poets.name: Anonymous Egyptian Poets
poets.credit: The Weighing of the Heart, from the Papyrus of Ani (Book of the Dead, c. 1250 BC; British Museum EA 10470) · An artifact, shown because no portrait exists for anonymous poets · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Egyptian poets are unnamed scribes, priests and court writers who set down hymns, laments and funerary songs in hieroglyphic and hieratic script on temple walls, tomb steles and papyrus. Their work spans the Middle and New Kingdoms, roughly the second millennium BC, and includes sun-hymns and litanies from the Book of the Dead, hymns to Amen and Osiris, and the festal songs sung at banquets for the dead.

The pieces given here are taken from Epiphanius Wilson’s collection Egyptian Literature (New York and London, The Colonial Press for the Co-operative Publication Society, 1901). Each is shown in the English version of the translator named in that volume (Budge, Chabas, Birch, Cook, Goodwin, Stern, Lushington, De Horrack, Naville). Several are printed there as continuous prose, and the Book of the Dead pieces appear without their rubrics.

poets.name: Anonymous Babylonian Poets
poets.credit: The Flood Tablet (Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, British Museum K.3375), Nineveh, 7th century BC · An artifact, shown because no portrait exists for anonymous poets · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Babylonian poets are unnamed scribes and singers who composed in Akkadian and wrote in cuneiform on clay tablets. Their works, among them the Epic of Gilgamish, survive in Old Babylonian, Hittite and Assyrian copies, the fullest being the seventh-century BC tablets from the royal library at Nineveh.
The Epic of Gilgamish is given here in R. Campbell Thompson's verse translation of 1928.

poets.name: Cynewulf
poets.credit: The runic signature of Cynewulf woven into the text of his poem ‘The Fates of the Apostles,’ Vercelli Book, folio 54r, 10th century — not a portrait (none survives), but the poet's own cryptographic signature in runes, the only trace of his identity. Public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: Cynewulf is one of only a handful of Old English poets known to us by name — not from any external record, but because he wove his own name in runic letters into the closing lines of four poems, as a kind of signed prayer for the reader's intercession.

Nothing certain is known of his life, not even his precise dates; scholars place him anywhere from the 8th to the 9th century based on his language and dialect. The four poems bearing his runic signature are Juliana and Christ II (the Ascension) in the Exeter Book, and Elene and The Fates of the Apostles in the Vercelli Book — all religious verse composed in the traditional alliterative meter inherited from pre-Christian heroic poetry.

Generations of scholars once attributed much more of the Old English corpus to him — Andreas, the Guthlac poems, The Phoenix, The Dream of the Rood — on stylistic grounds, but only the four signed poems can be assigned to him with confidence.

poets.name: Cædmon
poets.credit: A page from the so-called ‘Cædmon Manuscript’ (Bodleian Library, MS Junius 11, c. 1000) — the illustrated Old English paraphrase of Genesis, Exodus, and Daniel once (wrongly) believed to be Cædmon's own work. Not a portrait; no image of him survives. Public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: Cædmon is the first English poet known to us by name. According to the Venerable Bede's Ecclesiastical History (completed 731), he was an illiterate herdsman attached to the double monastery at Whitby who, ashamed of his inability to sing at feasts, received the gift of song in a dream: a stranger commanded him to “sing of the beginning of created things,” and he woke with the verses of what is now called Cædmon's Hymn already composed.

The Abbess Hild, recognizing the gift as divine, had him instructed in sacred history so that he might turn it into verse; he is said to have gone on to compose poems on Genesis, Exodus, and other scriptural subjects, though none of these survive under his name. Only the nine-line Hymn, preserved by Bede and copied into manuscripts of the Ecclesiastical History, can be attributed to him with any confidence.

For centuries the long biblical paraphrases of the Junius Manuscript (Genesis, Exodus, Daniel, Christ and Satan) were attributed to Cædmon on the strength of Bede's account, and the manuscript is still nicknamed for him, but modern scholarship treats those poems as the anonymous work of later, unrelated poets.

poets.name: Anonymous (Old English)
poets.credit: A full page of the Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library, MS 3501, c. 970–990) carrying the poem ‘Deor’ — one of the four great codices in which nearly the whole surviving corpus of Old English poetry is preserved. Public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: The great majority of surviving Old English poetry is anonymous. It comes down to us almost entirely through four manuscripts copied around the late 10th and early 11th centuries — the Exeter Book, the Vercelli Book, the Junius Manuscript, and the Nowell Codex (which also contains Beowulf) — plus a few poems preserved elsewhere, such as in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.

These poets, working in the alliterative, four-stress long line inherited from a common Germanic tradition, left behind elegies of exile and loss (The Wanderer, The Seafarer, The Wife's Lament), heroic fragments (The Battle of Maldon, The Fight at Finnsburg), riddles, saints' lives, and biblical paraphrase, alongside the single most revered poem of the corpus, The Dream of the Rood.

This entry gathers the many unsigned Old English poems in this archive — as distinct from Beowulf's anonymous poet, Cædmon, and the runically-signed Cynewulf — under one umbrella, in keeping with how they survive: unattributed, and copied by scribes who did not think to record whose voice they were preserving.

poets.name: Aneirin
poets.credit: Facsimile page of the Book of Aneirin (Cardiff MS 2.81, 13th century), from J. Gwenogvryn Evans, Facsimile and Text of the Book of Aneirin (1908) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Aneirin is the poet to whom the Gododdin is ascribed, an elegy for the warriors of the Votadini who rode from Din Eidyn (Edinburgh) to fall at Catraeth, perhaps about the end of the sixth century. It survives in the Book of Aneirin, a Welsh manuscript of the late thirteenth century, in a text of mixed age and layered authorship.
The poems are given in the Rev. D. Silvan Evans's translation, printed with the Welsh in William F. Skene's The Four Ancient Books of Wales (1868). The ascription to Aneirin is traditional.

poets.name: Taliesin
poets.credit: Facsimile page of the Book of Taliesin (NLW Peniarth MS 2, 14th century), from J. Gwenogvryn Evans, Facsimile and Text of the Book of Taliesin (1910) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Taliesin is the earliest named Welsh poet, a bard of the sixth century said to have sung at the courts of Urien of Rheged and his son Owain in the north of Britain. The poems collected under his name come down in the Book of Taliesin, a manuscript of the early fourteenth century; a handful of them may preserve genuinely early praise-poetry, while many others are later prophecy, mythological riddle and boast in the persona of a legendary Taliesin.

The ascription of every poem here is traditional, not established. They are given in the English translation by the Rev. Robert Williams, printed with the Welsh text in William F. Skene's The Four Ancient Books of Wales (1868), under Skene's titles and numbers.

poets.name: Myrddin Wyllt
bio: Myrddin Wyllt (Merlin the Wild) is the legendary prophet-poet of early Welsh tradition, said to have gone mad after the battle of Arderydd (about 573) and lived as a wild man in the Caledonian forest. Poems in his voice, mostly prophecies, appear in the Black Book of Carmarthen and the Red Book of Hergest, and the figure was later developed by Geoffrey of Monmouth into Merlin.

The poems here are those W. F. Skene groups under Myrdin in The Four Ancient Books of Wales (1868), in the translation of the Rev. D. Silvan Evans. The attribution is traditional, and the manuscripts date from the thirteenth and later centuries.

poets.name: Llywarch Hen
bio: Llywarch Hen (Llywarch the Aged) is a legendary sixth-century prince of the Men of the North, remembered in Welsh tradition for his long old age and the loss of his sons in war. Poems in his persona are found in the Red Book of Hergest (about 1400) and were written down long after the age they portray.

The poems here are those W. F. Skene groups as poems attributed to Llywarch Hen in The Four Ancient Books of Wales (1868), in the translation of the Rev. D. Silvan Evans. The attribution is traditional.

poets.name: Anonymous (Old Welsh)
poets.credit: A page of the Black Book of Carmarthen (NLW Peniarth MS 1, f. 4r), c. 1250 · An artifact, shown because no portrait exists for anonymous poets · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Welsh poems here are those of the Black Book of Carmarthen (about 1250) and the Red Book of Hergest (about 1400), including prophecy, praise, religious verse, the Verses of the Graves and the poem of Geraint son of Erbin, that carry no ascription or only a doubtful one. Their composition ranges from the early Middle Ages to the twelfth century.

They are given in the English translation by the Rev. D. Silvan Evans, printed with the Welsh in William F. Skene's The Four Ancient Books of Wales (1868), under Skene's titles and numbers. Where a poem is also found in the Book of Taliesin, Williams's version is credited too.

poets.name: Anonymous (Old Irish)
poets.credit: Folio 53 of the Book of Leinster (c. 1160) · No portrait exists for anonymous poets; a manuscript page is shown instead · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The early Irish poems gathered here were composed in Old and Middle Irish between roughly the eighth and the twelfth centuries, mostly by unnamed monks, scribes, hermits and court poets. They survive in medieval manuscripts such as the Book of Leinster and Lebor na hUidre, and many are tied by tradition to figures such as St Patrick, Colum Cille, Moling or King Cormac, though those attributions are legendary and the poems are treated here as anonymous.

The selection runs from sagas and the otherworld voyage of Bran to hymns, hermit songs, nature lyrics, love poems, bardic laments and the quatrains scribes wrote in the margins of their books, among them the poem of the monk and his cat Pangur. The English versions are by the Celtic scholar Kuno Meyer, from Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry (London, 1911).

poets.name: Classical Japanese Poets
poets.credit: Kakinomoto no Hitomaro, from the Sanjūrokkasen-gaku (Thirty-six Immortal Poets) by Kanō Tan'yū, 17th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons). An imagined likeness; no contemporary portrait of any of these poets survives.
bio: The poems collected here are the earliest voices of Japanese verse in this archive: ballads, love songs, elegies and short stanzas of the seventh to tenth centuries, the Nara and early Heian courts. Some carry the names of court poets, among them Hitomaro, Akahito, Okura, Sosei, Narihira and the Lady Komachi; many are anonymous, and a few are given only to a title or an editorial line. Because most of the named poets have just one to three pieces apiece, the archive gathers them under a single entry, and each poem's note gives its author exactly as the source prints it.

All the poems are in English by Basil Hall Chamberlain, taken from the 'Classical Poetry of Japan' section of the anthology Japanese Literature (The Colonial Press, 1900). Chamberlain turns the Japanese into rhymed English verse, so the five-and-seven-syllable counts of the originals are not kept; the Japanese long poems become ballad stanzas and the short poems become four-line stanzas. Dates here are approximate, as the volume gives none for its poets.

poets.name: Po Chü-i
poets.credit: Portrait of Bai Juyi (白樂天), traditional Chinese painting · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Po Chü-i (Bai Juyi, 772–846; also called Lo-t’ien) was one of the great poets of the T’ang dynasty. Born in Shansi and raised in Honan, he passed the examinations in 800, served at court as a scholar of the Han-lin Academy and a censor, and was banished in 815 to Chiang-chou (Hsün-yang) on the Yangtze. Later he governed Hangchow and Soochow and ended his life in retirement at Lo-yang.

He wrote in a deliberately plain style, said to have been tested on an old peasant woman, and he used it for satires on injustice and for quiet poems on illness, idleness, friendship, wine, old age and the death of a small daughter. His close friend was the poet Yüan Chēn. His poetry was admired in Japan during his lifetime. Arthur Waley’s versions, from A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918) and More Translations from the Chinese (1919), are presented here in Waley’s spelling of the poet’s name.

poets.name: Shi Jing (The Book of Songs)
poets.dates: poems c. 1000–600 BC; compilation traditionally ascribed to Confucius
poets.credit: Ma Hezhi (Song dynasty), Odes of the State of Bin, handscroll illustrating the Shijing, The Metropolitan Museum of Art · An artifact, shown because no portrait exists for anonymous poets · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Shi Jing (Classic of Poetry, also called the Book of Songs or Book of Odes) is the oldest surviving collection of Chinese verse: 305 anonymous poems in four parts, composed between about 1000 and 600 BC under the Zhou dynasty. They are the songs of the feudal States (Part I), the minor and greater odes of the royal court (Parts II and III), and the hymns of the ancestral temple and altar (Part IV). Tradition ascribes the compilation to Confucius, who is said to have chosen them from a much larger stock; by the Han dynasty the collection was one of the Five Classics.

These versions are James Legge's rhymed English verse translation, The She King; or, The Book of Ancient Poetry (London: Trübner & Co., 1876), which keeps his own romanised titles (for example Kwan-ts‘eu for the opening ode, now usually written Guanju). The Codex Note on each Legge poem is Legge's own one-line argument, set in plain case. Four odes are not given here: three that this edition prints only in Scots-dialect versions, and one whose text is cut short in the scan. A second English verse translation, William Jennings's The Shi King: The Old 'Poetry Classic' of the Chinese (1891), is added in selection; its odes carry no Codex Note and keep Jennings's own descriptive titles. Odes whose scan text is too corrupt to restore are omitted.

poets.name: The Rishis of the Rig Veda
poets.credit: Rig Veda manuscript on paper, India, early 19th century, Devanagari script (Rigveda MS2097) · A manuscript page, not a likeness · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Rig Veda is the oldest collection of Vedic Sanskrit hymns, and one of the oldest surviving religious texts in any Indo-European language. It is arranged in ten books, or mandalas, of hymns addressed chiefly to Agni, Indra, the Maruts, Ushas the Dawn and other gods. Tradition ascribes the hymns to rishis, the inspired seers, and assigns whole books to particular families of them: Book 2, for instance, to the Gritsamada family and Book 3 to Vishvamitra and his line. This attribution is traditional only. The individual poets are anonymous to us, and the hymns were composed and handed down orally over centuries, traditionally dated to about 1500–1000 BCE.

The English text is Ralph T. H. Griffith's verse translation, first published in 1889–92 and revised in 1896. Griffith, a Victorian Sanskritist and schoolmaster, kept the numbered verses of the original as stanzas and gave them an idiom of “thou”, “hath” and capitalised Gods that belongs to his own age rather than the Vedic one. This archive gives all ten books, as transcribed on Wikisource; 1.179 and the few other verses Griffith left in Latin are omitted. Each hymn is titled by its book and number with its first line, because that transcription gives Griffith’s deity headings for only two hymns (1.1 and 1.32).

poets.name: The Rishis of the Sama Veda
poets.credit: No portrait: the Samaveda has no author likeness
bio: The Samaveda is the Veda of chants (saman, melody), the third of the four Vedas and the liturgical book of the Udgatar priests who sang at the Soma sacrifice. It is not a collection of new compositions so much as a rearrangement: all but a small number of its verses are taken from the Rig Veda, chiefly from the Soma and Agni and Indra hymns, and reordered in the sequence in which they were sung. Tradition ascribes the verses to the same inspired seers, the rishis, as the Rig Veda; they are anonymous to us, and the text is traditionally dated to about 1200–1000 BCE, though the dating is uncertain.

The English text is Ralph T. H. Griffith's verse translation, published with a popular commentary in 1895; the commentary is not reproduced here. Griffith's work is in two parts. The First Part gives the verses in the order of the Archika, in books and chapters of decades (groups of about ten verses), and each decade is given here as one poem under its deity. The Second Part gives the verses in the order of the chants, in hymns of about three verses, and each hymn is titled by book, chapter and number with its first line. Griffith's verse numbers are kept. Many verses are Rig Veda verses in the same wording, which is the nature of the text; a few numbers and words are garbled in the digitised source and are left as printed.

poets.name: The Rishis of the Yajur Veda
poets.credit: No portrait: the Yajurveda has no author likeness
bio: The Yajurveda is the Veda of sacrificial formulae (yajus), the second of the four Vedas and the liturgical book of the Adhvaryu priests, who performed the physical work of the sacrifice and spoke or murmured its mantras as they did it. The White Yajurveda, the Vajasaneyi Samhita, is the form handed down in the school of Yajnavalkya: forty books of verses and prose formulae, many of the verses drawn from the Rig Veda, arranged in the order of the rites, from the New and Full Moon sacrifices and the Soma ritual to the Horse Sacrifice. Tradition ascribes the mantras to inspired seers, the rishis; they are anonymous to us, and the text is traditionally dated to about 1200–900 BCE, though the dating is uncertain.

The English text is Ralph T. H. Griffith's translation, published at Benares in 1899. It is given here as one work in forty books, with the numbered verses kept as separate paragraphs. The collection mixes metrical verses with short prose formulae, such as the opening of Book I, which are the mantras themselves. The last book is the Isa Upanishad, and Griffith's own notes and commentary are not reproduced.

poets.name: The Rishis of the Atharva Veda
poets.credit: Codex Cashmiriensis, folio 187a, from the Atharva-Veda Saṁhitā, ed. W. D. Whitney and C. R. Lanman (1905) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Atharva-Veda is the fourth of the four Vedas, the oldest sacred texts of India, composed in Vedic Sanskrit and traditionally dated to about 1200–900 BCE. Unlike the sacrificial hymns of the Rig-Veda, much of it is made up of charms and spells: prayers for healing and long life, incantations against disease, demons and rivals, blessings for kings, households and cattle, and spells of love and reconciliation. Its verses are traditionally attributed to the priestly families of the Atharvans and the Angirases.

The poets are anonymous and the attribution to the families is traditional, so the archive credits them as a group. The English text is Ralph T. H. Griffith's verse translation, The Hymns of the Atharva-Veda (two volumes, Benares, 1895–96), and each hymn carries Griffith's own descriptive heading. Books 1 to 14 and 17 to 19 are included (Books 15, 16 and 20 are omitted: the first two are prose, the last is almost wholly Rigvedic and already in the archive); a few hymns are still missing.

poets.name: The Bible (Authorized King James Version)
poets.dates: Hebrew originals c. 1000–300 BC; English version 1611
poets.credit: Title page of the first edition of the King James Bible (1611) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Hebrew Bible holds some of the oldest and most influential poetry in the world: the 150 Psalms, the dramatic dialogue of Job, the love lyrics of the Song of Songs, the meditations of Ecclesiastes and the funeral laments of Lamentations. Composed in Hebrew between roughly 1000 and 300 BC by many hands, these books are built on parallelism, in which a second line answers, repeats or deepens the first.

The English text here is the Authorized Version, published in 1611 under King James I by a company of scholars and clergy working in committees at Westminster, Oxford and Cambridge. Its cadences shaped English prose and verse for centuries, and its Psalms, Job and Ecclesiastes remain among the most quoted passages in the language.

poets.name: Homer
poets.credit: Portrait bust of Homer, Roman copy of a Hellenistic original — public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: Homer is the name tradition gives to the poet, or poets, credited with the Iliad and the Odyssey, the two foundational epics of ancient Greek literature. Nothing reliable is known of his life; ancient sources disagree even on his birthplace, and many scholars believe the poems as we have them are the culmination of centuries of oral epic tradition rather than the work of one man.

Whether historical individual or convenient legend, "Homer" is credited with shaping the Trojan War and the wanderings of Odysseus into the verse that became the bedrock of Greek and later Western literature and education.

This archive presents multiple English translations of the Iliad and the Odyssey side by side, so that the different choices each translator made — prose versus verse, plain diction versus ornate — can be compared directly. H. B. Cotterill's line-for-line translation of the Odyssey in English hexameters (1911) is among the Odysseys held here.

poets.name: Hesiod
poets.credit: Roman bust sometimes identified as Hesiod (identification uncertain), Neues Museum, Berlin · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Hesiod was a Greek poet of Boeotia who lived around 700 BC, roughly contemporary with Homer. In the Theogony he says the Muses called him to song while he was tending sheep on Mount Helicon, and in the Works and Days he describes his father’s move from Aeolian Cyme to Ascra, and a dispute with his brother Perses over their inheritance.

He is credited with the Theogony, an account of the origins of the gods, and the Works and Days, a poem of moral and practical instruction for farmers. The Shield of Heracles has long been attributed to him but is thought by most scholars to be a later composition. Both works are presented here in the 1914 prose translation by Hugh G. Evelyn-White.

poets.name: Archilochus
bio: Archilochus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to c. 700 BC. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of Meleager's Wreath, the Garland compiled about 100 BC.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book VI: 133).

poets.name: Sappho
poets.credit: Portrait bust of Sappho, Roman copy of a Greek original — public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: Sappho was a Greek lyric poet from the island of Lesbos, active around the turn of the 7th to 6th century BC. Ancient critics ranked her among the very greatest poets; Plato is said to have called her the "Tenth Muse."

Almost none of her work survives complete. What remains — quotations in later grammarians, and a few papyrus scraps recovered from Egypt — comes down to us as fragments, some no more than a phrase, prized for their directness of feeling and technical mastery of the Aeolic dialect and sapphic metre.
The fragments gathered here follow Henry Thornton Wharton’s 1885 literal prose translation, the edition that first made Sappho’s surviving words accessible to English readers in their entirety.

poets.name: Alcaeus of Lesbos
bio: Alcaeus of Lesbos is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 7th century BC. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of Meleager's Wreath, the Garland compiled about 100 BC.
This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book V: 10; Book VI: 218).

poets.name: Mimnermus
bio: Mimnermus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 7th century BC.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 50).

poets.name: Erinna
bio: Erinna is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to c. 600 BC. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of Meleager's Wreath, the Garland compiled about 100 BC.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book VI: 352).

poets.name: Anacreon
poets.credit: Statue of Anacreon from Monte Calvo, Roman copy (2nd century AD) after a Greek original, Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek, Copenhagen; photograph by ChrisO, cropped · CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Anacreon of Teos (c. 582 – c. 485 BC) was an Ancient Greek lyric poet of the Ionian coast who spent his career at the courts of Polycrates of Samos and of the Pisistratid rulers of Athens. He was celebrated in antiquity for short, polished songs of wine, love and good company, and his name became a byword for the light-hearted drinking song.

Only fragments of his own verse survive. The poems traditionally printed as the Odes of Anacreon — the Anacreontea — are in fact, for the most part, later Greek imitations composed centuries after his death and handed down under his name. They were widely read and imitated in Renaissance and eighteenth-century Europe. These odes are given here in Thomas Moore’s free English verse translation of 1800, numbered I to LXXVIII as in his edition; the lengthy scholarly notes he printed with them are omitted.

poets.name: Laozi (Lao Tzu)
poets.credit: Laozi Riding an Ox, painting by Zhang Lu (Ming dynasty, 16th century); a traditional depiction, not a likeness · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Laozi, "the Old Master", is the traditional author of the Tao Te Ching (Daodejing), the foundational book of Daoism. Chinese tradition places him in the 6th century BC and calls him an archivist at the court of Zhou, but nothing of his life can be established, and scholars disagree about whether he existed as one person or whether the book was assembled over generations. The attribution of the work to him is traditional.

The book is a collection of eighty-one short chapters on the Tao (the Way), on government, and on the conduct of the sage, written in a terse and largely rhymed Chinese. The text here is James Legge's translation, published in 1891 in the Sacred Books of the East (vol. 39) as the Tao Teh King. It is in prose, with Legge's occasional rhymed renderings of the verse passages; the words in parentheses are his own supplied additions.

poets.name: The Buddha (attributed)
poets.dates: traditionally 5th century BCE; the Dhammapada compiled c. 3rd century BCE
poets.credit: Standing Buddha, Gandhara (Kushan period, 1st-2nd century CE), Tokyo National Museum; photograph by World Imaging, 2004. An imagined likeness in sculpture, not a portrait from life · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Dhammapada is a Pali anthology of 423 verses in twenty-six chapters, preserved in the Khuddaka Nikaya of the Buddhist canon. Tradition ascribes the sayings to the Buddha himself, but the attribution is traditional: the verses were gathered from the oral teaching of the early community and compiled in their present form some two centuries or more after his death, around the 3rd century BCE.

The version here is F. Max Müller's translation from the Pali, published in 1881 as the tenth volume of the Sacred Books of the East. It is deliberately literal, and in English it reads close to prose, so the verses are given as paragraphs rather than lines. Each of the twenty-six chapters (vaggas) is kept whole as one poem, with Müller's introduction, notes and index omitted.

poets.name: Theognis of Megara
bio: Theognis of Megara was an archaic Greek elegiac poet, traditionally placed in the sixth century BC. A body of about 1,400 lines of elegiac couplets, the Theognidea, survives under his name, though much of it is probably the work of other hands and later date.

The two epigrams here come from the Greek Anthology and are printed in J. W. Mackail's Select Epigrams (1890); the saying that it is best never to have been born is one of the most quoted sentiments of Greek poetry.

poets.name: Valmiki
poets.credit: No authentic likeness survives.
bio: Valmiki is the sage-poet to whom Indian tradition ascribes the Ramayana, and is honoured as the Adi Kavi, the First Poet. Nothing about him is securely known as history; the epic itself and later legend present him as an ascetic who, moved by grief at the death of a bird, found the verse form of the shloka, and who sheltered Sita in his hermitage.

The Sanskrit Ramayana, the story of Rama, his exile, the abduction of Sita by the demon-king Ravana and her rescue, took shape over several centuries and is dated variously between about the fifth century BC and the second century AD. The standard Sanskrit epic is divided into seven books; Ralph T. H. Griffith's English verse translation (1870–1874), the version offered here, renders the first six, with the Uttarakanda summarised rather than versified.

poets.name: Vyasa
poets.dates: traditional; the Bhagavad Gita composed c. 400 BC – AD 200
poets.credit: Krishna and Arjuna in the chariot at Kurukshetra, illustrated Bhagavad Gita folio, 19th century, unknown artist (an illustration, not a portrait) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Vyasa (Krishna Dvaipayana) is the legendary sage to whom Indian tradition ascribes the Mahabharata, the compilation of the Vedas and the Puranas. His attribution is traditional: no historical author can be identified, and scholars regard the Mahabharata as the work of many hands over several centuries.

The Bhagavad Gita, 'the Song of the Lord', is a dialogue of 700 Sanskrit verses set in the sixth book of the Mahabharata, in which the god Krishna, as charioteer, counsels the warrior-prince Arjuna on the eve of battle at Kurukshetra. It is usually dated between about the 4th century BC and the 2nd century AD. It is read here in Sir Edwin Arnold's blank-verse rendering, The Song Celestial (1885). The archive now holds Kisari Mohan Ganguli’s complete English prose translation (1883–1896) in all eighteen books, from the Adi Parva to the Svargarohanika Parva, alongside Romesh Chunder Dutt’s verse condensation.

poets.name: Simonides of Ceos
poets.credit: Portrait: Michel Wolgemut, Wilhelm Pleydenwurff; Text: Hartmann Schedel — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Simonides of Ceos (c. 556 – 468 BC) was one of the great lyric poets of Greece and the most famous composer of epitaphs and dedicatory epigrams, among them the lines on the Greek dead of the Persian Wars. Many of the epigrams that circulated under his name are not his.
The epigrams here are those that Paton's first volume ascribes to him, a few of them with doubt.

poets.name: The Sisters of the Therigatha
poets.credit: Folios of the Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha (the nuns’ code of discipline) on gilded palm leaf, Burmese manuscript, c. 1846–53, British Library (Or. Man. Pali 21). A manuscript page of early Buddhist nuns’ literature, not a likeness · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons, CC0)
bio: The Therī-gāthā, the “Verses of the Elder Women”, is the Pali canon’s collection of poems by the first Buddhist nuns, in the Khuddaka Nikāya. Each psalm is traditionally ascribed to a named sister, from famous disciples such as Mahā-Pajāpatī, the Buddha’s foster-mother, to courtesans, widows and a goldsmith’s daughter, and some are given to groups of sisters. The attributions are traditional, and the date and authorship of the verses remain uncertain.

The translation is Mrs. C. A. F. Rhys Davids’s Psalms of the Sisters, the first volume of Psalms of the Early Buddhists, published in 1909 for the Pali Text Society. It numbers 73 psalms and 522 verses in sixteen cantos, arranged by length. The archive gives the verses only; the commentary’s origin-stories, Rhys Davids’s notes and her introductions are omitted.

poets.name: The Brethren of the Theragatha
poets.credit: Jataka relief (the jackal and the otters) from the Bharhut stupa, 2nd century BCE, a seated ascetic among animals; an early Buddhist relief, not a likeness of any thera · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Thera-gāthā, the “Verses of the Elder Monks”, is the Pali canon’s collection of poems by early Buddhist monks, in the Khuddaka Nikāya, the companion of the Therī-gāthā of the nuns. Each psalm is traditionally ascribed to a named thera, from chief disciples such as Sāriputta, Moggallāna and Ānanda to a fisherman, a barber, a potter and a former brigand, and a few are given to groups of friends. The attributions are traditional, and the date and authorship of the verses remain uncertain.

The translation is Mrs. C. A. F. Rhys Davids’s Psalms of the Brethren, the second volume of Psalms of the Early Buddhists, published in 1913 for the Pali Text Society. It numbers 264 psalms in twenty-one cantos, arranged by length from single verses to the seventy-one verses of Vangisa. The archive gives the verses only; the commentary’s origin-stories, Rhys Davids’s notes and her introductions are omitted.

poets.name: Pindar
poets.credit: Bust of Pindar, Roman marble copy after a Greek original of the 5th century BC, Capitoline Museums, Rome · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Pindar (c. 518 – c. 438 BC) was a Greek lyric poet from Thebes in Boeotia, and the most celebrated of the nine canonical lyric poets of the ancient world. He composed choral songs of many kinds, but the epinikia, or victory odes, are the only works of his that survive complete. They were commissioned to celebrate winners at the four great Greek games: the Olympian, Pythian, Nemean and Isthmian festivals.

His patrons included Hieron of Syracuse, Theron of Acragas, Arcesilas of Cyrene and the athletic families of Aegina and Thebes. The odes were sung by a chorus at the victor's home or at the festival, and they weave praise of the winner into myth and moral reflection. The 45 odes given here are in the prose translation by Sir John Sandys (1844–1922), published in the Loeb Classical Library in 1915, in the order of the four books: 14 Olympian, 12 Pythian, 11 Nemean and 8 Isthmian. A second prose version, by Ernest Myers (first published 1874), follows them, with the odes numbered as Myers numbers them (his Isthmian 3 runs the two parts that Sandys divides as Isthmian 3 and 4).

poets.name: Bacchylides
bio: Bacchylides is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 6th century BC. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of Meleager's Wreath, the Garland compiled about 100 BC.
This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book VI: 53, 313).

poets.name: Timocreon of Rhodes
bio: Timocreon of Rhodes was a lyric poet of the early fifth century BC, remembered above all for the invective verses in which he attacked Themistocles. Paton’s Index of Authors dates him to the 5th century BC.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XIII: 31.

poets.name: Lucretius
poets.credit: No authentic likeness survives.
bio: Titus Lucretius Carus was a Roman poet and Epicurean follower of the first century BC. Almost nothing is securely known of his life; he addressed his poem to the Roman aristocrat Memmius, and it was left unfinished at his death, to be edited, according to later tradition, by Cicero.

His single surviving work, De rerum natura (On the Nature of Things), is a didactic poem in six books of Latin hexameters setting out the atomic physics and ethics of Epicurus: the nature of atoms and void, the mortality of the soul, the origins of the world and of human society, and the causes of natural phenomena, all aimed at freeing readers from the fear of the gods and of death.

poets.name: Pythagoras
bio: Paton prints under the name of Pythagoras the one-line epitaph on the tomb of Zeus in Crete; the ascription to the philosopher is traditional but doubtful. Paton's Index of Authors includes the poet among those of Book VII. Paton's index of authors gives no date for the poet.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 746).

poets.name: Xenophanes
bio: Xenophanes of Colophon was a philosopher and poet of the sixth century BC. Paton's Index of Authors includes the poet among those of Book VII. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 6th century BC.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 120).

poets.name: Phocylides
bio: Phocylides is one of the named epigrammatists whose short poems are preserved in the Greek Anthology. Paton's Index of Authors dates the poet to the 6th century BC.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fourth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book X: 117.

poets.name: Aeschylus
poets.credit: Portrait: Tilemachos Efthimiadis — CC BY-SA 2.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Aeschylus (c. 525–456 BC) is the Athenian tragic poet; the epitaph Paton prints under his name is the one traditionally said to have been written for his own tomb. Paton's Index of Authors includes the poet among those of Book VII. The scan of Paton's index of authors used here does not give a date for the poet; the date shown is the conventional one.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 255).

poets.name: Sophocles
poets.credit: Photograph of the Lateran Sophocles (Museo Gregoriano Profano, Vatican), c. 1860–1900 · Rijksmuseum, CC0 (via Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sophocles (c. 497–406 BC) was born at Colonus, just outside Athens, and lived through the city’s greatest age. He was celebrated as a boy for his skill in music and dance, and in 468 BC won the tragic competition at the Dionysia over Aeschylus. He went on to win first prize many times and is said never to have taken third place.

He served the city as a treasurer of the Athenian empire and as one of its generals, and held a priesthood. Of well over a hundred plays, seven survive complete: Ajax, Antigone, Oedipus the King, Electra, Trachiniae, Philoctetes and Oedipus at Colonus. He is credited with adding a third actor and with developing painted scenery.

Antigone, Oedipus the King and Oedipus at Colonus, the Theban plays, were written years apart and not as a trilogy. Oedipus at Colonus was produced after his death, in 401 BC, by his grandson Sophocles.

poets.name: Euripides
bio: Euripides is one of the named epigrammatists whose short poems are preserved in the Greek Anthology. Paton's Index of Authors gives no date for the poet. The attribution is queried by Paton.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fourth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book X: 107.

poets.name: Anonymous (Classical Chinese)
bio: The Classical Chinese poems gathered here are anonymous: folk songs and ballads from the Book of Odes, short epigrams and proverbs with no author named, and a few poems that Giles prints with a poet’s name or date that the scan does not preserve in full.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898).

poets.name: Antimachus
bio: Antimachus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 5th century BC. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Wreath of Meleager, the Garland compiled in the first century BC.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 321).

poets.name: Demodocus
bio: Demodocus is one of the named epigrammatists whose short poems are preserved in the Greek Anthology. Paton's Index of Authors dates the poet to the 5th century BC.
This archive carries the 4 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the fourth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XI: 235, 236, 237, 238.

poets.name: Gaius Valerius Catullus
poets.credit: No authentic likeness survives.
bio: Gaius Valerius Catullus (c. 84 – c. 54 BC) was a Roman poet born at Verona in Cisalpine Gaul. He moved to Rome as a young man and belonged to the circle of the "new poets" who prized short, polished, personal verse on the Alexandrian model. His surviving book of about 116 poems ranges from love lyrics to savage invective, from occasional pieces to a few longer learned poems.

His best-known poems address a woman he calls Lesbia, usually identified with Clodia, and trace the course of an intense and unhappy love. He also wrote elegies for his brother, who died in the Troad, and epithalamia, the epyllion on Peleus and Thetis, and the Attis. This selection gives the whole surviving corpus in the English of Robinson Ellis (1871), who translated it in the metres of the originals.

poets.name: Parrhasius
bio: Parrhasius of Ephesus was a celebrated Greek painter of the late fifth century BC, active in Athens and a rival of Zeuxis. No work of his survives.
The boastful lines on the limits of his art that the Greek Anthology ascribes to him are of uncertain authenticity. Mackail prints one of them in his Select Epigrams (1890).

poets.name: Thucydides the Historian
bio: Paton prints under the name of Thucydides the historian an epitaph ascribed to him. Paton's Index of Authors includes the poet among those of Book VII. Paton's index of authors gives no date for the poet.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 45).

poets.name: Plato
poets.credit: Portrait: Marie-Lan Nguyen — CC BY 2.5 (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Plato (c. 428 – 348 BC) is credited in the Anthology with a number of short epigrams, love poems and epitaphs among them. Their authenticity is doubtful, and Paton's index gives them to Plato without comment.
The epigrams here are those that Paton's first volume ascribes to Plato.

poets.name: Sung Yü
bio: Sung Yü is dated by Giles to the 4th century BC. He is traditionally counted a follower of Ch’ü Yüan and a poet of the southern state of Ch’u.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Speusippus
bio: Speusippus was the nephew of Plato and his successor as head of the Academy at Athens. The Greek Anthology ascribes to him a short epitaph on Plato.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XVI: 31.

poets.name: Aeschines the Orator
bio: Aeschines the Orator is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 4th century BC.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book VI: 330).

poets.name: Ch’ü Yüan
bio: Ch’ü Yüan (332–295 BC) was a minister of the state of Ch’u and the author of the famous poem “Li Sao,” or “Falling into Trouble.” Finding that he could not influence the conduct of his prince, he withdrew into exile and finally drowned himself in the river Mi-lo; the Dragon Boat Festival is supposed to be held in his honour.

The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918); Arthur Waley’s version in More Translations from the Chinese (1919); L. Cranmer-Byng’s version in A Lute of Jade (1909), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Praxiteles the Sculptor
bio: Praxiteles of Athens, the greatest sculptor of the fourth century BC, made the Cnidian Aphrodite and the Eros of Thespiae. The Anthology ascribes to him a poem spoken in the person of his own Eros; the attribution is a literary fiction.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XVI: 204.

poets.name: Agis
bio: Agis is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 4th century BC. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of Meleager's Wreath, the Garland compiled about 100 BC.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book VI: 152).

poets.name: Lycophron
bio: Lycophron of Chalcis was a Greek poet and scholar of the early third century BC, said to have worked on the comedies in the Library of Alexandria under Ptolemy II.

The Alexandra, a 1474-line poem in iambic trimeters attributed to him, is a deliberately obscure prophecy delivered by Cassandra and reported by a slave. Mair’s Loeb prose translation (1921) is given in the Works section.

poets.name: Aratus of Soli
poets.credit: Portrait: unknown artist — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Aratus of Soli was a Greek poet of the early third century BC who worked at the court of Antigonus Gonatas of Macedon. He is known above all for the Phaenomena, a didactic hexameter poem on the constellations and on weather signs.

The Phaenomena, based on a prose work by the astronomer Eudoxus, was translated into Latin by Cicero and others and remained a school text for centuries. Mair’s Loeb prose translation (1921) is given in the Works section.

poets.name: Crates of Thebes
bio: Crates of Thebes, a pupil of Diogenes the Cynic, was a Cynic philosopher of the later fourth century BC. Paton's Index of Authors includes the poet among those of Book VII. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 4th century BC.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 326).

poets.name: Mnasalcas
bio: Mnasalcas is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 4th century BC (?). Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of Meleager's Wreath, the Garland compiled about 100 BC.
This archive carries the 5 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book VI: 9, 125, 128, 264, 268).

poets.name: Menander the comic poet
bio: Menander the comic poet is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 4th century BC.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 72).

poets.name: Diphilus
bio: Diphilus is one of the named epigrammatists whose short poems are preserved in the Greek Anthology. Paton's Index of Authors dates the poet to the 4th century BC. Paton's index calls him the comic poet.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fourth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XI: 439.

poets.name: Philiscus
bio: Philiscus is one of the named epigrammatists whose short poems are preserved in the Greek Anthology. Paton's Index of Authors dates the poet to the 4th century BC.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fourth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XI: 441.

poets.name: Callimachus
bio: Callimachus of Cyrene was a Greek poet and scholar who worked at the Library of Alexandria under the early Ptolemies. He wrote on a vast range of subjects, and his catalogue of the library’s holdings, the Pinakes, was a founding work of bibliography.

Of his poetry six hymns and a body of epigrams survive complete. This selection gives the six Hymns, to Zeus, Apollo, Artemis, Delos, Pallas and Demeter, in A. W. Mair’s prose translation for the Loeb Classical Library (1921).

poets.name: Demiurgus
bio: Demiurgus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors gives no date for the poet.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 52).

poets.name: Anonymous (Greek Anthology)
poets.credit: Page from the Codex Palatinus graecus 23 (the Palatine Anthology), 10th century, folio 5 recto, used here as an illustration of the Anthology itself, not a portrait · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Greek Anthology is the great collection of some four thousand short Greek poems, mostly epigrams, written between the archaic age and the Byzantine Middle Ages. Its main source is the tenth-century Palatine manuscript, itself built on earlier anthologies by Meleager, Philippus and Agathias.

This file gathers the epigrams in Books I–VI of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1916) whose author is not named, is not dated in Paton's index of authors, or is disputed. Where Paton names a possible author, the note on the poem says so.

poets.name: Ion (not the tragic poet)
bio: Ion (not the tragic poet) is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors gives no date for the poet.
This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 43, 44).

poets.name: Hegesippus
bio: Hegesippus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to c. 300 BC. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of Meleager's Wreath, the Garland compiled about 100 BC.
This archive carries the 3 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book VI: 124, 178, 266).

poets.name: Asclepiades of Samos
bio: Asclepiades of Samos was a Hellenistic epigrammatist of the early third century BC. He is counted among the poets who shaped the short Greek love poem, and Meleager's Garland drew heavily on his work.
The poems collected here are the epigrams that Paton's first volume ascribes to him, chiefly in Book V.

poets.name: Anyte
bio: Anyte of Tegea in Arcadia, an early third-century BC poet, wrote epitaphs, dedications and small scenes of country life, and was one of the women whom Meleager honoured in his Garland.
The epigrams here are the ones that Paton's first volume ascribes to her.

poets.name: Moero of Byzantium
bio: Moero of Byzantium is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to c. 300 BC. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of Meleager's Wreath, the Garland compiled about 100 BC.
This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book VI: 119, 189).

poets.name: Nossis
bio: Nossis of Locri, in southern Italy, wrote epigrams around 300 BC. Her short poems often record dedications by women and portraits of women, and she is often linked with Sappho.
The epigrams here are the ones that Paton's first volume ascribes to her.

poets.name: Perses
bio: Perses is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to c. 300 BC. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of Meleager's Wreath, the Garland compiled about 100 BC.
This archive carries the 3 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book VI: 112, 272, 274).

poets.name: Phaedimus
bio: Phaedimus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to c. 300 BC. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of Meleager's Wreath, the Garland compiled about 100 BC.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book VI: 271).

poets.name: Theocritus
poets.credit: Portrait bust of Theocritus in profile, after an antique marble (engraving, c. 1697–1702, from Gronovius's Thesaurus Graecarum antiquitatum; not an authentic likeness) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Theocritus was a Greek poet of the third century BC, born in Syracuse in Sicily and later at work in the Hellenistic courts of Cos and Alexandria. He is regarded as the founder of pastoral poetry, and his short hexameter poems, the Idylls, set the speech of herdsmen and the songs of love and loss against the Sicilian countryside.

The Idylls also include mythological narratives, a town mime and a panegyric for Ptolemy, and Virgil's Eclogues later took up his pastoral manner. This selection prints the verse translations of C. S. Calverley (1869), John Dryden (1684–85), W. R. Paton (1916–18) and J. M. Edmonds (1912, the Loeb Greek Bucolic Poets), together with the epigrams and epitaphs attributed to Theocritus.

poets.name: Herodas (Herodes)
poets.credit: Papyrus London 135 (P.Lit.Lond. 96), column i, with the opening of Mime I; the 1892 facsimile by E. Scott, British Museum (not a likeness; no portrait of Herodas survives) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Herodas, also written Herodes or Herondas, was a Greek poet of the third century BC who composed mimes in choliambics, the limping iambic verse of Hipponax. Little is known of his life; his scenes are set at Cos and in Ionian towns, and he probably worked at Cos or Alexandria. He was known only from a few quotations until a papyrus in the British Museum, discovered in 1891, restored the greater part of seven of his mimes.

The mimes are short dramatic sketches of everyday life: a procuress at work on a lonely wife, a pimp on trial, a schoolmaster flogging a truant, two women at the shrine of Asclepius, a cobbler's sale. This selection prints A. D. Knox's translation of the Mimes in the Loeb Classical Library volume of 1929, rendered in deliberately archaic English.

poets.name: Antagoras
bio: Antagoras is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 3rd century BC.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 103).

poets.name: Alexander of Aetolia

poets.dates: end of the 4th century BC (Paton’s date)

poets.name: Hedylus
bio: Hedylus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 3rd century BC. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of Meleager's Wreath, the Garland compiled about 100 BC.

poets.name: Leonidas of Tarentum
bio: Leonidas of Tarentum, a Hellenistic epigrammatist of the early third century BC, is known for epitaphs and for dedications by poor country folk and craftsmen, often with a touch of humour about poverty.
In this archive every epigram that Paton heads simply “Leonidas” is filed here; the isopsepha of Leonidas of Alexandria (Book VI, 321–329) are not included.

bio: Euphorion is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 3rd century BC. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of Meleager's Wreath, the Garland compiled about 100 BC.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book VI: 279).

poets.name: Posidippus
bio: Posidippus, a Macedonian poet of the third century BC, was one of the leading epigrammatists of the early Hellenistic age. His poems range from love epigrams to epitaphs and dedications.
The epigrams here are those that Paton's first volume ascribes to him without qualification; the uncertain ones are filed as anonymous.

poets.name: Nicias

bio: Pisander of Rhodes is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 3rd century BC.

poets.name: Micias
bio: Micias is known only as the name under which a single epigram, on a wayside fountain, is preserved in the Greek Anthology. Nothing secure is recorded of his life, and his date is uncertain.
This archive carries one poem ascribed to him, in Sir Rennell Rodd's 1916 rendering from the Greek Anthology.

poets.name: Phanias
poets.dates: between the 3rd and 1st century BC (Paton’s date)

This archive carries the 6 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book VI: 294, 295, 297, 299, 304, 307).

poets.name: Dioscorides
bio: Dioscorides was a Hellenistic epigrammatist whose several dozen poems in the Anthology include love poems, epitaphs and dedications. The editor places him in the late third century BC; Paton's index dates him to the second.
The epigrams here are the ones that Paton's first volume ascribes to him.

poets.name: Alcaeus of Messene

poets.name: Apollonius of Rhodes
poets.credit: No likeness survives. Death of Talos, Attic red-figure krater showing an episode of the Argonautic voyage (c. 400 BC) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Apollonius of Rhodes was a Greek poet of the third century BC, born at Alexandria or, according to some ancient sources, Naucratis. Ancient biographies connect him with the Library of Alexandria and with the poet Callimachus, and say that he later lived on Rhodes, from which his usual name comes.

His surviving work is the Argonautica, an epic in four books on Jason's voyage to Colchis for the Golden Fleece and on Medea's love for him. Written in the Homeric manner but with a learned Hellenistic sensibility, it strongly influenced later poets, Virgil among them.

poets.name: Artemidorus the Grammarian
bio: Artemidorus the Grammarian is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 3rd century BC. Paton's index describes him as a grammarian.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 205).

poets.name: Philip V, King of Macedon
bio: Philip V was king of Macedon from 221 BC until his death in 179 BC. The Greek Anthology preserves under his name a mocking couplet written in answer to an epigram of Alcaeus of Messene.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XVI: 26b.

poets.name: Liu Heng
bio: Liu Heng, who died in 157 BC, is the name Giles prints over a lament for a father’s death. Liu Heng is the personal name of the Han emperor known as Wen-ti.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Mei Sheng
bio: Mei Sheng is dated by Giles to the 2nd century BC, in the early Han dynasty. Two of his short poems appear in Giles’s anthology.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Wu-ti of Han
bio: Wu-ti (157–87 BC) was the sixth emperor of the Han dynasty and came to the throne when he was only sixteen. His “Autumn Wind” is the poem of an emperor on his state barge regretting a journey that leaves his mistress behind; when she, Li Fu-jēn, died, Waley tells us, he sent for wizards from all parts of China in the hope of seeing her spirit again.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s versions in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Moschus
bio: Moschus was a Greek bucolic poet who flourished in Syracuse in the second century BC.
Only a small collection of his works survives, the largest being the Europa; The Lament for Bion was formerly attributed to him but is now assigned to an unknown pupil of Bion.

poets.name: The Sibylline Oracles
poets.credit: The Delphic Sibyl by Michelangelo, Sistine Chapel ceiling (1508–12), shown because the Oracles are anonymous and no portrait of their authors exists · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Sibylline Oracles are a collection of prophecies in Greek hexameters, spoken in the name of the Sibyls, the inspired prophetesses of the pagan world. They were not written by the Sibyls of tradition but by anonymous Jewish and, later, Christian authors, who borrowed the old prophetic voice to announce the fall of empires, the judgment of the nations and the end of the world. The oldest parts belong to Hellenistic Jewish circles, probably in Egypt, around the second century BC; later books were added and reworked by Jewish and Christian hands down to about the fifth century AD.

Twelve books survive in the medieval manuscripts, and the collection was long known only in part. Milton S. Terry’s blank-verse translation of 1890, given here in full, numbers them I–VIII and IX–XII, with the manuscript numbers of the last four (XI–XIV) in parentheses.

poets.name: Herodicus of Babylon
bio: Herodicus of Babylon was a Greek grammarian of the second century BC, a follower of Crates of Mallos and an opponent of the school of Aristarchus. The one epigram preserved under his name is a satirical attack on the Aristarchans.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XVI: 19a.

poets.name: Crates the Grammarian
bio: Crates the Grammarian is one of the named epigrammatists whose short poems are preserved in the Greek Anthology. Paton's Index of Authors dates the poet to the 2nd century BC. Paton distinguishes this Crates, the grammarian, from Crates the philosopher.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fourth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XI: 218.

poets.name: Antipater of Sidon
bio: Antipater of Sidon was a Phoenician Greek epigrammatist active in the later second century BC. Cicero remembers him as a gifted improviser, and his surviving epigrams are largely epitaphs and dedications.
Only epigrams that Paton assigns to him by name are filed here; those headed merely “Antipater”, which Paton cannot place, stay with the anonymous file.

poets.name: Dionysius of Andros
bio: Dionysius of Andros is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors gives no date for the poet.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 533).

poets.name: Su Wu
bio: General Su Wu (c. 100 BC) was, with his friend Li Ling, a prisoner in the land of the Huns. After nineteen years Su Wu was released, while Li Ling chose to stay behind. Waley gives him one poem of farewell, addressed to his wife.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Philodemus of Gadara
bio: Philodemus of Gadara (c. 110 – c. 35 BC) was an Epicurean philosopher and a clever, light-hearted writer of epigrams. He lived in Italy under the patronage of Lucius Calpurnius Piso, and his library was found at Herculaneum.
The epigrams here are those that Paton's first volume ascribes to him by name.

poets.name: Bion of Smyrna
bio: Bion of Phlossa, near Smyrna, was a Greek bucolic poet who flourished in Sicily in the late second and early first centuries BC.
Only one complete poem, The Lament for Adonis, and a few small fragments of his other poems survive; the fragments are preserved in quotations by Stobaeus and others.

poets.name: Emperor Chao of Han
poets.credit: Emperor Zhao of Han, from the Portraits of the Emperors attributed to Yan Liben (7th century; later copy) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons); an illustration, not a lifelike portrait
bio: Emperor Chao of Han, called the "Bright Emperor" in Fir-Flower Tablets, came to the throne as a child in 87 B.C., succeeding his father Emperor Wu. The dates above are those the book's Contents gives.
The archive holds one poem from Fir-Flower Tablets (1921), a song of boating, singing and picking lotus on a clear autumn day.

poets.name: Han-chung
bio: Han-chung is a Chinese poet named in Charles Budd’s Chinese Poems (1912). Budd, who spells the name Han-chong, gives no dates or note for him beyond the word “ancient”.
The poems here are Charles Budd’s versions in Chinese Poems (1912), given under the poet’s name as Budd romanises it.

poets.name: Meleager of Gadara
bio: Meleager of Gadara, a Syrian Greek who grew up in Tyre and later lived on Cos, flourished around 100 BC. He compiled the first great anthology of Greek epigrams, the Garland (Stephanus), in which every poet is likened to a flower, and he added many short love poems of his own.
W. R. Paton prints Meleager's proem to his Garland as Book IV, 1, and attributes many of the amatory epigrams of Book V to him.

poets.name: Menecrates of Smyrna
bio: Menecrates of Smyrna is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors gives no firm date for the poet. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Wreath of Meleager, the Garland compiled in the first century BC.
This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 54, 390).

poets.name: Virgil
poets.credit: Virgil enthroned between Clio and Melpomene, Roman mosaic from Hadrumetum (Bardo National Museum, Tunis), 3rd century AD · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Publius Vergilius Maro, known in English as Virgil, was born near Mantua in 70 BC and became the greatest poet of Augustan Rome. His Eclogues and the Georgics, a poem on farming and the countryside, made his name; his patron Maecenas brought him into the circle around the emperor Augustus.

The Aeneid, left unfinished at his death in 19 BC, tells how the Trojan prince Aeneas escapes the burning of Troy and carries his gods and his people to Italy, where his descendants will found Rome. In twelve books it answers Homer in Latin and became the model for the Western epic. This archive presents it in John Dryden’s 1697 verse translation, in heroic couplets. It also holds James Rhoades’s blank-verse translation of the Aeneid (1893–96).

poets.name: Heracleitus
bio: Heracleitus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 1st century BC. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of Meleager's Wreath, the Garland compiled about 100 BC.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 465).

poets.name: Crinagoras of Mytilene
bio: Crinagoras of Mytilene (c. 70 BC – after AD 11) belonged to the circle of Augustus and Octavia and served as an envoy of his city to Rome. He is among the main poets of the Garland of Philippus.
The epigrams here are those that Paton's first volume ascribes to him.

poets.name: Horace (Quintus Horatius Flaccus)
poets.credit: Contorniate medallion with the head of Horace (late antique; Bibliotheque nationale de France, via Gallica), cropped · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons). Not a lifetime portrait: no ancient likeness of Horace survives.
bio: Quintus Horatius Flaccus (65–8 BC) was born at Venusia in southern Italy, the son of a freed slave. He was educated in Rome and Athens, fought on the losing side at Philippi (42 BC) under Brutus, and returned to Italy to find his family property confiscated. Through Virgil he met Maecenas, the great patron of the Augustan poets, who gave him a farm in the Sabine hills.

His Satires, Epodes, Odes and Epistles made him the leading lyric poet of Rome. The Odes, in four books, adapt the metres of the Greek lyricists Alcaeus and Sappho to Roman themes: wine and friendship, love, the brevity of life, the Augustan state. He also wrote the Carmen Saeculare for the Secular Games of 17 BC. The versions here are from John Conington's rhymed English translation of the Odes (which omits a few odes), C. S. Calverley's versions of a handful of odes, and Thomas Creech's 1684 English verse translation of the Odes, Epodes, Satires, Epistles and Art of Poetry.

poets.name: Archias
bio: Archias is the name of several epigrammatists in the Anthology, and Paton's index lists the author of these as probably the second of that name; the editor places him in the first century BC. His epigrams are mainly dedications and love poems.
The epigrams here are those that Paton's first volume ascribes to Archias without qualification.

poets.name: Zonas
bio: Zonas is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 1st century BC. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Wreath of Philippus, the Garland compiled in the first century AD.
This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book VI: 98, 106).

poets.name: Tibullus (Albius Tibullus)
poets.credit: No portrait known
bio: Albius Tibullus (c. 55–c. 19 BC) was a Roman poet of the Augustan age, a member of the circle of the patron and general Marcus Valerius Messalla Corvinus. He is remembered for two books of love elegies addressed to a woman he calls Delia, to a second mistress, Nemesis, and to a boy, Marathus, in which the pleasures of country life and peace are set against the greed and violence of war and wealth.

Ovid mourned his early death in a famous elegy. Tibullus's own work fills Books I and II of the Corpus Tibullianum; the later books are by other hands. This archive offers the English verse translation of Theodore C. Williams (1908), which includes the third book, ascribed to Lygdamus, and one poem from the fourth book.

poets.name: Anonymous (Latin)
poets.credit: No portrait
bio: The anonymous Latin poems preserved in the Anthologia Latina include the Pervigilium Veneris, the "Vigil of Venus", a lyric of some ninety lines in which a refrain bids those who have never loved, and those who have, love to-morrow. It celebrates a spring festival of Venus, with the goddess presiding over the woods and over the marriage of earth and sky.

Its date, authorship and place of origin are unknown. It survives in two manuscripts of the Anthologia Latina, both now in Paris, and was first printed in 1577. Scholars have placed it in the second century or between the late third and mid-fourth century, and it has sometimes been attributed to Tiberianus. This archive offers the prose translation of J. W. Mackail, printed in the Loeb Classical Library in 1913.

poets.name: Tullius Laureas
bio: Tullius Laureas is, in Paton's note, probably a freedman of Cicero. Paton's Index of Authors includes the poet among those of Book VII. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 1st century BC. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Wreath of Philippus, the Garland compiled in the first century AD.
This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 17, 294).

poets.name: The Lady Pan
bio: The Lady Pan is dated by Giles to the 1st century BC. She is the court lady of the Han dynasty whose poem of the autumn fan became a standard image of the discarded favourite.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Propertius
poets.credit: No portrait known · text from Propertius, trans. H. E. Butler (Loeb Classical Library, 1912), via the Internet Archive
bio: Sextus Propertius was born in Umbria about 50 BC, and his family lost land in the confiscations that followed the civil wars of the 40s. He made his career in Rome, where he joined the circle around Maecenas and wrote four books of love elegies. Book I, the "Monobiblos", centres on his turbulent affair with the woman he calls Cynthia, and it won him his standing among the Roman elegists.

His later books grow in range, with poems on poetry and patronage, on the Augustan regime, and, in Book IV, on the origins of Roman cults, places and legends, ending with the dead matron Cornelia speaking from the tomb. He is thought to have died by about 15 BC. The translations here are H. E. Butler's prose version for the Loeb Classical Library (1912), which gives each elegy as paragraphs of English.

poets.name: Erycius

This archive carries the 6 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 36, 174, 230, 368, 377, 397).

poets.name: Ovid
poets.credit: Portrait bust identified as Ovid — public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: Publius Ovidius Naso, known as Ovid, was one of the leading poets of Augustan Rome, admired in his lifetime for his wit and technical fluency in Latin verse.

His masterwork, the Metamorphoses, is a sprawling narrative poem in fifteen books that retells hundreds of Greek and Roman myths of transformation, from the creation of the world to the deification of Julius Caesar. In AD 8 Augustus banished Ovid to Tomis on the Black Sea for reasons that remain unclear; he died there without returning to Rome.

This archive presents the Metamorphoses in Henry T. Riley’s 1851 prose translation, long a standard English rendering of the poem, and the Heroides and Amores in Grant Showerman’s 1914 Loeb prose translation. J. H. Mozley's Loeb translation of the Art of Love and other poems (1929) is also included.

poets.name: Phaedrus
poets.credit: No authentic portrait survives
bio: Phaedrus was a Roman fabulist of the first century AD. By his own account he was born in Macedonia or Thrace and became a freedman of the emperor Augustus. He is the first author known to have turned the Greek fables attributed to Aesop into Latin verse, writing them in iambic senarii.

His five books of fables, composed in the reigns of Tiberius and after, mingle animal tales with anecdotes and with pointed remarks on his own critics and on life under the emperors. These English verse renderings are by Christopher Smart, as printed in Bohn's Classical Library (1887).

poets.name: Marcus Argentarius
bio: Marcus Argentarius was an epigrammatist of the Garland of Philippus, writing around the turn of the era. He is best known for sharply observed love and banquet epigrams.
The epigrams here are those that Paton's first volume ascribes to him by name.

bio: Antipater of Thessalonica wrote in the Augustan age and belongs to the Garland of Philippus. He addressed Roman patrons, among them Lucius Calpurnius Piso, in epigrams of many kinds.
Only epigrams headed “Antipater of Thessalonica” in Paton's volume are filed here.

poets.name: Alpheus of Mytilene
poets.dates: date uncertain (probably 1st century BC / 1st century AD)
bio: Alpheus of Mytilene is an epigrammatist represented in the Greek Anthology, where his poems are generally thought to come from the Garland of Philip of Thessalonica. His date is uncertain, but he probably belongs to the early imperial period.
His epigrams include prayers to Poseidon and reflections on the ruined cities of the heroic age, such as Troy and Mycenae. Mackail's Select Epigrams (1890) prints several of them.

poets.name: Addaeus
poets.dates: date uncertain (probably 1st century BC / 1st century AD)
bio: Addaeus is an epigrammatist whose short poems are preserved in the Greek Anthology; the Anthology's headings sometimes call him a Macedonian. His date is uncertain, but he is generally placed among the poets of the early imperial period.
Mackail's Select Epigrams (1890) prints two of his epigrams, one a request to a hero's shrine at Potidaea and one on the release of an old ox from labour.

poets.name: Silius Italicus
poets.credit: Silius Italicus in Joseph Wright of Derby, Virgil's Tomb by Moonlight, with Silius Italicus (1779) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons). No ancient portrait of the poet survives; this is a later imaginative painting.
bio: Tiberius Catius Asconius Silius Italicus (c. AD 26–101) was a Roman senator and orator who held the consulship in AD 68, the year of Nero's death. After a public career he retired to Campania, where he wrote the Punica.

The Punica, in seventeen books, is the longest surviving Latin epic. It tells the Second Punic War, from Hannibal's oath and the siege of Saguntum to Scipio's victory in Africa. Silius modelled it closely on Virgil's Aeneid. It is read here in the English heroic couplets of Thomas Ross (1661).

poets.name: Persius
poets.credit: No portrait known · text from Juvenal and Persius, trans. G. G. Ramsay (Loeb Classical Library, 1918; 1920 printing), via the Internet Archive
bio: Aulus Persius Flaccus was born in AD 34 at Volaterrae in Etruria and died young, in AD 62. A Roman of equestrian rank and a Stoic by training, he was a pupil and friend of the philosopher Cornutus, and his satires were published after his death.

His surviving work is a short prologue and six satires, dense and allusive, which mock bad poetry, empty prayers and moral laziness from a Stoic standpoint. The English here is G. G. Ramsay's prose translation in the Loeb Classical Library (1918), given without the facing Latin, his notes or his summaries.

poets.credit: Engraving from Thomas Stanley's History of Philosophy, 1655 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Empedocles of Acragas (Agrigentum) in Sicily was a Greek philosopher, physician and poet of the fifth century BC. He wrote in hexameter verse and taught that all things are made from four roots, fire, air, earth and water, which Love draws together and Strife pulls apart in endless cycles.

This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation of the Greek Anthology (Book IX: 569), and William Ellery Leonard's verse translation of the surviving fragments of his poems On Nature and The Purifications.

bio: Democritus, the author of an epigram on the Aphrodite of Apelles, is one of the named epigrammatists of the Greek Anthology. Paton’s Index of Authors gives no date for him.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XVI: 180.
