poets.name: Eugenes
bio: Eugenes is one of the named epigrammatists of the Greek Anthology. Paton’s Index of Authors gives no date for him.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XVI: 308.

poets.name: Lucan
poets.credit: Portrait bust identified as Lucan — public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: Marcus Annaeus Lucanus, known as Lucan, was a Roman poet born in Corduba (Córdoba, Spain) and raised in Rome, nephew of the philosopher Seneca the Younger.

His only surviving work, the Pharsalia (De Bello Civili), is an unfinished epic in ten books on the civil war between Julius Caesar and Pompey. Unusually for ancient epic, it dispenses with the gods entirely, focusing on human ambition and the collapse of the Roman Republic. Lucan fell out with the Emperor Nero, joined a conspiracy against him, and was forced to take his own life at twenty-five, reportedly reciting his own verses as he died.
This archive presents the Pharsalia in Sir Edward Ridley’s 1896 blank-verse translation.

poets.name: Lucillius
bio: Lucillius, a Greek epigrammatist of the first century AD, is one of the Anthology's satirical writers; not to be confused with the Roman satirist Lucilius.
Paton's first volume ascribes one epigram to him without qualification, a dedication in Book VI.

poets.name: Leonidas of Alexandria
bio: Leonidas of Alexandria is the Roman-period epigrammatist famed for his isopsepha, epigrams whose lines each add up to the same numerical value. Paton's Index of Authors includes the poet among those of Book VII. The scan of Paton's index of authors used here does not give a date for the poet; the date shown is the conventional one.
This archive carries the 6 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 547, 548, 549, 550, 668, 675).

poets.name: Nicarchus
bio: Nicarchus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 1st century AD.
This archive carries the 5 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book V: 38, 39, 40; Book VI: 31, 285).

poets.name: Ammianus
bio: Ammianus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 1st century AD (with a query).
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 573).

poets.name: Aceratus Grammaticus
bio: Aceratus Grammaticus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors gives no date for the poet.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 138).

bio: Xenocritus of Rhodes is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors gives no date for the poet.

poets.name: Aristodicus of Rhodes
bio: Aristodicus of Rhodes is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors gives no date for the poet.
This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 189, 473).

poets.name: Martial
poets.credit: Portrait: Unknown — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Martial (Marcus Valerius Martialis) was born at Bilbilis in Spain and made his career as an epigrammatist at Rome under the Flavian emperors. His twelve books of epigrams, brief and often barbed poems on the manners, vanities and vices of the city, made the epigram a lasting literary form.

The English verse here is the 1656 version by R. Fletcher, published as Ex otio negotium, or Martiall his epigrams translated. It renders the epigrams in rhymed couplets and stanzas, keeps the Latin addressees as headings, and preserves the spelling of the printed book. Walter C. A. Ker's Loeb prose translation (1919–20) is added after it, epigram by epigram; Ker left some of the most indecent epigrams untranslated or put them into Italian, and those are omitted here.

poets.name: Trajan
bio: Trajan is one of the named epigrammatists whose short poems are preserved in the Greek Anthology. Paton's Index of Authors gives no date for the poet. Paton's index lists him as the emperor Trajan.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fourth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XI: 418.

poets.name: Hadrian
bio: Hadrian is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 2nd century AD.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book VI: 332).

poets.name: Mesomedes of Crete
bio: Mesomedes of Crete was a freedman and court musician of the emperor Hadrian in the second century AD. He is best known for a small group of lyric hymns, and Paton’s Index of Authors places him in the time of Hadrian.
This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XIV: 63; Book XVI: 323.

poets.name: Strato of Sardis
poets.dates: probably the reign of Hadrian, 2nd century AD (Paton’s date)
bio: Strato, usually called Strato of Sardis, is the poet whose name gives its title to Book XII of the Greek Anthology, the Musa Puerilis, a collection of epigrams on the love of boys. In his introduction to that book Paton judges that Strato lived probably in the reign of Hadrian, and that it was a Byzantine compiler, perhaps Cephalas, who inserted into the book the many poems of Meleager and other earlier poets.

poets.name: Dionysius the Sophist
bio: Dionysius the Sophist is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 2nd century AD.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book V: 81).

poets.name: Statius
poets.credit: No portrait known · text from theoi.com (J. H. Mozley, Loeb Classical Library, 1928)
bio: Publius Papinius Statius was a Roman poet who flourished in the late first century AD, under the Emperor Domitian.

He wrote a collection of occasional poems, the Silvae, the twelve-book epic Thebaid on the Seven against Thebes, and the unfinished Achilleid on the youth of Achilles; the Silvae are not included here.

poets.name: Lucian
bio: Lucian is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 2nd century AD.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book VI: 164).

poets.name: Nestor of Laranda
bio: Nestor of Laranda is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 2nd century AD.
This archive carries the 3 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 129, 364, 537).

poets.name: Pollianus
bio: Pollianus is one of the named epigrammatists whose short poems are preserved in the Greek Anthology. Paton's Index of Authors dates the poet to the 2nd century AD (?).
This archive carries the 4 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the fourth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XI: 127, 128, 130, 167.

poets.name: Juvenal
poets.credit: No portrait known · text from Juvenal and Persius, trans. G. G. Ramsay (Loeb Classical Library, 1918; 1920 printing), via the Internet Archive
bio: Decimus Junius Juvenalis, known as Juvenal, was a Roman satirist who wrote in the late first and early second centuries AD. Little is certain about his life; he is traditionally linked with the town of Aquinum, and his sixteen hexameter satires, gathered in five books, belong to the reigns of Trajan and Hadrian.

The satires attack the vices of Rome: patronage and legacy-hunting, the bustle and danger of the city, the follies of women, the vanity of ambition and the abuses of wealth and power. The English here is G. G. Ramsay's prose translation in the Loeb Classical Library (1918), given without the facing Latin, his notes or his introduction.

poets.name: Asvaghosha
poets.credit: Gandhara relief of the Great Departure of the Buddha (c. 2nd–3rd century AD), Musée Guimet, photographed by Jastrow · an artifact, not a portrait of the poet, none being known · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Asvaghosha was a Buddhist poet, playwright and philosopher who is said to have flourished at the court of the Kushan king Kanishka in the first or second century AD. Tradition holds that he was born a Brahman and was converted to Buddhism; his dates and the details of his life rest on later Chinese and Tibetan reports and remain uncertain.

He is the author of the Buddhacarita, the Life of the Buddha, the earliest surviving Sanskrit court epic (mahakavya) on that subject, which follows the Buddha from his birth at Kapilavastu to his enlightenment and first teaching. Only about the first half of the Sanskrit text survives; the remainder is known from Tibetan and Chinese versions, and E. B. Cowell's English translation of 1894 supplies the closing books from the Chinese and Tibetan.

poets.name: Hsin Yen-nien
bio: Hsin Yen-nien is a Chinese poet named in Charles Budd’s Chinese Poems (1912). Budd, who spells the name Sin Yen-nien, places him in the Han dynasty and gives no further note for him.
The poems here are Charles Budd’s versions in Chinese Poems (1912), given under the poet’s name as Budd romanises it.

poets.name: Rufinus
bio: Rufinus wrote some of the most polished erotic epigrams in the Anthology. Nothing certain is known of him, and his date is uncertain, perhaps the second to the fourth century AD.

Paton's index lists a Rufinus Domesticus separately; the epigrams under that name are not filed here. The poems here are all those Paton heads “Rufinus” or attributes to him as “by the same”, mostly in Book V.

poets.name: Sung Tzŭ-hou
bio: Sung Tzŭ-hou is dated by Waley only to the second century AD. The poem translated here is a small dramatic ballad on a girl who breaks a branch of blossom, in which the tree and the girl speak in turn.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Emperor Ling of Later Han
bio: Emperor Ling (A.D. 156-189) ruled the Later (Eastern) Han dynasty from 168 until his death.
The archive holds one poem from Fir-Flower Tablets (1921), a short song of summer pleasure on a palace canal.

poets.name: Oppian
bio: Two Greek didactic poems come down under the name of Oppian: the Halieutica on fishing, which Mair's introduction attributes to Oppian of Cilicia and dates to the reign of Marcus Aurelius and his son Commodus, to whom it is addressed, and the Cynegetica on hunting.

Mair's introduction treats the Cynegetica as the work of a later Syrian poet of Apamea writing under Caracalla, so that the two poems are by two authors who have traditionally both been called Oppian.

poets.name: K’ung Jung
bio: K’ung Jung, who died in AD 208, was a scholar of the late Han dynasty. Giles prints one poem of his, on the death of a first-born child.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Hsü Kan
bio: Hsü Kan is dated by Giles to the 2nd and 3rd centuries AD, the last years of the Han dynasty. His poem here speaks in the voice of a wife whose husband is away.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Miu Hsi
bio: Miu Hsi died in AD 245. His “Bearer’s Song” belongs to the tradition of the Han burial songs, sung at funerals, and is spoken in the voice of the dead man.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Wei Wēn-ti
bio: Wei Wēn-ti (AD 188–227) was the son of Ts’ao Ts’ao, who founded the Wei dynasty and died in AD 220, and the elder brother of the poet Ts’ao Chih. Waley gives him a poem on the death of his father and two poems on a campaign against the southern state of Wu.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s versions in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Ts’ao Chih
bio: Ts’ao Chih (AD 192–233) was the third son of Ts’ao Ts’ao. He was a great favourite with his father until he made a mistake in a campaign. His poem on the ruins of Lo-yang, where he had once lived, was sacked by Tung Cho, and is one of the best known of the period.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s versions in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Diogenes Laertius
bio: Diogenes Laertius, author of the Lives of Eminent Philosophers (third century AD), is credited in Paton's index with the verse epitaphs on the philosophers that fill the middle of Book VII. Paton's Index of Authors includes the poet among those of Book VII. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 3rd century AD.

poets.name: Yüan Chi
bio: Yüan Chi (AD 210–263) is represented in this archive by one poem, “Regret,” in which a man who learned fencing in his youth looks back on his wasted years.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Fu Hsüan
bio: Fu Hsüan died in AD 278. Waley gives him two poems: a quiet night-piece on contentment with poverty, and “Woman,” a famous lament on the lot of women.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s versions in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Chi K’ang
bio: Chi K’ang (AD 223–262) is represented by one short Taoist song in Waley’s 1918 anthology, a poem of casting out wisdom and learning and letting the thoughts wander in the Great Void.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Asinius Quadratus
bio: Asinius Quadratus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 3rd century AD.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 312).

poets.name: Eupithius of Athens
bio: Eupithius of Athens is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 3rd century AD (with a query).
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 206).

poets.name: Fronto
bio: Fronto is one of the named epigrammatists whose short poems are preserved in the Greek Anthology. Paton's Index of Authors dates the poet to the 3rd century AD.
This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the fourth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XII: 174, 233.

poets.name: Orpheus (Orphic Hymns)
poets.dates: hymns c. 2nd–3rd c. AD (ascribed to the legendary Orpheus)
poets.credit: Orpheus and the beasts, Roman mosaic, Antakya Archaeological Museum · An artifact, shown because the hymns are anonymous and no portrait of any author exists · Photo: Dosseman, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Orphic Hymns are a collection of 87 short Greek hexameter hymns, each addressed to a god, a daimon or a personified power, together with a prefatory poem addressed to Musaeus, the pupil of Orpheus. The tradition ascribes them to Orpheus, the legendary singer of Thrace, but they are in fact anonymous late-antique poems, usually dated to about the second or third century AD and composed for the use of small cult groups. Each hymn was meant to be sung during an offering, and most carry a note naming the incense burned with it.

They are given here in Thomas Taylor's rhymed translation, first published in 1787 and reissued in a second edition in 1824; the text follows Bertram Dobell's 1896 facsimile reprint of that second edition. Taylor, the English Platonist, read the hymns through the Neoplatonic theology of Proclus, and his own long notes and dissertation, which fill most of the volume, are not part of the poems and are left out. His prose notes are omitted; only the verse is kept, with his fumigation headings recorded as each poem's note.

poets.name: Ch’ēng-kung Sui
bio: Ch’ēng-kung Sui died in AD 273. He is represented here by a single short poem, “Inviting Guests,” which describes a gathering of friends for talk and plain food.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Chang Tsai
bio: Chang Tsai lived in the third century AD. His poem on the desecration of the Han tombs describes the imperial burial-mounds north of Lo-yang plundered and overgrown.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Ch’ēng Hsiao
bio: Ch’ēng Hsiao is dated by Waley to about AD 250. The one poem translated here is a humorous satire on the habit of paying calls in the hottest month of the year.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Liu Hsün’s wife
bio: Liu Hsün’s wife lived in the third century AD. After she had been married to General Liu Hsün for a long while he sent her back to her home, because he had fallen in love with a girl of the Ssu-ma family, and she is credited with the poem on the curtain of the wedding bed.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Tso Ssŭ
bio: Tso Ssŭ lived in the third century AD. Waley’s two versions are “Day Dreams,” in which he recalls his youthful ambition, and “The Scholar in the Narrow Street,” a poem of poverty and neglect.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s versions in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Athenogenes
bio: John Brownlie's Hymns of the Greek Church (1900) heads its rendering of the evening hymn 'Phos hilaron' with the name of Athenogenes and the date 296 A.D. The sources used here give nothing else about him.
This file contains that single poem, Brownlie's translation beginning 'Light serene of holy glory', recorded with its translator.

poets.name: St. Methodius of Olympus
bio: John Brownlie describes Methodius as a prominent name in ecclesiastical history and a Father of the Church, born about the middle of the third century. He was first Bishop of Olympus in Lycia and, according to Jerome, ultimately Bishop of Tyre; he opposed certain views of Origen but seems to have been influenced by that theologian, and is said to have suffered martyrdom under Diocletian about 311.

Brownlie says the hymn from which his piece is taken is found in Methodius's Banquet of the Ten Virgins; it has twenty-four strophes beginning with the letters of the Greek alphabet in order and ending with a common refrain. This file gives Brownlie's 1900 cento, 'Behold the Bridegroom! Hark the cry'.

poets.name: Lu Chi
bio: Lu Chi is a Chinese poet named in Charles Budd’s Chinese Poems (1912). Budd, who spells the name Luh-Ki, gives no dates or note for him.
The poems here are Charles Budd’s versions in Chinese Poems (1912), given under the poet’s name as Budd romanises it.

poets.name: Lu Yün
bio: Lu Yün lived in the fourth century AD. Waley gives one short poem of his, “The Valley Wind,” in which a recluse stuffs his window with ferns and lets his cottage become a universe.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Tryphiodorus
bio: Tryphiodorus was a Greek poet and grammarian who flourished in Egypt in the 3rd or 4th century AD. His only surviving work is the short epic The Taking of Ilios; he also wrote the lost Marathoniaca and The Story of Hippodamea.

poets.name: Fu Mi
bio: Fu Mi is dated by Giles to the 3rd and 4th centuries AD. Giles prints two of his poems, both on the grief of separated lovers.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Quintus Smyrnaeus
poets.credit: Achilles slaying Penthesileia, Attic red-figure kylix by the Penthesilea Painter, c. 460 BC (Staatliche Antikensammlungen, Munich) — not a portrait (none survives), but a scene from the story he tells. Public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: Quintus Smyrnaeus (also called Quintus of Smyrna) was a Greek epic poet of the later Roman Empire, probably writing in the 4th century AD. His name suggests a link with Smyrna in Asia Minor; he says in his poem that he tended sheep there as a young man before the Muses taught him to sing.

His one surviving work is the Posthomerica, or The Fall of Troy, fourteen books of hexameter verse that carry the story on from the end of Homer's Iliad to the sack of Troy and the Greeks' departure. It imitates Homer's language and similes closely, and it was largely neglected until a manuscript was found in southern Italy in the 15th century.

poets.name: St. Hilary of Poitiers
poets.credit: St. Hilary of Poitiers, illustration, Wikimedia Commons · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Hilary was born at Poitiers early in the fourth century, became bishop of his native city about 350, and died in the later 360s. His feast day gives its name to Hilary Term.
John Brownlie's notes say that four Latin hymns are attributed to him. One of them, the morning hymn Jam meta noctis transiit, is given here in Brownlie's English version of 1896.

poets.name: Decimus Magnus Ausonius
poets.credit: The Neumagen wine ship (the “Mosel ship”), Roman funerary relief, early 3rd century AD, Rheinisches Landesmuseum Trier; photograph by Iris Reiff, U.S. Air Force, 2012 · An artifact, shown because no portrait of Ausonius exists · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Decimus Magnus Ausonius (c. AD 310 – c. 395) was born at Burdigala (Bordeaux), where he taught grammar and rhetoric for some thirty years. About 364 the emperor Valentinian I called him to Trier as tutor to his son Gratian; when Gratian became emperor in 375 Ausonius rose rapidly, becoming quaestor, prefect of Gaul and, in 379, consul. After Gratian's death in 383 he withdrew to his estates near Bordeaux and lived there until about 395.

His verse is the learned, occasional poetry of a professional teacher: the Parentalia and the Commemoratio Professorum Burdigalensium, in which he commemorates his kin and his colleagues; the Mosella, a poem on the river Moselle; Cupid Crucified; the verbal tours de force of the Technopaegnion and the Griphus; the Caesares; and many epistles and epigrams. The English prose given here is Hugh G. Evelyn-White's Loeb Classical Library translation (1919–21), which renders each verse piece as prose, so the lines of the originals do not appear as verse; only the pieces he translated are included.

poets.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
bio: Gregory of Nazianzus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 4th century AD.

This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book I: 92, 93), and now also the epigrams of Book VIII, “The Epigrams of Saint Gregory the Theologian”, in the second volume (Books VII–XII), 258 pieces in all, since Paton numbers four of them as 10a, 52a, 67a and 85a.

poets.name: Magnus the Physician
bio: Magnus the Physician is one of the named epigrammatists of the Greek Anthology. Paton’s Index of Authors dates him, with a query, to the 4th century AD.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XVI: 270.

poets.name: St. Ambrose of Milan
poets.credit: St. Ambrose, 5th-century mosaic in Sant'Ambrogio, Milan (cropped), Wikimedia Commons · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ambrose was born about 340 in Gaul and became Bishop of Milan in 374; he died on Easter Eve, 397. John Brownlie's notes record that he introduced antiphonal chanting into the Western Church.

Latin hymns in his manner were long called Ambrosian, and few can be certainly assigned to him. This page holds only the two that John Brownlie (1896) gives to him without real doubt, Deus creator omnium and Splendor paternae gloriae, in Brownlie's English.

poets.name: Chan Fang-shēng
bio: Chan Fang-shēng lived in the fourth century AD. His poem “Sailing Homeward” is a list of landscape features whose steadiness heals the pain of a traveller’s heart.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Prudentius
poets.credit: Prudentius, illustration from a Psychomachia manuscript (British Library, Add MS 24199, fol. 11v), Wikimedia Commons · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Aurelius Prudentius Clemens was born in 348 in the north of Spain, probably at Saragossa. After holding public offices he withdrew from secular life and devoted himself to Christian verse; he died about 413. In the Preface to his poems, here given in Pope's English, he looks back over a life of fifty-seven years and offers his verse to God as the fruit of his old age.

The Cathemerinon, 'Hymns for the Christian's Day', is a cycle of twelve hymns for the hours of the day and the feasts of the Christian year, from cock-crow to the Epiphany. It is given here in R. Martin Pope's Temple Classics translation of 1905, with its Preface and Epilogue. One of John Brownlie's 1896 versions of a breviary hymn drawn from his verse is added.

poets.name: T’ao Ch’ien
poets.credit: Portrait: Chen Hongshou (1599-1652) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: T’ao Ch’ien (AD 365–427) gave up official life to farm his own land, and his poems of retirement, wine, poverty and the pleasure of a small house and garden are among the best loved in Chinese. Waley devoted a whole chapter of his 1918 anthology to him.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s versions in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Synesius the Philosopher
bio: Synesius of Cyrene was a Neoplatonist philosopher, orator and poet who later became bishop of Ptolemais. Paton’s Index of Authors lists him as Synesius the Philosopher and dates him to the 5th century AD.
This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XVI: 76, 79.

poets.name: Kalidasa
poets.credit: Raja Ravi Varma, Shakuntala lost in thoughts (1901), an illustration of Kalidasa's heroine; no portrait of the poet exists · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Kalidasa is generally ranked the greatest poet and dramatist in Sanskrit. Almost nothing is known of his life: he is placed, on tradition and internal evidence, around the 4th or 5th century AD, probably under the Gupta kings.

He is credited with the play Shakuntala, the epics The Dynasty of Raghu and The Birth of the War-God, and the lyric Cloud-Messenger, in which an exiled Yaksha asks a passing cloud to carry word to his wife. The Seasons is also attributed to him, though its authorship has been doubted. Here he appears in the English verse of Ralph T. H. Griffith and Arthur W. Ryder.

poets.name: Bhartrihari
bio: Bhartrihari is the traditional name of a Sanskrit poet-grammarian said to have been a king of Ujjain who renounced the throne for a hermit's life; little about him is securely known, and the dating is uncertain, usually placed somewhere between the fifth and seventh centuries AD. His name is attached to the Shatakatraya, three centuries of epigrams on love, worldly wisdom and renunciation.

The poems given here are from Paul Elmer More's A Century of Indian Epigrams (Boston: Houghton, Mifflin, 1898), described on its title page as 'chiefly from the Sanskrit of Bhartrihari'. It is a free verse adaptation, not a literal translation: More selected from the traditional collection and, as he says in his introduction, added stanzas from other sources. The epigrams keep More's numbering.

poets.name: Tao-yün
bio: Tao-yün (c. AD 400) was the wife of General Wang Ning-chih. According to Waley the general was so stupid that she finally deserted him. Her poem, “Climbing a Mountain,” imagines a lodging for ever in a hollow among the rocks.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Palladas of Alexandria
bio: Palladas of Alexandria was a grammarian and the last great epigrammatist of pagan Alexandria, known for bitter, satirical verse. The editor dates him to the fourth century AD; Paton's index says the fifth.
The epigrams here are those that Paton's first volume ascribes to him.

poets.name: Andronicus
bio: Andronicus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 4th century AD (?).
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 181).

poets.name: Libanius
bio: Libanius, the Antiochene orator and rhetorician of the fourth century AD, is the poet to whom Paton ascribes the epitaph on the emperor Jovian. Paton's Index of Authors includes the poet among those of Book VII. The scan of Paton's index of authors used here does not give a date for the poet; the date shown is the conventional one.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 747).

poets.name: Apollinarius
bio: Apollinarius is one of the named epigrammatists whose short poems are preserved in the Greek Anthology. Paton's Index of Authors dates the poet to the 4th century AD (?).
This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the fourth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XI: 399, 421.

poets.name: Julian the Emperor
bio: Julian the Emperor is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors gives no firm date for the poet. Paton's index lists him as the emperor Julian.
This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 365, 368).

poets.name: Claudian
poets.credit: Portrait: Luca Signorelli — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Claudius Claudianus, called Claudian, has been named the last poet of classical Rome. He was born about 370, very probably in Alexandria, and wrote his first verses in Greek; he came to Rome around 394 and began to write in Latin in 395.

He then lived at the court of Milan as a kind of poet laureate to the general Stilicho, for whom he wrote panegyrics for the consuls and the emperor Honorius, invectives against the ministers Rufinus and Eutropius, epithalamia, and the unfinished mythological epic The Rape of Proserpine. He seems to have died in 404. The English prose here is Maurice Platnauer’s Loeb translation (1922).

poets.name: St. Anatolius of Constantinople
bio: J. M. Neale calls Anatolius the first poet who freed himself from the tyranny of the old laws and boldly struck out the new path of harmonious prose, and compares him to Venantius Fortunatus in the West. Neale's headnote records that he had been apocrisiarius, or legate, from Dioscorus to the Emperor's court, and that after the death of S. Flavian he was raised to the throne of Constantinople in 449. At the Council of Chalcedon he procured the enactment of the 28th Canon, which raised Constantinople to the second place among the Patriarchal Sees, and he died in 458 after eight years as Patriarch. John Brownlie also gives 458 as the year of his death.

Neale notes that Anatolius's compositions are not numerous and are almost all short, but usually very spirited. This file gives four of Neale's versions from Hymns of the Eastern Church (1862), including the stichera on the Lord stilling the storm and the Evening Hymn, and Brownlie's 1900 rendering of the Christmas hymn that begins 'What shall we bring to Thee?'. Each poem's translator is recorded.

poets.name: Theon of Alexandria
bio: Theon of Alexandria is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 5th century AD.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 292).

poets.name: Tiruvalluvar
poets.dates: traditionally c. 1st century BC – 5th century AD
bio: Tiruvalluvar is the traditional name of the Tamil poet-sage who composed the Tirukkural (the ‘Sacred Kural’), and almost nothing is securely known of his life; scholars have placed him anywhere between the first century BC and about the fifth century AD.

The Tirukkural consists of 1,330 couplets in 133 chapters of ten, arranged in three books on Virtue, Wealth and Love. It is given here, chapter by chapter, in G. U. Pope’s English verse translation of 1886.

poets.name: Eutolmius Scholasticus of Alexandria
bio: Eutolmius Scholasticus of Alexandria is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 5th century AD. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Cycle of Agathias, compiled in the sixth century AD.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book VI: 86).

poets.name: Helladius
bio: Helladius is one of the named epigrammatists whose short poems are preserved in the Greek Anthology. Paton's Index of Authors dates the poet to the 5th century AD (?).
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fourth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XI: 423.

poets.name: Pao Chao
bio: Pao Chao died in AD 466. Waley gives two soldier’s poems of his, “The Scholar Recruit” and “The Red Hills,” the second a description of a campaign in the poisonous south.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s versions in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Proclus
bio: Proclus was the leading Neoplatonic philosopher of the fifth century AD. Paton's Index of Authors includes the poet among those of Book VII. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 5th century AD.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 341).

poets.name: Marinus of Neapolis
bio: Marinus of Neapolis is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 5th century AD.
This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 196, 197).

poets.name: Boethius
poets.credit: Boethius with a monochord, medieval manuscript illustration, early 12th century · An artifact, shown as no contemporary portrait survives · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius was a Roman statesman and philosopher, born in Rome about AD 480 into a patrician family. He rose to be consul in 510 and later served as master of offices under the Ostrogothic king Theodoric, and he set himself to translate and comment on the works of Aristotle and Plato into Latin.

Accused of treason, he was imprisoned at Pavia and executed about 524. While in prison he wrote The Consolation of Philosophy, a dialogue with Lady Philosophy in alternating prose and verse. The thirty-nine verse songs are given here in the English version of H. R. James (1897), and the prose between them is left out.

poets.name: St. Ita
bio: St. Ita is the early Irish saint to whom tradition attributes a lullaby to the infant Jesus, which she is said to have sung while nursing him in her cell. George Sigerson, in Bards of the Gael and Gall (1907), dates her 480–570 and prints the poem under the title “Jesukin”.

The Irish original is preserved in the commentary to the Martyrology of Oengus, which Sigerson cites through Whitley Stokes. Only Sigerson’s version, made after the metre of the original, is given here.

poets.name: Christodorus of Coptus
bio: Christodorus of Coptus, in Egypt, was an epic poet of the reign of Anastasius I, around AD 500. Paton calls him Christodorus of Thebes in Egypt. Only one of his poems survives complete, thanks to its place in the Greek Anthology.
That poem is the description of the bronze statues in the public gymnasium called Zeuxippos at Byzantium, printed as the whole of Book II and destroyed with the building in the fire of 532.

poets.name: Colluthus
bio: Colluthus of Lycopolis was a Theban poet who flourished in the late 5th or early 6th century AD. His only surviving work is the epyllion The Rape of Helen; according to the Suda he also wrote the lost Calydoniaca, Persica and Encoinia.

poets.name: Tiberius Illustrius
bio: Tiberius Illustrius is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors gives no firm date for the poet. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Cycle of Agathias, with a query.
This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 2, 370).

poets.name: Eratosthenes Scholasticus
bio: Eratosthenes Scholasticus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors gives no firm date for the poet. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Cycle of Agathias, the sixth-century anthology.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 444).

poets.name: Cometas Chartularius
bio: Cometas Chartularius is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors gives no firm date for the poet. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Cycle of Agathias, the sixth-century anthology.
This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 586, 597).

poets.name: Marianus Scholasticus
bio: Marianus Scholasticus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors gives no firm date for the poet. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Cycle of Agathias, the sixth-century anthology.
This archive carries the 5 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 626, 627, 657, 668, 669).

poets.name: Arabius Scholasticus
bio: Arabius Scholasticus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors gives no firm date for the poet. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Cycle of Agathias, the sixth-century anthology.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 667).

poets.name: Ablabius Illustrius
bio: Ablabius Illustrius is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors gives no firm date for the poet. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Cycle of Agathias, the sixth-century anthology.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 762).

poets.name: Nilus Scholasticus
bio: Nilus Scholasticus is one of the named epigrammatists of the Greek Anthology. Paton’s Index of Authors gives no date for him; the title Scholasticus (a lawyer or man of letters) is common among the poets of the sixth century.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XVI: 247.

poets.name: Cosmas
bio: Cosmas is one of the named epigrammatists of the Greek Anthology. Paton’s Index of Authors gives no firm date for him.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XVI: 114.

poets.name: Damascius
bio: Damascius, the Neoplatonic philosopher, was the last head of the Platonic school at Athens in the sixth century AD. Paton's Index of Authors includes the poet among those of Book VII. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 6th century AD. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Cycle of Agathias, compiled in the sixth century AD.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 553).

poets.name: Chiang Yen
bio: Chiang Yen (AD 443–504) lived under the Southern dynasties. Giles prints one poem of his, on a battlefield and the forgotten names of the dead.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Macedonius the Consul
bio: Macedonius, called the Consul, was a Byzantine epigrammatist of the sixth century and a friend of Agathias and Paul the Silentiary; the title consul in his case was honorary.
The epigrams here are those that Paton's first volume ascribes to him, chiefly in Book V.

poets.name: Cyrus the Poet
bio: Cyrus the Poet is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 6th century AD. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Cycle of Agathias, compiled in the sixth century AD.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 557).

poets.name: Theodorus the Proconsul
bio: Theodorus the Proconsul is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 6th century AD. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Cycle of Agathias, compiled in the sixth century AD.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 556).

poets.name: Gabriel the Prefect
bio: Gabriel the Prefect was a high official and epigrammatist of the age of Justinian, in the sixth century AD. A portrait of a prefect named Gabriel at Byzantium is the subject of an epigram by Leontius Scholasticus in the same Book of the Anthology.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XVI: 208.

poets.name: Julian, Prefect of Egypt
bio: Julian, Prefect of Egypt, was a Byzantine official and epigrammatist of the sixth century, included in the Cycle of Agathias.
The epigrams here are those that Paton's first volume ascribes to him, including some in Book V and the dedications in Book VI.

poets.name: Theosebeia
bio: Theosebeia is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 6th century AD. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Cycle of Agathias, compiled in the sixth century AD.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 559).

poets.name: Diogenes, Bishop of Amisus
bio: Diogenes, Bishop of Amisus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 6th century AD. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Cycle of Agathias, compiled in the sixth century AD.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 613).

poets.name: Leontius Scholasticus
bio: Leontius Scholasticus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 6th century AD. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Cycle of Agathias, compiled in the sixth century AD.
This archive carries the 6 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 149, 150, 571, 573, 575, 579).

poets.name: Damocharis
bio: Damocharis is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 6th century AD.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book VI: 63).

poets.name: Julian Antecessor
bio: Julian Antecessor is one of the named epigrammatists whose short poems are preserved in the Greek Anthology. Paton's Index of Authors dates the poet to the 6th century AD (?).
This archive carries the 3 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the fourth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XI: 367, 368, 369.

poets.name: Michael the Grammarian
bio: Michael the Grammarian, called Michael Grammaticus in Paton’s Index of Authors, was one of the poets of the circle of Agathias in the sixth century AD.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XVI: 316.

poets.name: Thomas Scholasticus
bio: Thomas Scholasticus is one of the named epigrammatists of the Greek Anthology. Paton’s Index of Authors gives no firm date for him.
This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XVI: 315, 379.

poets.name: Synesius Scholasticus
bio: Synesius Scholasticus was a lawyer and epigrammatist of the sixth century AD. A statue of him in Berytus is the subject of an epigram by Joannes Barbocallus in the Planudean Appendix.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XVI: 267.

poets.name: Johannes Barbocallus
bio: Johannes Barbocallus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 6th century AD. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Cycle of Agathias, compiled in the sixth century AD.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book VI: 55).

poets.name: Theodoretus Grammaticus
bio: Theodoretus Grammaticus is one of the named epigrammatists of the Greek Anthology. Paton’s Index of Authors gives no date for him.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XVI: 34.

poets.name: Troilus Grammaticus
bio: Troilus Grammaticus is one of the named epigrammatists of the Greek Anthology. Paton’s Index of Authors gives no date for him.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XVI: 55.

poets.name: Agathias Scholasticus
bio: Agathias Scholasticus, born at Myrina in Asia Minor about 530, practised as a lawyer at Constantinople and wrote a history of Justinian's wars. He gathered the poems of his generation in the Cycle, a collection of new epigrams, around 567.
The epigrams here include the two proems of the Cycle (Book IV, 3 and 4) and the many love poems that Paton ascribes to him in Book V and dedications in Book VI.

poets.name: Venantius Fortunatus
poets.credit: Portrait: Unknown authorUnknown author — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Venantius Honorius Clementianus Fortunatus was a Latin poet born in northern Italy around 530. He travelled to Merovingian Gaul, where he became court poet and friend to Queen Radegund at Poitiers, and later served as bishop of Poitiers. He died there in the early seventh century.

His processional hymns for the Cross, written when relics of the True Cross reached Radegund's convent at Poitiers, passed into the Latin liturgy and are still sung. Both are given here in the English verse of John Mason Neale (1867), from Mediaeval Hymns and Sequences.

poets.name: Columcille (St. Columba)
bio: Columcille, or St. Columba, was born in 521 into a northern Irish royal kindred and became one of the great founders of early Irish monasticism, with churches at Derry and Durrow and, from 563, the island monastery of Iona off the Scottish coast. He died at Iona in 597.

Many poems of exile and homesickness were later ascribed to him. George Sigerson, in Bards of the Gael and Gall (1907), gives three under his name: the laments “Remembering Erinn” and “Delights in Erinn”, and the short stave “The Fall of the Book-Satchels”, which he places at the news of the death of the scholar Longarad. They are given here in Sigerson’s English versions.

poets.name: Pope Gregory the Great
poets.credit: Gregory the Great with the Holy Spirit, medieval illustration, Wikimedia Commons · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Gregory was born at Rome about 540 and became pope in 590. In 596 he sent Augustine on his mission to Britain, and he died in 604. He is counted among the four Latin Doctors of the Church.
Several hymns have been ascribed to him. This page holds the one that John Brownlie (1896) gives to him without a doubt, Lucis Creator optime, in Brownlie's English version.

poets.name: Hsieh T’iao
bio: Hsieh T’iao lived in the fifth century AD. His “Song of the Men of Chin-ling” was written for troops marching back into the capital.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Paul the Silentiary
bio: Paul the Silentiary, a court official under Justinian (d. c. 575), wrote the great verse description of Hagia Sophia as well as many polished epigrams, most of them erotic.
He is one of the best represented poets of the Cycle of Agathias in Book V, and the epigrams here are those that Paton ascribes to him.

poets.name: Wu-ti of Liang
bio: Wu-ti (AD 464–549) was emperor of the Liang dynasty. Waley gives two poems of his: “The Liberator,” a political allegory about a sparrow and a fowler, and a love-poem, “People Hide their Love.”
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s versions in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Theaetetus Scholasticus
bio: Theaetetus Scholasticus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 6th century AD. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Cycle of Agathias, compiled in the sixth century AD.
This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book VI: 27, 357).

poets.name: Phocas the Deacon
bio: Phocas the Deacon is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors gives no firm date for the poet.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 772).

poets.name: Joannes Barbucallus
bio: Joannes Barbucallus (John Barbucallus) is a Byzantine epigrammatist represented in the Greek Anthology. His date is uncertain.
Mackail's Select Epigrams (1890) prints two of his epigrams, a dedication by a newly married herdsman and the dying words of a contented wife.

poets.name: Sophronius the Patriarch
bio: Sophronius the Patriarch is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors gives no date for the poet.
This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 679, 680).

poets.name: Yü Yung
bio: Yü Yung is a Chinese poet named in Charles Budd’s Chinese Poems (1912). Budd, who spells the name Yuh Yong, places him in the Northern Wei dynasty and gives no further note for him.
The poems here are Charles Budd’s versions in Chinese Poems (1912), given under the poet’s name as Budd romanises it.

poets.name: Tsang Chih
bio: Tsang Chih lived in the sixth century. Waley prints a single four-line song of his, in the voice of a girl growing up under the walls of a castle.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Wang Seng-ju
bio: Wang Seng-ju is dated by L. Cranmer-Byng to the sixth century AD. He is represented by a single short lyric of tears.
The poems here are L. Cranmer-Byng’s version in A Lute of Jade (1909), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Ch’ien Wēn-ti of Liang
bio: The Emperor Ch’ien Wēn-ti of the Liang dynasty lived in the sixth century. Waley gives two short poems of his, one on the town of Lo-yang in spring and one on a lady waiting for her lover at a ferry.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s versions in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Hsü Ling
bio: Hsü Ling (AD 507–583) is represented here by “The Waters of Lung-t’ou,” a poem of the north-west frontier and the long road home to the capital.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Yüan-ti
bio: Yüan-ti (AD 508–554) is represented by a seven-line poem, “The Rejected Wife,” in which a woman meets her successor and her former husband in the same hour.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Menander Protector
bio: Menander Protector is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to c. AD 600.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book I: 101).

poets.name: Claudianus
bio: Claudianus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to Byzantine period. Paton's index describes him as a Byzantine poet.
This archive carries the 4 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 139, 140, 753, 754).

poets.name: Leo the Philosopher
bio: Leo the Philosopher is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to Byzantine period. Paton's index describes him as Byzantine.
This archive carries the 7 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 200, 201, 202, 214, 361, 578, 579).

poets.name: Photius the Patriarch
bio: Photius the Patriarch is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 9th century AD. Paton's index describes him as the Patriarch.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the third volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book IX: 203).

poets.name: Theophanes
bio: Theophanes is one of the Byzantine epigrammatists of the Greek Anthology. Paton’s Index of Authors gives his date as uncertain.
This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XV: 14, 35.

poets.name: Ignatius
bio: Ignatius is one of the Byzantine ecclesiastical writers whose epitaphs and verses are preserved in the Greek Anthology. Paton’s Index of Authors dates him, with a query, to the 10th century AD.
This archive carries the 4 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XV: 29, 30, 31, 39.

poets.name: Constantine of Sicily
bio: Constantine of Sicily was a Byzantine grammarian and epigrammatist. His epigram on his professorial chair drew a sharp reply from Theophanes.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XV: 13.

poets.name: Constantine of Rhodes
bio: Constantine of Rhodes, a native of Lindos and servant of the emperor Leo VI, wrote verses on a cross dedicated at Lindos and on the Mother of God. Paton prints him among the Byzantine poets of the Anthology.
This archive carries the 3 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XV: 15, 16, 17.

poets.name: Anastasius the Lisper
bio: Anastasius the Lisper is known to the Greek Anthology as the author of a short religious epigram on Christ crucified, one of the Byzantine pieces added in the fifteenth book.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XV: 28.

poets.name: Arethas the Deacon
bio: Arethas, deacon and later archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, was a Byzantine scholar and book-collector. The Anthology preserves under his name three epitaphs, two for his sister Anna and one for the nun Febronia.
This archive carries the 3 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the fifth volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Loeb, 1918): Book XV: 32, 33, 34.

poets.name: The Mu'allaqat Poets
poets.credit: The Holy Mosque at Mecca with the Kaaba, photograph by C. Snouck Hurgronje, 1889 (Bilder aus Mekka) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons). No portraits of the poets exist; the Kaaba, on which the odes were said to be hung, stands in for them.
bio: The Mu'allaqat are seven long odes of pre-Islamic Arabia, composed in the sixth century by Imru' al-Qais, Tarafa, Zuhayr, Labid, Antara, Amr ibn Kulthum and al-Harith ibn Hilliza. The name means 'the suspended' or 'the hanged' poems: a later tradition held that they were embroidered in gold and hung on the Kaaba at Mecca. Many scholars doubt that story, but the odes remain the great monuments of classical Arabic poetry, opening with a lament at the abandoned campsite of the beloved and moving on to journeys, horses and camels, hunting, war and tribal pride.

This archive offers them in the English of Sir William Jones, first published in 1782 as The Moallakát and reprinted by W. A. Clouston in 1881. Jones renders the Arabic as prose, numbered verse by verse, rather than as English verse, much as Butler's Homer is prose; the site keeps his numbering, one verse to a line.

poets.name: al-Husain ibn al-Humam
bio: Al-Husain ibn al-Humam al-Murri was a celebrated chief of the house of Sahm, of the tribe of Murrah, a sub-tribe of Dhubyan within the large Ghatafan group of north-central Arabia. In the introduction to his edition of the Mufaddaliyat, Charles Lyall describes him as living in the last age of the Ignorance; Abu 'Ubaidah is cited as saying he lived into Islam, a claim Lyall finds doubtful.

He was known by the title Mani' ad-dhaim, 'the Defender against wrong'. Two of his poems survive in the Mufaddaliyat, both relating to the War of the Huraqah, in which he defended a protected Quda'ite tribe against kinsmen of his own people. They are given here in Lyall's English prose translation of 1918.

poets.name: Ta'abbata Sharran
bio: Thabit ibn Jabir, called Ta'abbata Sharra, was a famous warrior of the tribe of Fahm, which dwelt in the Tihamah between Mecca and the sea. Lyall cannot say exactly when he lived but judges, from the contemporaries named in one of his poems, that he flourished about the time when the Prophet was living at Mecca.

He belonged to the class of warriors called the 'Ravens of the Arabs', born of Abyssinian mothers and Arab fathers, who made their raids on foot; he claims in his verse to be a runner of matchless speed, and he is linked in tradition with ash-Shanfara. His poems are thoroughly pagan in spirit.

poets.name: al-Kalhabah
bio: Hubairah ibn 'Abd-Manaf, called al-Kalhabah, belonged to a subdivision of the tribe of Yarbu' ibn Handhalah, a branch of Tamim, and had settled at Zarud among the men of Malik ibn Handhalah.
Lyall gives the occasion of Ode II: the tribe of Malik was raided by men of Taghlib, and the poet pursued them on his mare 'Aradah, 'the Locust'. Ode III, in the same vein, praises the mare.

poets.name: al-Jumaih
bio: Munqidh ibn at-Tammah, called al-Jumaih, was of the tribe of Asad; Lyall describes him as the son of a contemporary and enemy of Imra' al-Qais, and says that he fell at the battle of Shi'b Jabalah, fought in or about A.D. 570.
Three of his poems are in the Mufaddaliyat: a complaint against a wife set at variance with him by her people, a denunciation of a treacherous killing, and a lament for a chief.

poets.name: Salamah ibn al-Khurshub
bio: Salamah ibn al-Khurshub belonged to the Anmar, a stock celebrated, Lyall says, for producing men of mark. Lyall notes difficulties in the genealogy that connects him with the battle of ar-Raqam and doubts whether the first poem is rightly ascribed to him.
Ode V is addressed to 'Amir ibn at-Tufail; Ode VI, from verse 3 onward, praises his mare.

poets.name: al-Hadirah
bio: Qutbah ibn Mihsan, called al-Hadirah, was of the family of Tha'labah ibn Sa'd, of Dhubyan, a great stock of the Ghatafan group. The nickname means broad, stout and muscular in the shoulders and is said to have been given him by Zabban ibn Sayyar of Fazarah after a quarrel on a hunting trip.
Lyall places him, as Zabban's contemporary, in the latter half of the sixth century A.D.

poets.name: Mutammim ibn Nuwairah
bio: Mutammim ibn Nuwairah was a chief, with his elder brother Malik, of the Yarbu' branch of Tamim. Malik was put to death by Khalid ibn al-Walid after the fight at al-Butah in A.H. 11, and Mutammim lamented him in elegies, among them Ode LXVII; Ode IX is also attributed to Malik himself.
Lyall explains that 'Mutammim' is properly a title from the game of Maisir, designating a man who takes on several portions of a slaughtered camel.

poets.name: Bashamah ibn 'Amr
bio: Bashamah ibn 'Amr ibn Mu'awiyah was of Sahm. Lyall connects Ode CXXII with the situation of the War of the Huraqah described in his introduction to Ode XII.
Two of his poems are in the Mufaddaliyat.

poets.name: al-Musayyab
bio: Zuhair ibn 'Alas, called al-Musayyab, of the tribe of Dubai'ah ibn Rabi'ah, was the maternal uncle of the celebrated Maimun al-A'sha. Lyall judges that he flourished in the last half of the sixth century A.D. and was older than Tarafah.
He seems to have been a travelling composer of panegyrics who lived on the bounty of those he praised; Ode XI eulogizes al-Qa'qa' ibn Ma'bad ibn Zurarah, a chief of Tamim.

poets.name: A Man of 'Abd al-Qais
bio: Ode XIII is anonymous. According to the scholion, its author belonged to the 'Abd al-Qais, on the southern shore of the Persian Gulf, and was a confederate of the Banu Shaiban; another authority attributes the verses to Yazid ibn Sinan.
The fight it describes took place at Dhat ar-Rimth. Lyall says that, if the poem is really by Yazid, it belongs to the age immediately preceding Islam.

poets.name: al-Marrar ibn Munqidh
bio: Al-Marrar ibn Munqidh was a contemporary of Jarir and lived during the first century of Islam, as the Qur'anic quotation in Ode XIV shows. His tribe, the Bal-'Adawiyah, was a branch of Tamim.
Ode XIV is addressed to a woman who reproaches him for not being rich in camels; Lyall observes that Ode XVI is really two separate pieces.

poets.name: Muzarrid
bio: Yazid ibn Dirar, called Muzarrid, was the eldest of three brothers, the others being the more famous ash-Shammakh and Jaz'. All three were mukhadrims, born in paganism and converted to Islam, and lived into the Caliphate of 'Uthman.
Lyall judges that Muzarrid devoted himself chiefly to satire; Ode XVII is attributed by many authorities to his brother Jaz'.

poets.name: 'Abd-Allah ibn Salimah
bio: 'Abd-Allah ibn Salimah belonged to Ghamid, a division of the Azd Shanu'ah in the northern Sarat of the Yaman. Lyall records nothing of his age or history.
The two pieces in the Mufaddaliyat are fragments, only a small part of the poems they once belonged to.

poets.name: ash-Shanfara
bio: Ash-Shanfara of Azd is, in Lyall's words, one of the most interesting figures in ancient Arabia, and is the reputed author of the great Lamiyah. He left his own tribe to live among Fahm, where Ta'abbata Sharra was his companion in raids on foot, and pursued a blood-feud with another branch of the Azd.
Lyall suggests that he probably had African blood, and that he met his death in his attacks on that tribe.

poets.name: al-Mukhabbal
bio: Abu Yazid ar-Rabi' ibn Malik, called al-Mukhabbal, was of the Sa'd ibn Zaid-Manat branch of Tamim, whose lands lay at the head of the Persian Gulf. Lyall records that he lived to a ripe old age and became a Muslim after a long life in the Ignorance, as one of the mukhadrims.
On conversion he settled at al-Basrah, founded about A.D. 637-38. The lady celebrated in his ode, ar-Rabab, was of the same family.

poets.name: Salamah ibn Jandal
bio: Salamah ibn Jandal was of the Sa'd ibn Zaid-Manat branch of Tamim. Ibn Qutaibah calls him one who lived far back in the Ignorance and makes him a contemporary of 'Amr ibn Kulthum.
Lyall notes that, if a poem ascribed to him in the Asma'iyat is genuine, he outlived an-Nu'man Abu Qabus, who died between A.D. 602 and 607.

poets.name: 'Amr ibn al-Ahtam
bio: 'Amr ibn al-Ahtam was a near kinsman of Qais ibn 'Asim, chief of Sa'd, and, while still young, was one of the deputation of Tamim that went to the Prophet at Medina in A.H. 9 and accepted Islam.
Lyall says little is recorded of his later life beyond his fame for beauty; he shared in the tribe's apostasy after the Prophet's death and conformed again after the successes of Khalid ibn al-Walid.

poets.name: Tha'labah ibn Su'air
bio: Lyall says that nothing is known of this poet or his age. He wonders whether he is the Tha'labah ibn Su'air said to have become a Muslim and known Muhammad, though a statement in the scholion makes that impossible.
Only this one ode of his is in the Mufaddaliyat.

poets.name: al-Harith ibn Hillizah
bio: Al-Harith ibn Hillizah, of Yashkur, a branch of Bakr ibn Wa'il, was a contemporary of King 'Amr ibn Hind of al-Hirah (A.D. 554-69). His Mu'allaqa is held in the Mu'allaqat collection on this site and is not repeated here.
Two other pieces by him are in the Mufaddaliyat, Odes XXV and LXII, which are given here in Lyall's translation.

poets.name: 'Abdah ibn at-Tabib
bio: 'Abdah ibn at-Tabib was of the same tribe as Qais ibn 'Asim, the chief of Tamim, and shared his fortunes. He accepted Islam late in life, and Lyall dates his Ode XXVI after Tamim became Muslim, as it celebrates the victory of al-Muthanna over the Persians at Babylon in A.H. 13.
He is remembered only by two odes in the collection and a short elegy on Qais.

poets.name: al-Muthaqqib
bio: 'A'idh ibn Mihsan, called al-Muthaqqib, was of the Lukaiz division of 'Abd al-Qais on the Persian Gulf. His Ode XXVIII shows him to be a contemporary of an-Nu'man Abu Qabus, the last Lakhmite king of al-Hirah.
He was the maternal uncle of al-Mumazzaq.

poets.name: Dhu-l-Isba
bio: Hurthan, called Dhu-l-Isba', belonged to 'Adwan, a brother-tribe of Fahm in the Sarat mountains south-east of Mecca. Lyall describes it as once numerous and powerful, holding the privilege of giving the signal for dispersal at the pilgrimage.
Two of his poems are in the Mufaddaliyat.

poets.name: 'Abd-Yaghuth ibn Waqqas
bio: 'Abd-Yaghuth ibn Waqqas was chief of the Banu-l-Harith ibn Ka'b, of the Madhhij group of the Yaman, whose headquarters was Najran. In the account of the battle of al-Kulab the Second he led the Madhhij confederacy against Tamim.
Lyall dates that period to about A.D. 611-12.

poets.name: Wa'lah ibn al-Harith
bio: Wa'lah ibn al-Harith was of Jarm, a Quda'ite tribe settled in the northern Sarat of the Yaman. Lyall notes that the text calls the author al-Harith ibn Wa'lah, but that the correct name appears to be as given above.
In the battle of al-Kulab the Second he was standard-bearer of the confederacy of Madhhij under 'Abd-Yaghuth.

poets.name: Jubaiha
bio: Yazid ibn 'Ubaid, called Jubaiha or Jabha, was born and died in the reign of the Umayyad Caliphs (A.H. 36-132). He was a Bedouin of Ashja', a division of Ghatafan, who lived all his life in the Hijaz.
Lyall says he was known for graceful verse, though little survives, and that al-Farazdaq met him and admired his work.

poets.name: Shabib ibn al-Barsa
bio: Shabib ibn al-Barsa, a man of Murrah, was born in Islam. Lyall records that his father Yazid ibn Jamrah was chief of the branch of Murrah descended from Ghaidh, and that his mother was called al-Barsa.
Lyall dismisses as apocryphal a story in the Hamasah that the Prophet had sought his mother in marriage.

poets.name: 'Auf ibn al-Ahwas
bio: 'Auf ibn al-Ahwas was the son of the chief of 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah who commanded at Shi'b Jabalah (in or about A.D. 570), and himself one of the captains that day. He was grandfather of 'Alqamah ibn 'Ulathah, the rival of 'Amir ibn at-Tufail.
Lyall describes Ode XXXVI as a collection of fragments, wanting both beginning and end.

poets.name: Rabi'ah ibn Maqrum
bio: Rabi'ah ibn Maqrum, of Dabbah, the tribe of al-Mufaddal himself, was taken prisoner by the Persian King and later became a Muslim, fighting at the battles of Qadisiyah (A.H. 15) and Jalula. Lyall reports that he reached a great age.
The pieces by him in the Mufaddaliyat celebrate his own or his tribe's warlike deeds.

poets.name: Suwaid ibn Abi Kahil
bio: Suwaid ibn Abi Kahil, of Yashkur, a branch of Bakr ibn Wa'il, was a mukhadrim who lived far into the Islamic age. Lyall cites the Aghani for his imprisonment for satire under the governor of al-Kufah, who took office in A.H. 65.
He is said to have celebrated an exploit at the battle of Dhu Qar, fought probably in A.D. 610 or 611.

poets.name: al-Akhnas ibn Shihab
bio: Lyall says nothing is known of al-Akhnas ibn Shihab of Taghlib; he has no article in the Aghani or in Ibn Qutaibah, but his poem is celebrated and also appears in the Hamasah.
From the information in it Lyall dates it perhaps about A.D. 550.

poets.name: Jabir ibn Hunayy
bio: Jabir ibn Hunayy of Taghlib is unknown apart from this poem. Lyall says he belonged to the Christian faith the tribe accepted after its emigration to Babylonia, and was a remote kinsman of al-Akhnas.
The poem must be dated after the first battle of al-Kulab, and probably after the slaying of King 'Amr ibn Hind in A.D. 569.

poets.name: al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur
bio: Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur lived his whole life in the Ignorance, as a contemporary and boon-companion of an-Nu'man Abu Qabus, the last Lakhmite king of al-Hirah. He suffered from weak sight and in old age became quite blind.
Lyall believes that all of his verse that survives is in the Mufaddaliyat and the Aghani.

poets.name: Muraqqish the Elder
bio: Muraqqish the Elder belonged to the family of Sa'd ibn Malik of Qais ibn Tha'labah, of Bakr; he was uncle of Muraqqish the Younger. Lyall notes that the family fought in the War of al-Basus, and that he is chiefly of interest for his age.
Lyall remarks that the native critics speak slightingly of him, but that most of the pieces appear really old, especially Ode LIV.

poets.name: Muraqqish the Younger
bio: Rabi'ah ibn Sufyan, called Muraqqish the Younger, was the nephew of Muraqqish the Elder and paternal uncle of Tarafah. Lyall says he is reckoned a better poet than his uncle and was longer-lived.
Like him he took part in the war of al-Basus and is chiefly celebrated as the hero of a love-story, which Lyall connects with Fatimah, daughter of King al-Mundhir III of al-Hirah.

poets.name: Muhriz ibn al-Muka'bir
bio: Muhriz ibn al-Muka'bir, of Dabbah, celebrates in his ode the victory of his tribe with divisions of Tamim over Madhhij in the second battle of al-Kulab, probably fought in A.D. 611 or 612. He was not present at the battle.
Lyall adds that the poet was then a pagan but may have become a Muslim later in life.

poets.name: Tha'labah ibn 'Amr
bio: Tha'labah ibn 'Amr, also known as the Son of Umm Haznah, is said by Abu 'Ubaidah to have belonged to the 'Abd al-Qais, while al-Asma'i makes him a man of Shaiban settled among them. Lyall could ascertain nothing of his life or date.
He judges the first poem to have the stamp of the pre-Islamic time.

poets.name: 'Amirah ibn Ju'al
bio: 'Amirah ibn Ju'al of Taghlib lived under Islam; Ibn Qutaibah makes him and his brother Ka'b contemporaries of Yazid I (A.D. 680-83).
Lyall reports that he afterwards repented of having satirized his own tribe.

poets.name: Ufnun
bio: Suraim ibn Ma'shar, called Ufnun, of the Hubaib branch of Taghlib, lived before the promulgation of Islam, probably while his tribe was settled in 'Iraq. Lyall thinks he may have been a Christian.
Lyall gives the story that a diviner had warned him he would die at a place called Ilahah, where a snake bit him on a journey to Damascus.

poets.name: A Woman of Hanifah
bio: The author of Ode LXIX is an unnamed poetess of the tribe of Hanifah, who bewails Yazid ibn 'Abdallah ibn 'Amr, chief of the Banu Hanifah.
Lyall says the piece occurs in the small collection of elegies attributed to Ibn al-A'rabi.

poets.name: Bishr ibn 'Amr
bio: Bishr ibn 'Amr belonged to the house of Sa'd ibn Malik of Qais ibn Tha'labah, the family of the two Muraqqishes and of Tarafah, and was a kinsman of Maimun al-A'sha. Lyall says little about him is to be gathered from the usual sources.
The Aghani makes him a contemporary of an-Nu'man Abu Qabus.

poets.name: 'Abd al-Masih ibn 'Asalah
bio: 'Abd al-Masih ibn 'Asalah, whose name shows him to have been a Christian, belonged to the Shaiban branch of Bakr ibn Wa'il, in Mesopotamia. Lyall has no information about his date or history.
Ode LXXII describes a drinking-scene.

poets.name: Abu Qais ibn al-Aslat
bio: Abu Qais ibn al-Aslat was of the Aus-Manat of Yathrib. Lyall introduces him through the Prophet's migration to Yathrib (A.D. 622), which the quarrels between the Aus and the Khazraj helped to bring about.

poets.name: Yazid ibn al-Khadhdhaq
bio: Yazid ibn al-Khadhdhaq belonged to the Shann division of 'Abd al-Qais, on the north-western shore of the Persian Gulf. Lyall notes that Ode LXXVIII is sometimes ascribed to his brother Suwaid.
Both of his pieces defy an-Nu'man Abu Qabus (circa A.D. 582-605), who tried to levy taxation from the tribe.

poets.name: al-Mumazzaq
bio: Sha's ibn Nahar, called al-Mumazzaq, was the sister's son of al-Muthaqqib and, like him, of the Lukaiz division of 'Abd al-Qais. Lyall says very little of his work has survived.
In Ode LXXXI he mentions an-Nu'man Abu Qabus, the last king of al-Hirah.

poets.name: Murrah ibn Hammam
bio: Murrah ibn Hammam was of Dhuhl ibn Shaiban, a branch of Bakr ibn Wa'il long settled in al-'Iraq, near the royal house of al-Hirah. Lyall has no information to fix the date of his short poem.
It concerns a raid on his herd of camels by a man named 'Auf.

poets.name: Maqqas ibn 'Amr
bio: Maqqas ibn 'Amr, whose proper name was Mus-hir, belonged to the 'A'idhah, a branch of the Quraish descended from Khuzaimah, and became an adherent of Shaiban. Lyall calls him a contemporary of the Prophet.
His two odes praise Shaiban and the victory of the Bakrite tribe of 'Ijl at Falj.

poets.name: Rashid ibn Shihab
bio: Rashid ibn Shihab was a chief of Yashkur, a branch of Bakr ibn Wa'il, and is said to have borne the burden of numerous ransoms of prisoners, apparently in the time of King 'Amr ibn Hind.
His two pieces relate to an angry contention between Yashkur and the Shaiban under Qais ibn Mas'ud.

poets.name: al-Harith ibn Dhalim
bio: Al-Harith ibn Dhalim, of Murrah, is described by Lyall as one of the most famous and picturesque personages of old Arabian legend, a man of blood and violence. Raiders of the tribe of 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah had slain his father Dhalim and other members of his house, and the duty of avenging them began his adventures.
Two pieces are ascribed to him in the Mufaddaliyat.

poets.name: al-Khasafi
bio: 'Amir of Muharib, called al-Khasafi, wrote a rejoinder to Ode XC (by al-Husain ibn al-Humam). Lyall says little is heard of the tribe of Muharib, whose lands lay south of Jabal Salma between Tayyi' and Hawazin.
Ode XC is held in the file for al-Husain ibn al-Humam.

poets.name: as-Saffah ibn Bukair
bio: As-Saffah ibn Bukair of Yarbu', of Tamim, composed an elegy on his chief Yahya ibn Shaddad, who died as an adherent of Mus'ab, governor of 'Iraq for 'Abdallah ibn az-Zubair. Lyall dates it precisely to A.H. 72 (A.D. 691).
He calls the piece of much historical interest.

poets.name: Damrah ibn Damrah
bio: Damrah ibn Damrah of Nahshal, of Darim, of Tamim, was originally called Shiqqah or Shiqq, according to Lyall's authorities; the story is that a king of al-Hirah thought the boy puny and miserable.
Lyall gives the retort the boy is said to have made to the king.

poets.name: 'Auf ibn 'Atiyah
bio: 'Auf ibn 'Atiyah was a chief of the tribe of Taim, belonging to the Ribab group. Lyall dates him to the second half of the sixth century A.D. from his leadership of his tribe at the battle of Rahrahan, the year before Shi'b Jabalah.
He was also present at the defeat of 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah at an-Nisar.

poets.name: Bishr ibn Abi Khazim
bio: Bishr ibn Abi Khazim of Asad was, in Lyall's words, the most considerable poet of his tribe during the century before the Prophet. He was a contemporary of Hatim of Tayyi', of an-Nabighah of Dhubyan and of King an-Nu'man Abu Qabus.
Lyall mentions the battle of an-Nisar, about A.D. 575, as a point of time in his career.

poets.name: Sinan ibn Abu Harithah
bio: Sinan ibn Abu Harithah was a chief of the branch of Murrah descended from Ghaidh, of Dhubyan. Lyall notes that he is the man to whom the young prince of al-Hirah, slain by al-Harith ibn Dhalim, was entrusted for education.
Two pieces by him are in the Mufaddaliyat.

poets.name: Zabban ibn Sayyar
bio: Zabban ibn Sayyar of Fazarah, of the Mazin house, is the Zabban who, according to Lyall, nicknamed al-Hadirah. Lyall introduces his odes with the war of Dahis between the tribes of 'Abs and Dhubyan.
Two of his poems are in the Mufaddaliyat, Odes CII and CIII.

poets.name: Mu'awiyah ibn Malik
bio: Mu'awiyah ibn Malik was a son of Malik ibn Ja'far and Umm al-Banin, of the 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah, and brother of at-Tufail and 'Amir Abu Bara. Lyall says he took part in the deputation to King an-Nu'man early in that king's reign.
Two of his pieces are in the Mufaddaliyat.
