poets.name: 'Amir ibn at-Tufail
bio: 'Amir ibn at-Tufail, nephew of Mu'awiyah ibn Malik, was the famous cavalier and contemporary of the Prophet who was chief of the tribe of 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah. Lyall edited his Diwan in 1913.
Ode CVI is No. XI of the Diwan; the second piece is a rejoinder to Salamah ibn al-Khurshub.

poets.name: Khidash
bio: Khidash ibn Zuhair was of the 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah. Lyall says his ode relates to the fourth battle of the second war of the Fijar, at 'Ukadh, in which the Quraish leaders are said to have chained themselves to prevent flight.
He cites the poet's father, Zuhair ibn Rabi'ah, as killed in the course of the same war.

poets.name: Hajib ibn Habib
bio: Hajib ibn Habib was of Asad, though the commentators differ about his exact tribe. Marzuqi makes him grandson of Khalid ibn Nadlah, of the Faq'as division.
Ode CX sets out the merits of his horse Thadiq, which the poet's wife urges him to sell.

poets.name: Subai' ibn al-Khatim
bio: Subai' ibn al-Khatim was of Taim. Only this one ode of his is in the Mufaddaliyat.

poets.name: 'Abd-Allah ibn 'Anamah
bio: 'Abdallah ibn 'Anamah belonged to the same stock as Rabi'ah ibn Maqrum, his contemporary. Lyall says he quarrelled with his tribe and attached himself to the chiefs of Shaiban, to which his mother's family belonged.
He was constant in his devotion to Bistam ibn Qais and wrote a much-admired elegy upon him.

poets.name: 'Abd-Qais ibn Khufaf
bio: 'Abd-Qais ibn Khufaf, of the Barajim of Tamim, was a contemporary of Hatim of Tayyi', who helped him bear a burden of bloodwits that had fallen on him as chief of his tribe.
According to the Aghani he also frequented the court of an-Nu'man Abu Qabus.

poets.name: Aus ibn Ghalfah
bio: Aus ibn Ghalfah, of al-Hujaim, of Tamim, celebrates the victory of Yarbu' over 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah and a Kindite prince in the Day of Dhu Najab, fought about a year after Shi'b Jabalah, circa A.D. 571, by Lyall's reckoning.
Ode CXVIII is his only piece in the collection.

poets.name: 'Alqamah ibn 'Abadah
bio: 'Alqamah ibn 'Abadah, called al-Fahl, belonged to Tamim. Lyall calls his two odes among the most celebrated in ancient Arabic literature and says that the first can be fixed to the year and month in which it was composed.
Beyond these and one other long poem, a legend connects him with Imra' al-Qais.

poets.name: Khurashah ibn 'Amr
bio: Khurashah ibn 'Amr of 'Abs is not mentioned in the ordinary books of reference, and Lyall has no genealogy of him beyond his father's name; the name is also spelt Kharashah.
The title of the poem says it was composed on the Day of Shi'b Jabalah, when 'Abs was allied with 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah.

poets.name: Abu Dhu'aib
bio: Khuwailid ibn Khalid, called Abu Dhu'aib, was the most famous poet of the tribe of Hudhail, whose territory lay in the Hijaz and Tihamah north of Fahm. Lyall calls Ode CXXVI the most celebrated and admired composition of the tribe's poets.
Hudhail had many poets at the end of the Ignorance and in the first age of Islam; Abu Dhu'aib's Diwan survives in good manuscripts.

poets.name: Yang-ti
bio: Yang-ti was emperor of the Sui dynasty from AD 605 to 617. Waley gives one four-line poem of his, on the spring river by moonlight.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Lo Ping-wang
bio: Lo Ping-wang was a poet of the early seventh century, listed in the book among the T'ang poets. His poem here was written in prison, listening to a cicada.
The poem here is Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu's versions in The Jade Mountain (1929), given with the poet's name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Wang Chi
bio: Wang Chi is dated by Waley to about AD 700. His two short poems here are on wine and the contentment of a modest life.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s versions in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Wang Po
bio: Wang Po (AD 648–676) is counted among the four eminent poets of the early T’ang dynasty. He died young, by drowning on a voyage.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Tu Shen-yen
bio: Tu Shen-yen was a T’ang poet who lived between the seventh and eighth centuries; he is generally identified as the grandfather of Tu Fu.
The poem here is Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu’s version in The Jade Mountain (1929), given with the poet’s name as spelled here.

poets.name: St. Germanus of Constantinople
poets.credit: Fresco icon of St Germanos of Constantinople, St Bessarion's Monastery (Tzortzis Phouka, 16th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: J. M. Neale writes that Germanus was born in Constantinople about 634 (his heading prints 631), the son of a patrician, Justinian, whom the Emperor Constantine Pogonatus put to death. Germanus became a clergyman of the Great Church, was Bishop of Cyzicus, and was translated to the throne of Constantinople in 715. When the Emperor Leo the Isaurian moved against Icons his letters of opposition gave the first warning to the Church; he refused to sign the decrees of the synod of 730, was driven from his see and withdrew to his house at Platanias. Neale's heading gives 734 for his death.

Neale says the poetical compositions of Germanus are few: stanzas on S. Simeon Stylites, on the Prophet Elias and on the Decollation of S. John Baptist, and a Canon on the wonder-working image at Edessa. This file gives Neale's 1862 version of the simpler stanzas for a Sunday in the Week of the Great Fast. The portrait is a sixteenth-century fresco icon, not a likeness.

poets.name: St. Andrew of Crete
poets.credit: Fresco icon of St Andrew of Crete, Dionysiou Monastery, Mount Athos (Tzortzis Phouka, 1547) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: According to J. M. Neale's headnote, Andrew was born at Damascus about 660 and embraced the monastic life at Jerusalem, whence he sometimes takes his name. He was sent on church business to Constantinople, where he became a Deacon of the Great Church and Warden of the Orphanage, and under Philippicus Bardanes (711–714) he was raised to the Archbishopric of Crete. He took part in the synod of 712 that condemned the Sixth Oecumenical Council, but later returned to the faith of the Church, and he died on the island of Hierissus, near Mitylene, about 732.

Neale calls the Great Canon, sung right through on the Thursday of Mid-Lent week, his most ambitious composition, and praises his Triodia for Holy Week and his varied Idiomela. This file gives Neale's four versions from Hymns of the Eastern Church (1862), including a portion of the Great Canon, 'Whence shall my tears begin?'. The portrait is a sixteenth-century fresco icon, not a likeness.

poets.name: The Venerable Bede
bio: J. M. Neale attributes the hymn for the Holy Innocents 'Hymnum canentes Martyrum' to the Venerable Bede, and remarks that it compares unfavourably with the Salvete flores Martyrum of Prudentius and that, strangely, no part of it was introduced into any English Breviary. Neale gives no dates for him.

Neale points out that the first and last line of every verse are identical, a device he says Bede seems to have borrowed from the Elegy of Sedulius. This file gives that single version from Mediaeval Hymns and Sequences (1867).

poets.name: Ch’ēn Tzŭ-ang
bio: Ch’ēn Tzŭ-ang (AD 656–698) was famous for impromptu descriptive verse of the kind the Chinese call “Ying.” His passionate disposition brought him into trouble with the magistrate of his district, who had him cast into prison, where he died at the age of forty-two.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918); L. Cranmer-Byng’s version in A Lute of Jade (1909), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Chēng T’ien
bio: Chēng T’ien’s dates are printed as 656–698 in the Chronology of the Poets in Bynner’s The Jade Mountain.
The poems here are Witter Bynner’s versions, from the texts of Kiang Kang-hu, in The Jade Mountain (1929).

poets.name: Ho Chih-chang
bio: Ho Chih-chang, born in AD 659, was a T’ang official and poet, and an early admirer and friend of Li Po. His poem here is a homecoming after long absence.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Shen Ch'uan-ch'i
bio: Shen Ch'uan-ch'i was a T'ang poet who took his degree at the government examinations about AD 680 and died about AD 713. His two poems here concern wives left waiting while their husbands serve on the frontier.
The poems here are Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu's versions in The Jade Mountain (1929), given with the poet's name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Emperor Hsüan-tsung
bio: Emperor Hsüan-tsung (AD 685–761), known as Ming Huang, reigned from 713 to 755.
The poems here are Witter Bynner’s versions, from the texts of Kiang Kang-hu, in The Jade Mountain (1929).

poets.name: Sung Chih-wen
bio: Sung Chih-wen died in AD 710. According to Cranmer-Byng he was the son of a distinguished general who became involved in a palace intrigue, was banished and was finally put to death by order of the Emperor.
The poems here are L. Cranmer-Byng’s version in A Lute of Jade (1909), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: St. Cosmas of Jerusalem (the Melodist)
bio: J. M. Neale ranks Cosmas of Jerusalem second among the Greek ecclesiastical poets. According to his headnote he was left an orphan, was adopted by the father of S. John Damascene, and the two foster-brothers encouraged and polished each other's hymns. He became a monk of S. Sabas, was consecrated Bishop of Maiuma near Gaza against his will, and died about 760 at a good old age; the Eastern Church commemorates him on the 14th of October. John Brownlie likewise dates him to 760.

Neale describes his compositions as tolerably numerous, with a fondness for types and a boldness in applying them, and calls the Canon for Christmas Day perhaps the finest of his canons. This file gives Neale's 1862 versions, including that Canon (Odes I and III to IX, the second ode being omitted as in the Greek use) and a cento from the Transfiguration canon, together with two of Brownlie's 1900 translations.

poets.name: Emperor Tenji
bio: Poet of the Hyakunin Isshu (no. 1); Porter’s note gives the dates as: reigned 668–671.

poets.name: St. John of Damascus
poets.credit: Athonite fresco icon of Saint John of Damascus, Mount Athos (undated) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: St. John of Damascus (John Damascene) is called by J. M. Neale the greatest of the poets of the Eastern Church. Neale's headnote gives his death as c. 780 and records that he was born of a good family at Damascus, served under the Caliph, retired to the monastery of S. Sabas in Palestine, was an eloquent opponent of the Iconoclasts and was ordained priest of the Church of Jerusalem. John Brownlie likewise dates him to 780.

He had a principal share in the Octoechus, the Eastern Church's cycle of weekly hymns. His three great canons are those for Easter, the Ascension and S. Thomas's Sunday, and the Easter canon is known as the 'Golden Canon' or 'Queen of Canons'. This file gives the pieces Neale and Brownlie ascribe to him: Neale's 1862 versions, including the Easter and S. Thomas's Sunday canons joined ode by ode, and Brownlie's 1900 versions of the same Easter canon and two shorter hymns. Neale cautions that the 'Stichera of the Last Kiss' are attributed to John without any great cause. Each poem's translator is recorded.

poets.name: Chang Chiu-ling
bio: Chang Chiu-ling (died AD 740) was a T’ang minister and poet. Giles prints one poem of his, a lover’s moonlit longing.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Empress Jitō
bio: Poet of the Hyakunin Isshu (no. 2); Porter’s note gives the dates as: reigned 690–696.

poets.name: Kakinomoto no Hitomaro
poets.credit: Imagined likeness of Kakinomoto no Hitomaro by Kano Tan'yu, from the Sanjurokkasen-gaku (17th century); no contemporary portrait exists · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Kakinomoto no Hitomaro was a court poet of the late Asuka period and is regarded as the greatest poet of the Man'yoshu, the oldest anthology of Japanese poetry. Little is certain about his life beyond what his poems suggest: he served at the courts of the Empress Jito and the Emperor Mommu, wrote ceremonial laments and praise-poems for members of the imperial house, and is thought to have died in the province of Iwami. He is the first of the later Thirty-Six Immortals of Poetry.

These five poems come from Clara A. Walsh's The Master-Singers of Japan (1910), where he appears as Hitomaro, Kakinomoto no Asomi. They are English verse renderings made for a general audience: Walsh turns the long poems (choka) and their envoys (hanka) into rhymed English stanzas, and her versions are not literal.

poets.name: Yamabe no Akahito
bio: Poet of the Hyakunin Isshu (no. 4); Porter’s note gives the dates as: lived c. 700.

poets.name: Sarumaru no Dayū
bio: Poet of the Hyakunin Isshu (no. 5); Porter’s note gives the dates as: not later than 800.

poets.name: Wang Han
bio: Wang Han is dated by Giles to the 8th century AD. His poem here is a soldier’s drinking song.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: St. Stephen the Sabaite
bio: J. M. Neale's headnote says S. Stephen the Sabaite, so called from the monastery of S. Sabas, was the nephew of S. John Damascene, who placed him in that house at the age of ten. He spent fifty-nine years there and was the earliest of the hymnographers to live to see the final restoration of Icons; the Eastern Church commemorates him on 13 July. Neale's heading gives his years as 725 to 799.

Neale says he left few poetical compositions, the best being those on the Martyrs of the monastery of S. Sabas and on the Circumcision, and that his style seems formed on that of S. Cosmas rather than his uncle's. This file gives Neale's 1862 version of the idiomela for the week of the First Oblique Tone, which begins 'Art thou weary, art thou languid'.

poets.name: Paul the Deacon
poets.credit: Paul the Deacon, miniature in the Laurentian manuscript Plut. 65.35 (Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Paul the Deacon (Paulus Diaconus, c. 720–799) was a Lombard monk and historian, born in Friuli. He was educated at the court of the Lombard kings at Pavia, later entered the monastery of Monte Cassino, and spent several years at Charlemagne's court before returning there; he is best known for his History of the Lombards.

Tradition ascribes to him the hymn to St John the Baptist, Ut queant laxis, and its continuation Antra deserti, which the Roman Breviary used for the Baptist's feast on 24 June. The English given here is Edward Caswall's version from Lyra Catholica (1849).

poets.name: Wang Chih-huan
bio: Wang Chih-huan was a T’ang poet of the eighth century, whose quatrain on Heron Lodge is among the best known of its period.
The poems here are Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu’s versions in The Jade Mountain (1929), given with the poet’s name as spelled here.

poets.name: Meng Hao-jan
poets.credit: Portrait: Unknown authorUnknown author — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Meng Hao-jan (689–740) was the inseparable friend of the poet Wang Wei. He spent the first forty years of his life in study, but having failed to obtain his doctor’s degree he returned to the hills of his native province and gave his remaining years to composition.
The poems here are L. Cranmer-Byng’s versions in A Lute of Jade (1909), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Wang Wan
bio: Wang Wan was a T’ang poet who took his degree in AD 712, according to the chronology of poets in The Jade Mountain.
The poem here is Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu’s version in The Jade Mountain (1929), given with the poet’s name as spelled here.

poets.name: Wang Wei
poets.credit: Portrait: unknown artist — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Wang Wei (AD 699–759) was a T’ang poet, painter and devout Buddhist, famous for quiet poems of landscape and friendship.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Ch’iu Wei
bio: Ch'iu Wei (Qiu Wei) is a poet of the T'ang dynasty, dated by Ayscough and Lowell's Contents to circa A.D. 700.
The archive holds one poem from Fir-Flower Tablets (1921), the account of a climb to a hermit's hut that ends in a missed meeting.

poets.name: Tsu Yung
bio: Tsu Yung is dated by Giles to the 8th century AD. His poem here describes a woodland grotto and its quiet.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Chang Hsü
bio: Chang Hsü lived in the early 8th century AD.
The poems here are Witter Bynner’s versions, from the texts of Kiang Kang-hu, in The Jade Mountain (1929).

poets.name: Kao Shih
bio: Kao Shih (c. AD 700) was, Cranmer-Byng says, one of the most fascinating of all the T’ang poets: first a poor youth, then the lover of an actress, a secretary on a mission to Tibet, a soldier, and finally a poet of renown.
The poems here are L. Cranmer-Byng’s versions in A Lute of Jade (1909), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Wang Ch’ang-ling
bio: Wang Ch’ang-ling (c. AD 750) came from the district of Chiang-ning to the capital, where he took his doctor’s degree. He was eventually disgraced and exiled to Hunan and, according to Cranmer-Byng, was murdered by a censor at the time of An Lu-shan’s rebellion.
The poems here are L. Cranmer-Byng’s versions in A Lute of Jade (1909), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Li Shih-chih
bio: Li Shih-chih, who died in AD 747, was a minister of the T’ang dynasty and a friend of Li Po and Tu Fu. His poem here is on leaving office.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Li Ch'i
bio: Li Ch'i, a T'ang poet, took his degree at the government examinations in AD 725. The poems here are farewells, frontier songs and poems on music.
The poems here are Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu's versions in The Jade Mountain (1929), given with the poet's name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: St. Theodulph of Orleans
poets.dates: dates not given in the source
bio: J. M. Neale's note says the Palm Sunday processional hymn 'Gloria, laus, et honor' is said to have been composed by S. Theodulph at Metz, or at Angers according to others, while he was imprisoned on a false accusation, and sung by him from his dungeon window as the Emperor Louis and his Court went to the Cathedral. The good Bishop was then set free. Neale gives no dates for him.

Neale records that the original had ten stanzas besides the Chorus, that the Roman Missal keeps only the first five, and that he has added the sixth and tenth. This file gives that single translation (1867), made with a friend's help.

poets.name: Li Po
poets.credit: “Li Bai Strolling” by Liang Kai (13th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Li Po (701–762) is the most famous name in Chinese literature. A wanderer and a lover of wine, he was for a time a favourite at the court of the Emperor Ming Huang, but left it for a life as a guest of governors and mandarins, and was later swept up in the rebellion of An Lu-shan and imprisoned. He appears in two of the books drawn on here.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s versions in More Translations from the Chinese (1919); L. Cranmer-Byng’s versions in A Lute of Jade (1909), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Li Han-lin
bio: Li Han-lin is a Chinese poet named in Charles Budd’s Chinese Poems (1912). Budd attributes one T’ang-dynasty poem to him under this name, separately from Li T’ai-po, and gives no note for him.
The poems here are Charles Budd’s versions in Chinese Poems (1912), given under the poet’s name as Budd romanises it.

poets.name: St. Theophanes
bio: J. M. Neale's headnote on S. Theophanes, whom he places third among Greek Church-poets, says he was born in 759, the son of the Governor of the Archipelago. Betrothed in childhood to a lady named Megalis, he persuaded her on their wedding-day to take the monastic life, and he retired to the monastery of Syngriana. Nearly bedridden from his fiftieth year, he was one of the earliest victims of Leo the Armenian over the Icons, was imprisoned for two years and banished to Samothrace, and died there in 818. The dates are Neale's.

Neale says Theophanes is chiefly famous for his History, and that apart from S. Joseph of the Studium he is the most prolific of the Eastern hymnographers, though in his writings hymns begin to be composed to fill gaps in the Office-book rather than from the heart. This file gives Neale's two 1862 versions of his idiomela for Cheese-Sunday (Quinquagesima), one of which is called Adam's Complaint.

poets.name: Theodore of the Studium
bio: J. M. Neale writes that Theodore of the Studium, by his sufferings and his influence, did more for the cause of Icons than perhaps any other man. He was Hegumen of the great abbey of the Studium, was imprisoned for his firmness in the dispute over Constantine's marriage, and under Leo the Armenian was exiled, imprisoned and scourged. According to Neale he died in banishment on 11 November 826.

Neale judges his hymns superior to those of S. Theophanes and nearly equal to the works of S. Cosmas, and praises the fervent penitence and love they show. This file gives Neale's two 1862 pieces: the Canon for Apocreos (the Sunday of the Last Judgment), of which he translated Odes I, III, IV and IX, and the Orthodoxy Sunday hymn, which Neale thinks may have been written by Naucratius, Theodore's favourite disciple.

poets.name: Ts’ui Shu
bio: Ts’ui Shu was a T’ang poet who took his degree in AD 738, according to the chronology of poets in The Jade Mountain.
The poem here is Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu’s version in The Jade Mountain (1929), given with the poet’s name as spelled here.

poets.name: Ts’ui Hao
bio: Ts’ui Hao is dated by Giles to the 8th century AD. His poem here is set at the Yellow Crane Tower, a subject long associated with his name.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Chu Kuang-hsi
bio: Chu Kuang-hsi is a Chinese poet named in Charles Budd’s Chinese Poems (1912). Budd, who spells the name Chu Kwang-hi, describes him as a soldier of the T’ang dynasty who passed the highest literary examinations and was appointed a member of the Censorate by the Emperor Hsuan Tsung.
The poems here are Charles Budd’s versions in Chinese Poems (1912), given under the poet’s name as Budd romanises it.

poets.name: Liu Ch’ang-ch’ing
bio: Liu Ch’ang-ch’ing is dated by Giles to the 8th century AD, in the T’ang dynasty. His poem here is set at a washerwoman’s grave.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Rabanus Maurus (Hrabanus Maurus)
bio: J. M. Neale calls him S. Hrabanus Maurus, Archbishop of Mayence, born in 777 and deceased in 850.

This file gives Neale's 1867 version of his hymn 'Tibi, Christe, Splendor Patris'. Neale says it was so completely altered in the Te Splendor et Virtus Patris of the modern Roman Breviary that scarcely a trace of the original remains, and that it is one of the few hymns without rhyme.

poets.name: Liu Shen-hsu
bio: Liu Shen-hsu was a T'ang poet who flourished about AD 742–755. His poem here is printed in the book with the note that its title is lost.
The poem here is Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu's versions in The Jade Mountain (1929), given with the poet's name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Chi Wu-ch’ien
bio: Chi Wu-ch'ien (also written Ch'i Wu-ch'ien) is a poet of the T'ang dynasty, dated by Ayscough and Lowell's Contents to circa A.D. 733.
The archive holds one poem from Fir-Flower Tablets (1921), a spring evening on the pool of Jo Ya.

poets.name: Niu Hsi-chi
bio: Niu Hsi-chi is a poet of the T'ang period whom Florence Ayscough's Contents dates to circa A.D. 733. That date is the book's own; later scholarship may place him differently.
The archive holds one lyric from Fir-Flower Tablets (1921), a poem of parting written to the tune "The Unripe Hawthorn Berry".

poets.name: Tu Fu
poets.credit: Portrait: Unknown authorUnknown author — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Tu Fu (712–770), whom his countrymen called the God of Verse, was the friend of Li Po and a master of craftsmanship. Cranmer-Byng describes his work as underlain by a continual sadness, and notes his poems of rural life and of the horrors of civil war.
The poems here are L. Cranmer-Byng’s versions in A Lute of Jade (1909), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Huang-fu Jan
bio: Huang-fu Jan (AD 714–767) was a T’ang poet.
The poems here are Witter Bynner’s versions, from the texts of Kiang Kang-hu, in The Jade Mountain (1929).

poets.name: Chang Chi (I)
poets.dates: graduated between AD 742 and 755; lived to AD 780
bio: Chang Chi (I) graduated at the government examinations between AD 742 and 755 and lived to 780.
The poems here are Witter Bynner’s versions, from the texts of Kiang Kang-hu, in The Jade Mountain (1929).

poets.name: St. Methodius I, Patriarch of Constantinople
bio: J. M. Neale's headnote says S. Methodius I was a native of Syracuse who became a monk at Constantinople. Sent as legate from Pope Paschal to Michael the Stammerer, he was imprisoned for nine years for defending Icons, was scourged under the Emperor Theophilus, escaped, and when peace returned to the Church was raised to the throne of Constantinople. He assembled the synod that restored the Icons, which the Greeks celebrate on Orthodoxy Sunday, and died on 4 November 846. Neale's heading gives 836 instead.

Neale says his compositions are very few and are chiefly confined to Idiomela. This file gives Neale's 1862 version of the idiomela for a Sunday of the Fourth Tone, 'Are thy toils and woes increasing?'. He is a different man from Methodius of Olympus, the earlier martyr whose hymn Brownlie translated.

poets.name: Ch’ien Ch’i
bio: Ch’ien Ch’i graduated at the government examinations in AD 751.
The poems here are Witter Bynner’s versions, from the texts of Kiang Kang-hu, in The Jade Mountain (1929).

poets.name: Han Hung
bio: Han Hung graduated at the government examinations in AD 754.
The poems here are Witter Bynner’s versions, from the texts of Kiang Kang-hu, in The Jade Mountain (1929).

poets.name: Chiang Ts’ai-p’in
bio: Chiang Ts'ai-p'in (Jiang Caipin), known as Mei Fei, the "Plum-Blossom" concubine, was a favourite of the T'ang emperor Ming Huang before Yang Kuei-fei supplanted her. The date above is the one Ayscough and Lowell's Contents gives.
The archive holds one poem from Fir-Flower Tablets (1921), the thank-you for a gift of pearls that is traditionally attributed to her.

poets.name: Yang Kuei-fei
bio: Yang Kuei-fei (Yang Guifei, 719-756) was the imperial concubine of the T'ang emperor Ming Huang, remembered as the "White Poplar" beauty of his court. The date above is the one Ayscough and Lowell's Contents gives.
The archive holds one poem from Fir-Flower Tablets (1921), a poem of a dance, set down as four brief pictures.

poets.name: Otomo no Yakamochi
poets.credit: Imagined likeness of Otomo no Yakamochi by Kano Tan'yu, from the Sanjurokkasen-gaku (17th century); no contemporary portrait exists · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Otomo no Yakamochi was a Nara-period nobleman and statesman, a member of the powerful Otomo clan, who served as provincial governor in Etchu and elsewhere and died in 785. He is the most prolific poet of the Man'yoshu, with more than four hundred poems, and is generally credited with its final compilation; the last poem in the anthology, dated 759, is his. He is counted among the Thirty-Six Immortals of Poetry.

The eleven poems here are taken from Clara A. Walsh's The Master-Singers of Japan (1910), where he appears as Yakamochi, Ohotomo no Sukune Yakamochi. They are free English verse renderings of his long poems (choka) and short poems (tanka), with Walsh's own dates and titles; her versions are not literal.

poets.name: Chia Chih
bio: Chia Chih (AD 718–772) was a T’ang official and poet. His poem here is a spring poem of sorrow.

poets.name: Abe no Nakamaro

poets.name: Seng Chiao-jan

poets.name: Chang Wen-chang

poets.name: Li Hua
bio: Li Hua is dated by Cranmer-Byng to about AD 850. He is represented by “An Old Battle-field,” a long poem on a desolate field where the dead of many dynasties are said to be heard at night.
The poems here are L. Cranmer-Byng’s version in A Lute of Jade (1909), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Ts’en Ts’an
bio: Ts’en Ts’an (c. AD 750) was an intimate friend of Tu Fu and, Cranmer-Byng tells us, a censor under the Emperor Su Tsung who rose to be governor of Chia-chou. Most of his surviving verse takes the form of quatrains.
The poems here are L. Cranmer-Byng’s version in A Lute of Jade (1909), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Yüan Chieh
bio: Yüan Chieh was a contemporary of Li Po and flourished about AD 740–770. Waley notes that he had not before been mentioned in any European book, and translates two of his poems.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s versions in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Ch’ang Ch’ien
bio: Ch’ang Ch’ien (c. AD 720) was, according to Cranmer-Byng, a philosopher-poet of the Taoist school who spent his life far from the court, trying to set himself in harmony with the universe.
The poems here are L. Cranmer-Byng’s version in A Lute of Jade (1909), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Ssu-k’ung Shu
bio: Ssu-k’ung Shu is dated by Giles to the 8th century AD. His poem here is a farewell to a friend.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Anonymous (Old High German)
poets.credit: A page of the Hildebrandslied manuscript (Kassel, Universitätsbibliothek, 2° Ms. theol. 54, c. 830s) - a manuscript leaf, not a portrait of any poet. Public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: The Lay of Hildebrand (Hildebrandslied) is the only surviving heroic lay in Old High German, composed in alliterative verse and probably written down in the 830s. It survives in a single manuscript, copied by two scribes at the monastery of Fulda onto the blank outer leaves of a theological codex, and is now kept in Kassel. The text breaks off before the end, and in places shows a mixture of Upper German and Low German forms.

The lay tells how Hildebrand, returning after some thirty years of exile in the service of Theoderic (Dietrich of Bern), meets his grown son Hadubrand between two armies. Hadubrand takes the stranger for a deceiver and refuses the gift of arm-rings offered in peace, so that father and son are driven toward combat; in the surviving text the outcome is not given. The poem is among the oldest witnesses to the Germanic heroic tradition, and the version here is Francis B. Gummere's English rendering of 1909.

poets.name: Keng Wei

poets.name: Liu Chung-yung

The poem here is Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu's versions in The Jade Mountain (1929), given with the poet's name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Li I

The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Chang Chih-ho
bio: Chang Chih-ho (c. AD 750) was a Taoist philosopher who held office under the Emperor Su Tsung. Exiled for some offence, he became a lonely wanderer and called himself the “Old Fisherman of the Mists and Waters.”
The poems here are L. Cranmer-Byng’s version in A Lute of Jade (1909), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: St. Joseph of the Studium
poets.dates: dates not given in the source
bio: J. M. Neale calls S. Joseph of the Studium the most voluminous writer of Greek hymns, with whom the third period of Greek hymnology opens. He was a Sicilian who left his country when the Mahometans occupied it in 830, became a monk at Thessalonica and then at Constantinople, went to Rome during the second Iconoclastic persecution, was captured by pirates and enslaved for some years in Crete, and on his return stood high in favour with Ignatius and then Photius, whom he accompanied into exile. Recalled after Photius's death, he gave himself entirely to hymnology, and the Eastern Church commemorates him on 3 April. Neale gives no dates of birth or death.

Neale judges most of Joseph's saints' canons tedious and bombastic, but calls the Canon for Ascension Day the crowning glory of the poet, in which he must be pronounced superior to S. John Damascene. This file gives Neale's 1862 versions: the complete Ascension canon, with its alphabetical stanzas and the Catavasias, and four shorter pieces, among them 'Stars of the Morning' and 'And wilt Thou pardon, Lord'.

poets.name: Ono no Takamura
bio: Poet of the Hyakunin Isshu (no. 11); Porter’s note gives the dates as: d. 852.

poets.name: Yang Chü-yüan

poets.name: Henjō

poets.name: Meng Chiao
bio: Meng Chiao (Meng Jiao) was a poet of the T'ang dynasty. Ayscough and Lowell's Contents dates him to circa A.D. 790; the editor's reference dates for him are about 751-814.
The archive holds one short poem from Fir-Flower Tablets (1921), a mother's thread sewn into a travelling son's clothes, which the book prints under the air "The Wanderer".

poets.name: Ch’üan Te-yü
bio: Ch’üan Te-yü (AD 759–818) was a T’ang official and poet. His poem here is a brief verse addressed to a bride.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Emperor Yōzei

poets.name: Li Chia-yu

poets.name: Han Yü
poets.credit: Portrait: unknown artist — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)

poets.name: Ts’ui Hu

poets.name: Liu Yü-hsi

poets.name: Theoctistus of the Studium
bio: J. M. Neale's headnote says only that Theoctistus of the Studium is said to have been a friend of S. Joseph, and that he is known to us by the Suppliant Canon to Jesus, found at the end of the Paracletice. His heading gives the year of death as about 890.
This file gives Neale's single piece, a cento formed from that Suppliant Canon, which begins 'Jesu, Name all names above' (Hymns of the Eastern Church, 1862).

poets.name: Metrophanes of Smyrna
bio: According to J. M. Neale, Metrophanes was Bishop of Smyrna toward the close of the ninth century and is principally famous for his Canons in honour of the Blessed Trinity, eight in number, one for each Tone, sung at Matins on Sundays. He was a vigorous supporter of S. Ignatius and a partisan of Rome in her contest with Photius, and Neale's heading gives about 910 as the year of his death.

Neale found it impossible to translate a whole Triadic Canon without wearying the reader, so this file gives his 1862 cento from the Canon for the Sunday of the Second Tone, 'O Unity of Threefold Light'. Neale remarks that his translations need not be carried beyond Metrophanes.

poets.name: Emperor Kōkō

poets.name: Leo VI, the Wise (the Philosopher)
bio: J. M. Neale calls Leo VI the Philosopher a royal poet who reigned from 886 to 917 and left behind the Idiomela, or detached stanzas, on the Resurrection, sung at Lauds; they are better, he says, than might have been expected from an imperial author. His heading gives 917 as the year of death, while John Brownlie's heading for the hymn given here says he died in 911.
This file contains the one poem the sources attribute to him, Brownlie's 1900 translation of a hymn headed 'By the Emperor Leo VI.', which begins 'Come ye people, come adore Him'.

poets.name: Cormac mac Cuilennain
bio: Cormac mac Cuilennain was king and bishop of Cashel, and is traditionally credited with the Psalter of Cashel and with the glossary known as Sanas Cormaic. Sigerson, in Bards of the Gael and Gall (1907), gives his dates as 837–903 and quotes O’Curry’s judgement that he was among the most distinguished scholars of his time; he is generally said to have been killed in battle in 908.

The poem “The Heavenly Pilot”, in which a sailor asks God to steer his frail boat, is taken from the Book of Leinster. Sigerson notes that it anticipates the thought of Tennyson’s “Crossing the Bar”. It is given here in his English version.

poets.credit: Chola-period bronze image of Manikkavacakar (11th-12th century), Linden-Museum Stuttgart, photographed by Daderot · an image of the saint, not a portrait · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Manikka Vasahar (Manikkavacakar) is one of the Tamil Saivite saints whose hymns are sung in the worship of the god Siva. According to the tradition summarised by his translators, he served as prime minister to a Pandyan king at Madura before turning from worldly life to devotion.

His chief work is the Tiruvasagam ("Holy Utterances"); he is also credited with the Tirukkovaiyar. His translators in this 1921 volume write that scholarly opinion was converging on a date in the latter half of the ninth or the first half of the tenth century. The poems here are the selection of the hundred-odd stanzas in the Kingsbury and Phillips volume, grouped under the titles given there.

poets.name: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poets.credit: Imagined portrait by Kahlil Gibran (1917), no contemporary likeness exists · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri (973–1057) was a blind poet, philosopher and sceptic born in Ma'arrat al-Nu'man in northern Syria. Blinded by smallpox in childhood, he studied in Aleppo and Antioch, spent a short period in Baghdad, and returned to his home town, where he lived for decades as a celebrated ascetic and teacher, a vegetarian who called himself a prisoner of three things: blindness, solitude and the body. His verse questions revelation, priestly authority and the claims of every rival creed, and he has often been called the Voltaire or Lucretius of the Arabs.

His two great collections are Saqt al-zand (Sparks of the Tinder) and the Luzum ma la yalzam (The Necessity of What Is Not Necessary), the latter known as the Luzumiyat. The poems here are from Ameen Rihani's 1918 English version, a free rendering in quatrains selected from those books; they follow the sense and spirit of the Arabic rather than its form, which is monorhymed and in a different metre.

poets.name: St. Fulbert of Chartres
poets.dates: dates not given in the source
bio: J. M. Neale says the Paschal hymn 'Chorus novae Jerusalem' is the composition of S. Fulbert of Chartres. It is not common in continental Breviaries but was adopted in the English one, where it occurs at the First Vespers of Low Sunday. Neale gives no dates for him.
This file gives Neale's single version from Mediaeval Hymns and Sequences (1867), 'Ye Choirs of New Jerusalem!'.

poets.name: Mael-Isu of Derry
bio: Mael-Isu (“Servant of Jesus”) of Derry is named in Eleanor Hull's The Poem-Book of the Gael as the author of the Irish hymn “Deus Meus”, and is dated there by his obit, 1038.
The English version of his hymn gathered here is by the Irish poet and physician George Sigerson, printed in Hull's anthology (London, 1913).

poets.name: Godescalcus
poets.dates: dates not given in the source
bio: J. M. Neale describes Godescalcus as the most famous writer, next to S. Notker himself, of the Proses named from Notker, and warns that he is not to be confused with his predestinarian namesake. Neale gives no dates for him.

This file gives Neale's verse translation of the Alleluiatic Sequence 'Cantemus cuncti', which he says was written for the Deposition of Alleluia at Septuagesima and which he first translated for the Hymnal Noted (Mediaeval Hymns and Sequences, 1867). His other two versions of Godescalcus are literal prose and are not included.

poets.name: St. Peter Damian
bio: J. M. Neale describes S. Peter Damiani as Cardinal Bishop of Ostia and the great coadjutor of S. Gregory VII in his reform of the Church. He gives his years as 1002 to 1072 and says he spent the last years of his life at his Abbey of S. Croce d'Avellano after resigning his Cardinalate.

Neale calls 'Gravi me terrore pulsas, vitae dies ultima' the Dies irae of individual life, and notes that 'Crux mundi benedictio' follows the Vexilla Regis and does not seem to have been used publicly by the Church. This file gives Neale's 1867 versions of both.

poets.name: Ou-yang Hsiu
poets.credit: Portrait: unknown artist — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ou-yang Hsiu (1007–1072) was a statesman and man of letters of the Sung dynasty. With the historian Sung Ch’i he prepared a history of the T’ang dynasty, and he held the office of Grand Examiner. His “Autumn” is often held to be among the finest pieces in Chinese literature.
The poems here are L. Cranmer-Byng’s versions in A Lute of Jade (1909), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Wen T’ung
poets.credit: “Bamboo in Monochrome Ink” by Wen Tong (11th century), National Palace Museum, Taipei · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Wen T’ung (1018–1079) was a Chinese poet, calligrapher and painter of the Northern Sung dynasty, best remembered for his ink paintings of bamboo, and a cousin and friend of the poet Su Tung-p’o.
The poems here are L. Cranmer-Byng’s versions in A Feast of Lanterns (1916), given under the poet’s name as spelled there.

poets.name: Solomon ibn Gabirol
bio: Solomon ibn Gabirol (c. 1021 to c. 1058) was a Hebrew poet and philosopher of Muslim Spain, born in Malaga and raised in Zaragoza. He wrote in Hebrew, and also in Arabic, and is counted among the foremost poets of the Spanish Hebrew tradition, both for his devotional verse and for shorter poems of grief, friendship and nature. His philosophical work, the Fountain of Life, was known to Latin scholars as the work of Avicebron.

The poems here come from two English translators. Emma Lazarus rendered ten of his shorter poems in Poems, vol. II (1889), among them Night-Piece, Hymn and A Degenerate Age. Israel Zangwill’s Selected Religious Poems of Solomon ibn Gabirol (1923) gives fifty devotional pieces, ending with the long cosmic hymn The Royal Crown (Keter Malkhut), which appears here as a single poem with its numbered cantos. No portrait of Gabirol survives.

poets.name: Marbodius of Rennes
bio: J. M. Neale calls Marbodus (Marbodius) successively Archdeacon of Angers and Bishop of Rennes, and says he died in 1125. His poem on precious stones, de Gemmis, had a high reputation in its time.

This file gives Neale's 1867 version of the prose 'Cives coelestis patriae', a sequence on the mystical meaning of precious stones. Neale says the ruggedness of his translation merely copies that of the original, which he thinks was meant for a high festival, probably a dedication.

poets.name: Máel Ísu Ua Brolcháin
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Máel Ísu Ua Brolcháin (Maelisu ua Brolchain) was an Irish monk and religious poet of the eleventh century, who died in 1086. His name means "servant (or tonsured one) of Jesus".

Two of his hymns, to the Archangel Michael and to the Holy Spirit, are given here in the English verse of Alfred Perceval Graves in A Celtic Psaltery (1917). Graves's headnote gives 1051 as the year of his death.

poets.name: Beowulf Poet
poets.credit: The Sutton Hoo helmet, c. early 7th century — an Anglo-Saxon warrior’s helmet contemporary with the world Beowulf describes; a symbolic image for this anonymous poet, not a portrait. Public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: The author of Beowulf is unknown — an anonymous Anglo-Saxon poet whose single surviving epic, composed in Old English somewhere between the 8th and early 11th centuries, is the longest and most celebrated poem to survive from that period.

The poem survives in one manuscript, the Nowell Codex (British Library, Cotton Vitellius A.xv), damaged by fire in 1731 and now held by the British Library. It tells of the Geatish hero Beowulf's battles with the monster Grendel, Grendel's mother, and, in old age, a dragon.

This text is the 1910 verse translation by the American philologist Francis Barton Gummere, prepared for the Harvard Classics and long in the public domain; it preserves the original's alliterative, four-stress line.

poets.name: Su Tung-p’o
poets.credit: Portrait of Su Shi (Su Dongpo) attributed to Zhao Mengfu (13th–14th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Su Tung-p’o (Su Shi, 1036–1101) was one of the foremost poets of the Sung dynasty. Waley includes his well-known humorous quatrain written on the birth of a son.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: King Alfred
poets.credit: The Alfred Jewel (Ashmolean Museum, late 9th century), inscribed ‘AELFRED MEC HEHT GEWYRCAN’; photograph by Geni, 2025 · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alfred (849–899) was king of the West Saxons from 871 until his death, and the only English king to be called “the Great.” He is remembered for his defence of Wessex against the Danes and for his programme of learning, in which he sponsored, and by his own account took part in, English translations of Latin works, among them Gregory the Great’s Pastoral Care and Boethius’s Consolation of Philosophy.

The verse attributed to him is the metrical preface and epilogue to the Pastoral Care and the Old English Meters of Boethius, which turn the verse sections of the Consolation into alliterative English. The Proem to the Meters names Alfred as the author, but whether he wrote them, or someone in his circle did, is debated.

poets.name: The Avesta
poets.dates: the Gathas c. 1500–1000 BC (ascribed to Zarathustra); the Yashts later; dates uncertain
bio: The Avesta is the scripture of Zoroastrianism, the collected sacred texts of the ancient Iranian religion, composed in the Avestan language.
The Gathas are its oldest part and are traditionally ascribed to Zarathustra himself; the Yashts are hymns to the yazatas, composed later.

poets.name: Firdausi
poets.credit: The Court of Gayumars, folio from the Shahnameh of Shah Tahmasp (Sultan Muhammad, c. 1522–25); a manuscript painting, not a portrait of the poet · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Abu'l-Qasim Firdausi (also spelled Ferdowsi, Firdusi), born near Tus in Khurasan around 940, was the great epic poet of Persia. He spent some thirty years, until about 1010, composing the Shahnameh, the Book of Kings, a poem of some fifty thousand couplets that follows the legendary and historical kings of Iran from the first king, Kaiumers, to the Arab conquest.

By tradition he dedicated the poem to Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni and felt himself ill rewarded, and the satire attributed to him is one of the best-known stories of Persian literary history, though its details are legendary. He is thought to have died around 1020 in Tus. The English version here is James Atkinson's 1832 abridgement, which renders the most famous episodes in verse and links them with prose summary; it is in this form a free adaptation, not a literal translation. The archive also holds the Warners' complete blank-verse translation (1905-1925), of which volumes I–VIII are given so far.

poets.name: Bilhana
poets.credit: Champavati by a Lotus Pond, miniature from a Chaurapanchasika series, 16th century (artist unknown; Lalbhai Dalpatbhai Museum) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons). No portrait of Bilhana exists.
bio: Bilhana was a Kashmiri Sanskrit poet of the 11th century. His exact dates are unknown; the birth year used to place him in the archive is only a sort key. He is best known as the poet to whom the Chaurapanchasika, "Fifty Stanzas of the Thief", is attributed.

In the tradition that grew up around the poem, the stanzas are the thoughts of a lover awaiting execution who recalls, one after another, his nights with a princess. The poem is read here in E. Powys Mathers's free English version, Black Marigolds (1919).

poets.name: Omar Khayyam
poets.credit: Portrait: The original uploader was Atilin at French Wikipedia. — CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Omar Khayyam (Ghiyath al-Din Abu'l-Fath Umar ibn Ibrahim al-Khayyam, 1048–1131) was a Persian mathematician, astronomer and philosopher born at Nishapur. He is remembered in the sciences for his work on cubic equations and for his part in reforming the Persian calendar, and in the West chiefly for the quatrains (ruba'iyat) attributed to him.

The English version here is E. H. Whinfield's 1883 translation, which he made from several Persian manuscripts and which numbers 500 quatrains. The attribution of many ruba'iyat to Omar is disputed, and scholars have long argued over which are genuinely his; the quatrains turn on wine, the tavern, the brevity of life and the mystical and sceptical questions of fate and faith. For Edward FitzGerald's celebrated freer rendering, already in this archive, see the poet FitzGerald.

poets.name: Moses ibn Ezra
bio: Moses ibn Ezra was a Hebrew poet and critic of Muslim Spain, born in Granada about 1055. He belonged to a distinguished Jewish family, and after the Almoravid conquest of Granada he spent his later life in exile in Christian northern Spain, where he lamented his lost homeland and circle of friends.

He was a master of the Andalusian school of Hebrew verse, writing secular poems of wine, friendship and love as well as penitential hymns for the synagogue. His Book of Tarshish, a collection of wine poems, and his Arabic treatise on poetics are among his best-known works. These versions are by Emma Lazarus, from her 1889 Poems.

poets.name: Liu Tzu-hui
bio: Liu Tzu-hui (1101–1147) was a Chinese poet and scholar of the Sung dynasty. L. Cranmer-Byng gives him two poems in A Feast of Lanterns (1916).
The poems here are L. Cranmer-Byng’s versions in A Feast of Lanterns (1916), given under the poet’s name as spelled there.

poets.name: Judah Halevi
bio: Judah Halevi (c. 1075 to 1141) was a Hebrew poet and philosopher of Muslim and Christian Spain, a physician by profession and a pupil of the Andalusian school of Hebrew verse. He wrote love songs, wedding poems, poems of friendship and a large body of devotional and liturgical verse, and in prose the Kuzari, a defence of Judaism. Late in life he left Spain for the Land of Israel; his poems of Zion and of the sea voyage there are the best known of his work.

The poems here come from two English translators. Emma Lazarus gave seven of them in Poems, vol. II (1889), among them Longing for Jerusalem and To the West Wind. Nina Salaman's Selected Poems of Jehudah Halevi (Jewish Publication Society, 1924) gives eighty, in four groups (the journey to Zion, love and bridal songs, poems of friendship, devotional poems), followed by thirteen of them in rhymed versions, which appear here with the label (rhymed version). Where both translators render the same poem, both versions are kept. No portrait of Halevi survives.

poets.name: St. Bernard of Clairvaux
poets.credit: Juan Correa de Vivar, San Bernardo (Museo del Prado), 16th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Bernard was born near Dijon in 1090, entered Citeaux, became the first Abbot of Clairvaux, and preached the Second Crusade. He died in 1153.
The hymn Jesu dulcis memoria is generally ascribed to him, taken from a long poem on the name of Jesus known as the Joyful Rhythm. It is given here in John Brownlie's English version of 1896.

poets.name: Anonymous (Old French)
poets.credit: Roland at Roncevaux: the Battle of Roncevaux Pass in eight stages, illumination by Simon Marmion from the Grandes Chroniques de France, 15th century (an illustration of the story, not a portrait; the poet is anonymous) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Chanson de Roland, the oldest major work of French literature, was composed in Old French around 1100 by a poet whose identity is unknown. It is a chanson de geste of some 4,000 lines in assonanced laisses, built on the defeat of Charlemagne's rearguard at Roncevaux in 778 and the vengeance that follows.

The earliest and best text survives in the Oxford manuscript, Digby 23, in the Bodleian Library, copied in Anglo-Norman England in the twelfth century. Its last line names a certain Turoldus ("Ci falt la geste que Turoldus declinet"), but whether he was the author, a copyist or a reciter has never been settled, and the poem is credited to no one with certainty.

poets.name: Chrétien de Troyes
poets.credit: Engraving traditionally considered a representation of Chrétien de Troyes in his study (c. 1530; no authentic likeness survives) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Chrétien de Troyes was a French poet who wrote at the courts of Champagne and Flanders in the later twelfth century. Little is known of his life beyond what his own prologues say: he served Countess Marie of Champagne, daughter of Louis VII and Eleanor of Aquitaine, and later Count Philip of Flanders.

He is the earliest known author of Arthurian verse romances in French, and the poems that fixed the matter of Britain for later writers: Erec and Enide, Cligés, Yvain (The Knight with the Lion), Lancelot (The Knight of the Cart), and the unfinished Perceval. He also wrote courtly lyrics and, by his own account, translations from Ovid.

poets.name: Bernard of Cluny
bio: Bernard was a Benedictine monk of the abbey of Cluny who flourished about 1140. He is the author of the long Latin satirical and devotional poem De contemptu mundi, whose opening words are 'Hora novissima'.

The most famous part of the poem, on the glories of heaven, is given here as The Celestial Country in the English verse of John Mason Neale, as printed in C. C. Nott's The Seven Great Hymns of the Mediaeval Church (1902).

poets.name: Nizami Ganjavi
poets.credit: Nizami addressing his son (detail), attributed to Behzad, from a Layla and Majnun manuscript, 1482 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Nizami Ganjavi (Nizami of Ganja, in present-day Azerbaijan) lived from about 1141 to 1209 and is counted among the greatest romantic poets in Persian. He spent his life largely in Ganja and addressed his poems to the local and Seljuk-era rulers of the region, but the details of his biography are sparse and partly legendary.

His fame rests on the Khamsa (the Quintet), five long narrative poems in rhyming couplets: the Makhzan al-Asrar (Treasury of Secrets), Khusraw and Shirin, Layli and Majnun, the Haft Paykar (Seven Portraits) and the Iskandarnama (Book of Alexander). The text here is James Atkinson's English verse translation of Layli and Majnun, published in London in 1836.

poets.name: Farid al-Din Attar
poets.credit: Portrait: Hossein Behzad — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Farid al-Din Attar was a Persian Sufi poet born at Nishapur in Khorasan, who worked as a pharmacist or perfumer (the name Attar means 'druggist'). He is the author of the Mantiq al-Tair (The Conference of the Birds), the Ilahi-nama and a prose biographical collection of Sufi saints, and tradition places his death at about 1221, at the Mongol sack of Nishapur.

He is represented here by Edward FitzGerald's free abridgement of the Mantiq al-Tair, published after FitzGerald's death in 1889 as Bird Parliament, in which the birds of the world seek their king and find him in themselves. It is given as a single long work.

poets.name: Lu Yu
bio: Lu Yu (1125–1209) was a poet of the Sung dynasty. The four short poems here are Waley’s versions of village scenes and a day on the water.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s versions in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poets.name: Jayadeva
bio: Jayadeva was a Sanskrit poet of eastern India, traditionally associated with the court of King Lakshmanasena of Bengal and with the Jagannath temple at Puri in Odisha. His dates are not fixed by any record: he is placed only in the twelfth century, and the birth year used to order him in this archive (1150) is an estimate for sorting, not a biographical fact.

He is remembered for the Gita Govinda, a sequence of twelve cantos (sargas) of songs about the love of Krishna and Radha, in which the pastoral story of their separation, quarrel and reunion is also an image of the soul's longing for the divine. It became one of the most widely sung and imitated texts of devotional Hindu poetry. It is given here in Sir Edwin Arnold's English verse rendering, The Indian Song of Songs (1875), as reprinted in Indian Poetry (Kegan Paul, eighth impression, 1904).

poets.name: Adam of St. Victor
bio: J. M. Neale calls Adam of St. Victor the greatest of mediaeval poets. He says Adam was born in Britannia, whether Great or Little cannot be known, and that the school of the Abbey of S. Victor at Paris produced three of the great men of the twelfth century, Hugh, Adam and Richard. Neale thinks it probable that Adam died in 1192.

Neale notes that Adam's sequences were long thought to number 37 or 38, but that M. Gautier's edition of 1858 gives more than a hundred. This file gives Neale's English versions of ten of them from Mediaeval Hymns and Sequences (3rd ed., 1867), each recorded with its translator and the Latin first line in the note.

poets.name: Marcabru
bio: Marcabru (spelled Marcabrun in Farnell) is among the earliest of the troubadours. The Life Farnell translates says he was a foundling left at a great man's door, brought up by Lord Aldric of Vilar, taught by the troubadour Cercamon, and known as Panperdut before he took the name Marcabrun.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Jaufre Rudel
bio: Jaufre Rudel was lord of Blaye. The Life Farnell translates tells how he loved the Countess of Tripoli without having seen her, took the Cross to reach her, and died in her arms; Farnell calls it one of the most beautiful of the Lives and one of the least authentic.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Bertran de Born
poets.credit: Bertran de Born, miniature from a 13th-century chansonnier (BnF ms. 12473, fol. 160) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Bertran de Born was lord of the castle of Autafort (Hautefort) in Périgord and, in Farnell's words, one of the most remarkable representatives of the second half of the twelfth century. He was drawn into the quarrels of the sons of Henry II of England, mourned the Young King Henry in the poem given first below, and was set by Dante among the sowers of discord in the Inferno.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are approximate, and the Old Occitan originals are not included.

poets.name: Bernart de Ventadorn
bio: Bernart de Ventadorn is described by Farnell as the first great Provençal poet and one of the greatest medieval love-poets in Europe. The Life she translates makes him the son of a servant at the castle of Ventadorn in Limousin, who loved the viscount's wife, then served the Duchess of Normandy and Count Raymond of Toulouse, and ended his days in the monastery of Dalon.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Comtessa de Dia
bio: The Countess of Dia is one of the few women whose songs survive from the troubadour period. The Life Farnell translates calls her the wife of Lord Guillem of Poitiers and says she loved Lord Raembaut of Orange and made many poems of him.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Anonymous (Old Norse)
poets.credit: A page of the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270) — a manuscript page, not a portrait of any poet. Public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: The mythological and heroic lays of the Old Norse tradition are anonymous. They were composed and handed down orally over several centuries, some of them perhaps as early as the 9th century, and were written down only in Iceland in the 13th. Their chief witness is the Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to), an Icelandic manuscript copied around 1270 and rediscovered in the 17th century, which gathers most of the poems now known as the Poetic Edda; a few further lays survive in other manuscripts and in prose sagas.

The lays fall into two groups: poems of the gods, such as the Voluspo, the Hovamol and the Lokasenna, and poems of the heroes, such as the Volund, Helgi and Sigurth cycles and the lays of Guthrun and Atli. They are composed in short alliterative lines, often in speeches and dialogue, with brief prose links (kept in this archive) that supply the story between the verses. The collection is the principal source for Norse mythology and for the legends that later fed the Volsunga saga and the Nibelungenlied.

poets.name: Richard Coeur-de-Lion
bio: Richard I of England, king from 1189 to 1199, appears in Farnell's book among the troubadours as a maker of verse as well as a patron. Her chapter on him gives the lament he is said to have composed while a prisoner in Germany on his return from the Crusade, probably about 1193.
The verse is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896); the prose of her chapter is not reproduced here, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Arnaut de Maruelh
bio: Arnaut de Maruelh (Arnaut of Marvoil in Farnell) came from the diocese of Périgord. The Life she translates calls him a clerk of low degree who took to wandering the world as a singer and loved the Countess of Burlatz, daughter of Count Raymond and wife of the Viscount of Béziers.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Pons de Capduelh
bio: Pons de Capduelh (Pons of Capduoil) sang of Azalais of Mercuer. The poem given here laments the death of a lady named Azalais and is addressed to his friend Andrew.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Der von Kürenberg
poets.credit: Der von Kürenberg, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Der von Kürenberg, the earliest named lyric poet of the German minnesong, was active in the Danube region around the middle of the twelfth century and is known for his short long-line stanzas, among them the celebrated falcon song.
Seven of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Dietmar von Aist
poets.credit: Dietmar von Aist, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Dietmar von Aist, a nobleman from Aist in Upper Austria documented between 1139 and 1171, wrote some of the earliest German love lyrics, notably women’s songs such as the lady and the falcon.
Three of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Friedrich von Hausen
poets.credit: Friedrich von Hausen, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Friedrich von Hausen, a Rhenish nobleman in the service of Frederick Barbarossa, brought Proven00e7al and northern French models into German minnesong and died on the Third Crusade in 1190.
Five of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Heinrich von Veldeke
poets.credit: Heinrich von Veldeke, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Heinrich von Veldeke, from the Maas region near Maastricht, wrote the courtly romance of the Eneit and was one of the first German poets to take up the Romance forms of courtly love song.
Six of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Meinloh von Sevelingen
poets.credit: Meinloh von Sevelingen, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Meinloh von Sevelingen was an early minnesinger of the later twelfth century whose name points to a place in south-west Germany, usually identified with Söflingen near Ulm.
Two of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Burggraf von Rietenburg
poets.credit: Burggraf von Rietenburg, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Burggraf von Rietenburg is one of the earliest named German minnesingers, a nobleman of the Bavarian Danube region in the second half of the twelfth century, of whom only a few strophes survive.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Guiraut de Bornelh
bio: Guiraut de Bornelh (Giraut of Borneil in Farnell) was a troubadour whose gentle love-songs the King of Aragon, in the Life of Bertran de Born that Farnell translates, is said to have paired with Bertran's warlike sirventes. She notes that he travelled with two singers who performed his songs for him.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Peire Vidal
bio: Peire Vidal was a troubadour of Toulouse whom Farnell treats as one of the most colourful figures of the age. The first poem given here is a boastful self-portrait, the second a canzone in praise of love.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Heinrich von Morungen
poets.credit: Heinrich von Morungen, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Heinrich von Morungen, probably from Thuringia and associated with the court of the margraves of Meissen, is regarded as the most imaginative of the minnesingers before Walther von der Vogelweide.
Eight of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Liu Ch’ang
bio: Liu Ch’ang is a Chinese poet whom L. Cranmer-Byng dates to about A.D. 1150. He is not to be confused with the Tang poet Liu Ch’ang-ch’ing, who is a different man.
The poems here are L. Cranmer-Byng’s versions in A Feast of Lanterns (1916), given under the poet’s name as spelled there.

poets.name: Marie de France
poets.credit: Marie de France writing, miniature from BnF Arsenal MS 3142 (late 13th c.) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Marie de France was a poet who lived in the second half of the twelfth century and wrote in Anglo-Norman French, probably in England. Nothing certain is known of her life beyond the name she gives in her own verse: “Marie ai nun, si sui de France.” She is the earliest known woman poet to write in French, and her short narrative poems, called lays, drew on Breton tales of love, loss and enchantment.

The twelve lays given here are those preserved in the London manuscript, British Library Harley 978. They are read in the English prose of Eugene Mason (Everyman’s Library, 1911), which renders her octosyllabic couplets as continuous prose, preceded by her dedicatory prologue.

poets.name: Anonymous (The Lay of Igor's Campaign)
poets.credit: After the Battle of Igor Svyatoslavich with the Polovtsy by Viktor Vasnetsov, 1880 (an historical image; the poet is anonymous) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Lay of Igor's Campaign (Slovo o polku Igoreve) is the great anonymous epic of medieval Rus'. Composed in Old East Slavic probably soon after 1185, it recounts the failed raid of Igor Svyatoslavic, Prince of Novgorod-Seversk, against the nomadic Polovtsy, his defeat and capture, and his escape. Its author is unknown, and he moves between the heroic narrative, the lament of Igor's wife Yaroslavna, and a plea to the quarrelling princes of Rus' to unite.

The poem survives through a single manuscript, discovered in the 1790s and first printed in 1800. That manuscript was burnt in the fire of Moscow in 1812, so the printed edition and a copy made for Catherine the Great are all that remain. Its authenticity was long debated but is now widely accepted. Leonard A. Magnus's 1915 English prose translation, given here, was the first English edition.

poets.name: Folquet de Marseilla
bio: Folquet de Marseilla (Folquet of Marseilles) enjoyed the favour of Richard of England, Raymond V of Toulouse and Barral of Marseilles. Farnell notes that after the war against the Arabs in 1195 the poet gave way to the ecclesiastic, who persecuted the Albigensian heretics and became Bishop of Toulouse.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Raimbaut de Vaqueiras
bio: Raimbaut de Vaqueiras (Raembaut of Vaqueiras in Farnell) was the follower and friend of Boniface, Marquis of Montferrat. Farnell relates that in 1202 he made ready, unwillingly, to join his master on the crusade that ended with the conquest of Constantinople and Boniface's kingdom of Thessalonica.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Peirol
bio: Peirol was, according to the Life Farnell translates, a poor knight of Auvergne. The poem given here is a tenson in which Love and the poet dispute whether he should keep to song or take the Cross.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Guillem de Saint Leidier
bio: Guillem de Saint Leidier was, in the Life Farnell translates, a powerful castellan of Veillac in the diocese of Puy Sainte Marie, a stout knight and a generous giver who paid court to the Marchioness of Polomiac.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Monk of Montaudon
bio: The Monk of Montaudon came from Auvergne, was made a monk of the abbey of Orllac, and was given the priory of Montaudon. Farnell's Life says that he made coblas and sirventes while still in the monastery.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Rudolf von Fenis
poets.credit: Rudolf von Fenis, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Rudolf von Fenis, count of Neuchâtel in what is now Switzerland (d. 1192), wrote minnesongs that follow Proven00e7al and French models closely.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Reinmar von Hagenau
poets.credit: Reinmar von Hagenau, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Reinmar von Hagenau, called Reinmar the Elder, was the leading minnesinger at the Babenberg court in Vienna in the 1190s and a master of the courtly lament.
Eight of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Guillem de Cabestanh
bio: Guillem de Cabestanh was, in the Life Farnell translates, a knight of Roussillon, handsome and renowned in arms, who loved Lady Soremonda, wife of Sir Raymond of Castel-Roussillon.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Ibn al-Arabi
poets.credit: Portrait: Unknown authorUnknown author — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Muhyi al-Din Ibn al-Arabi was born in Murcia in Muslim Spain in 1165 and educated in Seville. He left al-Andalus for the East in 1200, travelled through North Africa, Mecca, Anatolia and Syria, and settled in Damascus, where he died in 1240. He wrote some hundreds of works and is among the most influential thinkers of Sufism, best known for his prose Meccan Revelations (al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya).

The Tarjuman al-Ashwaq (“Interpreter of Desires”), completed in Mecca in 1215, is a sequence of short love lyrics in the manner of the classical Arabic ode. Ibn al-Arabi later wrote a commentary on it himself, explaining the beloved and the desert imagery as mystical. The poems here follow Reynold A. Nicholson’s English version of 1911, with the verses printed as numbered lines in the translation; the commentary is not reproduced.

poets.name: Judah al-Harizi
bio: Judah al-Harizi (Judah ben Solomon al-Harizi, c. 1165-1225) was a Hebrew poet and translator born in Toledo, in Christian Spain. He translated works from Arabic into Hebrew, including Maimonides' Guide of the Perplexed in a version that competed with Ibn Tibbon's, and he travelled widely through the Near East. His best-known original work is the Tahkemoni, a Hebrew collection of rhymed prose narratives (maqamat) in the Arabic manner, which established the form in Hebrew literature.

poets.name: Hartmann von Aue
poets.credit: Hartmann von Aue, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Hartmann von Aue was a Swabian knight and one of the great poets of the Middle High German court epic, ranked with Wolfram von Eschenbach and Gottfried von Strassburg. He introduced the Arthurian romance into German in his Erec and Iwein, adapting Chrétien de Troyes, and also wrote the legends Gregorius and Der arme Heinrich, together with courtly love lyrics. His dates are uncertain: he was active from about 1180 to about 1200 and is thought to have died c. 1210.

Der arme Heinrich (“Poor Henry”) tells of a nobleman struck with leprosy, who can be cured only by the willing death of a maiden. Dante Gabriel Rossetti translated it in verse as a young man in 1846, under the title Henry the Leper; it was not published until his Collected Works of 1886.

poets.name: Spervogel
poets.credit: Spervogel, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Spervogel is the name given to two itinerant poets of the later twelfth century, distinguished by scholars as Spervogel I and Spervogel II, whose short moral and proverbial stanzas are among the oldest German Spruchdichtung.
Eight songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), five marked as Spervogel I and three as Spervogel II as in his book.

poets.name: Wolfram von Eschenbach
poets.credit: Wolfram von Eschenbach in armour, Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848, fol. 149v), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
