bio: Wolfram von Eschenbach was a Bavarian knight and poet who wrote in Middle High German in the early thirteenth century, and is generally ranked with Gottfried von Strassburg and Hartmann von Aue as one of the three great court epic poets of his age. Little is known of his life beyond what he says of himself in his poems: that he was a knight, that he could not read well, and that he worked at the courts of Hermann of Thuringia and others.

His Parzival, completed around 1210 and based on Chrétien de Troyes's Perceval, tells of the education and failures of a young knight who becomes king of the Grail. He also left the unfinished epics Titurel and Willehalm and a handful of dawn-songs. Parzival later provided the ground for Wagner's Parsifal.

poets.name: Bernger von Horheim
poets.credit: Bernger von Horheim, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Bernger von Horheim, a knight of south-west Germany who flourished in the later twelfth century, is best known for a playful “lying song” of exaggerated boasts.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Walther von der Vogelweide
poets.credit: Walther von der Vogelweide, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848, fol. 124r), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Walther von der Vogelweide is the greatest lyric poet of the German Middle Ages. Born around 1170, probably in the Austrian or Tyrolean region, he is thought to have learned his art at the Vienna court of the Babenbergs, where the older poet Reinmar was his master, before leaving to wander from court to court. He died around 1230 and is traditionally said to be buried at Würzburg.

He wrote courtly love-songs, dawn-songs and songs in praise of simple, mutual love ("niedere Minne"), as well as religious verse, crusading songs and a large body of political Sprüche, in which he spoke for the Hohenstaufen emperors and attacked the papacy. These versions come from Frank C. Nicholson's Old German Love Songs (1907).

poets.name: Shota Rustaveli
poets.credit: Fresco portrait of Rustaveli, Monastery of the Holy Cross, Jerusalem (13th c.), photograph · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Shota Rustaveli (c. 1172 – after 1216) is the national poet of Georgia. Little is known of his life beyond what his poem and later tradition say: he served at the court of Queen Tamar, who reigned from 1184 to 1213, and is traditionally held to have spent his last years in the Georgian monastery of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, where a fresco portrait of him survives.

His one surviving work is the epic Vepkhistqaosani, 'The Man in the Panther's Skin', composed around 1200 in some 1,600 quatrains of sixteen-syllable lines. It tells of the knights Avt'handil and Tariel and their love for Tinatin and Nestan-Daredjan, and has been cherished in Georgia ever since. It is given here in the prose translation by Marjory Scott Wardrop (1912).

poets.name: Bligger von Steinach
poets.credit: Bligger von Steinach, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Bligger von Steinach, a nobleman of Neckarsteinach near Heidelberg who died in 1209, was praised by Gottfried von Strassburg, but only a single song survives under his name.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Shinran Shōnin
poets.credit: Portrait of Shinran (Nara National Museum), Kamakura period · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Shinran Shōnin (1173–1263) was a Japanese Buddhist priest, the disciple of Hōnen and the founder of the Jōdo Shinshū, or True Pure Land, school. Because the nembutsu movement was suppressed, he was defrocked and exiled in 1207, and he later lived and taught among ordinary people in eastern Japan before returning to Kyoto.

The poems here are his wasan, hymns in praise of Amida Buddha, the Pure Land and the line of teachers who handed down the faith. They follow the English version by S. Yamabe and L. Adams Beck, published as Buddhist Psalms in the Wisdom of the East series (London: John Murray, 1921), rendered as numbered prose-verse. The translators' own dates are not established, but the book's date is.

poets.name: Albrecht von Johannsdorf
poets.credit: Albrecht von Johannsdorf, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Albrecht von Johannsdorf, a Bavarian ministerial documented between 1185 and 1209, wrote both love songs and crusading songs that weigh service to a lady against service to God.
Three of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Der von Kolmas
poets.credit: No portrait is known; a monogram is shown.
bio: Der von Kolmas is a minnesinger of the later twelfth century known only by the name of his place of origin.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Heinrich von Rugge
poets.credit: Heinrich von Rugge, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Heinrich von Rugge, a Swabian knight of the later twelfth century, wrote love songs and a long religious leich calling on Christians to take the Cross, probably composed in 1190.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Rubin
poets.credit: Rubin, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Rubin was a minnesinger of the generation of Walther von der Vogelweide, known from the few songs preserved under his name in the Codex Manesse.
Two of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Wachsmut von Mühlhausen
poets.credit: Wachsmut von Mühlhausen, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Wachsmut von Mühlhausen was a minnesinger of about 1200 whose songs are preserved in the Codex Manesse.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Murdoch O'Daly (Muredach Albanach)
bio: Murdoch O'Daly, called Murdoch “the Scotchman” (Muredach Albanach) on account of his affection for Scotland, is described in Eleanor Hull's The Poem-Book of the Gael as born in Connaught towards the close of the twelfth century.

The three poems gathered here are religious and monastic verses: a consecration, a prayer to the Trinity and a poem on his shaving as a monk, when he entered the monastic life together with Cathal of the Red Hand, King of Connaught. Their English versions are by Eleanor Hull and by Standish Hayes O'Grady, from Hull's anthology (1913).

poets.name: Carol O'Daly
bio: Carol O'Daly is dated by Eleanor Hull's The Poem-Book of the Gael to the early thirteenth century, and is given there as the author of the love-song “Eileen Aroon”.
The English version gathered here is unsigned in Hull's anthology (London, 1913), so by the book's own rule it is Eleanor Hull's.

poets.name: Hartwig von Raute
poets.credit: Hartwig von Raute, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Hartwig von Raute was a minnesinger of the late twelfth century, known from a small group of songs preserved in the great Heidelberg manuscripts.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Gaucelm Faidit
bio: Gaucelm Faidit was of Uzerche in Limousin. The Life Farnell translates says he sang worse than any man alive yet made many good melodies and canzones, and became a jongleur after losing everything at dice.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Raimon de Miraval
bio: Raimon de Miraval (Raymond of Miraval in Farnell) was, in the Life she translates, a poor knight of the Carcassès who owned a fourth part of the castle of Miraval, and who was loved and prized by Count Raymond for his poetry and his knowledge of courtly love.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Der Markgraf von Hohenburg
poets.credit: Der Markgraf von Hohenburg, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Markgraf von Hohenburg, a Bavarian margrave who flourished around 1200 and is usually identified with Diepold von Hohenburg, is known for a single dawn-song.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Neidhart von Reuenthal
poets.credit: Neidhart von Reuenthal, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Neidhart von Reuenthal, a Bavarian knight who later lived at the Babenberg court in Vienna, created the genre of the village courtship song with its summer and winter songs.
Seven of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Der Truchsess von Sankt Gallen
poets.credit: Der Truchsess von Sankt Gallen, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Der Truchsess von Sankt Gallen is identified with Ulrich von Singenberg, steward to the abbot of St Gallen, a minnesinger of Walther von der Vogelweide’s generation.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Hiltbold von Schwangau
poets.credit: Hiltbold von Schwangau, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Hiltbold von Schwangau, a knight from Schwangau near Füssen in the Allgäu, was a minnesinger of the early thirteenth century whose songs are preserved in the Codex Manesse.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Uc de Saint Circ
bio: Uc de Saint Circ (Hugh of Saint Circ) was of Quercy, the son of a poor vavasour. Farnell's translation of the Life of Bernart de Ventadorn is given in his own voice ("this that I, Hugh of Saint Circ, have written").

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Guiraut de Calanso
poets.dates: fl. first half of the 13th century
bio: Guiraut de Calanso was a Gascon jongleur whom the Life Farnell translates calls learned and subtle in the making of poetry, though little liked in Provence.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Guillem Figueira
poets.dates: fl. first half of the 13th century
bio: Guillem Figueira was of Toulouse, the son of a tailor and himself a tailor. After the French took Toulouse he settled in Lombardy, and the sirvente of his given here is directed against Rome.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Peire de Barjac
bio: Peire de Barjac was a knight, the companion of Guillem de Balaun. The Life Farnell translates tells of his love for the wife of a vavasour of the castle of Javiac.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Gillabride Mac Conmide
bio: Gillabride Mac Conmide (Gilla Brighde Mac Conmidhe) was a bard of Ulster, known also as Albanach because of his visits to Scotland. Sigerson, in Bards of the Gael and Gall (1907), dates his two poems here to 1230 and 1260, and calls him Chief Bard of Ulster and friend of Brian O’Neill, who was killed at the battle of Down in 1260.

“The Harp that Ransomed” concerns the harp of the O’Briens, which he was sent to recover and could not; “The Exiled Head” laments the head of Brian O’Neill, sent to the English king. Both are given in Sigerson’s English versions.

poets.name: Burkhard von Hohenfels
poets.credit: Burkhard von Hohenfels, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Burkhard von Hohenfels, a Swabian nobleman from the Lake Constance region, wrote songs in the manner of Neidhart and Gottfried von Neifen.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Narayana (Hitopadesa)
poets.credit: No portrait exists for Narayana; a monogram tile is shown.
bio: Narayana is the name given as the author or compiler of the Hitopadesa, the Sanskrit "Book of Good Counsel", a collection of animal fables and maxims in prose and verse, drawn in large part from the older Panchatantra. Nothing secure is known of his life, and the date of the work is uncertain.
The verses printed here are the proverbs of the Hitopadesa as selected and rendered by Sir Edwin Arnold, who first published them in 1861 as the Book of Good Counsels.

poets.name: Ulrich von Lichtenstein
poets.credit: Ulrich von Lichtenstein, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ulrich von Lichtenstein, a Styrian knight, wrote the autobiographical Frauendienst (1255), in which he tells of his service to a lady in tournaments and in song.
Three of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Burggraf von Lüenz
poets.credit: Burggraf von Lüenz, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Burggraf von Lüenz, a burgrave of Lienz in the Tyrol, was a minnesinger of the thirteenth century whose songs are preserved in the Codex Manesse.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Reinmar von Zweter
poets.credit: Reinmar von Zweter, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Reinmar von Zweter, a Rhinelander who worked at Vienna and at the Bohemian court of King Wenzel I, was a leading Spruchdichter of the thirteenth century.
Ten of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Aimeric de Peguilhan
bio: Aimeric de Peguilhan was of Toulouse, the son of a burgher and cloth merchant. The Life Farnell translates says that he sang ill but that love of a neighbour's wife taught him to make poetry.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Gottfried von Neifen
poets.credit: Gottfried von Neifen, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Gottfried von Neifen, a Swabian nobleman, was one of the most prolific minnesingers of the thirteenth century, known for polished dance songs and summer lyrics.
Two of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Ulrich von Winterstetten
poets.credit: Ulrich von Winterstetten, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ulrich von Winterstetten, a Swabian nobleman at the Hohenstaufen court, wrote songs and long leiche in the courtly tradition of the thirteenth century.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Peire Cardenal
bio: Peire Cardenal was of Velay, of the city of Puy Notre Dame, and was sent as a boy to the canonry there. Farnell compares the audacity of his attacks on the Church with those of Walther von der Vogelweide.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Der Marner
poets.credit: Der Marner, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Der Marner was a travelling Swabian poet of the mid-thirteenth century who wrote in Latin and German and composed love songs, riddles and didactic verse.
Two of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Anonymous (Russian Byliny)
poets.credit: Not a portrait of a poet (the byliny are anonymous): Viktor Vasnetsov, Bogatyrs (1898), showing the heroes Ilya of Murom, Dobrynya Nikitich and Alyosha Popovich · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The byliny are the heroic oral songs of Russia, chanted by unlettered peasant singers, above all in the far north, long after the age of princes they recall. They tell of the bogatyrs, the champions of Holy Russia, and gather in cycles. The Kiev cycle surrounds Prince Vladimir the Fair Sun and his court at Kiev, with Ilya of Murom, Dobrynya Nikitich and Alyosha Popovich as its chief heroes, against steppe raiders, dragons and the Nightingale the Robber. The Novgorod cycle belongs to a merchant republic and sings of the gusli-player Sadko and the unruly Vasily Buslaevich. Older, half-mythical figures such as Svyatogor and Volga Vseslavich stand behind both.

The songs were first gathered in writing in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, from the Kirsha Danilov collection onward, and reached English readers through Isabel Florence Hapgood, whose The Epic Songs of Russia (New York: Scribner, 1886; with an introductory note by Francis James Child) is read here in full as a prose rendering. Her introduction, notes, appendix and connecting commentary are left out; only the songs themselves come in.

poets.name: Graf von Leiningen
poets.credit: Graf von Leiningen, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Graf von Leiningen, a count of the Palatinate house of Leiningen, was a minnesinger of the thirteenth century whose songs are preserved in the Codex Manesse.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Christian von Hamle
poets.credit: No portrait is known; a monogram is shown.
bio: Christian von Hamle was a thirteenth-century minnesinger known from the songs preserved under his name in the Codex Manesse, of whom little else is recorded.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Walther von Metz
poets.credit: No portrait is known; a monogram is shown.
bio: Walther von Metz was a thirteenth-century minnesinger known from songs preserved in the Codex Manesse and from a mention in a poem by Reinmar von Brennenberg.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Der Hardegger
poets.credit: Der Hardegger, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Der Hardegger was a minnesinger of the mid-thirteenth century known from the songs preserved under his name in the Codex Manesse.
Two of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Tannhäuser
poets.credit: Tannhäuser, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Tannhäuser was a wandering minnesinger of the mid-thirteenth century, at the court of Duke Frederick II of Austria, about whom later legend made him the knight of the Venusberg.
Three of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Reinmar von Brennenberg
poets.credit: Reinmar von Brennenberg, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Reinmar von Brennenberg, a Bavarian knight of the Regensburg region, was killed in 1276 and left songs that include a lament for the poets who had died before him.
Two of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Der von Wildonie
poets.credit: Der von Wildonie, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Herrand von Wildonie, a Styrian nobleman, wrote minnesongs and short verse tales in the second half of the thirteenth century.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Der Wilde Alexander
poets.credit: Der Wilde Alexander, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Der Wilde Alexander was a wandering poet of the later thirteenth century, known for songs and moral verse preserved in the Codex Manesse.
Two of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Sordello
bio: Sordello was of Mantua, the son of a poor knight. The Life Farnell translates says he delighted in the learning of canzones and made coblas and sirventes before coming to the court of the Count of Saint Boniface.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Der von Suneck
poets.credit: No portrait is known; a monogram is shown.
bio: Der von Suneck is a thirteenth-century minnesinger known from the songs preserved under his name in the Codex Manesse.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Albrecht von Rapperswil
poets.credit: Albrecht von Rapperswil, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Albrecht von Rapperswil was a Swiss minnesinger of the later thirteenth century whose songs are preserved in the Codex Manesse.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Boppe
poets.credit: Boppe, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Boppe was a late thirteenth-century wandering Spruchdichter praised by the later Meistersinger for his long, elaborate stanzas.
Two of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Steinmar
poets.credit: Steinmar, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Berthold Steinmar von Klingnau, a Swiss nobleman, wrote harvest and drinking songs in the late thirteenth century.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: König Konrad der Junge
poets.credit: No portrait is known; a monogram is shown.
bio: Konrad der Junge, known as Conradin, was the last Hohenstaufen king and was executed at Naples in 1268 at the age of sixteen; songs are ascribed to him in the Codex Manesse.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Herzog Johann von Brabant
poets.credit: Herzog Johann von Brabant, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John I, duke of Brabant and victor of the battle of Worringen in 1288, was a prince who also wrote songs, preserved in the Codex Manesse.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Heinrich von Breslau
poets.credit: Heinrich von Breslau, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Heinrich IV Probus, duke of Silesia and lord of Breslau, was a patron of German poets, and songs are ascribed to him in the Codex Manesse.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Frauenlob
poets.credit: Frauenlob, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Heinrich von Meissen, called Frauenlob (“praise of women”), was a wandering Spruchdichter famed for his Marian hymns and elaborate song who died at Mainz in 1318.
Two of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Der Guter
poets.credit: No portrait is known; a monogram is shown.
bio: Der Guter was a late thirteenth-century poet whose verse on the vanity of the world draws on the legend of the knight and Dame World.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Regenbogen
poets.credit: Regenbogen, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Regenbogen was an itinerant Spruchdichter of the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries, remembered as a rival of Frauenlob and revered by the later Meistersinger.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Christian von Luppin
poets.credit: Christian von Luppin, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Christian von Luppin was a minnesinger of about 1300 whose songs are preserved in the Codex Manesse.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: König Wenzel von Böhmen
poets.credit: König Wenzel von Böhmen, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: King Wenceslas II of Bohemia, a patron of German poets, is credited in the Codex Manesse with a small group of songs.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Bertolome Zorzi
bio: Bertolome Zorzi was a gentleman of Venice who, in the Life Farnell translates, was taken captive by the Genoese, who were at war with the Venetians.

The verse in this selection is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896), where it stands beside a prose Life of the poet; the prose Life is not reproduced here. The dates are those Farnell prints for the period in which the poet was active, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poets.name: Anonymous (Poem of the Cid)
poets.credit: The Tizona, the sword traditionally (though not verifiably) attributed to El Cid, now displayed at the Museum of Burgos — a symbolic image for this anonymous tradition, not a portrait. Public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: The medieval Spanish accounts of Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, "El Cid" (c. 1043–1099), the Castilian warlord who became Spain’s national hero, were composed and compiled by unknown authors in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. The great narrative poem on his exploits, the Cantar de Mio Cid, survives in a single incomplete manuscript and is itself anonymous.

This archive presents Robert Southey’s 1808 "Chronicle of the Cid," an English translation and compilation drawn chiefly from the medieval Crónica General de España together with other early chronicle and ballad material about the Cid — the fullest and best-known public-domain English account of the legend, though it is a prose chronicle rather than a verse rendering of the Cantar itself.

poets.name: Hadlaub
poets.credit: Hadlaub, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Johannes Hadlaub, a citizen of Zurich, was a minnesinger of the early fourteenth century associated with the circle that gathered the Codex Manesse.
Two of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Anonymous (Middle High German)
poets.credit: First page of the Nibelungenlied, Manuscript C (Donaueschingen, 13th century) - a manuscript leaf, not a portrait of any poet. Public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: The Nibelungenlied, the great Middle High German heroic epic, is anonymous. It was composed in the Danube region, probably in Austria, around 1200, and survives in several dozen manuscripts and fragments, of which the chief are Manuscripts A, B and C, copied in the 13th century. Its author drew on older Germanic legends of Siegfried and of the fall of the Burgundians, and set them in the courtly world of the Hohenstaufen age.

The poem is written in four-line stanzas of long lines, each divided by a mid-line pause (the caesura), and tells in thirty-nine "adventures" how Siegfried wins Kriemhild, is murdered through Hagen's treachery, and how Kriemhild, now married to Etzel, king of the Huns, brings about the destruction of the Burgundians. It is the national epic of the German-speaking world and a source for Wagner's Ring cycle.

poets.name: Jalal al-Din Rumi
poets.credit: Meeting of Rumi and Shams al-Din, folio from the Jami al-Siyar (Topkapi Palace Museum, H 1230), late 16th or early 17th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Jalal al-Din Rumi (1207–1273) was a Persian Sufi poet, born at Balkh, who settled at Konya in Anatolia, where he taught and wrote for the rest of his life. After he met the wandering dervish Shams of Tabriz, his devotion poured out in lyric odes (ghazals) addressed to his master and, through him, to God, and the collection is named the Divan of Shams of Tabriz.

The English versions here are R. A. Nicholson’s translations of forty-eight odes from the Divan, published at Cambridge in 1898. Nicholson printed the Persian beside his English; only the English is given here.

poets.name: Dafydd Benfras
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Dafydd Benfras was a court poet of the Welsh princes of Gwynedd, who flourished, according to the Dictionary of Welsh Biography, between about 1230 and 1260. He wrote praise poems for Llywelyn ap Iorwerth and Llywelyn ap Gruffydd and elegies for sons of Llywelyn the Great.
The poem here is George Borrow's English version, from his Quarterly Review article on Welsh poetry, printed in Welsh Poems and Ballads (1915).

poets.name: Hsieh Fang-te
bio: Hsieh Fang-te (AD 1226–1289) was a Sung loyalist who refused to serve the Mongol court.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Yeh Li
bio: Yeh Li is dated by Giles to the 13th century AD. His poem here is a scholar’s spring among his books.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Yüan I-shan
bio: Yüan I-shan is a Chinese poet named in Charles Budd’s Chinese Poems (1912). Budd, who spells the name Yuen I-shan, gives no dates or note for him.
The poems here are Charles Budd’s versions in Chinese Poems (1912), given under the poet’s name as Budd romanises it.

poets.name: Guido Cavalcanti
poets.credit: Imagined likeness, engraving from Rime (1813), no contemporary portrait exists · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Guido Cavalcanti (c. 1255–1300) was a Florentine poet and philosopher, the leading figure after Guinizzelli of the dolce stil novo, the 'sweet new style' of love poetry. Born into a wealthy Guelf family, he was drawn into the strife between the Black and White factions of Florence and was banished in 1300, spending his exile at Sarzana, where he fell ill; he returned to the city and died that same year. Dante called him his 'first friend' and dedicated the Vita Nuova to him.

His surviving verse, about fifty pieces, treats love as a dark, near-fatal force acting on the soul and its spirits, and is among the most intense of its age. The texts given here are Dante Gabriel Rossetti's English versions in The Early Italian Poets (1861), the translator's own selection of twenty-nine poems, which follow the Italian forms (sonnet, ballata and canzone) and rhyme patterns. Poems that Rossetti prints as the replies of other poets, and Dante's sonnets to Guido, are not included.

poets.name: Heinrich von Mügeln
poets.credit: No portrait is known; a monogram is shown.
bio: Heinrich von Mügeln, a poet from the Meissen region who worked at the court of the Emperor Charles IV, was one of the last writers in the minnesong tradition.
One of his songs appears here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poets.name: Yunus Emre
bio: Yunus Emre is the first recorded native poet of the Western Turks: a mystic who wrote in Anatolian Turkish rather than in the Persian forms that Ottoman court poets later preferred. Ottoman biographers describe him as nearly unlettered, a disciple of the holy man Tapduk Emre, whose verse was held to be a direct gift of God.

Only a little is known of his life, and the early sources disagree. E. J. W. Gibb, whose History of Ottoman Poetry (1900) gives the first English account of him, notes that one of his own poems dates his devotion to the Path to the year 707 AH (1307–8), which places him about a century before the dates given by later biographers.

poets.name: Thomas of Celano
poets.credit: Tommaso da Celano, illustration, Wikimedia Commons · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas of Celano was an Italian Franciscan friar, best known as the first biographer of St. Francis of Assisi. He is traditionally held to be the author of the Latin sequence Dies irae.

Seven English versions of the Dies irae are given here, as collected in C. C. Nott's The Seven Great Hymns of the Mediaeval Church (1902), by Abraham Coles, Richard Crashaw, John Adams Dix, William Josiah Irons, Franklin Johnson, the Earl of Roscommon and Edward Slosson.

poets.name: The Goliards (Wandering Scholars)
poets.credit: The Wheel of Fortune, from the Codex Buranus (Carmina Burana manuscript, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Clm 4660), c. 1230 · A manuscript image, not a portrait · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The goliards were the wandering clerks and students of twelfth- and thirteenth-century Europe, men trained in the schools and cathedral chapters who lived by their wits, drifting between universities and patrons. They wrote in Medieval Latin, in rhymed and accentual stanzas, on spring, love, wine, dice, poverty and the hypocrisy of the Church. Their verse is almost entirely anonymous, and is preserved chiefly in manuscripts of the period.

The largest surviving collection is the Carmina Burana, copied in the early thirteenth century at a Bavarian monastery and now in Munich. Among the best known goliardic poems is the 'Confession of Golias', long attributed to the Archpoet. The translations here are by John Addington Symonds, from his Wine, Women, and Song (1884), where they are set within his essay on the student songs.

poets.name: St. Thomas Aquinas
poets.dates: dates not given in the source
bio: In Mediaeval Hymns and Sequences J. M. Neale calls Thomas Aquinas the Angelic Doctor and attributes to him the Eucharistic hymn 'Adoro Te devote', which he says was never in public use in the mediaeval Church but was appended to most Missals as a private devotion. Neale gives no dates for him.
This file gives Neale's two versions (1867): 'Humbly I adore Thee, hidden Deity' and 'Of the glorious Body telling', his rendering of the Corpus Christi hymn 'Pange lingua gloriosi'.

poets.name: Jacopone da Todi
bio: Jacopone da Todi was an Italian Franciscan friar and poet who died in 1306. The Stabat Mater, the hymn on the sorrows of Mary at the Cross, is traditionally ascribed to him, as is the companion Christmas hymn Mater speciosa.
Three versions of the Stabat Mater and one of the Mater speciosa are given here, from C. C. Nott's The Seven Great Hymns of the Mediaeval Church (1902).

poets.name: Anonymous (Danish ballads)
bio: The Danish ballads (folkeviser) are anonymous songs of the Middle Ages, sung to a dance with a leader and a chorus that answers with a burden or refrain. They were composed over several centuries, from about the 13th, and were written down chiefly in the 16th century in the manuscript song-books of Danish noble families, which preserve them in great numbers.

This selection of twenty-nine is taken from Danish Ballads, translated by E. M. Smith-Dampier (Cambridge University Press, 1920); thirteen more ballads are in George Borrow's versions from Romantic Ballads (1826). It runs from the historical ballads on Valdemar, Queen Dagmar and the murder of King Erik Klipping, through legendary ballads of heroes and of magic with mermen and elves, to miscellaneous ballads of love and chance. The translator's introduction, head-notes and end-notes are not reproduced; the stanza numbers of the printed edition are omitted.

poets.name: Anonymous Latin Hymns
bio: Hymns of the Latin Church whose authorship is unknown, doubtful or disputed: breviary hymns, sequences and anonymous compositions of the early and later Middle Ages, together with a few whose authors are named in the source but are not otherwise represented in this archive.

They are given mainly in three English versions: the Breviary and Missal hymns of Edward Caswall's Lyra Catholica (1849), John Mason Neale's translations (1867), and John Brownlie's Hymns of the Early Church (1896), whose source notes on authorship are reproduced in the poem notes. Catherine Winkworth's version of the Veni Sancte Spiritus, from C. C. Nott's The Seven Great Hymns of the Mediaeval Church (1902), is also included. Each poem's note gives the Latin first line and its place in the source.

poets.name: Dante Alighieri
poets.credit: Portrait of Dante by Sandro Botticelli, c. 1495 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Dante Alighieri was born in Florence in 1265 and became one of the city's political figures as well as its greatest poet. His early lyrics and the prose-and-verse Vita Nuova (c. 1294) celebrate Beatrice, the woman he loved from afar and who later became his guide in the Paradiso.

In 1302, on the losing side of Florence's factional struggles, he was sentenced to exile and never returned. During those years he wrote the Divine Comedy, a vision in rhymed tercets of the soul's journey through Hell, Purgatory and Heaven, composed in the Tuscan vernacular rather than Latin. He died in Ravenna in 1321, soon after finishing it.

poets.name: Namdev
poets.credit: Oleograph of Namdev by Laxman Pralhad Mule, Pandharpur (c. 1920) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Namdev (Nama) is one of the earliest and most widely loved saint-poets of Maharashtra, whom Macnicol places in the 14th century. A devotee of Vithoba (Vitthal) of Pandharpur, he is often counted among the circle of Jnanesvar, and his Marathi songs (abhangs) are sung to this day by pilgrims on the road to Pandharpur.
The twelve hymns here are drawn from Macnicol's Psalms of Maratha Saints (1919), which cites Avate's edition of the poet for most of them.

poets.name: Jnanesvar
bio: Jnanesvar (also Jnanadev or Dnyaneshwar) is the earliest of the great Marathi saint-poets, placed by Macnicol in the 13th century. He is remembered as the author of the Jnanesvari, a Marathi commentary in verse on the Bhagavad Gita, and as one of the founding voices of the devotional (bhakti) tradition centred on Vithoba of Pandharpur.

The eight hymns here are rendered by Nicol Macnicol in Psalms of Maratha Saints (1919); the first four are taken from the Jnanesvari itself, and the remainder are short devotional songs (abhangs) in praise of the divine Name.

poets.name: Mukta Bai
bio: Mukta Bai (Muktabai) is a Marathi woman saint-poet of the 13th century, traditionally the younger sister of Jnanesvar and a member of the same circle of Maharashtrian devotional (bhakti) poets.
Macnicol's Psalms of Maratha Saints (1919) gives two of her short songs (abhangs): a riddling poem of the topsy-turvy world of the enlightened soul, and a plea to her brother to open the door.

poets.name: 'Ashiq Pasha
bio: Gibb calls 'Ashiq Pasha the earliest writer of the Ottomans, who flourished in the reign of Orkhan and lived in the town of Qir-Shehr in Anatolia; his title Pasha is a spiritual one, as he was a chief among mystics rather than a leader of warriors.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Sa'di of Shiraz
poets.credit: Sa'di in a Rose Garden, attributed to Govardhan (Mughal, repainted c. 1645) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sa'di (Muslih al-Din Sa'di) was born in Shiraz, in southern Persia, around 1210, and was educated at the Nizamiyya college in Baghdad. By his own account he spent some thirty years travelling, through Syria, Anatolia, Egypt, Arabia and beyond, working as a preacher and wayfarer before he went back to Shiraz, where he lived on in retirement and died in 1291. Anecdotes of his captivity, his poverty and his encounters on the road are scattered through his writings, though the traditional life is hard to separate from the stories he tells.

He wrote the Bustan (The Orchard, or Garden of Fruit) in 1257 and the Gulistan (The Rose Garden) in 1258, both dedicated to the ruler of Fars, the atabak Abu Bakr ibn Sa'd. The Bustan is a verse masnavi in ten chapters of moral stories; the Gulistan is chiefly prose with verses. Neither of the English books here is the Gulistan. The poems are the twenty-four pieces of Arthur N. Wollaston's Sadi's Scroll of Wisdom (1906), in rhymed verse; the work is A. Hart Edwards's Bustan (1911), which renders the original in English prose.

poets.name: Anonymous (Irish Gaelic, later)
bio: The Irish-language poems gathered here are anonymous songs, laments, prayers, charms, lullabies and working songs, most of them known from oral tradition and from later manuscripts, and placed by Eleanor Hull after the early Christian poems in her anthology, The Poem-Book of the Gael (London, 1913). They include the laments of the dark days, the religious verse of the people, and the love-songs of the west.

The English versions are by many hands, among them Douglas Hyde, Sir Samuel Ferguson, George Sigerson, Robin Flower, P. H. Pearse, Thomas MacDonagh, Padraic Colum, Lady Wilde and Lady Gregory; each poem records its own translator, and poems the book leaves unsigned are by Hull herself. Most of the poems are undated in the book, so the dates given for the group are approximate.

poets.name: Anonymous (Middle English)
poets.credit: No portrait: these are the voices of unnamed singers and scribes, and no author’s name survives for any of them. They are known from manuscripts such as British Library Harley 978 (the ‘Cuckoo Song’), Harley 2253 (the Harley Lyrics) and Sloane 2593 (carols and songs).
bio: Most of the short poems that survive from medieval England carry no author’s name. They are songs, hymns, carols, ballads and charms, copied by clerks, friars and minstrels onto the spare leaves of larger books, and they reach us through a handful of manuscripts: the Reading Abbey volume that preserves ‘Sumer is icumen in’, the Harley miscellany (MS Harley 2253) with its love-songs and spring-songs, the song-book Sloane 2593 with its carols, and the Balliol commonplace book of Richard Hill, which holds ‘Lully, lulley’.

The poems gathered here run from about 1225 to the edge of the sixteenth century, with one later record of a far older custom. They include some of the earliest English love-songs, the plain and piercing carols of the fifteenth century, early ballads such as ‘Judas’ and ‘Robyn and Gandelyn’, the ‘Erthe upon erthe’ tradition of the memento mori, and the Yorkshire ‘Lyke-Wake Dirge’. The spelling is Middle English as the editors printed it.

poets.name: Mahmud Shabistari
poets.credit: Folio from a copy of the Gulshan-i Rāz made by Ja'far Bāysonghorī (Āstān-e Quds Razavī Library, no. 10579) · An artifact, shown because no portrait of the poet exists · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sa'd ud-Dīn Mahmūd Shabistarī was a Persian Sufi poet and scholar, born at Shabistar near Tabriz in north-western Iran. His dates are uncertain: Florence Lederer, whose translation is given here, places his birth about 1250, while other accounts put his life at about 1288 to about 1340. Little is known of his career beyond his learning in Sufi thought and his authorship of two prose treatises, Haqq al-Yaqīn and Risāla-yi Shādī.

He is remembered above all for the Gulshan-i Rāz (The Secret Rose Garden), a short mystical poem in rhyming couplets, written in 1311 in answer to questions put by a Sufi scholar of Herat. It treats unity, the soul's journey, the world as reflection and the language of wine and beauty as symbols of the divine. The English text offered here is Florence Lederer's selective 1920 version.

poets.name: Janabai
bio: Janabai (Jani Bai) is a Marathi woman saint-poet of the 14th century, remembered as a maidservant in the household of Namdev and a devotee of Vithoba of Pandharpur.
Her songs (abhangs) draw on the labours of household life, as in the grinding-mill hymn. Macnicol's Psalms of Maratha Saints (1919) gives three of them.

poets.name: Richard Rolle of Hampole
bio: Richard Rolle (c. 1300–1349), born at Thornton Dale in Yorkshire, left Oxford without a degree to live as a hermit, and became the most widely read English mystic of the fourteenth century. He wrote chiefly in Latin, notably the Incendium Amoris, but also composed English prose treatises and lyrics for devout readers, and an English commentary on the Psalter.

He died in 1349, reputedly at the Cistercian nunnery of Hampole near Doncaster, and was venerated locally as a saint. The lyric printed here, in his northern Middle English, is the only piece by him in The Oxford Book of English Mystical Verse (1917); its spelling is kept as the editors give it, with thorn (þ) and yogh (ȝ) restored.

poets.name: Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch)
poets.credit: Portrait of Francesco Petrarca (called Petrarch), French school, 17th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), known in English as Petrarch, was born in Arezzo to a Florentine notary exiled from his native city, and grew up in Avignon, then the seat of the papacy. He studied law at Montpellier and Bologna but gave himself to classical letters, recovering and copying Latin authors, and was crowned poet laureate on the Capitol in Rome in 1341. He spent his later years in northern Italy and died at Arquà, near Padua.

His Italian lyrics, the Rerum vulgarium fragmenta or Canzoniere, record his love for a woman named Laura, first seen in Avignon in 1327, whose death in 1348 divides the collection into poems written in her life and after her death. Their sonnet form and manner of address shaped European love poetry for centuries. The English versions here are from the 1879 Bohn volume, which prints several translations of most poems by different hands; the first version of each is given.

poets.name: Liu Chi
bio: Liu Chi (AD 1311–1375) was a scholar and adviser to the first Ming emperor, and a poet.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Hafiz
poets.credit: Anselm Feuerbach, Hafis vor der Schenke (1852); an imagined likeness, as no contemporary portrait of Hafez exists · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Shams al-Din Muhammad Hafez of Shiraz (c. 1315–1390) is the most beloved lyric poet of Persia. He is remembered chiefly for his ghazals, short rhymed lyrics of love, wine and mystical longing, gathered after his death into the Divan. His pen-name, Hafiz, means one who has memorised the Qur'an. He lived in Shiraz, where his tomb remains a place of pilgrimage, and his verses are still consulted and recited across the Persian-speaking world.

The poems here are three English versions: forty-three free rhymed renderings from Gertrude Lowthian Bell's Poems from the Divan of Hafiz (London: Heinemann, 1897), one song translated by Sir William Jones (1771), and a selection of forty-two odes in Herman Bicknell's translation, as printed in the Colonial Press Persian Literature (1909). Bell's introduction and notes and the volume's introduction and footnotes are left out. The 1917 Four Seas edition of Edna Worthley Underwood's Songs of Hafiz is also included; its title page says 'newly translated from the Persian', but the notes quote Julius Hart's German essay and the names follow German spelling, so she likely worked through German versions.

poets.name: Yang Chi
bio: Yang Chi was a native of Kiang-su who became a district magistrate and afterwards secretary to the Minister of War. According to L. Cranmer-Byng, he was sent to Shansi as Treasurer-General to the Forces, was impeached and falsely accused, and was condemned to life-long exile, during which he wrote the poem given here.
The poem here is L. Cranmer-Byng’s version in A Feast of Lanterns (1916), given under the poet’s name as spelled there.

poets.name: Dafydd ap Gwilym
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Dafydd ap Gwilym was a Welsh poet of the fourteenth century, a contemporary of Chaucer, and is generally counted the greatest of the medieval poets of Wales. Born in Ceredigion, he made the cywydd the leading Welsh metre and wrote lyrics of love, nature and wit.
The two poems here, "My Burial" and "The Last Cywydd", are serious pieces rendered into English verse by Alfred Perceval Graves in A Celtic Psaltery (1917).

poets.name: Iolo Goch
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Iolo Goch ("Iolo the Red") was a Welsh court poet of the fourteenth century, from the Vale of Clwyd in north Wales, who wrote praise poems for the nobility and was a patron-bard to Owain Glyndwr.
His cywydd on the labourer is given in English verse by Alfred Perceval Graves in A Celtic Psaltery (1917).

poets.name: John Barbour
bio: John Barbour (c. 1320–1395) was a Scottish churchman and poet, Archdeacon of Aberdeen from 1357. He travelled to Oxford and France to study and served as an auditor of the royal exchequer under Robert II.

His long poem The Bruce (c. 1375), written in Older Scots octosyllabic couplets, tells of the life and deeds of Robert the Bruce and Sir James Douglas in the Wars of Independence, and is the earliest major work of Scottish literature. Its address to freedom, 'A! fredome is a noble thing!', is among the best-known lines in Scots.

poets.name: John Gower
poets.credit: Photograph of Gower's tomb effigy, Southwark Cathedral — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Gower (c. 1330–1408) was an English poet, a friend and contemporary of Chaucer, who wrote major long works in all three literary languages of his day: French (Mirour de l'Omme), Latin (Vox Clamantis), and English (Confessio Amantis).

A man of some property in Kent, he spent his later years at the Priory of St Mary Overie in Southwark, where his elaborate tomb, with its painted effigy resting its head on his three books, still stands in what is now Southwark Cathedral.

Confessio Amantis, his English masterwork, frames some hundred and forty tales as a lover's confession to a priest of Venus, moving through the Seven Deadly Sins toward a final meditation on age and the end of love — dedicated, in its first version, to Richard II.

poets.name: Gerald, Earl of Desmond
bio: Gerald FitzGerald, Earl of Desmond, called Gearoid Iarla, was a Hiberno-Norman nobleman who wrote verse in Irish. Sigerson, in Bards of the Gael and Gall (1907), calls him Gerald the Bard, notes that he was Lord Justice of Ireland in 1367, and says he composed many Irish and some Norman-French poems.
“Womankind”, a warning against women’s wiles, is taken from the Book of the Dean of Lismore. It is given here in Sigerson’s English version, which keeps the repeating rhyme of the original.

poets.name: Gruffudd Gryg
poets.dates: fl. second half of the 14th century
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Gruffudd Gryg was an Anglesey bard of the second half of the fourteenth century, a contemporary of Dafydd ap Gwilym with whom he exchanged a famous poetic controversy that ended in an elegy each wrote for the other.
The poem here is a free English version after him, taken from George Borrow's Wild Wales and printed in Welsh Poems and Ballads (1915).

poets.name: William Langland
poets.credit: Portrait: Lepidus Magnus — CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Langland is the name traditionally given to the presumed author of Piers Plowman, one of the great alliterative poems of medieval England, on the strength of a fifteenth-century manuscript note naming a “William de Langlond” as its maker.

Little is known of his life beyond what can be inferred from the poem: he seems to have received a clerical education, lived for a time in London, and moved in the world of minor clergy and the poor rather than the court.

Piers Plowman survives in three successive versions (the A, B, and C texts), which Langland appears to have revised and expanded over some twenty years. It follows a dreamer, Will, through a series of visions in search of Do-well, Do-bet, and Do-best — a sweeping allegorical satire of fourteenth-century church and society.

poets.name: Owain Glyndŵr
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Owain Glyndŵr (c. 1354–1416), Prince of Wales, led the Welsh revolt against English rule from 1400. He was the patron of the poet Iolo Goch, who celebrated his house at Sycharth.
The quatrain here is attributed to him in Borrow's source, as translated in Welsh Poems and Ballads (1915); the attribution is traditional and uncertain.

poets.name: Sir John Clanvowe
bio: Sir John Clanvowe (c. 1341-1391) was a Herefordshire knight and a member of the household of Richard II, a friend of Chaucer's circle at court, and one of the so-called Lollard knights. He wrote a short devotional prose treatise, The Two Ways, and served on diplomatic and military missions abroad.

He died near Constantinople in 1391 while returning from a campaign with Sir William Neville. Skeat, in Chaucerian and Other Pieces (1897), printed The Cuckoo and the Nightingale under Clanvowe's name on the strength of its colophon, and later scholars have generally accepted the attribution; the poem is a debate between the two birds set at the court of the God of Love.

poets.name: Geoffrey Chaucer
poets.credit: Portrait of Geoffrey Chaucer (manuscript detail) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343–1400) was an English poet, civil servant, and diplomat, widely called the father of English poetry for demonstrating that the vernacular could carry the full weight of serious literary art.

He served in the royal household under three kings, worked as a customs official and clerk of the king's works, and travelled on diplomatic missions to France and Italy, where he likely encountered the work of Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio.

His masterwork, The Canterbury Tales, left unfinished at his death, gathers a fellowship of pilgrims riding to Canterbury and telling stories in turn — a panorama of medieval English society in verse of astonishing variety and wit. He was buried in Westminster Abbey, in the corner that later became Poets' Corner.

poets.name: Anonymous (Serbian)
poets.credit: Not a portrait of a poet (the ballads are anonymous): King Marko Mrnjavčević, fresco (1376) in the church of Marko's Monastery near Skopje · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Marko ballads are Serbian heroic songs, sung to the one-stringed gusle by anonymous singers from the fourteenth century down to the nineteenth. Their hero is Marko Kraljević (Prince Marko), son of King Vukašin, a vassal of the Turkish Sultan who in song becomes the champion of the Serbian people, a drinker, a fighter and a defender of the weak.

They are read here in the English version of D. H. Low, The Ballads of Marko Kraljević (Cambridge University Press, 1922), made chiefly from the collections of Vuk Karadžić and rendered in unrhymed lines that follow the long line of the originals. Low's introduction, notes and apparatus are left out; the thirty-one ballads, including the variants and one fragment, follow the order of the book. Added to them are the Kosovo songs, which centre on the Serbian defeat at Kosovo in 1389, in Helen Rootham's English version, Kossovo: Heroic Songs of the Serbs (Oxford: Blackwell, 1920), and a further selection of Kosovo, Marko and other heroic ballads in the rhymed version of George Rapall Noyes and Leonard Bacon, Heroic Ballads of Servia (Boston, 1913); the introductions and notes of those books are likewise left out.

poets.name: Layamon
bio: Layamon (Laȝamon) names himself at the opening of his Brut as a priest at Areley Kings, on the banks of the Severn, where he says he read books and conceived the plan of telling the history of the English. Nothing more is known of his life beyond what he tells us there.

The Brut is an English alliterative chronicle of about 16,000 long lines, running from the Trojan Brutus to the last British king, Cadwalader. It is drawn chiefly from Wace's Anglo-Norman Roman de Brut, which Layamon expands considerably, and it is the first English poem to tell the story of King Arthur, including the Round Table and his passing to Avalon.

poets.name: Vidyapati
bio: Vidyapati Thakur was a Maithili poet at the court of Mithila, in what is now northern Bihar. He enjoyed the patronage of Raja Shivasimha, who granted him the village of Bisapi in 1400, and he also wrote in Sanskrit. He is best known for his songs (padas) on the love of Radha and Krishna, composed in his mother tongue.

His songs became household poetry in Bengal and Bihar and are the source of the Bengali Vaishnava padavali tradition, taken up by Chaitanya and the poets who followed. The 138 songs given here are from the Bangiya Padabali as translated by Ananda Coomaraswamy and Arun Sen (Old Bourne Press, London, 1915); each is titled by its first line, with its section and number from that edition in the note.

poets.name: Ahmedî
bio: Ahmedi, born at Sivas, is described by Gibb as the first and perhaps the greatest of the Ottoman epic poets, whose Iskender-Nama is an epitome of Oriental history, mysticism, philosophy and science.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Gawain Poet
poets.credit: A page from the unique manuscript of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (British Library, Cotton Nero A.x) — a symbolic image for this anonymous poet, not a portrait. Public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: Known also as the Pearl Poet, this anonymous author wrote in a north-west Midlands dialect of Middle English in the late fourteenth century, a contemporary of Chaucer working in a very different, alliterative tradition.

Four poems in a single surviving manuscript (British Library, Cotton Nero A.x) are usually attributed to this one poet on grounds of dialect, style, and shared concerns: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Pearl, Patience, and Cleanness (also called Purity). Nothing certain is known of the poet's identity.

Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, the best known of the four, is a chivalric romance and moral test of a Round Table knight, told with intricate structure and a rare sensitivity to the turning of the seasons.

poets.name: Thomas Chestre
bio: Thomas Chestre is known only from the closing stanza of Sir Launfal, which names him as its maker. The poem survives in a single manuscript, British Library Cotton Caligula A.ii, and nothing else is certainly known of him.

Sir Launfal is a tail-rhyme Breton lay of about 1,040 lines, adapted from Marie de France's Lanval and the anonymous Graelent. It tells how a knight of Arthur's court, impoverished and slighted by Queen Guinevere, is loved by the fairy Tryamour.

poets.name: Hsieh Chin
bio: Hsieh Chin (AD 1369–1415) was an early Ming scholar and the chief editor of the great Yung-lo encyclopaedia.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Thomas Hoccleve
poets.credit: Hoccleve presenting the Regement of Princes to Prince Henry (British Library, Arundel MS 38, f. 37, c. 1411–13) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Hoccleve (c. 1368–1426) spent most of his working life as a clerk in the Office of the Privy Seal at Westminster, a post he held from about 1387, copying and drawing up the writs and letters that carried the king's seal. His poems return again and again to the pinch of that career: an uncertain annuity, a hungry purse, and a clerk's anxiety about his standing.

He called Chaucer his master and wrote in his teacher's metres, but his own voice, candid, self-mocking and often anxious, is unmistakable. His early confession La Male Regle (1406) looks back on a wasted youth, and in the Series (c. 1420–22) he speaks frankly of a mental breakdown and his recovery. Several of his poems survive in manuscripts written in his own hand.

The Regement of Princes, written about 1411 for Henry, Prince of Wales (the future Henry V), is his longest poem. It sets a dialogue between the poet and an old beggar before a mirror for princes drawn largely from Giles of Rome, Jacobus de Cessolis and the Secretum secretorum, and it was widely copied through the fifteenth century.

poets.name: Vemana
poets.dates: dates disputed (placed between the 14th and 17th centuries)
bio: Vemana was a Telugu moralist and mystic poet whose short verses, ending in the signature ‘Vema’, are still widely quoted and revered in the folk tradition of Andhra. His dates are disputed, and scholars have placed him anywhere between the 14th and 17th centuries.

His verses teach plain living and yogic self-knowledge, and often mock caste pride, ritual and the claims of priests. C. P. Brown’s prose version, published at Madras in 1829, was the first printed translation of a Telugu classic into English.

poets.name: John Lydgate
poets.credit: Portrait of John Lydgate (illuminated manuscript) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Lydgate (c. 1370–c. 1451) was a Benedictine monk of Bury St Edmunds and, in his own lifetime, probably the most prolific and widely read poet in England — his surviving output runs to well over a hundred thousand lines.

He wrote in conscious imitation of Chaucer, whom he revered as his master, producing enormous works such as the Troy Book and the Fall of Princes alongside occasional verse, saints' lives, and courtly dream visions for patrons that included the royal house of Lancaster.
Modern taste has generally preferred Chaucer's economy to Lydgate's copiousness, but he was central to how English poetry was read and valued through the fifteenth century.

poets.name: Sheykhî
bio: Sheykhi, whose real name was Sinan, was born in Germiyan in Asia Minor and, Gibb notes, was the first of the Ottomans to write a romantic poem; his pen-name marks his standing as sheykh, or chief, of the poets of his age.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Charles d’Orléans
bio: Charles d’Orléans (1394–1465) was a French prince and poet, Duke of Orléans, who was taken prisoner at Agincourt in 1415 and held in England for twenty-five years. During his captivity he wrote many ballades, rondeaux and songs.
The poem here is Henry Francis Cary’s English version of one of his lyrics, as printed in the Library of Poetry and Song edited by William Cullen Bryant (1871).

poets.name: Anonymous (Spanish ballads)
bio: The romances, or Spanish ballads, are short narrative poems in assonanced, mostly eight-syllable lines that were sung and recited in Castile from the fourteenth century onward and were gathered into printed songbooks, the Cancioneros and Romanceros, in the sixteenth. They are anonymous: none of the ballads in this selection can be assigned to a named author. Their subjects are the history and legend of Spain — the fall of the Gothic kingdom under King Roderick, Bernardo del Carpio, the Cid, Pedro the Cruel — together with the frontier ballads of the Moors of Granada and romances of chivalry.

These English versions are by John Gibson Lockhart (1794–1854), the Scottish writer and biographer of Walter Scott, who published them as Ancient Spanish Ballads, Historical and Romantic (Edinburgh: William Blackwood, 1823). By his own account most were made from pieces in the collection of Christoph Friedrich Depping (Leipzig, 1817). Lockhart arranged them in three groups, the historical, the Moorish and the romantic ballads, and rendered them in English ballad measures, in places omitting stanzas of the Spanish. The Spanish ballad texts are anonymous and centuries old; the translations are Lockhart's own.

poets.name: Siôn Cent
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Siôn Cent was a Welsh poet of the early fifteenth century, associated with Kentchurch in Herefordshire, whose verse turns on the vanity of worldly pride and the certainty of death.
His poem "The Noble's Grave" is given in English verse by Alfred Perceval Graves in A Celtic Psaltery (1917).

poets.name: Chao Ts’ai-chi
bio: Chao Ts’ai-chi is dated by Giles to the 15th century AD. Her poem here is a lover’s message.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Yaziji-Oglu
bio: Yaziji-Oglu, also called Ibn-Katib, lived at Gallipoli with his brother Bijan, who was likewise a mystic poet; the poem here comes from his Muhammediyya.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Fang Shu-shao
bio: Fang Shu-shao is dated by Giles to the 15th century AD. His poem here is addressed to his own coffin.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Sultan Murad II
bio: Murad II, sixth sovereign of the House of 'Osman, is described by Gibb as the earliest Ottoman monarch to encourage poetry by his own example, the first of the long line of poet-sultans.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Jami
poets.credit: Kamal al-Din Bihzad (attributed), Yusuf Flees from Zulaikha, folio from a Bustan of Sa'di, 1488 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons); an illustration of the story, not a portrait of Jami
bio: Nur al-Din Abd al-Rahman Jami (1414–1492) was born at Jam in Khorasan and spent most of his life at Herat, then the cultural capital of the Timurid world. Poet, Sufi of the Naqshbandi order, scholar and biographer, he is generally counted the last great classical Persian poet, and his Haft Awrang (Seven Thrones) gathers his long narrative poems, among them Yusuf and Zulaikha.

Here he is represented by Ralph T. H. Griffith's English verse translation of Yusuf and Zulaikha (London, 1882), which retells the Qur'anic and Biblical story of Joseph and the vizier's wife as a Sufi allegory of the soul's longing for divine beauty. It is given as a single long work.

poets.name: Dafydd Nanmor
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Dafydd Nanmor was a fifteenth-century Welsh poet, named from Nanmor near Beddgelert. He wrote love poems in the manner of Dafydd ap Gwilym and later found patrons in South Wales; the Dictionary of Welsh Biography calls him a poet of note but dates him only to the fifteenth century.
The poem here is George Borrow's English version, taken from his Wild Wales and printed in Welsh Poems and Ballads (1915).

poets.name: 'Adenî (Mahmud Pasha)
bio: 'Adeni was the pen-name of the Grand Vezir Mahmud Pasha, who died in 1474.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Anonymous (Chaucerian apocrypha)
bio: These are Middle English poems of unknown authorship that were once printed as Chaucer's own. From the first collected editions in the sixteenth century onward, publishers filled out the Chaucer volume with whatever looked Chaucerian, and for three centuries readers took The Flower and the Leaf, The Court of Love and The Assembly of Ladies for his work.

In the nineteenth century scholars showed from their language and metre that the poems were later, most of them of the fifteenth century, and in 1897 W. W. Skeat gathered the doubtful pieces in Chaucerian and Other Pieces, a supplement to his edition of Chaucer. This page holds the anonymous verse from that volume: the dream-visions and love poems, a short envoy and a virelai, a balade in praise of Chaucer, and the Lollard satire The Plowmans Tale.

The authors are unknown, though some of the dream-visions may be by women: The Flower and the Leaf describes itself as the work of a lady. Skeat's own spelling and word-forms are kept, without his line numbers or notes.

poets.name: Âfitâbî
bio: Gibb says that Afitabi, a native of Amasya, gained admittance to the court of Sultan Bayezid II but was driven from it by the envy of courtiers, and in retirement wrote a qasida giving an account of his misfortunes.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: François Villon
poets.credit: Woodcut of Villon from the 1489 Pierre Levet edition of Le Grand Testament · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: François Villon (born in Paris in 1431) took his master's degree at the University of Paris in 1452 and then lived by his wits on the margins of the city. In 1455 he killed a priest in a street quarrel and fled; he was later imprisoned at Meung-sur-Loire and released in 1461, and in 1462–63 he was condemned to be hanged in Paris and had the sentence commuted to banishment. After January 1463 nothing certain is known of him.

His reputation rests on two mock wills: the Lesser Testament (Le Lais), written at Christmas 1456, and the Greater Testament (Le Testament), begun about 1461, into which he set ballads such as the Ballad of Old-Time Ladies with its refrain about last year's snow, together with the Epitaph in Ballad Form, usually known as the Ballad of the Hanged. These texts are John Payne's English verse translation of 1878, as reprinted by Thomas Bird Mosher of Portland, Maine, in 1909; the Payne volume leaves out a few ballads, which the book itself marks as omitted.

poets.name: Lewys Glyn Cothi
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Lewys Glyn Cothi was a fifteenth-century Welsh poet from the Cothi valley in Carmarthenshire, a wandering bard who sang for patrons across Wales and the borders.
His elegy for his young son Siôn is given in English verse by Alfred Perceval Graves in A Celtic Psaltery (1917).

poets.name: Gwilym ab Ieuan Hen
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Gwilym ab Ieuan Hen was a Welsh poet who flourished, according to the Dictionary of Welsh Biography, between about 1440 and 1480. Little is known of his life, though many of his poems survive in manuscript.
The poem here is George Borrow's English version, taken from his Wild Wales and printed in Welsh Poems and Ballads (1915).

poets.name: Isabel Stuart, Countess of Argyll
bio: Isabel Stuart was the second daughter of Stuart, Lord of Lorn, and married Archibald, first Earl of Argyll, whose title dates from 1457. Sigerson, in Bards of the Gael and Gall (1907), dates her poem to 1459.
“Love Untold” is preserved in the Book of the Dean of Lismore, and Sigerson reads in it a hidden romance. It is given here in his English version.

poets.name: Robin Ddu
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Robin Ddu (Robin Ddu ap Siencyn Bledrydd of Anglesey) was a Welsh poet who flourished about 1450. Around ninety of his poems survive in manuscript, many of them prophetic; he sided with the Tudors and made a pilgrimage to Rome in 1450.
The poem here is a fragment of an ode to Anglesey in George Borrow's English version, from Wild Wales, printed in Welsh Poems and Ballads (1915).

poets.name: 'Avnî (Sultan Mehmed II)
bio: 'Avni was the pen-name of Sultan Mehmed II, who was girt with the scimitar of 'Osman at twenty-one and two years later took Constantinople, ending the Roman Empire.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Zeyneb
bio: Zeyneb, whose father was a judge, was a woman poet who made a Divan of Turkish and Persian poems and dedicated it to Sultan Mehmed II; Gibb notes that she seems never to have married.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Kabir
poets.credit: Kabir with a disciple, Company-school painting (c. 1825), an imagined likeness by an unknown artist · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Kabir was a Hindi-language mystic poet and weaver of Benares (Varanasi), traditionally dated c. 1440 to 1518. Born, by tradition, into a Muslim weaving family, he is said to have received initiation from the Hindu teacher Ramananda, and he rejected the claims of both Hindu and Muslim orthodoxy in favour of direct devotion to a single, formless God.

His short songs and couplets were transmitted orally and later collected in the Bijak, the Adi Granth of the Sikhs and other anthologies.
