The English Songs of Kabir (1915) were rendered by Rabindranath Tagore with the help of Evelyn Underhill, who wrote the introduction; this edition gives the hundred songs of that volume.

poets.name: Ahmed Pasha
bio: Ahmed Pasha, the son of Veliyyu-'d-Din, is called by Gibb the first really great lyric poet of the Ottomans; he was raised to the rank of vezir by Sultan Mehmed II.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Sir Richard Ros
bio: Sir Richard Ros (c. 1429 to after 1482) was an English gentleman and poet, known as the translator of Alain Chartier's French poem La Belle Dame sans Mercy. Few details of his life are certain, and no portrait of him survives.

His English version, made about 1460 from Chartier's poem of 1424, keeps the original's eight-line stanzas and its debate between a courtly lover and a lady who refuses him. It was long printed among the works of Chaucer, as in Thynne's edition of 1532, until Skeat edited it separately in 1897.

poets.name: Robert Henryson
poets.credit: No authentic portrait of Henryson survives · Texts from W. M. Metcalfe's edition, The Poems and Fables of Robert Henryson (Paisley: Alexander Gardner, 1917) · Public domain
bio: Robert Henryson (c. 1430–c. 1506) was a Scottish poet writing in Middle Scots in the second half of the fifteenth century. Almost nothing is known of his life: he is described in early sources as a schoolmaster, and is generally linked with Dunfermline, where William Dunbar's Lament for the Makaris places his death.

He is best known for The Morall Fabillis of Esope the Phrygian, thirteen beast fables in rime royal, each closed by a moralitas; for The Testament of Cresseid, a tragic sequel to Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde; and for Orpheus and Eurydice and the pastoral Robene and Makyne. With Dunbar and Gavin Douglas he is counted among the great Scottish makars.

poets.name: Blind Hary
poets.credit: Portrait: D.j.c — CC0 (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Blind Hary, also called Henry the Minstrel, was a Scottish poet of the second half of the fifteenth century. Little is securely known of his life: later tradition holds that he was blind from birth and lived by reciting verse before Scottish nobles, and the accounts of James IV's treasurer record payments to him in the 1490s.

He is the author of The Wallace (c. 1477), a long Older Scots poem in decasyllabic couplets on the life and deeds of Sir William Wallace, drawing on an earlier Latin life that Hary cites. Vivid, partisan and freely inventive where history fails him, it became one of the most widely read books in Scotland for centuries.

poets.name: Anonymous (English and Scottish Ballads)
bio: The popular ballads of England and Scotland are anonymous narrative songs, passed on by voice for generations before collectors wrote them down, mostly between the 15th and 18th centuries, so each ballad often survives in several differing versions. They tell of elves and ghosts, outlaws, border raids, feuds and unhappy lovers in plain, repeated formulas and refrains.

This archive follows the selection of Arthur Quiller-Couch in The Oxford Book of Ballads (Clarendon Press, 1910), which gathers 176 ballads in seven books, from the supernatural and romantic pieces to the outlaw, historical and later broadside ballads. The editor keeps the Scots spellings of his sources.

poets.name: Anonymous (English nursery rhymes)
poets.credit: No portrait: traditional rhymes, collected by James Orchard Halliwell (The Nursery Rhymes of England, 1842).
bio: The English nursery rhymes are anonymous traditional verses of the cradle and the playground: lullabies, riddles, counting-out and game rhymes, jingles, charms and short tales in rhyme. Most were handed down by voice for generations, and the earliest of them were written down in the seventeenth century, although many are certainly older.

This archive follows The Nursery Rhymes of England, collected by James Orchard Halliwell (first edition, London, 1842), which arranges more than six hundred rhymes in eighteen classes, from the historical and the literal to games, lullabies and relics. The text is taken from the Project Gutenberg edition of the Warne printing of 1886, illustrated by W. B. Scott. Halliwell's class is given in each poem's note; his notes and the directions for games are omitted.

poets.name: Traditional Ballads (Child collection)
poets.credit: Francis James Child (1825–1896), who collected the ballads; photograph, date unknown (the ballads themselves are anonymous) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The English and Scottish Popular Ballads is the great scholarly collection of traditional ballads in English and Scots, edited by the Harvard professor Francis James Child (1825–1896) and published in ten parts between 1882 and 1898. Child gathered 305 ballads, each given a number that is still how scholars cite it, and printed every version he could find, lettered A, B, C and so on, from manuscripts, broadsides, printed miscellanies and oral tradition.

The ballads range from elfin knights, ghosts and riddling lovers to Border raids, Robin Hood and sea-fights. Their texts were written down between about the 13th and the 19th century, and most were sung long before that. This archive gives version A of every ballad, with later versions added where they tell the story in substantially different words, and keeps Child's titles and spellings; his headnotes, sources and variant readings are left out.

poets.name: Nejâtî
bio: Nejati, whose real name was 'Isa (Jesus), was born, according to Qinali-Zada, at Adrianople but brought up at Kastamonu, and won his first laurels at Bursa.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Mesîhî
bio: Mesihi, born at Pristina near Skopje, is held by Gibb to be a poet of high merit whose strength, like Lami'i's, lay in elegant descriptions of the beauties of nature.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Mihrî
bio: Mihri is a poet of the early sixteenth century whom Gibb's anthology represents with two gazels; Gibb's heading dates the death to about 1514.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Prince Jem
bio: Prince Jem was the younger brother of Sultan Bayezid II, with whom he contested the throne, and after his defeat at Yeni-Shehr he fled abroad.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: William Dunbar
poets.credit: Portrait of William Dunbar — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Dunbar was a Scottish makar (court poet) attached to the household of King James IV, celebrated for the range and metrical virtuosity of his verse.
His poems move between satire, comic invective, and devotional lyric, and include the famous elegy ‘Lament for the Makers,’ with its refrain ‘Timor Mortis conturbat me.’

poets.name: John Skelton
poets.credit: Portrait of John Skelton — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Skelton was an English poet and tutor to the young Prince Henry, later Henry VIII, remembered for the idiosyncratic short-lined verse form later called ‘Skeltonics.’
He wrote both courtly lyrics of praise and sharp satire of clergy and court, and was crowned poet laureate by three universities.

poets.name: Harîmî (Prince Qorqud)
bio: Prince Qorqud, who wrote under the pen-name Harimi, was a son of Sultan Bayezid II and a brother of Selim I.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Selîmî (Sultan Selim I)
bio: Selim I wrote verse under the pen-name Selimi; he came to the throne in 1512 on the abdication of his father Bayezid II and in a reign of less than nine years doubled the extent of the Ottoman Empire.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Figânî
bio: Figani, of Qaraman, was a secretary to Prince 'Abdu-'llah, one of Sultan Bayezid's sons.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Ludovico Ariosto
poets.credit: Portrait of Ludovico Ariosto, woodcut from the Ferrara edition of the Orlando Furioso (1532) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ludovico Ariosto (1474–1533) was born at Reggio Emilia and spent most of his life in the service of the Este family of Ferrara, first under Cardinal Ippolito d'Este and then, after 1517, under Duke Alfonso I. He wrote comedies and satires as well as lyrics, and was governor of the mountainous Garfagnana district for the duke from 1522 to 1525.

His masterpiece, the Orlando Furioso (first printed in 1516, revised in 1521 and again in the final edition of 1532), continues Boiardo's unfinished Orlando Innamorato in forty-six cantos of ottava rima. It weaves the madness of Orlando (Roland), the love of Ruggiero and Bradamante, and the war between Charlemagne and the Saracens into a single mock-heroic romance, and it deeply influenced Tasso, Spenser and later English poets. The version here is by William Stewart Rose, published in eight volumes by John Murray between 1823 and 1831.

poets.name: Gavin Douglas
bio: Gavin Douglas (c. 1474–1522) was a Scottish poet, churchman and statesman, a son of Archibald Douglas, 5th Earl of Angus, and from 1516 Bishop of Dunkeld. He was educated at St Andrews and later took a prominent part in the politics of the minority of James V.

His Eneados, completed in 1513, is a Middle Scots verse translation of Virgil's Aeneid with an original prologue to each book and Maffeo Vegio's thirteenth book; it is generally counted the first complete translation of the Aeneid into any form of English. It is read in the archive under Virgil's Aeneid, beside the English versions by later translators.

poets.name: Stephen Hawes
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Stephen Hawes was an English poet who served as a groom of the chamber to Henry VII, best known for his allegorical romance ‘The Pastime of Pleasure.’
His verse bridges medieval allegory and the new humanism of the early Tudor court, and he was among the last English poets to write in the tradition of Chaucer and Lydgate.

poets.name: Michelangelo Buonarroti
poets.credit: Portrait of Michelangelo by Daniele da Volterra (c. 1545) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475–1564) was born at Caprese in Tuscany and trained in Florence. He is remembered above all as a sculptor, painter and architect, of the David, the Sistine Chapel ceiling and the dome of St Peter’s, but he also wrote poetry throughout his long life, working at madrigals and sonnets in the Tuscan tradition of Dante and Petrarch.

His surviving verse, about three hundred poems, was not published as a book in his lifetime. It speaks of beauty, love and art, of his friendships with Tommaso de’ Cavalieri and Vittoria Colonna, and, in old age, of death and the longing for God. This selection is John Addington Symonds’s rhymed English version of 1878; where Michelangelo left two versions of a sonnet, both are given.

poets.name: Lâmi'î
bio: Gibb ranks Lami'i, born in Bursa, among the very best and most fruitful writers of the Ottomans, a man of quiet and uneventful life given wholly to study.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Girolamo Fracastoro
poets.credit: Portrait of Girolamo Fracastoro after Titian (c. 1528, National Gallery, London) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Girolamo Fracastoro (c. 1478–1553) was a physician, astronomer and poet of Verona, a friend of Pietro Bembo and a student at Padua. He is remembered both for early work on contagion and for his Latin verse.

His didactic poem Syphilis sive de morbo Gallico, in three books, appeared in 1530; it tells the story of the shepherd Syphilus, from whom the disease took its name. This edition gives Nahum Tate's English verse translation, A Poetical History of the French Disease (1686); the Latin original was published in 1530.

poets.name: Ghazâlî
bio: Ghazali is the pen-name of Muhammed Chelebi, a distinguished poet of Bursa, nicknamed Deli Birader, Mad Brother, for his jovial but dissolute habits.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Kemâl Pasha-Zâde
bio: Kemal Pasha-Zade is represented in Gibb's anthology by a passage from his elegy on the death of Sultan Selim I.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Ishâq Chelebi
bio: Ishaq Chelebi, the son of a sword-cutler of Skopje, was noted for his drunken and abandoned life.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Fuzuli
bio: Fuzuli (Mehmed bin Süleyman, c. 1483–1556) was one of the greatest poets of the sixteenth-century Turkish world. He wrote in Azerbaijani Turkish, Ottoman Turkish, Persian and Arabic, and is remembered above all for his romance Leyla and Mejnun, the tale of the lover driven mad by his love for Leyla.

E. J. W. Gibb, whose Ottoman Poems (1882) gives the first English translations of his ghazels, noted that Fuzuli's Leyla and Mejnun contains many touching passages of great beauty. The poems below are from that volume.

poets.name: Sir David Lyndsay
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir David Lyndsay · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir David Lyndsay of the Mount was a Scottish courtier, diplomat and poet who served the young James V and later held the office of Lord Lyon King of Arms. He is often called the Scottish Juvenal for his satires on the abuses of court and church.

His best-known work is the morality play "Ane Pleasant Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis". His narrative and satiric poems, among them "The Dreme", "The Testament of the Papyngo" and "Squyer Meldrum", were widely read in Scotland for generations. Eyre-Todd (1892) prints his Middle Scots text from David Laing's edition.

poets.name: Martin Luther
poets.credit: Martin Luther by Lucas Cranach the Elder, 1528 (Veste Coburg) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Martin Luther was born at Eisleben in 1483 and died there in 1546. An Augustinian friar and professor at the University of Wittenberg, he was the leading figure of the German Reformation, and he wrote some three dozen hymns, among them Ein feste Burg and Christ lag in Todesbanden, which helped establish congregational singing in German.
The English versions here are Catherine Winkworth's in Lyra Germanica (1855).

poets.name: Zâtî
bio: Zati was born in the province of Qarasi, where his father was a shoemaker, made his fortune in Constantinople, and was one of the poetic lights of the reigns of Bayezid II and Selim I.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Muhibbî (Sultan Suleyman I)
bio: Suleyman I, surnamed Qanuni, the Lawgiver, the most illustrious of the Ottoman monarchs, left a Divan of gazels under the pen-name Muhibbi.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Lutfî
bio: Lutfi, an Albanian by birth, was Grand Vezir and brother-in-law of Sultan Suleyman I, and was disgraced and banished to Demotika after a quarrel with his wife.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Henry VIII
bio: Henry VIII (1491–1547) was King of England from 1509 until his death. A skilled musician and a patron of court music, he is credited with a number of songs and ballads, most of them preserved in the manuscript known as the Henry VIII Book (British Library, Additional MS 31922), compiled about 1518.

The pieces given here are the lyrics printed under his name in Early English Lyrics (1907): the holly-and-ivy song, the farewell lyric "Whereto should I express", and the famous "Pastime with Good Company". The attribution of individual songs to the king rests on the manuscript and on tradition.

poets.name: John Bellenden
bio: John Bellenden was a Scottish churchman and translator, Archdeacon of Moray, who made a Scots version of Hector Boece's Latin history of Scotland and a Scots Livy for the court of James V.
The poems gathered here are the verse prefaces to those translations and the opening stanzas of "The Benner of Pietie", printed by Eyre-Todd in 1892.

poets.name: Sir Richard Maitland
bio: Sir Richard Maitland of Lethington was a Scottish judge and Lord Privy Seal, who in old age lost his sight yet went on writing. He is remembered also as the collector of the Maitland Folio and Quarto manuscripts, which preserve much older Scots poetry.
His own verse is mostly short moral satire on the vanity of the age, the dress of town ladies and the corruption of the court and the Borders. Eyre-Todd (1892) prints six of these pieces.

poets.name: Garcilaso de la Vega
poets.credit: Portrait traditionally identified as Garcilaso de la Vega (anonymous, 16th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Garcilaso de la Vega was a Spanish soldier and poet, born at Toledo around 1501 into a noble family. He served Emperor Charles V in his campaigns, fought in the expedition to Tunis in 1535, and was fatally wounded in 1536 while leading an assault at Le Muy in Provence.

Often called the prince of Castilian poets, he brought the Italian forms of Petrarch and Sannazaro into Spanish verse: the sonnet, the hendecasyllabic line, the eclogue and the elegy. His poems were published after his death alongside those of his friend Juan Boscán. This archive holds J. H. Wiffen's English verse translation of his works, published in London in 1823.

poets.name: Khiyâlî
bio: Khiyali was a native of Asia Minor who came to Constantinople, according to Gibb's Biographical Notices.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Sir Thomas Wyatt
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir Thomas Wyatt — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Thomas Wyatt was a Kentish courtier and diplomat under Henry VIII, credited with introducing the sonnet form into English poetry after his travels in Italy.
His lyrics of love and court intrigue circulated in manuscript during his lifetime and were first printed posthumously in Tottel’s Miscellany (1557).

poets.name: St. Francis Xavier
poets.credit: Portrait of St. Francis Xavier, Wikimedia Commons · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Francis Xavier was born at the Castle of Xavier, near Pamplona, in 1506. He studied at Paris, where he met Ignatius Loyola, and as a Jesuit missionary worked in India and the East. He died in 1552.
The hymn O Deus, ego amo Te is attributed to him. It is given here in John Brownlie's English version of 1896.

poets.name: Gruffudd Hiraethog
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Gruffudd Hiraethog (died 1564) was a Welsh bard and herald, best known as the teacher of the next generation of poets, among them Wiliam Llŷn and Siôn Tudur. He also compiled a Welsh dictionary and a collection of proverbs. He is not the nineteenth-century poet Gwilym Hiraethog.
The poem here is a couplet in George Borrow's English version, from Wild Wales, printed in Welsh Poems and Ballads (1915).

poets.name: Thomas Phaer
poets.credit: No portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Phaer was a lawyer and physician who wrote on medicine and began a verse translation of Virgil’s Aeneid, which he left unfinished at his death (Thomas Twyne completed it). He contributed the legend of Owen Glendower to A Mirror for Magistrates.
The poem here is taken from Joseph Haslewood’s 1815 reprint of Part III, where it is signed Th. Ph.

poets.name: George Ferrers
poets.credit: No portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: George Ferrers was an English lawyer, member of parliament and courtier, who was put in charge of the Christmas entertainments at the court of Edward VI. He was one of the principal contributors to A Mirror for Magistrates, helping Baldwin to complete the work.
The legends here, signed G. F. in the printed text, are taken from Joseph Haslewood’s 1815 reprint of Part III.

poets.name: Fazlî
bio: Fazli, nicknamed Qara Fazli, Black Fazli, was the son of a saddler of Constantinople, a dervish of the Khalveti order and a clerk by occupation, and a disciple of the poet-laureate Zati.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Chu Hou-tsung
bio: Chu Hou-tsung was a Ming emperor. His poem here is addressed to a general sent against the barbarians.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: William Baldwin
poets.credit: No portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Baldwin was a Tudor writer and clergyman, the original editor of A Mirror for Magistrates (first printed 1559), whose prose dialogues link its tragedies. He also wrote the prose satire Beware the Cat (composed 1553, printed 1570), often called the earliest English novel.
The legends here are those that Joseph Haslewood’s 1815 reprint assigns to him, most of them as “attributed to Baldwin”. The attributions are Haslewood’s and are not certain.

poets.name: Nishânî
bio: Nishani, Jelal-Zade Mustafa, was the great historian of Suleyman's reign and held some of the highest offices of state, among them that of Nishanji, Cipher-writer to the Sultan.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: King James V of Scotland
poets.credit: Portrait of James V of Scotland (1512–1542) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James V became King of Scotland as an infant in 1513 after his father fell at Flodden, and ruled in his own right from 1528 until his death in 1542. Tradition tells of his wandering among his subjects in disguise as the "Gudeman of Ballengeich".

Four comic poems have long been attributed to him: "Peblis to the Play", "Christis Kirk on the Grene", "The Gaberlunzieman" and "The Jolly Beggar". Eyre-Todd follows the traditional attribution; the authorship of all four is disputed.

poets.name: Mukhlisî (Prince Mustafa)
bio: Prince Mustafa, heir to Suleyman's throne, is represented by Gibb's sources as talented, courageous, generous and refined; he wrote under the pen-name Mukhlisi.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey
poets.credit: Portrait of Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey, was an English nobleman and poet who, alongside his friend Sir Thomas Wyatt, helped pioneer the English sonnet and was the first to write English verse in blank verse.
He was executed for treason in the last weeks of Henry VIII’s reign, at the age of twenty-nine.

poets.name: Chao Li-hua
bio: Chao Li-hua is dated by Giles to the 16th century AD. Her poem here is a lover’s plea.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: John Harington the Elder
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Harington the Elder, father of the translator Sir John Harington, was a courtier who was imprisoned in the Tower under Queen Mary for carrying messages to the princess Elizabeth, and was rewarded by her after her accession. Gilfillan, who spells the name Harrington, gives his dates as 1534 to 1582.
He is credited with a handful of amatory verses. Gilfillan prints two of them: a sonnet on Isabella Markham and verses on a stony-hearted maiden.

poets.name: Nicholas Grimald
bio: Nicholas Grimald (1519–1562), also spelled Grimalde, was an English scholar, poet and playwright, a member of Christ Church, Oxford, and the author of the Latin play Christus Redivivus.
He was a leading contributor to Tottel’s Miscellany (1557), where his poems appeared with those of Surrey and Wyatt.

poets.name: Joachim du Bellay
poets.credit: Portrait of Joachim du Bellay, 16th-century engraving · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Joachim du Bellay (1522–1560) was a French poet of the Pléiade, born in Anjou. His manifesto La Défense et illustration de la langue française (1549) argued that French could rival Latin and Italian, and he followed it with the sonnet sequence L'Olive. He spent some years in Rome in the service of his kinsman Cardinal Jean du Bellay, and returned to Paris in 1557.

His Roman years produced the Regrets and Les Antiquitez de Rome (1558), sonnets on the fallen grandeur of the ancient city; the related Songe (Dream) sequence closed the same volume. Edmund Spenser translated both as a young man, and printed them in his Complaints (1591) as Ruines of Rome and The Visions of Bellay. The versions here are Spenser's, in his own spelling.

poets.name: Alexander Scott
bio: Alexander Scott was a Scottish makar of the mid-sixteenth century, whose short love lyrics are preserved chiefly in the Bannatyne Manuscript. Eyre-Todd calls him the earliest of the more distinctly lyrical Scottish poets.
He also wrote a comic burlesque, "The Justing and Debait vp at the Drum". Little is securely known of his life.

poets.name: Siôn Tudur
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Siôn Tudur (died 1602) was a Welsh poet of Wigfair near St Asaph, Denbighshire, who served for a time at the court in London and was made apprentice chief bard at the Caerwys eisteddfod of 1568. The Dictionary of Welsh Biography gives only his death date, 3 April 1602.
The poem here is George Borrow's English version, taken from his Wild Wales and printed in Welsh Poems and Ballads (1915).

poets.name: Luís de Camões
poets.credit: Portrait of Luís de Camões, attributed to Fernão Gomes (16th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Luís Vaz de Camões was a Portuguese poet, widely regarded as the greatest in the Portuguese language. He served in the Portuguese enterprises in North Africa and the East, losing the sight of one eye in battle at Ceuta, and spent many years abroad in India and Macao before returning to Lisbon.

His epic Os Lusíadas, published in 1572, celebrates Vasco da Gama's voyage to India and the history of the Portuguese people in ten cantos of ottava rima. He is also remembered for his lyric poetry, and died in Lisbon in 1580. This archive holds Sir Richard Francis Burton's English version of the epic, published in 1880.

poets.name: Thomas Churchyard
poets.credit: No portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Churchyard was an English soldier, courtier and prolific verse-writer who served in the wars in Scotland, France and the Low Countries, and in Ireland. He was in the household of the Earl of Surrey as a young man, and he published verse and prose for more than half a century, down to the reign of James I.

This selection is drawn from A Pleasaunte Laborinth called Churchyardes Chance (London: Ihon Kyngston, 1580): epitaphs for noble and gentle friends, verses presented to Queen Elizabeth, and miscellaneous poems on court, friendship, love and the world. Spelling is that of the printed book.

poets.name: Selîmî (Sultan Selim II)
bio: Selim II wrote verse under the pen-name Selimi, the same pen-name used by his grandfather Selim I.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Pierre de Ronsard
poets.credit: Portrait of Ronsard by Benjamin Foulon (19th century, after a 16th-century portrait) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Pierre de Ronsard (1524-1585) was born at the manor of La Possonnière in the Vendômois, in the Loir valley, and began his career as a page at the French court. An illness that left him largely deaf turned him from a court and military career to study and poetry. At the Collège de Coqueret he studied the classics under Jean Dorat with Joachim du Bellay and others, and became the leader of the group of poets later known as the Pléiade.

His first books of Odes appeared in 1550 and his Amours in 1552; later works include the Hymns, the Sonnets pour Hélène (1578) and the unfinished epic La Franciade. Honoured as the Prince of Poets under several French kings, he died in 1585 at the priory of Saint-Cosme near Tours. These English versions are from Curtis Hidden Page's Songs and Sonnets of Pierre de Ronsard (1903), a selection that gathers them under headings of its own.

poets.name: Sir Thomas Chaloner
poets.credit: No portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir Thomas Chaloner was an English diplomat and writer, ambassador to Spain under Elizabeth I, and the translator of Erasmus’s Praise of Folly (1549). He contributed the legend of Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk, to A Mirror for Magistrates.
The poem here is taken from Joseph Haslewood’s 1815 reprint of Part III, where it is signed T. Ch.

poets.name: Shâhî (Prince Bayezid)
bio: Prince Bayezid, a son of Sultan Suleyman I, led an unsuccessful revolt against his brother Selim, was defeated on the plain of Qonya and fled to Persia.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Shemsî Pasha
bio: Shemsi Pasha, confidant and governor of the palace of Selim II and Murad III, was born in Hungary and was the last scion of the House of Qizil-Ahmedli.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Bâqî
bio: Bâqî, whose full name was Mahmud 'Abdu-'l-Baqi, is, by the unanimous verdict of the Ottoman critics Gibb cites, the greatest lyric poet the Ottoman nation has produced; he was born in Constantinople in 1526.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Richard Edwardes
bio: Richard Edwardes (1523?–1566) was an English poet, composer and dramatist, a gentleman and later Master of the Children of the Chapel Royal under Elizabeth I, and author of the play Damon and Pithias.
His poems appeared in The Paradise of Dainty Devices (1576), the miscellany he is chiefly associated with.

poets.name: Yahyâ Beg
bio: Yahya Beg was an Albanian janissary who devoted himself with success to literature and wrote an elegy on his friend Iskender Chelebi.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Thomas Tusser
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Tusser was an English farmer and poet who also worked, at different times, as a chorister, a courtier and a schoolmaster. He farmed in Suffolk, Essex and elsewhere with little lasting success.

He is remembered for his rhymed farming manual, A Hundreth Good Pointes of Husbandrie (1557), later enlarged as Five Hundreth Pointes of Good Husbandrie. Gilfillan's Specimens prints two short pieces from it.

poets.name: Eknath
bio: Eknath (Ekanath) was a Marathi saint-poet of Paithan, a disciple of the teacher Janardan, and a leading figure in the devotional (bhakti) tradition of Maharashtra between Jnanesvar and Tukaram. He is remembered for his Marathi commentary on the eleventh book of the Bhagavata Purana and for his abhangs. The dates 1548-99 are those printed by Macnicol; other authorities place his birth earlier, around 1533.
Macnicol's Psalms of Maratha Saints (1919) gives seven of his pieces, from both his commentary and his short songs.

poets.name: Queen Elizabeth I
bio: Elizabeth I (1533–1603), daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn, was Queen of England and Ireland from 1558 until her death. Educated in Latin, Greek and several modern languages, she wrote a handful of poems, many of them circulated in manuscript.
'The Doubt of Future Foes', composed about 1571, is generally read as a response to the presence in England of Mary, Queen of Scots, who had fled there in 1568.

poets.name: Edward de Vere, Earl of Oxford
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Edward de Vere, seventeenth Earl of Oxford, was an Elizabethan courtier and poet. Palgrave's index gives his dates as 1534 to 1604; modern scholarship places his birth in 1550.
Palgrave includes his poem "A Renunciation".

poets.name: George Gascoigne
poets.credit: Portrait of George Gascoigne — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Gascoigne was an English soldier, courtier and poet whose ‘A Hundreth Sundrie Flowres’ (1573) is considered one of the first substantial collections of original English verse and prose.
He also wrote what is often called the first original prose comedy in English and an early treatise on the art of English versification.

poets.name: Thomas Sackville
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Sackville, 1st Earl of Dorset, by John de Critz the Elder · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Sackville, first Earl of Dorset, was an English statesman, Lord High Treasurer and poet. With Thomas Norton he wrote the tragedy Gorboduc (1561). His Induction and Complaint of Henry, Duke of Buckingham first appeared in the 1563 edition of A Mirror for Magistrates and are generally regarded as the finest verse in the collection.
The poems here are taken from Joseph Haslewood’s 1815 reprint of Part III.

poets.name: George Turberville
poets.credit: Portrait: Unknown authorUnknown author — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Turberville (c. 1540 – c. 1610) was an Elizabethan poet and translator, born in Dorset and educated at Winchester College and at Oxford before he entered the Inns of Court in London. In 1568 he went to Russia as secretary to Thomas Randolph, Elizabeth's ambassador to Ivan the Terrible, and wrote verse letters home about the country and its customs, which Richard Hakluyt later printed.

His Epitaphes, Epigrams, Songs and Sonets (1567) mixes love complaints, epigrams and funeral verses, and gathers a loosely told love story of Tymetes and Pyndara. He also translated Ovid's Heroides (1567), the eclogues of Mantuan (1567) and Italian tales, and wrote two popular manuals on falconry and hunting (1575). This edition is the 1567 text, with the spelling kept as printed.

poets.name: O'Gnive
bio: O'Gnive was the bard of Shane O'Neill, and is dated in Eleanor Hull's The Poem-Book of the Gael to about 1560.
His poem on the downfall of the Gael is given here in the English version by Sir Samuel Ferguson, as printed in Hull's anthology (London, 1913).

poets.name: John Higgins
poets.credit: No portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Higgins revised and extended A Mirror for Magistrates, the Tudor collection of verse “tragedies” in which fallen princes and nobles speak their own downfall. His First Part of the Mirror (1574, enlarged in later editions) carries the story back to the legendary kings of Britain and the Roman emperors, and begins with his own verse Induction.

The poems here are taken from Joseph Haslewood’s 1815 reprint, which follows the 1587 text of Part I collated with the editions of 1575 and 1610. Each legend is given with the Lenvoy that Higgins prints after it. One further legend, the death of Sir Nicholas Burdet, is credited to Higgins in the contents of Part III.

poets.name: Torquato Tasso
poets.credit: Portrait of Torquato Tasso aged 22 by Jacopo Bassano (c. 1566) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Torquato Tasso (1544–1595) was an Italian poet born at Sorrento, the son of the courtier-poet Bernardo Tasso. He studied at Padua and Bologna and from the 1560s served the Este court at Ferrara, where he wrote the pastoral play Aminta (1573) and worked for years on his epic of the First Crusade.

Gerusalemme liberata (Jerusalem Delivered), first published in 1581, tells of the Christian siege of Jerusalem under Godfrey of Bouillon and became one of the most influential epics of the late Renaissance. Tasso suffered long periods of mental distress and confinement in the 1570s and 1580s, and later revised the poem as Gerusalemme conquistata. He died in Rome in 1595. Edward Fairfax's English version appeared in 1600.

poets.name: Guillaume de Salluste Du Bartas
poets.credit: Portrait engraved by Nicolas de Larmessin (late 17th or early 18th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Guillaume de Salluste, seigneur Du Bartas (1544–1590), was a Huguenot poet and soldier-diplomat from Gascony who served Henry of Navarre, the future Henri IV. He is remembered above all for La Sepmaine (1578), a long poem on the seven days of Creation, and for its unfinished sequel, La Seconde Sepmaine.

The Sepmaine was a European success, reprinted and translated many times within a few years. Josuah Sylvester's English version, Du Bartas his Divine Weekes and Workes, was completed in the folio of 1611, and the poem was read by Milton among others. It is held here as a work under Du Bartas, following the archive's practice for translated epics.

poets.name: Francis Segar
poets.credit: No portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Francis Segar (also spelt Seager) is known chiefly for The Schole of Vertue, a book of manners in verse printed in 1557. He contributed the legend of Richard, Duke of Gloucester, to the 1563 edition of A Mirror for Magistrates.
The poem here is taken from Joseph Haslewood’s 1815 reprint of Part III, where it is signed F. Seg.

poets.name: John Dolman
poets.credit: No portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Dolman is known as the contributor of the legend of Lord Hastings to the 1563 edition of A Mirror for Magistrates; little else is certain about him.
The poem here is taken from Joseph Haslewood’s 1815 reprint of Part III.

poets.name: Cavyll
poets.credit: No portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Cavyll (also printed Cavil or Cauyll) is known only by the name signed to two tragedies in A Mirror for Magistrates, those of the two Rogers Mortimer and of the Blacksmith and Lord Audley. Haslewood gives no dates or Christian name for him.
The poems here are taken from Joseph Haslewood’s 1815 reprint of Part III.

poets.name: Francis Dingley
poets.credit: No portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Francis Dingley is known only as the author of The Battle of Brampton, or Flodden Field, a poem on the Scottish defeat of 1513 included in A Mirror for Magistrates. Haslewood gives no dates for him.
The poem here is taken from Joseph Haslewood’s 1815 reprint of Part III, where it is signed “qd. Frauncis Dingley”.

poets.name: Sir Edward Dyer
bio: Sir Edward Dyer was a courtier and, with Fulke Greville, one of the "worthy and fellow-poets" whom Sir Philip Sidney celebrated in a pastoral on their meeting.

England's Helicon (1600) prints six poems over the initials "S. E. D." (once "S. E. Dyer"). A. H. Bullen, following Francis Davison's manuscript list of the contributors, reads them as Dyer's, though he thinks one of them, "To Phyllis the fair Shepherdess", really belongs to Thomas Lodge, whose Phillis (1593) contains it. The poems here are all from that anthology, as printed in Bullen's 1887 edition.

poets.name: Thomas Deloney
bio: Thomas Deloney (c. 1543–1600) was a silk-weaver of Norwich and London who became one of the best-known ballad-writers of Elizabethan England, and later wrote prose tales of the clothing trades. His ballads were collected in The Garland of Good Will.

The poem here is the ballad on the defeat of the Spanish Armada and the capture of the great galleass, signed T. D. in the broadside text, as printed in C. H. Firth's Naval Songs and Ballads (Navy Records Society, 1908).

poets.name: Alexander Montgomerie
poets.credit: Portrait of Alexander Montgomerie — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alexander Montgomerie was a Scottish Jacobean courtier and makar, master poet at the court of James VI, best known for the allegorical dream-poem ‘The Cherrie and the Slae.’
A Catholic at a Protestant court, he later fell from royal favour over his religion and political dealings.

poets.name: Tadg O’Bruadin
bio: Tadg O’Bruadin was a bard whom Sigerson, in Bards of the Gael and Gall (1907), dates to 1580. The poem given here is part of a longer address to Doncad O’Brien, fourth Earl of Thomond, on his election as chieftain of his clan.
Sigerson points to the plain speaking of the bard’s advice to a ruler. “A King’s Lesson” is given in his English version.

poets.name: Nicholas Breton
poets.credit: Portrait of Nicholas Breton — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Nicholas Breton was a prolific English poet and prose writer of the Elizabethan and Jacobean periods, admired for pastoral lyrics such as ‘Phillida and Coridon.’
He wrote across a remarkable range of genres, from devotional verse to satire, over a career of some fifty years.

poets.name: Muradî (Sultan Murad III)
bio: Murad III wrote verse under the pen-name Muradi; Gibb's anthology gives one gazel of his.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Teig Dall O'Higgin
bio: Teig Dall O'Higgin was the bard of Brian O'Rourke “of the Bulwarks”, and is dated in Eleanor Hull's The Poem-Book of the Gael to about 1566.
His address to O'Rourke, urging him to rise against the English, is given here in the English version printed in Hull's anthology (London, 1913), where no other translator is named.

poets.name: Giles Fletcher the Elder
poets.credit: Title page of Giles Fletcher, Of the Russe Common Wealth (1591) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons); no portrait of the poet is known
bio: Giles Fletcher the Elder (c. 1549–1611) was an English diplomat, civil servant and poet. Educated at Eton and King's College, Cambridge, he served in Parliament and as a commissioner abroad, and in 1588–89 was Queen Elizabeth's ambassador to Russia. His account of that embassy, Of the Russe Common Wealth (1591), was suppressed at first and later became a much-read description of Muscovy.

His sonnet sequence Licia, or Poemes of Love (1593), issued with a verse dedication, an ode, a dialogue from Lucian, a love-maze and three elegies, is a modest, conventional Elizabethan love cycle; it was printed together with a historical complaint, The Rising to the Crowne of Richard the third. He was the father of the poets Giles Fletcher the Younger and Phineas Fletcher, and uncle of the dramatist John Fletcher.

poets.name: Thomas Blenerhasset
poets.credit: No portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Blenerhasset wrote the Second Part of A Mirror for Magistrates (1578), a series of twelve complaints spoken by British kings and queens from the Roman conquest down to Harold, the last Saxon king. Each is introduced by a short prose dialogue between Memory and Inquisition. He later wrote A Direction for the Plantation in Ulster (1610).
The complaints here are taken from Joseph Haslewood’s 1815 reprint, which follows the 1578 text collated with the edition of 1610. The prose Inductions are left out.

poets.name: Sir Walter Raleigh
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir Walter Raleigh — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Walter Raleigh was an English courtier, explorer and poet, a favourite of Elizabeth I who later fell from favour and was ultimately executed under James I.
His surviving poems, several written while imprisoned in the Tower of London, meditate with stoic clarity on time, fortune and mortality.

poets.name: Edmund Spenser
poets.credit: Portrait of Edmund Spenser — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edmund Spenser was an English poet best known for his epic ‘The Faerie Queene,’ but he also wrote a substantial body of shorter verse, including the pastoral ‘Shepheardes Calender,’ the sonnet sequence ‘Amoretti,’ and the wedding hymns ‘Epithalamion’ and ‘Prothalamion.’
He spent much of his career in Ireland as a colonial administrator, and his poetry stands at the centre of English Renaissance literature.

poets.name: John Lyly
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Lyly was an Elizabethan courtier, prose stylist and dramatist, author of Euphues. Songs from his court comedies are among the earliest English stage lyrics.
Palgrave includes "Cupid and Campaspe", a song from his play Campaspe.

poets.name: Thomas Watson
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Watson was an Elizabethan poet and translator, a friend of Christopher Marlowe, who published the sonnet sequence Hekatompathia (1582) and the madrigals of The First Set of Italian Madrigals Englished (1590). Gilfillan gives his dates as 1560 to about 1592.
Gilfillan prints a short song, The Nymphs to Their May-Queen, and a sonnet.

poets.name: George Peele
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: George Peele (1556–1596) was an English poet and dramatist, born in London and educated at Christ's Hospital and at Oxford. One of the "University Wits" who wrote for the Elizabethan stage, he made his living as a playwright and as a writer of civic pageants, and is best remembered for The Arraignment of Paris, The Old Wives' Tale and David and Bethsabe.

The songs in this file are those A. H. Bullen printed from his plays and from the tilt-yard poem Polyhymnia in Lyrics from the Dramatists of the Elizabethan Age (1889), among them "His golden locks Time hath to silver turned" and the snatches of song in The Old Wives' Tale. Bullen's attributions are followed; his introduction and notes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Thomas Lodge
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Lodge was an English poet, dramatist and prose romancer whose pastoral romance ‘Rosalynde’ (1590) later supplied Shakespeare with the plot of ‘As You Like It.’
His lyric poems, many embedded as songs within his prose fictions, are prized for their musicality and pastoral grace.

poets.name: Alexander Hume
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Alexander Hume was a Scottish poet and minister, a younger son of the Humes of Polwarth, who held the living of Logie in Stirlingshire. Gilfillan says he was born about the middle of the sixteenth century and died in 1609.

He is best known for Of the Day Estivall, a descriptive poem of a summer day published in his Hymnes or Sacred Songs (1599), here printed under Gilfillan's title Thanks for a Summer's Day. He is not to be confused with the nineteenth-century Alexander Hume also in this archive.

poets.name: Robert Greene
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Greene — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Greene was an Elizabethan playwright, pamphleteer and poet, notorious in his own time for his dissolute life and for a posthumous pamphlet often read as an attack on the young William Shakespeare.
His lyric poems, many sung by characters in his prose romances, are notable for their pastoral grace and simplicity.

poets.name: Thomas Kyd
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait
bio: Thomas Kyd (1558–1594) was an English dramatist, born in London and educated at the Merchant Taylors' School. He wrote for the Elizabethan public stage in the late 1580s and early 1590s, and for a time shared a writing room with Christopher Marlowe.

His The Spanish Tragedy, a play of murder, madness and revenge introduced by the ghost of a slain courtier, was among the most popular plays of its age and helped establish the revenge tragedy later taken up by Shakespeare and others. Arrested in 1593 on suspicion of heresy, he died the following year, in his mid-thirties.

poets.name: William Warner
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Warner (c. 1558–1609) was an Elizabethan attorney and poet, best known for Albion's England, a fourteener history of Britain from Noah and Brutus down to the Tudors that was much read in its day.

Francis Meres, writing in 1598, ranked Warner beside Spenser among the English poets. The archive carries the 1597 edition of the poem, twelve books in all; the later additions of 1602–1612 are not included.

poets.name: George Chapman
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of George Chapman by William Hole, frontispiece to The Whole Works of Homer (1616) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Chapman (c. 1559–1634) was an English poet, dramatist and translator. He wrote comedies and tragedies for the Elizabethan and Jacobean stage, and is best remembered for his translations of Homer, the Iliad (1611) and the Odyssey (1614–15), whose rolling fourteeners were celebrated by Keats in his sonnet “On First Looking into Chapman's Homer.”

After Christopher Marlowe's death in 1593 left Hero and Leander unfinished, Chapman completed it in four further Sestiads, published in 1598. His Homer translations are kept in this archive under Homer, with his translator credit; here he appears as a poet in his own right through his continuation of Marlowe's poem.

poets.name: Anthony Munday
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Anthony Munday (1560–1633) was a London writer who worked as an actor, playwright, pamphleteer, translator of romances and, later, as the city's pageant-poet. He wrote the two plays about Robin Hood as Earl of Huntington (acted 1598, printed 1601) with Henry Chettle.
The two songs here are taken from the play's death scenes as printed in A. H. Bullen's Lyrics from the Dramatists of the Elizabethan Age (1889), where they are credited to Munday.

poets.name: Bartholomew Yong
bio: Bartholomew Yong (or Young) translated Jorge de Montemayor's Spanish pastoral romance Diana into English. A. H. Bullen records that the manuscript was finished on 1 May 1583 and that the translation was published in 1598.

England's Helicon (1600) prints some two dozen of the verse passages from his Diana over the signature "Bar. Yong"; Bullen's notes say they are taken from that translation. The poems here are all from that anthology, as printed in Bullen's 1887 edition, and are Yong's English versions of Montemayor's Spanish verse.

poets.name: Anonymous (Elizabethan miscellanies)
bio: "Ignoto", Italian for "the unknown", is the signature England's Helicon (1600) prints under many of its poems. The anthology, first published in 1600 by the stationer John Flasket and enlarged in 1614, was edited under the initials "A. B."; the poems it prints are credited, in this archive, to the poets whose signatures they bear, and Anthony Munday's "Shepherd Tony" is not identified here, since A. H. Bullen argues that Munday was not that poet.

This page gathers the poems of Bullen's 1887 edition that carry no usable name: those signed "Ignoto" or "Anonymous", the poems signed with initials Bullen does not identify (T. B., W. H., I. F., I. G.), the signature "M. N. Howell", of whom Bullen says nothing is known, the "Shepherd Tony" poems, two poems signed with the Earl of Surrey's name that first appeared among the Uncertain Authors of Tottel's Miscellany (1557), and the madrigal and song-book pieces printed without a name. Each note gives the signature as printed.

poets.name: John Wootton
bio: John Wootton is known only as the signer of two pastoral songs in England's Helicon (1600). A. H. Bullen reports that Brydges supposed him to be Sir John Wotton, half-brother of Sir Henry Wotton, a gentleman knighted by Queen Elizabeth who died young; the identification is a supposition.
Both poems here, "Damsetas' Jig in praise of his Love" and "Damsetas' Madrigal in praise of his Daphnis", are from that anthology, as printed in Bullen's 1887 edition.

poets.name: Sir John Harington
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir John Harington by Hieronimo Custodis, c. 1590s · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir John Harington (1560–1612) was an English courtier, translator and epigrammatist, born at Kelston in Somerset. A godson of Queen Elizabeth I, he made his name at court with wit that sometimes cost him her favour; he translated Ariosto's Orlando Furioso into English verse (1591) and wrote a satirical pamphlet on a water closet, The Metamorphosis of Ajax.

His Latin-flavoured English epigrams, pointed and often bawdy or political, circulated in manuscript during his lifetime and were collected after his death. This selection follows the 1618 printing, The Most Elegant and Witty Epigrams, in four books, taken from the Text Creation Partnership transcription. Epigrams whose transcription is too badly damaged to be read with their point intact have been left out.

poets.name: Simon Wastell
bio: Simon Wastell (c. 1560–1632) was an English schoolmaster, born in Westmorland and educated at Queen’s College, Oxford. He became master of the free school at Northampton.

He published A True Christians Daily Delight (1623), a verse summary of the chapters of the Bible, enlarged as Microbiblion (1629). The meditation “Man’s Mortality”, which begins “Like as the damask rose you see”, was long anthologised.

poets.name: Anonymous (Elizabethan songs)
poets.credit: No portrait: these songs come from A. H. Bullen's Lyrics from the Song-Books of the Elizabethan Age and Lyrics from the Dramatists of the Elizabethan Age.
bio: Between 1588 and about 1630 English composers printed hundreds of songs for voices and lute: madrigals, ballets, airs and rounds by Byrd, Dowland, Morley, Wilbye, Jones, Ford, Ravenscroft and others. The words were usually printed without a poet's name, and the composer named on the title-page is not the author of the lyric.

This file gathers the lyrics of A. H. Bullen's Lyrics from the Song-Books of the Elizabethan Age (1887; second edition 1891), each with its song-book in the note, together with the few songs in his Lyrics from the Dramatists of the Elizabethan Age (1889) that belong to anonymous plays and masques. Lyrics that Bullen firmly gives to a named poet are not included here, and Thomas Campion's airs are on his own page.

poets.name: Sir Robert Ayton
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir Robert Ayton (1570–1638) was a Scottish courtier and poet who wrote in Latin, English and Scots. Educated at St Andrews, he rose at the court of James VI and I, was knighted, and served as secretary to Queen Anne of Denmark and later to Henrietta Maria.

The 2 poems here are the pieces printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Anonymous (English broadside ballads)
bio: The broadside ballad was the cheap newspaper, song sheet and picture of early modern England: a single sheet printed on one side with a woodcut, a long title, the name of a tune to sing it to, and verses on love, marriage, murder, wonders, war, trade and politics. London printers issued them by the thousand from the reign of Elizabeth to the end of the seventeenth century, usually without the author's name, and they were pasted on walls and sold in the streets by pedlars.

The texts come from the Text Creation Partnership (EEBO-TCP), whose volunteers hand-keyed early English printed books from the Early English Books Online page images and released them free of restriction. Each ballad is printed here from its TCP transcription with long s normalised and the printers' VV set as W; the original spelling is otherwise kept, and only verse is taken, without imprints, woodcut descriptions or prose paragraphs. A ballad that survives in several printings appears once, from the earliest clean one, and the note lists the other printings. The refrain cues printed as "&c." are kept as printed. A text with any illegible letter in the transcription was left out.

poets.name: Robert Southwell
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Southwell — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Southwell was an English Jesuit priest and poet who was arrested, tortured and executed for treason under Elizabeth I because of his underground Catholic ministry.
His devotional verse, most famously ‘The Burning Babe,’ was admired even by contemporaries hostile to his faith.

poets.name: Francis Bacon
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Francis Bacon, Viscount St Alban, was an English lawyer, statesman and philosopher who rose to be Lord Chancellor. He is remembered chiefly for his essays and his writings on natural philosophy rather than for verse.
Palgrave gives him the short meditation "Life".

poets.name: Henry Constable
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Henry Constable was an Elizabethan sonneteer, author of the sequence Diana (1592). His birth and death dates are uncertain.
Palgrave includes his pastoral song "Diaphenia".

poets.name: Joshua Sylvester
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Joshua Sylvester was an English poet and translator, known for his English version of Du Bartas, Divine Weeks and Works; the translation itself is held in this archive under Guillaume de Salluste Du Bartas, as The Divine Weeks.
Palgrave includes his lyric "Love's Omnipresence".

poets.name: Mark Alexander Boyd
bio: Mark Alexander Boyd (1563–1601) was a Scottish soldier and scholar who spent much of his life on the Continent and wrote Latin verse.
He is remembered chiefly for a single sonnet in Scots, “Fra bank to bank, fra wood to wood I rin.”

poets.name: John Davies of Hereford
poets.credit: 1611 woodcut after Rowland Lockey, facsimile in Grosart's Complete Works (1878) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Davies of Hereford (c. 1565–1618) was an Anglo-Welsh poet and the writing-master of Hereford, later teaching penmanship in Oxford and London. He added "of Hereford" to his name to distinguish himself from his contemporary Sir John Davies, the author of Nosce Teipsum, who has a separate entry in this archive.

The Muses Sacrifice, or Divine Meditations (1612) gathers his devotional verse: meditations and penitential poems, versions of the seven penitential psalms in The Dolefull Dove, funeral elegies in Obit-Rights, and a long run of fourteen-line Essaies. It is dedicated to the Countesses of Bedford and Pembroke and to Lady Cary.

poets.name: Thomas Bastard
poets.credit: No known portrait · text from Chrestoleros (1598), EEBO-TCP A05458 (CC0)
bio: Thomas Bastard (1565/6–1618) was an English clergyman and epigrammatist, born in Blandford Forum, Dorset. He was educated at Winchester College and New College, Oxford, and later held church livings in Dorset, including Bere Regis.

His Chrestoleros: Seven Bookes of Epigrames (1598), dedicated to Lord Mountjoy, is a collection of short satirical and moral verses on lawyers, doctors, preachers, courtiers and fools, together with epitaphs and poems of praise. It is among the best-known English epigram books of the Elizabethan age.

poets.name: Alessandro Tassoni
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of Alessandro Tassoni (c. 1806–1830), Rijksmuseum · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alessandro Tassoni (1565–1635) was a poet and critic from Modena. Born into a noble family, he studied at Bologna, Pisa and Ferrara and spent much of his life in the service of cardinals and princes in Rome and Savoy. He was a combative writer: his Considerazioni sopra le Rime del Petrarca (1609) criticised Petrarch and his imitators, and his Pensieri diversi (1612) questioned received opinion on many subjects.

His best-known work, La secchia rapita (The Rape of the Bucket), published in 1622, is generally regarded as the first Italian mock-heroic epic. Built on a real medieval quarrel between Modena and Bologna that began over a wooden bucket carried off from a well, it sets the gods of Olympus, grand battles and high speeches against comically petty motives. It strongly influenced later mock-epics such as Boileau's Le Lutrin and Pope's Rape of the Lock. James Atkinson's English version appeared in 1825.

poets.name: 'Adlî (Sultan Mehmed III)
bio: Mehmed III, son of Murad III, wrote verse under the pen-name 'Adli.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex
bio: Robert Devereux, 2nd Earl of Essex (1565–1601), was an Elizabethan courtier and soldier, favourite of Queen Elizabeth I, executed for treason after his rising of 1601.
The lyric “A Wish” is traditionally attributed to him and was printed under his name in Palgrave’s The Golden Treasury (1861).

poets.name: Thomas Campion
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Campion — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Campion was an English composer, physician and poet who wrote and set to music his own delicate, classically influenced lyrics.
He also published a treatise arguing for quantitative, unrhymed verse in English, though his own most enduring songs are rhymed airs.

poets.name: Tommaso Campanella
poets.credit: Portrait of Tommaso Campanella by Francesco Cozza (17th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Tommaso Campanella (1568–1639) was a Calabrian Dominican friar, philosopher and poet. He was imprisoned by the Spanish authorities in Naples for twenty-seven years after a failed conspiracy against Spanish rule in 1599, and wrote much of his philosophy, including the utopia The City of the Sun, in prison.

His Italian poems, the Scelta d’alcune poesie filosofiche, mix metaphysics, political protest and religious prophecy in sonnets and canzoni. They were first published in Germany in 1622. This selection of his sonnets is John Addington Symonds’s rhymed English version of 1878.

poets.name: Thomas Nashe
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Nashe was an Elizabethan satirist, pamphleteer and dramatist. Palgrave gives his dates as 1567 to 1601?.
Palgrave opens his anthology with Nashe's "Spring", a song from the play Summer's Last Will and Testament.

poets.name: Sir Henry Wotton
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir Henry Wotton was an English diplomat and Provost of Eton College. He wrote a few poems that circulated widely.
Palgrave includes "Character of a Happy Life" and his lines to Elizabeth of Bohemia.

poets.name: Sir John Davies
poets.credit: Portrait: Unknown authorUnknown author — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir John Davies was an English poet, lawyer and politician who later served as Attorney General for Ireland.
He is best remembered for ‘Nosce Teipsum,’ a long philosophical poem on the nature of the soul, and for witty, compact epigrams on the paradox of human self-knowledge.

poets.name: John Dickenson
bio: John Dickenson is known here as the author of three pastoral lyrics printed in England's Helicon (1600) over the initials "I. D." and "I. M.". A. H. Bullen's notes identify all three as his, from The Shepherds Complaint (c. 1594), a copy of which had been found at Lamport Hall, Northamptonshire.
Earlier guesses had given the poems to Sir John Davies, John Marston, Gervase Markham and John Donne. The three poems here are from the anthology, as printed in Bullen's 1887 edition.

poets.name: Aemilia Lanyer
bio: Aemilia Lanyer (born Aemilia Bassano, 1569–1645), the daughter of a court musician of Venetian descent, grew up in London and was for a time the ward of the Countess of Kent. She later married Alfonso Lanyer, also a court musician, and spent her last decades on the edges of the Jacobean court.

Her Salve Deus Rex Judaeorum (1611) is the first volume of original poems in English published by a woman who sought patronage. It joins a long narrative of the Passion, with a defence of Eve, to verse dedications addressed to the Queen and to the great ladies of the court, and closes with “The Description of Cooke-ham,” among the earliest English country-house poems.

poets.name: Thomas Dekker
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Dekker was a London dramatist and pamphleteer of the age of Shakespeare. The dates of his birth and death are uncertain.
Palgrave includes his song "The Happy Heart", from a play.

poets.name: Barnabe Barnes
bio: Barnabe Barnes (c. 1571–1609) was the son of Richard Barnes, Bishop of Durham, and studied at Brasenose College, Oxford. In 1591 he served with the Earl of Essex's expedition to Normandy.

His sonnet sequence Parthenophil and Parthenophe (1593) was dedicated to William Percy, and A Divine Centurie of Spirituall Sonnets followed in 1595. His tragedy The Devil's Charter was acted before King James in 1607. The poems here are taken from the original editions, in their old spelling.

poets.name: Tobias Hume
bio: Tobias Hume (c. 1569–1645) was a soldier and composer for the viol and lute, who died in the Charterhouse, London.
His First Part of Ayres (1605) contains songs with words of his own, among them the one given here.

poets.name: Bartholomew Griffin
poets.credit: No portrait of the poet is known
bio: Bartholomew Griffin (fl. 1596) was an Elizabethan sonneteer who was buried at Coventry in 1602 and is otherwise little known.

His sonnet cycle Fidessa, More Chaste than Kind (1596) was dedicated to William Essex of Lamebourne in Berkshire, and its third sonnet was pirated in 1599 in a volume printed under Shakespeare's name.

poets.name: William Smith
poets.credit: No portrait of the poet is known
bio: William Smith (fl. 1596) was an Elizabethan poet of whom nothing certain is known beyond his one surviving work.

That work, Chloris, or the Complaint of the Passionate Despised Shepherd (1596), is a pastoral sonnet cycle in the Shakespearean rhyme scheme, opening with sonnets of homage to Spenser as the shepherd Colin Clout.

poets.name: Richard Barnfield
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Richard Barnfield was an English poet whose pastoral and erotic verse, including ‘The Affectionate Shepherd,’ was controversial in its own time for its open homoeroticism.
Some of his lyrics, including ‘As it fell upon a day,’ were long misattributed to his contemporary William Shakespeare.

poets.name: Joseph Hall
poets.credit: Engraving of Joseph Hall by John Payne, 1628 (Emmanuel College, Cambridge) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Joseph Hall (1574–1656) was an English bishop, satirist and moralist, born at Bristow Park in Ashby-de-la-Zouch and educated at Emmanuel College, Cambridge. His contemporaries called him the English Seneca for the plainness and fullness of his prose, and in later life he served as Bishop of Exeter and then of Norwich.

In 1597–98 he published Virgidemiarum, six books of verse satires, which he boasted was the first English satire in the manner of Juvenal and Persius. The first three books, the Toothless Satires, mock bad poets, the universities and the follies of daily life; the last three, the Biting Satires, turn to the vices of the great. Only those pieces that survive intact in the early printed texts are given here.

poets.name: Edmund Bolton
bio: Edmund Bolton was the author of The Elements of Armories (1610) and of the treatise Hypercritica (c. 1618). A. H. Bullen, who calls him one of the most learned men of his time, adds that he was a retainer of George Villiers, Duke of Buckingham, whom he accompanied to Spain in 1623, and that he died about 1633.

England's Helicon (1600) prints one poem over his full name, "A Canzon Pastoral in honour of her Majesty", and four more signed only "E. B."; Bullen's notes take the initials to be Bolton's. All five poems here are from that anthology, as printed in Bullen's 1887 edition.

poets.name: John Marston
poets.credit: No known portrait
bio: John Marston (1575?–1634) was an English satirist, poet and dramatist, born in Oxfordshire and educated at Brasenose College, Oxford, and the Middle Temple. In 1598 he published two books of verse, The Metamorphosis of Pigmalions Image and Certaine Satyres, and The Scourge of Villanie, the second under the pseudonym W. Kinsayder. The satires are harsh, crowded and deliberately obscure, and their rough manner made them a landmark of the Elizabethan verse-satire fashion of the 1590s.

In 1599 the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Bishop of London issued the Bishops' Ban, ordering Marston's two books, with other satires, to be burned. He turned to the stage, writing plays such as Antonio and Mellida, The Malcontent and The Dutch Courtesan, and quarrelled in print and on stage with Ben Jonson. He was ordained in 1609 and served as rector of Christchurch, Hampshire, from 1616 until he resigned the living in 1631; he died in 1634. Only his verse from the 1598 volumes is gathered here, not his plays.

poets.name: Francis Davison
poets.credit: No portrait is known. Poems from A. H. Bullen's edition of Davison's Poetical Rhapsody (1890–91).
bio: Francis Davison (born about 1575; died in or before 1619) was the eldest son of William Davison, Queen Elizabeth's Secretary of State, who was driven from office after the execution of Mary Queen of Scots. He was admitted to Gray's Inn in 1593, wrote speeches for the Gray's Inn masque of 1594, and in May 1595 set out on his travels abroad.

In 1602 he published A Poetical Rhapsody, an anthology of his own poems, his brother Walter's, those of friends he names only 'Anomos', and pieces by Sidney, Campion, Raleigh, Donne and others; a second edition followed in 1608, a third in 1611, and a fourth in 1621, after his death. This page gathers the poems that A. H. Bullen's edition (1890–91) credits to Francis himself: the eclogues, sonnets, odes, madrigals, epigrams and elegies that carry his name.

poets.name: John Chalkhill
bio: John Chalkhill (fl. c. 1600) is known chiefly through Izaak Walton, who described him as a friend of Edmund Spenser, printed songs signed with his name in The Compleat Angler, and in 1683 published his pastoral romance Thealma and Clearchus. Little else is recorded of his life.
Both pieces given here come from Walton's Compleat Angler: Coridon's country song and Piscator's song in praise of the angler's life.

poets.name: Christopher Marlowe
poets.credit: Portrait of Christopher Marlowe — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Christopher Marlowe (1564-1593) was an English poet and dramatist, the most celebrated of the University Wits and the leading figure of Elizabethan tragedy before Shakespeare.

Alongside his plays he left a body of non-dramatic verse, including the unfinished mythological poem Hero and Leander and a translation of Ovid's Amores, and was killed in a Deptford tavern brawl at twenty-nine.

poets.name: William Shakespeare
poets.credit: Portrait of William Shakespeare — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Shakespeare (1564-1616) was an English poet and playwright from Stratford-upon-Avon, widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language.
Beyond his plays, his non-dramatic verse includes the 154 Sonnets, the narrative poems Venus and Adonis and The Rape of Lucrece, and the shorter pieces collected as The Passionate Pilgrim.

poets.name: Ben Jonson
poets.credit: Portrait of Ben Jonson — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ben Jonson (1572-1637) was an English poet and playwright, the dominant literary figure of the Jacobean stage and a rival and friend of Shakespeare.

Beyond his comedies and tragedies, he wrote a substantial body of lyric and occasional verse, including epigrams and elegies collected here from a posthumous volume of his poems and prose "Discoveries."

poets.name: Sir Philip Sidney
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir Philip Sidney · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Philip Sidney (1554–1586) was an English poet, courtier, and soldier, killed at the Battle of Zutphen at thirty-one.
His sonnet sequence Astrophel and Stella (1591) is the first great sequence in English, chronicling an unrequited, thinly-veiled autobiographical love.

poets.name: Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke
poets.credit: Miniature identified as Mary Sidney Herbert, by Nicholas Hilliard (c. 1590s) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke (1561–1621), was the sister of Sir Philip Sidney and the centre of the literary circle at Wilton, where she acted as patron to a generation of poets.

After her brother's death in 1586 she completed the metrical psalter he had begun, revising his Psalms 1–43 and writing Psalms 44–150 herself. The Sidney Psalter, with its extraordinary range of stanza forms, circulated in manuscript and was first printed in 1823.

poets.name: William Bradford
bio: William Bradford (c. 1590–1657) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “New England's Growth”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Roger Williams
bio: Roger Williams (1604–1683) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “God Makes a Path”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Fulke Greville
poets.credit: Unknown artist, c. 1620 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Fulke Greville, Lord Brooke (1554–1628), was an English poet and statesman, the close friend and biographer of Philip Sidney.
His philosophical sequences, published posthumously as Certaine Learned and Elegant Workes, weigh monarchy, religion, and human frailty in dense, difficult verse.

poets.name: Samuel Daniel
poets.credit: Portrait: Unknown authorUnknown author — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Samuel Daniel (1562–1619) was an English poet and historian, admired for the plain, measured elegance of his style.
His sonnet sequence Delia and the narrative poem The Complaint of Rosamond made his early reputation.

poets.name: Michael Drayton
poets.credit: Portrait: Sylvester Harding — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Michael Drayton (1563–1631) was an English poet whose vast body of work spans the sonnet sequence Idea, historical verse, and the topographical epic Poly-Olbion.
His Barons' Wars retells the civil strife of Edward II's reign in stately ottava rima.

poets.name: Thomas Heywood
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Heywood was an English actor and a prolific dramatist. His dates of birth and death are uncertain.
Palgrave includes his song "Pack, clouds, away, and welcome day".

poets.name: John White
poets.credit: No known portrait · text from Davids Psalms in Metre (1655), EEBO-TCP A76568 (CC0)
bio: John White (1575–1648) was an English Puritan clergyman, rector of Holy Trinity, Dorchester, in Dorset, where his long ministry earned him the nickname the ‘Patriarch of Dorchester’. He took a close interest in the colonisation of New England and was instrumental in organising the Dorchester Company and in the founding of the Massachusetts Bay Company.

His metrical version of the Psalms, made for congregational singing in common tunes, was left in the care of his son and printed posthumously in 1655 as Davids Psalms in Metre, with a preface by his successor Stanley Gower. The Psalms here are the 1655 text, with its original spelling. Fourteen psalms whose source pages are damaged or illegible are omitted.

poets.name: William Barton
poets.credit: No known portrait — text from The Book of Psalms in Metre (1644), EEBO-TCP A27789 (CC0)
bio: William Barton (1598?–1678) was an English hymnodist and metrical psalmist. His versification of the Psalms was offered to Parliament as a replacement for the older version of Sternhold and Hopkins.

The Psalms here are the 1644 text of The Book of Psalms in Metre, with its original spelling. All 150 psalms are included, none omitted. Psalms made up of several parts, such as Psalm 119, are given as a single poem, and the printed musical notation, tune directions, argument and marginal notes are left out. A bullet (•) marks a letter that is illegible in the digitised source.

poets.name: Anonymous (American Ballads and Songs)
poets.credit: Archibald Willard, “The Spirit of '76” (originally titled Yankee Doodle), 1876; an illustrative image for the anonymous ballads, not a portrait · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: These ballads, songs, epigrams and satires are printed without an author's name in Burton E. Stevenson's Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922), where they illustrate events from the colonial period to the Civil War.

They are given here in the order of the book, which arranges its poems by historical chapter, from early voyages and settlements through the Revolution, the War of 1812 and the war between the States. Stevenson's own headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: John Fletcher
poets.credit: Portrait: unknown artist — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Fletcher was an English dramatist who collaborated with Francis Beaumont and later with Shakespeare. Songs scattered through his plays are admired for their lyric grace.
