Palgrave includes his song "Melancholy".

poets.name: Henry Peacham
poets.credit: Title page of The Compleat Gentleman (1622) by Henry Peacham, not a portrait (no authenticated likeness is used here) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Peacham was an English emblem writer, schoolmaster and author, best known for The Compleat Gentleman (1622), a guide to the education and accomplishments of a gentleman. He was educated at Cambridge, taught school, and travelled on the Continent; the dates usually given for his birth and death (about 1576 and about 1643) are uncertain, and some sources place his birth in 1578.

Minerva Britanna, or a Garden of Heroical Devices (1612), dedicated to Henry, Prince of Wales, is a book of emblems, each a woodcut or engraving with a Latin motto, English verses and Latin glosses, addressed to patrons, friends and public figures. Only the English verses are given here, under the Latin mottoes that head each emblem.

poets.name: Robert Burton
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Robert Burton was an English scholar and clergyman, a long-time student of Christ Church, Oxford, and the author of the encyclopaedic prose work The Anatomy of Melancholy (1621). Gilfillan gives his birth year as 1576.
His one celebrated poem, the lyric Abstract of Melancholy, stands at the head of the Anatomy and is printed by Gilfillan under the title On Melancholy.

poets.name: Hâfiz Pasha
bio: Hafiz Pasha was the Grand Vezir who, early in the reign of Murad IV, made an unsuccessful attempt to recover Bagdad.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: George Sandys
poets.credit: Portrait of George Sandys (engraving), reproduced by Robert Alonzo Brock and Virgil Anson Lewis · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Sandys (1578–1644) was an English traveller, colonist and poet. In 1610 he journeyed through the Ottoman Empire, Egypt and the Holy Land, and published an account of it as A Relation of a Journey (1615), one of the most widely read travel books of its day. From 1621 he was in Virginia as treasurer of the Virginia Company, and there he worked on his English translation of Ovid's Metamorphoses, published in full in 1632.

Back in England he turned to sacred verse: A Paraphrase upon the Psalms of David (1636) and A Paraphrase upon the Divine Poems (1638), which added Job, Ecclesiastes, Lamentations and the scriptural songs, with musical settings by Henry Lawes. The 1638 volume is the source of the poems here, given in the original spelling.

poets.name: William Alexander, Earl of Stirling
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Alexander, later Earl of Stirling, was a Scottish courtier and poet who served James VI and I. He published the sonnet sequence Aurora in 1604 and a set of verse tragedies, the Monarchicke Tragedies.
Palgrave includes one poem by him, the song "To Aurora".

poets.name: 'Atâ'î
bio: 'Ata'i Nev'i-Zade, the most distinguished man of letters of his time, studied first under his father Nev'i, tutor to Sultan Murad III, and entered the legal profession.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Nef'î
bio: Nef'i, of Erzurum, was the greatest poet of the reign of Murad IV; his book of satirical verses, the Siham-i Qaza, The Shafts of Fate, brought on him the Sultan's anger.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Thomas Middleton
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of Thomas Middleton, from Two New Playes (1657) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Middleton (baptised 1580, buried 1627) was one of the most versatile English dramatists of his day, writing city comedies, tragedies, masques and civic pageants, often in collaboration. A Chaste Maid in Cheapside, The Changeling (with William Rowley) and Women Beware Women are the plays most often revived, and A Game at Chess (1624) was a political sensation.

The lyrics here are those printed in A. H. Bullen's Lyrics from the Dramatists of the Elizabethan Age (1889), including songs from A Mad World, My Masters and The Widow. Songs Bullen lists under Middleton and Rowley jointly, or under Middleton with a query, say so in their notes.

poets.name: Sean Mac Walter Walsh
bio: Sean Mac Walter Walsh is dated by Sigerson, in Bards of the Gael and Gall (1907), to 1604. His dirge for Oliver Grace is described there as composed by the descendant of a Welshman for the descendant of an Anglo-Norman family.
The piece is given here in Sigerson’s English version.

poets.name: Andreas Mac Marcuis
bio: Andreas Mac Marcuis is dated by Sigerson, in Bards of the Gael and Gall (1907), to 1607, the year of the departure of the Ulster earls O’Neill and O’Donnell from Ireland.
His lament for the flight of the earls is given here in Sigerson’s English version.

poets.name: John Webster
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Webster was an English dramatist, author of The White Devil and The Duchess of Malfi. His birth date is unknown.
Palgrave includes "A Land Dirge", a song from The White Devil.

poets.name: John Taylor
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of John Taylor, the Water Poet, by Thomas Cockson, from All the Workes of John Taylor (1630) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Taylor (1580–1653), known as “the Water Poet”, was a Thames waterman who made himself a prolific pamphleteer and verse-writer. He worked the river as a ferryman and sculler, served the navy in his youth, and later enjoyed the notice of the court of James I.

The Sculler (1612) and The Nipping and Snipping of Abuses (1614), both gathered here, are early miscellanies of satires, epigrams, sonnets and anagrams. They mix anti-Catholic invective, jibes at the manners of the city, and verses of compliment to patrons and fellow writers.

poets.name: Walter Davison
poets.credit: No portrait is known. Poems from A. H. Bullen's edition of Davison's Poetical Rhapsody (1890–91).
bio: Walter Davison (born 1581) was the youngest son of William Davison, Queen Elizabeth's Secretary of State, and the brother of Francis Davison, who edited A Poetical Rhapsody (1602). He was serving as a soldier in the Low Countries in 1602, and his brother says he was not eighteen when he wrote the poems, which were printed without his knowledge.

A. H. Bullen's edition (1890–91) assigns to him the 'Roundelay' among the pastorals and the sonnets, odes and elegy that open the second volume (Rhapsody, ii. 1–20), which end with the signature 'W. D.'.

poets.name: John Reynolds
bio: John Reynolds is an English poet of the sixteenth century, of whom little is known; the Oxford Book of English Verse places him in that century. He is not to be confused with the Romantic poet John Hamilton Reynolds (1794–1852).
Quiller-Couch’s Oxford Book of English Verse (1900) prints his song “A Nosegay”, in which a lover asks the flowers whether they have seen his mistress.

poets.name: Sir John Beaumont
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir John Beaumont (1583–1627), 1st Baronet, was born at Grace-Dieu in Leicestershire, the elder brother of the dramatist Francis Beaumont, whose death he mourns in one of the epitaphs printed here. He was a country gentleman and a baronet rather than a professional writer, and his poems circulated among friends and were not collected in his lifetime.

His verse appeared posthumously in Bosworth-field, with a Taste of the Variety of Other Poems (1629), set forth by his son. The book joins a long historical poem on the battle that ended the Wars of the Roses with devotional pieces, verses to the Stuart court and the Duke of Buckingham, elegies and epitaphs, and translations from Virgil, Horace, Persius, Juvenal, Ausonius, Claudian and Prudentius. His easy, balanced couplets are often seen as a forerunner of the polished heroic couplet of later in the century. The 1629 text is damaged in the EEBO-TCP transcription, so lost letters and words are shown in square brackets; two pages of the book (181 and 182), following the epitaph on Lord Wriothesley, are missing from that transcription altogether.

poets.name: Philip Massinger
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of Philip Massinger by Charles Grignion the Elder, c. 1750 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Philip Massinger (1583–1640), born at Salisbury and educated at Oxford, wrote or co-wrote some forty plays, among them A New Way to Pay Old Debts and The City Madam, and often collaborated with John Fletcher, Thomas Dekker and Nathaniel Field. He was buried in London in March 1640.

Bullen thought lyric verse was not Massinger's gift; the two songs here, from The Emperor of the East and The Guardian, are the ones he printed in Lyrics from the Dramatists of the Elizabethan Age (1889).

poets.name: Aurelian Townshend
bio: Aurelian Townshend (born by 1583, died after 1643) was an English court poet of the reign of Charles I. He wrote the masques Albion’s Triumph and Tempe Restored (both 1632) and a handful of songs that were set to music and circulated in manuscript.
His poems were first gathered and edited by E. K. Chambers in 1912. Herbert Grierson included two of them in Metaphysical Lyrics & Poems of the Seventeenth Century (1921).

poets.name: Edward Herbert, Lord Herbert of Cherbury
bio: Edward Herbert, first Baron Herbert of Cherbury (1583–1648), was a Welsh soldier, diplomat, historian, and philosopher, the elder brother of the poet George Herbert. He is remembered for his deist treatise De Veritate (1624) and for his Autobiography.
His poems were published after his death, in Occasional Verses (1665). Herbert Grierson included two of them in Metaphysical Lyrics & Poems of the Seventeenth Century (1921).

poets.name: Phineas Fletcher
poets.credit: No authentic portrait is known.
bio: Phineas Fletcher (1582–1650), the elder son of Giles Fletcher the elder and brother of the poet Giles Fletcher the younger, was educated at Eton and King's College, Cambridge. He took holy orders, and from 1621 until his death he was rector of Hilgay in Norfolk. He is generally regarded as the leading Spenserian poet of his generation.

His chief work, The Purple Island, or The Isle of Man, an allegorical poem in twelve cantos on the human body and soul, was printed at Cambridge in 1633 together with Piscatorie Eclogs and Poeticall Miscellanies. Those two shorter collections are given here: seven eclogues in which fishermen take the place of shepherds, and a miscellany of occasional verses, epigrams, translations from Boethius, psalm paraphrases and hymns. The Purple Island itself is given in full as a work.

poets.name: William Basse
bio: William Basse (c. 1583–c. 1653) was an English poet and a follower of Edmund Spenser, author of Three Pastoral Elegies (1602) and of Great Britain's Sunset (1613), an elegy on Prince Henry.

He is remembered above all for his short elegy on Shakespeare, first printed in 1633, and for the Angler's Song that Izaak Walton printed in The Compleat Angler (1653). The texts here follow R. W. Bond's edition of his Poetical Works (1893).

poets.name: Richard Niccols
poets.credit: No portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Richard Niccols was an English poet educated at Magdalen Hall, Oxford. For the 1610 edition of A Mirror for Magistrates he added ten new tragedies of English kings and princes from Arthur to Richard III, preceded by an Induction, and he rearranged the whole work in chronological order. He also wrote The Cuckow (1607) and The Furies (1614).
The poems here are taken from Part IV of Joseph Haslewood’s 1815 reprint. His long poem England’s Eliza (Part V) is not included here.

poets.name: William Rowley
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Rowley (c. 1585–1626) was an English actor and dramatist who wrote many plays in collaboration with Thomas Middleton, Thomas Dekker, John Ford and others; The Changeling (1622), written with Middleton, is the best known. He died in 1626.
The songs here are those Bullen assigns to Rowley from The Thracian Wonder, a play printed in 1661 whose authorship is uncertain, in his Lyrics from the Dramatists of the Elizabethan Age (1889).

poets.name: William Drummond of Hawthornden
poets.credit: Portrait: Abraham van Blijenberch — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Drummond of Hawthornden (1585–1649) was the first considerable Scottish poet to write in English rather than Scots.
His polished sonnets and elegies were shaped by his wide reading in French and Italian verse.

poets.name: Johann Heermann
poets.credit: Portrait of Johann Heermann, 17th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Johann Heermann was born at Raudten in Silesia in 1585 and died at Lissa (Leszno) in 1647. He was a Lutheran pastor at Köben from 1611, and his ministry was disturbed by illness and by the troubles of the Thirty Years' War; he left Köben for Lissa in 1638.
His hymns appeared in collections such as Devoti musica cordis (1630). The English versions here are Catherine Winkworth's in Lyra Germanica (1855).

poets.name: Giles Fletcher the Younger
poets.credit: No authentic portrait is known.
bio: Giles Fletcher the Younger (c. 1586–1623) was a Cambridge poet and divine, the younger brother of Phineas Fletcher and a disciple of Spenser.
His Christ's Victory and Triumph, first published at Cambridge in 1610, is his major work, and Milton read it.

poets.name: John Donne
poets.credit: Portrait of John Donne by Isaac Oliver · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Donne (1572–1631) was an English poet and cleric, the foremost of the metaphysical poets.
His verse — by turns erotic, witty, and devout — moved from the love poems of his youth to the religious sonnets of his years as Dean of St Paul's.

poets.name: Rhys Prichard
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Rhys Prichard, "the Vicar Prichard", was vicar of Llandovery, whose moral verses in the free metres of the folk-song, collected as Canwyll y Cymry ("The Welshmen's Candle"), were loved in Wales for two centuries.
His poem "A Good Wife" is given in English verse by Alfred Perceval Graves in A Celtic Psaltery (1917).

poets.name: Richard Corbet
poets.credit: Portrait of Richard Corbet, Bishop of Norwich, engraved by Sylvester Harding · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Corbet was born at Ewell in Surrey in 1582, was educated at Westminster School and Christ Church, Oxford, and became a celebrated wit among the university poets. He rose to be Dean of Christ Church, then Bishop of Oxford in 1628 and Bishop of Norwich in 1632, and died on 28 July 1635. He was a friend of Ben Jonson and a famous humorist in the pulpit and out of it.

His poems circulated in manuscript and were first printed after his death, in 1647 and again in 1648 and 1672. The fourth edition, edited by Octavius Gilchrist in 1807, is used here. The English poems are given in order: the mock-heroic Iter Boreale, the verse letters, elegies and epitaphs, and the ballad The Faeryes Farewell, his best-known piece.

poets.name: Francis Beaumont
poets.credit: Portrait: Francis Kyte — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Francis Beaumont was an English dramatist, best known for his plays written in collaboration with John Fletcher. His own poems were collected and published after his death.
Palgrave includes his lines on the tombs in Westminster Abbey.

poets.name: John Ford
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Ford (baptised 1586 in Devon, died about 1639) trained at the Middle Temple and wrote for the Caroline stage, both alone and with Thomas Dekker and William Rowley. His best-known plays are 'Tis Pity She's a Whore, The Broken Heart and Perkin Warbeck.

The two songs here, from The Lover's Melancholy (1629) and The Broken Heart (1633), are the ones printed under his name in A. H. Bullen's Lyrics from the Dramatists of the Elizabethan Age (1889). Songs from The Sun's Darling, which he wrote with Dekker, are filed under Dekker.

poets.name: 'Azîzî
bio: 'Azizi was the pen-name of a certain Mustafa of Constantinople, who held the appointment of provost of the Seven Towers and is known mainly from his Shehr-engiz.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Nathaniel Field
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Nathaniel Field (1587–1620) began as a boy actor, became a leading player of his generation and also wrote plays: A Woman Is a Weathercock and Amends for Ladies, and The Fatal Dowry with Philip Massinger.
The two songs here are those Bullen printed from his comedies in Lyrics from the Dramatists of the Elizabethan Age (1889).

poets.name: Sir Francis Kynaston
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir Francis Kynaston (also spelled Kinaston) was born at Oteley in Shropshire in 1587. He matriculated at Oriel College, Oxford, in 1601, took his B.A. from St Mary Hall in 1604, took his M.A. from Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1609, and was reincorporated at Oxford two years later. He was knighted in 1618, sat in Parliament for Shropshire from 1621, served as a proctor at Cambridge in 1635, and died in 1642. He was also known for translating part of Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde into Latin.

His chief English poems appeared in 1642 as Leoline and Sydanis, a romance in rhyme royal, together with Cynthiades, a series of amorous lyrics addressed to a mistress under the name of Cynthia. The texts here are taken from George Saintsbury's edition (Minor Poets of the Caroline Period, vol. II, 1906); the long romance is filed under Works and the Cynthiades are given as separate poems.

poets.name: Anonymous (Naval Songs and Ballads)
bio: The songs and ballads in this collection are by unknown hands: sailors, ballad-writers and the printers of broadside sheets, who sang of sea-fights, press-gangs, pirates, storms, the pay of seamen and the farewells of lovers. They run from the fourteenth-century ballad on the battle of Sluys to the sea songs of the Crimean War.

They are taken from Naval Songs and Ballads, selected and edited by C. H. Firth (Navy Records Society, vol. 33, 1908), which draws on manuscripts, broadsides and songsters. The spelling of each text is kept, with Firth's titles and any date or attribution printed with the broadside given in the note; his introduction, headnotes and notes are left out. Songs whose authors Firth names appear under those poets, and ballads already held elsewhere in the archive are not repeated.

poets.name: George Herbert
poets.credit: Portrait of George Herbert · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Herbert (1593–1633) was a Welsh-born English poet and priest, a central figure of the metaphysical school.
His single collection, The Temple (1633), published just after his death, gathers the devotional lyrics for which he is loved.

poets.name: Izaak Walton
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Izaak Walton was an English biographer and angler, the author of The Compleat Angler (1653) and of the Lives of Donne, Wotton, Hooker, Herbert and Sanderson.
Gilfillan prints one poem under his name, The Angler's Wish, a short pastoral lyric of the fisherman's contented life.

poets.name: Thomas May
bio: Thomas May (1595–1650) was an English poet, dramatist and historian, educated at Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge, and Gray's Inn. He wrote several plays and translated Virgil's Georgics, but he is remembered chiefly for his rhymed English version of Lucan's Pharsalia (1627) and for his own continuation of Lucan's story.

His Continuation of Lucan's Historicall Poem (1630), in seven books, carries the narrative to the death of Julius Caesar. In the 1640s he became the historian of the Long Parliament. This archive presents his Continuation here, and his Pharsalia under Lucan.

poets.name: Thomas Carew
poets.credit: Portrait: Anthony van Dyck — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Carew (1595–1640) was an English Cavalier poet at the court of Charles I, admired for the polish of his amorous lyrics.
His Poems (1640) circulated widely and shaped the courtly style later followed by Lovelace and Suckling.

poets.name: James Shirley
poets.credit: Portrait: unknown artist — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James Shirley was an English dramatist of the reign of Charles I, one of the last playwrights of the Jacobean and Caroline stage.
Palgrave includes two of his lyrics, "The Last Conqueror" and "Death the Leveller".

poets.name: Simon Dach
poets.credit: Portrait of Simon Dach, 17th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Simon Dach was born at Memel in 1605 and died at Königsberg in 1659. He became professor of poetry at the University of Königsberg in 1639 and was the centre of a circle of poets in that city, writing a large body of occasional verse and some hymns.
The English versions here are Catherine Winkworth's in Lyra Germanica (1855).

poets.name: Arthur Capel, 1st Baron Capel
poets.credit: Arthur Capel, 1st Baron Capel, by Henry Peart the elder, c. 1660 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Arthur Capel, 1st Baron Capel (1604–1649), was a Royalist commander in the English Civil War. Captured after the fall of Colchester in 1648, he was imprisoned in the Tower of London and beheaded in 1649; the poem "Loyalty Confined", traditionally attributed to him, is said to have been written there.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Christopher Harvey
bio: Christopher Harvey (1597–1663) was an English clergyman and poet. His best-known book, The Synagogue (1640), was written in imitation of George Herbert’s The Temple, and was long printed with it.
The poems printed here are those given in The Oxford Book of English Mystical Verse (1917), edited by D. H. S. Nicholson and A. H. E. Lee; the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Jasper Mayne
bio: Jasper Mayne (1604–1672) was an English clergyman, scholar and dramatist, a student of Christ Church, Oxford, and later Archdeacon of Chichester.
He wrote the plays The City Match and The Amorous War, translated Lucian, and contributed commendatory and occasional verse.

poets.name: Tukaram
poets.credit: Oleograph of Tukaram, Ravi Varma Press (before 1945) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Tukaram (1608-49) was a Marathi poet-saint of the village of Dehu, near Pune, and the most popular of the Varkari devotional poets of Maharashtra. A devotee of Vithoba (Vitthal) of Pandharpur, he composed many short songs (abhangs) in plain Marathi, addressed to God as mother, father and friend, and often turned against pride, hypocrisy and empty ritual.

These seventy-six hymns are Nicol Macnicol's verse renderings in Psalms of Maratha Saints (1919), in The Heritage of India series; each abhang is cited there to the Indu Prakash edition of Tukaram's works.

poets.name: Sir John Suckling
poets.credit: Portrait: Anthony van Dyck — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir John Suckling (1609–1641) was an English Cavalier poet and courtier, famed for his wit and his invention of the card game cribbage.
His collected verse, Fragmenta Aurea (1646), mixes light, conversational love lyrics with plays and prose.

poets.name: Sidney Godolphin
bio: Sidney Godolphin (1610–1643) was an English poet and Member of Parliament, a friend of Thomas Hobbes and of Lord Falkland and the Great Tew circle. He was killed fighting for the king at Chagford, Devon, in February 1643.
His few lyrics circulated in manuscript; they are among the finest short love poems of the Cavalier generation and were prized by H. J. C. Grierson in his anthology of seventeenth-century lyrics.

poets.name: Martin Parker
bio: Martin Parker (died about 1656) was one of the most prolific London ballad-writers of the reign of Charles I, supplying the printers of Cheapside and the Old Bailey with moral, comic, news and love ballads, many signed with his initials M. P. Little is known of his life, and the dates given here are the catalogue's own uncertain ones.

The ballads in this archive are single-sheet broadsides, each from the Text Creation Partnership (EEBO-TCP) transcription of its printed sheet. Attribution follows the TCP catalogue, which names Parker, or the printed signature M. P.; initials alone cannot prove authorship, and the note on each ballad records its TCP number and printing date. Long s is normalised and the original spelling otherwise kept.

poets.name: Charles I
bio: Charles I (1600–1649), King of England, Scotland and Ireland from 1625, was executed at Whitehall on 30 January 1649 after defeat in the Civil War.
Verses attributed to him circulated in print soon after his death; "Majesty in Misery", said to have been written during his imprisonment at Carisbrooke Castle in 1648, is the best known.

poets.name: Pedro Calderón de la Barca
poets.credit: Engraving from Las Glorias Nacionales, 1852 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Pedro Calderón de la Barca (1600–1681) was born in Madrid and educated by the Jesuits before studying at Alcalá and Salamanca. After soldiering in Italy and Flanders he became court dramatist to Philip IV, was made a knight of the Order of Santiago, and in 1651 was ordained a priest. He wrote for the court theatre and the public stage, and he was the chief author of the sacred one-act plays called autos sacramentales.

Among the best known of his comedias are La vida es sueño and El alcalde de Zalamea. Edward FitzGerald, later famous for the Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám, translated eight of them very freely: six were printed in 1853 and two more in 1865. Those versions are given here as eight verse plays, with the prose speeches of the comic servants kept as FitzGerald wrote them.

poets.name: William Strode
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Strode (1601–1645) was an English poet and clergyman, Public Orator of Oxford University and Canon of Christ Church. His verse circulated in manuscript and was first collected long after his death.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: William Cartwright
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Cartwright was an English clergyman, playwright and poet, educated at Westminster School and Christ Church, Oxford. He became a succentor of Salisbury Cathedral in 1642 and died of camp fever in the first years of the Civil War.
His Comedies, Tragi-comedies, With other Poems appeared in 1651 with commendatory verses by many of the leading writers of the day. Gilfillan prints three of his poems.

poets.name: Laurence Price
bio: Laurence (or Lawrence) Price was a London ballad-writer and pamphleteer who was at work from the 1620s and, by the catalogue's reckoning, into the 1680s, writing for the popular press on murders, monsters, wonders, love and the quarrels of his day, often signing L. P. Nothing is firmly known of his life.

The ballads in this archive are broadside sheets from the Text Creation Partnership (EEBO-TCP) transcriptions. Attribution follows the TCP catalogue, which names Price, or the printed signature L. P.; the note on each ballad records its TCP number and printing date. Long s is normalised and the original spelling otherwise kept.

poets.name: Nathaniel Whiting
poets.credit: No portrait of Whiting is known.
bio: Nathaniel Whiting was a Cambridge-educated poet and later a Puritan minister. He took his B.A. at Queens' College, Cambridge, in 1631 and his M.A. in 1635, and in 1637 published, under the initials N. W., the long verse romance Le Hore di Recreatione, or The Pleasant History of Albino and Bellama. He later became minister of Aldwincle in Northamptonshire and was deprived of the living at the Restoration.

Albino and Bellama, printed with the dream-poem Il Insonio Insonnadado that defends poetry against its critics, is written in an odd, inventive diction. The text here follows George Saintsbury's Minor Poets of the Caroline Period, vol. III (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1921).

poets.name: Thomas Jordan
poets.credit: No portrait is known; none sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Jordan (c. 1612–1685) was an English actor, dramatist and poet. He began as a player in London before the theatres were closed in 1642, and published his verse in small, miscellaneous volumes through the Civil War, the Interregnum and the Restoration.

His Divine Raptures (1646) turns everyday sights — a weathercock, a windmill, a ship — into pious meditations; the later volumes gathered here, Divinity and Morality in Robes of Poetry and The Muses Melody, both printed undated, mix moral epigrams, elegies, acrostics and occasional verse with amorous and satirical pieces.

poets.name: James Graham, Marquess of Montrose
bio: James Graham, 1st Marquess of Montrose (1612–1650), was a Scottish nobleman and Royalist general in the Civil Wars, executed in Edinburgh in 1650.
His verse, a few lyrics and a famous epitaph for Charles I, has outlived most of his contemporaries’ more ambitious work.

poets.name: Sir William Davenant
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir William Davenant · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir William Davenant (1606–1668) was an English poet and playwright who served as Poet Laureate from 1638. A bridge between the ages of Shakespeare and Dryden, he helped reopen and reshape the English theatre after the Restoration.
His most ambitious work is the unfinished heroic poem Gondibert (1651); the collection Madagascar; with Other Poems (1638) gathers his courtly and occasional verse.

poets.name: Johann Rist
poets.credit: Portrait of Johann Rist, 17th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Johann Rist was born at Ottensen near Hamburg in 1607 and died at Wedel in 1667. A Lutheran pastor at Wedel from 1635, he was also a dramatist and a prolific poet; he was crowned imperial poet laureate in 1644 and ennobled in 1653, and he wrote hundreds of hymns.
The English versions here are Catherine Winkworth's in Lyra Germanica (1855).

poets.name: Paul Gerhardt
poets.credit: Portrait of Paul Gerhardt, 17th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Paul Gerhardt was born in Gräfenhainichen in Saxony in 1607 and died at Lübben in 1676. A Lutheran pastor, he served at Mittenwalde from 1651 and from 1657 as deacon of St Nicholas's church in Berlin; in 1666 he lost that post for refusing to sign an edict restricting doctrinal controversy, and from 1669 he was archdeacon at Lübben.
His hymns, many of them set to melodies by Johann Crüger, are among the best known in German Protestant worship. The English versions here are Catherine Winkworth's in Lyra Germanica (1855).

poets.name: Piers Ferriter
bio: Piers Ferriter was a poet of Norman descent and a Kerry soldier. Sigerson, in Bards of the Gael and Gall (1907), describes him as a cultured poet and the last of the Catholic cavaliers to hold out against Cromwell; he was executed at Killarney in 1653, after the fall of Ross Castle.
“Lay Thine Arms Aside, Young Maid” is a gallant love-song in which the poet begs a girl to hide her charms. It is given here in Sigerson’s English version.

poets.name: Sir William Killigrew
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir William Killigrew by Anthony van Dyck, 1638 (Tate Britain) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir William Killigrew (1606–1695), of Kempton Park, Middlesex, was an English court official who served under both Charles I and Charles II. He was the brother of the dramatist Thomas Killigrew, and Anthony van Dyck painted his portrait in 1638.

In old age he published Mid-night and Daily Thoughts, in Prose and Verse (1694), a book of short devotional meditations, each followed or replaced by a rhymed poem on a Christian theme: repentance, faith, time, the Christian festivals and the fear of death. The poems collected here are the verse of that book.

poets.name: Mirza Khan Ansari
bio: Mirza Khan Ansari was probably a descendant of Pir Roshan, founder of the Roshanian sect among the Eastern Afghans. Raverty reports that he began writing poetry in A.H. 1040 (about A.D. 1630), and that his odes were later gathered into a Diwan under his name.

Some claimed that his real name was Fath Khan of the Yusufzi tribe, but Raverty argues from old manuscripts that Mirza Khan Ansari is the name he bore. His poems are Sufi and mystical in tone, and the selection includes several built on the letters of the Arabic alphabet.

poets.name: Henry King
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Henry King (1592–1669) was an English poet and Bishop of Chichester.
He is remembered above all for ‘The Exequy,’ his elegy for his young wife — one of the great grief poems of the century.

poets.name: John Milton
poets.credit: Portrait, Christ’s College, Cambridge · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Milton (1608–1674) was an English poet and polemicist, author of the epic Paradise Lost. He went blind in mid-life and composed his greatest work by dictation.
Though he predates the Romantic movement, his blank verse and his figure of Satan shaped nearly every English poet who followed.

poets.name: Sir Aston Cokain
poets.credit: Engraving of Sir Aston Cokain, published 1796 (after an earlier print) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Aston Cokain (also spelt Cokayne or Cockayne, 1608–1684) was a Derbyshire gentleman, Royalist and minor poet and dramatist, born at Ashbourne Hall. He was educated at Trinity College, Cambridge, and travelled in France and Italy before settling into the life of a country squire. He was created a baronet in 1642 and sided with the King in the Civil War, after which his estates were much reduced.

Cokain moved in literary circles and was a friend and admirer of Philip Massinger and John Fletcher, on whose shared grave in Southwark he wrote an epitaph, and a kinsman of Charles Cotton. His chief book, A Chain of Golden Poems (1658), gathers epigrams, love and funeral elegies, songs, eclogues, verse letters and a satire, together with two comedies, The Obstinate Lady and Trappolin Suppos'd a Prince. It is a lively record of Cavalier manners and of the Derbyshire gentry around him.

poets.name: Sir Richard Fanshawe
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir Richard Fanshawe was an English diplomat and royalist who served the Stuarts in Spain and Portugal. Gilfillan says he was born at Ware in 1607 or 1608 and was in Madrid in 1666.
He is best known as a translator, notably of Guarini's Il Pastor Fido (1647/48), and he published some original poems as well. Gilfillan prints his version of a Spanish sonnet, The Spring.

poets.name: Anne Bradstreet
poets.credit: Title page of The Tenth Muse (London, 1650); no authentic portrait of Bradstreet survives · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Anne Bradstreet (c. 1612–1672), born Anne Dudley in Northampton, England, emigrated to Massachusetts in 1630 with her husband Simon Bradstreet and her parents, Thomas and Dorothy Dudley. She raised eight children and is regarded as the first English-language poet of the American colonies, writing amid the work of a household in the new settlements, and she died at North Andover.

Her brother-in-law took a manuscript to London, where it appeared without her knowledge as The Tenth Muse Lately Sprung Up in America (1650). A revised and enlarged edition, Several Poems, was printed in Boston in 1678, six years after her death, and is the source of this selection; it holds her long quaternions and historical poems alongside the shorter personal poems, 'Contemplations' and the verses to her husband and children.

poets.name: Richard Crashaw
poets.credit: Portrait: Unknown artistUnknown artist — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Crashaw (1613–1649) was an English metaphysical poet known for the ecstatic, ornate devotion of his sacred verse.
A convert to Catholicism, he collected his poems as Steps to the Temple (1646), consciously following George Herbert.

poets.name: John Cleveland
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of John Cleveland, frontispiece to his Works (1687) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Cleveland (1613–1658) was an English Royalist poet and satirist, a fellow of St John's College, Cambridge, who lost his post when the Civil War came and served the King's cause with his pen. He is best known for his sharp political satires against Scots, Parliament men and Puritans, and for love poems in the most extravagant 'strong-lined' conceited style.

Cleveland's verse was enormously popular in the 1650s and was reprinted many times, though the collections that carry his name also contain pieces by other hands. The text here follows George Saintsbury's Minor Poets of the Caroline Period, vol. III (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1921), using the poems he prints as Cleveland's and leaving out those he marks as disputed.

poets.name: Samuel Butler
poets.credit: Samuel Butler, attributed to Pieter Borsseler, c. 1665 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Samuel Butler (1613–1680) was an English poet, the author of Hudibras (1663–78), a mock-heroic satire on the Puritans written in galloping octosyllabic couplets. Little is known of his early life, and he died poor.

The archive also holds the whole of Hudibras, in three parts, as a work of its own. The short pieces listed here are those that James Parton printed as his epigrammatic and satirical verses in his anthology of English humorous poetry.

poets.name: Khushhal Khan Khattak
bio: Khushhal Khan, chief of the Khattak tribe, was born in 1613 and succeeded his father in 1640 after the latter was wounded fighting the Yusufzis. He served the Mughal emperors Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb, then fell under Aurangzeb's suspicion, was sent away as a prisoner, and afterwards led Afghan resistance to the Mughals, dying free in the mountains.

Raverty calls him alike a warrior and a poet. Unlike the Sufi poets in this volume he writes on whatever was on his mind: spring and love, wine, the faults of tribes and rulers, and the call to Afghan unity against the Mughals.

poets.name: Jeremy Taylor
bio: Jeremy Taylor (1613–1667) was an English clergyman, chaplain to Charles I and later Bishop of Down and Connor. He is best known for his prose devotions Holy Living (1650) and Holy Dying (1651).
A few devotional poems and hymns of his are still anthologised, among them the hymn on Heaven.

poets.name: William Hammond
poets.credit: No known portrait · Text from EEBO-TCP A87057 (Poems. By W. H., London, 1655)
bio: William Hammond is a Royalist-period lyric poet known from a single book, Poems, published in London by Thomas Dring in 1655. Its title page gives only the initials "W. H."; the attribution to William Hammond, born in 1614, comes from the library catalogue record of the volume.

The book gathers love lyrics, pastoral dialogues, verse letters, elegies and English versions of Horace. Many of the poems are addressed to a close family circle: his kinsman T. S., a brother, H. S., mourned as drowned, a sister, Mrs. S., and an uncle, Mr. G. Sandys. Little else about his life can be stated from the book itself.

poets.name: Richard Baxter
poets.credit: After Robert White, engraving, c. 1670 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Baxter (1615–1691) was an English Puritan minister, theologian and controversialist, long associated with Kidderminster in Worcestershire. A prolific author of devotional prose, he was a leading Nonconformist voice after the Restoration and suffered fines and imprisonment for his beliefs.

His metrical Paraphrase on the Psalms of David was published in 1692, the year after his death, 'left fitted for the press by his own hand', together with a handful of hymns. In it he marks his own additions to the biblical text in square brackets. Several psalms are followed by alternative versions, including one by George Herbert.

poets.name: Abraham Cowley
poets.credit: Portrait of Abraham Cowley by Sir Peter Lely · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Abraham Cowley (1618–1667) was among the most celebrated English poets of his century, a child prodigy admired for his metaphysical wit.
His 1656 Poems gathers odes, elegies, and the love sequence The Mistress.

poets.name: Johann Franck
bio: Johann Franck was born at Guben in Lusatia in 1618 and died there in 1677. A lawyer, he served as burgomaster of Guben and as its representative in the Lusatian diet, and wrote hymns and occasional verse alongside his public duties.
The English versions here are Catherine Winkworth's in Lyra Germanica (1855).

poets.name: Edward Sherburne
bio: Sir Edward Sherburne (1618–1702) was an English Royalist, scholar and poet, Clerk of the Ordnance, and translator of Seneca and Manilius.
His Salmacis, Lyrian and Sylvia, Forsaken Lydia, The Rape of Helen … with Severall other Poems and Translations appeared in 1651.

poets.name: Joseph Beaumont
bio: Joseph Beaumont (1616–1699) was an English clergyman and devotional poet. Educated at Peterhouse, Cambridge, he later became Master of that college and Regius Professor of Divinity. His long religious poem Psyche, or Love's Mystery appeared in 1648.

His shorter poems stayed in manuscript until they were edited, with their seventeenth-century spelling, by Eloise Robinson as The Minor Poems of Joseph Beaumont (1914). They are printed here from that edition.

poets.name: William Chamberlayne
poets.credit: Portrait: unknown artist — CC BY 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Chamberlayne (1619–1689) was a physician of Shaftesbury in Dorset who is recorded as having fought on the royalist side at Newbury.
He is remembered for Pharonnida (1659), a long heroic poem in rhymed couplets, which is given here in full.

poets.name: Richard Lovelace
poets.credit: Portrait: William Dobson — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Lovelace (1617–1657) was an English Cavalier poet who fought and was imprisoned for the Royalist cause.
Best remembered for ‘To Althea, from Prison’ and ‘To Lucasta, Going to the Wars,’ his posthumous Lucasta volumes appeared in 1659.

poets.name: Sir John Berkenhead
bio: Sir John Berkenhead (1617–1679) was a royalist journalist and satirist, editor of the Oxford newsbook Mercurius Aulicus during the Civil War, and later a member of Parliament and a knight.
The poem here is the ballad on the St James's Day fight of 1666 against the Dutch, which C. H. Firth prints in Naval Songs and Ballads (Navy Records Society, 1908) with the attribution to Berkenhead.

poets.name: William Habington
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Habington (1605–1654) was an English poet whose single collection, Castara (1634), celebrates — unusually for the age — his courtship and marriage to one woman.

poets.name: Sir John Denham
poets.credit: Portrait: unknown artist — CC BY 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir John Denham (1615–1669) was an English poet best known for Cooper's Hill (1642), a landscape meditation that founded the English topographical poem.
His couplets were much admired by Dryden and Pope for their balance and control.

poets.name: Jacob Steendam
bio: Jacob Steendam was a seventeenth-century Dutch poet associated with New Netherland, the Dutch colony that became New York.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “The Praise of New Netherland” and “The Complaint of New Amsterdam”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Thomas Randolph
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Randolph · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Randolph (1605–1635) was an English poet and dramatist, a celebrated wit at Cambridge and an adopted ‘son’ of Ben Jonson.
He died at twenty-nine; his collected Poems appeared three years later.

poets.name: Edmund Waller
poets.credit: Portrait of Edmund Waller · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edmund Waller (1606–1687) was an English poet and politician whose smooth, regular couplets influenced the coming Augustan style.
He wrote equally fluent verse for both sides of the Civil War, a flexibility that shadowed his reputation.

poets.name: Sir Charles Sedley
poets.credit: Portrait: Engraving after a painting by Michael Van der Gucht — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Charles Sedley (1639–1701) was an English Restoration poet, playwright, and courtier known for his wit and libertine reputation at the court of Charles II.

poets.name: George Wither
poets.credit: Portrait: Original uploader was Algabal at en.wikipedia — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Wither (1588–1667) was a prolific English poet and pamphleteer whose early verse, collected as Juvenilia, made him one of the most popular poets of his generation before his turn to satire and religious controversy.

poets.name: Donncad O’Futail
bio: Donncad O’Futail is dated by Sigerson, in Bards of the Gael and Gall (1907), to 1619. The poem given here is an extract from a longer piece printed in the Miscellany of the Celtic Society, on two Irish soldiers who went to serve abroad, one of them Concobar O’Driscoll, son of Sir Fingein O’Driscoll.
“Two Champions of Christendom” is given in Sigerson’s English version.

poets.name: Richard Brathwaite
poets.credit: Richard Brathwaite, engraving by Charles Pye after George Clint (1823), from a print by Robert Vaughan prefixed to The English Gentleman · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Brathwaite (also spelled Brathwait, c. 1588-1673) was an English poet and prose writer from Westmorland, in the north of England. He studied at Oxford and Cambridge, spent most of his life in the north, and wrote a long run of conduct books, moral treatises and verse, among them The English Gentleman (1630).

The poems here come from two early volumes. A Strappado for the Divell (1615) mixes satirical epigrams, verse addresses to the townsfolk of Kendal, and the Ovidian tale of Pyramus and Thisbe. Natures Embassie (1621) gathers satires, funeral elegies, pastoral eclogues and the bird poems that give the book its name. Poems too badly damaged in the digital transcription of the printed text have been left out.

poets.name: William Browne of Tavistock
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Browne of Tavistock (1590–1645) was an English pastoral poet from Devon, educated at Exeter College, Oxford, and the Inner Temple. A follower of Spenser, he is best known for Britannia's Pastorals (1613–16), a long poem of the Devon countryside, and for The Shepherd's Pipe (1614), to which his friend George Wither also contributed.

He also wrote the masque of the Inner Temple, the sonnet sequences gathered here under Cælia and Visions, and a celebrated epitaph on Mary Sidney, Countess of Pembroke. His verse is prized for its close, affectionate observation of birds, flowers, rivers and rural customs.

poets.name: Bakhtî (Sultan Ahmed I)
bio: Ahmed I wrote verse under the pen-name Bakhti.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Fârisî (Sultan 'Osman II)
bio: 'Osman II was named Sultan in 1618, in the fourteenth year of his age, when the imbecile Mustafa I was removed from the throne, and wrote verse under the pen-name Farisi.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Nâ'ilî
bio: Of Na'ili little is known, says Gibb, save that he was a native of Constantinople, that his real name was Yeni-Zade Mustafa Efendi, and that he held a position under government.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Muradî (Sultan Murad IV)
bio: Murad IV ascended the throne at twelve years of age, at a time when the Empire was in a state of woeful disorder, and wrote verse under the pen-name Muradi.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Robert Herrick
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Herrick · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Herrick (1591–1674) was an English poet and clergyman, the most prolific of the Cavalier poets.
His single vast collection, Hesperides (1648), moves between pagan celebration, courtly love, and country ritual — over a thousand short poems in one book.

poets.name: Francis Quarles
poets.credit: Portrait of Francis Quarles (engraving, c. 1640) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Francis Quarles (1592–1644) was an English poet and prose writer, born in Essex and educated at Christ's College, Cambridge, and Lincoln's Inn. He served as cupbearer to Elizabeth of Bohemia, the daughter of James I, and later as secretary to James Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh, in Ireland. In 1639 he was appointed chronologer of the City of London, and he remained a committed royalist during the Civil War.

Quarles was among the most widely read devotional writers of the seventeenth century. His Divine Fancies (1633) gathers epigrams, meditations and observations in verse; his best-known work, Emblemes (1635), pairs engraved emblems with sacred poems, and was followed by Hieroglyphikes of the Life of Man (1638). His popularity endured for generations among readers of plain, pointed religious verse.

poets.name: Thomas Bancroft
poets.credit: No known portrait
bio: Thomas Bancroft (fl. 1633–1658) was an English epigrammatist and verse satirist. Little is securely recorded of his life; his poems are addressed to gentry and neighbours of the English Midlands, and he published two books of epigrams and epitaphs in London in 1639.

Two Bookes of Epigrammes, and Epitaphs was dedicated to Sir Charles Shirley, Baronet, and William Davenport, Esquire, and printed by I. Okes for Matthew Walbancke. The first book is largely satirical and occasional, mixing portraits of types and named acquaintances with epitaphs; the second turns often to scriptural and devotional themes. A later volume, Time's out of Tune, appeared in 1658.

poets.name: Andrew Marvell
poets.credit: Portrait of Andrew Marvell · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Andrew Marvell (1621–1678) was an English metaphysical poet and politician.
Celebrated for lyrics such as ‘To His Coy Mistress’ and ‘The Garden,’ most of his poems appeared posthumously in the Miscellaneous Poems of 1681.

poets.name: Jean de La Fontaine
poets.credit: Portrait of Jean de La Fontaine by Hyacinthe Rigaud, 1690 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Jean de La Fontaine (1621–1695) was a French poet born at Château-Thierry in Champagne. After an unsettled early career in law and the administration of forests and waters, he found patrons in Paris, among them Nicolas Fouquet and later Madame de La Sablière, and became one of the glories of the age of Louis XIV; he was elected to the Académie française in 1684.

His Fables, published in collected books between 1668 and 1694, retell the stories of Aesop, Phaedrus and the Indian tradition in supple, irregular verse of great wit and economy. Under the guise of animals they observe the manners, vanities and cruelties of court and town. This selection follows the English verse translation by Walter Thornbury (London, 1886), printed with Gustave Doré's illustrations.

poets.name: Molière
poets.credit: Pierre Mignard, c. 1658 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Molière was the stage name of Jean-Baptiste Poquelin (1622–1673), born in Paris, the son of a royal upholsterer. He gave up the law for the theatre, spent years touring the provinces as actor and company manager, and from 1658 won the favour of Louis XIV in Paris, where he acted in, directed and wrote the plays of his troupe. He died in 1673 after being taken ill while playing the title role of his last comedy, Le Malade imaginaire.

He is the master of French comedy of manners and character, and his great comedies, among them Tartuffe, Le Misanthrope and L'Avare, are written in rhymed alexandrine couplets. Tartuffe, first performed in 1664, was banned for years as an attack on religious hypocrisy before it was allowed on the stage in 1669.

poets.name: Henry Vaughan
poets.credit: Title-page emblem from Silex Scintillans (1650) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Vaughan (1621–1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet and physician who styled himself ‘the Silurist.’
He is best known for the sacred poems of Silex Scintillans (1650), written under the deep influence of George Herbert.

poets.name: Margaret Cavendish, Duchess of Newcastle
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Margaret Cavendish, Duchess of Newcastle, was a maid of honour to Queen Henrietta Maria, married William Cavendish, later Duke of Newcastle, in Paris in 1645, and published prolifically in poetry, drama, philosophy and fiction. Her Poems and Fancies appeared in 1653.
Gilfillan prints two companion pieces from her pictures of Mirth and Melancholy.

poets.name: Angelus Silesius (Johann Scheffler)
poets.credit: Portrait of Johannes Scheffler (Angelus Silesius), 17th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Johann Scheffler was born at Breslau in 1624 and died there in 1677. He trained as a physician, was received into the Roman Catholic Church in 1653 and ordained priest in 1661, and took the name Angelus Silesius, the Silesian Angel, for his poetry. His devotional hymns appeared in Heilige Seelenlust (1657), the same year as his epigram collection Der Cherubinische Wandersmann.
The English versions here are Catherine Winkworth's in Lyra Germanica (1855).

poets.name: Thomas Stanley
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Stanley, 1660 · Public domain (Wikipedia)
bio: Thomas Stanley (1625–1678) was an English poet, translator and scholar, remembered for his History of Philosophy (1655–62) and for his edition of Aeschylus. Educated at Cambridge, he lived in London and moved among Royalist writers such as Shirley and Fanshawe.

His own poems, first printed in 1647 and reprinted in 1651 and 1656, are polished, graceful love lyrics addressed mostly to a lady called Chariessa or Celia. This selection takes his original poems from George Saintsbury's Minor Poets of the Caroline Period, vol. III (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1921) and leaves out the pieces that Stanley translated from other poets.

poets.name: John Hall
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Hall of Durham was educated at Cambridge, studied law, and published a volume of poems while still young. Gilfillan records that he was born at Durham in 1627 and died in 1656, in his twenty-ninth year.
Gilfillan quotes one poem of his, The Morning Star, in the memoir of Joseph Hall, whom he is careful to distinguish from the poet.

poets.name: John Bunyan
bio: John Bunyan (1628–1688) was an English Baptist preacher and writer, imprisoned for unlicensed preaching, and author of The Pilgrim’s Progress.
Songs and rhymes occur throughout his prose works and in A Book for Boys and Girls.

poets.name: Charles Cotton
poets.credit: Charles Cotton, British (English) School, 17th century (National Trust) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Cotton (1630–1687) was an English poet and translator from Beresford Hall in Staffordshire, on the river Dove. He was the friend and adopted "son" of Izaak Walton, and wrote the second part of The Compleat Angler (1676), the treatise on fly-fishing added to Walton's book. His translation of Montaigne's Essays (1685) remained the standard English version for generations.

His burlesques, Scarronides (a travesty of Virgil, 1664) and A Voyage to Ireland in Burlesque, made him a leading comic poet of the Restoration, while his love lyrics, odes and "quatrains" of the countryside show a quieter, more personal voice. Poems on Several Occasions appeared posthumously in 1689; the text here follows that edition (EEBO-TCP), including its closing section of translations from Horace, Martial, Catullus, Johannes Secundus and French and Italian poets, and leaving out the commendatory verses by another hand.

poets.name: Katherine Philips
poets.credit: Portrait of Katherine Philips · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Katherine Philips (1632–1664), called ‘the Matchless Orinda,’ was an English poet and translator.
She was admired above all for her poems of female friendship; her collected Poems appeared in 1664 and 1667.

poets.name: John Dryden
poets.credit: Portrait of John Dryden by an unknown artist, after Sir Godfrey Kneller · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Dryden (1631–1700) was England’s dominant literary figure of the later 17th century — poet, satirist, playwright, and critic — and was made the first official Poet Laureate in 1668.
His satires — Absalom and Achitophel, Mac Flecknoe, The Medal — and his public odes set the model for Augustan verse that Pope and Swift would inherit.

poets.name: Michael Wigglesworth
bio: Michael Wigglesworth (1631–1705) was born in Yorkshire, England, and taken as a child of seven to New England, where his family settled at New Haven. He graduated from Harvard in 1651, served there as a tutor and fellow, and in 1656 became minister of the church at Malden, Massachusetts, a charge he held for the rest of his life although long periods of ill health kept him from the pulpit. He also practised as a physician.

The Day of Doom; or, A Poetical Description of the Great and Last Judgment, published in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1662, is a Calvinist vision of the Last Judgment in 224 eight-line ballad stanzas. It is generally counted the first American best-seller: the first printing of about 1,800 copies sold out within a year, and the poem was reprinted for generations and learned by heart by New England children. It was followed by Meat out of the Eater (1670) and God's Controversy with New England (1662, printed 1871).

This selection follows the New York reprint of 1867, edited by John Ward Dean from the 1715 sixth edition. It gives The Day of Doom with its prefatory and closing verses ('To the Christian Reader', 'A Prayer unto Christ the Judge of the World', 'A Short Discourse on Eternity' and 'A Postscript unto the Reader') and the shorter poems printed with it. The editor's memoir, the notes, the marginal Scripture references and summaries, the commendatory verses by J. Mitchel and the funeral sermon and epitaph by Cotton Mather are left out.

poets.name: Samuel Pordage
bio: Samuel Pordage (1633–1691?) was an English poet and dramatist, the son of the Behmenist mystic John Pordage. His dates are uncertain; the year of his death is given only as a probable one.

His Poems upon Several Occasions appeared in 1660, signed “S. P. Gent.”, and includes panegyrics on Monck and on Charles II. He is also remembered as the author of Azaria and Hushai (1682), a reply to Dryden’s Absalom and Achitophel.

poets.name: Anton Ulrich, Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel
poets.credit: Portrait of Duke Anton Ulrich by Christoph Bernhard Francke · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Anton Ulrich was born at Hitzacker in 1633 and died at Salzdahlum in 1714. He ruled the duchy of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, from 1685 jointly with his brother and from 1704 alone, and in 1710 he converted to the Roman Catholic Church. Besides his hymns he wrote long courtly prose romances, notably Die durchlauchtige Syrerin Aramena.
The English versions here are Catherine Winkworth's in Lyra Germanica (1855).

poets.name: Ashraf Khan Khattak
bio: Ashraf Khan, eldest son of Khushhal Khan, was born in 1634 and became chief of the Khattaks in 1681 when his father stepped down. His brother Bahram intrigued against him, and he was betrayed to the Mughals and sent to the fortress of Bijapur in the Deccan.

He died in captivity in 1693, aged about sixty, and Raverty says his poems were written in his leisure hours. They are chiefly poems of exile and longing, signed with a pen-name that the translator renders as 'the Separated'.

poets.name: Thomas Flatman
poets.credit: Thomas Flatman, self-portrait miniature · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Flatman (1635–1688) was an English poet and miniature painter, born in London, educated at Winchester and New College, Oxford, and called to the bar at the Inner Temple. He became a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1668 and was admired for his portrait miniatures as much as for his verse.

His Poems and Songs went through four editions between 1674 and 1686. They range from Pindaric odes on the deaths of public figures, through devotional pieces such as the Hymn for the Morning, to witty songs and satires. The text here follows George Saintsbury's Minor Poets of the Caroline Period, vol. III (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1921), leaving out his Latin pieces and his translations and paraphrases of Horace, Ovid and others.

poets.name: Thomas Shipman
poets.credit: No portrait known · text from Carolina, or Loyal Poems (1683), EEBO-TCP A59967 (CC0)
bio: Thomas Shipman (1632–1680) was a Royalist gentleman-poet of Nottinghamshire. He wrote steadily from the last years of the Commonwealth through the Restoration, and his verse is largely occasional: elegies for friends and for Charles I, verse-letters and thank-you poems to neighbouring gentry, drinking songs in praise of Canary wine, and prologues written for players. Many of the poems carry the year of composition in their titles.

Almost nothing of his verse was printed in his lifetime. Carolina, or Loyal Poems appeared in 1683, three years after his death, published by friends. It opens with poems on the execution of Charles I and the Restoration and closes with a long Pindaric poem on Belvoir Castle, the seat of the Earls of Rutland. The Resolute Courtier is the poem by which he is most often anthologised.

poets.name: Thomas Traherne
bio: Thomas Traherne was an English clergyman and religious writer, born in Hereford, probably in 1636 or 1637, the son of a shoemaker. He studied at Brasenose College, Oxford, became rector of Credenhill in Herefordshire, and later served as chaplain to Sir Orlando Bridgeman at Teddington, where he died in 1674. Almost nothing of his work was printed in his lifetime.

His poems and prose meditations lay forgotten in manuscript for more than two centuries. They were found on a London bookstall in the 1890s and, once identified as his, edited by Bertram Dobell, whose Poetical Works appeared in 1903 and in a second edition in 1906. The poems, centred on childhood, wonder and the delight of the created world, are given here from Dobell's second edition (1906), together with the poems first printed in H. I. Bell's Poems of Felicity (1910).

poets.name: Robert Heath
poets.credit: No known portrait · text from Clarastella (1650), EEBO-TCP A86166 (CC0)
bio: Robert Heath, styled Esquire on his title page, was an English poet of the Caroline and Interregnum years. Very little is securely known of his life, and he is remembered almost entirely for a single printed volume, which gives its name to a wider circle of friends and patrons named only by their initials in his dedications and elegies.

Clarastella, together with Poems Occasional, Elegies, Epigrams, Satyrs was printed in London in 1650 for Humphrey Moseley. It opens with a sequence of love poems addressed to the fictional Clarastella, then turns to occasional verse, elegies for friends and for Royalist casualties of the Civil War, two books of short satirical epigrams, and four longer verse satires on the follies of the age.

poets.name: Samuel Woodford
poets.credit: Thomas Flatman, Samuel Woodforde DD (1661) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Samuel Woodford (1636-1700) was an Anglican clergyman and poet, born in London and educated at St Paul's School and Wadham College, Oxford. He studied at the Inner Temple, where his chamber-fellow was the poet Thomas Flatman, and was elected to the Royal Society in 1664. He took holy orders in 1669 and held livings and canonries in Hampshire, Chichester and Winchester, taking his D.D. in 1677.

He is best known for his verse paraphrases of scripture: a Paraphrase upon the Psalms (1667) and A Paraphrase upon the Canticles (1679), the latter gathering the Song of Solomon, hymns and psalms from the New and Old Testaments, and occasional odes and sonnets, among them poems to Izaak Walton and Sir John Denham. He drew his inspiration from Abraham Cowley, and wrote in the irregular, Pindaric stanzas of the Cowleyan ode.

poets.name: Sir George Etherege
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir George Etherege (1636–1692) was an English Restoration dramatist, author of The Comical Revenge, She Would if She Could and The Man of Mode. He served as a diplomat at Constantinople and Ratisbon, and wrote a handful of polished songs and lyrics.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Charles Sackville, Earl of Dorset
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Charles Sackville, sixth Earl of Dorset, was a courtier, wit and patron of writers under Charles II and later reigns. Gilfillan notes that he was rather a patron of poets than a poet, and gives his birth as 24 January 1637.
He is remembered chiefly for the song To all you Ladies now at Land, said to have been written at sea on the eve of the Dutch naval battle of 1665, which Gilfillan prints in full.

poets.name: Thomas Ken
bio: Thomas Ken (1637–1711) was an English clergyman, educated at Winchester College and Oxford, who became Bishop of Bath and Wells in 1685. He was one of the seven bishops tried and acquitted for resisting James II's Declaration of Indulgence in 1688, but as a non-juror he refused the oath to William III and was deprived of his see in 1691.

His morning, evening and midnight hymns were written for the boys of Winchester College and printed in later editions of his Manual of Prayers. The closing doxology of the morning and evening hymns, 'Praise God from whom all blessings flow', became one of the most widely sung verses in the English language.

poets.name: Philip Ayres
poets.credit: No known portrait · text from Lyric Poems (1687), EEBO-TCP A26293 (CC0)
bio: Philip Ayres (1638–1712) was an English poet and translator, born at Cottingham and educated at Westminster and St John's College, Oxford. He became tutor in the family of Montague Garrard Drake of Amersham, Buckinghamshire, and lived with them until his death on 1 December 1712.

His chief work is Lyric Poems, Made in Imitation of the Italians (1687), a collection of sonnets, songs and original pieces together with many translations from Italian, Spanish, Latin and Greek poets. One copy of verses is addressed to his friend John Dryden.

poets.name: Zeb-un-Nissa (Makhfi)
poets.credit: Mughal miniature inscribed as a portrait of a daughter of Alamgir (Aurangzeb), Bodleian Library MS. Ouseley Add. 170, 17th century · Illustrative image only, not an authenticated likeness · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Zeb-un-Nissa (1639–1702) was a Mughal princess, the eldest daughter of the emperor Aurangzeb, and is remembered as a learned woman, a patron of scholars and a poet in Persian. She wrote under the pen-name Makhfi, “the Hidden One”. The editors of the 1913 volume give her birth year as 1639. No authentic portrait of her is known; the image shown is a period miniature used for illustration.

The ghazals here come from The Diwan of Zeb-un-Nissa, rendered into English verse by Magan Lal and Jessie Duncan Westbrook (Wisdom of the East series, John Murray, London, 1913). The editors themselves acknowledge that the attribution of the Diwan to Zeb-un-Nissa is disputed. The translations turn on divine and mystical love, and the numbering of the ghazals follows that book.

poets.name: Khwajah Muhammad Bangash
bio: Khwajah Muhammad belonged to the Bangash tribe of Afghans around Kohat and lived in the reign of Aurangzeb. Raverty says materials for his life are meagre: he lived as a poor darwesh of the Chishti order, made the pilgrimage to Mecca and Medina, and gave up poetry after his return.
His Diwan survives in a single copy known to Raverty. The poems are deeply tinged with Sufi mysticism, but some lament the loss of friends and the pain of separation.

poets.name: Aphra Behn
poets.credit: Portrait of Aphra Behn by Sir Peter Lely (c. 1670) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Aphra Behn (1640–1689) was among the first Englishwomen to earn a living by her pen. Little is certain about her early life; she is said to have spent time in Surinam, and in 1666 she was sent to Antwerp as a spy for Charles II, writing under the code name Astrea. Back in London she turned to the stage, and from The Forc’d Marriage (1670) to The Rover (1677) and beyond she became one of the most successful playwrights of the Restoration, later adding prose fiction such as Oroonoko (1688). She was buried in the cloisters of Westminster Abbey.

Her verse was published in Poems upon Several Occasions (1684) and in A Miscellany (1685), and further pieces appeared after her death. It ranges from songs written for her plays, Pindaric odes and pastoral dialogues to satires, epistles to friends and patrons, and elegies for Rochester and Waller. This selection takes her own short and occasional poems from the sixth volume of Montague Summers’s edition (1915); her translations from Tallemant, A Voyage to the Isle of Love and Lycidus, are left out.

poets.name: Köroğlu
bio: Köroğlu (Kurroglou in older English spellings) is the legendary bandit-poet of Turkish and Turkic folklore. He robbed the caravans on the road between Persia and the Ottoman lands, and is remembered above all for the improvised songs he is said to have sung. He is the hero of a large cycle of tales and songs carried by wandering minstrels among the Turkic peoples of Anatolia, Azerbaijan and Central Asia.

The cycle is traditional, and its authorship is not known: no single author can be named, and the songs were passed on orally and changed with each telling. The English version used here is from Alexander Chodzko's Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842), which places the hero in northern Khorasan in the second half of the seventeenth century. Chodzko's versions are set within his prose narrative, so the songs are given as paragraphs rather than as verse lines.

poets.name: Benjamin Keach
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of Benjamin Keach, 17th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Benjamin Keach (1640–1704) was an English Baptist preacher, born at Stoke Hammond in Buckinghamshire. He was imprisoned and put in the pillory in 1664 for his children's primer 'The Child's Instructor', and from 1668 he served as pastor of a Baptist congregation in Southwark, London, which later met at Horsleydown.

Keach wrote prolifically in prose and verse. 'Spiritual Melody, containing near three hundred sacred hymns' (1691) was among the first collections of hymns written for congregational singing in English Baptist worship, a move that was controversial in his own day. The hymns, plain in diction and built on scriptural images, are set out in nine parts.

poets.name: Nâbî
bio: Nabi, born at Urfa, came to Constantinople in the reign of Muhammed IV and attached himself to that monarch's favourite Mustafa Pasha, whom he accompanied on his Morean campaign.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: P’u Sung-ling
bio: P’u Sung-ling was a writer of the early Ch’ing dynasty, best known for his collection of tales, Strange Stories from a Chinese Studio.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: John Mason
bio: John Mason (1646?–1694) was an English clergyman, rector of Water Stratford in Buckinghamshire. He is remembered for his Spiritual Songs, first published in 1683, which were among the first English hymns written for congregational singing.

The collection pairs thirty-three Songs of Praise (thirty are given here, three being too damaged in the source) on the great occasions of Christian life with a verse rendering and a paraphrase of the Song of Songs, which Mason reads as a dialogue between Christ and his Church. The text here is the sixth edition of 1699, five years after his death.

poets.name: John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester
poets.credit: Portrait of John Wilmot, 2nd Earl of Rochester, attributed to Peter Lely (17th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Wilmot, second Earl of Rochester (1647–1680), was an English courtier and poet at the court of Charles II, and the most celebrated of the Restoration 'Court Wits'. Famed for his libertine life, he wrote satires, songs, lyrics and verse epistles, and died at thirty-three.
Texts and attributions follow The Works of the Right Honourable John, Earl of Rochester (London, 1718); some pieces in that collection are of disputed authorship.

poets.name: Sidqî
bio: Sidqi, Gibb says, was a daughter of Qamer Muhammed Efendi, a member of the 'ulema, and besides her Divan wrote two mystic poems; several poets have written under the name of Sidqi.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: John Sheffield, Duke of Buckingham and Normanby
bio: John Sheffield, Earl of Mulgrave and later Duke of Buckingham and Normanby (1648–1721), was an English statesman and poet, a patron of Dryden and the author of An Essay upon Poetry and An Essay upon Satire.
Arthur Quiller-Couch included two of his lyrics in The Oxford Book of English Verse (1900).

poets.name: Ernst Lange
poets.credit: No portrait available (monogram tile). Text: G. Osborn (ed.), The Poetical Works of John and Charles Wesley, 13 vols (London: Wesleyan-Methodist Conference Office, 1868–72), from Internet Archive scans (OCR).
bio: Ernst Lange (1650–1727) was a German hymn-writer whose “O Gott, du Tiefe sonder Grund” appears in the Herrnhuth Collection (No. 9) and in Knapp’s Evangelischer Liederschatz.
The single piece here is John Wesley’s English translation, printed in Hymns and Sacred Poems (1739); Osborn’s footnote names Lange as the author of the German original.

poets.name: Henry Aldrich
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Henry Aldrich (1648–1710) was an English scholar, logician and amateur architect and composer. He became Dean of Christ Church, Oxford, in 1689 and is remembered for his Artis logicae compendium and for a set of Latin and English verses on the five reasons for drinking.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Jane Barker
poets.credit: Portrait: Barker, Jane — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Jane Barker (1652–1732) was an English poet and novelist, born at Blatherwycke in Northamptonshire and later associated with Wilsthorpe in Lincolnshire. She was a Catholic and a Jacobite, and followed the exiled James II to the court at Saint-Germain in France after 1688, returning to England in the early eighteenth century.

Her first printed verse appeared as Part I of Poetical Recreations (1688), a miscellany of epistles, songs, odes and elegies, several of them addressed to friends and to her brother, with a second part by other hands. She later published further poems and the prose fictions Love Intrigues (1713), Exilius (1715) and A Patch-Work Screen for the Ladies (1723).

poets.name: Abd-ul-Kadir Khan Khattak
bio: Abd-ul-Kadir Khan, a son of Khushhal Khan and brother of Ashraf, was born in 1652. Raverty calls him the most eloquent writer and poet among Khushhal's sons, and says he was as good with the sword as with the pen, fighting the Mughals with the confederate Afghans.

He disputed the chieftainship with his nephew Afzal, and was put to death with ten of his brothers and a number of their sons at Zaman Garrai. His odes are deeply coloured by Sufi mysticism and are highly valued by Afghans.

poets.name: Thomas Otway
bio: Thomas Otway (1652–1685) was an English dramatist, best known for the tragedies The Orphan and Venice Preserv’d.
He also published poems, including The Poet’s Complaint of his Muse and lyrics such as “The Enchantment.”

poets.name: John Oldham
poets.credit: Portrait of John Oldham, engraved (after William Dobson?) by Scheneker, in The Biographical Mirrour (1795) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Oldham (1653–1683) was an English satirist, the son of a Nonconformist minister in Gloucestershire. After St Edmund Hall, Oxford, he worked as an usher (assistant schoolmaster) at a school in Croydon. His Satyrs upon the Jesuits (1681), written in the vein of Juvenal, made his name, and he followed it with imitations and paraphrases of Latin and French poets, among them Juvenal, Horace, Boileau, Catullus and Anacreon.

The 1683 volume from which these poems are taken, Poems, and Translations, is anonymous on its title page (‘by the author of the Satyrs upon the Jesuits’); the author is identified as John Oldham by the TCP/ESTC catalogue record. He died of smallpox at the age of thirty. Dryden, who admired his work, wrote the elegy ‘To the Memory of Mr. Oldham’, and the archive also holds Gould’s elegy on him.

poets.name: Abd-ur-Rahman
bio: Mulla Abd-ur-Rahman, of the Ghoriah Khel clan of the Mohmand tribe, lived in the village of Hazar-Khani near Peshawar. By Raverty's account he was a learned recluse who lived as a darwesh, absorbed in prayer, and he is counted among the most popular of the Afghan poets.

His odes, collected in a Diwan after his death, are religious and moral in character and chiefly concern divine love in the Sufi manner. Raverty notes their fiery energy and natural simplicity; he places the poet as a young man during Khushhal Khan's last years, and one poem refers to events of 1711.

poets.name: Robert Gould
