bio: Robert Gould (died about 1709) was an English poet and satirist of the Restoration. Little is securely known of his early life; he is generally said to have risen from domestic service in a noble household, and to have won the patronage of the Earl of Dorset and other grandees, several of whom he addresses in his verse.

He made his name with Love Given O'er (1682), a savage satire on women that provoked printed replies, followed by The Play-House (1685) and A Satyr upon Man. His collected Poems, chiefly consisting of Satyrs and Satyrical Epistles (1689) joined these to love songs, verse letters, funeral elegies and pindarick odes. He also wrote plays, and a posthumous Works appeared in 1709.

poets.name: Thomas D'Urfey
poets.credit: Thomas D'Urfey, engraving by Edward Gouge, c. 1819 (National Portrait Gallery, London) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas D'Urfey (1653-1723) was an English songwriter, poet and playwright, born in Exeter of Huguenot descent. He came to London to study law but turned to the stage and wrote some thirty plays, among them Madam Fickle (1676) and The Comical History of Don Quixote (1694-96). He was a familiar figure at the courts of Charles II, James II, William III and Anne, and was known above all as a writer and singer of comic and bawdy songs.

New Poems, consisting of Satyrs, Elegies and Odes, together with a Choice Collection of the Newest Court Songs (1690), from which this selection is drawn, mixes verse satires, prologues and epilogues, epithalamia and elegies with songs, several of them set by Henry Purcell and John Blow. D'Urfey later gathered songs, his own and others', into Wit and Mirth: or Pills to Purge Melancholy (1698-1720), the best-known song collection of its age.

poets.name: Sir Richard Blackmore
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir Richard Blackmore (engraving, artist unknown) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Richard Blackmore (1654–1729) was an English physician and poet. He practised medicine in London, became a Fellow of the College of Physicians, and served as physician in ordinary to William III, who knighted him in 1697. He is best known for his heavily moralising epics Prince Arthur (1695) and King Arthur (1697), and for the philosophical poem Creation (1712). His first epic, Prince Arthur, is included here in full, from the 1695 first edition.

His verse was a favourite target of Dryden and Pope, and he became a byword for dull ambition in the satirical tradition. The poems here come from A Paraphrase on the Book of Job (1700), which turns the chapters of Job, with the songs of Moses and Deborah, David's lament for Saul and Jonathan, four psalms, five chapters of Isaiah and the third chapter of Habakkuk, into rhymed English verse. The text follows the 1700 printing, with its original spelling.

poets.name: Mary Lee, Lady Chudleigh
bio: Mary Lee, Lady Chudleigh (1656–1710), born Mary Lee at Winkleigh in Devon, married Sir George Chudleigh in 1685 and spent her life largely at Ashton, near Exeter. She was among the earliest English women to write publicly in defence of her sex, notably in her verse satire The Ladies' Defence (1701).
Her Poems on Several Occasions appeared in 1703 and her Essays upon Several Subjects in Prose and Verse in 1710, the year she died.

poets.name: John Dennis
poets.credit: John Vandergucht, line engraving, 1734 (National Portrait Gallery, London) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Dennis (1657–1734) was an English critic and dramatist, educated at Harrow and Cambridge. He wrote tragedies and comedies and a body of critical prose, and became notorious as the longtime antagonist of Alexander Pope, who satirised him in print.

His Miscellanies in Verse and Prose (1693) is an early volume of his verse: a Pindaric ode on William III, occasional and amatory pieces, burlesque fables with their morals, and versions of Horace, Boileau and Juvenal.

poets.name: John Norris
bio: John Norris (1657–1711) was an English philosopher and divine, a Platonist of the Cambridge school and rector of Bemerton, the parish of George Herbert.
His “Hymn to Darkness” was included in Palgrave’s The Golden Treasury (1861).

poets.name: 'Ârif
bio: 'Arif was a distinguished member of the legal profession, famed for his learning and for the elegance with which he wrote the taliq script; he composed a long poem on the Prophet's Night-journey and a complete Divan.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Wolfgang Christoph Dessler
poets.credit: No portrait available (monogram tile). Text: G. Osborn (ed.), The Poetical Works of John and Charles Wesley, 13 vols (London: Wesleyan-Methodist Conference Office, 1868–72), from Internet Archive scans (OCR).
bio: Wolfgang Christoph Dessler (1660–1722) was a German hymn-writer whose “Mein Jesu, dem die Seraphinen” appears in the Herrnhuth Collection and in Knapp’s Evangelischer Liederschatz.
The single piece here is John Wesley’s English translation, printed in Hymns and Sacred Poems (1739); Osborn’s footnote names Dessler as the author of the German original.

poets.name: Charles Mordaunt, Earl of Peterborough
poets.credit: Charles Mordaunt, 3rd Earl of Peterborough, by Sir Godfrey Kneller, 1715 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Mordaunt, 3rd Earl of Peterborough (1658–1735), was an English soldier and diplomat, famous for his campaign in Spain in the War of the Spanish Succession. He was a friend of Pope and Swift and wrote a few polished lyrics.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Thomas Southerne
poets.credit: Thomas Southerne, engraved portrait reproduced in Read's volume of 1879 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Southerne (1660–1746) was an Irish-born English dramatist, author of the tragedies The Fatal Marriage (1694) and Oroonoko (1695), and a friend of Dryden. He also wrote prologues and songs.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Anne Finch, Countess of Winchilsea
bio: Anne Finch, Countess of Winchilsea (1661–1720), née Kingsmill, was a maid of honour to Mary of Modena and married Heneage Finch in 1684. After the Revolution of 1688 the couple retired to the country, where she wrote most of her poems. She published Miscellany Poems, on Several Occasions in 1713 and often called herself Ardelia in her verse.

Her ‘Nocturnal Reverie’ was singled out by Wordsworth as a rare piece of fresh nature description in its century, and her ode ‘The Spleen’ is among the earliest English poems on melancholy as a condition. She also wrote fables, satires, songs and religious poems.

poets.name: John Cutts, Lord Cutts
bio: John Cutts, Baron Cutts of Gowran (1661–1707), was an English soldier who served under William III and Marlborough, nicknamed “the Salamander” for his courage under fire.
He also wrote occasional verse, collected in his Poetical Exercises (1687).

poets.name: Sir Samuel Garth
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir Samuel Garth by Sir Godfrey Kneller (Kit-Cat Club series) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Samuel Garth (1661–1719) was an English physician and poet, a leading member of the Whig Kit-Cat Club and a friend of Addison, Pope and Dryden, whose funeral oration he delivered in 1700. He was knighted in 1714 on the accession of George I.

His mock-heroic poem The Dispensary (1699) satirised the 1690s quarrel between the College of Physicians, who backed a free dispensary for the poor, and the apothecaries who opposed it, and became one of the most admired English burlesque epics of its day.

poets.name: Samuel Wesley
poets.credit: Portrait: A. H. Hyde — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Samuel Wesley (1662–1735) was an English clergyman and poet, born in Dorset and educated at Oxford. He became rector of Epworth in Lincolnshire in 1696 and held the living until his death. He is best remembered as the father of John Wesley, the founder of Methodism, and of the hymn-writer Charles Wesley.

Before his long career in the Church he published Maggots, or Poems on Several Subjects (1685), a book of comic verse written in his youth. Its mock-heroic and burlesque poems on trifling subjects, a hog's grunting, a cheese, a tobacco pipe, a louse, are the playful side of a man later known for pious and learned writing.

poets.name: Ludwig Andreas Gotter
poets.credit: No portrait available (monogram tile). Text: G. Osborn (ed.), The Poetical Works of John and Charles Wesley, 13 vols (London: Wesleyan-Methodist Conference Office, 1868–72), from Internet Archive scans (OCR).
bio: Ludwig Andreas Gotter (1661–1735) was a German hymn-writer whose “Sei hochgelobt, barmherziger Gott” appears in the Herrnhuth Collection and in Knapp’s Evangelischer Liederschatz (Osborn’s scanned text prints his name as “Cotter”).
The single piece here is John Wesley’s English translation, printed in Hymns and Sacred Poems (1740); Osborn’s footnote gives the German as a comparison.

poets.name: Richard Bentley
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Richard Bentley was the great English classical scholar and Master of Trinity College, Cambridge, famous for the Dissertation on the Epistles of Phalaris.
Gilfillan prints a single piece of English verse which he calls Bentley's sole poetical composition.

poets.name: William Walsh
poets.credit: William Walsh, by Sir Godfrey Kneller · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Walsh (1662–1708) was an English critic and poet and a member of parliament, an early friend and adviser of Alexander Pope, who praised him in An Essay on Criticism. He wrote amorous verse and the Dialogue Concerning Women (1691).

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Peter Anthony Motteux
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Peter Anthony Motteux (1663–1718) was a Huguenot refugee from Rouen who settled in London. He translated Rabelais and Don Quixote, edited the Gentleman's Journal (1692–94), and wrote songs and plays.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Matthew Prior
bio: Matthew Prior (1664–1721) was the son of a joiner, educated at Westminster School and Cambridge, and made his career as a diplomat. He served as secretary to the embassy at The Hague and in Paris, and took part in the negotiations that led to the Treaty of Utrecht, and was imprisoned for a time after the Whig ministry came to power in 1715.

As a poet he was admired for his light, polished verse: songs and epigrams addressed to Cloe, tales and fables, and longer poems such as Alma and Solomon. His Poems on Several Occasions was published by subscription in 1718.

poets.name: Iqbâlî (Sultan Mustafa II)
bio: Mustafa II succeeded his uncle Ahmed II in 1695 and led his army against the Austrians; he wrote verse under the pen-name Iqbali.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Lady Grisell Baillie
bio: Lady Grisell Baillie (1665–1746), born Grisell Hume, was a Scottish songwriter, the daughter of Sir Patrick Hume, later Earl of Marchmont, and the wife of George Baillie of Jerviswood.
She is remembered for the song "Werena my heart's licht I wad dee", which Quiller-Couch prints in The Oxford Book of English Verse.

poets.name: Alexander Brome
poets.credit: No portrait available · monogram tile
bio: Alexander Brome (1620 – 30 June 1666) was an English poet and attorney, a staunch Royalist who made his name with satirical ballads, drinking songs and love lyrics written during the Civil War and the Interregnum, many of which circulated in manuscript and print against the Parliamentary cause.

Songs and Other Poems appeared in 1661 and in an enlarged second edition in 1664, the text used here. It gathers his songs, ballads, verse epistles to friends, and a section of epigrams translated from the classical tradition, together with pieces on the Restoration of Charles II in 1660.

poets.name: Sir John Vanbrugh
poets.credit: Sir John Vanbrugh, by Sir Godfrey Kneller, c. 1704–10 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir John Vanbrugh (1664–1726) was an English dramatist and architect, author of The Relapse (1696) and The Provok'd Wife (1697), and designer of Castle Howard and Blenheim Palace.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Demeter Csáthi
bio: Hungarian poet and Franciscan monk, presumed author of a national ballad on the Magyar conquest of Pannonia (Bowring calls his date uncertain).
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: Miklós Zrínyi
bio: Hungarian-Croatian soldier, statesman and poet, author of the epic Zrínyiad, who died in 1664 (Bowring gives 1616–1665).
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: Huw Morus
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Huw Morus (Hugh Morris, "Eos Ceiriog") was a Welsh poet of the seventeenth century from the Ceiriog valley, a Royalist who wrote satire, love lyrics and, late in life, religious verse.
Two of his poems, "The Bard's Death-Bed Confession" and "Quick, Death!", are given in English verse by Alfred Perceval Graves in A Celtic Psaltery (1917).

poets.name: Jonathan Swift
poets.credit: Portrait of Jonathan Swift by Charles Jervas, c. 1718 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Jonathan Swift (1667–1745), Dean of St Patrick’s Cathedral in Dublin, is remembered above all for his prose satires, but his verse — plain-spoken, often savage, sometimes tender — was equally his own invention.

Poems like A Description of a City Shower and The Lady’s Dressing-Room turned unflinching, unglamorous observation into satire, while Cadenus and Vanessa and the Stella poems show a gentler, more private side of a famously guarded man.

poets.name: John Pomfret
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Pomfret was an English clergyman and poet who became rector of Maulden in Bedfordshire. He published a volume of poems in 1699, including Pindaric essays in the manner of Cowley.
His poem The Choice, a wish for a quiet country life, became one of the most widely read short poems of its time and is printed in full by Gilfillan.

poets.name: Wali Deccani
bio: Wali of the Deccan is called in the book the first to write an Urdu diwan and the Father of Urdu poetry; born at Aurungabad, he wrote in the latter half of the seventeenth century, held a just balance between Sunnis and Shiahs, and did not flatter any ruler in his verses.

The one piece given here is drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. It is a free rendering, not a literal translation, and the original Urdu poem is untitled; it is named here by its first line.

poets.name: William Congreve
poets.credit: William Congreve, by Sir Godfrey Kneller, 1709 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Congreve (1670–1729) was the leading comic dramatist of the English Restoration stage, author of Love for Love (1695) and The Way of the World (1700). He also wrote songs, odes and translations, and was admired by Dryden and Pope.

The 4 poems here are the pieces printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Johann Joseph Winkler
poets.credit: No portrait available (monogram tile). Text: G. Osborn (ed.), The Poetical Works of John and Charles Wesley, 13 vols (London: Wesleyan-Methodist Conference Office, 1868–72), from Internet Archive scans (OCR).
bio: Johann Joseph Winkler (1670–1722) was a German pietist hymn-writer; his “Sollt ich aus Furcht vor Menschenkindern” appears in the Herrnhuth Collection and in Knapp’s Evangelischer Liederschatz.
The single piece here is John Wesley’s English translation, printed in Hymns and Sacred Poems (1739); Osborn’s footnote names Winkler as the author of the German original.

poets.name: Joachim Lange
poets.credit: No portrait available (monogram tile). Text: G. Osborn (ed.), The Poetical Works of John and Charles Wesley, 13 vols (London: Wesleyan-Methodist Conference Office, 1868–72), from Internet Archive scans (OCR).
bio: Joachim Lange (1670–1744) was a pietist theologian at Halle and a hymn-writer; his “O Jesu, süßes Licht” appears in the Herrnhuth Collection (No. 308) and in Knapp’s Evangelischer Liederschatz.
The single piece here is John Wesley’s English translation, printed in Hymns and Sacred Poems (1739); Osborn’s footnote names Joachim Lange as the author of the German original.

poets.name: Johann Anastasius Freylinghausen
poets.credit: No portrait available (monogram tile). Text: G. Osborn (ed.), The Poetical Works of John and Charles Wesley, 13 vols (London: Wesleyan-Methodist Conference Office, 1868–72), from Internet Archive scans (OCR).
bio: Johann Anastasius Freylinghausen (1670–1739) was a pietist theologian at Halle, the son-in-law of A. H. Francke, and the editor of the Geistreiches Gesangbuch (1704), a principal hymn-book of German Pietism; he also wrote hymns.
The single piece here is John Wesley’s English translation, printed in Hymns and Sacred Poems (1739); Osborn’s footnote names Freylinghausen as the author of the German original.

poets.name: Richard Leveridge
bio: Richard Leveridge (1670–1758) was an English bass singer, actor and composer, long a mainstay of the London theatres in the early eighteenth century. He composed theatre songs and published them as a Collection of Songs with the Musick (1727).
He is remembered above all for the patriotic song in praise of old English roast beef, printed in The British Musical Miscellany in 1735.

poets.name: Colley Cibber
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Colley Cibber was an English actor-manager and playwright who became Poet Laureate in 1730. His stage comedies and his autobiography, An Apology for the Life of Mr. Colley Cibber, are better known than his verse.
Palgrave includes his song "The Blind Boy".

poets.name: Nedim
bio: Ahmed Nedim was one of the most celebrated Ottoman poets of the early 18th century, the age later called the Tulip Era, a period of peace, luxury and garden-pavilion culture in Istanbul. He wrote the courtly ghazel and became librarian and boon-companion of the Grand Vezir Ibrahim Pasha.

He died in October 1730, when the palace was stormed in the uprising that overthrew Sultan Ahmed III. E. J. W. Gibb, whose History of Ottoman Poetry gives the first sustained English account of him, warned that Nedim's delicate verbal music could scarcely survive translation. The poems below are Gibb's renderings of ghazels from the fourth volume of that history.

poets.name: Turlough O’Carolan
bio: Turlough O’Carolan (Toralach O’Cearbhallain) was a blind Irish harper and composer, born at Nobber in Meath in 1670, who played for patrons in many parts of Ireland and died in 1738; Sigerson says he was buried at Kilronan.

Sigerson, in Bards of the Gael and Gall (1907), says that his genius gave fresh life to Irish song. His “Mabel ni Kelly” is given here in Sigerson’s English version, which tries to reproduce the original’s irregular metre.

poets.name: Egan O’Reilly
bio: Sigerson, in Bards of the Gael and Gall (1907), prints two visionary poems of the early eighteenth century under the name Egan O’Reilly. The first, “The Brightness of Brightness”, is an aisling, or vision-poem, in which a radiant woman who stands for Ireland appears to the poet.

Sigerson’s own note on the poet’s life treats him as John Mor O’Reilly of Cavan. The poem is generally attributed in the Irish tradition to Egan O’Rahilly of Kerry. Both pieces are given here as Sigerson prints them, in his English versions.

poets.name: Joseph Addison
poets.credit: Portrait of Joseph Addison after Sir Godfrey Kneller, c. 1703–12 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Joseph Addison (1672–1719) was an English essayist, poet and politician, educated at Charterhouse and Magdalen College, Oxford. With Richard Steele he wrote The Tatler and The Spectator, the periodical essays that made his prose a model of the polite style.

His verse includes The Campaign (1704), written in praise of Marlborough's victory at Blenheim, A Letter from Italy, An Account of the Greatest English Poets and a handful of hymns and odes first printed in The Spectator, among them 'The spacious firmament on high'. His translations of Ovid and Virgil, and his drama Cato, are not included here.

poets.name: Sir Richard Steele
bio: Sir Richard Steele (1672–1729) was born in Dublin and educated at the Charterhouse and Oxford. Essayist, dramatist and Whig politician, he founded The Tatler in 1709 and, with Joseph Addison, The Spectator in 1711.
His plays include The Conscious Lovers (1722). He wrote little verse; the song here was printed in The Muses Mercury in 1707.

poets.name: Charles Goodall
poets.credit: No known portrait · text from Poems and Translations (1689), EEBO-TCP A41430 (CC0)
bio: Charles Goodall (1671–1689) is known only through one posthumous-looking book, Poems and Translations, Written upon Several Occasions, and to Several Persons (1689), whose title page says merely that it is "by a late Scholar of Eaton". The attribution to Goodall, and his dates of 1671 to 1689, come from the catalogue record of the EEBO-TCP transcription, not from the printed book; on those dates he died at about eighteen.

The volume carries a prose dedication to the Countess of Clarendon and a verse dedication to Mr. Roderick, Upper-Master of Eaton-School. Its contents are schoolboy and undergraduate-age verse: love poems and epigrams to a Hemiera and an Idera, verse letters to friends and to his brother, an elegy on Oldham, and versions of Anacreon, Bion, Theocritus, Catullus, Ovid, Seneca and Juvenal, with Greek epigrams in English. The spelling of the 1689 print is kept here.

poets.name: John Oldmixon
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Oldmixon (1673–1742) was an English Whig historian and pamphleteer, author of a critical history of England and a target of Pope's Dunciad. He also wrote songs and light verse.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: William Somervile
poets.credit: Portrait of William Somervile, unknown artist, c. 1695–1710 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Somervile (1675–1742) was an English poet and country gentleman who lived on his estate at Edstone in Warwickshire. He was a keen fox-hunter and a magistrate, and a friend of several writers of his day.

He is remembered for The Chase (1735), a poem in blank verse on hunting, in four books, which treats hounds, kennels, the hare, the stag and the fox with a mixture of practical instruction and Miltonic and Virgilian manner. The text here is from Gilfillan's edition (Edinburgh, 1859), which spells his name Somerville.

poets.name: Abd-ul-Hamid
bio: Abd-ul-Hamid was born in the Mohmand village of Mashu Khel near Peshawar and was brought up for the priesthood. Raverty could not fix his birth year but places it about the middle of the last half of the seventeenth century, and gives his death as about A.D. 1732 on village testimony.

Raverty calls him the cynical poet of the Afghans, compared with Sa'di in Persian, and says that Persian critics knew him as 'Hamid the Hair-splitter'. His odes, from the Diwan 'Dur-o-Marjan' ('Pearls and Corals'), mix moral satire and contempt for worldly vanity with Sufi doctrine.

poets.name: Nicholas Rowe
bio: Nicholas Rowe (1674–1718) was an English dramatist and poet, author of the tragedies Tamerlane (1701), The Fair Penitent (1703) and Jane Shore (1714). He edited Shakespeare (1709) and became Poet Laureate in 1715.
His verse translation of Lucan's Pharsalia appeared in 1718; the archive holds it as a work. The poem given here is his pastoral ballad Colin's Complaint.

poets.name: Ambrose Philips
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Ambrose Philips was an English poet best known for his Pastorals (1709). Henry Carey gave his light verses to children the nickname "namby-pamby".
Palgrave includes his lines "To Charlotte Pulteney".

poets.name: Ellis Wynne
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Ellis Wynne (Elis Wyn) was a Welsh clergyman and writer, born at Lasynys in Merioneth, best known for his prose work The Visions of the Sleeping Bard (1703).
His verse "Counsel in View of Death" is given in English by Alfred Perceval Graves in A Celtic Psaltery (1917).

poets.name: Benjamin Schmolck
poets.credit: Portrait of Benjamin Schmolck, 18th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Benjamin Schmolck was born at Brauchitschdorf in Silesia in 1672 and died at Schweidnitz in 1737. A Lutheran pastor, he served at Schweidnitz from 1702 and became one of the most prolific hymn writers of his age, with well over a thousand hymns to his name.
The English versions here are Catherine Winkworth's in Lyra Germanica (1855).

poets.name: Isaac Watts
poets.credit: Portrait of Isaac Watts, from the National Portrait Gallery, London (c. 1727) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Isaac Watts (1674–1748), born in Southampton, was an English Congregationalist minister, theologian and hymn-writer, often called the father of English hymnody. The son of a Nonconformist who was imprisoned for his beliefs, he was educated at the Dissenting academy in Stoke Newington and from 1702 served as pastor of the Independent congregation at Mark Lane, London. Poor health limited his preaching, and from 1712 he lived under the protection of the Abney family at Theobalds and Stoke Newington.

His Hymns and Spiritual Songs (1707–09) broke with the English habit of singing only metrical psalms, and The Psalms of David Imitated in the Language of the New Testament (1719) recast the Psalter for Christian worship; it gave English-speaking churches such hymns as “O God, Our Help in Ages Past” and “Joy to the World.” His Divine Songs Attempted in Easy Language for the Use of Children (1715) became one of the most widely read children’s books of the eighteenth century, and a famous parody of its “How doth the little busy bee” appears in Lewis Carroll’s Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland.

poets.name: John Philips
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Philips was an English poet born at Bampton in Oxfordshire and educated at Christ Church, Oxford. He is not to be confused with his contemporary Ambrose Philips or with Katherine Philips.
His best-known poem is The Splendid Shilling (1701), a burlesque of Milton's blank verse, which Gilfillan prints complete.

poets.name: Charles Webbe
bio: Little is known of Charles Webbe, who is dated about 1678 by the Oxford Book of English Verse.
He is remembered for one lyric, “Against Indifference,” which has been anthologised since the seventeenth century.

poets.name: George Sewell
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: George Sewell was an English physician and miscellaneous writer who died in 1726.
Palgrave includes his poem "The Dying Man in His Garden".

poets.name: Christian Friedrich Richter
poets.credit: No portrait available (monogram tile). Text: G. Osborn (ed.), The Poetical Works of John and Charles Wesley, 13 vols (London: Wesleyan-Methodist Conference Office, 1868–72), from Internet Archive scans (OCR).
bio: Christian Friedrich Richter (1676–1711) was a physician and pietist hymn-writer at Halle, where he was connected with the institutions of A. H. Francke. Several of his hymns passed into the Herrnhuth Collection and Knapp’s Evangelischer Liederschatz.

The pieces here are John Wesley’s English translations of 1738–42. Osborn’s footnotes name Richter (“Dr. C. F. Richter, of Halle”) as author of the German originals; for “In Affliction or Pain” he gives the reference as a comparison.

poets.name: John Hopkins
poets.credit: No portrait is known; none sourced for this archive.
bio: John Hopkins (fl. 1700) was an English poet of the turn of the eighteenth century, remembered for a single large work, Amasia, or, The Works of the Muses, published in London in 1700 in three volumes. Little is recorded of his life, and the catalogue gives only a floruit.

Amasia gathers love poems and verse epistles addressed to a lady under that name, together with occasional pieces, Ovidian tales in the manner of the day, and poems to friends. He should not be confused with John Hopkins, the sixteenth-century psalmist, or with Gerard Manley Hopkins.

poets.name: Thomas Parnell
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of Thomas Parnell, artist unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Parnell (1679–1718) was an Anglo-Irish poet and clergyman, born in Dublin and educated at Trinity College, who became Archdeacon of Clogher in 1706. He was a friend of Swift, Pope, Gay and Arbuthnot, took part in the Scriblerus Club, and wrote the essay on Homer prefixed to Pope's Iliad.

He died at Chester in 1718, on a journey to Ireland. Pope edited his Poems on Several Occasions (1722). A Night-Piece on Death is often seen as an early forerunner of Gray's Elegy, and The Hermit, a moral tale in couplets, was widely reprinted through the eighteenth century.

poets.name: Abel Evans
bio: Abel Evans (1679–1737) was an English clergyman and wit, a member of St John's College, Oxford, and an acquaintance of Pope. He was known in his own day for his epigrams and for Latin and English verse.
His best-remembered lines are the mock epitaph on the architect Sir John Vanbrugh, whose buildings included Blenheim Palace.

poets.name: Barton Booth
bio: Barton Booth (1681–1733) was an English actor, famous in the part of Cato in Addison's tragedy (1713), and from 1713 a joint manager of the Drury Lane theatre.
He also wrote occasional verse; his song “Sweet are the Charms of her I love” was printed in The Hive in 1726 and widely reprinted.

poets.name: Edward Young
bio: Edward Young (1683–1765) was born in Hampshire and educated at Oxford, where he became a fellow of All Souls. He made his name with a poem on the Last Judgment, a series of satires called The Love of Fame, and some tragedies, and took holy orders in middle age, becoming rector of Welwyn in Hertfordshire in 1730.

His blank-verse The Complaint, or Night Thoughts (1742–1745), a long meditation in nine Nights on life, death and immortality, was one of the most widely read poems in Europe in the later eighteenth century. William Blake made a famous series of designs for it.

poets.name: Elijah Fenton
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Elijah Fenton was born at Shelton near Newcastle-under-Lyme in Staffordshire and studied at Cambridge. He was a schoolmaster and secretary, and translated part of the Odyssey for Pope.
Gilfillan prints one of his odes, written in the spring of 1716 to Lord Gower.

poets.name: Shah Mubarak Abru
bio: The introduction to Hindustani Lyrics says that Abru was born at Lucknow, lived at Delhi, was a darwesh of the Order of Kalenders, and wrote an Urdu diwan much appreciated for the ingenious allegories in which it abounds. Abru is his takhallus, or pen-name.

The one piece given here is drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. It is a free rendering, not a literal translation, and the original Urdu poem is untitled; it is named here by its first line.

poets.name: David Lewis
bio: David Lewis (1683?–1760) was a poet and editor, a friend of Alexander Pope, who edited the anthology Miscellaneous Poems by Several Hands (1726). His own Miscellaneous Poems appeared in 1730.
The lines here, addressed to Pope in the years of the Dunciad quarrels, were printed in 1732.

poets.name: John Gay
bio: John Gay (1685–1732) was an English poet and dramatist, born in Barnstaple, Devon. A friend of Pope, Swift and Arbuthnot, he wrote Trivia, a mock-georgic on walking the streets of London, and The Beggar’s Opera (1728), a ballad opera that was a great popular success.

His Fables, published in two series in 1727 and 1738, are short verse stories in which animals speak and act as foils to human folly. They were widely read for generations and are the part of his verse that still has readers.

poets.name: George Berkeley
bio: George Berkeley (1685–1753), born in County Kilkenny, was an Anglo-Irish philosopher and clergyman, Bishop of Cloyne from 1734. He is best known for his philosophical idealism, set out in A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge (1710), and for his scheme of founding a college in Bermuda.

His one famous poem, the verses on the prospect of planting arts and learning in America, was written about 1726 while he waited for support for that scheme. Its last stanza, "Westward the course of empire takes its way," became one of the most quoted lines of the eighteenth century.

poets.name: Thomas Tickell
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Tickell was a friend and follower of Joseph Addison, a Fellow of Queen's College, Oxford, and an under-secretary of state. Gilfillan gives his birth as 1686 at Bridekirk near Carlisle.
His elegy To the Earl of Warwick, on the Death of Mr Addison (1721), prefixed to Addison's Works, is generally counted his finest poem and is printed in full.

poets.name: Aaron Hill
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Aaron Hill (1685–1750) was an English dramatist, poet and projector, a patron of younger writers and a correspondent of Pope and Richardson. His verse was collected in his Works (1753).

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Henry Carey
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Henry Carey was an English poet, songwriter and musician who wrote the words and often the music of popular ballads and stage pieces. He died in 1743.
His best-known song is "Sally in Our Alley", which Palgrave includes.

poets.name: Allan Ramsay
poets.credit: Portrait: William Aikman — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Allan Ramsay was a Scottish poet, wig-maker and bookseller in Edinburgh, born at Leadhills in Lanarkshire. He founded a circulating library, edited the Tea-Table Miscellany and wrote the pastoral drama The Gentle Shepherd. He is not to be confused with the nineteenth-century John Ramsay also in this archive.
Gilfillan prints two of his songs, Lochaber No More and The Last Time I Came o'er the Moor.

poets.name: Stephen Tilden
bio: Stephen Tilden (1686–1766) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “The British Lyon Roused” and “Braddock's Fate”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Thomas Sheridan
bio: Thomas Sheridan (1687–1738) was an Irish clergyman and schoolmaster in Dublin, a close friend of Jonathan Swift and the grandfather of the dramatist Richard Brinsley Sheridan. He was known for his wit and for the verse exchanges he kept up with Swift.
The pieces here are those that James Parton assigned to him in his anthology of English humorous poetry.

poets.name: Alexander Pope
poets.credit: Portrait of Alexander Pope by Michael Dahl, c. 1727 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alexander Pope (1688–1744) was the foremost English poet of the early 18th century, master of the heroic couplet and the sharpest satirist of his age.

Barred by his Catholicism and ill health from university or public office, he made a career (and a fortune) from his verse and his acclaimed translation of Homer; The Rape of the Lock and An Essay on Man remain his best-loved works.

poets.name: Mazhar Jan-i Janan
bio: Mazhar of Delhi, of a family originally from Bokhara, is described in the book as learned in jurisprudence as well as poetry, with many favourite poets among his pupils, a Sunni who professed spiritual poverty and was reputed able to work miracles. The book says he was killed by a fanatic because he disagreed with the Shiah mourning for the death of Hussein, and died in 1780, aged nearly a hundred years.

The 5 pieces given here are drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. They are free renderings, not literal translations, and the original Urdu poems are untitled; each is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Thomas Warton the Elder
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Warton the Elder was a clergyman and Professor of Poetry at Oxford, father of the poets and critics Joseph and Thomas Warton the Younger. Gilfillan gives the years 1687 to 1745.
Gilfillan prints two of his short poems.

poets.name: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu
poets.credit: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, by Jonathan Richardson the younger, c. 1725 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu (1689–1762) was an English aristocrat, letter-writer and poet, famous for her Turkish Embassy Letters and for introducing smallpox inoculation to England. Her town eclogues and verse epistles circulated in manuscript and print in her lifetime.

The two poems 'The Lover' and 'On Seeing a Portrait of Sir Robert Walpole' follow Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867); the other verse here follows The Works of the Right Honourable Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, vol. V: Poems (London, 1817, ed. Dallaway), with the letters, essays and notes left out and the Italian and French pieces omitted. Of the six Town Eclogues, five are given here; Roxana and Thursday ('The Bassette Table') are held under Pope.

poets.name: William Broome
bio: William Broome (1689–1745) was an English clergyman and poet who collaborated with Alexander Pope on the translation of Homer’s Odyssey, translating eight of its books himself.
Arthur Quiller-Couch included two of his short poems in The Oxford Book of English Verse (1900).

poets.name: Sean Clarach Mac Donnell
bio: Sean Clarach Mac Donnell was born in Co. Cork in 1691 and is said by Sigerson, in Bards of the Gael and Gall (1907), to have died in 1751. He kept up the custom of holding sessions of bards, and was known for his learning in Irish, Latin and Greek.
Three of his songs are given here in Sigerson’s English versions: “Over the Hills and Far Away”, “Grainne Mael” and “The Dells of Orrerie”.

poets.name: Johann Andreas Rothe
poets.credit: No portrait available (monogram tile). Text: G. Osborn (ed.), The Poetical Works of John and Charles Wesley, 13 vols (London: Wesleyan-Methodist Conference Office, 1868–72), from Internet Archive scans (OCR).
bio: Johann Andreas Rothe (1688–1758) was a German pastor and hymn-writer; his “Ich habe nun den Grund gefunden” (1722) was written while he served at Berthelsdorf, where Count Zinzendorf was patron.
The single piece here is John Wesley’s abridged English translation, printed in Hymns and Sacred Poems (1740); Osborn’s footnote names Rothe as the author of the German original.

poets.name: John Byrom
poets.credit: Portrait of John Byrom (18th-century portrait, artist unknown) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Byrom (1691–1763), born at Kersal near Manchester, was educated at Merchant Taylors' School and Trinity College, Cambridge, where he became a fellow. He devised a system of shorthand, and is remembered for the Christmas hymn ‘Christians, awake, salute the happy morn’.

A follower of the mystic William Law, he put passages from the writings of Jakob Boehme (Behmen) into English verse. The poems printed here are those given in The Oxford Book of English Mystical Verse (1917), edited by D. H. S. Nicholson and A. H. E. Lee; the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Samuel Wesley the Younger
bio: Samuel Wesley the younger (1690–1739), the eldest son of the rector of Epworth and elder brother of John and Charles Wesley, was an usher at Westminster School and later headmaster of Blundell's School at Tiverton. He is not to be confused with his father, Samuel Wesley the elder (1662–1735), also a poet.
He wrote hymns, satires and epigrams, collected in Poems on Several Occasions (1736), and was a friend of Francis Atterbury, Bishop of Rochester.

poets.name: George Bubb Dodington, Lord Melcombe
bio: George Bubb Dodington (1691?–1762), created Baron Melcombe in 1761, was an English politician and a patron of writers, and the author of a widely read political diary.
His occasional verse is represented in The Oxford Book of English Verse by "Shorten Sail".

poets.name: Philip Dormer Stanhope, Earl of Chesterfield
poets.credit: Portrait of the 4th Earl of Chesterfield by Allan Ramsay, 1765 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Philip Dormer Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield (1694–1773), was a statesman, diplomat and celebrated wit, now best known for his Letters to his Son on manners and the conduct of life.
The epigram here is the one James Parton printed under his name in his anthology of English humorous poetry.

poets.name: Voltaire
poets.credit: Portrait of Voltaire by Nicolas de Largillière (c. 1718) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: François-Marie Arouet, called Voltaire (1694–1778), was the central writer of the French Enlightenment: dramatist, historian, satirist, letter-writer and the author of the philosophical tale Candide. He spent the years 1726–28 in exile in England, where he met the circle of Pope and Swift and began to publish his epic poem.

La Henriade, first printed as La Ligue in 1723 and revised until its definitive text of 1728, takes the civil wars of religion under Henri IV as its subject and is the only French epic in ten cantos in the classical manner. It was long counted among the great poems of the age. It appears here in a rhymed English version of the eighteenth century.

poets.name: Robert Crawford
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Robert Crawford was a Scottish songwriter who contributed to Allan Ramsay's Tea-Table Miscellany. Gilfillan records that he was drowned while returning from France in 1733.
His song The Bush aboon Traquair is one of the early Scots songs of the eighteenth century revival.

poets.name: William Oldys
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Oldys was an English antiquary and bibliographer who died in 1761. He is the author of a famous short lyric about a fly drinking from his cup.
Gilfillan prints the song, Busy, Curious, Thirsty Fly, here under his own title.

poets.name: Sabqatî (Sultan Mahmud I)
bio: Mahmud I succeeded his uncle Ahmed III in 1730 and wrote verse under the pen-name Sabqati.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Matthew Green
bio: Matthew Green (1696–1737) was an English poet born of Nonconformist parents, who for many years held a post in the Custom House in London and was known among his friends as a wit.
His chief work, The Spleen, an epistle in octosyllabic couplets, was published after his death, in 1737. The poem given here is taken from The Spleen and Other Poems (1796).

poets.name: Richard Savage
bio: Richard Savage (1697/8–1743) was an English poet and satirist whose year of birth is contested: he himself claimed to be the illegitimate son of the Countess of Macclesfield and Earl Rivers, and the dates given for his birth vary, so 1697 or 1698 is only an approximation. He lived by his pen and by patrons, was condemned to death for a tavern killing in 1727 and pardoned, and died in Bristol's Newgate debtors' prison in 1743.

The Wanderer (1729), dedicated to Lord Tyrconnel, is his best-known poem, a visionary meditation in five cantos in heroic couplets that sets the still life against the active. His friend Samuel Johnson told his story in the Life of Mr Richard Savage (1744), which shaped his later reputation and from which much of what is told about his origins derives.

poets.name: Gerhard Tersteegen
bio: Gerhard Tersteegen was born at Moers in 1697 and died at Mülheim an der Ruhr in 1769. A ribbon weaver by trade, he became a lay preacher and spiritual counsellor in the Reformed Pietist tradition, and published his hymns in Geistliches Blumengärtlein (1729) and later collections.
The English versions here are Catherine Winkworth's in Lyra Germanica (1855).

poets.name: Robert Blair
bio: Robert Blair (1699–1746) was a Scottish minister and poet, born in Edinburgh and for many years parish minister of Athelstaneford in East Lothian. He wrote little verse that survives.

His blank-verse poem The Grave (1743) is a gloomy meditation on death and the churchyard in the manner of the so-called graveyard poets, and was often reprinted, notably with William Blake’s designs in 1808.

poets.name: Shah Hatim
bio: The book calls Hatim one of the early Urdu poets, born about 1700 and living till near the end of the century: a soldier by profession who in old age renounced the world and became a darwesh, with his cell near the gate of the Imperial Palace, where many resorted to him for counsel. The foreword names him, with Wali, as one of the first to write an Urdu diwan.

The one piece given here is drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. It is a free rendering, not a literal translation, and the original Urdu poem is untitled; it is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Alexander Ross
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Alexander Ross was a Scottish schoolmaster at Lochlee in Forfarshire and author of the pastoral poem Helenore, or the Fortunate Shepherdess (1768), written in the Scots of the north-east.
Gilfillan prints two of his songs, Woo'd and Married and A' and The Rock an' the Wee Pickle Tow.

poets.name: John Dyer
poets.credit: John Dyer, engraving by the Brothers Dalziel (1855), from a portrait supplied by W. H. Longstaffe · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Dyer was a Welsh poet and painter, born in Carmarthenshire in 1699. He trained as a painter, travelled in Italy in the 1720s, and brought a painter's eye for hill, valley and ruin into his verse.

Grongar Hill, a poem about the Towy valley near his home, first appeared in 1726 and became one of the most anthologised English poems of the century. The Ruins of Rome (1740) came out of his Italian journey; Dyer later took holy orders and served as a country clergyman in Lincolnshire.

His last and longest work was The Fleece (1757), a blank-verse poem in four books on sheep, wool and the cloth trade, published in the year he died. Wordsworth honoured him in a sonnet addressed to the poet of the Fleece.

poets.name: Thomas Whittle
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Whittle is represented here by verse printed in John Bell's Rhymes of Northern Bards (Newcastle, 1812), 5 pieces.
John Bell's collection describes Thomas Whittle as a Northumbrian by birth who lived long near Cambo; the date given is the year of the wager with William Carstairs that Bell's note mentions.

poets.name: Thomas Edwards
bio: Thomas Edwards (1699–1757) was an English lawyer and critic. His Canons of Criticism (1748) attacked Warburton's edition of Shakespeare, and he wrote sonnets in the manner of Milton.
The sonnet given here, on a picture of his brothers and sisters, was printed in the second volume of Dodsley's Collection of Poems (1748).

poets.name: James Thomson
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: James Thomson was a Scottish poet who made his name with The Seasons (1726-30), a landmark of eighteenth-century nature poetry.
Palgrave includes "Rule Britannia", written for the masque Alfred, and a short love song.

poets.name: Yakrang
poets.dates: dates not given in the source
bio: The book says Yakrang was one of the officers of the Emperor Muhammad Shah (r. 1719–48), who lived in dignity and honour at Delhi. It gives no dates for him.

The one piece given here is drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. It is a free rendering, not a literal translation, and the original Urdu poem is untitled; it is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Mac Aib
bio: Mac Aib (now Mac Cabe) is the bard to whom Sigerson, in Bards of the Gael and Gall (1907), attributes an elegy on the death of the harper Turlough O’Carolan in 1738, and he calls him a brother bard.
The elegy is given here in Sigerson’s English version.

poets.name: Andrias Mac Cuirtin
bio: Andrias Mac Cuirtin is dated by Sigerson, in Bards of the Gael and Gall (1907), to 1737. His “Doreen le Poer” is a poem in praise of a young lady, one of the society verses and madrigals that Sigerson says helped to sweeten society under the Penal Code.
It is given here in Sigerson’s English version.

poets.name: Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf
poets.credit: No portrait available (monogram tile). Text: G. Osborn (ed.), The Poetical Works of John and Charles Wesley, 13 vols (London: Wesleyan-Methodist Conference Office, 1868–72), from Internet Archive scans (OCR).
bio: Nikolaus Ludwig, Count von Zinzendorf (1700–1760), born in Dresden, was the patron of the Moravian community at Herrnhut and later a bishop of the Moravian Church. He was a prolific hymn-writer, and his hymns circulated in the Herrnhuth hymn-book that the Wesleys knew.

The pieces here are John Wesley’s English translations of 1738–42, in which Osborn’s footnotes name Zinzendorf as the author of the German original (citing the Herrnhuth Collection and Knapp’s Evangelischer Liederschatz). Osborn sometimes hedges the identification with “compare” or “is said to be”.

poets.name: Anonymous (Scottish Gaelic)
poets.dates: traditional; collected in the Highlands and Islands 1855–1899
poets.credit: No portrait: these are anonymous oral prayers, charms and songs, gathered by Alexander Carmichael and published in Carmina Gadelica (1900).
bio: The prayers, blessings, songs and charms gathered here come from the Gaelic-speaking Highlands and Hebrides, where they were recited from memory by crofters, fishermen, shepherds and women at the quern and the loom. They belong to no single author: the same invocations turn up in different islands in different versions, and they blend Christian devotion with older customs of the hearth, the byre, the sea and the seasons.

They were written down between 1855 and 1899 by Alexander Carmichael, an excise officer and folklorist, and published with his English translations as Carmina Gadelica (Ortha nan Gaidheal), volume I, in 1900. The poems here are Carmichael’s English versions of the 121 pieces in that volume, which he arranged under the headings Invocations, Seasons and Labour, with the Gaelic title of each given in its note. His prose headnotes, notes, and the short inset fragments in small type are left out.

poets.name: Lewis Morris
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Lewis Morris (Llewelyn Ddu o Fôn, 1701–1765) was an Anglesey poet and scholar, a leading figure in the eighteenth-century revival of Welsh letters and the patron and friend of Goronwy Owen.
The poem here is George Borrow's English version of a Welsh song of Merioneth, from Borrow's manuscripts, printed in Welsh Poems and Ballads (1915).

poets.name: Lu Chu-ch’i
bio: Lu Chu-ch’i is dated by Giles to the 18th century AD. His poem here is an impromptu couplet.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Tsing-nien
bio: Tsing-nien is a Chinese poet named in Charles Budd’s Chinese Poems (1912). Budd, who calls the piece a modern poem composed by a successful student, attributes it to a poet of the Ch’ing (his T’sing) dynasty and gives no note for him.
The poems here are Charles Budd’s versions in Chinese Poems (1912), given under the poet’s name as Budd romanises it.

poets.name: Chang Hsüan
bio: Chang Hsüan is a Chinese poet named in Charles Budd’s Chinese Poems (1912). Budd, who spells the name Chang-Hsuen, places him in the Ch’ing (his T’sing) dynasty and gives no further note for him.
The poems here are Charles Budd’s versions in Chinese Poems (1912), given under the poet’s name as Budd romanises it.

poets.name: Cheng-cheng
bio: Cheng-cheng is a Chinese poet named in Charles Budd’s Chinese Poems (1912). Budd attributes to him a prize poem of the Ch’ing (his T’sing) dynasty and gives no further note for him.
The poems here are Charles Budd’s versions in Chinese Poems (1912), given under the poet’s name as Budd romanises it.

poets.name: Lu-teh
bio: Lu-teh is a Chinese poet named in Charles Budd’s Chinese Poems (1912). Budd places him in the Ch’ing (his T’sing) dynasty and gives no further note for him.
The poems here are Charles Budd’s versions in Chinese Poems (1912), given under the poet’s name as Budd romanises it.

poets.name: Ferenc Faludi
bio: Hungarian Jesuit poet, born at Güssing, sometimes called the father of the new Hungarian lyric.
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: Stephen Duck
bio: Stephen Duck (1705–1756) was an English poet, born in Wiltshire and working as an agricultural labourer when he began to write verse. His poem The Thresher's Labour, which describes the farm worker's year of toil, became known beyond his village and brought him to the notice of Queen Caroline, who gave him a pension and a place at court.

He later took holy orders and served as a clergyman and as keeper of the Queen's library at Richmond. Poems on Several Occasions (1736), the collection drawn on here, gathers his verse, including The Thresher's Labour, longer narrative poems such as Avaro and Amanda, and imitations of Horace.

poets.name: Belîg
bio: Belig was the son of a certain Qara Bag 'Ali Efendi of Kayseri and came to Constantinople in 1703, where he lived in one of the medreses of the mosque of Mehmed II.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Sâmî
bio: Sami is the annalist whose history forms one of the volumes of the Imperial Historiographers; Gibb calls him particularly strong in the mufred, the single couplet.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Nev-res
bio: Nev-res was a poet of the times of Mahmud I and Mustafa III, whose praises he sings; he was banished to Bursa in 1761 and died there shortly afterwards.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Philip Doddridge
poets.credit: Engraving by George Vertue, 1751 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Philip Doddridge (1702-1751) was an English Nonconformist minister, teacher and writer. Born in London, he became pastor of the Independent congregation at Northampton in 1729 and ran an academy there for training ministers. His best-known prose works include The Family Expositor and The Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul.

He wrote many hymns, usually composed to accompany the conclusion of his Sunday sermons, and they circulated in manuscript and in print among Dissenting congregations. The present collection of 370 hymns was published after his death in 1755 from his manuscript by his friend Job Orton. Several of its hymns, such as O God of Bethel, by whose hand, remained in common use.

poets.name: Benjamin Stillingfleet
bio: Benjamin Stillingfleet (1702–1771) was an English naturalist and writer, a friend of Elizabeth Montagu and her circle of learned women.
The sonnet given here, addressed to his friend Williamson, was written in 1746 and printed in Todd's edition of Milton (1801).

poets.name: Robert Craggs Nugent, Earl Nugent
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Robert Craggs, afterwards Robert Craggs Nugent and Earl Nugent, was an Irish-born politician, who published a small body of verse.
Gilfillan prints his Ode to Mankind.

poets.name: William Hamilton of Bangour
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Hamilton of Bangour was a Scottish poet and Jacobite who was forced into exile after the rising of 1745 and died at Lyons in 1754.
His ballad The Braes of Yarrow, a lament modelled on the older Border ballads, is printed in full by Gilfillan.

poets.name: John Wesley
poets.credit: Portrait of John Wesley, a copy after George Romney (original of 1789) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Wesley (1703–1791) was born at Epworth, Lincolnshire, educated at Charterhouse and Christ Church, Oxford, and became a fellow of Lincoln College. With his brother Charles he led the Oxford “Holy Club”. After a mission to Georgia (1735–38), where he learned German from the Moravians and began to translate their hymns, and his evangelical conversion in May 1738, he became the organiser of the Methodist movement.

In this archive he appears as the editor and translator of hymns. Osborn’s edition (G. Osborn (ed.), The Poetical Works of John and Charles Wesley, 13 vols (London: Wesleyan-Methodist Conference Office, 1868–72), from Internet Archive scans (OCR)) reprints the Collection of Psalms and Hymns that John Wesley published in 1741, of which only the pieces Osborn could not trace to other authors are given here, and records his translations from the German and Spanish. German pieces whose original author Osborn names stand under that author’s name.

poets.name: August Gottlieb Spangenberg
poets.credit: No portrait available (monogram tile). Text: G. Osborn (ed.), The Poetical Works of John and Charles Wesley, 13 vols (London: Wesleyan-Methodist Conference Office, 1868–72), from Internet Archive scans (OCR).
bio: August Gottlieb Spangenberg (1704–1792) was a leader and bishop of the Moravian Church and the author of several hymns in the Herrnhuth Collection.

The single piece here is John Wesley’s English translation “God’s Husbandry”, printed in 1742; Osborn’s footnote names Spangenberg (“Bishop A. G. Spangenberg”) as the author of the German hymn with which it should be compared.

poets.name: Isaac Hawkins Browne
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Isaac Hawkins Browne was an English poet and member of parliament, born at Burton-on-Trent in 1705. He is best remembered for the Pipe of Tobacco (1736), a set of imitations of Thomson, Pope, Swift and other poets, in which he praised tobacco in their manner.
Gilfillan prints three of the imitations, of Thomson, Pope and Swift.

poets.name: Robert Lambe
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Robert Lambe is represented here by verse printed in John Bell's Rhymes of Northern Bards (Newcastle, 1812), 1 piece.
Bell's heading names him Robert Lambe, Vicar of Norham, and prints his ballad of the Laidley Worm of Spindleston Heugh.

poets.name: Soame Jenyns
poets.credit: Soame Jenyns, engraving by William Dickinson after Sir Joshua Reynolds, 1776 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Soame Jenyns (1704–1787) was an English writer and member of parliament, author of the poem The Art of Dancing (1730) and of A Free Inquiry into the Nature and Origin of Evil (1757), which drew a famous review from Samuel Johnson.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: David Mallet
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: David Mallet, who altered the Scottish form of his surname Malloch, was a Scottish poet, dramatist and man of letters who worked in London and was the friend of James Thomson and Pope.
Gilfillan prints two of his ballads, William and Margaret and The Birks of Invermay.

poets.name: Benjamin Franklin
poets.credit: Portrait of Benjamin Franklin, by Joseph-Siffred Duplessis · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) was an American Founding Father and polymath.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “The Downfall of Piracy” and “The Mother Country”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Henry Fielding
poets.credit: Portrait of Henry Fielding · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Fielding (1707–1754) was an English novelist and dramatist, the author of Tom Jones (1749), and later a London magistrate. Before the novels he wrote satirical plays and verse aimed at the government of Sir Robert Walpole.
The poem here is the one James Parton printed under his name in his anthology of English humorous poetry, where it is introduced as addressed by Fielding to Walpole.

poets.name: Mather Byles
poets.credit: Mezzotint of Mather Byles by Peter Pelham (18th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mather Byles (1707–1788) was a Congregational minister in Boston and the best-known American poet of his generation. A nephew of Cotton Mather, he corresponded with Alexander Pope and others in England, and his Poems on Several Occasions was published in Boston in 1744.
Celebrated in Boston for his wit and his punning, he served the Hollis Street Church for decades. He remained loyal to the Crown during the Revolution and was dismissed from his pulpit in 1776.

poets.name: Charles Wesley
poets.credit: Portrait of Charles Wesley, 18th century (painter not named in the Wikimedia Commons record) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Wesley (1707–1788) was born at Epworth, Lincolnshire, the youngest surviving son of Samuel and Susanna Wesley and the brother of John Wesley. Educated at Westminster School and Christ Church, Oxford, he joined the small band of students nicknamed the “Holy Club” or “Methodists”, was ordained in 1735 and went with John to Georgia, returning in 1736. After his evangelical conversion in May 1738 he became, with his brother, a leader of the Methodist revival, and wrote the hymns for which he is chiefly remembered; more than six thousand are credited to him.

The texts here are transcribed from G. Osborn (ed.), The Poetical Works of John and Charles Wesley, 13 vols (London: Wesleyan-Methodist Conference Office, 1868–72), from Internet Archive scans (OCR). Osborn does not distinguish the brothers in the publications of 1739–49 that bore both their names, so pieces from those collections carry a note to that effect; the thirteen volumes also include Charles Wesley’s separate collections, his Short Hymns on Select Passages of the Holy Scriptures (1762) and his scattered poems. Pieces that Osborn marks as taken from Herbert or other poets, or as the work of Samuel Wesley the elder, John Gambold or John Byrom, are not included.

poets.name: Mary Jones
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Mary Jones (c. 1707–1778) was an English poet who lived at Oxford with her brother, a clergyman, and was a friend of Lady Bridgeman. Her Miscellanies in Prose and Verse appeared in 1750.

The poem here is the one printed under her name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Sir Charles Hanbury Williams
poets.credit: Sir Charles Hanbury Williams by John Giles Eccardt, c. 1746 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Charles Hanbury Williams (1708–1759) was a diplomat and member of parliament who served as British envoy at several European courts and wrote satirical and occasional verse that circulated widely in manuscript. His works were first collected in 1822.
The poem here is the fable that James Parton included in his anthology of English humorous poetry.

poets.name: John Armstrong
poets.credit: Portrait: Joshua Reynolds — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Armstrong (1709–1779) was a Scottish physician and poet trained in medicine at Edinburgh. He practised in London, served as physician to the army, and was a friend of James Thomson, whose The Castle of Indolence includes a stanza by him.

His best-known poem is The Art of Preserving Health (1744), a four-book work in blank verse on air, diet, exercise and the passions, praised in its day for bringing didactic verse to a medical subject. He also published essays and later poems.

poets.name: Samuel Johnson
poets.credit: Portrait of Samuel Johnson by Sir Joshua Reynolds, c. 1772 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Samuel Johnson (1709–1784) — lexicographer, essayist, critic, and the dominant literary figure of mid-18th-century England — also wrote poetry of severe, weighty moral force.
London and The Vanity of Human Wishes, both close imitations of Juvenal’s satires, and his plain elegy for his friend Robert Levet, show the same unflinching realism that marks his prose.

poets.name: George Lyttelton, 1st Baron Lyttelton
poets.credit: George Lyttelton, 1st Baron Lyttelton, portrait by an unknown artist, c. 1756 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Lyttelton, 1st Baron Lyttelton (1709–1773), was an English politician, patron of James Thomson, Henry Fielding and Alexander Pope, and the author of verse, dialogues and a History of Henry II. He is the Lord Lyttelton of Samuel Johnson's Lives of the Poets.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: George Alexander Stevens
poets.credit: George Alexander Stevens (with Mrs Paul Sandby), by Paul Sandby · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Alexander Stevens (1710–1784) was an English actor, dramatist and songwriter, born in London. After years as a strolling player he made his name on the London stage and, above all, as a solo entertainer: his comic monologue 'A Lecture upon Heads' (1764) was a long-running success in Britain and abroad.

His convivial and topical songs were performed at taverns, clubs and his own entertainments, and he gathered them in 'Songs, Comic and Satyrical' (1772). They mock fashion, politics, quackery and fashionable folly in the broad manner of the Augustan ballad, and many were set to popular tunes of the day.

poets.name: Paul Whitehead
bio: Paul Whitehead (1710–1774) was an English satirical poet, author of the verse satires Manners (1739) and Honour (1747), and a steward of Sir Francis Dashwood's Medmenham brotherhood.
His Hunting Song was sung in the ballad-opera Apollo and Daphne (1734, or later) and is the poem given here, from the Oxford Book of Eighteenth Century Verse (1926).

poets.name: Mikhail Lomonosov
poets.credit: Portrait of Mikhail Lomonosov, engraving by L. Miropolsky (1787) after Georg Caspar Prenner · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mikhail Vasilyevich Lomonosov (1711–1765) was born near Kholmogory in the far north of Russia, the son of a fisherman. He studied in Moscow and in Germany, became a professor at the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences, took part in founding Moscow University (1755), and worked as both scientist and poet. He helped fix the rules of Russian versification and the literary language, and his solemn odes made him the leading Russian poet of the mid-eighteenth century.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: James Hammond
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: James Hammond was an English politician and poet, educated at Westminster School and attached to the household of the Prince of Wales. He sat in parliament for Truro and died in 1742.
He is remembered for his Love Elegies, published after his death, of which Gilfillan prints the thirteenth.

poets.name: Donnchad Ruadh MacNamara
bio: Donnchad Ruadh MacNamara is dated in Eleanor Hull's The Poem-Book of the Gael to about 1730, and is given there as the author of “The Fair Hills of Eire”.
The English version gathered here is by George Sigerson, printed in Hull's anthology (London, 1913).

poets.name: William Inglis
bio: William Inglis (often wrongly given as English) was born at Newcastle in Co. Limerick, taught classics for a time, and wrote some well-known Irish songs. Sigerson, in Bards of the Gael and Gall (1907), says he gave up song-writing on becoming an Augustinian friar, and that he died in 1778 in Cork.
His song “The Flower of Love” is given here in Sigerson’s English version.

poets.name: Charles Wyndham, 2nd Earl of Egremont
poets.credit: Charles Wyndham, 2nd Earl of Egremont, by William Hoare, 1762 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Wyndham, 2nd Earl of Egremont (1710–1763), was an English politician who served as Secretary of State for the Southern Department from 1761 to 1763. A single light poem, "The Fair Thief", is traditionally given to him.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: John Gambold
poets.credit: Engraving of John Gambold by Jonathan Spilsbury after Abraham Louis Brandt, 1771 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Gambold (1711–1771) was born at Puncheston, Pembrokeshire, and educated at Christ Church, Oxford, where he knew the Wesleys. Ordained in the Church of England, he became vicar of Stanton Harcourt, Oxfordshire; in 1742 he joined the Moravian Church, of which he became a bishop in 1754.

He did not publish his poems himself; several were first printed by the Wesleys in Hymns and Sacred Poems (1739). The pieces here are those that Osborn marks as Gambold’s in that volume (G. Osborn (ed.), The Poetical Works of John and Charles Wesley, 13 vols (London: Wesleyan-Methodist Conference Office, 1868–72), from Internet Archive scans (OCR)), where he cites Gambold’s Works (Bath, 1789).

poets.name: Alison Cockburn
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Alison Cockburn (née Rutherford) was a Scottish society hostess in Edinburgh, a friend of Hume, Scott and Burns, and the author of one of the best-known versions of The Flowers of the Forest.
Gilfillan prints her version, which opens 'I've seen the smiling', beside the older version by Jean Elliot.

poets.name: Edward Moore
bio: Edward Moore (1712-1757) was born at Abingdon, Berkshire, the son of a dissenting minister. He was apprenticed to a linen-draper and set up in trade in London, but his business failed and he turned to writing. His Fables for the Ladies (1744), light verse apologues on love, vanity and the manners of the town, won him wide popularity and a long afterlife in the anthologies.

Moore also wrote for the stage, notably the comedy The Foundling (1748) and the domestic tragedy The Gamester (1753), and he conducted the periodical The World (1753-56) with Lord Chesterfield and other wits. This selection follows the verse in the 1782 Bell's Poets edition: the sixteen Fables, two Odes, the satirical and occasional pieces of the Miscellanies, and the Songs.

poets.name: Gedeon Ráday
bio: Hungarian nobleman, poet and translator, Count Gedeon Ráday de Ráda.
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: Richard Glover
poets.credit: Portrait: Friedrich Fleischmann — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Glover was a London merchant, politician and poet, best known for the epic Leonidas (1737) and for the ballad Admiral Hosier's Ghost (1739), which he wrote on the capture of Porto Bello.
Gilfillan prints the ballad in full.

poets.name: Mesech Weare
bio: Mesech Weare (1713–1786) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “The Blasted Herb”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: William Shenstone
poets.credit: Portrait of William Shenstone by Edward Alcock, 1760 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Shenstone (1714–1763) was an English poet and landscape gardener, born at Halesowen in Shropshire (now the West Midlands) and educated at Pembroke College, Oxford. He is remembered for The School-Mistress (1742), a gently comic imitation of Spenser, and for his Elegies, Odes, Songs and Ballads, which were widely admired in the middle of the eighteenth century.

From 1745 he lived on his family estate, The Leasowes, near Halesowen, which he laid out as a ferme ornee, a working farm shaped into a landscape of walks, cascades and inscriptions. Visitors came from across Britain to see it, and it helped shape the English taste for the picturesque garden. His Works in Verse and Prose appeared after his death, and the poems here follow the two-volume Poetical Works of 1778.

poets.name: Taban
bio: The book describes Taban of Delhi as famous for his beauty as for his poetic talent, a pupil of Hatim and a friend of Mazhar and Sauda, descended from the Prophet on both his father’s and mother’s side.

The 2 pieces given here are drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. They are free renderings, not literal translations, and the original Urdu poems are untitled; each is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Robert Mackay (Rob Donn)
bio: Robert Mackay (Rob Donn) (c. 1714–1778) wrote in Gaelic; Charles Rogers printed English verse renderings of the bard's songs in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 English rendering from the Gaelic in volumes 1 and 2 of the anthology; each is credited to the translator whom Rogers names. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir.

poets.name: William Whitehead
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Whitehead was an English poet and dramatist, educated at Winchester and Clare Hall, Cambridge, who succeeded Colley Cibber as Poet Laureate in 1757. He is not to be confused with the satirist Paul Whitehead.
Gilfillan prints his verse tale Variety.

poets.name: Richard Jago
poets.credit: Richard Jago, portrait by an unknown artist, 18th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Jago (1715–1781) was an English clergyman and poet, a friend and Oxford contemporary of William Shenstone. He is known for his topographical poem Edge-Hill (1767) and for short lyrics such as "Absence".

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Thomas Gray
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Gray by John Giles Eccardt, 1747-48 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Gray (1716–1771) was a reclusive Cambridge scholar who published only a handful of poems in his lifetime, yet his Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard became one of the most quoted poems in the English language.
His Pindaric odes The Progress of Poesy and The Bard helped carry English verse from Augustan restraint toward the Romantic sublime.

poets.name: Anne Steele
poets.credit: Title page and frontispiece of Poems on Subjects Chiefly Devotional, by Theodosia (Bristol, 1780, vol. 1) · An artifact, shown because no authentic portrait of Anne Steele is known · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Anne Steele (1717–1778) was an English Baptist hymn-writer who spent her whole life at Broughton in Hampshire, where her father was a Dissenting minister and pastor of the congregation. Her health was never firm, and she wrote chiefly for her family and friends; it was only with reluctance that she allowed any of it to be published, under the name “Theodosia”. Her Poems on Subjects Chiefly Devotional appeared in two volumes in 1760, and a third volume of Miscellaneous Pieces in Prose and Verse was published after her death, in 1780, by the Rev. Caleb Evans of Bristol. Her hymns, among them “Father of mercies, in thy word”, made her the first major woman hymn-writer in English.

The texts given here follow the Boston edition of 1808 (volume I: the hymns and the occasional poems), with the Psalm versions and the posthumous miscellaneous poems taken from the Bristol edition of 1780. The prose meditations and essays of those volumes are not included.

poets.name: Elizabeth Carter
bio: Elizabeth Carter (1717–1806) was an English scholar, translator and poet, born at Deal in Kent. Her translation of Epictetus appeared in 1758, and she was one of the learned women of the bluestocking circle.
Her Ode to Wisdom first appeared in The Gentleman's Magazine in December 1747.
