poets.name: William Williams Pantycelyn
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Williams, called Pantycelyn after his home, was a leading Welsh Methodist preacher and the greatest of Welsh hymn-writers, often called the national poet of Wales.
His hymn "Marchog Jesu!" is given in English verse by Alfred Perceval Graves in A Celtic Psaltery (1917).

poets.name: Yüan Mei
bio: Yüan Mei was a Ch’ing poet and critic. His poem here is a sceptical epigram on the gods.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Horace Walpole, Earl of Orford
poets.credit: Horace Walpole, by Sir Joshua Reynolds, c. 1756–57 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Horace Walpole, 4th Earl of Orford (1717–1797), was an English writer, collector and politician, author of the Gothic novel The Castle of Otranto (1764) and of the great series of Letters. He built Strawberry Hill and wrote graceful occasional verse.

The 2 poems here are the pieces printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: David Garrick
poets.credit: David Garrick, by Thomas Gainsborough, c. 1770 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: David Garrick (1717–1779) was the foremost English actor of the eighteenth century and manager of the Drury Lane Theatre. He also wrote prologues, epilogues, epigrams and songs, among them "Heart of Oak".

The 3 poems here are the pieces printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Lőrinc Orczy
poets.credit: Portrait of Lőrinc Orczy, c. 1740s, artist unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Hungarian nobleman, general and poet.
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: Johann Wilhelm Ludwig Gleim
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Johann Wilhelm Ludwig Gleim lived for most of his life at Halberstadt. He wrote Anacreontic songs and, in 1758, the patriotic Prussian War Songs of a Grenadier, and was a generous friend to younger poets.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Johann Elias Schlegel
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Johann Elias Schlegel was born at Meissen. A dramatist and critic of the early German Enlightenment, he died young while teaching in Denmark.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Francis Fawkes
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Francis Fawkes was an English clergyman and translator of Anacreon, Sappho, Theocritus and Apollonius Rhodius.
Gilfillan prints his drinking-song The Brown Jug.

poets.name: James Merrick
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: James Merrick was an English clergyman and scholar of Trinity College, Oxford, who versified the Psalms and wrote fables.
His poem The Chameleon is a fable about two travellers who quarrel over the colour of a chameleon; Gilfillan prints it in full.

poets.name: Conor O'Riordan
bio: Conor O'Riordan is dated in Eleanor Hull's The Poem-Book of the Gael to about 1750, and is given there as the author of a hymn to the Virgin Mary.
The English version gathered here is the one printed in Hull's anthology (London, 1913), where no other translator is named.

poets.name: Tobias Smollett
poets.credit: Portrait of Tobias Smollett by Nathaniel Dance-Holland, c. 1770 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Tobias Smollett (1721–1771) was a Scottish surgeon and writer, born at Dalquhurn in Dunbartonshire and trained in Glasgow. He served as a naval surgeon's mate, settled in London, and made his name with the picaresque novels Roderick Random (1748), Peregrine Pickle (1751) and Humphry Clinker (1771).

His verse is the smaller part of his work: the satires Advice and Reproof, The Tears of Scotland, written after Culloden in 1746, and the Ode to Independence, published after his death. He died near Livorno in Italy in 1771.

poets.name: Mark Akenside
bio: Mark Akenside (1721–1770) was born in Newcastle upon Tyne, the son of a butcher, and studied at Edinburgh and Leiden before practising as a physician in London. He was lame from a boyhood accident.

His blank-verse The Pleasures of Imagination (1744), a philosophical poem on the sources of aesthetic pleasure, made him famous when he was in his early twenties, and he later reworked it at length. His Odes and Hymn to the Naiads share its classical models and its enthusiasm for liberty.

poets.name: Henry Jones
bio: Henry Jones (1721–1770) was born at Beaulieu, near Drogheda in County Louth, and was brought up to the trade of bricklayer, which earned him the label "the bricklayer poet". He taught himself to write verse, and lines of his on the death of Pope won the notice of Lord Chief Justice Singleton, who lived at Beaulieu.

Through Singleton his verses reached the Earl of Chesterfield, then Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, who became his patron and took him to London in 1748. His Poems on Several Occasions (1749) was published by subscription, with Chesterfield's name at its head; his tragedy The Earl of Essex followed at Covent Garden in 1753. Later pieces, among them Merit, The Relief, The Royal Vision, Clifton and The Isle of Wight, are occasional and topographical poems. This selection omits the tragedy. Clifton and The Isle of Wight are given as separate works.

poets.name: William Collins
bio: William Collins (1721–1759) was born in Chichester and educated at Winchester and Oxford. He went to London to live by his pen, and his small output of odes, published in 1746, made little stir at first but is now ranked among the finest lyric poetry of the century.

His odes to Evening, Fear and Simplicity, and ‘How sleep the brave,’ are often seen as turning eighteenth-century verse toward feeling and imagination. His mind failed in his later years and he died in Chichester at thirty-seven.

poets.name: John Skinner
bio: John Skinner (1721–1807) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 9 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 1 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William O’Leanain
bio: William O’Leanain is dated by Sigerson, in Bards of the Gael and Gall (1907), to 1750. His song “Shiela Gal ni Connolan” is an aisling set to an old air, in which a radiant woman of the fairy world stands for Ireland.
It is given here in Sigerson’s English version.

poets.name: Kazim Khan Shaida
bio: Kazim Khan, surnamed Shaida, was a great-grandson of Khushhal Khan, born in the five years after A.H. 1135 (A.D. 1722). Quarrelling with his elder brother Asad-ullah, who held the chieftainship, he left home as a young man, wandered in Kashmir, and settled at Rampur.

A disappointment in love led him to remain unmarried. His poems were gathered alphabetically into a volume in A.D. 1767, and Raverty describes the surviving copy as the only one; they are largely love ghazals in the Persian manner.

poets.name: Mir Soz
bio: The book says that Mir Soz was of Bokhari ancestry, had to leave his country in time of peril in the dress of a fakir, and came to Lucknow, where he became tutor to the Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula.

The 2 pieces given here are drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. They are free renderings, not literal translations, and the original Urdu poems are untitled; each is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Sauda
bio: Sauda was born at Delhi about 1720, according to the book, a soldier by profession, much esteemed in his lifetime and a favourite at Court. He is said to have excelled in all kinds of poetry, chiefly the ghazal, the qasidah and satire; the book glosses the name Sauda as the folly of love.

The 3 pieces given here are drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. They are free renderings, not literal translations, and the original Urdu poems are untitled; each is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Ahmad Shah Abdali
poets.credit: Portrait: AnonymousUnknown author — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ahmad Shah, of the Saddozi family of the Abdali tribe, was freed from captivity in Kandahar by Nadir Shah and crowned king of Afghanistan in 1747, when Raverty says he was about twenty-three. He founded the Durrani monarchy, conquered Kashmir and the Panjab, and entered Delhi, and died in June 1773.

Raverty's notice speaks of the Shah as a Molawi who held regular assemblies of learned men and had time for literature. The poems chosen here are mainly poems of love and longing, with two on divine themes.

poets.name: Thomas Blacklock
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Blacklock was a Scottish poet, blind from infancy, who became a clergyman and a teacher in Edinburgh. He encouraged the young Robert Burns.
Gilfillan prints two of his poems, one a humorous self-portrait.

poets.name: James Grainger
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: James Grainger was a Scottish physician and poet who practised in the West Indies. He wrote the georgic poem The Sugar-Cane (1764) and translated Tibullus.
Gilfillan prints his Ode to Solitude.

poets.name: Mir
poets.dates: dates not given in the source
bio: The contents of Hindustani Lyrics list a poet under the plain heading MIR, separate from MIR SOZ, MIR TAQI and MIR DARD; the book gives no biographical note for him and no dates. It is not certain which Mir is meant, so he is kept here as his own entry rather than being merged with Mir Taqi Mir or any other poet.

The one piece given here is drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. It is a free rendering, not a literal translation, and the original Urdu poem is untitled; it is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Mir Dard
bio: The book calls Mir Dard the author of a famous Urdu diwan, skilled in the sacred music sung at the assemblies of the Sufis, who lived the life of a sage; the Padishah often came to him for counsel, though he himself never sought the Emperor’s court.

The one piece given here is drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. It is a free rendering, not a literal translation, and the original Urdu poem is untitled; it is named here by its first line.

poets.name: William Wilkie
bio: William Wilkie (1721–1772) was born in West Lothian, the son of a farmer, and studied at Edinburgh. He became a minister of the Church of Scotland and later professor of natural philosophy at St Andrews, where he was known for his absent-minded habits and his love of the potato, which earned him the nickname Potato Willie.

His epic The Epigoniad (1757, enlarged in a second edition of 1759) retells the war of the Epigoni against Thebes in nine books of heroic couplets after Homer, and won him the name of the Scottish Homer. He also wrote Moral Fables in Verse (1768).

poets.name: Mir Taqi Mir
bio: Mir Taqi Mir was born at Agra and in his later days lived at Lucknow under the protection of the Nawab of Oudh. The book says he wrote many kinds of verse but excelled in the ghazal and the masnawi, was the author of a biography of poets, and wrote his own autobiography in Persian, as well as Persian poetry. He is generally counted among the greatest Urdu poets.

The 2 pieces given here are drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. They are free renderings, not literal translations, and the original Urdu poems are untitled; each is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Mary Leapor
poets.credit: Engraved frontispiece portrait of Mary Leapor, from Poems upon Several Occasions (1748) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mary Leapor (1722–1746) was an English poet, the daughter of a gardener at Marston St Lawrence, Northamptonshire, who worked as a kitchen-maid in the household at Weldon and later at Brackley, where she wrote verse in the margins of her duties. She taught herself to read and write, and modelled her heroic couplets on Pope, Dryden and Gay. She died of measles at the age of twenty-four, before her work could appear.

Her Poems upon Several Occasions was published by subscription in 1748, after her death, and a second volume followed in 1751. Her verse mixes satire on vanity and marriage, pastoral, fables, biblical paraphrase and sharp reflections on class and women's lot; the poems about 'Mira', such as 'Mira's Will', are generally read as self-portraits of the poet.

poets.name: Christopher Smart
bio: Christopher Smart (1722–1771) was born in Kent and educated at Cambridge, where he became a fellow of Pembroke Hall. He lived in London as a hack writer and was confined for mental illness between 1756 and 1763. He died in a debtors’ prison.

His A Song to David (1763) is the poem by which he is chiefly remembered; its ecstatic language was thought a sign of his madness and it was little read for a century. His Hymns for the Amusement of Children appeared in 1771, and Jubilate Agno, written in confinement, was not published until the twentieth century.

poets.name: Fighan
bio: Fighan of Delhi was, according to the book, the foster-brother of the Emperor Ahmad Shah (r. 1748–1754) and one of the principal officers at the Imperial Court, famous for his piquant and witty conversation and greatly skilled in wordplay. The book spells his name Fighan.

The 2 pieces given here are drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. They are free renderings, not literal translations, and the original Urdu poems are untitled; each is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Duncan Macintyre
bio: Duncan Macintyre (1724–1812) wrote in Gaelic; Charles Rogers printed English verse renderings of the bard's songs in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 English rendering from the Gaelic in volume 1 of the anthology; each is credited to the translator whom Rogers names. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir.

poets.name: Joseph Warton
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Joseph Warton was an English poet and critic, headmaster of Winchester College, whose Essay on the Genius and Writings of Pope (1756) helped to change taste, and brother of Thomas Warton the Younger.
Gilfillan prints his Ode to Fancy.

poets.name: Sir Gilbert Elliot
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir Gilbert Elliot, 3rd Baronet (1722–1777), was a Scottish lawyer and politician who held office as Treasurer of the Chamber. He is remembered as the author of the pastoral song "Amynta" ("My sheep I neglected").

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Jane Elliot
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Jane Elliot was a Scottish poet of the eighteenth century, remembered for one famous lament.
Palgrave includes her "Lament for Flodden", a version of "The Flowers of the Forest".

poets.name: Sir William Blackstone
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir William Blackstone was the English jurist whose Commentaries on the Laws of England (1765-69) became the standard account of English law. He was also, in his youth, a writer of verse.
Gilfillan prints his poem The Lawyer's Farewell to his Muse.

poets.name: Goronwy Owen
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Goronwy Owen was a Welsh poet and clergyman, born in Anglesey, who restored the strict metres to eighteenth-century Welsh verse. He emigrated to Virginia in 1757 and died there.
An extract from his ode on the Day of Judgment is given in English verse by Alfred Perceval Graves in A Celtic Psaltery (1917).

poets.name: Edward Lovibond
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Edward Lovibond was a gentleman-poet born at Hampton in Middlesex who contributed verse to the periodical The World and died in 1775.
Gilfillan prints his poem The Tears of Old May-Day, written on the change of the calendar in 1752.

poets.name: Friedrich Gottlieb Klopstock
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Friedrich Gottlieb Klopstock was born at Quedlinburg. He wrote the religious epic Der Messias and a body of odes in classical metres that opened the way for German poetry of feeling.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Frances Greville
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Frances Greville (died 1789), born Frances Macartney, was an English poet and society hostess, wife of Fulke Greville. Her "Prayer for Indifference" (1759) was one of the most admired and quoted poems by a woman of her time.

The poem here is the one printed under her name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: John Newton
poets.credit: After John Russell's portrait of John Newton (1788) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Newton (1725–1807) was an English clergyman and hymn-writer. The son of a merchant sea captain, he went to sea as a boy and later served on slave ships, including as a captain; after a near-fatal storm in 1748 he underwent a religious conversion, and he left the slave trade in 1754. He was ordained in the Church of England in 1764 and served as curate of Olney, Buckinghamshire, until 1780, then as rector of St Mary Woolnoth in London. In later life he spoke publicly against the slave trade and supported William Wilberforce's campaign for abolition.

At Olney he befriended the poet William Cowper, and together they compiled Olney Hymns (1779), in three books, for use in Newton's parish meetings. Newton wrote the great majority of the 348 hymns and Cowper 67 of them; Newton's include 'Amazing Grace' and 'Glorious Things of Thee Are Spoken'. The Olney Hymns remained a staple of English-language evangelical worship.

poets.name: William Mason
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Mason was an English clergyman and poet, friend and biographer of Thomas Gray, and author of the tragedies Elfrida and Caractacus and the long poem The English Garden.
Gilfillan prints his epitaph on his wife and his satire An Heroic Epistle to Sir William Chambers.

poets.name: William Kenrick
poets.credit: Engraving of William Kenrick by Thomas Worlidge, 1766 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Kenrick (1725?–1779) was an English novelist, playwright, translator and satirist who spent much of his career lampooning his fellow writers. He translated Rousseau's Emilius into English and wrote for the stage, and he later edited the London Review.

This selection is drawn from his verse book Poems; Ludicrous, Satirical, and Moral (1768). Alongside long philosophical epistles in couplets it includes fables, topical satires on the London theatres and their rivals, and prologues written for Drury Lane.

poets.name: Chao I
bio: Chao I (AD 1727–1814) was a Ch’ing historian and poet.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Mir Hasan
bio: The book gives his name as Mir Shulam Hasan (that is, Ghulam Hasan), born at Delhi, who passed his youth in Faizabad and then came to Lucknow to join the literary circle there. It describes him as handsome in person as in mind, and says his verse is still popular. He wrote as Hasan.

The one piece given here is drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. It is a free rendering, not a literal translation, and the original Urdu poem is untitled; it is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Hester Chapone
bio: Hester Chapone (1727–1801), born Hester Mulso, was an English writer and a member of the bluestocking circle, best known for her Letters on the Improvement of the Mind (1773).
Her poem To Stella, written by 1755, was printed in her Miscellanies (1775).

poets.name: Oliver Goldsmith
poets.credit: Portrait of Oliver Goldsmith after Sir Joshua Reynolds · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Oliver Goldsmith (1728–1774) was an Irish-born writer of extraordinary range — poet, playwright, and novelist — whose warmth and clarity made him one of the best-loved authors of his age.
The Deserted Village, his elegy for a vanishing rural England, and Retaliation, his affectionate mock-epitaphs on his own dinner-table friends, remain his most-read poems.

poets.name: Thomas Hull
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Hull, unknown artist (1760s; National Portrait Gallery, London) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Hull (1728–1808) was an English actor and dramatist, long associated with the Covent Garden theatre. Alongside his stage work, which included plays such as The Fairy Favour and Henry the Second, he published verse: A Collection of Poems and Translations, in English and Latin (printed at Bath, 1758), the legendary tale Richard Plantagenet (1774) and, late in life, two volumes of Moral Tales in Verse, Founded on Real Events (1797).

This selection gives his English verse only: the odes, songs, paraphrases and imitations of 1758 (his Latin poems and the Latin versions printed beside them are left out), the single-part moral tales and the verse addresses and introductions of 1797. His multi-part tales (Foscue, Alleyne, Cadwal, Edward and Orra) and Richard Plantagenet are placed in the Works section. Texts come from early printed editions via ECCO-TCP, with the long s modernised.

poets.name: Thomas Warton the Younger
bio: Thomas Warton (1728–1790) was an English poet, critic and literary historian, born at Basingstoke, the younger son of Thomas Warton the Elder and the brother of Joseph Warton. A Fellow of Trinity College, Oxford, he was Professor of Poetry at Oxford from 1757 to 1767, Camden Professor of Ancient History from 1785, and Poet Laureate from 1785 until his death.

His History of English Poetry (1774–81) and Observations on the Faerie Queene (1754) did much to revive interest in medieval and Spenserian verse. His own poems, among them The Pleasures of Melancholy (1747), The Triumph of Isis (1749) and a group of antiquarian sonnets, anticipate the Romantic taste for ruins and the Middle Ages.

poets.name: Mercy Warren
poets.credit: Portrait of Mercy Warren, by John Singleton Copley · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mercy Warren (1728–1814) was an American writer.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Massachusetts Song of Liberty”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Thomas Barnard, Bishop of Limerick
poets.credit: Dr Thomas Barnard, Bishop of Limerick, drawn by George Dance (1793), etched by William Daniell (1812) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Barnard (1728–1806) was an Irish churchman, successively Bishop of Killaloe and, from 1794, Bishop of Limerick. He belonged to the circle of Samuel Johnson and the Literary Club, and wrote occasional verse.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: John Cunningham
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Cunningham was an actor and pastoral poet, born in Dublin, who spent much of his life in the north of England and died at Newcastle in 1773.
Gilfillan prints his ballad May-Eve, or Kate of Aberdeen.

poets.name: Thomas Percy
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Percy, Bishop of Dromore · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Percy (1729–1811), born in Bridgnorth, Shropshire, was an English clergyman who became Bishop of Dromore in Ireland in 1782. He is remembered above all for Reliques of Ancient English Poetry (1765), the collection of old ballads and songs that did much to start the Romantic revival of interest in popular poetry.

Besides editing, he composed or reworked pieces of his own for the Reliques. "The Friar of Orders Gray", which weaves together scraps of old songs and lines from Shakespeare into a new ballad, is the best known of them.

poets.name: Patrick Mac Gearoit (Fitzgerald)
bio: Patrick Mac Gearoit, also given as Fitzgerald, is dated by Sigerson, in Bards of the Gael and Gall (1907), to 1764. His vision-poem is set by the lake at Blarney, where a fairy woman foretells that warriors from Spain will come to free Ireland.
“The Spirit of Song” is given here in Sigerson’s English version.

poets.name: John Scott of Amwell
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Scott of Amwell was a Quaker poet and writer on prisons and roads, who lived at Amwell in Hertfordshire.
Gilfillan prints two of his odes.

poets.name: Edward Botwood
bio: Edward Botwood (c. 1730–1759) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Hot Stuff”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Thomas Osbert Mordaunt
bio: Thomas Osbert Mordaunt (1730–1809) was an English poet, distinct from Charles Mordaunt, Earl of Peterborough.
His verses written during the war of 1756–1763 were printed in The Bee, or Literary Weekly Intelligencer (Edinburgh) on 12 October 1791.

poets.name: William Cowper
poets.credit: Portrait of William Cowper by Lemuel Francis Abbott, 1792 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Cowper (1731–1800) wrote from a life shadowed by recurring breakdowns and religious despair, retired to the Buckinghamshire village of Olney under the care of friends.

His comic ballad John Gilpin made him briefly famous, but his lasting achievement is The Task, a long meditative poem on rural retirement, and the Olney Hymns he wrote with John Newton, including “God Moves in a Mysterious Way.”

poets.name: Samuel Bishop
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Samuel Bishop was an English clergyman and headmaster of Merchant Taylors' School, who wrote light verse. Gilfillan gives the years 1731 to 1795.
Gilfillan prints two of his poems addressed to his wife.

poets.name: Erasmus Darwin
poets.credit: Portrait of Erasmus Darwin by Joseph Wright of Derby (1792) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Erasmus Darwin (1731–1802) was an English physician, natural philosopher and inventor, born in Nottinghamshire and long in practice at Lichfield and later Derby. He was a leading member of the Lunar Society of Birmingham and the grandfather of Charles Darwin.

His verse made natural science fashionable: The Botanic Garden (1791) set the Linnaean system and contemporary chemistry, geology and engineering in glittering heroic couplets, and was widely admired and parodied in its day.

poets.name: Charles Churchill
poets.credit: Portrait of Charles Churchill by John Stone Clifford Schaack, 1764 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Churchill (1732–1764) was an English satirist, born in Westminster and educated at Westminster School. A clergyman who had taken orders for want of other prospects, he became famous overnight with The Rosciad (1761), a satire on the actors of the London stage, and gave up the ministry to live by his pen.

A friend and ally of John Wilkes, he turned his verse to politics in The Prophecy of Famine (1763), Gotham and The Times, and to personal satire in The Ghost and The Duellist. He died at Boulogne in November 1764, aged thirty-two. The texts here are from George Gilfillan's edition of his poetical works (Edinburgh, Nichol), with the editor's life, dissertation and notes omitted.

poets.name: William Falconer
poets.credit: Portrait of William Falconer, engraved by J. Fittler after Daniel · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Falconer (1732–1770) was a Scottish sailor and poet, born in Edinburgh. He served at sea from boyhood and survived the wreck of the merchant ship Britannia off Cape Colonna, in Attica, an experience that underlies his best-known poem.

The Shipwreck (1762), in three cantos, is a narrative of a voyage and its loss, written in heroic couplets and notable for its accurate sea language. His other verse includes The Demagogue (1764) and a few occasional pieces. He is said to have been lost at sea in the frigate Aurora, which disappeared on its voyage out in 1769–70.

poets.name: Christoph Martin Wieland
poets.credit: Portrait of Christoph Martin Wieland by Anton Graff (1794) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Christoph Martin Wieland was born in 1733 near Biberach in Swabia, the son of a Pietist pastor, and spent most of his working life as a poet, translator, editor and teacher. His early poems were devout and Klopstockian; in the 1760s he turned to a lighter, ironic, Rococo manner, and in Biberach he began his German translation of Shakespeare's plays, the first of its kind.

In 1772 he went to Weimar as tutor to the young Duke Karl August, and there edited the Teutscher Merkur. His verse romance Oberon, in twelve cantos, appeared in 1780 and was widely admired, among others by Goethe. It was translated into English by William Sotheby (1798), and later gave Weber the subject for his opera. Wieland died at Weimar in 1813. His other principal works include the novel Geschichte des Agathon, often called the first German Bildungsroman.

poets.name: James Beattie
poets.credit: Engraving of James Beattie by Ridley, 1801 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James Beattie (1735–1803) was a Scottish poet and moral philosopher, for many years professor of moral philosophy at Marischal College, Aberdeen. He was also known for his Essay on the Nature and Immutability of Truth (1770), written against Hume.

His best-known poem is The Minstrel (1771–74), in Spenserian stanzas, which traces the growth of a young poet, Edwin, among the hills and shepherds of the Scottish countryside. It was much admired by later eighteenth- and early nineteenth-century readers. The texts here are from Gilfillan's edition of Beattie, Blair and Falconer.

poets.name: John Wolcot (Peter Pindar)
poets.credit: Portrait of John Wolcot by John Opie · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Wolcot (1738–1819), who wrote as 'Peter Pindar', was born in Devon and trained as a physician before turning to satire. His Lyric Odes to the Royal Academicians (1782) and the long run of comic verse that followed, much of it aimed at George III, his court and the painters of the Royal Academy, made him one of the most widely read humorous poets of the 1780s and 1790s.

'Peter Pindar' is only a pen-name: he is not the Greek lyric poet Pindar, who has a page of his own in the archive. The poems here are those that James Parton printed under the name in his anthology The Humorous Poetry of the English Language.

poets.name: Cuthbert Shaw
bio: Cuthbert Shaw (1738–1771) was an English poet and satirist who died young.
His best-known poem, Monody to the Memory of a Young Lady (1768), laments the death of his wife in childbirth and went through several editions.

poets.name: Robert Lloyd
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Robert Lloyd was a London poet, the son of a master at Westminster School and a friend of Charles Churchill and George Colman. He died in 1764.
Gilfillan prints one of his satires on the poet's hard life.

poets.name: Vasily Petrov
bio: Vasily Petrovich Petrov (1736–1799), born in Moscow, was a court poet under Catherine II. He wrote ceremonial odes on Russian victories and translated Virgil’s Aeneid into Russian verse.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: William Julius Mickle
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Julius Mickle was a Scottish poet who translated the Lusiad of Camoens into English verse in 1775.
Palgrave includes "The Sailor's Wife", the song also known by the words "There's nae luck about the house".

poets.name: John Langhorne
bio: John Langhorne (1735–1779) was an English poet and clergyman, born in Westmorland and later rector of Blagdon in Somerset. With his brother William he translated Plutarch's Lives (1770).
His verse includes The Country Justice (1774–77) and Fables of Flora (1771), the latter a set of short poems on flowers.

poets.name: Robert Graham of Gartmore
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Robert Graham of Gartmore was a Scottish landowner and politician who also wrote verse.
Palgrave signs his song "If doughty deeds my lady please" with the name Graham of Gartmore.

poets.name: William Sutton
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Sutton is represented here by verse printed in John Bell's Rhymes of Northern Bards (Newcastle, 1812), 1 piece.
Bell prints his song written for the year 1764 on the people and affairs of Stockton.

poets.name: James Macpherson
poets.credit: Portrait: George Romney — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James Macpherson was a Scottish writer born at Ruthven in Inverness-shire, who published the prose-poems attributed to Ossian between 1760 and 1763. They had a European influence and a long controversy over their authenticity.
Gilfillan prints several Ossianic passages in prose, which are not taken here, and one poem in rhyme, The Cave, which is.

poets.name: Paul Revere
poets.credit: Portrait of Paul Revere, by John Singleton Copley · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Paul Revere (1735–1818) was an American silversmith and military officer.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Unhappy Boston”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Francis Hopkinson
bio: Francis Hopkinson (1737–1791) was a Philadelphia lawyer, judge and composer, and a signer of the Declaration of Independence for New Jersey. He wrote satirical songs and ballads for the patriot cause; The Battle of the Kegs is the best known.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: The Battle of the Kegs.

poets.name: Thomas Paine
bio: Thomas Paine (1737–1809), born in England, emigrated to Pennsylvania in 1774 and became the great pamphleteer of the American Revolution, author of Common Sense (1776) and The American Crisis. His song Liberty Tree appeared in the Pennsylvania Magazine in 1775.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: Liberty Tree.

poets.name: Edward Jerningham
poets.credit: William Ridley, engraving after Samuel Drummond's portrait of Edward Jerningham (1800) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward Jerningham (1737?–1812) was a poet and dramatist born into the Catholic Jerningham family of Costessey (Cossey) Hall, Norfolk, and was educated on the Continent. He moved in fashionable London literary and theatrical society, and wrote sentimental narrative poems, elegies, album verses and a few stage pieces; the plays are not included here.

His chief successes were the pathetic verse tales and occasional poems of the 1760s to the 1790s, among them Il Latte, The Deserter, Yarico to Inkle, The Nun, Faldoni and Teresa (1773) and The Fall of Mexico (1775), and the longer poems The Shakspeare Gallery, Enthusiasm and Abelard to Eloisa. This selection follows his collected Poems of 1796 (a new edition, in two volumes, from the ECCO-TCP transcription), together with the separately published pieces from 1773 to 1796 that the collection did not reprint.

poets.name: Dávid Baróti Szabó
bio: Hungarian Jesuit priest, poet, writer and linguist.
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: Isobel Pagan
bio: Isobel Pagan (c. 1741–1821) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Hugh Downman
poets.credit: Hugh Downman, line engraving by James Fittler after John Downman (Wellcome Collection) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Hugh Downman (1740–1809) was an English physician, poet and dramatist, the son of Hugh Downman of Newton House, near Exeter. Educated at Exeter grammar school and Balliol College, Oxford, he was ordained in 1763 but turned to medicine, studying at Edinburgh, where he boarded with the blind poet Thomas Blacklock. He practised in Exeter for most of his life and died at Alphington, near Exeter, in 1809.

His first publication, The Land of the Muses (1768), was a Spenserian poem addressed to Blacklock; his best-known work, the didactic poem Infancy (1774–76), is not included here. This selection draws on his Poems (second edition, Exeter, 1790) — odes, elegies, sonnets and the Death-Song of Ragnar Lodbrach, rendered from the Latin of Olaus Wormius — together with the Poems to Thespia (1781) and the earlier Land of the Muses volume (1768), where these add pieces not in the 1790 book.

poets.name: Joseph Warren
poets.credit: Portrait of Joseph Warren, by John Singleton Copley · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Joseph Warren (1741–1775) was an American physician and Founding Father.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Free America”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Dermot O'Curnan
bio: Dermot O'Curnan is given in Eleanor Hull's The Poem-Book of the Gael as born in 1740, and as the author of the love-song “Love's Despair”.
The English version gathered here is by George Sigerson, printed in Hull's anthology (London, 1913).

poets.name: Arthur Lee
bio: Arthur Lee (1740–1792) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “A Prophecy”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Augustus Montague Toplady
bio: Augustus Montague Toplady (1740–1778) was an English Anglican clergyman, Calvinist controversialist and hymn-writer, vicar of Broadhembury in Devon.
His hymn Rock of Ages appeared in the Gospel Magazine in 1775 and, as A Prayer, living and dying, in his Psalms and Hymns for Public and Private Worship (1776).

poets.name: Anna Seward
poets.credit: Portrait of Anna Seward by Tilly Kettle (1762) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Anna Seward (1742–1809), born at Eyam in Derbyshire and raised in Lichfield, where her father was a canon of the cathedral, was known in her own day as the “Swan of Lichfield”. She was educated at home on progressive lines and became a prominent figure in the literary society of the Midlands, publishing an elegy on Captain Cook, a monody on Major André and the poetical novel Louisa (1784).

Her Original Sonnets on Various Subjects, and Odes Paraphrased from Horace appeared in 1799. The hundred sonnets, many in the Petrarchan and Miltonic manner and some of them nature poems or elegies, helped to revive the English sonnet in the years before Wordsworth, and the Horatian paraphrases freely expand their originals. Her letters were published posthumously in 1811.

poets.name: John Collins
bio: John Collins (1742–1808) was an English actor, lecturer and writer of songs and verse.
His song “Tomorrow” was included in Palgrave’s The Golden Treasury (1861).

poets.name: Anne Hunter (Mrs John Hunter)
bio: Anne Hunter (Mrs John Hunter) (1742–1821) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 7 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 1 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: James Muirhead, D.D.
bio: James Muirhead, D.D. (1742–1806) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 2 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: George Ogle
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: George Ogle (1739–1814) represented Dublin city in parliament and voted against the Union in 1799.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Ippolit Bogdanovich
bio: Ippolit Fyodorovich Bogdanovich (1743–1803), of Ukrainian origin, served as a state official and wrote light, graceful verse. His best-known work is Dushenka (1783), a free adaptation of La Fontaine’s tale of Psyche, which earned him Bowring’s title of “the Russian Anacreon”.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Matthias Claudius
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Matthias Claudius was a German poet and journalist, editor of the Wandsbecker Bote, whose plain, devout songs ("Der Mond ist aufgegangen", "Der Tod und das Mädchen") became part of German family life.
The English versions here are George MacDonald's, printed in Rampolli (1897).

poets.name: Anna Laetitia Barbauld
bio: Anna Laetitia Barbauld (1743–1825), née Aikin, was born in Leicestershire, the daughter of a Dissenting minister and schoolmaster, and grew up at Warrington Academy. Her Poems (1773) went through several editions within a year, and she went on to write hymns, children’s books and essays and to teach at a school she ran with her husband.

Her later work includes the long political poem Eighteen Hundred and Eleven (1812), which looks forward to the decline of Britain and the rise of America. She was a friend of Joseph Priestley and a figure in the Dissenting and literary circles of her day.

poets.name: Alexander, Duke of Gordon
bio: Alexander, Duke of Gordon (1743–1827) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 1 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Johannes Ewald
poets.credit: Portrait of Johannes Ewald, attributed to Eric Paulsen, c. 1780 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Johannes Ewald (1743–1781) was a Danish poet and dramatist, born in Copenhagen. He ran away to serve in the Prussian and Austrian armies as a young man, and afterwards lived by his pen, in poor health, under the protection of friends and patrons.

His verse drama The Death of Balder (1773) and the singspiel The Fishermen (1779) were landmarks of the Danish literary revival, and the latter contains the royal anthem "King Christian stood by the lofty mast", the Danish national song of naval praise, which is the poem given here in George Borrow's translation.

poets.name: Hannah Cowley
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of Hannah Cowley, 18th century (engraver unidentified); crop by Shashankg165 · Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 (underlying engraving public domain)
bio: Hannah Cowley (1743–1809), born Hannah Parkhouse at Tiverton in Devon, was an English playwright and poet. After her marriage to Thomas Cowley she turned to the stage, and her comedies, above all The Belle's Stratagem (1780), kept the London theatres supplied for more than a decade; none of her plays is included here.

In 1787–88 she took part, as "Anna Matilda", in the Della Crusca exchange, an ornate verse correspondence with Robert Merry published in the newspaper The World. This selection gives her share of it from The Poetry of Anna Matilda (London: John Bell, 1788), with the other pieces in that volume, and her descriptive poem The Scottish Village: or, Pitcairne Green (1787). Her reply to a poem signed "Reuben" is included; Reuben's own piece is not. She died at Tiverton in 1809.

poets.name: George Saville Carey
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: George Saville Carey (1743–1807) was an English comic writer, lecturer and entertainer, and a writer of songs, epigrams and occasional verse.
He was the son of the poet and songwriter Henry Carey.

poets.name: Gavrila Derzhavin
poets.credit: Portrait of Gavrila Derzhavin by Vladimir Borovikovsky (1811) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Gavrila Romanovich Derzhavin (1743–1816), born near Kazan, served as a soldier and then as a state official: secretary to Catherine II, governor of provinces, and later Minister of Justice. His odes “Felitsa” (1782) and “God” (1784) brought him fame, and he is usually counted the greatest Russian poet before Pushkin. “God” was translated into many languages, and Bowring’s version of it is among the best known in English.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Johann Gottfried Herder
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Johann Gottfried Herder was a philosopher, critic and clergyman who settled at Weimar. His collection of folk songs from many nations, published in 1778–79, helped to shape the Romantic interest in popular poetry.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Mrs Grant of Carron
bio: Mrs Grant of Carron (c. 1745–c. 1814) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 1 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: James Wilson
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: James Wilson is represented here by verse printed in John Bell's Rhymes of Northern Bards (Newcastle, 1812), 4 pieces and in The Newcastle Song Book; or, Tyne-side Songster (Newcastle: W. & T. Fordyce, 1842), 1 piece.
Bell says James Wilson belonged to Hexham, taught school there and later at Cawsey Park, and published a volume of poems at Newcastle in 1778.

poets.name: Arzu
bio: The book describes Arzu as a poet of Gwalior who held an important Government post in the days of Shah Alam II (r. 1759–1806), wrote his poems mostly in Persian, and was the author of a dictionary of mystical words. He is not identified here with Khan-i Arzu of Delhi, since the book’s description does not match; no dates are given.

The one piece given here is drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. It is a free rendering, not a literal translation, and the original Urdu poem is untitled; it is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Hector Macneill
bio: Hector Macneill (1746–1818) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 9 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 1 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William Hayley
poets.credit: Portrait of William Hayley by Henry Howard · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Hayley (1745–1820) was an English poet and biographer, born in Chichester and educated at Eton and Trinity Hall, Cambridge. He lived most of his life in Sussex, first at Eartham and later at Felpham, and was a friend and patron of the painter George Romney, the poet William Cowper and, in his last years at Felpham, William Blake.

In his own day Hayley was a celebrated verse writer. The Triumphs of Temper (1781), a mock-heroic poem in six cantos, was reprinted many times, and his philosophical verse essays in heroic couplets on history, painting, epic poetry and sculpture, each addressed to a friend, were widely read. He also wrote odes, sonnets, plays and a Life of Milton (1796), and later a Life of Cowper (1803). This selection draws on the volumes printed between 1779 and 1800.

poets.name: Hannah More
poets.credit: Portrait of Hannah More by Henry William Pickersgill, c. 1821 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Hannah More (1745–1833) was born near Bristol and made her name in London in the 1770s as a dramatist and as a friend of David Garrick, Samuel Johnson and the Bluestocking circle. Her early verse, among it Sir Eldred of the Bower (1776), the Ode to Dragon (1777), Florio and The Bas Bleu (1786), and Slavery, a Poem (1788), was written for that polite literary world, and the last of these joined the campaign against the slave trade.

From the 1790s she turned to religious and moral writing for a wider public. Her ballads, songs and verse tracts for the Cheap Repository (1795–1800), written in plain language to be sold cheaply and sung or read aloud, are represented here alongside the earlier poems. She spent her last years near Bristol and died at Clifton in 1833. The texts follow the early printed editions (via ECCO-TCP), with the long s modernised.

poets.name: Charles Dibdin
poets.credit: Portrait of Charles Dibdin by Thomas Phillips · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Dibdin (1745–1814), born at Southampton, was a singer, composer, actor and dramatist who wrote the words and the music of his own songs. He first won notice at Drury Lane in the late 1760s, and went on to write a long run of comic operas and other pieces for the London stage.

From the late 1780s he gave one-man “table entertainments”, in which he sang his own songs at the keyboard, and the ballads of the sea that he wrote for them made his name. The songs here come from his own 1790 selection, taken from his table entertainments and from songs printed without any stage piece; songs from his operas and other stage pieces are left out.

poets.name: Ivan Khemnitser
bio: Ivan Ivanovich Khemnitser (1745–1784), of German descent, was a mining engineer and later a Russian consul in Smyrna, where he died. He is remembered for his fables, first published in 1779, whose plain, humorous style set an example for Krylov.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Fitnet Khânim
bio: Fitnet Khanim is represented in Gibb's anthology by a gazel and a museddes in praise of spring.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Shâhin Girây (Khan of the Crimea)
bio: Shahin Giray, the last of the Khans of the Crimea, was a talented and accomplished prince who lacked political foresight; after losing his throne he fled to Constantinople and was executed at Rhodes.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Michael Bruce
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Michael Bruce was a Scottish poet, a weaver's son from Kinnesswood in Kinross-shire, who studied at Edinburgh, taught school, and died of consumption at twenty-one.
Gilfillan prints under his name To the Cuckoo and an elegy written in spring. The authorship of the cuckoo poem was later disputed in favour of John Logan, who published it in 1770.

poets.name: Sir William Jones
poets.credit: Sir William Jones, by Sir Joshua Reynolds, 1767 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir William Jones (1746–1794) was a British orientalist and judge in Calcutta, founder of the Asiatic Society (1784), who first proposed the kinship of Sanskrit with Greek, Latin and the other Indo-European languages. He wrote English verse as well as translations from Persian and Sanskrit.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Susanna Blamire
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Susanna Blamire, called the Muse of Cumberland, was born at Cardew Hall near Carlisle. She wrote in standard English and in Scots, and her poems were collected and published after her death.
Gilfillan prints two of her songs, The Nabob and What Ails this Heart o' Mine?

poets.name: Charles Morris
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Captain Charles Morris (1745–1838) was an English army officer and songwriter, long the laureate of the Beefsteak Club and a favourite of the Prince of Wales's circle. His convivial songs were gathered in Lyra Urbanica (1840).

The 2 poems here are the pieces printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Gottfried August Bürger
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Gottfried August Bürger was a German poet associated with Göttingen. His ballad Lenore (1773) was widely translated and was a strong influence on English Romantic poetry.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: John Logan
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Logan was a Scottish minister and poet. He published a volume of poems in 1781.
Palgrave gives him "The Braes of Yarrow", a poem whose authorship has been disputed.

poets.name: Jonathan Mitchell Sewall
bio: Jonathan Mitchell Sewall (1748–1808) was a New England lawyer and poet of the Revolutionary period; his war song War and Washington was sung during the war. Eggleston prints the name as Seward.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: War and Washington.

poets.name: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
poets.credit: Portrait of Goethe by Joseph Karl Stieler (1828) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (1749–1832) was born in Frankfurt am Main and studied law before the success of his novel The Sorrows of Young Werther (1774) made him famous across Europe. In 1775 he moved to Weimar at the invitation of Duke Karl August, where he served as a minister of state and director of the court theatre, and from 1794 he was the close friend and collaborator of Friedrich Schiller.

Best known for the drama Faust, he wrote lyrics, ballads, odes, elegies and epigrams throughout his life, from the early songs and the Roman Elegies and Venetian Epigrams of his Italian years to the West-Eastern Divan (1819), inspired by the Persian poet Hafiz. The English versions here are from Edgar Alfred Bowring’s 1853 The Poems of Goethe, translated in the original metres; it is a selection from his shorter verse.

poets.name: Samuel Jackson Pratt
poets.credit: Portrait of Samuel Jackson Pratt by Thomas Lawrence · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Samuel Jackson Pratt (1749–1814) was an English writer born at St Ives in Huntingdonshire, who worked for a time as an actor before settling to authorship. He published much of his work under the pen-name Courtney Melmoth, among it the poems The Tears of Genius (1774), on the death of Goldsmith, and The Shadows of Shakespeare (c. 1780), on the death of Garrick, and sentimental novels such as The Pupil of Pleasure (1776) and Emma Corbett (1780).

His longer verse includes Sympathy (1781) and Humanity, or the Rights of Nature (1788), a poem in two books that condemns the slave trade. He later published travel writing and miscellanies. He died in Birmingham in 1814. This selection draws on the early printed editions (via ECCO-TCP) and gives only his verse; the two longer poems, Humanity and Sympathy, and Garrick’s Looking-Glass, are placed in the Works section.

poets.name: Charlotte Smith
poets.credit: Portrait of Charlotte Smith by George Romney (1792) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charlotte Smith (1749–1806) was an English poet and novelist, born Charlotte Turner and raised in Sussex and Surrey. Married young to a spendthrift husband who was imprisoned for debt in 1783, she turned to writing to support her many children.

Her Elegiac Sonnets (1784), expanded through many editions, is often credited with reviving the English sonnet as a form for personal feeling, and its melancholy landscapes of the Sussex downs and coast lie behind much Romantic poetry. She was also a successful novelist, and her long blank-verse poem Beachy Head appeared after her death in 1807.

poets.name: Arthur Dawson
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Arthur Dawson was a Baron of the Exchequer in Ireland and a contemporary of the harper Turlough O'Carolan; "Bumpers, Squire Jones" was written to one of Carolan's tunes.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Brian Merriman
bio: Eleanor Hull's The Poem-Book of the Gael describes Brian Merriman as having died in Limerick in 1808. He is the author of the Irish comic poem “The Midnight Court”.
Only the prologue is gathered here, in the English version printed in Hull's anthology (London, 1913), where no other translator is named.

poets.name: Anonymous Hungarian Popular Songs
poets.credit: Not a portrait (the songs are anonymous): the engraving "A Hungarian nobleman and peasant" from Robert Townson, Travels in Hungary (1797) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The anonymous popular songs of the Hungarians, sung in the villages and inns of the Magyar lands.
They are read here in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: Lady Anne Lindsay
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Lady Anne Lindsay, later Lady Anne Barnard, was a Scottish writer. She wrote the ballad "Auld Robin Gray" in 1771.
Palgrave includes "Auld Robin Gray", her best-known poem.

poets.name: Phillis Wheatley
bio: Phillis Wheatley (c. 1753–1784) was born in West Africa, kidnapped and brought to Boston as a child in 1761, and purchased by the merchant John Wheatley. Taught to read and write in his household, she began publishing verse as a teenager.

Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral (1773) was the first book of poems published by an African American. A group of Boston notables attested in its front matter that she had written the poems; she was freed shortly after the book appeared.

poets.name: Henry Rowe
bio: Henry Rowe (1750–1819) was an English poet of the late eighteenth century.
Arthur Quiller-Couch included his two odes, “Sun” and “Moon”, in The Oxford Book of English Verse (1900).

poets.name: John Philpot Curran
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Philpot Curran was an Irish barrister, orator and politician, born in Newmarket, County Cork. He defended many of the United Irishmen and served as Master of the Rolls in Ireland from 1806 to 1814.
His best-known song, "The Deserter's Meditation", is included in W. B. Yeats's A Book of Irish Verse (1900).

poets.name: Benjamin Tompson
bio: Benjamin Tompson (1753–1814) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “On a Fortification at Boston Begun by Women”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Lady Anne Barnard
bio: Lady Anne Barnard (1750–1825) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 1 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Qalandar Bakhsh Jurat
bio: Jurat of Delhi is described in the book as celebrated for his skill in music, astronomy and poetry; he became blind while still young and was pensioned by Nawab Muhabbat Khan and afterwards by Suleiman Shikoh. He is the author of an enormous volume of ghazals and love-poems in the modern taste, and also wrote satires on the rain, the cold, smallpox and the like.

The one piece given here is drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. It is a free rendering, not a literal translation, and the original Urdu poem is untitled; it is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Ludwig Heinrich Christoph Hölty
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Ludwig Heinrich Christoph Hölty was a member of the Göttingen Hainbund. He wrote delicate songs and elegies on nature, friendship and early death, and died of consumption at twenty-eight.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: John Trumbull
poets.credit: Portrait of the poet by his cousin, the painter John Trumbull, 1793 (Detroit Institute of Arts) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Trumbull (1750–1831) was an American poet and lawyer, born in Watertown, Connecticut. He entered Yale as a child prodigy, later became a tutor there, and was a leading member of the Connecticut Wits. He trained in law under John Adams and practised in Hartford, serving also as a state judge.

His best-known work, M'Fingal (first part 1775, complete 1782), is a Hudibrastic mock-epic satirising a Tory squire in revolutionary Massachusetts. It was among the most widely read American poems of its age and went through dozens of editions.

poets.name: Peter St. John
bio: Peter St. John, of Norwalk, Connecticut, is named as the author of the Revolutionary ballad Taxation of America in Eggleston’s anthology; his dates are not given there.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: Taxation of America.

poets.name: Robert Couper, M.D.
bio: Robert Couper, M.D. (1750–1818) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 1 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Chang Wen-t’ao
bio: Chang Wen-t’ao is dated by Giles to the 18th century AD. His poem here is advice to girls on marriage.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poets.name: Anonymous Chinese nursery rhymes
bio: The rhymes gathered here are the nursery rhymes of Peking, recited by nurses and mothers to the children in their care. They are anonymous and orally transmitted, and the collection records what was current in the Chinese capital in the 1890s, in the last decades of the Qing dynasty.

They survive in English thanks to Isaac Taylor Headland (1859–1942), a missionary educator who taught at Peking University and who rendered them into rhymed English verse for Chinese Mother Goose Rhymes (New York: Fleming H. Revell, 1900). The English renderings are his; they follow the sense and spirit of the spoken originals rather than their Chinese wording.

poets.name: John Tait
bio: John Tait (died 1817) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 1 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Friedrich Leopold zu Stolberg-Stolberg
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of Friedrich Leopold zu Stolberg, artist unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Friedrich Leopold, Count zu Stolberg-Stolberg (1750–1819) was a German poet, translator and diplomat, born at Bramstedt in Holstein. A member of the Göttingen Hainbund and a friend of Klopstock and Goethe in his youth, he wrote odes, ballads and verse dramas, and translated Homer and Aeschylus.

In 1800 he became a Roman Catholic, to the scandal of many of his friends, and spent his later years writing a large history of the Christian religion. "Ode to a Mountain-torrent" is given here in George Borrow's English version of 1826.

poets.name: Richard Brinsley Sheridan
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Richard Brinsley Sheridan was born in Dublin and became one of the leading English-language dramatists of his century, the author of The Rivals and The School for Scandal. He was also manager of the Drury Lane Theatre and a Whig Member of Parliament.
The song "Thou canst not boast" is included in W. B. Yeats's A Book of Irish Verse (1900).

poets.name: George Pickering
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: George Pickering is represented here by verse printed in John Bell's Rhymes of Northern Bards (Newcastle, 1812), 2 pieces and in The Newcastle Song Book; or, Tyne-side Songster (Newcastle: W. & T. Fordyce, 1842), 1 piece.
Bell's book gives no dates for this writer, so the date above is the year of the collection in which the verse appears. The dialect spelling of the printed texts is kept.

poets.name: Mushafi
bio: The book says Mushafi belonged to a distinguished family of Amroha, lived at first at Lucknow and then went to Delhi, where he held famous literary reunions at which gathered many poets of whom he was the inspirer and teacher.

The 2 pieces given here are drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. They are free renderings, not literal translations, and the original Urdu poems are untitled; each is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Thomas Erskine, Lord Erskine
poets.credit: Thomas Erskine, 1st Baron Erskine, by William Charles Ross, 1823 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Erskine, 1st Baron Erskine (1750–1823), was one of the most celebrated English advocates of his day and served briefly as Lord Chancellor in 1806–07.
The epigram here is the one James Parton printed under the name Erskine in his anthology of English humorous poetry.

poets.name: Robert Fergusson
poets.credit: Portrait: Photo: MaccoinnichStatue: David Annand[2] — CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Fergusson was a Scottish poet born in Edinburgh, who wrote in Scots and in English and died in the city's asylum at twenty-three. Robert Burns revered him as a forerunner.
Gilfillan prints his Scots poem The Farmer's Ingle, a picture of a farmhouse evening that was one of the models for Burns's The Cotter's Saturday Night.

poets.name: John Lowe
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Lowe was a Scottish poet and tutor, born at Kenmure in Galloway, who emigrated to Virginia and died in 1798.
He wrote the ballad Mary's Dream, which Gilfillan prints complete.

poets.name: Joseph Stansbury
bio: Joseph Stansbury (1750–1809) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “A New Song” and “The Lords of the Main”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Johann Martin Miller
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Johann Martin Miller was a member of the Göttingen Hainbund and a clergyman at Ulm. He wrote songs and the sentimental novel Siegwart.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: William Cameron
bio: William Cameron (died 1811) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 1 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: John André
poets.credit: Portrait of John André, by George Engleheart · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John André (1751–1780) was a British Army officer, executed as a spy in 1780 during the American Revolution.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “The Cow-Chace”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Thomas Chatterton
bio: Thomas Chatterton (1752–1770) was born in Bristol, the posthumous son of a schoolmaster and church official, and was writing remarkable verse before he was in his teens. He invented a fifteenth-century Bristol priest named Thomas Rowley and wrote a body of poems in an imitation medieval English, passing them off as Rowley's recovered manuscripts.

He went to London in 1770 hoping to live by his pen and died there in August of that year, aged seventeen. The question whether the Rowley poems were genuine was argued for decades, but they are now known to be his own. Wordsworth called him ‘the marvellous Boy,’ and Keats dedicated Endymion to his memory.

poets.name: Insha Allah Khan
bio: The book says Insha was born in Murshedabad, lived in Lucknow about the end of the eighteenth century, and enjoyed the favour of Prince Suleiman Shikoh. He wrote verse in Turkish, Arabic and Persian, but was most famous for his Urdu poems, described as elegant in style and conception.

The one piece given here is drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. It is a free rendering, not a literal translation, and the original Urdu poem is untitled; it is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Yury Neledinsky-Meletsky
bio: Yury Aleksandrovich Neledinsky-Meletsky (1752–1828) was a court official who served under Catherine II and Paul I. He is remembered for songs written in the manner of Russian folk lyrics, many of which were set to music and sung widely.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: William Dudgeon
bio: William Dudgeon (died 1813) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 1 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: George Ellis
bio: George Ellis (1753–1815) was an English satirist, antiquary and diplomat, editor of Specimens of the Early English Poets (1790) and a contributor to the Rolliad and the Anti-Jacobin.

The rondeau given here, mocking the salary of William Eden's commercial mission to Versailles, appeared in The European Magazine in December 1785; the Oxford Book of Eighteenth Century Verse attributes it to Ellis with a query.

poets.name: Philip Freneau
poets.credit: Engraving of Philip Freneau by Frederick Halpin (1901) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Philip Freneau (1752–1832) was an American poet and journalist, born in New York City. He studied at Princeton alongside James Madison and became known as the “Poet of the American Revolution” for his satires on the British and his patriotic verse.
He later edited the National Gazette in Philadelphia. His nature lyrics, such as “The Wild Honey Suckle” (1786), are often seen as early signs of Romanticism in American poetry.

poets.name: St. George Tucker
bio: St. George Tucker (1752–1827) was a Bermuda-born American jurist and poet, a law professor at the College of William and Mary and later a judge in Virginia.
Griswold included 1 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Timothy Dwight
poets.credit: Portrait: John Trumbull — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Timothy Dwight (1752–1817) was an American Congregational minister, educator and poet, born in Northampton, Massachusetts. A member of the Connecticut Wits, he was president of Yale College from 1795 until his death.
Griswold included 10 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: David Humphreys
bio: David Humphreys (1752–1818) was an American soldier, diplomat and poet, born in Derby, Connecticut. A Yale graduate and one of the Connecticut Wits, he served on Washington's staff during the Revolution.
Griswold included 4 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Sean O’Coileann
bio: Sean O’Coileann (O’Cullane) was, according to Sigerson in Bards of the Gael and Gall (1907), one of the O’Coileanns, chiefs of Castlelyons, born about 1754 in Co. Cork and dead in 1816. He composed a lament for Timoleague Abbey that was translated by Sir Samuel Ferguson.
Two of his vision-songs, “The Dear White Youth” and “The Forest Fair”, are given here in Sigerson’s English versions.

poets.name: Christoph August Tiedge
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Christoph August Tiedge was a German poet best known for his long didactic poem Urania (1801). He lived for many years at Dresden.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: George Crabbe
bio: George Crabbe (1754–1832) was born at Aldeburgh on the Suffolk coast, trained as a surgeon and apothecary, and went to London in 1780 to try his fortune as a poet. Edmund Burke took him up, and he afterward became a clergyman. The Village (1783), which Samuel Johnson read in manuscript, set out to show the real life of the rural poor against the conventions of pastoral.

His later narrative poems, The Parish Register, The Borough and the Tales, tell the lives of ordinary people in plain, exact couplets and were widely read in his day. Peter Grimes, from The Borough, is the source of Benjamin Britten’s opera.

poets.name: Benedek Virág
bio: Hungarian poet, translator and priest of the generation before Kazinczy.
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: Yermil Kostrov
