bio: Yermil Ivanovich Kostrov (1755–1796) studied at Moscow University and made a name as a translator. He rendered part of Homer’s Iliad into Russian verse and worked on a version of Ossian, which, as Bowring notes, was completed after his early death by Gnedich.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Pál Ányos
bio: Hungarian poet of the late eighteenth century who died in his late twenties (Wikisource gives his name as Pál István Ányos).
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: János Endrődy
bio: Hungarian monk, teacher, priest and poet.
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: John Dunlop
bio: John Dunlop (1755–1820) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 4 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William Drennan
poets.credit: William Drennan, attributed to Robert Home, c. 1790 (Ulster Museum) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Drennan (1754–1820) was a Belfast physician and poet who helped found the Society of United Irishmen and drafted many of its addresses. He was tried for sedition in 1794 and acquitted, and is credited with the phrase "Emerald Isle".
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Sir John Henry Moore
bio: Sir John Henry Moore (1756–1780) was an English baronet and poet. His Poetical Trifles (1778) appeared anonymously and was reprinted several times; his poems were collected in Park's edition of the British Poets (1808).
He is remembered for light verse, tales and songs, and for an Elegy Written in a College Library.

poets.name: Robert Merry
bio: Robert Merry (1755–1798) was an English poet and dilettante, born in London into a family with ties to the Hudson's Bay Company; his mother was a daughter of Sir John Willes, Lord Chief Justice. He lived for some years in Italy, where he was admitted to the Accademia della Crusca of Florence, and he took the name "Della Crusca" from it when he began printing verse in the London newspapers.

As "Della Crusca" he conducted the celebrated verse correspondence with Hannah Cowley's "Anna Matilda" in The World (1787–88), the high point of the sentimental, ornate manner later mocked as the Della Cruscan school. The poems here are only his contributions as printed in The Poetry of Anna Matilda (London: John Bell, 1788); they are attributed by the signature at the end of each piece. He emigrated to America in the 1790s and died at Baltimore in 1798.

poets.name: Prince Hoare
bio: Prince Hoare (1755–1834) was an English painter and dramatist who wrote librettos and plays for the London stage, including the opera The Lock and Key, with music by William Shield.

The poem here is the sea song of the frigate Arethusa, which C. H. Firth prints in Naval Songs and Ballads (Navy Records Society, 1908), noting that its words are by Prince Hoare and the music by Shield.

poets.name: Mrs Anne Grant of Laggan
bio: Mrs Anne Grant of Laggan (1755–1838) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 1 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Joel Barlow
poets.credit: Portrait: Robert Fulton — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Joel Barlow (1754–1812) was an American poet and diplomat, born in Reading, Connecticut, and one of the Connecticut Wits. He is remembered for The Columbiad (1807) and the mock-pastoral The Hasty-Pudding.
Griswold included 5 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Stuart Lewis
bio: Stuart Lewis (c. 1756–1818) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William Blake
poets.credit: Portrait by Thomas Phillips (1807) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Blake (1757–1827) was an English poet, painter, and printmaker, largely unrecognised in his lifetime and now seen as a seminal figure of the Romantic age.
He engraved and hand-coloured his own illuminated books, most famously Songs of Innocence and of Experience, where word and image are inseparable.

poets.name: Mikhail Muravyov
bio: Mikhail Nikitich Muravyov (1757–1807) was a poet and teacher who served as tutor to the future Alexander I and later as a curator of Moscow University. His gentle, personal verse looked forward to the sentimental school of Karamzin and Zhukovsky.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Ferenc Verseghy
bio: Hungarian poet of the late eighteenth century, active in the Hungarian literary revival.
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: Mary Robinson
poets.credit: Thomas Gainsborough, 'Mrs. Mary Robinson (Perdita)', 1781 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mary Robinson (1757–1800), born Mary Darby in Bristol, became an actress at Drury Lane in the 1770s. Her performance as Perdita in The Winter's Tale (1779) caught the eye of the Prince of Wales, later George IV, and she was known afterwards as 'Perdita'. Their liaison was brief, and she later lived on a pension and on her writing.

In the 1790s she turned to poetry, publishing Sappho and Phaon (1796), a sequence of sonnets, as well as novels, essays and political writing, and she contributed verse to the Morning Post. Lyrical Tales (1800), a volume of narrative poems that took its title in answer to Wordsworth and Coleridge's Lyrical Ballads, appeared in the year of her death; she died in December 1800 at Englefield Green, Surrey.

poets.name: Vasily Kapnist
bio: Vasily Vasilyevich Kapnist (1758–1823), of Greek-Ukrainian family, wrote odes, songs and the satirical comedy Chicane (1798). Bowring notes that he wrote “on a variety of subjects”.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Andrew Scott
bio: Andrew Scott (1757–1839) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 7 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 1 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Jean Glover
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Jean Glover (1758–1801) was a Scottish singer and songwriter, the daughter of a weaver at Kilmarnock, who married a strolling player and wandered through the west of Scotland singing her own songs.
Her song 'O'er the Muir amang the Heather' was taken down for the Scots Musical Museum and became a classic of Scottish song; Lyra Celtica prints it.

poets.name: Robert Burns
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Burns by Alexander Nasmyth, 1787 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Burns (1759–1796), Scotland’s national poet, turned the everyday life and speech of Ayrshire farming folk into poetry of remarkable warmth, wit, and force.

Writing in Scots and English by turns, he ranged from the comic terror of Tam O’ Shanter to the tenderness of A Red, Red Rose and the satire of Holy Willie’s Prayer; his spelling is kept exactly as printed here.

poets.name: Ferenc Kazinczy
poets.credit: Portrait of Ferenc Kazinczy by János Donát, 1812 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Hungarian author, poet, translator and language reformer who led the renewal of Hungarian literature around 1800.
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: Janet Little
bio: Janet Little (1759–1813), known as 'the Scotch Milkmaid', was a Scottish poet who worked as a dairymaid and servant in the household of Flora, Countess of Loudoun, at Loudoun Castle in Ayrshire. Her Poetical Works were published by subscription at Ayr in 1792.

The volume mixes English and Scots verse: epistles, elegies, songs and tales, several addressed to friends in the Loudoun household, with an epistle to Robert Burns and a poem on her visit to him. The dedication and list of subscribers are omitted here.

poets.name: Helen Maria Williams
poets.credit: Portrait of Helen Maria Williams, unidentified engraver (London: Dean and Munday, 1816) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Helen Maria Williams (1759–1827) was an English poet, novelist and translator, brought up in Berwick-upon-Tweed and later in London. Her first poem, the legendary tale Edwin and Eltruda, appeared in 1782, and Peru, a Poem in Six Cantos followed in 1784, a lament for the fall of the Inca empire to the Spanish conquerors. Her two-volume Poems of 1786 was published by subscription.

A religious Dissenter, she supported the abolition of the slave trade and, from 1790, the ideals of the French Revolution, and she settled in France, where she wrote the Letters from France and was imprisoned for a time during the Terror. She died in Paris in 1827. Wordsworth printed his early sonnet to her in 1787. The poems held here are those of her Poems (1786); Peru stands as a separate work.

poets.name: Ivan Dmitriev
poets.credit: Portrait: Vasily Andreevich Tropinin — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ivan Ivanovich Dmitriev (1760–1837), born in the Simbirsk province, was a poet of the sentimental school and a close friend of Karamzin. He is best known for his songs and fables, and later served as Minister of Justice (1810–1814).

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: John Mayne
bio: John Mayne (1759–1836) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 5 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 1 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Sarah Wentworth Morton
poets.credit: Portrait of Sarah Wentworth Morton, by Gilbert Stuart · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sarah Wentworth Morton (1759–1846) was an American poet.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “To Aaron Burr, Under Trial for High Treason”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Richard Porson
poets.credit: Richard Porson, engraving by B. Holl after John Hoppner, 19th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Porson (1759–1808) was an English classical scholar, Regius Professor of Greek at Cambridge, celebrated for his editions of Euripides and for his epigrams.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Richard Alsop
bio: Richard Alsop (1761–1815) was a poet and satirist of Middletown, Connecticut, associated with the Connecticut Wits and a co-author of the satires The Echo and The Political Greenhouse.
Griswold included 1 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Semyon Bobrov
bio: Semyon Sergeyevich Bobrov (c. 1763–1810) was a poet and official. His long poem Khersonida (1804), set in the Crimea, is the source of the three pieces given here; Bowring calls it “an oriental epic poem”. His writing is known for its obscure, ornate style.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: James Nugent Reynolds
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: James Nugent Reynolds was an Irish writer who died in 1802. He is remembered chiefly as the author of the ballad "Kathleen O'More".
Yeats includes the ballad in A Book of Irish Verse (1900).

poets.name: Ivan Dolgorukov
bio: Prince Ivan Mikhailovich Dolgorukov (1764–1823) was a courtier, poet and memoirist. Bowring includes his poem “The Legacy” in the second part of the Specimens.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: John Hamilton
bio: John Hamilton (died 1814) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 7 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 1 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Şeyh Galip
bio: Mehmed Esad, known as Şeyh Galip or Galib Dede (1757–1799), was a Mevlevi dervish and sheikh of the Galata convent in Istanbul, and one of the foremost poets of the late Ottoman Romantic school. Sultan Selim III conferred on him the office of sheikh.

His masterpiece is the mystical romance Husn ü Aşk ('Beauty and Love'), from which two passages are given here. E. J. W. Gibb, who gave the first English account of his diwan, praised the strong and glowing verse of his lyric poems.

poets.name: Royall Tyler
poets.credit: Portrait of Royall Tyler · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Royall Tyler (1757–1826) was an American judge.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Independence Day”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Friedrich von Matthisson
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Friedrich von Matthisson was a German poet of landscape and sentiment whose poem Adelaide was set to music by Beethoven. He spent his later life in Württemberg and Anhalt.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Aloys Schreiber
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Aloys Schreiber was a German writer and poet, best known for his guidebooks to the Rhine and Baden and for occasional verse.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Friedrich Schiller
poets.credit: Portrait: Ludovike Simanowiz — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Friedrich Schiller was born at Marbach in Württemberg and became, with Goethe, one of the two great figures of Weimar Classicism. He wrote the plays The Robbers, Wallenstein and William Tell, as well as ballads and philosophical poems, among them the Ode to Joy and The Song of the Bell.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: August von Kotzebue
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: August von Kotzebue was a prolific German dramatist, born at Weimar, whose plays were performed across Europe. He was assassinated at Mannheim in 1819.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Ilhâmî (Sultan Selim III)
bio: Selim III wrote verse under the pen-name Ilhami; he made the poet Galib Sheykh of Galata.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Fâzil Beg
bio: Fazil Beg was the son of Tahir Pasha, the Sheykh Daher of Volney and Savary, the accomplice of 'Ali Beg of Egypt in his revolt against the Ottoman Porte.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Râmiz Pasha
bio: Ramiz Pasha was the Qapudan, or Lord High Admiral, and an intimate friend of Sultan Mustafa IV; after the revolution that dethroned that monarch he fled to Russia, where he wrote gazels showing how he yearned for his friend and his native land.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Wâsif
bio: Gibb distinguishes this Wasif from the historian of the same name, who died in 1806, because the poet's Divan contains beyts as late as 1820.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Mary Lamb
poets.credit: Unknown artist, c. 1847 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mary Lamb was an English writer and the elder sister of Charles Lamb. Her prose and verse appeared mostly in collaboration with her brother, notably the children's books Tales from Shakespeare (1807) and Mrs. Leicester's School (1809).

After a family tragedy in 1796 she lived for long periods in the care of her brother, who looked after her for the rest of his life. Her own verse, mostly occasional pieces, was printed alongside his in the Works of Charles Lamb.

poets.name: St. John Honeywood
bio: St. John Honeywood (1763–1798) was an American lawyer and poet, a native of Leicester, Massachusetts, educated at Yale College, who taught at Schenectady and practised law in New York State.
Griswold included 4 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: George Monck Berkeley
poets.credit: Portrait of George Monck Berkeley by William Peters (1796) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Monck Berkeley was the grandson of Bishop George Berkeley, the philosopher, and a member of the Inner Temple. He died in 1793 at the age of twenty-nine, and his mother, Eliza Berkeley, published his Poems in 1797.

poets.name: Nikolay Karamzin
poets.credit: Portrait of Nikolay Karamzin by Vasily Tropinin (1818) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Nikolay Mikhailovich Karamzin (1766–1826), born near Simbirsk, was the leading figure of Russian sentimentalism. His Letters of a Russian Traveller (1791–92) and the tale Poor Liza (1792) set a new, polished prose style, and his History of the Russian State (begun 1803, published from 1818) made him a national writer. Bowring called him “the most successful and the most popular” of Russia’s living writers.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Samuel Rogers
poets.credit: Wood engraving after Sir Thomas Lawrence, 1855 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Samuel Rogers was an English banker and poet whose The Pleasures of Memory (1792) made his name. He was a well-known host and patron in London literary society.
Palgrave includes two of his short poems.

poets.name: Benjamin Pye
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Benjamin Pye is represented here by verse printed in John Bell's Rhymes of Northern Bards (Newcastle, 1812), 1 piece.
Bell's heading styles him Benjamin Pye, LL.D.

poets.name: Joanna Baillie
poets.credit: Portrait: Mary Ann Knight — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Joanna Baillie (1762–1851) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 12 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 1 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Robert Lochore
bio: Robert Lochore (1762–1852) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 4 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 2 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Mrs Agnes Lyon
bio: Mrs Agnes Lyon (c. 1762–1840) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 4 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 2 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Thomas Russell
bio: Thomas Russell (1762–1788) was an English poet and sonneteer, educated at Winchester College and New College, Oxford. He died young, of consumption, in 1788.
His Sonnets and Miscellaneous Poems were published after his death, in 1789, and the sonnets in particular were admired by later poets of the Romantic generation.

poets.name: William Lisle Bowles
poets.credit: Portrait of William Lisle Bowles, undated engraving · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Lisle Bowles (1762–1850) was an English clergyman and poet, rector of Bremhill in Wiltshire. His Fourteen Sonnets (1789), written during journeys through England, Scotland and the Rhineland, were warmly admired by the young Coleridge and helped to revive the sonnet as a form of personal reflection.

His longer poems include The Spirit of Discovery (1804), The Missionary (1813) and several narrative and devotional poems. In the 1820s he took part in a famous controversy with Byron and others about the poetry of Pope. The texts here are from Gilfillan's edition (Edinburgh, Nichol, 1855), volumes I and II; translations, the editor's memoir and notes are omitted.

poets.name: Alexander Campbell
bio: Alexander Campbell (1764–1824) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 1 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Karel Sudimír Šnajdr
poets.credit: No portrait in the public domain was found.
bio: Karel Sudimír Šnajdr (1766–1835) was a Czech and German poet of the Czech National Revival. Bowring calls him Karel Sudimír Šnaidr, notes that his German name was Schneider, and describes him as one of the liveliest and most humorous of the Bohemian poets.

He first made a name as a writer of German verse, then turned to Czech. Bowring gives two pieces in English: a short lament that the Czech muse came to him so late, and the ballad of the silver bell, built on a popular superstition.

poets.name: Andrew Cherry
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Andrew Cherry (1762–1812) was a printer, actor and dramatist born in Limerick. His plays included The Soldier's Daughter, and his songs "The Bay of Biscay" and "The Green Little Shamrock of Ireland" remained popular.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: William Reid
bio: William Reid (1764–1831) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 5 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 1 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Grigory Khovansky
bio: Grigory Khovansky (1767–1796) was a minor Russian poet of the late eighteenth century who died young. Bowring prints one of his songs in the second part of the Specimens.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Edward Lysaght
poets.credit: Portrait from Edward Lysaght's Poems (1811), artist unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward Lysaght (1763–1810), born at Brickhill, County Clare, was a barrister, wit and song-writer, active in the Volunteer and anti-Union movements. Only a few of his songs and poems survive.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: George Colman the Younger
poets.credit: George Colman the Younger, engraving by William Ridley and Blood, 1809 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Colman the Younger (1762–1836) was an English dramatist and humorous poet, author of the comedies The Heir at Law and John Bull. He later served as Examiner of Plays, and his comic verse was collected in Broad Grins (1802) and My Night-Gown and Slippers (1797).

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Johann Gaudenz von Salis-Seewis
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Johann Gaudenz von Salis-Seewis was a Swiss officer and poet from Graubünden, whose graceful songs of nature and melancholy were widely set to music.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Jean Paul (Johann Paul Friedrich Richter)
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Jean Paul, born Johann Paul Friedrich Richter at Wunsiedel, was a German novelist and humorist whose long novels include Siebenkäs and Titan. He is usually listed under his pen-name.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Helen D'Arcy Stewart (Mrs Dugald Stewart)
bio: Helen D'Arcy Stewart (Mrs Dugald Stewart) (1765–1838) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 1 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Nikolay Shatrov
bio: Nikolay Ivanovich Shatrov (1767–1841) was a Russian poet who wrote patriotic odes. Bowring prints his ode “To the Army of the Don”, written during the war with Napoleon. Bowring’s volumes give no separate notice of his life, so the dates are those supplied by the archive’s editor.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Michael Og O’Longain
bio: Michael Og O’Longain belonged, Sigerson says in Bards of the Gael and Gall (1907), to a respectable and learned family, and settled near Carrignavar in Co. Cork. He took part in the insurrection of 1798 and narrowly escaped death.
His “Song of the Dead Insurgent” is given here in Sigerson’s English version.

poets.name: Henry Luttrell
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Henry Luttrell (c. 1765–1851) was an Irish-born wit, diner-out and poet of Holland House and the circle of Samuel Rogers. His chief work was Advice to Julia: a Letter in Rhyme (1820).

The 4 poems here are the pieces printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Catherine Maria Fanshawe
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Catherine Maria Fanshawe (1765–1834) was an English poet and amateur artist and a friend of Horace Walpole. Her witty verses circulated in manuscript and were collected after her death; she is best known for her riddle on the letter H and her parody of Wordsworth.

The 2 poems here are the pieces printed under her name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Ivan Krylov
poets.credit: Portrait of Ivan Krylov by Karl Bryullov (1839) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ivan Andreyevich Krylov (1769–1844) began as a satirical journalist and playwright. He turned to fables in 1809, many adapted from La Fontaine and Aesop, and became Russia’s best-loved fabulist; from 1812 he worked at the Imperial Public Library in St Petersburg. Bowring printed two of his fables in the first part.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Carolina Nairne
poets.credit: Portrait: John Watson Gordon — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Carolina Nairne, Lady Nairne, was a Scottish songwriter who adapted and wrote songs in the Scots tradition, often anonymously.
Palgrave includes her song "The Land o' the Leal".

poets.name: Robert Bloomfield
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Bloomfield by Henry Bone · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Bloomfield (1766–1823) was an English poet of labouring-class origins, born in Suffolk. He worked as a farm boy and then as a shoemaker in London, where he composed The Farmer's Boy in his head while he worked.

The Farmer's Boy (1800), a poem of rural life in four seasons, was introduced to the public by Capel Lofft and had a very large sale. Rural Tales, Ballads, and Songs followed in 1802 and May-Day with the Muses in 1822. He died in poverty at Shefford, Bedfordshire. The texts here are from early editions on Project Gutenberg; the prefaces and prose supplements are omitted.

poets.name: Antonín Jaroslav Puchmajer
poets.credit: Portrait of Antonín Jaroslav Puchmajer (19th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Antonín Jaroslav Puchmajer (1769–1820) was a Czech priest, poet, philologist and editor, a leading figure of the Czech National Revival. Bowring spells his name Antonín Puchmayer and says he died at Prague, an ecclesiastic of Radnice.
Bowring credits the poetry collection he edited with reawakening interest in the Czech language and literature. From it he translates the ode to the Hussite commander Jan Žižka.

poets.name: Gábor Dayka
poets.credit: Portrait of Gábor Dayka, artist unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Hungarian poet, born at Miskolc, who died young at Ungvár.
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: Alexander Wilson
bio: Alexander Wilson (1766–1813) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 1 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: John Quincy Adams
bio: John Quincy Adams (1767–1848) was the sixth President of the United States, and a diplomat, congressman and occasional poet.
Griswold included 3 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Richard Alfred Milliken
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Richard Alfred Milliken was an Irish lawyer and humorous writer from County Cork. He is remembered for the burlesque song "The Groves of Blarney", written in the 1790s.
Yeats includes the song in A Book of Irish Verse (1900).

poets.name: Alexander Balfour
bio: Alexander Balfour (1767–1829) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 2 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: James Nicol
bio: James Nicol (1769–1819) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 4 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 1 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Bahadur Shah Zafar
poets.credit: Portrait of Bahadur Shah II, unknown artist, c. 1850 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Zafar, or Bahadur Shah, was the Padishah of Delhi and the last Mogul Emperor, son of Akbar II. The book gives his dates as 1768–1862 (other sources give 1775–1862). It says he was over sixty when he came to the throne, a poet and a good judge of music and painting, skilled in all kinds of poetry, author of a voluminous diwan, and a clever calligraphist. After the Mutiny of 1857 he was taken prisoner and sent to Rangoon, where he continued to write verses.

The 4 pieces given here are drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. They are free renderings, not literal translations, and the original Urdu poems are untitled; each is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Charles Dibdin the Younger
bio: Charles Isaac Mungo Dibdin (1768–1833), the son of the songwriter Charles Dibdin, was a dramatist, songwriter and theatre manager, long connected with Sadler's Wells.
The poem here is the song on the frigate La Loire, which C. H. Firth prints in Naval Songs and Ballads (Navy Records Society, 1908) as written by Mr C. Dibdin, junior, and sung at Sadler's Wells.

poets.name: John Shield
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Shield is represented here by verse printed in John Bell's Rhymes of Northern Bards (Newcastle, 1812), 5 pieces and in The Newcastle Song Book; or, Tyne-side Songster (Newcastle: W. & T. Fordyce, 1842), 4 pieces.
A writer of Tyneside songs in the local dialect; the spelling of the printed texts is kept as the books give it.

poets.name: Ebenezer Picken
bio: Ebenezer Picken (c. 1769–1816) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William Robert Spencer
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Robert Spencer (1769–1834) was an English poet and wit, a celebrated writer of vers de société. His ballad "Beth Gêlert" (1800) was widely read, and he moved in the Holland House and Samuel Rogers circles.

The 4 poems here are the pieces printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Ernst Moritz Arndt
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Ernst Moritz Arndt was born on the island of Rügen. A historian and patriotic poet of the wars against Napoleon, he wrote the song Was ist des Deutschen Vaterland? and later taught at Bonn.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: William Wordsworth
poets.credit: ‘Wordsworth on Helvellyn’ by Benjamin Robert Haydon (1842) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) was an English Romantic poet who, with Coleridge, launched the movement in Lyrical Ballads (1798).
He made ordinary life and the natural world his subject, and served as Poet Laureate from 1843 until his death.

poets.name: Joseph Hopkinson
bio: Joseph Hopkinson (1770–1842) was a Philadelphia lawyer, congressman and judge, the son of Francis Hopkinson, and the author of the national song Hail, Columbia (1798).
Griswold included 1 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: William Charles Wentworth
bio: William Charles Wentworth (1790–1872) was an Australian explorer, barrister, newspaper proprietor and statesman, one of the three who first crossed the Blue Mountains in 1813.
While a student at Cambridge he wrote the poem Australasia (1823) for the Chancellor's medal, where it came second to Winthrop Mackworth Praed's entry; Stevens's anthology prints its opening lines.

poets.name: János Kis
bio: Hungarian Lutheran pastor, bishop, poet and translator.
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: James Hogg
poets.credit: Portrait of James Hogg by Sir John Watson Gordon · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James Hogg (1770–1835) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).

This archive holds songs from volume 2 of Rogers's anthology, together with the shorter poems, ballads, songs and parodies of The Poetical Works of the Ettrick Shepherd (Blackie, Glasgow, 1838–40, five volumes). The long poems are in the Works section. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir.

poets.name: George Canning
poets.credit: George Canning, after Thomas Lawrence, 1820s · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Canning (1770–1827) was a British statesman, Foreign Secretary and, briefly, Prime Minister in 1827. In 1797–98 he was one of the writers of The Anti-Jacobin, a weekly paper that ridiculed radical politics and fashionable verse by parody.
The poem here is the song James Parton ascribed to him in his anthology of English humorous poetry. Pieces that Parton credits only to the Anti-Jacobin, or to several hands, are not included.

poets.name: John Robertson
bio: John Robertson (c. 1770–1810) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).

poets.name: Sir Walter Scott
poets.credit: Portrait: Henry Raeburn — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Walter Scott (1771–1832) was a Scottish poet and novelist whose verse romances — The Lay of the Last Minstrel, Marmion, The Lady of the Lake — made him the best-selling poet in Europe before Byron eclipsed him, and whose Waverley novels effectively invented the historical novel.

Trained as a lawyer in Edinburgh, Scott drew on a lifelong passion for Scottish Border ballads and Highland history; a private financial ruin late in life led him to write at a furious pace to pay off his debts, at the cost of his health.

poets.name: Thomas Browne
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Browne (1771–1798) was born at Lastingham, the son of the vicar, and began as a schoolmaster at Yeddingham and then Bridlington. In 1797 he moved to Hull to edit the newly founded Hull Advertiser; he took orders and married, and died the following year.

His friends published Poems on Several Occasions in 1800. Most of it is in standard English, but the few dialect pieces, in which F. W. Moorman saw the influence of Burns, circulated widely in Yorkshire. The three poems here come from Moorman's Yorkshire Dialect Poems (1916).

poets.name: Sydney Smith
poets.credit: Portrait of Sydney Smith, 1858 print · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sydney Smith (1771–1845) was an English clergyman, essayist and conversationalist, a founder of the Edinburgh Review in 1802 and later a canon of St Paul's Cathedral. He was famous in his own day as a wit.
Verse was a sideline for him. The pieces here are the few that James Parton included in his anthology of English humorous poetry, among them the comic 'Recipe for Salad'.

poets.name: James Montgomery
poets.credit: Portrait of James Montgomery, early 19th century engraving · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James Montgomery (1771–1854) was born in Irvine, Ayrshire, the son of a Moravian minister, and was educated at the Moravian school at Fulneck in Yorkshire. He settled in Sheffield, where he edited the Sheffield Iris newspaper, was twice imprisoned for political publications, and wrote on humanitarian causes including the abolition of the slave trade and the plight of child chimney sweeps.

He published long poems such as The Wanderer of Switzerland and The World before the Flood, but is remembered chiefly as one of the foremost English hymn writers; ‘Hail to the Lord’s Anointed’ and ‘Angels from the realms of glory’ remain widely sung. This selection is drawn from Sacred Poems and Hymns, for Public and Private Devotion (1854), with the author’s latest corrections.

poets.name: Thomas John Dibdin
bio: Thomas John Dibdin (1771–1841) was an English dramatist and songwriter, the son of the songwriter Charles Dibdin. He wrote a great many stage pieces and songs for the London theatres.
His best-known song, "The Snug Little Island", was written for the entertainment The British Raft (1797–98) and became hugely popular in the years of the French invasion scare.

poets.name: James Orr
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: James Orr (1770–1816), the "Bard of Ballycarry", was a weaver who contributed to the Northern Star, joined the United Irishmen and fought at Antrim in 1798. He wrote "Song of an Exile" on a voyage into exile, soon returned, and died at his loom.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Peter Buchan

This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William Clifton
bio: William Clifton (1772–1799) was a Philadelphia poet from a Quaker family who died young; he is known for his verse epistle To William Gifford.
Griswold included 2 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.credit: Wood engraving of Sándor Kisfaludy by Gusztáv Morelli, from Az Osztrák-Magyar Monarchia írásban és képben (1887–1901) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Hungarian lyric poet whose chief work is the love-song cycle Himfy's Loves, and the elder brother of Károly Kisfaludy.
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: Thomas Green Fessenden
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Green Fessenden · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Green Fessenden (1771–1837) was an American author and editor.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Ye Sons of Columbia”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: William Martin Johnson
bio: William Martin Johnson (c. 1771–1797) was an American physician and poet who died at Jamaica, Long Island. Specimens of his poems were published by John Howard Payne in the Democratic Review in 1838.

poets.name: Siegfried August Mahlmann
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Siegfried August Mahlmann was a German poet and journalist who lived at Leipzig, where he edited a fashionable newspaper and published songs and light verse.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Mary Tighe
poets.credit: Mary Tighe, by George Romney, c. 1794–95 (National Gallery of Ireland) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mary Tighe (née Blachford, 1772–1810) was an Irish poet, born in Dublin on 9 October 1772, the daughter of the clergyman William Blachford and the Methodist leader Theodosia Tighe. At twenty-one she married her first cousin Henry Tighe, a member of the Irish Parliament; she later lived in London, where she knew Thomas Moore, and spent her last years in failing health, dying of tuberculosis at Woodstock, County Kilkenny, on 24 March 1810.

Her Psyche, or the Legend of Love, a retelling of the tale of Cupid and Psyche from Apuleius in six cantos of Spenserian stanzas, was privately printed in 1805. It was published in 1811, the year after her death, together with a gathering of her shorter poems, sonnets and songs, and won her wide admiration, Keats among her readers. The texts here are from Psyche, with Other Poems (London, 1811).

poets.name: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
poets.credit: Portrait of Coleridge at age 42 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) was an English poet, critic, and philosopher, co-founder of the Romantic movement.
His visionary poems ‘The Rime of the Ancient Mariner’ and ‘Kubla Khan’ remain touchstones of the imagination he spent his life theorising.

poets.name: Robert Treat Paine
bio: Robert Treat Paine (1773–1811) was a Boston lawyer and poet, born Thomas Paine, who adopted the name Robert Treat Paine in 1801. His song Adams and Liberty (1798) was widely sung.
Griswold included 2 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: William M'Laren

This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 2 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Dorothy Payne Madison
bio: Dorothy Payne Madison (1772–1849) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “La Fayette”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Novalis (Friedrich von Hardenberg)
poets.credit: Portrait of Novalis by Franz Gareis (1799) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Friedrich von Hardenberg, who wrote as Novalis, was born in 1772 at Oberwiederstedt in Saxony and trained as a lawyer and mining administrator while moving in the Jena circle of early German Romanticism. The death in 1797 of his young betrothed, Sophie von Kühn, became the centre of his work.

His Hymns to the Night (1800) and Spiritual Songs (1802) turn that bereavement into a mystical devotion to night, death and Christ. He died of consumption in 1801, aged twenty-eight. The English versions here are George MacDonald's, printed in Rampolli (1897).

poets.name: Mihály Csokonai Vitéz
poets.credit: Portrait of Mihály Csokonai Vitéz, artist unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Hungarian poet and a leading figure in the Hungarian literary revival.
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: Josef Jungmann
poets.credit: Portrait of Josef Jungmann by Antonín Machek · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Josef Jungmann (1773–1847) was a Czech linguist and poet, one of the main architects of the modern Czech literary language. Bowring writes his name Joseph Jungmann and describes him as professor of poetry and oratory at the Academical Gymnasium of Prague.
Bowring notes his Czech version of Paradise Lost and his prose works. The single poem here, a song of rural contentment, is the one lyric Bowring prints in full.

poets.name: Robert Southey
poets.credit: Peter Vandyke, 1795 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Southey (1774–1843) was an English poet and man of letters, Poet Laureate from 1813 until his death, and one of the “Lake Poets” alongside his friends Wordsworth and Coleridge (whose sister-in-law he married).

He was, in his own day, best known for his grim and often macabre ballads of guilt, folklore and the supernatural, and for prose-poem “Eclogues” that gave a plain, compassionate voice to the rural poor — work that has aged rather better than the long epics on which he staked his reputation.

poets.name: Francis Jeffrey, Lord Jeffrey
poets.credit: Francis Jeffrey, Lord Jeffrey, by Andrew Geddes · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Francis Jeffrey, Lord Jeffrey (1773–1850), was a Scottish lawyer, judge and critic, editor of the Edinburgh Review for nearly three decades. He wrote little verse; the lines here were written for a lady's album.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Henry Vassall-Fox, 3rd Baron Holland
poets.credit: Henry Richard Vassall-Fox, 3rd Baron Holland, by Sir George Hayter · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Richard Vassall-Fox, 3rd Baron Holland (1773–1840), was a Whig statesman and nephew of Charles James Fox. Holland House, Kensington, was under him the centre of Whig society and of a famous literary circle; he wrote occasional verse and translations.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Ludwig Tieck
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Ludwig Tieck was born in Berlin and became a leading figure of early German Romanticism. He wrote fairy-tale comedies, novellas and lyric poems, and edited the works of other Romantic writers.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: John Leyden
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of John Leyden · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Leyden (1775–1811) was a Scottish poet, physician and orientalist, born at Denholm in Roxburghshire, the son of a shepherd. He studied at Edinburgh, became a friend and helper of Walter Scott, and supplied him with ballad material and original ballads for the Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border.

His own poems include Scenes of Infancy (1803). He went to India as an assistant surgeon in 1803, held posts in Mysore and Calcutta, studied Indian languages, and died of fever at Batavia in Java in 1811.

poets.name: William Munford
bio: William Munford (1775–1825) was a Virginia lawyer and legislator, born in Mecklenburg County, and the translator of Homer's Iliad, published after his death in 1846.
Griswold included 2 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: R. S. Sharpe
bio: R. S. Sharpe (Richard Scrafton Sharpe) was an English writer of songs in the early nineteenth century, remembered for “The Minute-Gun,” which was set to music and widely sung.
The song here is taken from the Library of Poetry and Song edited by William Cullen Bryant (1871); little else is recorded of him there.

poets.name: Matthew Gregory Lewis
poets.credit: Portrait of Matthew Gregory Lewis by George Lethbridge Saunders, after an unknown artist · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Matthew Gregory Lewis (1775–1818), known as “Monk” Lewis, was an English novelist, playwright and poet, born in London. His Gothic novel The Monk (1796) made him famous, and he wrote plays and the ballad collections Tales of Wonder and Tales of Terror.
He was an early friend of Walter Scott, to whose Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border he contributed a ballad, and he died of yellow fever at sea in 1818 on a voyage home from his Jamaican estates.

poets.name: William Dobie
bio: William Dobie (born 1790) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Thomas Dermody
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Dermody by Charles Allingham, 1802 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Dermody (1775–1802), born at Ennis, was a precocious poet sometimes called the "Chatterton of Ireland". Poverty and drink dogged him, and he died in a hovel near Sydenham.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Matthew Arnold
poets.credit: Portrait of Matthew Arnold · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Matthew Arnold (1822–1888) was an English poet and cultural critic, Professor of Poetry at Oxford.
His poems — among them ‘Dover Beach’ and ‘The Scholar-Gipsy’ — register the anxious loss of religious certainty at the heart of the Victorian age.

poets.name: Walter Savage Landor
poets.credit: J. Brown, Beaumaris, c. 1850 (National Library of Wales, Welsh Portrait Collection) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Walter Savage Landor (1775–1864) was an English writer best known for Imaginary Conversations, a vast series of prose dialogues between historical figures, and for a small body of exquisitely polished short poems and epigrams that later poets — Swinburne, Pound, and others — prized above almost anything else of his era for their classical restraint.

Quarrelsome and litigious by temperament (he was expelled from Oxford and later drove himself into exile in Italy more than once), Landor lived to eighty-nine, still writing crisp, controlled verse almost to the end — including his own epitaph-poem, ‘I strove with none.’

poets.name: Charles Lamb
poets.credit: Portrait: After Henry Hoppner Meyer — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Lamb was an English essayist and critic, famous for the Essays of Elia, and a close friend of Samuel Taylor Coleridge. He also wrote a small body of verse.
Palgrave includes several of his short poems, among them "The Old Familiar Faces".
