poets.name: Thomas Campbell
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Campbell by Sir Thomas Lawrence · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Campbell (1777–1844) was a Scottish poet, born in Glasgow, the youngest of eleven children. He made his name at twenty-one with The Pleasures of Hope (1799), a didactic poem on hope, liberty and the wrongs of Poland and Africa, and followed it with the Pennsylvania tale Gertrude of Wyoming (1809).

He is best remembered for his patriotic and martial lyrics — ‘Ye Mariners of England’, ‘The Battle of the Baltic’, ‘Hohenlinden’ — and for the ballads ‘Lord Ullin’s Daughter’ and ‘Lochiel’s Warning’. He was also an early promoter of University College London and served as Lord Rector of Glasgow University; he died at Boulogne and is buried in Westminster Abbey.

poets.name: Mrs G. G. Richardson
bio: Mrs G. G. Richardson (1777–1853) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 4 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 2 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Alexey Merzlyakov
bio: Alexey Fyodorovich Merzlyakov (1778–1830) was a poet and critic and professor of rhetoric at Moscow University. His songs written in the folk manner were widely sung in Russia. Bowring prints his version of Isaiah’s oracle on the fall of Babylon and a pastoral “Duett”.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: John Shaw
bio: John Shaw (1778–1809) was an American physician and poet, born in Annapolis, Maryland, and a graduate of St. John's College, who served as a ship's surgeon and died abroad.
Griswold included 3 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: James Kirke Paulding
bio: James Kirke Paulding (1778–1860) was a New York essayist, novelist and poet, and later Secretary of the Navy. His poem The Backwoodsman appeared in 1818.
Griswold included 5 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Mihály Vitkovics
poets.credit: Portrait of Mihály Vitkovics, early 19th century, artist unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Serbian-Hungarian poet, translator and lawyer, born in Eger and active in Hungarian literary life in Pest (Wikisource gives his name as Mihailo Vitković).
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: George Scott
bio: George Scott (1777–1853) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 2 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Thomas Brown, M.D.
bio: Thomas Brown, M.D. (1778–1820) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 2 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William Blacker
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Blacker (1777–1855) was a lieutenant-colonel born at Carrickblacker, County Armagh, where he also died. His Orange ballad "Oliver's Advice" became almost a war-song; his poems were never collected in his lifetime.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Friedrich de la Motte Fouqué
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Friedrich de la Motte Fouqué was a Prussian officer and Romantic writer, best known for the tale Undine (1811) and for his chivalric romances.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Philipp Otto Runge
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Philipp Otto Runge was a German Romantic painter, born at Wolgast, who also wrote on colour theory and wrote some verse. He died in Hamburg at the age of thirty-three.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Henry Brougham, Lord Brougham
poets.credit: Henry Brougham by Thomas Lawrence, 1825 (National Portrait Gallery) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Brougham, 1st Baron Brougham and Vaux (1778–1868), was a Scottish-born lawyer, reformer and statesman who served as Lord Chancellor from 1830 to 1834 and helped found the Edinburgh Review.
The epitaph here is the one James Parton printed under his name in his anthology of English humorous poetry.

poets.name: Thomas Moore
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Moore by Sir Thomas Lawrence (Trinity College, Cambridge; date not given on Wikimedia Commons) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Moore (1779–1852) was Ireland's national poet in the Romantic era, celebrated above all for the Irish Melodies (issued in installments from 1808 to 1834), verses written to fit traditional Irish airs, which carried Irish nationalist feeling and folklore to drawing rooms across Britain and America.

A close friend of Byron (whose memoirs he controversially burned after the poet's death) and a fixture of literary London, Moore was also the author of the wildly popular Oriental verse-romance Lalla Rookh, though it is the Melodies — "The Minstrel Boy," "The Last Rose of Summer," "Believe Me, if All Those Endearing Young Charms" — that have lasted.

poets.name: Clement C. Moore
bio: Clement C. Moore (1779–1863) was an American scholar of Hebrew and Greek, a professor at the General Theological Seminary in New York, and the author of A Visit from St. Nicholas.
Griswold included 2 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Washington Allston
poets.credit: Portrait: Washington Allston — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Washington Allston (1779–1843) was a South Carolina-born painter, the leading American Romantic painter of his day, who also published verse, including The Sylphs of the Seasons (1813).
Griswold included 13 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Francis Scott Key
bio: Francis Scott Key (1779–1843) was a Maryland lawyer who wrote the words of The Star-Spangled Banner during the British bombardment of Fort McHenry in September 1814.
Griswold included 1 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Daniel Webster
bio: Daniel Webster (1782–1852) was the American statesman and orator, a congressman and senator for Massachusetts and twice Secretary of State. He wrote only a few poems, which appeared posthumously in his Private Correspondence (1856).

poets.name: Adam Oehlenschläger
poets.credit: Portrait of Adam Oehlenschläger by Christian Albrecht Jensen, 1825 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Adam Oehlenschläger (1779–1850) was a Danish poet and dramatist, born in Copenhagen. His poem "The Golden Horns" (1802) and the collection Poems of 1803 opened the Romantic movement in Danish literature, and he went on to write verse tragedies such as Hakon Jarl and Axel and Valborg, and the oriental drama Aladdin. In 1810 he became professor of aesthetics at the University of Copenhagen, and in 1829 the Swedish poet Esaias Tegnér crowned him in Lund cathedral as the laureate of the North.

Much of his work draws on Norse myth and saga. Nordens Guder (1819) is a cycle of poems on the Norse gods, here in William Edward Frye's English version, The Gods of the North (1845), which follows Thor and the trickster Lok through thirty cantos. He wrote also in German, and he is remembered in Denmark as the author of the national song 'There is a lovely land'.

poets.name: William Chalmers
bio: William Chalmers (1779–1843) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 2 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Muztar
poets.dates: dates not given in the source
bio: The book says Muztar was born and educated at Lucknow, that his ancestors occupied an honourable rank at Delhi, and that he was a pupil of Mushafi. It gives no dates.

The one piece given here is drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. It is a free rendering, not a literal translation, and the original Urdu poem is untitled; it is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Horace Smith
bio: Horace Smith (1779–1849) was a London stockbroker, novelist and poet. With his brother James he wrote Rejected Addresses (1812), a book of parodies of the leading poets of the day, supposedly submitted for the opening of the rebuilt Drury Lane Theatre.
The poems here are the pieces that James Parton assigned to Horace Smith in his anthology The Humorous Poetry of the English Language.

poets.name: Charles James Finlayson
bio: Charles James Finlayson (born 1790; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Alexander Voeikov
bio: Alexander Fyodorovich Voeikov (1779–1839) was a poet, critic and translator, and for a time a professor at the University of Dorpat. Bowring prints his poem “To My Future Bride” in the second part of the Specimens.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Robert Davidson
bio: Robert Davidson (1779–1855) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Joseph Train
bio: Joseph Train (1779–1852) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 2 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: John Gibson
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Gibson is represented here by verse printed in John Bell's Rhymes of Northern Bards (Newcastle, 1812), 1 piece.
Bell's book gives no dates for this writer, so the date above is the year of the collection in which the verse appears. The dialect spelling of the printed texts is kept.

poets.name: Anthony Raftery
bio: Eleanor Hull's The Poem-Book of the Gael describes Anthony Raftery as having died at Craughwell, Co. Galway, in October 1835. He was an Irish-language poet.

The three poems gathered here are given in the English versions printed in Hull's anthology (London, 1913), by Douglas Hyde and Lady Gregory, and, for “The Shining Posy”, where no translator is named, by Hull herself.

poets.name: John Marriott
bio: The Reverend John Marriott (1780–1825) was an English clergyman and poet, tutor to the family of the Duke of Buccleuch, the chief of Walter Scott’s clan, and later a curate and rector in Devon.
He wrote verses on Border subjects for the later editions of Scott’s Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border, including The Feast of Spurs and Archie Armstrong’s Aith.

poets.name: Sir Robert Grant
bio: Sir Robert Grant (1779–1838) was a British lawyer and politician, later Governor of Bombay, whose hymns include “O worship the King”.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: George Croly
bio: George Croly (1780–1860) was an Irish-born clergyman, poet, novelist and historian. Born in Dublin, he was ordained in 1804, moved to London, and from 1835 until his death was rector of St Stephen Walbrook.
His Poetical Works appeared in two volumes in 1830; his best-known novel is Salathiel (1828). The poems given here are taken from the Poetical Works.

poets.name: William Dunbar, D.D.
bio: William Dunbar, D.D. (dates not given by Rogers) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William Lamb, Viscount Melbourne
poets.credit: William Lamb, 2nd Viscount Melbourne, by John Partridge, 1844 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Lamb, 2nd Viscount Melbourne (1779–1848), was a Whig statesman who served twice as Prime Minister (1834 and 1835–1841) and was Queen Victoria's first political adviser. A few youthful verses are traditionally credited to him.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Robert Jamieson
bio: Robert Jamieson (c. 1780–1844) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 2 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William Laidlaw
bio: William Laidlaw (1780–1845) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 2 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: John Macdonald, Jun.
bio: John Macdonald, Jun. (dates not given by Rogers) wrote in Gaelic; Charles Rogers printed English verse renderings of the bard's songs in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 English rendering from the Gaelic in volume 6 of the anthology; each is credited to the translator whom Rogers names. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir.

poets.name: Joseph Macgregor
bio: Joseph Macgregor (died c. 1845) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Walter Watson
bio: Walter Watson (1780–1854) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 5 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 2 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: James Kenney
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: James Kenney (1780–1849) was an English dramatist whose farce Raising the Wind (1803) introduced the character Jeremy Diddler. He wrote many comedies, operettas and melodramas for the London stage.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Théophile Gautier
poets.credit: Portrait of Théophile Gautier by Nadar, c. 1856 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Théophile Gautier (1811–1872) was a French poet, novelist and critic, born in Tarbes and raised in Paris, where he first trained as a painter before turning to literature. A champion of Romanticism from the 1830s and the principal voice of "art for art's sake", he served as a journalist and theatre critic for most of his working life, and he is much admired by later poets, including the Parnassians and Baudelaire, who dedicated Les Fleurs du mal to him.

Émaux et Camées (Enamels and Cameos), first published in 1852 and enlarged until 1872, gathers his polished, sculptural short poems, in which he treats verse as a craft of enamel, marble and carved gem; the closing poem, "Art", is its manifesto. The original poems are in French. The English shown here is the translation by Agnes Lee, published in 1903 in the Complete Works of Théophile Gautier.

poets.name: Charles Kirkpatrick Sharpe
bio: Charles Kirkpatrick Sharpe (c. 1781–1851) was a Scottish antiquary, artist and wit, of the family of Hoddom in Dumfriesshire. He was educated at Oxford and became a noted collector of ballads, folklore and curious historical anecdote.
He contributed Border ballads to Walter Scott’s Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border and later edited Kirkton’s history of the Church of Scotland and other works.

poets.name: Esaias Tegnér
poets.credit: Johan Gustaf Sandberg, 1826 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Esaias Tegnér (1782–1846) was a Swedish poet, professor of Greek at Lund University and, from 1824, Bishop of Växjö. He was the leading voice of Swedish Romanticism and is regarded as the father of modern Swedish poetry.

His best-known work is Frithiofs saga (1825), a cycle of twenty-four cantos retelling an Icelandic saga, which was translated into English many times in the nineteenth century. This archive carries the 1876 version by Thomas A. E. Holcomb and Martha A. Lyon Holcomb.

poets.name: 'Izzet Molla
bio: 'Izzet Molla was one of Sultan Mahmud II's Vice-Chancellors and the author of the Mihnet-Keshan; Gibb places him among the highest poets of the nineteenth century.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: John S. B. Monsell
poets.credit: Title page of ‘Spiritual Songs’ for the Sundays and Holydays (London: Parker, Son, and Bourn, 3rd ed., 1861), from the Internet Archive scan · An artifact, shown because no clearly public-domain likeness of Monsell could be found · Public domain
bio: John Samuel Bewley Monsell (1811–1875) was an Irish-born Anglican clergyman, the son of the Archdeacon of Derry, who was educated at Trinity College, Dublin, and ordained in 1834. He served in Ireland, as Rector of Ramoan in County Antrim, and from 1853 as Vicar of Egham in Surrey, where he was also Rural Dean; in 1870 he became Rector of St Nicholas, Guildford. He died in 1875 after a fall during the rebuilding of that church.

Monsell was a prolific hymn-writer, with some three hundred hymns to his name, among them ‘O worship the Lord in the beauty of holiness’ and ‘Fight the good fight’. This selection draws on four of his books: Spiritual Songs for the Sundays and Holydays (1861), Hymns of Love and Praise for the Church’s Year (1866), Parish Musings, or Devotional Poems (the Rivington edition of 1863) and The Passing Bell and Other Poems (1868), whose long title poem is given as a separate work.

poets.name: Theodore Parker
bio: Theodore Parker (1810–1860) was an American Unitarian minister, Transcendentalist and reformer, born at Lexington, Massachusetts, and minister in Boston.
A leading abolitionist and a prolific preacher and writer, he left a few devotional poems that have been widely anthologised.

poets.name: John Grieve
bio: John Grieve (1781–1836) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William Makepeace Thackeray
poets.credit: Daguerreotype of W. M. Thackeray by Jesse Harrison Whitehurst, c. 1855 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Makepeace Thackeray (1811–1863) was born in Calcutta and is best known as the novelist of Vanity Fair, but he was also a prolific writer of comic verse. Much of it first appeared in Punch in the 1840s and early 1850s, including the 'Policeman X' ballads in comic cockney dialect, often under the name Titmarsh.
The poems here are the ones James Parton chose for his anthology The Humorous Poetry of the English Language.

poets.name: Robert Browning
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Browning · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Browning (1812–1889) was an English poet and playwright, master of the dramatic monologue — a poem spoken entirely in an invented character's voice.

This selection gathers his early collections Dramatic Lyrics (1842) and Dramatic Romances (1845); his stage plays and longer closet-dramas (Pauline, Paracelsus, Pippa Passes) are not included here; Sordello is given as a work of its own.

poets.name: James Stirrat
bio: James Stirrat (1781–1843) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Charles Dickens
poets.credit: Charles Dickens, photograph by Jeremiah Gurney (c. 1867) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Dickens (1812–1870) was the leading English novelist of the Victorian age. He wrote little verse; the song given here is "The Ivy Green", sung in his first novel, The Pickwick Papers (1836–37).
It is taken from Edmund H. Garrett's anthology Victorian Songs: Lyrics of the Affections and Nature (Boston: Little, Brown, 1895).

poets.name: William Bell Scott
poets.credit: William Bell Scott, portrait by Arthur Hughes · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Bell Scott (1812–1890; dates as printed in the anthology) was a Scottish painter and poet, a friend of Dante Gabriel Rossetti and master of the government school of design at Newcastle. His verse was gathered in Poems (1875).
The poems given here are taken from Edmund H. Garrett's anthology Victorian Songs (Boston: Little, Brown, 1895) and R. Brimley Johnson's Popular British Ballads (1894).

poets.name: William Stanley Roscoe
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Stanley Roscoe (1782–1843) was an English poet, banker and abolitionist.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: John Kenyon
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Kenyon (1784–1856) was an English verse-writer and philanthropist, now remembered as a patron of Robert Browning.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: William Edmondstoune Aytoun
poets.credit: Bust of W. E. Aytoun by James Charles Armytage, 1867 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Edmondstoune Aytoun (1813–1865) was a Scottish lawyer, poet and critic, Professor of Rhetoric and Belles Lettres at Edinburgh and a regular contributor to Blackwood's Magazine. He is best known for the Lays of the Scottish Cavaliers (1849) and, with Theodore Martin, for the parodic Bon Gaultier ballads.
The pieces here are the comic verses that James Parton printed under his name in his anthology of English humorous poetry, several of them parodies of fashionable poets of the day.

poets.name: John Finlay
bio: John Finlay (born 1782) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 4 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Ebenezer Elliott
poets.credit: Portrait of Ebenezer Elliott · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ebenezer Elliott (1781–1849) was an English poet and Sheffield iron merchant, known as the “Corn Law Rhymer” for the verse he wrote against the Corn Laws.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 2, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: John Mitford
bio: John Mitford, clergyman and editor, was born in 1781. In 1814 he edited the works of Gray, and in 1851 those of Milton; he also edited Parnell for the Aldine Poets.
A collection of his own verse, Miscellaneous Poems, appeared in 1858. He died in 1859.

poets.name: Edward Hovell-Thurlow, Lord Thurlow
bio: Edward Hovell-Thurlow, 2nd Baron Thurlow (1781–1829), was an English poet and nephew of the Lord Chancellor of the same title. He published several volumes of verse in the 1810s and 1820s.
His lyric "May" is printed in The Oxford Book of English Verse.

poets.name: Charles Gray
bio: Charles Gray (1782–1851) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 4 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Emil Buczy
bio: Hungarian poet of the early nineteenth century.
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: William Jerdan
bio: William Jerdan (born 1782) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Ann Taylor
bio: Ann Taylor (1782–1866), later Mrs Gilbert, was an English writer of verse for children. With her sister Jane Taylor she published Original Poems for Infant Minds (1804) and other books of moral rhymes that were read throughout the nineteenth century.
The Pin and The Cow are among her best-remembered short poems.

poets.name: Vasily Zhukovsky
poets.credit: Portrait of Vasily Zhukovsky by Karl Bryullov (1837) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Vasily Andreyevich Zhukovsky (1783–1852) was the founder of Russian Romanticism. His free translations and adaptations of English and German poetry, among them Gray’s “Elegy”, Bürger’s ballads and the ballad “Svetlana” (1813), brought a new emotional range to Russian verse. He later served as tutor to the future Alexander II and was an early mentor and friend of Pushkin.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: William Nicholson
bio: William Nicholson (1782–1849) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 4 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: John M'Diarmid
bio: John M'Diarmid (1790–1852) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Alexander Bald
bio: Alexander Bald (born 1783) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Leigh Hunt
poets.credit: Portrait of Leigh Hunt by Benjamin Robert Haydon · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Leigh Hunt (1784–1859) was an English poet, essayist and editor, best remembered today as the friend and champion of Keats and Shelley. As editor of The Examiner he was imprisoned from 1813 to 1815 for libelling the Prince Regent, and he received visitors in his cell.
His own poems range from the narrative Story of Rimini (1816) to light verse, sonnets and short lyrics. “Abou Ben Adhem” and “Jenny Kiss’d Me” are the two that most readers know.

poets.name: Denis Davydov
bio: Denis Vasilyevich Davydov (1784–1839) was a cavalry officer, a leader of partisan raids against Napoleon’s army in 1812, and the poet of the “hussar” style of lively, convivial verse. Bowring prints a single short poem under the name “Davidov”; the archive’s editor identifies him with Denis Davydov, but Bowring himself gives no notice of the author.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Samuel Woodworth
poets.credit: Portrait of Samuel Woodworth, from The National Cyclopaedia of American Biography (1893) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Samuel Woodworth (1784–1842) was an American poet, journalist and editor, born at Scituate, Massachusetts. He worked as a printer and edited several periodicals in New York, including the New-York Mirror, which he founded with George Pope Morris.
He is remembered chiefly for “The Bucket”, better known as “The Old Oaken Bucket”, written in 1817 and one of the most popular American songs of the nineteenth century.

poets.name: John Selkirk
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Selkirk is represented here by verse printed in John Bell's Rhymes of Northern Bards (Newcastle, 1812), 2 pieces.
A writer of Tyneside songs in the local dialect; the spelling of the printed texts is kept as the books give it.

poets.name: Levi Frisbie
bio: Levi Frisbie (1784–1822) was an American scholar and professor of moral philosophy at Harvard, the son of a clergyman of Ipswich, Massachusetts.
Griswold included 1 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Thomas Hastings
bio: Thomas Hastings (1784–1872) was an American composer, music teacher and hymn writer, born in Washington, Connecticut.
From 1842 he worked in New York City as a church musician and writer on sacred music. His hymns include “Hail to the brightness of Zion’s glad morning”.

poets.name: Reginald Heber
poets.credit: Portrait of Reginald Heber by Thomas Phillips (c. 1822) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Reginald Heber (1783–1826) was an English Anglican bishop of Calcutta, a man of letters and a hymn-writer.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included. Further poems come from The Poetical Works of Reginald Heber, D.D. (London and New York: Frederick Warne, The Lansdowne Poets).

poets.name: Jane Taylor
bio: Jane Taylor (1783–1824) was an English poet and prose writer, best known for the verses for children that she wrote with her sister Ann. Her poem "The Star", in Rhymes for the Nursery (1806), is the source of "Twinkle, twinkle, little star".
She lived most of her life at Ongar, in Essex, where she died at the age of forty.

poets.name: Allan Cunningham
poets.credit: Portrait: Henry Room (died 1850) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Allan Cunningham was a Scottish poet and man of letters who began as a stonemason. He wrote songs in the Scots tradition and compiled collections of Scottish song.
Palgrave includes his sea song "A wet sheet and a flowing sea".

poets.name: Washington Irving
poets.credit: Washington Irving, attributed to Charles Robert Leslie, c. 1820 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Washington Irving (1783–1859) was an American essayist, short-story writer and diplomat, author of The Sketch Book (1819–20), including "Rip Van Winkle" and "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow". His few poems are album and occasional verses.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Phoebe Hinsdale Brown
bio: Phoebe Hinsdale Brown (1783–1861) was an American hymn-writer, born at Canaan, New York, and later a resident of Connecticut, Massachusetts and Illinois. Her hymn "I love to steal awhile away" was written in 1818.

poets.name: Max von Schenkendorf
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Max von Schenkendorf was born at Tilsit and became one of the patriotic poets of the wars of liberation against Napoleon. He died at Koblenz.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Alexander Rodger
bio: Alexander Rodger (1784–1846) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 5 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: George Wilson
bio: George Wilson (born 1784; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: John Pierpont
poets.credit: Portrait: Mathew Benjamin Brady — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Pierpont (1785–1866) was a Unitarian minister, poet and reformer, born in Litchfield, Connecticut, and author of Airs of Palestine (1816). He was long minister of the Hollis Street Church in Boston.
Griswold included 14 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Henry Kirke White
poets.credit: Portrait of Henry Kirke White by Thomas Barber · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Kirke White (1785–1806) was born in Nottingham, the son of a butcher, and was put to work early in a stocking-loom and then a lawyer's office while he taught himself languages and wrote verse. His first volume, Clifton Grove (1803), won him the notice of Robert Southey, and with the help of patrons he went up to St John's College, Cambridge, to study for the church.

Overwork and the strain of competing for university honours broke his health, and he died of consumption at Cambridge at the age of twenty-one. Southey edited his Remains (1807), and Lord Byron's lines on his early death in English Bards and Scotch Reviewers made his name widely known. The poems here follow the Poetical Works with a memoir by Sir Harris Nicolas.

poets.name: 'Adlî (Sultan Mahmud II)
bio: Mahmud II wrote verse under the pen-name 'Adli.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Pál Szemere
bio: Hungarian writer of the early nineteenth-century literary revival.
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: Gábor Döbrentei
poets.credit: Portrait of Gábor Döbrentei, published in Vasárnapi Ujság, 1858, artist unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Hungarian philologist, antiquary and poet, and one of Bowring's Hungarian correspondents.
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: Konstantin Batyushkov
poets.credit: Portrait of Konstantin Batyushkov by an unknown artist (1810s) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Konstantin Nikolayevich Batyushkov (1787–1855), born in Vologda, served as an officer in the Napoleonic wars and was wounded in 1807 and 1813–14. His smooth, sensuous elegies and epistles, drawing on Italian and French models, were a strong influence on the young Pushkin. From about 1821 he suffered from mental illness and wrote nothing more; he died in Vologda in 1855.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Bernard Barton
bio: Bernard Barton (1784–1849) was known as the Quaker poet.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Archibald Crawford
bio: Archibald Crawford (1785–1843) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: John Wilson
bio: John Wilson (1785–1854) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Andrews Norton
poets.credit: Portrait: Christopher Pearse Cranch — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Andrews Norton (1786–1853) was a Unitarian theologian and biblical scholar at Harvard, born in Hingham, Massachusetts.
Griswold included 15 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: John Younger
bio: John Younger (born 1785; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Thomas Love Peacock
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Love Peacock by Henry Wallis (1858) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Love Peacock (1785–1866) was an English novelist and poet, a close friend of Percy Bysshe Shelley and, for most of his working life, an official of the East India Company. He is best known for his conversational satirical novels, among them Headlong Hall (1816), Nightmare Abbey (1818) and The Misfortunes of Elphin (1829).

His verse is mostly scattered through those novels as songs. "The War-Song of Dinas Vawr", sung by the Welsh warriors of The Misfortunes of Elphin, is the most often reprinted; the editor of this anthology also prints two Welsh-legend ballads, "The Cauldron of Ceridwen" and "Llyn-y-Dreiddiad-Vrawd".

poets.name: David Vedder
bio: David Vedder (1790–1854) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 7 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: John Mitchell
bio: John Mitchell (1786–1856) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 4 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Gulian Crommelin Verplanck
bio: Gulian Crommelin Verplanck (1786–1870) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Prophecy”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Caroline Bowles Southey
bio: Caroline Anne Bowles (1786–1854) was born at Buckland, near Lymington in Hampshire, and became known as a poet and prose writer. She corresponded with Robert Southey for many years and married him in 1839.
She is a different writer from her husband; her poem "To Death" appears in The Oxford Book of English Verse.

poets.name: Samuel Beazley
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Samuel Beazley (1786–1851) was an English architect and playwright. He designed several London theatres, including the St James's Theatre, and wrote a long run of farces, operettas and melodramas for the stage.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Justinus Kerner
poets.credit: Portrait: Friedrich Brandseph — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Justinus Kerner was a physician and poet of the Swabian school who lived at Weinsberg in Württemberg. He is also known for his account of the clairvoyant Friederike Hauffe, The Seeress of Prevorst (1829).
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: William Johnson Fox
bio: William Johnson Fox (1786–1864), born in Suffolk, was a Unitarian preacher, journalist and reforming politician. He was a radical minister at Chichester and later at Finsbury Chapel in London, wrote for the periodicals, and was a noted orator in the cause of reform.
A memorial edition of his works appeared in twelve volumes in 1868. The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s A Victorian Anthology, 1837–1895 (1895).

poets.name: Alexander Laing
bio: Alexander Laing (born 1787; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 8 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Richard Henry Dana
bio: Richard Henry Dana (1787–1879) was a Boston poet, critic and lawyer, a founder of the North American Review and the author of The Buccaneer (1827). He was the father of the author of Two Years Before the Mast.
Griswold included 6 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Sarah Josepha Hale
bio: Sarah Josepha Hale (1788–1879) was an American writer and editor, born in New Hampshire. As editor of Godey's Lady's Book for four decades she was among the most influential figures in American letters, and she campaigned for a national Thanksgiving holiday.
Her verse includes Poems for Our Children (1830), which contains Mary's Lamb.

poets.name: David Webster
bio: David Webster (1787–1837) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Bryan Waller Procter (Barry Cornwall)
poets.credit: Bryan Waller Procter ("Barry Cornwall") by William Brockedon (c. 1830) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Bryan Waller Procter (1787–1874), who wrote as "Barry Cornwall", was an English poet and lawyer, a friend of Charles Lamb and Leigh Hunt and the father of the poet Adelaide Anne Procter. He is best remembered for his songs, collected in English Songs and Other Small Poems (1832).
The songs given here are taken from Edmund H. Garrett's anthology Victorian Songs: Lyrics of the Affections and Nature (Boston: Little, Brown, 1895).

poets.name: Joseph Hutton
bio: Joseph Hutton (1787–1828) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “The Tomb of the Brave”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Emma Hart Willard
bio: Emma Hart Willard (1787–1870) was an American educator who founded the Troy Female Seminary in New York. She is remembered as a verse-writer chiefly for "Rocked in the Cradle of the Deep", set to music by Joseph P. Knight.

poets.name: Lavinia Stoddard
bio: Lavinia Stoddard (born Lavinia Stone, 1787–1820) was an American poet, born at Guilford, Connecticut, who conducted an academy at Troy, New York, with her husband, Dr. William Stoddard. Her best-known poem is "The Soul's Defiance".

poets.name: Ludwig Uhland
poets.credit: Portrait: Gottlob Wilhelm Morff — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ludwig Uhland was born at Tübingen and trained as a lawyer. A leading poet of the Swabian school, he is best known for his ballads and songs, and he was also a scholar of medieval German and French literature.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Lord Byron
poets.credit: Portrait by Thomas Phillips (1813) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Lord Byron (George Gordon Byron, 1788–1824) was an English Romantic poet and satirist, one of the most celebrated — and scandalous — figures of his age.
He died at Missolonghi while supporting the Greek war of independence, and gave his name to the brooding ‘Byronic hero.’

poets.name: Károly Kisfaludy
poets.credit: Wood engraving of Károly Kisfaludy by Gusztáv Morelli, from Az Osztrák-Magyar Monarchia írásban és képben (1887–1901) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Hungarian dramatist, poet and painter, brother of Sándor Kisfaludy, and a founder of the national drama.
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: László Ungvárnémeti Tóth
bio: Hungarian poet of the early nineteenth century.
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: Milota Zdirad Polák
poets.credit: No portrait in the public domain was found.
bio: Milota Zdirad Polák (1788–1856) was a Czech poet and soldier. Bowring calls him M. Z. Polak and says he served in the army, was adjutant to Baron Koller, and twice went with the Austrian troops to Italy.

His best-known work is the didactic poem Vznešenost přírody (Sublimities of Nature). Bowring translates three songs of parting and longing, two of them a dialogue between the lovers Kráska and Květoslav.

poets.name: Richard Henry Wilde
poets.credit: Portrait of Richard Henry Wilde · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Henry Wilde (1789–1847) was an American lawyer, congressman and poet, born in Dublin, Ireland, and raised in Augusta, Georgia. He represented Georgia in Congress and later settled in New Orleans, where he died of yellow fever.
His short lyric “My Life is Like the Summer Rose”, sometimes called “The Lament of the Captive”, became one of the most widely reprinted American poems of its day.

poets.name: James A. Hillhouse
bio: James A. Hillhouse (1789–1841) was a Connecticut poet of New Haven, author of the dramatic poem Hadad (1825) and the poem The Judgment.
Griswold included 1 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: William Midford
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Midford is represented here by verse printed in The Newcastle Song Book; or, Tyne-side Songster (Newcastle: W. & T. Fordyce, 1842), 16 pieces.
A writer of Tyneside songs in the local dialect; the spelling of the printed texts is kept as the books give it.

poets.name: John M. Harney
bio: John M. Harney (1789–1825) was a physician and poet, born in Sussex County, Delaware, who lived in Kentucky and Louisiana. He is the author of Crystalina (1816).
Griswold included 4 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Sir Aubrey de Vere
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir Aubrey de Vere (1788–1846), born at Curragh Chase, County Limerick, was a poet and friend of Wordsworth, whose example strongly influenced him. He was the father of the poet Aubrey Thomas de Vere.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Hannah Flagg Gould
bio: Hannah Flagg Gould (1789–1865) was born in Lancaster, Vermont, and lived most of her life in Newburyport, Massachusetts. She was a popular American writer of light and children's verse, as well as of occasional, sacred and memorial poems, and her work appeared in periodicals and in several volumes of poetry for children and adults.

The poems here come from two of her books: The Mother's Dream, and Other Poems (Boston: Crosby, Nichols, 1853) and The Youth's Coronal (1851), a gift book of verse for young readers. Poems that appear in both books are given once, in their 1853 text.

poets.name: George Jehoshaphat Mountain
bio: George Jehoshaphat Mountain (1789–1863), born in England, was the Anglican Bishop of Quebec from 1836 until his death.
He published a small volume of verse, Songs of the Wilderness (1846). One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: James Fenimore Cooper
bio: James Fenimore Cooper (1789–1851) was the American novelist of The Last of the Mohicans and The Pilot. The few songs scattered through his novels are usually put in the mouths of his characters; "My Brigantine" appears in The Water-Witch (1830).

poets.name: Fitz-Greene Halleck
poets.credit: Photograph of Fitz-Greene Halleck, Brady-Handy Photograph Collection (Library of Congress) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Fitz-Greene Halleck (1790–1867) was an American poet, born at Guilford, Connecticut. He worked as a clerk and later as a business agent for John Jacob Astor in New York, and wrote satirical verse with Joseph Rodman Drake as the “Croakers”.
His elegy on Drake, “Green be the turf above thee”, and the ballad “Marco Bozzaris” were among the most admired American poems of the early nineteenth century.

poets.name: Alexander H. Everett
bio: Alexander Hill Everett (1790–1847) was a Boston diplomat, editor and writer, the brother of Edward Everett, who published a volume of Poems in 1845.
Griswold included 2 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Ferenc Kölcsey
bio: Hungarian poet, critic, orator and politician, author of the words of the Hungarian national anthem.
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: Richard Harris Barham (‘Thomas Ingoldsby’)
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of Richard Harris Barham, frontispiece to The Ingoldsby Legends · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Harris Barham (1788–1845) was born in Canterbury and became a clergyman of the Church of England; he was a minor canon and later a priest in ordinary of the Chapel Royal, and from 1824 a minor canon of St Paul’s Cathedral in London, where he also held a parish living. He wrote under the name ‘Thomas Ingoldsby’.

His comic and macabre verse legends first appeared in Bentley’s Miscellany from 1837 and were collected as The Ingoldsby Legends in three series (1840, 1842 and 1847). Mixing medieval saints, ghosts, devils and Kentish folklore with rattling, outrageous rhymes and puns, they included ‘The Jackdaw of Rheims’, and were hugely popular through the Victorian age.

poets.name: Alexander Carlile
bio: Alexander Carlile (born 1788; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William Park
bio: William Park (1788–1843) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William Glen
bio: William Glen (1789–1826) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 9 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

bio: Alexander Jamieson (1789–1826) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.
