bio: William Knox (1789–1825) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Thomas Pringle
poets.credit: Portrait: William Finden — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Pringle (1789–1834) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).

This archive holds 5 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling, and 23 poems printed under his name in The Poetry of South Africa, collected and arranged by A. Wilmot (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle & Rivington; Cape Town: J. C. Juta & Co., 1887), in Wilmot's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir.

poets.name: William Thom
bio: William Thom (1789–1848) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 5 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Friedrich Rückert
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Friedrich Rückert was born at Schweinfurt and was both an orientalist and a poet. He made German versions of Persian, Arabic and Sanskrit poetry and wrote a large body of lyric verse of his own.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Joseph von Eichendorff
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Joseph von Eichendorff was born at Lubowitz in Silesia and became one of the best loved poets of German Romanticism. His songs of woods, wandering and longing were set by many composers, and he also wrote the tale Aus dem Leben eines Taugenichts.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Lydia Huntley Sigourney
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of Lydia Sigourney, 19th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Lydia Huntley Sigourney (1791-1865) was born in Norwich, Connecticut, and lived most of her life in Hartford. She was among the best-known American poets of her day, nicknamed the "Sweet Singer of Hartford", and published some fifty books of verse and prose as well as many contributions to periodicals.

The poems here are the "In Memoriam" section of The Man of Uz, and Other Poems (Hartford, 1862), a sequence of elegies on neighbours, clergymen, children and public figures of Hartford and beyond who died between 1859 and 1862, a form of memorial verse for which she was especially known.

poets.name: Charles Wolfe
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Charles Wolfe was an Irish clergyman and poet who died young. He is remembered for one poem.
Palgrave includes it: "The Burial of Sir John Moore at Corunna".

poets.name: Josiah Conder
poets.credit: Portrait: Benjamin Haydon — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Josiah Conder (1789–1855) was a British writer, editor and hymn-writer.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Charlotte Elliott
bio: Charlotte Elliott (1789–1871) was an English evangelical Anglican poet, hymn-writer and editor, best known for the hymn “Just as I Am”.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Friedrich August von Heyden
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Friedrich August von Heyden was a Silesian poet and writer, best remembered for his epic Reginald.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Zauq
bio: Zauq is called in the book a celebrated poet at the court of Bahadur Shah (r. 1837–57) and his teacher in the arts of verse, compiler of an anthology of poems, said to have written one hundred thousand verses and still highly popular and much quoted.

The one piece given here is drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. It is a free rendering, not a literal translation, and the original Urdu poem is untitled; it is named here by its first line.

poets.name: John Howard Payne
bio: John Howard Payne (1791–1852) was a New York-born actor and dramatist, best known as the author of the song Home, Sweet Home, and later United States consul at Tunis.
Griswold included 1 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Samuel Gilman
bio: Samuel Gilman (1791–1858) was a Unitarian minister in Charleston, South Carolina, born in Gloucester, Massachusetts, and the author of the Harvard song Fair Harvard.
Griswold included 1 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Charles Sprague
poets.credit: Portrait: Southworth & Hawes — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Sprague (1791–1875) was a Boston banker and poet, born in Boston, known for his Shakspeare Ode (1823) and the poem Curiosity.
Griswold included 13 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Margaret Mercer
bio: Margaret Mercer (1791–1846), born at Annapolis, Maryland, was the daughter of John Mercer, governor of Maryland. She wrote religious verse and spent most of her life teaching school.

poets.name: Václav Hanka
poets.credit: Portrait of Václav Hanka (1821) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Václav Hanka (1791–1861) was a Czech philologist, librarian and poet of the Czech National Revival; Bowring writes his name Waslaw Hanka and notes his appointment as librarian of the National Museum at Prague in 1818. He is also remembered as the forger of the Králové Dvůr manuscript.

The four songs here are given by Bowring as Hanka's own; he says two of them come from the collection Dvanáctero písní (1816). They are love songs in a folk manner; nothing from the forged manuscripts is included.

poets.name: George Petrie
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: George Petrie (1790–1866), born in Dublin, was an antiquary and artist who devoted his life to collecting and preserving the art, music and literature of Ireland.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Charlotte Elizabeth Tonna
bio: Charlotte Elizabeth Tonna (1790–1846), who wrote under the name "Charlotte Elizabeth", was an English evangelical author born in Norwich. She lived for some years in Ireland, edited the Christian Lady's Magazine and later the Protestant Magazine, and wrote many tracts, novels and social studies.
"The Maiden City", her ballad in praise of the defence of Londonderry in 1689, was widely sung in Ulster and was included in R. Brimley Johnson's 1894 anthology.

poets.name: Joseph Christian von Zedlitz
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Joseph Christian von Zedlitz was an Austrian poet and dramatist of Silesian birth. His ballad Die nächtliche Heerschau, on the ghost of Napoleon's army, was widely known.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Robert Hendry, M.D.
bio: Robert Hendry, M.D. (born 1791; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: James Edmeston
bio: James Edmeston, architect, was born at Wapping, London, in 1791, and became a well-known writer of hymns.
He published his first volume of poems in 1817 and a select collection in 1847. He died at Homerton in 1867.

poets.name: Theodor Körner
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Theodor Körner was born at Dresden. A poet and dramatist, he joined the Lützow Free Corps in 1813 and was killed in action that August; his war songs, collected as Leyer und Schwert, made him a hero of the wars of liberation.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Henry Hart Milman
bio: Henry Hart Milman (1791–1868), born in London, was a clergyman, historian and poet. He was Professor of Poetry at Oxford, wrote the dramatic poem The Fall of Jerusalem, and became Dean of St Paul’s in 1849.
His hymns are still sung. The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s A Victorian Anthology, 1837–1895 (1895).

poets.name: Percy Bysshe Shelley
poets.credit: Portrait by Alfred Clint · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Percy Bysshe Shelley (1792–1822) was an English Romantic poet, radical in politics and idealist in temper.
Author of ‘Ozymandias’ and ‘Ode to the West Wind,’ he drowned off the Italian coast before his thirtieth birthday.

poets.name: Seba Smith
bio: Seba Smith (1792–1868) was a Maine journalist and humorist, born in Buckfield, a graduate of Bowdoin College and the creator of Major Jack Downing.
Griswold included 2 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Augustus Lucas Hillhouse
bio: Augustus Lucas Hillhouse (1792–1859) was an American poet and hymn-writer, born in New Haven, Connecticut, and the brother of the poet James Abraham Hillhouse.
He is represented in Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900) by a short hymn on the joy of forgiveness.

poets.name: Pyotr Vyazemsky
bio: Prince Pyotr Andreyevich Vyazemsky (1792–1878) was a poet, critic and wit, a friend of Pushkin and a prominent member of the Arzamas circle. Bowring, who spells the name “Væsemsky”, prints three of his poems in the second part.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Mikhail Milonov
bio: Mikhail Vasilyevich Milonov (1792–1821) was a Russian poet who wrote satires and elegies and died young. Bowring prints his poem “The Fall of the Leaf” in the second part.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: John Keble
poets.credit: Portrait of John Keble by Miss Donkin (19th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Keble (1792–1866) was an English Anglican priest and poet, born in Fairford, Gloucestershire. He took a double first at Oxford, became a fellow of Oriel College, and served as Oxford's Professor of Poetry from 1831 to 1841. He spent most of his working life as a country parish priest at Hursley in Hampshire.

His Assize Sermon on National Apostasy (1833) is traditionally taken as the starting point of the Oxford Movement. His best-known book of verse, The Christian Year (1827), gives a poem to each Sunday and holy day of the Book of Common Prayer and was among the most widely read volumes of the nineteenth century. Keble College, Oxford, was founded in his memory.

poets.name: John D'Alton
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John D'Alton (1792–1867) was an historian, translator and antiquarian, born in Westmeath and long resident in Dublin. He wrote many works on the history and archaeology of Ireland.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Jefferys Taylor
bio: Jefferys Taylor (1792–1853) was an English author of books for children, and a member of the Taylor family of Ongar; his sisters Ann and Jane Taylor were the authors of Original Poems for Infant Minds and Rhymes for the Nursery.
His Aesop in Rhyme, with Some Originals (1820) retells Aesop's fables in light verse. He also wrote prose works for young readers, among them The Young Islanders and The Farm.

poets.name: John Castillo
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Castillo (1792–1845) was born near Dublin of Roman Catholic parents and brought up at Lealholm Bridge in the Cleveland country, where he learnt the trade of a journeyman stone-mason. In 1818 he joined the Wesleyan Methodist Society and became a popular local preacher in the North Riding.

His best-known poem, Awd Isaac, was first printed at Northallerton in 1831 and gave its name to a volume published at Whitby in 1843. He died at Pickering. The poem here is taken from Moorman's Yorkshire Dialect Poems (1916).

poets.name: William Howitt
bio: William Howitt (1792–1879) was an English writer, born at Heanor in Derbyshire and brought up a Quaker. He wrote widely on country life, travel and history, and with his wife Mary Howitt produced many volumes of verse and prose.
His best-known poem is “The Departure of the Swallow”, a short lyric that Stedman placed among the English song writers in A Victorian Anthology (1895).

poets.name: Nathaniel L. Frothingham
bio: Nathaniel L. Frothingham (1793–1870) was a Unitarian minister of the First Church in Boston, born in Boston and a graduate of Harvard.
Griswold included 2 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Henry Rowe Schoolcraft
bio: Henry Rowe Schoolcraft (1793–1864) was an American ethnologist and Indian agent, born near Albany, New York, who wrote widely on the Ojibwe and other Native peoples.
Griswold included 4 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: John Neal
poets.credit: Portrait: Unknown photographer — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Neal (1793–1876) was a Portland, Maine, novelist, critic and poet, and an early champion of an American literature.
Griswold included 9 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Samuel G. Goodrich
bio: Samuel Griswold Goodrich (1793–1860) was a Connecticut-born publisher and author, better known under the pen name Peter Parley.
Griswold included 5 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Hew Ainslie
bio: Hew Ainslie (born 1792; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 7 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William Finlay
bio: William Finlay (1792–1847) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Thomas Lyle
bio: Thomas Lyle (dates not given by Rogers) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: John Nevay
bio: John Nevay (born 1792; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Peter Roger
bio: Peter Roger (1792–1856) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: John Clare
poets.credit: Portrait: William Hilton — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Clare (1793–1864) was an English labouring-class poet, the son of a Northamptonshire farm labourer, whose closely observed poems of birds, insects and the vanishing open fields of his native Helpston mark him as one of the great nature poets in the language.

His early success gave way to poverty and the destruction of the rural world he wrote from, as the enclosure acts fenced in the commons he had grown up roaming. He spent the last decades of his life in asylums, where he continued to write some of his most haunting poems, including "I Am."

poets.name: Sir John Bowring
bio: Sir John Bowring (1792–1872) was a British political economist, traveller, writer, translator and hymn-writer.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Maria Gowen Brooks
bio: Maria Gowen Brooks (c. 1794–1845), who wrote as “Maria del Occidente”, was an American poet born at Medford, Massachusetts. She published Judith, Esther, and Other Poems in 1820, lived for some years in Cuba, and finished her long narrative poem Zophiël, or the Bride of Seven, in England with the encouragement of Robert Southey.
The poem here is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin, 1900).

poets.name: Carlos Wilcox
bio: Carlos Wilcox (1794–1827) was a Congregational minister and poet, born in Newport, New Hampshire. His poems were collected posthumously in 1828.
Griswold included 10 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Henry Ware, Jr.
bio: Henry Ware Jr. (1794–1843) was a Unitarian minister in Boston and professor at Harvard Divinity School, born in Hingham, Massachusetts.
Griswold included 3 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: William B. Tappan
bio: William B. Tappan (1794–1849) was a religious poet, born in Beverly, Massachusetts, who worked for the American Sunday School Union.
Griswold included 4 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Edward Everett
bio: Edward Everett (1794–1865) was an orator, scholar and statesman, born in Dorchester, Massachusetts: professor of Greek at Harvard, governor of Massachusetts and United States Secretary of State.
Griswold included 2 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Jan Kollár
poets.credit: Portrait of Ján Kollár (19th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Jan Kollár (Ján Kollár, 1793–1852) was a Slovak poet who wrote in Czech, a Protestant minister and a leading voice of Slavic literary solidarity. Bowring calls him John Kollár and describes him as a Bohemian minister at Pesth, in Hungary.

His sonnet cycle Slávy dcera (The Daughter of Sláva) joins love for his Mína to grief and hope for the Slavic peoples. Bowring translated a large selection, keeping the sonnet form; the numbered sonnets here keep Kollár's numbering, and seven further sonnets Bowring received in manuscript are unnumbered.

poets.name: Felicia Hemans
poets.credit: Portrait of Felicia Hemans by William Edward West (before 1835) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Felicia Hemans (1793–1835), born Felicia Dorothea Browne in Liverpool and raised largely in Wales, published her first volume of poems at fourteen and became one of the most widely read poets of her day, in Britain and in America.

After her husband left for Italy in 1818 she brought up her five sons alone and supported them by her writing. Her best-known collections include Records of Woman (1828) and Songs of the Affections (1830), and poems such as “Casabianca” and “The Homes of England” were learned by heart by generations of schoolchildren. She died in Dublin at forty-one.

poets.name: Henry Francis Lyte
poets.credit: Portrait of Henry Francis Lyte · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Francis Lyte (1793–1847) was a British Anglican clergyman, hymn-writer and poet, the author of “Abide with Me”.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: William Maginn
bio: William Maginn was born in Cork in 1793, entered Trinity College, Dublin, as a boy of ten, and took his LL.D. at twenty-three.
He wrote for Blackwood’s and was connected with Fraser’s Magazine; he was a prolific humorist and ballad writer, and the author of a series of Homeric Ballads. He died at Walton-on-Thames in 1842.

poets.name: John Gibson Lockhart
bio: John Gibson Lockhart (1794–1854) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Robert Emery
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Robert Emery is represented here by verse printed in The Newcastle Song Book; or, Tyne-side Songster (Newcastle: W. & T. Fordyce, 1842), 19 pieces.
A writer of Tyneside songs in the local dialect; the spelling of the printed texts is kept as the books give it.

poets.name: Thomas Mathers
bio: Thomas Mathers (1794–1851) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Alajos Szentmiklóssy
bio: Hungarian writer, lawyer and poet.
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: Thomas Furlong
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Furlong (1794–1827), born near Ferns, County Wexford, was a poet and a friend and supporter of Daniel O'Connell. He is now remembered chiefly as a translator of Irish poems into English verse.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: William Carleton
poets.credit: Portrait of William Carleton by John Slattery · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Carleton (1794–1869) was an Irish novelist and short-story writer, born into a Catholic farming family in County Tyrone. He became famous for Traits and Stories of the Irish Peasantry (1830–33), which drew on his own rural upbringing, and for later novels such as Fardorougha the Miser (1839).
"Sir Turlough; or, The Churchyard Bride" is among his few poems; its refrain names Killeevy, in County Armagh.

poets.name: John Hamilton Reynolds
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Hamilton Reynolds (1794–1852) was an English poet and lawyer, a close friend of John Keats and a brother-in-law of Thomas Hood, with whom he wrote Odes and Addresses to Great People (1825).

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Anna Brownell Jameson
bio: Anna Brownell Jameson was born in Dublin in 1794, the eldest daughter of the miniature-painter D. Brownell Murphy. She became a governess at sixteen and in 1825 married Robert Jameson.
She is best known as a writer on art, notably Sacred and Legendary Art. She died at Ealing in 1860.

poets.name: John Keats
poets.credit: Portrait by William Hilton (c. 1822) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Keats (1795–1821) was an English Romantic poet whose odes are among the most celebrated in the language.
He trained as a surgeon before devoting himself to poetry, and died of tuberculosis in Rome at just twenty-five.

poets.name: James Gates Percival
poets.credit: Portrait: Percival (first name unknown) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James Gates Percival (1795–1856) was a Connecticut poet, physician and geologist, born in Berlin, Connecticut, and a graduate of Yale.
Griswold included 23 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Sidney Walker
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sidney Walker (1795–1846) was an English critic and scholar, remembered for his textual studies of Shakespeare's verse. He also wrote occasional verse.

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Pavel Josef Šafařík
poets.credit: Portrait of Pavel Jozef Šafárik (19th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Pavel Josef Šafařík (Pavel Jozef Šafárik, 1795–1861) was a Slovak-born poet, philologist and literary historian who wrote in Czech. Bowring calls him Paul Joseph Šafarík, professor at the gymnasium of Neusatz, and praises his history of the Slavonic language and literature.
Bowring translates two of his poems: the long ballad of Prince Oldřich and the peasant girl Božena, and a lyric, Jarmila to Slawislaw.

poets.name: Isaac Clason
bio: Isaac Clason (c. 1796–1830) was a New York poet and graduate of Columbia College (1813) who wrote the Seventeenth and Eighteenth Cantos of Don Juan (1825) as a continuation of Byron's poem.
Griswold included 4 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: John G. C. Brainard
poets.credit: Portrait: Described as "From an unfinished pencil sketch by Wentworth" — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John G. C. Brainard (1796–1828) was a Connecticut poet and newspaper editor, whose Occasional Pieces of Poetry appeared in 1825.
Griswold included 18 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: William B. Walter
bio: William B. Walter (c. 1796–1823) was a young American poet of a New England clerical family, a descendant of Nehemiah Walter and Increase Mather.
Griswold included 2 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: George Hill
bio: George Hill (1796–1871) was a poet and diplomat, a native of Guilford, Connecticut, and a Yale graduate, who served as a professor of mathematics in the United States Navy. His poem The Ruins of Athens appeared in 1839.
Griswold included 8 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: William Augustus Muhlenberg
bio: William Augustus Muhlenberg (1796–1877) was an American Episcopal clergyman, educator and hymn-writer, born in Philadelphia.
He founded St. Luke's Hospital in New York, and is best remembered for the hymn 'I would not live alway'.

poets.name: Jeremiah Joseph Callanan
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Jeremiah Joseph Callanan was born in Cork and studied at Maynooth and Trinity College Dublin. He worked as a tutor, made English versions of Irish songs, and died in Lisbon in 1829.
Yeats credited his translations from the Irish with first giving English-speaking Ireland an honest style. Yeats's anthology misprints his death year as 1839.

poets.name: Walter Colton
bio: Walter Colton (1797–1851) was a clergyman and navy chaplain, born in Rutland County, Vermont, and a graduate of Yale. He later served as alcalde of Monterey, California.
Griswold included 2 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Mirabeau Bonaparte Lamar
bio: Mirabeau Bonaparte Lamar (1798–1859) was born in Georgia and became the second President of the Republic of Texas. He also wrote verse, collected as Verse Memorials (1857).
He is represented in Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900) by a serenade, “The Daughter of Mendoza.”

poets.name: James Wallis Eastburn
bio: James Wallis Eastburn (1797–1819) was a New York clergyman and poet, the collaborator of Robert C. Sands on the Indian poem Yamoyden (1820).
Griswold included 2 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: George Darley
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: George Darley was born in Dublin and spent most of his working life in London, where he was a poet, mathematician and art and drama critic for The Athenaeum. His works include Sylvia; or, The May Queen (1827) and Nepenthe (1835).
He suffered from a severe stammer and wrote little for a wide audience in his lifetime.

poets.name: Heinrich Heine
poets.credit: Portrait of Heinrich Heine by Moritz Daniel Oppenheim (1831) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Heinrich Heine (1797–1856) was born in Düsseldorf to a Jewish family and studied law at Bonn, Berlin and Göttingen, taking his degree in 1825 after converting to Protestant Christianity. His Book of Songs (Buch der Lieder, 1827), with its plain, musical lyrics of love and disappointment, made him one of the most widely read German poets, and many of its poems were set to music by Schumann, Schubert and Mendelssohn.

In 1831 Heine moved to Paris, where he lived for the rest of his life, writing travel pieces, criticism and satirical verse, among them Germany: A Winter's Tale and Atta Troll. His work was banned in several German states. From the mid-1840s he suffered from a progressive paralysis and spent his last years confined to what he called his mattress-grave, producing the Romancero (1851) and the late poems. The translations here are by Edgar Alfred Bowring (1908 edition of the complete poems, in the original metres).

poets.name: Janet Hamilton
bio: Janet Hamilton (1795–1873) was a self-taught Scottish working-class poet who lived at Langloan, near Coatbridge, in the industrial west of Scotland. She learned to write late and lost her sight in her later years.

Her verse, in Scots and English, appeared in volumes from the 1860s such as Poems and Essays and Poems and Ballads; “A Ballad of Memorie”, in Scots, is the piece chosen for Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Thomas Carlyle
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Carlyle (1795–1881) was a Scottish essayist, historian and philosopher, known as the "sage of Chelsea". He is remembered above all for his prose; verse was a small part of his output.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: John Malcolm
bio: John Malcolm (c. 1795–1835) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: František Turinský
poets.credit: No portrait in the public domain was found.
bio: František Turinský (1797–1852) was a Czech poet and playwright. Bowring writes his name Fr. Turínsky, gives his birth year as 1796, and says he was a lawyer in Moravia; his best-known work was the tragedy Angelina.
Bowring includes one short ballad by him, The Maiden by the Stream, and closes the anthology with it.

poets.name: Alexander M'Lachlan
bio: Alexander M'Lachlan (dates not given by Rogers) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Hartley Coleridge
poets.credit: Portrait of Hartley Coleridge, engraving by Day & Son (c. 1850) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Hartley Coleridge was an English poet and essayist, the eldest son of Samuel Taylor Coleridge. He spent much of his life in the Lake District, writing sonnets and short lyrics.
Palgrave includes one of his lyrics, "She is not fair to outward view".

poets.name: Giacomo Leopardi
poets.credit: Portrait of Giacomo Leopardi by A. Ferrazzi (c. 1820) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Giacomo Leopardi (1798–1837) was born in Recanati, in the Papal States, and educated in his father's great library, where he mastered the classical languages and ruined his health by study. He is regarded as the greatest Italian lyric poet of the nineteenth century, and a profound pessimist whose thought is also preserved in his prose Operette morali and the Zibaldone.

His Canti move from patriotic odes on Italy's fallen glory to the brief, intense idylls such as “The Infinite” and “To Silvia”, and finally to the late, stoic “The Genista”. He died in Naples in 1837, aged thirty-eight. The selection here is Francis Henry Cliffe's English verse translation of 1893.

poets.name: Adam Mickiewicz
poets.credit: Daguerreotype of Adam Mickiewicz, Paris, 1842 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Adam Mickiewicz (1798–1855) was born near Nowogródek in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, then under Russian rule, and studied at the University of Wilno, where he joined secret student societies. In 1823 he was arrested for this activity and in 1824 exiled to Russia, where he lived in Odessa, Crimea and Moscow and became friends with Russian writers including Pushkin. In 1829 he left Russia and never returned to his homeland.

He settled in Paris after the failed uprising of 1830–31 and lectured on Slavic literature at the Collège de France. Regarded as the national poet of Poland, he is the author of the drama Dziady (Forefathers' Eve) and the epic Pan Tadeusz (1834), which recalls the Lithuanian countryside of his childhood. He died in Constantinople in 1855. The work here is George Rapall Noyes's English prose translation of 1917.

poets.name: Alexander Pushkin
poets.credit: Portrait of Alexander Pushkin by Orest Kiprensky (1827) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alexander Sergeyevich Pushkin (1799–1837) was born in Moscow into an old noble family and educated at the Tsarskoye Selo Lyceum. His early verse brought him fame, and his liberal poems led the authorities to send him into exile in southern Russia in 1820 and then to his family estate at Mikhailovskoye. He is widely regarded as the founder of modern Russian literature and its literary language.

Besides the verse novel Eugene Onegin, the drama Boris Godunov and the narrative poem The Bronze Horseman, he wrote many short lyrics, ballads and tales in verse. He died in St Petersburg in 1837 of a wound received in a duel. The versions here are by Ivan Panin (1888), who aimed at literal, line-for-line renderings, unrhymed, rather than at the music of the originals.

poets.name: Robert C. Sands
bio: Robert C. Sands (1799–1832) was a New York lawyer, journalist and poet, co-author of Yamoyden and an editor of the Atlantic Magazine.
Griswold included 13 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: William B. O. Peabody
bio: William B. O. Peabody (1799–1847) was a Unitarian minister of Springfield, Massachusetts, born in Exeter, New Hampshire, and a graduate of Harvard.
Griswold included 4 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Grenville Mellen
bio: Grenville Mellen (1799–1841) was a lawyer and poet, born in Biddeford, Maine, the son of Chief Justice Prentiss Mellen.
Griswold included 5 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: George W. Doane
bio: George W. Doane (1799–1859) was an Episcopal clergyman, bishop of New Jersey from 1832, and the author of Songs by the Way (1824).
Griswold included 10 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Mary Howitt
poets.credit: Picture of Mary Howitt, artist unknown (no later than 1889) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mary Howitt (née Botham, 1799–1888) was an English poet and writer, born at Coleford in Gloucestershire and brought up in a Quaker family in Staffordshire. Married to the writer William Howitt, she was widely read for her ballads and for verse written for children, above all “The Spider and the Fly”, and she later translated Hans Christian Andersen and Fredrika Bremer into English.

The poems here are taken from the Philadelphia edition of 1844, which gathers her hymns and fireside verses, poems of birds, flowers and country things, sketches of natural history, tales in verse and miscellaneous pieces. The memoir, the dramatic pieces The Poor Scholar and The Sorrow of Teresa, and a dramatic sketch for a parrot are not included.

poets.name: John Banim
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Banim was born in Kilkenny and became a novelist, dramatist and poet. With his brother Michael he wrote the O'Hara Tales, a series of stories of Irish life.
His song "Soggarth Aroon" ("Priest, dear") is included in W. B. Yeats's A Book of Irish Verse (1900).

poets.name: James Brown
bio: James Brown (1796–1836) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 4 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Thomas Haynes Bayly
poets.credit: Thomas Haynes Bayly, portrait by an unknown artist, before 1840 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Haynes Bayly (1797–1839) was an English songwriter and dramatist, born at Bath. His sentimental ballads, among them "I'd be a butterfly" and "Oh! no, we never mention her", were widely sung in the 1820s and 1830s.

The 2 poems here are the pieces printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: J. C. Denovan
bio: J. C. Denovan (1798–1827) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Robert Gilchrist
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Robert Gilchrist is represented here by verse printed in The Newcastle Song Book; or, Tyne-side Songster (Newcastle: W. & T. Fordyce, 1842), 17 pieces.
A writer of Tyneside songs in the local dialect; the spelling of the printed texts is kept as the books give it.

poets.name: Robert Fraser
bio: Robert Fraser (1798–1839) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Robert Gilfillan
bio: Robert Gilfillan (1798–1850) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 6 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: George Bancroft
bio: George Bancroft (1800–1891) was a historian and statesman, author of the History of the United States, who published a volume of poems in 1823.
Griswold included 4 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: John Goldie
bio: John Goldie (1798–1826) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: George Moses Horton
bio: George Moses Horton was born into slavery in North Carolina around 1798 and spent most of his life on the farm of his owner in Chatham County. Unable at first to write, he composed verses in his head and, on Sundays, walked to Chapel Hill, where students of the University of North Carolina paid him to compose love poems for them.

His first book, The Hope of Liberty (1829), is generally recognised as the first book of poetry by a Black author published in the South. Its poems were reissued in Philadelphia in 1837 as Poems by a Slave, the edition from which these pieces are taken. He remained enslaved until 1865, when Union forces arrived in North Carolina and he gained his freedom.

poets.name: James Hislop
bio: James Hislop (1798–1827) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: David Macbeth Moir
poets.credit: Portrait of David Macbeth Moir · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: David Macbeth Moir (1798–1851) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Robert Pollok
bio: Robert Pollok (1798–1827) was a Scottish poet, a divinity student of the Secession Church. His blank-verse epic The Course of Time (1827), a vision of human history to the Last Judgement, went through many editions; it was published by Blackwood of Edinburgh only months before his early death from consumption.

Charles Rogers also included one song under his name, 'The African Maid', in volume 4 of The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57); it is kept here in Rogers's spelling, and is not part of The Course of Time.

poets.name: Richard Robert Madden
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Richard Robert Madden (1798–1886), born in Dublin, was a surgeon, colonial official and prolific author, best known for his lives and history of the United Irishmen.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Henry Scott Riddell
bio: Henry Scott Riddell (born 1798; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 20 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Alexander Smart
bio: Alexander Smart (born 1798; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Thomas Hood
poets.credit: Unknown artist, National Portrait Gallery, London · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Hood (1799–1845) was an English poet and humorist, famous in his own lifetime chiefly for comic verse and outrageous puns, but remembered today at least as much for a handful of serious social poems — above all ‘The Song of the Shirt’ and ‘The Bridge of Sighs’ — written from genuine anger at the suffering of the poor.

Chronically ill for most of his adult life, he supported a family through unrelenting magazine work, editing and writing comic annuals even as his health failed; he died at forty-five, not long after a government pension was finally arranged for him.

poets.name: Erskine Conolly
bio: Erskine Conolly (1796–1843) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: John Imlah
bio: John Imlah (1799–1846) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 9 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Thomas Noel
bio: Thomas Noel (1799–1861) was an English poet, born at Kirby Mallory, Leicestershire, who died at Brighton. His verse appeared in Rhymes and Roundelays (1841).
He is a different writer from the later poet Roden Noel. His winter song "Old Winter" and the satirical ballad "The Pauper's Drive" were long reprinted in anthologies.

poets.name: Thomas Cogswell Upham
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Cogswell Upham · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Cogswell Upham (1799–1872) was an American poet and philosopher.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Song of the Pilgrims”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Thomas Atkinson
bio: Thomas Atkinson (c. 1800–1833) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: James G. Brooks
bio: James G. Brooks (1801–1841) was a New York journalist and poet, born at Red Hook, New York, and a graduate of Union College.
Griswold included 5 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: William Leggett
bio: William Leggett (1801–1839) was a New York journalist and political writer, a former navy midshipman and a radical Jacksonian editor of the Evening Post.
Griswold included 5 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: George W. Cutter
bio: George W. Cutter (1801–1865) was a poet who lived in Kentucky and Ohio, whose Buena Vista, and Other Poems appeared in 1848.
Griswold included 3 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Theodore Dwight Woolsey
bio: Theodore Dwight Woolsey (1801–1889) was an American scholar, professor of Greek at Yale from 1831 and president of Yale from 1846 to 1871.

poets.name: William Blair
bio: William Blair (born 1800; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Mihály Vörösmarty
poets.credit: Portrait of Mihály Vörösmarty by Miklós Barabás (lithograph printed by Josef Axmann), 1857 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Hungarian poet and dramatist, a leading voice of Hungarian Romanticism.
His poems here are read in John Bowring's English versions from Poetry of the Magyars (1830), an early English anthology of Hungarian verse.

poets.name: Amos Bronson Alcott
bio: Amos Bronson Alcott (1799–1888) was an American teacher, philosopher and Transcendentalist, born at Wolcott, Connecticut. He taught young children in Connecticut and Boston, founded the Temple School in Boston in 1834 and later lived in Concord, Massachusetts, among Emerson and Thoreau. He was the father of Louisa May Alcott.
His verse is mostly sonnets in honour of his friends and contemporaries, gathered in Sonnets and Canzonets (1882). Stedman printed eight of them in An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Thomas Dick
bio: Thomas Dick (dates not given by Rogers) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: George Donald
bio: George Donald (1800–1851) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William Ferguson
bio: William Ferguson (dates not given by Rogers) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Henry Grattan Curran
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Henry Grattan Curran was a son of the orator John Philpot Curran and helped with the translations in Hardiman's collection of Irish minstrelsy. Sparling notes that no account of his life seemed to be accessible.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Joseph O'Leary
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Joseph O'Leary was for many years a writer on the London press and the author of several songs that enjoyed great vogue in their day.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Elias Lönnrot
poets.credit: Portrait of Elias Lönnrot, artist unknown, nineteenth century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Elias Lönnrot (1802–1884) was a Finnish physician and philologist, born in Sammatti in southern Finland. From 1828 he made a series of collecting journeys through Finland and Russian Karelia, on foot, on horseback, by sledge and by canoe, writing down the rune-songs that country singers still chanted from memory. In 1835 he published the first Kalevala, and in 1849 an enlarged edition of fifty runes; the Finnish Literature Society, which he helped to found, issued both.

Lönnrot is the compiler-author of the Kalevala, not its sole poet. The verses are drawn from oral folk songs, which he selected, ordered and joined into a continuous narrative of the hero Wainamoinen, the smith Ilmarinen and the Sampo, in the unrhymed trochaic metre of the tradition. The poem became a foundation of Finnish national culture. He later served as professor of Finnish at Helsinki and compiled a Finnish dictionary. This archive holds John Martin Crawford's 1888 English translation.

poets.name: William Gardiner
bio: William Gardiner (c. 1800–1845) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Thomas Babington Macaulay
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Babington Macaulay (1800–1859) was a British historian, poet and Whig politician, best known for his History of England and for his ballads in the Lays of Ancient Rome.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Sir Henry Taylor
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir Henry Taylor (1800–1886) was an English dramatist and poet who also served as an official in the Colonial Office; his best-known work is the verse drama Philip van Artevelde.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: George Henderson
bio: George Henderson (born 1800; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Daniel Weir
poets.credit: Portrait: John Fleming — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Daniel Weir (1796–1831) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 9 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 3 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: James Home
bio: James Home (dates not given by Rogers) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 5 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Edward Coote Pinkney
poets.credit: Frontispiece portrait of Edward Coote Pinkney, from The Life and Works of Edward Coote Pinkney (Macmillan, 1926) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward Coote Pinkney (1802–1828) was an American poet, born in London and raised in Baltimore, who served as a midshipman in the United States Navy and later practised law. He died at the age of twenty-five.
His slender output, including Poems (1825), contains a few graceful songs that earned him a lasting place in anthologies, notably “A Health”.

poets.name: George P. Morris
poets.credit: Portrait: Henry Inman — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George P. Morris (1802–1864) was a Philadelphia-born New York editor and songwriter, co-editor of the New-York Mirror and author of Woodman, Spare That Tree.
Griswold included 11 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Fortunatus Cosby
bio: Fortunatus Cosby (born 1802) was a Kentucky poet, born at Harrod's Creek, Jefferson County, the son of a Louisville judge, and a graduate of Yale College (1819).
Griswold included 1 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Lydia Maria Child
bio: Lydia Maria Child (1802–1880) was a New England novelist, editor and abolitionist, author of An Appeal in Favor of That Class of Americans Called Africans (1833) and of the Thanksgiving poem “Over the River and Through the Wood.”
Edmund Clarence Stedman included her poem on trust and kindness in An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: William Henry Furness
bio: William Henry Furness (1802–1896) was a Unitarian minister of Philadelphia, a writer on the life of Christ and a friend of Emerson, who also wrote hymns and verse.
Edmund Clarence Stedman included his “Evening Hymn” in An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: James William Miller
bio: James William Miller (c. 1802–1829) was a young American poet of refined character who died in his twenties.
Griswold included 1 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Albert G. Greene
bio: Albert G. Greene (1802–1868) was a Rhode Island lawyer and judge, born in Providence and a graduate of Brown University, and the author of the humorous ballad Old Grimes.
Griswold included 5 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: George D. Prentice
bio: George D. Prentice (1802–1870) was a Connecticut-born newspaper editor and poet, long the editor of the Louisville Journal.
Griswold included 6 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: John Hunter
bio: John Hunter (dates not given by Rogers) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Winthrop Mackworth Praed
poets.credit: Engraving of W. M. Praed, from The Poems of Winthrop Mackworth Praed (1864) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Winthrop Mackworth Praed (1802–1839) was an English poet and Tory politician, educated at Eton and Trinity College, Cambridge. He is remembered for light, polished society verse such as 'The Belle of the Ball' and 'The Vicar', in which a quick comic rhythm carries a gentle irony.
His poems were collected only after his death. The pieces here are the ones that James Parton chose for his anthology of English humorous verse.

poets.name: Letitia Elizabeth Landon (L.E.L.)
poets.credit: Portrait of Letitia Elizabeth Landon, engraving after Daniel Maclise · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Letitia Elizabeth Landon (1802–1838), who wrote under the initials L.E.L., was born in Chelsea, London. Her poems began to appear in William Jerdan’s Literary Gazette in 1820, signed with those initials, and The Improvisatrice (1824) made her one of the best-known poets of her day.

It was followed by The Troubadour (1825), The Golden Violet (1827) and The Venetian Bracelet (1829), long verse romances and tales that dwell on love, loss and the life of the woman poet. She also contributed constantly to the annuals and gift-books of the time and edited Fisher’s Drawing Room Scrap Book.
In June 1838 she married George Maclean, governor of Cape Coast Castle on the Gold Coast, and sailed with him to West Africa. She died there on 15 October 1838, at the age of thirty-six.

poets.name: Harriet Martineau
poets.credit: Portrait of Harriet Martineau by Richard Evans (exhibited 1834) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Harriet Martineau (1802–1876) was an English writer and social theorist, born at Norwich, best known for her prose: the Illustrations of Political Economy (1832–34), Society in America (1837) and her abridged English version of Comte's philosophy. She was deaf from youth.

Her verse is slight beside her prose, but her brief hymn-like lyric “Onward” was chosen by Elizabeth A. Sharp to open Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890). She spent her later years at Ambleside in the Lake District.

poets.name: Sara Coleridge
poets.credit: Portrait of Sara Coleridge (1852) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sara Coleridge (1802–1852) was the daughter of Samuel Taylor Coleridge and Sara Fricker, and the wife of her cousin Henry Nelson Coleridge. She was a translator and editor of her father's work, and published Pretty Lessons in Verse for Good Children (1834).
Her fairy romance Phantasmion (1837), a prose tale threaded with songs, is the source of several of the lyrics Elizabeth A. Sharp chose for Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Mrs Mary Macarthur

poets.name: Victor Hugo
poets.credit: Photograph of Victor Hugo by Étienne Carjat, c. 1876 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Victor Hugo (1802–1885) was born in Besançon and became the leading figure of French Romanticism, as poet, novelist and dramatist. His early odes won royalist favour, but after Napoleon III's coup of December 1851 he went into exile in Jersey and then Guernsey, remaining abroad until 1870. From there he published the satirical Les Châtiments (1853), the elegiac Les Contemplations (1856) and the epic sequence La Légende des siècles (1859–83).

The English shown here is drawn from the anthology Poems by Victor Hugo (1888), in which many hands render single poems from his collections. Only those poems whose translator is named in that book's contents are included; each carries the translator's name as printed there, and the original French incipit is recorded in the Codex Note.

The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Thomas Lovell Beddoes
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Lovell Beddoes by Nathan Cooper Branwhite (1824) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Lovell Beddoes (1803–1849) was an English poet, dramatist and physician, educated at Charterhouse and Oxford. He spent most of his adult life on the Continent, studying medicine in Germany and Switzerland.

His great work, the blank-verse tragedy Death’s Jest-Book, was begun in the 1820s and published only after his death in 1850. It is full of grave-haunted lyrics, such as “Dream-Pedlary” and “Old Adam, the Carrion Crow,” for which he is now chiefly read. He died in Basel in 1849.

poets.name: Sumner Lincoln Fairfield
bio: Sumner Lincoln Fairfield (1803–1844) was a poet and editor, born in Warwick, Massachusetts, a Harvard student and the author of The Last Night of Pompeii (1832).
Griswold included 3 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Rufus Dawes
bio: Rufus Dawes (1803–1859) was a poet of an old Massachusetts family, author of Geraldine (1839) and other poems.
Griswold included 6 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Sarah Helen Whitman
bio: Sarah Helen Whitman (1803–1878) was a poet and critic of Providence, Rhode Island, author of Hours of Life, and Other Poems (1853). She was briefly engaged to Edgar Allan Poe in 1848.
Edmund Clarence Stedman printed four of her sonnets in An American Anthology (1900); they are untitled and are given here by their first lines.

poets.name: George Lunt
bio: George Lunt (1803–1885) was a Newburyport, Massachusetts, lawyer, poet and politician, a graduate of Harvard.
Griswold included 6 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Robert Stephen Hawker
poets.credit: Photograph of Robert Stephen Hawker by Richard Budd, 1864 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Stephen Hawker (1803–1875) was an English clergyman, poet and antiquary of an old Cornish family, born at Plymouth, who was vicar of the remote Cornish parish of Morwenstow from 1834 until his death. His best-known book is Cornish Ballads (1869).
Lyra Celtica prints two of his poems, 'Featherstone's Doom' and 'Trebarrow'; this file also holds 'The Doom-Well of St Madron' from Popular British Ballads (1894).

poets.name: James Telfer
bio: James Telfer (born c. 1800) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Edward Bulwer Lytton
poets.credit: Portrait of Edward Bulwer-Lytton by Henry William Pickersgill (c. 1831) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward Bulwer-Lytton (1803–1873), created Baron Lytton in 1866, was an English novelist, dramatist, politician and poet. He is remembered chiefly for his novels, but he wrote verse throughout his career and gathered it, revised, in several editions of his Poetical Works.

The poems here are taken from the Routledge edition of 1860: the satire The New Timon, the narrative poems Milton, Constance and The Fairy Bride, the twelve-book romance King Arthur, the “Narrative Lyrics” and the short lyrics of Corn-Flowers and Earlier Poems. His plays, prose notes and pieces headed as translations or imitations are not included.

poets.name: Samuel Lover
poets.credit: Portrait: unknown artist — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Samuel Lover was a Dublin-born novelist, songwriter, painter and miniaturist. His novels include Rory O'More and Handy Andy, and he wrote and performed Irish songs and entertainments.
He died in Jersey in 1868.

poets.name: Mirza Ghalib
poets.credit: Photograph of Mirza Ghalib, 19th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mirza Asadullah Beg Khan, who wrote as Ghalib, was born in Agra in 1797 and lived most of his life in Delhi, where he died in 1869. He wrote in Urdu and in Persian, and is generally counted among the greatest Urdu poets of the ghazal. The book from which these pieces come describes him as coming of a distinguished Turkish family of Samarkand, and as Poet Laureate at the court of Bahadur Shah, the last Mughal emperor.

The six pieces given here are drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook; five appear in the main series and one among the closing fragments. They are free renderings, not literal translations.

poets.name: Chauncy Hare Townshend
bio: Chauncy Hare Townshend was born in 1798, educated at Trinity Hall, Cambridge, and took his M.A. in 1824.
He published Jerusalem (1828), Sermons in Sonnets, with Other Poems (1851) and The Shell Gates (1859). He died in 1868.

poets.name: Thomas Kibble Hervey
bio: Thomas Kibble Hervey was born at Paisley in 1799, studied law, and about 1820 went to London to follow a literary career.
He contributed to the Art Journal and edited the Athenaeum for several years. His poems were collected, with a memoir, by his widow in 1866. He died at Kentish Town in 1859.

poets.name: J. H. Dixon
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: James Henry Dixon (1803–1876) was a local historian and antiquary of the Craven country, who edited for the Percy Society the collection Ancient Poems, Ballads, and Songs of the Peasantry of England (1846).

He wrote comparatively little verse of his own; Moorman singles out "The Milkin'-Time" for its lilt, and mentions a longer poem, "Slaadburn Faar" (1871). The poem here is taken from Moorman's Yorkshire Dialect Poems (1916).

poets.name: James Clarence Mangan
poets.credit: Portrait: David M. Jensen (Storkk) — CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James Clarence Mangan was born in Dublin and worked as a scrivener's clerk and library assistant. He contributed poems and translations, many of them English versions from the Irish, to The Nation and other periodicals.
He lived in poverty and ill health and died of cholera in 1849. His "Dark Rosaleen" is the most widely known of his poems.

poets.name: Momin Khan Momin
bio: Momin of Delhi is described in the book as the author of six long masnawis, skilled in medicine, astronomy and astrology, and deeply read in poetry. He is said at first to have lived a gay and reckless life, and in old age to have given himself to prayer and fasting, acquiring great contemporary fame; his work is called the most delicate flower of Urdu expression.

The one piece given here is drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. It is a free rendering, not a literal translation, and the original Urdu poem is untitled; it is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Francis Lieber
poets.credit: Portrait of Francis Lieber, by Mathew Brady · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Francis Lieber (1800–1872) was a German-American jurist, gymnast and political philosopher.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “The Ship Canal from the Atlantic to the Pacific”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Harvey Rice
bio: Harvey Rice (1800–1891) was an American politician.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Cuba”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Robert White
bio: Robert White (dates not given by Rogers) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 6 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Johan Ludvig Runeberg
poets.credit: Portrait of Johan Ludvig Runeberg by Albert Edelfelt (1893) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Johan Ludvig Runeberg (1804–1877) is honoured as Finland's national poet, though he wrote in Swedish, the language of the educated class of his day. Born in Jakobstad (Pietarsaari) on the Ostrobothnian coast, he studied at Turku and Helsinki, taught for a time as a tutor in the Finnish interior, and spent most of his working life in the town of Porvoo, where he was a schoolmaster and lived until his death.

His best-known work is The Songs of Ensign Stål (Fänrik Ståls sägner), a cycle of narrative and lyric poems on the Finnish War of 1808–09, in which Sweden lost Finland to Russia. The first series appeared in 1848 and the second in 1860. An old, half-forgotten soldier tells the stories, and the cycle turns defeat into a moral portrait of a people, in the figures of the common soldier, the officer, and the women who wait at home.

The prologue, 'Our Land' (Vårt land), was set to music by Fredrik Pacius in 1848 and became the national anthem of Finland. The English text here is the first complete English translation, by Clement Burbank Shaw (New York: G. E. Stechert, 1925), in the original metres. Only the cantos of the 1848 series that the Wikisource transcription has fully proofread from the scan so far are given here.

poets.name: Edmund D. Griffin
bio: Edmund D. Griffin (1804–1830) was a poet and Episcopal clergyman, born in the Wyoming Valley of Pennsylvania and a Columbia College graduate; his writings were collected after his early death.
Griswold included 4 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: J. H. Bright

Griswold included 3 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

Edmund Clarence Stedman included his poem “The Star of Calvary” in An American Anthology (1900).
