poets.name: William Lloyd Garrison
bio: William Lloyd Garrison (1805–1879) was an American journalist and reformer, born at Newburyport, Massachusetts, and the leading voice of the radical abolitionists.
He founded the anti-slavery newspaper The Liberator in 1831, and wrote occasional verse, chiefly sonnets, in the cause of freedom.

poets.name: Francis Sylvester Mahony
poets.credit: Portrait of Francis Sylvester Mahony ("Father Prout"), artist not stated · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Francis Sylvester Mahony (c. 1804–1866), born in Cork and known as "Father Prout", trained as a priest but left his cure for a life of letters, becoming a celebrated wit and essayist. He died in Paris.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield (1804–1881), was a British statesman and writer who twice served as Prime Minister. He published verse as well as novels.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Laman Blanchard
poets.credit: Laman Blanchard, by Daniel Maclise, 1846 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Samuel Laman Blanchard (1804–1845) was an English journalist and poet, a friend of Charles Lamb and Edward Bulwer-Lytton and and editor of several periodicals. He died in 1845; Bulwer-Lytton wrote a memoir for his Sketches from Life (1846).

The poem here is the one printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poets.name: Alfred Henry Forrester (Alfred Crowquill)
bio: Alfred Henry Forrester (1804–1872), who wrote and drew as "Alfred Crowquill", was an English illustrator, caricaturist and humorist, a contributor to Bentley's Miscellany and Punch.
He was the brother of the illustrator Charles Robert Forrester, and published comic verse and books for children alongside his drawings.

poets.name: Bartholomew Simmons
bio: Bartholomew Simmons (1804–1850) was an Irish poet, born at Kilworth, County Cork. He entered the Excise service in 1830 and later lived in London.
He contributed to Blackwood’s Magazine and other periodicals, and his poems were collected as Legends, Lyrics, and Other Poems (1843).

poets.name: Charles Whitehead
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Charles Whitehead (1804–1862) was an English poet, novelist and dramatist.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: William Barnes
poets.credit: Photograph of William Barnes, 19th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Barnes (1801–1886) was an English poet, philologist and clergyman, born at Rushay in the Vale of Blackmore, Dorset. A largely self-taught scholar, he worked as a schoolmaster in Dorchester and later became rector of Winterborne Came, near Dorchester.

He is best known for his poems in the Dorset dialect, collected in three series of Poems of Rural Life in the Dorset Dialect (1844, 1859, 1862) and gathered in one volume in 1879. Thomas Hardy, who knew him in Dorchester, admired him and wrote of his death in a poem.

poets.name: Gerald Griffin
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Gerald Griffin was born in Limerick and became a novelist, dramatist and poet; his best-known novel is The Collegians (1829). In 1838 he joined the Christian Brothers.
He died in Cork in 1840.

poets.name: Jane Welsh Carlyle
poets.credit: Portrait of Jane Welsh Carlyle by Samuel Laurence · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Jane Baillie Welsh Carlyle (1801–1866) was born at Haddington in Scotland and in 1826 married the historian Thomas Carlyle. She is remembered above all for her letters, which are among the most admired of the century.
She wrote little verse and published almost none in her lifetime; the poem “To a Swallow Building under our Eaves” is the piece by which she is usually represented in anthologies.

poets.name: William Wilson
bio: William Wilson (born 1801; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 7 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Charles Swain
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Charles Swain (1801–1874) was an English poet and engraver, born in Manchester. He was honorary professor of poetry at the Manchester Royal Institution and received a civil list pension in 1856.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Henry Glassford Bell
bio: Henry Glassford Bell (dates not given by Rogers) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 5 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Alexander Macansh
bio: Alexander Macansh (born 1803; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: James Pringle
bio: James Pringle (born 1803) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Edward Walsh
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Edward Walsh was born in Londonderry and worked as a schoolmaster. He is known for his English versions of Irish songs, collected in Irish Popular Songs (1847).
He died in Cork in 1850.

poets.name: William Pitt Palmer
bio: William Pitt Palmer (1805–1884) was an American poet of New York, the son of a sea captain, whose verses appeared in the magazines of his day.
Griswold included 3 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: George W. Bethune
bio: George W. Bethune (1805–1862) was a Dutch Reformed minister, born in New York, who served in Utica, Philadelphia and Brooklyn and edited an edition of Walton's Compleat Angler.
Griswold included 4 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Frederic Henry Hedge
bio: Frederic Henry Hedge (1805–1890) was a Unitarian minister, a founder of the Transcendental Club and later a professor at Harvard, and a translator of German literature. He also made hymns, among them a version of Luther’s “Ein’ feste Burg.”
Edmund Clarence Stedman included the paraphrase in An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Nathaniel Ingersoll Bowditch
bio: Nathaniel Ingersoll Bowditch (1805–1861) was a Boston man of business and antiquarian, the son of the navigator Nathaniel Bowditch and author of Suffolk Surnames (1857).
Edmund Clarence Stedman included his short poem “A World Beyond” in An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Edward Sanford
bio: Edward Sanford (1805–1876) was a New York lawyer and poet, the son of Chancellor Sanford and a graduate of Union College (1824).
Griswold included 2 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Elizabeth Oakes Smith
bio: Elizabeth Oakes Smith (1806–1893) was an American poet, novelist and lecturer, born near Yarmouth, Maine, who spoke and wrote in support of women's rights.
Her best-known poem is The Sinless Child (1843); The Drowned Mariner is among her most anthologised shorter pieces.

poets.name: Lionel Johnson
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Lionel Johnson (1867–1902) was an English poet and critic associated with the Rhymers' Club and the Decadent movement of the 1890s.
A convert to Catholicism, his spare, disciplined verse turned repeatedly to faith, monastic ideals, and the pull of dissipation he struggled against.

poets.name: José-Maria de Heredia
poets.credit: Etching by Adolphe Lalauze, c. 1897 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: José-Maria de Heredia (1842–1905) was born in Cuba of Spanish-descended family and educated in France, where he settled and became one of the leading Parnassian poets. He published his poems slowly, in periodicals, and was elected to the Académie française in 1894.

His single book, Les Trophées (1893), gathers some hundred and eighteen sonnets on Greek and Roman antiquity, the Middle Ages and Renaissance, the conquistadors, the Orient and the sea. These versions are by the San Francisco jurist Edward Robeson Taylor, from the fifth edition of 1913.

poets.name: Oscar Wilde
poets.credit: Portrait of Oscar Wilde · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Oscar Wilde (1854–1900) was an Irish poet, playwright, and wit, one of the most celebrated figures of Victorian literary London before his 1895 trial and imprisonment.
His early verse is lush and Romantic in the Keatsian mode, while The Ballad of Reading Gaol, written after his release from prison, is a stark, plainspoken account of suffering and remorse.

poets.name: Douglas Brooke Wheelton Sladen
bio: Douglas Sladen (1856–1947) was an English-born poet and novelist who lectured at the University of Sydney from 1879 to 1884.
He edited the anthologies A Century of Australian Song and Australian Ballads and Rhymes (both 1888), and wrote many novels.

poets.name: Lewis Frank Tooker
bio: Lewis Frank Tooker (1855–1925) was an American editor and poet, for many years associated with the staff of The Century Magazine. He wrote verse and prose, including sea poems and memoirs of his years in magazine editing.
Knowles included his poem “The Return” in his anthology of American lyrics.

poets.name: Emile Verhaeren
poets.credit: Portrait of Emile Verhaeren by Théo van Rysselberghe, 1915 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Emile Verhaeren was born in 1855 at Sint-Amands, near Antwerp, and grew up on the banks of the Scheldt amid the Flemish plains. He studied at Ghent and Louvain, was called to the Bar at Brussels in 1881, and soon gave up law for literature, publishing his first volume of poems in 1883 and writing for the review L'Art Moderne. He was a friend of Maeterlinck and a leading figure of the Belgian literary revival known as Young Belgium.

His work moves from the vigorous Flemish scenes of Les Flamandes through the anguished books of the 1880s to the visionary village and city poems of Les Villages illusoires and Les Villes tentaculaires, and to the tender love-songs of Les Heures claires, written for his wife. A master of free verse, he died in 1916. The English versions gathered here are by Alma Strettell (1915), Jethro Bithell (1911) and F. S. Flint (1916), with one poem by Osman Edwards (1896).

poets.name: Thomas Hardy
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Hardy · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928) is best known as a novelist, but after finishing Jude the Obscure in 1895 he devoted the rest of his long career chiefly to poetry.
His verse is plain-spoken and often bleak, preoccupied with chance, loss, rural Wessex life, and the death of his first wife Emma, which produced some of his most admired elegies.

poets.name: Patrick Moloney
bio: Patrick Moloney (1843–1904) was a Melbourne doctor and writer of light and occasional verse.
His poem on Melbourne appeared in An Easter Omelette (1879).

poets.name: Thomas Bracken
bio: Thomas Bracken (1843–1898) was an Irish-born journalist, politician and poet who settled in New Zealand.
He published Musings in Maoriland (1890) and wrote the words of 'God Defend New Zealand', later the national hymn.

poets.name: Sarah Pratt McLean Greene
bio: Sarah Pratt McLean Greene (1856–1935) was an American writer, born at Simsbury, Connecticut, and educated at Mount Holyoke College. She is known for books of Cape Cod life such as Cape Cod Folks and Vesty of the Basins.
Rittenhouse included her dialect poem “De Massa ob de Sheepfol’”, which she judged destined to hold a lasting place.

poets.name: H. T. Mackenzie Bell
bio: Henry Thomas Mackenzie Bell (1856–1930) was a critic and poet born in Liverpool, who contributed to the Academy and other periodicals.
His verse volumes include The Keeping of the Vow (1879), Verses of Varied Life (1882) and Old Year Leaves (1883); he also wrote a biographical and critical study of Christina Rossetti (1898).

poets.name: Leylâ Khânim
bio: Leyla Khanim is a woman poet represented in Gibb's anthology by a tarikh on the death of 'Andelib Khanim, the Sultan's adopted sister, and a tahmis on a gazel of Baqi.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Ziyâ Beg (Ziya Pasha)
bio: Ziya Beg, the son of an Albanian father, was one of the most distinguished men of letters of modern Turkey, a member of the Young Turkey party who withdrew to London after losing the favour of Sultan 'Abdu-'l-'Aziz, whose secretary he was.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Ref'et Beg
bio: Ref'et Beg is represented in Gibb's anthology by a patriotic sharqi, a song of the Ottoman soldier, from the Tanzimat period; Gibb prints no dates for him.
The poems here are taken from E. J. W. Gibb's Ottoman Poems (1882), the first English verse translations of Ottoman poetry; dates and biographical details follow Gibb's Biographical Notices.

poets.name: Namık Kemal
poets.credit: Photograph of Namık Kemal, 1878 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Namık Kemal (1840–1888) was an Ottoman poet, journalist, playwright and political thinker, born in Tekirdağ. A leading figure of the Young Ottomans, the reform-minded circle of the Tanzimat era, he argued for liberty, constitutional government and love of the fatherland in newspapers, plays and verse, and was later known as the "poet of the fatherland" (vatan şairi).

His writing brought him repeated trouble with the authorities: he spent years in exile in Europe in the 1860s, and after his patriotic play Vatan yahut Silistre (1873) he was banished to Magosa (Famagusta) in Cyprus. He later served as an Ottoman provincial governor and died on the island of Chios on 2 December 1888. The eight pieces here are taken from Turkish Wikisource, which lists his death year as 1889; the standard date is 1888.

poets.name: Wilfrid Scawen Blunt
poets.credit: Portrait photograph of Wilfrid Scawen Blunt (undated), via the William Morris Society · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Wilfrid Scawen Blunt (1840–1922) was an English poet, diplomat and landowner, born in Sussex and educated for the diplomatic service, in which he served in several European capitals before leaving it. With his wife, Lady Anne Blunt, he travelled in Arabia and the Middle East and founded the Crabbet Arabian Stud at his Sussex estate.

He was a vocal opponent of British imperial policy in Egypt, India and Ireland, and was imprisoned in Ireland in 1888 for his part in the land agitation, writing the sonnets of In Vinculis there. His love poetry, collected as The Love Sonnets of Proteus (1881), and his later sequences were gathered with his narrative and political poems in the two-volume Poetical Works of 1914, the text used here.

poets.name: Austin Dobson
poets.credit: Frank Brooks, 1911 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Austin Dobson (1840–1921) was an English poet and man of letters who spent his working life as a clerk in the Board of Trade. In his spare hours he became the chief English master of light verse and of the French fixed forms — the rondeau, ballade, triolet and villanelle — which he handled with polish and wit.
He was also a respected biographer and essayist of the eighteenth century, writing lives of Hogarth, Fielding and Goldsmith, among others. His Collected Poems appeared in 1895.

poets.name: Frank T. Marzials
bio: Frank Thomas Marzials (1840–1912) was born at Lille, France, and spent his working life in the English War Office. He was an elder brother of the poet and composer Theo Marzials.
He wrote biographies (Life of Charles Dickens, 1887; Life of Victor Hugo, 1888), edited the Great Writers series, and published his verse in Death's Disguises (1889).

poets.name: Alice Brown
poets.credit: Photograph of Alice Brown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alice Brown (1857–1948) was an American writer, born at Hampton Falls, New Hampshire, and educated at Robinson Seminary, Exeter. She is chiefly known as a novelist and short-story writer of New England life, with books such as Meadow Grass and Tiverton Tales.
In poetry she published one volume, The Road to Castaly (1896), reprinted with new poems in 1917. In 1915 her play Children of Earth won a ten-thousand-dollar prize and was produced in New York.

poets.name: Recaizade Mahmut Ekrem
poets.credit: Photograph of Recaizade Mahmut Ekrem, before 1900, photographer unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Recaizade Mahmut Ekrem (1847–1914) was a writer of the Tanzimat period, the Ottoman reform era, and one of the figures who helped turn Turkish literature toward new subjects and a plainer prose. He was born in Istanbul. He is remembered above all for his novel Araba Sevdası (1896) and for his critical writing, and he also wrote plays and a good deal of verse.

Nağme-i Seher ('Song of the Dawn') was a collection of his poems, dated 1288 AH (about 1871). It gathers classical forms (tevhîd and na't, praise poems, chronogram verses, gazels) alongside lighter songs (şarkı). The poems below are given in the Vikikaynak (tr.wikisource.org) Latin-alphabet transcription of the 1871 book, which keeps the book's circumflexed Ottoman spelling.

poets.name: William Ernest Henley
poets.credit: Portrait of William Ernest Henley · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Ernest Henley (1849–1903) was an English poet and editor whose leg was amputated in youth after tubercular illness, an experience recorded directly in his sequence In Hospital.
He is best remembered for Invictus, and his robust, muscular verse and criticism made him an influential figure among younger writers of the 1890s.

poets.name: Harriet Eleanor Hamilton King
bio: Harriet Eleanor Hamilton King (1840–1920) was an English poet whose long narrative poems were inspired by the Italian struggle for unification, in which she took a warm interest. Her works include Aspromonte and Other Poems (1869) and The Disciples (1873).
Her heroic ballad “Baron Giovanni Nicotera”, on the Italian patriot imprisoned by the Bourbon government, is printed in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Edmund Gosse
poets.credit: Edmund Gosse by John Singer Sargent (1886) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Edmund Gosse (1849–1928) was an English poet, critic and librarian of the House of Lords. He published verse early, in On Viol and Flute (1873), and became better known as a man of letters, author of the memoir Father and Son (1907).
The poem given here is taken from Edmund H. Garrett's anthology Victorian Songs: Lyrics of the Affections and Nature (Boston: Little, Brown, 1895).

poets.name: Selwyn Image
bio: Selwyn Image (1849–1930) was educated at Brighton College, Marlborough and New College, Oxford. Ordained in 1872, he gave up clerical work about 1880 to become an artist and designer.
With Herbert Horne he started the Hobby Horse in 1886, and later wrote verse in the manner of the Century Guild circle.

poets.name: Philip Bourke Marston
poets.credit: No known portrait
bio: Philip Bourke Marston (1850–1887) was an English poet, the son of the dramatist and critic Westland Marston. He lost his sight in childhood and spent his short life as a blind poet in London, where his circle included Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Arthur O’Shaughnessy and Oliver Madox Brown. Much of his verse is shaped by bereavement: the early death of his betrothed, then of friends and of his sister Cicely.

The poems given here are taken from The Collected Poems of Philip Bourke Marston (Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1892), which gathers his three lifetime books, Song-Tide, All in All and Wind-Voices, with the posthumous A Last Harvest and Aftermath. The biographical sketch by Louise Chandler Moulton and her dedicatory sonnet are not reproduced. The text comes from an optical scan of the printed book and has been corrected for obvious scanning errors; stanza breaks are reconstructed and may not always match the page.

poets.name: John Arthur Blaikie
bio: John Arthur Blaikie (born London, 1850) was a minor Victorian poet and a member of the staff of the Saturday Review.
His first book, Poems by Two Friends (1876), was published jointly with Edmund Gosse.

poets.name: William Douw Lighthall
poets.credit: Portrait of William Douw Lighthall, from Canadian Singers and Their Songs (c. 1919) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Douw Lighthall (1857–1954) was a Montreal lawyer, author and civic reformer, later mayor of Westmount, who edited a series of anthologies of Canadian poetry.
His own verse appeared in Thoughts, Moods and Ideals (1887); the poems here are those he included in his own anthology, Songs of the Great Dominion (1889).

poets.name: Charles Henry Luders
bio: Charles Henry Luders (1858–1891), also spelled Lüders, was an American poet, who died young at the age of thirty-three. Little is recorded of his life in the sources used for this archive.
Knowles included his lyric “The Four Winds” in his anthology of American songs and lyrics.

poets.name: Rosa Mulholland, Lady Gilbert
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Rosa Mulholland was born in Belfast and became a prolific novelist and poet. In 1891 she married the historian Sir John Gilbert and was afterwards known as Lady Gilbert.
Yeats's anthology prints her poem under the name Rosa Gilbert.

poets.name: Clement Scott
bio: Clement William Scott (1841–1904) was an English drama critic, playwright and poet, born in London. He worked as a clerk in the War Office before becoming dramatic critic of the Daily Telegraph in 1879.
His verse appeared in Lays of a Londoner (1882) and Lays and Legends (1888). The poem here comes from Edmund Clarence Stedman's A Victorian Anthology (1895).

poets.name: A. E. Housman
poets.credit: Portrait of A. E. Housman · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: A. E. Housman (1859–1936) was an English classical scholar and poet whose reputation rests on two slim volumes, A Shropshire Lad (1896) and Last Poems (1922).
His terse, ballad-like lyrics of doomed youth, soldiering, and rural England were composed in a private grief masked by classical restraint.

poets.name: James Kenneth Stephen
bio: James Kenneth Stephen (1859–1892), known as J. K. S., was the son of Sir James Fitzjames Stephen. He was educated at Eton and King's College, Cambridge, where he became a Fellow, and was for a time tutor to Prince Albert Victor; he was called to the Bar in 1884.
He is remembered for his parodies and light verse in Lapsus Calami (1891), and also published Quo, Musa, Tendis? (1891).

poets.name: Arthur Conan Doyle
bio: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle (1859–1930) was born in Edinburgh and trained as a physician before becoming the author of the Sherlock Holmes stories and of historical romances such as The White Company. He died at Crowborough, Sussex.
He also wrote spirited ballad verse, collected in Songs of Action (1898) and Songs of the Road (1911).

poets.name: Henry Abbey
bio: Henry Abbey (1842–1911) was an American poet, born at Rondout, New York. He worked for some years as a journalist in New York City and afterwards as a merchant in his native town, and published May Dreams (1862), Ballads of Good Deeds (1872), The City of Success (1883) and a collected Poems (1886).
The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin, 1900).

poets.name: Charles Warren Stoddard
bio: Charles Warren Stoddard (1843–1909) was an American poet and travel writer, born at Rochester, New York. Bret Harte edited his first book, Poems (1867); he spent years in the Hawaiian Islands and the South Seas, wrote South Sea Idyls (1873), and later taught English literature at Notre Dame and lectured at the Catholic University in Washington.
The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin, 1900).

poets.name: Edward Dowden
poets.credit: Frontispiece, Poems (London: J. M. Dent, 1914), via Project Gutenberg · Public domain
bio: Edward Dowden was born in Cork and became Professor of English Literature at Trinity College Dublin. He is best known for his Shakespeare criticism and his Life of Shelley.
He also published several volumes of verse.

poets.name: Violet Fane
bio: Violet Fane was the pen name of Mary Montgomerie Singleton (1843–1905), later Lady Currie, an English poet and novelist of the 1870s and 1880s. Her volumes include From Dawn to Noon (1872) and Denzil Place (1875).
Two of her lyrics, “Rest” and “Forbidden Love”, appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Margaret Veley
bio: Margaret Veley (1843–1887) was an English poet and novelist, the daughter of a solicitor at Braintree in Essex. She began writing verse young and contributed both prose and poetry to the leading magazines of her day.
Her poems were collected after her death, with a biographical preface by Leslie Stephen.

poets.name: Frederic W. H. Myers
poets.credit: Portrait: William Clarke Wontner — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Frederic William Henry Myers (1843–1901) was a British poet, classicist and philologist, and a founder of the Society for Psychical Research.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 8, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Charles M. Doughty
poets.credit: Portrait of Charles M. Doughty, photogravure by Emery Walker (from Wanderings in Arabia, 1908) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Montagu Doughty (1843–1926) was an English poet and traveller, born in Suffolk and educated at Cambridge. He is best known for Travels in Arabia Deserta (1888), his account of two years among the Bedouin, written in a deliberately archaic English modelled on Chaucer and the Elizabethans.

He turned to verse late in life. The Dawn in Britain (1906), a blank-verse epic in twenty-four books on the early history of Britain, was followed by Adam Cast Forth (1908), The Cliffs (1909), The Clouds (1912), The Titans (1916) and Mansoul (1920). His poems were little read in his lifetime, but admired by later poets for their austere, Spenserian diction.

poets.name: Andrew Lang
poets.credit: Portrait of Andrew Lang · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Andrew Lang (1844–1912) was a Scottish man of letters, folklorist, and translator, remembered today chiefly for his coloured Fairy Books but also a prolific poet.
His verse favours French forms revived by the 1870s ballade craze, along with translations and tributes to French and English poets he admired.

poets.name: Caroline Blanche Elizabeth, Lady Lindsay
bio: Caroline Blanche Elizabeth FitzRoy, Lady Lindsay (1844–1912), was an English poet, prose writer and musician, a daughter of Henry FitzRoy and a granddaughter of Baron Nathan Mayer Rothschild. She married Sir Coutts Lindsay, the painter who founded the Grosvenor Gallery.
Her verse appeared in Lyrics (1890), A Child’s Dream and A String of Beads (1893).

poets.name: Gerard Manley Hopkins
poets.credit: Photograph of Gerard Manley Hopkins, before 1889, photographer unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Gerard Manley Hopkins (1844–1889) was an English poet, Roman Catholic convert and Jesuit priest. Born in Stratford, Essex, he studied at Balliol College, Oxford, became a Catholic in 1866 under the influence of John Henry Newman, and entered the Society of Jesus in 1868. He burned his early verses on joining the order and wrote little for several years, until the wreck of the Deutschland in December 1875 drew from him the long ode that opened his mature manner.

His poems, built on what he called sprung rhythm and a dense, coined vocabulary of sound and image, found almost no readers in his lifetime. He worked as a teacher and parish priest, and from 1884 as professor of Greek at University College, Dublin, where he wrote the so-called terrible sonnets and died of typhoid in 1889. His friend Robert Bridges published the first collected Poems in 1918, and Hopkins has since been counted among the major Victorian poets.

poets.name: Robert Bridges
poets.credit: Photograph of Robert Bridges, late 19th century, photographer unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Bridges (1844–1930) was an English poet and physician. Born at Walmer in Kent, he was educated at Eton and Corpus Christi College, Oxford, and trained in medicine at St Bartholomew's Hospital, practising until ill health led him to retire in 1882 and devote himself to poetry. He was a close friend of Gerard Manley Hopkins, whose poems he preserved and, in 1918, brought to the public.

His own verse, notable for its delicate lyrics and metrical experiment, including syllabic measures modelled on Milton's Samson Agonistes, appeared in small private editions such as the Daniel Press Poems of 1884. He became Poet Laureate in 1913, published the long philosophical poem The Testament of Beauty in 1929, and died at Boars Hill, near Oxford, in 1930.

poets.name: John Jeffrey
bio: John Jeffrey (born 1822; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Paul Verlaine
poets.credit: Photograph of Paul Verlaine by Otto Wegener, 1893 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Paul Verlaine (1844–1896) was a French poet born in Metz and raised in Paris, where he worked briefly as a clerk at the Hôtel de Ville while publishing his first book, Poèmes saturniens (1866). His Fêtes galantes (1869) and La Bonne Chanson (1870), the latter written for his young fiancée Mathilde Mauté, established him as a master of fluid, musical verse among the Parnassian poets.

In 1871 he met Arthur Rimbaud, and in 1873 he was imprisoned in Belgium after shooting him; Romances sans paroles (1874) was written in these years and Sagesse (1881), a book of Catholic devotion, in the aftermath. He later published Jadis et naguère (1884) and Parallèlement (1889), and was named the leading living poet by the Symbolists, though he spent his last years in poverty and illness in Paris. These versions are from Gertrude Hall's English translation of 1895.

poets.name: Amy Levy
poets.credit: Portrait of Amy Levy · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Amy Levy (1861–1889) was an English poet and novelist, among the first Jewish women to study at Cambridge, who took her own life at twenty-seven.
Her poems of London street life, unrequited love, and urban melancholy anticipate the modern lyric's compression and irony.

poets.name: George MacDonald
poets.credit: Portrait of George MacDonald · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George MacDonald (1824–1905) was a Scottish minister turned author, celebrated for fantasy novels such as Phantastes and The Princess and the Goblin, and a lifelong writer of devotional and reflective verse.
His poems return often to faith, fatherhood, nature, and the soul's struggle toward trust in a loving God.

poets.name: Frances Ellen Watkins Harper
poets.credit: Portrait of Frances E. W. Harper from Women of Distinction (1893) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Frances Ellen Watkins Harper (1825–1911) was born free in Baltimore and became one of the most widely read African American poets of the nineteenth century, as well as a lecturer, abolitionist and suffragist. Her verse, from the ballads of her early books to the dialect monologues of Aunt Chloe in Sketches of Southern Life (1891), took up slavery, emancipation, temperance, the rights of women and Christian faith.
The poems here come from Poems (1895), Sketches of Southern Life (1891) and Idylls of the Bible (1901), which includes the long dramatic poem Moses: A Story of the Nile, given one chapter to a poem.

poets.name: George Meredith
poets.credit: Portrait of George Meredith · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Meredith (1828–1909) was an English novelist and poet whose sonnet sequence Modern Love (1862) gave unusually candid, ironic voice to a marriage's collapse.
His nature poetry, especially The Lark Ascending, prizes close observation and intellectual vigour over conventional sentiment.

poets.name: Gerald Massey
poets.credit: Gerald Massey, photograph (1856; photographer unknown) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Gerald Massey (1828–1907) was an English poet of working-class origins, born at Tring in Hertfordshire. His early collections, such as Poems and Chansons (1846) and The Ballad of Babe Christabel (1854), won him a wide readership.
The poems here come from The Poetical Works of Gerald Massey (1861) and My Lyrical Life (1889).

poets.name: George Walter Thornbury
poets.credit: George Walter Thornbury, portrait (c. 1876; artist unknown) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Walter Thornbury (1828–1876) was an English poet, journalist and writer on London and on the painter Turner. His best-known verse is Songs of the Cavaliers and Roundheads (1857).
The poems given here are taken from Edmund H. Garrett's anthology Victorian Songs (Boston: Little, Brown, 1895) and R. Brimley Johnson's Popular British Ballads (1894).

poets.name: Henrik Ibsen
poets.credit: Eilif Peterssen, 1895 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henrik Ibsen (1828–1906) was a Norwegian dramatist, born in Skien, who after years in the theatres of Bergen and Christiania left Norway in 1864 and lived abroad, in Italy and Germany, for most of the next twenty-seven years. He is remembered above all as the founder of modern prose drama.

His two great verse dramas belong to the years of exile. Brand (1866), the story of an uncompromising pastor who demands of himself and others all or nothing, made his name in Scandinavia; Peer Gynt (1867), its fantastic, wandering counterpart, follows a self-deceiving dreamer from the Norwegian mountains to Morocco, Egypt and back.
Both plays are held here as complete works in the English translations of 1907, Brand by C. H. Herford and Peer Gynt by William and Charles Archer.

poets.name: John Boyle O'Reilly
poets.credit: John Boyle O'Reilly, photograph by Augustus Marshall, c. 1870 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Boyle O'Reilly (1844–1890), born at Dowth Castle, County Meath, was a Fenian transported to Western Australia, from which he escaped in 1869. He settled in Boston, became editor and part-owner of the Pilot, and published several volumes of verse.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Charles Baudelaire
poets.credit: Portrait of Charles Baudelaire by Étienne Carjat (c. 1862) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Baudelaire (1821–1867) was a French poet, critic and translator of Edgar Allan Poe. Born in Paris, he spent his short life in the city's literary and artistic circles, and is widely regarded as a founder of modern poetry and a forerunner of the Symbolists.

His one major collection of verse, Les Fleurs du Mal (1857), drew a prosecution for offending public morality, and six of its poems were suppressed. Its themes of spleen, beauty, desire, the city and death shaped later poets across Europe. These versions are from Cyril Scott's English translation of 1909.

poets.name: Charles P. O'Conor
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Charles P. O'Conor was known as "Ireland's Peasant Poet" and published Wreaths of Fancy in 1870. Sparling praises the simple, tuneful vigour of his verse.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Attie O'Brien
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Attie (Frances) O'Brien (1840–1885) was born at Peafield, near Ennis, County Clare. She wrote many poems and some short stories.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Dora Greenwell
poets.credit: Photograph of Dora Greenwell · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Dora Greenwell (1821–1882) was an English poet and devotional writer born in County Durham. Her volumes include Poems (1848) and Carmina Crucis (1869), and she wrote essays on religious and social questions.
Her poem “Songs of Farewell: Death”, a meditation on the seasons that will return when the speaker is gone, was chosen for Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Colin Rae Brown
bio: Colin Rae Brown (born 1821; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: John Halliday
bio: John Halliday (born 1821) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: James Little
bio: James Little (born 1821) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 4 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William Logan
bio: William Logan (born 1821) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Nikolay Nekrasov
poets.credit: Photograph by Vezenberg & Co., 1870s · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio:
Nikolay Alekseyevich Nekrasov (1821–1878) was a Russian poet, editor and publisher, born in Podolia and raised on his father's estate on the Volga. He settled in St. Petersburg, where he edited the journals The Contemporary and, later, Notes of the Fatherland, and became the leading voice of Russian civic poetry.

His verse turned from the drawing-room to the lives of peasants, city poor and serf-haulers, written in a language close to folk song. His last great work, Who Can Be Happy and Free in Russia?, was left unfinished at his death on 27 December 1877 (Old Style), which is 8 January 1878 in the modern calendar, and was first published in 1879.

poets.name: Frederick Locker-Lampson
poets.credit: Photograph of Frederick Locker-Lampson, 1867 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Frederick Locker-Lampson (1821–1895), known as Frederick Locker for most of his writing life, was an English poet. Born at Greenwich Hospital, he worked as a clerk in the Admiralty and published London Lyrics in 1857, a slim volume of polished society verse that he went on revising and enlarging through many later editions.

His light, graceful, gently ironical manner is often set beside that of Praed. The poems here come from the 1904 Methuen edition of London Lyrics (the early pieces of 1857) and from a selection of his works printed by Edward Moxon in 1865.

poets.name: Sir Richard Francis Burton
poets.credit: Frederic Leighton, c. 1872–75 (National Portrait Gallery, London) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Richard Francis Burton (1821–1890) was an English explorer, soldier, diplomat and Arabist. He travelled to Mecca in disguise, sought the source of the Nile, and is best remembered as the translator of The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night (the Arabian Nights) and of other Eastern texts.

His verse includes The Kasidah (1880), his own English poem published as a translation from a fictitious Persian poet, Haji Abdu, and his rendering of Camões's The Lusiads (1880), which is already in this archive under Camões.

poets.name: Mary Jane O'Donovan Rossa
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Mary Jane O'Donovan Rossa (b. 1845, Clonakilty) was the wife of the Fenian leader Jeremiah O'Donovan Rossa. She published a volume of Irish Lyrical Poems in New York in 1868.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Charlotte Grace O'Brien
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Charlotte Grace O'Brien (1845–1909), daughter of William Smith O'Brien, was a novelist and poet who also devoted herself to the welfare of Irish emigrants.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: John Addington Symonds
poets.credit: Portrait of John Addington Symonds, 1889 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Addington Symonds (1840–1893) was an English poet, literary critic and cultural historian.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 6, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Cosmo Monkhouse
poets.credit: Portrait of Cosmo Monkhouse by John McLure Hamilton · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Cosmo Monkhouse (1840–1901) was a British poet and critic.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 6, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson
poets.credit: Portrait of Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson by Erwin Raupp, before 1909 (restored by Adam Cuerden; National Library of Norway) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson (1832–1910) was a Norwegian poet, novelist, dramatist and public campaigner, one of the “four great ones” of nineteenth-century Norwegian literature. He wrote the words of the national hymn “Yes, We Love This Land Forever,” and was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1903.

The poems here are Arthur Hubbell Palmer’s English versions, made in the original meters and published as Poems and Songs (American-Scandinavian Foundation, 1915); Bjørnson’s originals are in Norwegian. Many began as songs inside his peasant tales and plays, such as Synnøve Solbakken and Arne, others as occasional verse for national causes.

poets.name: William Morris
poets.credit: Portrait of William Morris · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Morris (1834–1896) was an English designer, socialist, and poet, a central figure of the Pre-Raphaelite circle whose vast output includes the narrative cycle The Earthly Paradise and the Icelandic-inspired epic Sigurd the Volsung. His first long narrative poem, The Life and Death of Jason (1867), tells the story of Jason and the Argo in seventeen books of rhymed couplets.
In later years his political convictions produced the direct, rallying verse of Chants for Socialists and The Pilgrims of Hope.

poets.name: James Thomson (B.V.)
poets.credit: Photographic portrait of James Thomson (B.V.), 1860 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James Thomson (1834–1882), who wrote as "B.V.", was a Scottish poet and essayist who made his living in London as a clerk and journalist. His best-known work, The City of Dreadful Night, appeared in the National Reformer in 1874 and in book form in 1880.

The poems filed here come from three volumes: The City of Dreadful Night and Other Poems (1880), Vane's Story, Weddah and Om-el-Bonain, and Other Poems (1881), and A Voice from the Nile, and Other Poems (1884). His "Attempts at Translation from Heine" are filed under Heinrich Heine, and The City of Dreadful Night itself stands as a work.

poets.name: James Brunton Stephens
bio: James Brunton Stephens (1835–1902) was a Scottish-born poet who emigrated to Queensland in 1866 and worked as a teacher and civil servant.
His books include Convict Once (1871) and Miscellaneous Poems; his poem The Dominion of Australia (1877) looked forward to federation.

poets.name: Joseph Ashby-Sterry
bio: Joseph Ashby-Sterry (1836–1917) was an English poet and novelist, an enthusiast for boating on the Thames, much of whose light verse celebrates river and drawing-room life.
He wrote regularly for the press and was on the staff of the London Graphic; his verse was collected in volumes such as Boudoir Ballads (1876).

poets.name: Alfred Austin
poets.credit: Alfred Austin, photograph by Russell & Sons (before 1901) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alfred Austin (1835–1913) was an English poet and journalist, born near Leeds. He wrote for the Standard and the National Review, and in 1896 succeeded Tennyson as Poet Laureate, an office he held until his death.
The poem given here is taken from Edmund H. Garrett's anthology Victorian Songs: Lyrics of the Affections and Nature (Boston: Little, Brown, 1895).

poets.name: Lord de Tabley (John Leicester Warren)
poets.credit: John Leicester Warren, Lord de Tabley, portrait · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Leicester Warren, third Baron de Tabley (1835–1895), was an English poet, classical scholar and student of botany and numismatics. His mature verse appeared in Poems, Dramatic and Lyrical (1893; a second series followed in 1895) and was admired by later poets.
The poems given here are taken from Edmund H. Garrett's anthology Victorian Songs: Lyrics of the Affections and Nature (Boston: Little, Brown, 1895).

poets.name: Richard Garnett
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of Richard Garnett, Illustrated London News (1892) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Garnett (1835–1906) was an English librarian, scholar, biographer and poet. He worked in the British Museum Library from 1851 and became Keeper of Printed Books in 1890; he also wrote many biographies and contributed widely to the Dictionary of National Biography.

His own verse includes Io in Egypt and other poems (1859), the sonnets and lyrics of Poems (1893) besides the tales of The Twilight of the Gods (1888) and several ballads such as the two printed here.

poets.name: Charles Henry Webb
bio: Charles Henry Webb (1834–1905) was an American humorist, journalist and poet, born at Rouse’s Point, New York. He went to sea as a boy, wrote for the New York Times and Tribune under the name “John Paul”, and founded the San Francisco weekly The Californian in 1864.
The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin, 1900).

poets.name: William B. C. Riddell
bio: William B. C. Riddell (1835–1856) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: George du Maurier
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: George du Maurier (1834–1896) was a French-British cartoonist, illustrator and novelist, known for his work in Punch and for the novels Peter Ibbetson and Trilby.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Mary Emily Bradley
bio: Mary Emily Bradley (1835–1898) was an American poet and writer of stories for girls, born at Easton, Maryland, and later living in New York and Washington. She was encouraged in her verse-writing by Richard Henry Stoddard and published the volume Hidden Sweetness in 1886.
The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin, 1900).

poets.name: W. S. Gilbert
poets.credit: Photograph of W. S. Gilbert by Elliott & Fry, c. 1882 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Schwenck Gilbert (1836–1911) was an English dramatist, librettist and comic poet. Before he turned to the stage he made his name with the Bab Ballads, comic verses he published in magazines from the 1860s and illustrated with his own drawings, built on topsy-turvy logic and a deadpan manner.

With the composer Arthur Sullivan he wrote fourteen comic operas for the Savoy Theatre, among them H.M.S. Pinafore, The Pirates of Penzance, Iolanthe and The Mikado. Songs of a Savoyard gathers his own favourites among the lyrics of those pieces, patter songs and ballads that satirise class, law, fashion and officialdom.

poets.name: Alexander Wilmot
bio: Alexander Wilmot (1836–1923) collected and arranged The Poetry of South Africa (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle & Rivington; Cape Town: J. C. Juta & Co., 1887), an anthology of verse from the Cape Colony, Natal and the Transvaal, and printed some of his own verse in it.

This archive holds 6 poems printed under this name in that volume, in Wilmot’s spelling. His own pieces concern the 1820 Settlers, the drought lands and the Transvaal. Dates are those of a standard reference.

poets.name: Thomas Ashe
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Ashe, Illustrated London News (11 January 1890) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Ashe (1836–1889) was an English poet, born in Stockport and educated at St Catharine's College, Cambridge. His collections include The Sorrows of Hypsipyle (1866), Poems (1886) and Songs Now Forgotten (1888).
The songs given here are taken from Edmund H. Garrett's anthology Victorian Songs: Lyrics of the Affections and Nature (Boston: Little, Brown, 1895).

poets.name: Celia Thaxter
poets.credit: Portrait: Childe Hassam — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Celia Laighton Thaxter (1835–1894) was an American poet and essayist, born at Portsmouth, New Hampshire. She grew up on the Isles of Shoals, where her father kept the lighthouse, and lived much of her life on Appledore Island; her books include Among the Isles of Shoals (1873) and a volume of Poems (1872).
The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin, 1900).

poets.name: Matilda Betham-Edwards
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Matilda Betham-Edwards (1836–1919) was an English novelist, travel writer and Francophile, and a prolific poet, who also wrote a number of children's books.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Frances Ridley Havergal
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of Frances Ridley Havergal (frontispiece, Project Gutenberg eText 18444) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Frances Ridley Havergal (1836–1879) was an English poet, hymn writer and singer, born at Astley in Worcestershire, the youngest child of the Rev. William Henry Havergal, a clergyman and composer. She was a gifted pianist and linguist, and her hymns, among them ‘Take my life, and let it be’ and ‘Who is on the Lord’s side?’, were sung throughout the English-speaking world. She died at Caswell Bay in Wales at the age of forty-two.

Her books of verse include The Ministry of Song (1869), Under the Surface (1874) and Loyal Responses (1878). The poems here are taken from an undated Toronto printing (Willard Tract Depot) of the Author’s Authorized Edition, with a prefatory note by her sister Maria V. G. Havergal. The book’s own groups are kept in each poem’s collection field, and the text comes from an OCR scan, so a few readings may still need correction.

poets.name: Edward Ernest Bowen
bio: Edward Ernest Bowen (1836–1901) was an English schoolmaster, for more than forty years a master at Harrow School. He wrote the words of a number of Harrow school songs, among them "Forty Years On" (1872).
His occasional verse, much of it on school and religious themes, was printed in magazines and anthologies; "Shemuel," a poem on the first Christmas night, appears in The Home Book of Verse (1912).

poets.name: Theodore Harding Rand
poets.credit: Portrait of Theodore H. Rand, after a painting by J. W. L. Porter, frontispiece of Song-Waves (1900) · Public domain (Project Gutenberg)
bio: Theodore Harding Rand (1835–1900) was a Canadian educator and poet, a Doctor of Civil Law who served as Superintendent of Education in Nova Scotia and in New Brunswick and later taught at McMaster University, Toronto. He is also named on the title page of Song-Waves as the author of A Treasury of Canadian Verse.

His verse appeared in At Minas Basin, and Other Poems (Toronto: William Briggs, 1897), mostly sonnets and lyrics of the Bay of Fundy and the Annapolis Valley, and in Song-Waves (Toronto: William Briggs, 1900), a sequence of short untitled lyrics followed by a handful of titled poems.

poets.name: Vítězslav Hálek
poets.credit: Portrait of Vítězslav Hálek, from Humoristické listy (10 October 1874) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Vítězslav Hálek (1835–1874) was a Czech poet, prose writer and journalist, a leading figure of the Czech literary generation of the 1850s and 1860s. His lyric collection Večerní písně (Evening Songs, 1859) made his name with its tender, song-like poems of love and nature.
The poems here are drawn from Joseph Štýbr's English translation of Evening Songs, published in Boston in 1920.

poets.name: Giosuè Carducci
poets.credit: Photograph of Giosuè Carducci, late 19th or early 20th century (photographer unknown) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Giosuè Carducci (1835–1907) was the leading Italian poet of his age and the first Italian to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1906. A professor of Italian literature at Bologna for over four decades, he set his classical learning and republican, anticlerical convictions against what he saw as the sentimental excesses of Italian Romanticism.

He is best known for the pagan, defiant “Hymn to Satan” and for the Odi barbare, which adapted Greek and Latin metres to Italian verse. The translations here are by the American writer Frank Sewall, from his 1893 English introduction to Carducci's work.

poets.name: Rabindranath Tagore
poets.credit: Rabindranath Tagore, 1909 photograph, published in Les Prix Nobel 1913 (1914) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Rabindranath Tagore (1861–1941) was a Bengali poet, songwriter, playwright, novelist and educator, born into a prominent family in Calcutta. He wrote chiefly in Bengali, founded a school at Santiniketan, and in 1913 became the first non-European to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature.

The poems here are his own English prose renderings of his Bengali verse: Gitanjali (Song Offerings, 1912), the devotional poems that W. B. Yeats introduced to English readers, and The Gardener (1915), a gathering of love lyrics and poems of youth and life. Tagore translated them himself, and the English is often freer than the Bengali, abridging or paraphrasing as he saw fit. Two further books of 1916 are also gathered here: Stray Birds, his book of short aphoristic poems, and Fruit-Gathering, a further collection of lyrics. The Crescent Moon (1913), his book of poems about children and their mothers, is gathered here too.

poets.name: Katharine Tynan Hinkson
poets.credit: Photograph of Katharine Tynan, c. 1890s–1910s · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Katharine Tynan Hinkson (dates as printed in Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920): 1861–1931) was an Irish poet and novelist, born in Dublin. A friend of the young W. B. Yeats and part of the Irish literary revival, she wrote devotional and pastoral verse as well as a great many novels.
She married the barrister Henry Hinkson. Her poems here come from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: Owen Seaman
bio: Sir Owen Seaman (1861–1936) was an English parodist and light-verse writer who edited the humorous magazine Punch from 1906 to 1932. He was created a baronet in 1933.
His verse, as in To an Old Fogey and the war poem Thomas of the Light Heart, mixes satire with patriotic sentiment. The poems here come from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: Henry Cust
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Henry John Cockayne Cust, known as Harry Cust (1861–1917), was an English politician and newspaper editor who also wrote verse.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Gabriel Setoun
bio: Gabriel Setoun was the pen name of the Scottish poet and author Thomas Nicoll Hepburn (1861–1930). He is remembered chiefly for The Child World (1896), a book of verses for children.
He also wrote prose sketches of Scottish life, among them Robert Urquhart (1896) and Sunshine and Haar (1898), and a life of Robert Burns.

poets.name: May Byron
bio: Mary Clarissa Byron, née Gillington (1861–1936), wrote as May Byron. A British writer and poet, she is best known for her abridgements of J. M. Barrie's Peter Pan and for the "A Day with" series of anthologies.
Her own verse was gathered in The Wind on the Heath: Ballads and Lyrics (1911).

poets.name: Maurice Hewlett
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Maurice Henry Hewlett (1861–1923) was an English historical novelist, poet and essayist.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Ethel Castilla
bio: Ethel Castilla (1861–1937) was an Australian poet, journalist and story writer, born at Kyneton, Victoria, and long resident in Melbourne. She was a founder of the Austral Salon, a meeting place for women writers and thinkers.
Her best-known poem, "An Australian Girl", first appeared in a Melbourne newspaper and gave its name to her collection The Australian Girl, and Other Verses (1900).

poets.name: Mary E. Coleridge
poets.credit: Photograph of Mary Elizabeth Coleridge, 1883 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mary Elizabeth Coleridge (1861–1907) was born in London into the family of Samuel Taylor Coleridge, to whom she was related as a great-great-niece. She wrote novels, essays and reviews, but her poems, which she published only anonymously or under the pseudonym Anodos ("Wanderer", taken from George MacDonald's Phantastes), are what last. They first appeared in Fancy's Following (1896, a private-press edition of 125 copies) and Fancy's Guerdon (1897).

She wished her verse to stay unsigned during her lifetime, fearing to tarnish a famous name. After her death Henry Newbolt gathered the seventy-seven pieces already printed, together with the rest of her uncollected work, in Poems (1908). The book shows her in the short lyric: terse, musical and intimate, with an eye for the strange and the uncanny. Robert Bridges, who knew her, was among her early admirers.

poets.name: Henry Newbolt
poets.credit: Portrait of Henry Newbolt · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Newbolt (1862–1938) was an English poet best known for patriotic and naval verse such as Vitài Lampada and Drake's Drum, written to celebrate duty, empire, and the sea.
His confident public rhetoric made him one of the most widely recited poets of the pre-1914 era.

poets.name: Gilbert Parker
poets.credit: Gilbert Parker in 1922, photograph by Keystone View · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Gilbert Parker (1862–1932) was born at Camden East, Ontario, and became a novelist, best known for his stories of Canada and the Pacific, before settling in England. He sat as a Conservative Member of Parliament for Gravesend from 1900 to 1918 and was made a baronet in 1915.

His two books of verse are here: A Lover’s Diary (1894), a sequence of sonnets, and Embers (1895), a miscellany of ballads, songs and lyrics of memory, the north and the East. Several of the Embers lyrics were later set to music, among others by Sir Edward Elgar. The texts are from the Project Gutenberg editions of the complete books, which carry the author’s later prefatory notes.

poets.name: Francis William Lauderdale Adams
bio: Francis William Lauderdale Adams (1862–1893) was a poet and journalist, born in Malta and educated in England, who went to Australia in 1884.
He published Songs of the Army of the Night (1888) and died young.

poets.name: William Pember Reeves
poets.era: Australian and New Zealand (19th and early 20th century)
poets.credit: Portrait of William Pember Reeves (photographer unidentified), c. 1887 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Pember Reeves (1857–1932) was a New Zealand politician, historian and writer, born in Lyttelton. He served as a cabinet minister in the Liberal government, then as New Zealand's agent-general and High Commissioner in London, and later directed the London School of Economics.
He is best known for the history The Long White Cloud; his poem New Zealand is widely anthologised.

poets.name: Norman Gale
bio: Norman Gale (1862–1942) was an English poet whose light, pastoral lyrics made his name in the 1890s, notably in Orchard Songs (1893).
The songs given here are taken from Edmund H. Garrett's anthology Victorian Songs: Lyrics of the Affections and Nature (Boston: Little, Brown, 1895).

poets.name: Hubert Church
poets.era: Australian and New Zealand (19th and early 20th century)
bio: Hubert Church (1857–1932) was a New Zealand poet.
Two of his poems appear in The Oxford Book of Australasian Verse (1918).

poets.name: James Hebblethwaite
poets.era: Australian and New Zealand (19th and early 20th century)
bio: James Hebblethwaite (1857–1921) was an Australian poet whose verse appeared in the Sydney Bulletin and in book form.
Walter Murdoch included three of his poems in The Oxford Book of Australasian Verse (1918).

poets.name: Percy F. Sinnett
bio: Percy F. Sinnett was born at Norwood, South Australia, and died at North Adelaide at the age of twenty-two. He wrote a number of political poems.
His poem on the loss of the steamer Tararua, written when he was eighteen, was reprinted in Stedman's Victorian Anthology (1895).

poets.name: Thomas William Heney
bio: Thomas William Heney (1862–1928) was an Australian journalist, poet and novelist, born in Sydney, who later edited the Sydney Morning Herald.
His verse was collected in In Middle Harbour, and Other Verse.

poets.name: J. P. Bourke
poets.era: Australian and New Zealand (19th and early 20th century)
bio: John Phillip Bourke (1860–1914) was an Australian poet.
One of his poems appears in The Oxford Book of Australasian Verse (1918).

poets.name: John Bernard O'Hara
bio: John Bernard O'Hara (1862–1927) was an Australian poet.
His books include Songs of the South and Lyrics of Nature.

poets.name: G. W. L. Marshall-Hall
poets.era: Australian and New Zealand (19th and early 20th century)
bio: George William Louis Marshall-Hall (1862–1915) was an English-born composer and conductor who became the first Ormond Professor of Music at the University of Melbourne.
He also wrote verse, and two of his sonnets appear in The Oxford Book of Australasian Verse (1918).

poets.name: Arthur Christopher Benson
poets.credit: Portrait: Allen Hastings Fry — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Arthur Christopher Benson (1862–1925) was an English essayist, poet and academic, Master of Magdalene College, Cambridge. He wrote the words of the Coronation Ode of 1902, including the song "Land of Hope and Glory".
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Inez K. Hyland
bio: Inez K. Hyland (1863–1892) was an Australian poet who died young.
Her verse was collected in In Sunshine and in Shadow.

poets.name: Arthur W. Jose
poets.era: Australian and New Zealand (19th and early 20th century)
bio: Arthur Wilberforce Jose (1863–1934) was an English-born Australian historian and writer, author of a History of Australasia.
He also wrote verse, and three of his poems appear in The Oxford Book of Australasian Verse (1918).

poets.name: John Sandes
bio: John Sandes (1863–1938) was an Australian journalist and poet.
His verse includes Ballads of Battle.

poets.name: Elizabeth Craigmyle
bio: Elizabeth (Bessie) Craigmyle (1863–1933) was a Scottish poet and translator.
Her books include Poems and Translations (1886) and A Handful of Pansies (1888). She is represented here by a Scots ballad lyric from Stedman’s Victorian Anthology (1895).

poets.name: George Essex Evans
bio: George Essex Evans (1863–1909) was an English-born poet who emigrated to Queensland as a young man and farmed on the Darling Downs.
His books include Loraine, and Other Verses (1898), and he wrote the Federation 'Ode for Commonwealth Day'.

poets.name: Mary Colborne-Veel
bio: Mary Colborne-Veel (1863–1923) was a New Zealand poet and writer.
Her verse was collected in The Fairest of the Angels, and Other Verse.

poets.name: Sydney Jephcott
bio: Sydney Jephcott (1864–1951) was an Australian poet and journalist who lived on the upper Murray in Victoria.
His books include The Secrets of the South (1892).

poets.name: Herbert P. Horne
bio: Herbert Percy Horne (1864–1916) was an English architect, art historian and poet, born in London. About 1882 he began the study of art with Selwyn Image, and with him started the Hobby Horse in 1886, later becoming its sole editor.
He was an authority on printing and book decoration; his one small volume of verse, Diversi Colores, appeared in 1891.

poets.name: C. H. Souter
poets.era: Australian and New Zealand (19th and early 20th century)
bio: C. H. Souter (Charles Henry Souter, 1864–1944) was an Australian poet.
Two of his poems, 'The Mallee Fire' and 'Bound for Sourabaya!', appear in Walter Murdoch's Oxford Book of Australasian Verse (1918).

poets.name: Charles Murray
bio: Charles Murray (1864–1941) was born at Alford in Aberdeenshire and trained as an engineer. In 1888 he went out to South Africa, where he worked on the Rand and in the Transvaal, and later became a senior official in the Public Works Department.

Far from home he wrote verse in the Scots of the Aberdeenshire country he had left, much of it first printed in Scottish periodicals. His first volume, Hamewith, appeared in Aberdeen in 1900, and the enlarged collection, with an introduction by Andrew Lang and many new poems, was published in London by Constable in 1916; that is the book printed here.
Murray retired to Banchory in Aberdeenshire in 1924 and died there in 1941.

poets.name: Andrew Barton 'Banjo' Paterson
poets.credit: Portrait of A. B. Paterson, c. 1890 (National Library of Australia) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Andrew Barton 'Banjo' Paterson (1864–1941) was an Australian bush poet, solicitor and journalist, born near Orange, New South Wales, who reported the Boer War as a correspondent.
He published The Man from Snowy River and Other Verses (1895) and Rio Grande's Last Race (1902), and wrote the words of 'Waltzing Matilda'.

poets.name: Jessie Mackay
bio: Jessie Mackay (1864–1938) was a New Zealand poet and journalist, born in Canterbury.
Her first volume was The Spirit of the Rangatira and Other Ballads (1889); she was a leading New Zealand verse writer of her time.

poets.name: Barry Pain
bio: Barry Pain (1864–1928) was an English humorist and writer of light verse and short stories, educated at Sedbergh and at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge.
He is remembered for the comic monologues of Eliza (1900) and for his parodies, of which The Poets at Tea is the best known.

poets.name: Moira O'Neill
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Moira O'Neill was the pseudonym of Agnes Shakespeare Higginson (1864–1955), an Irish-Canadian poet who wrote ballads and other verse inspired by County Antrim, where she lived at Cushendun.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Arthur O'Shaughnessy
poets.credit: Portrait of Arthur O'Shaughnessy · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Arthur O'Shaughnessy (1844–1881) was an English poet who worked as a herpetologist at the British Museum while publishing richly musical, melancholy verse.
His Ode, beginning "We are the music makers," is his most famous poem and a manifesto for the visionary power of artists.

poets.name: Marcus Clarke
bio: Marcus Clarke (1846–1881) was an English-born journalist and novelist who settled in Melbourne in 1863.
He is best known for the convict novel For the Term of His Natural Life (1874), and also wrote essays, plays and occasional verse.

poets.name: Ada Cambridge
bio: Ada Cambridge (1844–1926) was an English-born novelist and poet who emigrated to Australia in 1870 as the wife of a clergyman and lived in Victoria.
Her verse appeared in Unspoken Thoughts (1887) and later volumes, and she wrote the memoir Thirty Years in Australia (1903).

poets.name: James Ashcroft Noble
bio: James Ashcroft Noble (1844–1896) was an English journalist, critic and minor poet who wrote for the periodical press and lived for years in Liverpool. He is best remembered for his critical essays, collected in The Sonnet in England and Other Essays (1893).
The one poem included here, "The Red Thread of Honour", a ballad of a British regiment in India, was printed in R. Brimley Johnson's 1894 anthology.

poets.name: Alexander Bathgate
bio: Alexander Bathgate (1845–1930) was a Scottish-born lawyer and writer who settled in Otago, New Zealand.
His verse was collected in Far South Fancies.

poets.name: Mary Hannay Foott
bio: Mary Hannay Foott (1846–1918) was a Scottish-born poet who emigrated to Australia as a girl and later lived on a Queensland station.
Her books include Where the Pelican Builds and Other Poems (1885) and Morna Lee and Other Poems.

poets.name: Richard Watson Gilder
poets.credit: Photograph of Richard Watson Gilder (before 1913) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Watson Gilder (1844–1909) was an American poet and editor, born at Bordentown, New Jersey. From 1881 until his death he edited The Century Magazine, one of the most influential American periodicals of the period.
His own poems, including the sonnet sequence The New Day (1875) and later lyrics, were admired for their delicacy and were frequently anthologised.

poets.name: Maurice Thompson
poets.credit: Portrait of Maurice Thompson (before 1900) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Maurice Thompson (1844–1901) was an American novelist, poet, and essayist, born at Fairfield, Indiana, and raised in Georgia. He served in the Confederate army, then practised as an engineer and lawyer in Indiana, and became an expert on archery.
He is best known for the novel Alice of Old Vincennes (1900). His lyric poems on nature, such as “Fertility”, were collected in volumes including Songs of Fair Weather (1883).

poets.name: Samuel Waddington
bio: Samuel Waddington (1844–1923) was a British civil servant, traveller and poet.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 8, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Ernest Myers
bio: Ernest Myers (1844–1921) was an English poet, classicist and author.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 8, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: John Banister Tabb
bio: John Banister Tabb (1845–1909) was an American poet and Roman Catholic priest, born in Amelia County, Virginia. He served in the Confederate army, was captured and imprisoned at Point Lookout, where he met Sidney Lanier, and later taught at St Charles College in Maryland.
He wrote very short, finished lyrics, often of four lines, on nature, childhood, and faith.

poets.name: Louisa S. Bevington
bio: Louisa Sarah Bevington (1845–1895) was an English poet and essayist, a freethinker and later an anarchist. Her verse appeared in Key Notes (1876), Poems, Lyrics and Sonnets (1882) and Liberty Lyrics (1895).
Her long poem “The Valley of Remorse” is printed in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Emily H. Hickey
bio: Emily Henrietta Hickey (1845–1924) was an Irish poet and critic, born in County Wexford. She helped Frederick Furnivall to found the Browning Society in 1881.
Her poems include Verse Tales, Lyrics and Translations (1889); “Harebells”, “Madonna della Vita” and “A Sea Story” are in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Alexander Anderson
bio: Alexander Anderson (1845–1909), known by his pen name “Surfaceman”, was a Scottish poet born at Kirkconnel in Dumfriesshire. He worked as a railway labourer and later in the library of Edinburgh University.
His books include Songs of Labour (1873), The Two Angels and Other Poems (1875), Songs of the Rail (1877) and Ballads and Sonnets (1879).

poets.name: Emily Lawless
poets.credit: Photograph of Emily Lawless, photographer unknown (late 19th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Hon. Emily Lawless (1845–1913) was an Irish novelist, poet and naturalist, born in County Kildare, daughter of Lord Cloncurry. She is best known for her novels Hurrish and Grania and for the poems of With the Wild Geese, and her love of the Burren and the Atlantic coast of the west of Ireland runs through her verse.

The poems here are taken from The Inalienable Heritage, and Other Poems, privately printed in 1914, the year after her death. Many were written during her last years of illness. Edith Sichel’s preface to the volume is not reproduced.

poets.name: George Francis Savage-Armstrong
bio: George Francis Savage-Armstrong (1845–1906) was an Irish poet and scholar, Professor of History and English Literature at Queen's College, Cork, from 1871 to 1905. He published many volumes of verse, including Ballads of Down (1901).
"The Wreck off Mizen-Head" is a ballad of a rescue from a shipwreck off the Cork coast and was chosen by R. Brimley Johnson for his 1894 collection.

poets.name: Walter Crane
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Walter Crane (1845–1915) was a British artist and book illustrator and an advocate of socialism and the Arts and Crafts movement. He also wrote occasional verse.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Eugene Lee-Hamilton
poets.credit: Photograph of Eugene Lee-Hamilton, photographer unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Eugene Lee-Hamilton (1845–1907) was an English poet, born in London and brought up largely on the Continent; he was the half-brother of the writer Vernon Lee. A long illness left him an invalid for many years, a circumstance that colours much of his work, and he is remembered chiefly as a sonneteer, the author of Sonnets of the Wingless Hours (1894).

The poems here are taken from Apollo and Marsyas, and Other Poems (London: Elliot Stock, 1884): dramatic dialogues, narrative poems and odes, followed by a closing group of sonnets. The prose Introduction to the volume is not included.

poets.name: Lloyd Mifflin
bio: Lloyd Mifflin (1846–1921) was an American poet and painter, born at Columbia, Pennsylvania, on the Susquehanna, where he lived most of his life. He is remembered chiefly for his sonnets, which draw on the classical world and the landscape of his own river valley.
Several of his short poems were included by Knowles in his anthology of American lyrics, and Jessie Rittenhouse later placed him among the older poets of the period.

poets.name: William Canton
poets.credit: Portrait of William Canton by Russell, Baker Street, 1896 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Canton (1845–1926) was a British poet, journalist and writer, best known for his writing for children.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 8, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Michael Field
poets.credit: Photograph of Katharine Bradley and Edith Cooper, before 1913, photographer unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Michael Field was the shared pen name of two English women, the aunt Katharine Harris Bradley (1846–1914) and her niece Edith Emma Cooper (1862–1913), who lived and wrote together for most of their adult lives.
