Their early verse dramas appeared under the name in the 1880s, and for a time critics took “Michael Field” for a man; Robert Browning was among the first to praise the work. In later years both women became Roman Catholics, and their last books are devotional.

The poems here come from three books. Sight and Song (1892) answers paintings in European galleries, each poem taking the picture’s title and naming painter and gallery in its note. Underneath the Bough, in the 1898 edition with new songs added (preface dated 8 September 1898), gathers lyrics in numbered Books of Songs. From A Selection from the Poems of Michael Field (The Poetry Bookshop, 1923) only poems not already taken from those two books are included; the note on each says which earlier volume it was first printed in, among them Long Ago, Wild Honey, Poems of Adoration and Mystic Trees.

poets.name: Robert Cameron Rogers
bio: Robert Cameron Rogers (1862–1912) was an American poet, born at Buffalo, New York, who died at Santa Barbara, California, in 1912.
He is remembered chiefly for his song-lyric “The Rosary”, which was set to music by Ethelbert Nevin and became one of the most popular parlour songs of its time.

poets.name: Algernon Charles Swinburne
poets.credit: Portrait of Algernon Charles Swinburne · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Algernon Charles Swinburne (1837–1909) was an English poet notorious in his own day for the sensuous, metrically dazzling, and often scandalous verse of Poems and Ballads.
An ardent republican, he also wrote fervent political verse cheering Italian unification and liberty, alongside a huge later output of odes, elegies, and sonnets.

poets.name: Alexander Hay Japp
bio: Alexander Hay Japp (1837–1905) was a Scottish journalist, critic and biographer, born in Forfarshire. He wrote much under the pseudonym H. A. Page, and published lives of De Quincey and Robert Louis Stevenson.
His verse includes Circle of the Year, a sonnet sequence (1893), and Dramatic Pictures, English Rispetti, Sonnets, and Other Verse (1894).

poets.name: Henry Kendall
poets.credit: Photograph of Henry Kendall · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Kendall (1839–1882) was an Australian poet, born at Ulladulla, New South Wales, who worked as a clerk, a journalist and finally an inspector of forests.
His books include Poems and Songs (1862), Leaves from Australian Forests (1869) and Songs from the Mountains (1880).

poets.name: William Dean Howells
poets.credit: Photograph of William Dean Howells by Underwood & Underwood · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Dean Howells (1837–1920) was an American novelist, critic and editor, born at Martins Ferry, Ohio. He edited The Atlantic Monthly from 1871 to 1881, and championed literary realism in novels such as The Rise of Silas Lapham.
He began as a poet and, with John James Piatt, published Poems of Two Friends (1860); he continued to write occasional verse throughout his life.

poets.name: Byron Forceythe Willson
poets.credit: Portrait of Byron Forceythe Willson, from The Magazine of Poetry · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Byron Forceythe Willson (1837–1867) was an American poet born in Little Genesee, New York, and raised in Ohio. He wrote patriotic verse during the Civil War, including “The Old Sergeant”, which appeared in The Atlantic Monthly in 1863.
He died young, in 1867. Knowles included his lyric “No More” in his anthology of American lyrics.

poets.name: John Todhunter
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Todhunter was born in Dublin, practised as a physician and later turned to literature, writing poems and verse plays. He settled in Bedford Park, London.
Yeats printed his poems "The Banshee" and "Aghadoe" in A Book of Irish Verse (1900).

poets.name: Herman Charles Merivale
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Herman Charles Merivale (1839–1906) was an English dramatist and poet, the son of the civil servant and historian Herman Merivale.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: James Ryder Randall
poets.credit: Photograph of James Ryder Randall by Blessing & Co., Baltimore (before 1908) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James Ryder Randall (1839–1908) was an American poet and journalist, born at Baltimore, Maryland. He was teaching at Poydras College in Louisiana in April 1861 when news of the Baltimore riot moved him to write “Maryland, My Maryland”.
Set to the tune of “O Tannenbaum”, the poem became a rallying song of the Confederacy. Randall later worked as a newspaper editor in Georgia.

poets.name: John Hartley
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Hartley (1839–1915) was a Halifax writer of Yorkshire dialect verse and prose. Moorman's anthology calls him the most versatile dialect writer Yorkshire had produced: for some fifty years he poured out lyric song and prose tale, most of it in the Halifax Original Illuminated Clock Almanac, which he began in 1867 and edited until his death. His Yorkshire Lyrics appeared in 1898.

This selection gathers the verse of Yorkshire Ditties (First and Second Series), Yorkshire Lyrics, including its closing section of fugitive verses not in dialect, and two poems from F. W. Moorman's Yorkshire Dialect Poems (1916). Poems that appear in more than one volume are given once; the prose pieces of the Ditties volumes are left out. Dialect spelling is kept as printed.

poets.name: Rossiter Johnson
bio: Rossiter Johnson (1840–1931) was an American author, editor and historian, who also wrote verse.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: A Woman of the War.

poets.name: Joseph O’Connor
bio: Joseph O’Connor is named as the author of the Civil War poem The White Rose in Eggleston’s anthology; his dates are not given there.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: The White Rose.

poets.name: Rossiter Worthington Raymond
bio: Rossiter Worthington Raymond (1840–1918) was an American mining engineer, Union soldier, editor and author who also wrote verse. Eggleston prints his Civil War songs under R. W. Raymond and Rossiter W. Raymond.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where they are printed under his or her name: The Banner of the Stars; Cavalry Song.

poets.name: Lady Charlotte Elliot
bio: Lady Charlotte Elliot (1839–1880) was an English poet, the author of Medusa and Other Poems (1878).
Her poem “The Wife of Loki”, on the Norse myth, is included in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: John White Chadwick
poets.credit: Portrait of John White Chadwick · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John White Chadwick (1840–1904) was an American writer and Unitarian clergyman.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “Mugford's Victory” and “Full Cycle”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Constance Fenimore Woolson
bio: Constance Fenimore Woolson (1840–1894) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Kentucky Belle”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Mary Bolles Branch
bio: Mary Bolles Branch (1840–1922) was an American poet and writer, born in Connecticut.
Her best-known poem, "The Petrified Fern", was widely reprinted and was included in Edmund Clarence Stedman's An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Toru Dutt
poets.credit: Portrait of Toru Dutt, reproduced in Harihar Das, Life and Letters of Toru Dutt (1921) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Toru Dutt (1856-1877) was born in Calcutta into a Bengali Christian family and educated in France and England. After returning to India in 1873 she taught herself Sanskrit, and before her death from consumption at twenty-one she published translations from the French and a French novel.

Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan, her English retellings of Sanskrit legends, appeared posthumously in 1882 with a memoir by Edmund Gosse; the 1885 edition added the miscellaneous poems given here, among them the two sonnets and Our Casuarina Tree.

poets.name: Sidney Royse Lysaght
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sidney Royse Lysaght (1856–1941) was a British writer of Irish ancestry.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Jane Barlow
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Jane Barlow (1856–1917) was an Irish writer noted for novels and poems about the lives of the Irish peasantry, chiefly in the fictional villages of Lisconnell and Ballyhoy.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: John Davidson
poets.credit: Portrait: James Russell (1809-1899) photographer — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Davidson (1857–1909) was a Scottish poet, playwright and novelist, born in Barrhead, Renfrewshire. He came to London in the 1890s and made his name with Fleet Street Eclogues and the Ballads and Songs of 1894.

His verse ranges from vigorous ballads of city life to the Testaments of his later years. He took his own life in 1909. Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920) printed his long Ballad of Hell, given here.

poets.name: Duncan Campbell Scott
poets.credit: Portrait: unknown artist — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Duncan Campbell Scott (1862–1947), born in Ottawa, was a civil servant in the Department of Indian Affairs and one of the Confederation poets.

His first collection, The Magic House and Other Poems, appeared in 1893; the poems here predate it. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Thomas William Rolleston
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas William Rolleston was born in County Offaly and was a poet, translator and essayist of the Irish literary revival. He co-edited a Treasury of Irish Poetry with Stopford Brooke.
He died in 1920.

poets.name: Ernest Radford
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Ernest William Radford (1857–1919) was an English poet, critic and socialist, a follower of William Morris and an organiser of the Arts and Crafts movement.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: William Watson
bio: William Watson (1858–1935) was an English poet, born at Burley-in-Wharfedale, Yorkshire. He made his reputation in the 1890s with poems on public themes and with elegant, formal lyrics, and was often spoken of as a possible poet laureate.
He was knighted in 1917. His volumes include Wordsworth's Grave and Other Poems and The Hope of the World (1897). The poems here come from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: Victor James Daley
bio: Victor James Daley (1858–1905) was an Irish-born poet who came to Australia in 1878 and became a leading figure of Sydney's bohemian literary circle.
His books include At Dawn and Dusk (1898); Wine and Roses appeared after his death.

poets.name: Francis Thompson
poets.credit: Portrait of Francis Thompson · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Francis Thompson (1859–1907) was an English poet who spent years destitute and addicted to opium on the streets of London before his talent was discovered and he found refuge among Catholic friends.
His best-known poem, The Hound of Heaven, describes a soul fleeing and finally yielding to divine pursuit.

poets.name: George Sigerson
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: George Sigerson (1836–1925), born near Strabane, County Tyrone, was a Dublin physician, scholar and translator, author of Modern Ireland and Munster Poets and Poetry.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Alice Werner
bio: Alice Werner (1859–1935) was a British scholar of African languages and poet, later a professor at the School of Oriental Studies in London.
Her early verse, which includes the Australian ballad Bannerman of the Dandenong, was collected in A Time and Times.

poets.name: J. B. B. Nichols
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Bowyer Buchanan Nichols (1859–1939), known as Bowyer Nichols, was an English poet and artist, educated at Winchester and Balliol College, Oxford. With H. C. Beeching and J. W. Mackail he published the verse collections Love in Idleness (1883) and Love's Looking Glass (1891).
The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman's anthology A Victorian Anthology, 1837–1895 (Houghton Mifflin, 1895).

poets.name: Frederick Peterson
bio: Frederick Peterson was an American neurologist and poet, born in Faribault, Minnesota, in 1859 and a graduate of the University of Buffalo; he taught nervous and mental diseases at Columbia University.
He published Poems and Swedish Translations (1883) and In the Shade of Ygdrasil (1893).

poets.name: Lucy Evangeline Tilley
bio: Lucy Evangeline Tilley was born in Chatham, Ohio, in 1859 and died in Medina, Ohio, in 1890, having moved to Medina early in life.
Many of her poems appeared in magazines and weekly papers; they were collected in Little Rhymes in Brown (1886) and Verses (1892).

poets.name: Henry Charles Beeching
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Henry Charles Beeching (1859–1919) was a British clergyman, writer and poet, Dean of Norwich from 1911 to 1919.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Helen Gray Cone
bio: Helen Gray Cone (1859–1934) was an American poet and teacher, born in New York City. She graduated from the Normal College in 1876 and from 1899 was professor of English literature at Hunter College.
Her volumes of verse include Oberon and Puck (1885), The Ride to the Lady (1893) and Soldiers of the Light (1911).

poets.name: Edward J. Wheeler
bio: Edward Jewitt Wheeler (1859–1922) was an American editor and poet, born at Cleveland, Ohio. He edited The Literary Digest from 1895 to 1905 and Current Opinion from 1905, and was literary editor of Funk and Wagnalls.
He was one of the founders of the Poetry Society of America in 1909 and served as its first president.

poets.name: Rose Kavanagh
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Rose Kavanagh was an Irish poet and journalist, born in County Tyrone, who wrote for Irish periodicals. She died young, in 1891.
Her poem "Lough Bray" was included by Yeats in A Book of Irish Verse (1900).

poets.name: Arthur Reed Ropes
bio: Arthur Reed Ropes (1859–1933) was an English poet and librettist, born near London, the son of an American merchant settled in England. He was a Fellow of King's College, Cambridge, and published Poems in 1884.
He later wrote lyrics for the musical stage under the name Adrian Ross, and edited selections from the letters of Lady Mary Wortley Montagu.

poets.name: Susie Frances Harrison
bio: Susie Frances Harrison (1859–1935), who wrote under the pen-name Seranus, was a Canadian poet, novelist, music critic and composer, born in Toronto.
Her poems include the collection Pine, Rose and Fleur de Lis. The poem here comes from Edmund Clarence Stedman's A Victorian Anthology (1895).

poets.name: Ernest Rhys
poets.credit: Portrait of Ernest Rhys, from The Sketch, 1 July 1896 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ernest Rhys (1859–1946) was a Welsh-descended poet, editor and critic, born in London and brought up partly in Carmarthen. He founded and edited Everyman's Library for J. M. Dent, and his own poems appeared in the Rhymers' Club books and in A London Rose and Other Rhymes (1894).
Lyra Celtica calls him the leader of the neo-Celtic movement in Wales and prints 'The Night Ride' and part of 'The House of Hendra'.

poets.name: Charles F. Lummis
poets.credit: Portrait of Charles F. Lummis · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles F. Lummis (1859–1928) was an American journalist.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “John Charles Frémont”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Wallace Rice
poets.credit: Portrait of Wallace Rice · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Wallace Rice (1859–1939) was an American vexillographer.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “The First American Sailors”, “The Sudbury Fight”, “The Minute-Men of Northboro”, “Firstfruits in 1812” and “Defeat and Victory” among others; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Charles G. D. Roberts
poets.credit: Photograph of Charles G. D. Roberts, 1904 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Charles George Douglas Roberts (1860–1943) was a Canadian poet and prose writer, born in Douglas, New Brunswick. He studied at the University of New Brunswick, taught and edited in Toronto and New York, and became famous for his animal stories as well as his poems.
His volumes of verse include Orion, and Other Poems (1880), Songs of the Common Day (1893) and New York Nocturnes (1898). Anthologists of his own time grouped him with the American poets.

poets.name: George Santayana
bio: George Santayana (1863–1952) was a philosopher, essayist and poet, born in Madrid and raised in Boston. He taught philosophy at Harvard and wrote The Sense of Beauty (1896) and Interpretations of Poetry and Religion (1900).
His poetry, mostly in sonnet form, includes Sonnets and Other Verses (1894) and Lucifer (1899). Rittenhouse printed three of his sonnets in 1913.

poets.name: Alfred Perceval Graves
poets.credit: Portrait: Unknown authorUnknown author — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alfred Perceval Graves was born in Dublin and worked as a school inspector, while writing songs and verse and collecting Irish and Welsh folk music. His song "Father O'Flynn" became widely popular.
He was the father of the poet Robert Graves and died in 1931.

poets.name: Lewis Carroll
poets.credit: Portrait of Lewis Carroll · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Lewis Carroll, the pen name of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson (1832–1898), was an Oxford mathematician best known for the Alice books, whose fondness for nonsense and wordplay also produced a distinctive body of comic and whimsical verse.
The Hunting of the Snark and the parodies collected in Phantasmagoria remain classics of English nonsense poetry.

poets.name: Adam Lindsay Gordon
poets.credit: Photograph of Adam Lindsay Gordon by S. Milbourn, 1860 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Adam Lindsay Gordon (1833–1870) was an Anglo-Australian poet, born in the Azores and educated in England, who emigrated to South Australia in 1853 and worked as a mounted trooper, horse-breaker and steeplechase rider.
He published Sea Spray and Smoke Drift (1867) and Bush Ballads and Galloping Rhymes (1870), and died by his own hand at Brighton, Victoria.

poets.name: Margaret Crawford
bio: Margaret Crawford (born 1833) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 5 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: George Gordon McCrae
poets.era: Australian and New Zealand (19th and early 20th century)
bio: George Gordon McCrae (1833–1927) was a Scottish-born Australian poet and painter who came to Port Phillip as a child and worked for many years as a civil servant in Melbourne.
He published verse including The Story of Balladeadro and Mamba, and his poems draw on Australian scenery and Aboriginal subjects.

poets.name: Joseph Skipsey
poets.credit: Joseph Skipsey, photograph (1898; photographer unknown) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Joseph Skipsey (1832–1903) was an English poet from Northumberland who went down the pit as a child and worked as a miner for years. His lyrics were praised by Victorian critics and collected in Carols from the Coal-Fields (1886) and other volumes.
The songs given here are taken from Edmund H. Garrett's anthology Victorian Songs: Lyrics of the Affections and Nature (Boston: Little, Brown, 1895).

poets.name: Sir Edwin Arnold
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir Edwin Arnold (photograph, 19th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edwin Arnold (1832–1904) was an English poet, journalist and orientalist. Educated at King's College School, London, and University College, Oxford, he became principal of the Government Sanskrit College at Poona, India, in 1856, and returned to England in 1861.

He then worked for many years on the staff of the Daily Telegraph, serving as its editor-in-chief, and was made a Knight Commander of the Star of India. His verse epic The Light of Asia (1879), a life of the Buddha, was immensely popular in Britain and America and did much to introduce Buddhism to Western readers. He also translated Indian and Persian works and wrote further poems on Eastern themes.

poets.name: James Macfarlan
bio: James Macfarlan (born 1832; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Mary Woolsey Howland
bio: Mary Woolsey Howland (1832–1864) was an American poet from a New York family, one of the Woolsey sisters, who died in 1864. She is represented in this archive by a single poem, “In the Hospital”, which Knowles included in his anthology of American lyrics.
The poem was written during the years of the Civil War and is a quiet meditation on suffering and consolation.

poets.name: Edmund Clarence Stedman
poets.credit: Photograph of Edmund Clarence Stedman by Alman and Company, New York · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edmund Clarence Stedman (1833–1908) was an American poet and critic, born at Hartford, Connecticut. He earned his living as a stockbroker in New York while writing poetry and criticism, and edited, with Ellen Mackay Hutchinson, the Library of American Literature.
His critical books Victorian Poets (1875) and Poets of America (1885) were standard works; his own verse includes the satirical “Pan in Wall Street”.

poets.name: Sarah Anne Curzon
poets.credit: Portrait of Sarah Anne Curzon, Godey's Magazine (July 1897) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sarah Anne Curzon (1833–1898) was an English-born Canadian writer and advocate of women's suffrage, who lived in Toronto.
She wrote the poem and play Laura Secord, the Heroine of 1812 (1887). One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Annie Adams Fields
poets.credit: Portrait of Annie Adams Fields by John Singer Sargent, 1890 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Annie Adams Fields (1834–1915) was an American writer and literary hostess, born in Boston. As the wife of the publisher James T. Fields, she presided over a salon at 148 Charles Street, attended by Hawthorne, Longfellow, Dickens and other leading writers.
She wrote poems, memoirs and biographies, including Authors and Friends (1896) and Life and Letters of Harriet Beecher Stowe (1897).

poets.name: Rudyard Kipling
poets.credit: Portrait of Rudyard Kipling · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) was an English author born in Bombay, awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1907, whose verse gave voice to soldiers, machines, and the British imperial experience in vigorous, ballad-like rhythms.
Poems such as If—, Gunga Din, and Recessional made him one of the most quoted poets in the English language.

poets.name: John Keegan Casey
poets.credit: Convict photograph of John Keegan Casey, attributed to Thomas Larcom, before 1870 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Keegan Casey (1846–1870), who wrote as "Leo", was a poet and Fenian born near Mullingar, County Westmeath, the son of a peasant. Imprisoned in 1867, he died at twenty-three, and his funeral drew a very large crowd.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: J. Laurence Rentoul
poets.era: Australian and New Zealand (19th and early 20th century)
bio: James Laurence Rentoul (1846–1926) was an Irish-born Presbyterian minister who became a professor at Ormond College in the University of Melbourne.
He published collections of verse, and two of his poems appear in The Oxford Book of Australasian Verse (1918).

poets.name: Joseph I. C. Clarke
bio: Joseph I. C. Clarke (1846–1925) was an American dramatist.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “The Fighting Race”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: James Logie Robertson
bio: James Logie Robertson (1846–1922) was a Scottish schoolmaster, critic and poet who wrote in Scots under the pen-name Hugh Haliburton. His best-known verse collection is Horace in Homespun (1886).
His poem "Spring on the Ochils" is printed in The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse.

poets.name: Arthur Symons
poets.credit: Portrait: Coburn, Alvin Langdon, 1882-1966 -- Photographer — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Arthur Symons (1865–1945) was a Welsh-born poet and critic, a leading figure of the Decadent and Symbolist movements in Britain in the 1890s. His books of verse include Silhouettes (1892) and London Nights (1895).

His critical study The Symbolist Movement in Literature (1899) introduced French poets such as Verlaine and Mallarmé to English readers. The poems here come from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: Laurence Hope
poets.credit: Portrait of Adela Florence Nicolson (“Laurence Hope”) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Laurence Hope was the pen name of Adela Florence Nicolson (née Cory, 1865–1904), who was raised partly in India and married Colonel Malcolm Nicolson. She took her own life in 1904, two months after his death.

Her passionate verse was presented as translated from Indian poets, but the poems are her own, and she is best known for ‘Kashmiri Song’ (‘Pale hands I love beside the Shalimar’), which was set to music and made famous. The poems here come from India’s Love Lyrics (the American title of The Garden of Kama, 1901) and the posthumous Last Poems (1905).

poets.name: William Gay
bio: William Gay (1865–1897) was a Scottish-born poet who emigrated to Australia.
He published Christ on Olympus, and Other Poems (1893) and a volume of sonnets.

poets.name: Herbert Trench
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Frederic Herbert Trench (1865–1923) was an Irish poet.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Douglas Ainslie
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Douglas Ainslie (1865–1948) was a Scottish poet, translator, critic and diplomat, born in Paris and educated at Eton and at Balliol and Exeter Colleges, Oxford. He contributed to The Yellow Book.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Edward Dyson
bio: Edward Dyson (1865–1931) was an Australian journalist, poet and story writer, born in Victoria, who worked as a miner before turning to writing.
His books include Rhymes from the Mines, and Other Lines (1896).

poets.name: Alfred Cochrane
bio: Alfred Cochrane (1865–1948) was an English writer of light verse. Educated at Oxford, he played first-class cricket for Derbyshire (1884–86) and for Oxford University (1885–88), and wrote on sport.
His books of verse include The Kestrel's Nest and Other Verses (1894), Collected Verses (1903) and Later Verses (1918). The poems given here come from the first two.

poets.name: Dowell O'Reilly
bio: Dowell O'Reilly (1865–1923) was an Australian poet and short-story writer, born in Sydney, who also sat in the New South Wales parliament.
His verse was collected in Tears and Triumph (1913).

poets.name: Robert W. Chambers
bio: Robert William Chambers (1865–1933) was an American writer and illustrator, born in Brooklyn, New York, who became a popular novelist; his best-known book is the weird-fiction collection The King in Yellow (1895).
He is not to be confused with the Scottish publisher Robert Chambers (1802–1871). His comic dialect poem “The Recruit” is printed in Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Frank S. Williamson
poets.era: Australian and New Zealand (19th and early 20th century)
poets.credit: Portrait of Frank S. Williamson, 1920 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Frank S. Williamson (1865–1936) was an Australian poet whose verse was published by the Lothian Book Publishing Company.
Walter Murdoch included five of his poems in The Oxford Book of Australasian Verse (1918).

poets.name: A. G. Stephens
poets.era: Australian and New Zealand (19th and early 20th century)
poets.credit: Portrait of A. G. Stephens, c. 1910 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alfred George Stephens (1865–1933) was an Australian critic, editor and publisher, born in Toowoomba, Queensland. As editor of the Red Page of the Bulletin and later of the Bookfellow he was among the most influential literary critics in Australia.
He also wrote verse, and one poem, Babylon, appears in The Oxford Book of Australasian Verse (1918).

poets.name: Stephen Phillips
bio: Stephen Phillips (1868–1915) was an English poet and verse dramatist. He won sudden fame with his Poems of 1897 and with the plays Paolo and Francesca (1899), Herod (1900) and Ulysses (1902), which revived blank-verse drama on the London stage.
His popularity faded within a few years, and he died in 1915. The two short lyrics here come from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920); the extract from Herod printed there is not included.

poets.name: Jennings Carmichael
bio: Jennings Carmichael (1868–1904) was an Australian poet.
Her verse was published in a volume of Poems.

poets.name: Arthur Shearly Cripps
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Arthur Shearly Cripps (1869–1952) was an English-born Anglican priest, missionary, activist, short-story writer and poet who spent most of his life in Southern Rhodesia.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Henry Dawson Lowry
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Henry Dawson Lowry (1869–1906) was an English journalist, short-story writer, novelist and poet who wrote as H. D. Lowry.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Lord Alfred Douglas
bio: Lord Alfred Douglas (1870–1945) was an English poet, the younger son of the Marquess of Queensberry, and the close companion of Oscar Wilde, whose trials in 1895 made both their names notorious.
His own sonnets and lyrics, written in a clear late-Romantic manner, appeared in volumes such as The City of the Soul (1899). The poem here comes from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: Nora Hopper Chesson
bio: Nora Hopper Chesson (1871–1906) was a poet and story-writer of Irish descent, born in Exeter, who drew on Irish folklore and song. She belonged to the Celtic revival of the 1890s and was praised by W. B. Yeats.
She married the writer W. H. Chesson in 1901 and died young, in 1906. Her poem here comes from Untermeyer's Modern British Poetry (1920).

poets.name: Theodore Wratislaw
bio: Theodore Wratislaw (1871–1933) was born at Rugby, of an old Bohemian family long settled in England.
A poet of the 1890s, he published two small books of verse in 1892 and Caprices in 1893.

poets.name: Maurice Baring
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Maurice Baring (1874–1945) was an English man of letters, known as a dramatist, poet, novelist, translator and essayist, and as a travel writer and war correspondent with a particular knowledge of Russia.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Alice Meynell
poets.credit: Portrait of Alice Meynell · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alice Meynell (1847–1922) was an English poet, essayist, and suffragist, admired in her lifetime for the precision and restraint of her devout, closely observed lyrics.
A convert to Catholicism, she wrote often of motherhood, nature, and quiet spiritual attention.

poets.name: Walter Learned
bio: Walter Learned (1847–1915) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “The Last Reservation”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: James Jeffrey Roche
poets.credit: Portrait of James Jeffrey Roche · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James Jeffrey Roche (1847–1908) was an American journalist.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “Washington”, “Reuben James”, “Jack Creamer”, “The Fight of the Armstrong Privateer” and “The Constitution's Last Fight” among others; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Anne Glenny Wilson
bio: Anne Glenny Wilson (1848–1930), who published as Mrs James Glenny Wilson, was an Australian poet and writer.
Her verse was collected in A Book of Verses.

poets.name: George John Romanes
bio: George John Romanes (1848–1894) was a Canadian-born British biologist, a friend and disciple of Charles Darwin, known for his work on animal intelligence and on evolution. He also wrote verse, collected after his death.
Francis Turner Palgrave included two of his short poems in the Second Series of The Golden Treasury (1897).

poets.name: Frederic Edward Weatherly
bio: Frederic Edward Weatherly (1848–1929) was an English barrister and lyricist, born at Portishead in Somerset and educated at Hereford Cathedral School and Brasenose College, Oxford. He wrote the words of a very large number of popular songs, among them “Nancy Lee”, “The Holy City” and “Danny Boy”.
The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s A Victorian Anthology, 1837–1895 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin, 1895).

poets.name: John Vance Cheney
poets.credit: Portrait of John Vance Cheney (1896) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Vance Cheney (1848–1922) was an American poet and librarian, born at Groveland, New York. He was librarian of the San Francisco Free Public Library from 1887 to 1894, and of the Newberry Library in Chicago until 1899, and then lived in California.
His volumes of verse include Thistle Drift (1887), Out of the Silence (1897), The Time of Roses (1908) and At the Silver Gate (1911).

poets.name: George Barlow
bio: George Barlow (1847–1913) was an English poet who sometimes wrote under the pseudonym James Hinton.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 8, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Lilla Cabot Perry
bio: Lilla Cabot Perry (1848–1933) was an American painter and poet, born in Boston, who studied and worked in the circle of Claude Monet at Giverny.
She was married to the critic Thomas Sergeant Perry and published several volumes of verse, among them Impressions (1898).

poets.name: Fanny Parnell
poets.credit: Portrait of Fanny Parnell (halftone etching, c. 1870s, artist unknown) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Fanny Parnell (1848–1882) was an Irish poet and nationalist, born at Avondale, County Wicklow, and a sister of Charles Stewart Parnell. She wrote fiery verse for the nationalist press, notably 'Hold the Harvest' (1879), and took an active part in the Land League agitation, dying at Bordentown, New Jersey, in 1882.
Lyra Celtica includes her lyric 'After Death'.

poets.name: Charles de Kay
bio: Charles de Kay (1848–1935) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “The Draft Riot”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Will Henry Thompson
bio: Will Henry Thompson (1848–1918) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “The High Tide at Gettysburg”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Robert Leighton
bio: Robert Leighton (born 1822; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Arthur Hugh Clough
poets.credit: Portrait of Arthur Hugh Clough · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Arthur Hugh Clough (1819–1861) was an English poet and close friend of Matthew Arnold, whose verse candidly registers the Victorian crisis of religious faith and doubt.
His long poems Amours de Voyage and The Bothie of Tober-na-Vuolich experiment with conversational, unglamorous realism unusual for their time.

poets.name: Michael Mullen
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Michael Mullen (1833–1869) was a priest and song-writer born at Kilmore, County Galway, who died at Chicago. Sparling notes that the Society for the Preservation of the Irish Language was then working against the fears he voices in "The Celtic Tongue".
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Francis Robert St. Clair-Erskine, Earl of Rosslyn
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Francis Robert St Clair-Erskine, Earl of Rosslyn (1833–1890), was a British peer who also wrote verse.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: John Nichol
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Nichol (1833–1894) was a Scottish literary scholar and writer, the first Regius Professor of English Language and Literature at the University of Glasgow, and the author of the drama Hannibal.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Percy Addleshaw
bio: Percy Addleshaw (1866–1916) was an English barrister, born at Bowdon, Cheshire, and educated at Christ Church, Oxford. He was called to the bar in 1893.
Writing also under the name Percy Hemingway, he published a volume of short stories, Out of Egypt (1894), and a book of verse, The Happy Wanderer and Other Poems (1895).

poets.name: Sir Lewis Morris
poets.credit: Woodburytype portrait of Lewis Morris, 1880s · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Lewis Morris (1833–1907) was a Welsh poet writing in English, best known for The Epic of Hades (1876–77).

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 5, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Richard Watson Dixon
poets.credit: Portrait of Richard Watson Dixon · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Watson Dixon (1833–1900) was an English poet and clergyman, and a correspondent of Gerard Manley Hopkins.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 5, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Ernest Dowson
poets.credit: Portrait of Ernest Dowson · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ernest Dowson (1867–1900) was an English poet of the 1890s Decadent movement, associated with the Rhymers' Club, who died of tuberculosis and drink at thirty-two.
His hallmark is a wistful, musical melancholy, most famous in the refrain "I have been faithful to thee, Cynara! in my fashion," from his poem Non Sum Qualis Eram.

poets.name: Henry Lawson
poets.credit: Photograph of Henry Lawson by May Moore, c. 1915 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Lawson (1867–1922) was an Australian poet and short-story writer, born near Grenfell, New South Wales.
His books include In the Days When the World Was Wide, and Other Verses (1896) and While the Billy Boils (1896); he is regarded as the voice of the bush and the working man.

poets.name: Charles Tennyson Turner
bio: Charles Tennyson Turner (1808–1879) was an English clergyman and poet, born Charles Tennyson at Somersby, Lincolnshire, and the elder brother of Alfred Tennyson; the two brothers appeared together in Poems by Two Brothers. He added the surname Turner after inheriting property from a relative, and spent much of his life as a parish priest in Lincolnshire.

He is remembered chiefly for his sonnets, which turn small observed things—a lark, a rainbow, a drowned spaniel, the bell of a buoy—into brief pictures with a moral or elegiac turn. The poems here are taken from Collected Sonnets, Old and New (London: C. Kegan Paul, 1880), the posthumous gathering of the sonnets he published in 1830, 1864, 1868 and 1873 together with those first printed there, and the few lyrics at its end.

poets.name: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
poets.credit: Portrait of Alfred, Lord Tennyson · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1809–1892) was Poet Laureate of Great Britain for over four decades and the most popular and representative poet of the Victorian age.
His work ranges from the intimate grief of In Memoriam A.H.H., written for a dead friend, to the martial narrative verse of Enoch Arden and the ballad-like Maud.

poets.name: John Hanmer, 1st Baron Hanmer
bio: John Hanmer, 1st Baron Hanmer (1809–1881), was an English politician and poet, educated at Eton and Christ Church, Oxford, and an advocate of political reform. He published Fra Cipolla and Other Poems (1839) and Sonnets (1840), and died at Knotley Hall, near Tunbridge Wells.
The sonnet here is the one printed under his name in A Victorian Anthology, 1837–1895, ed. Edmund Clarence Stedman (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1895).

poets.name: Lord Houghton (Richard Monckton Milnes)
poets.credit: Richard Monckton Milnes, Lord Houghton, portrait (19th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Monckton Milnes, first Baron Houghton (1809–1885), was an English poet, politician and patron of letters. He wrote the first biography of Keats (Life, Letters and Literary Remains of John Keats, 1848) and published verse such as Poems of Many Years (1838).
The poems given here are taken from Edmund H. Garrett's anthology Victorian Songs: Lyrics of the Affections and Nature (Boston: Little, Brown, 1895).

poets.name: Francis A. Fahy
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Francis A. Fahy (1854–1935), who wrote under the name "Dreoilin", was counted by Sparling among the best known and most genuinely lyrical of the younger Irish poets of his day. He published a volume of verse and contributed to the national newspapers.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: William James Dawson
poets.credit: Portrait: not stated — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William James Dawson (1854–1928) was an English clergyman, lecturer, poet, hymn-writer and author.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 8, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: F. W. Bourdillon
bio: Francis William Bourdillon (1852–1921) was an English poet and translator, educated at Worcester College, Oxford. His best-known lyric, "The Night Has a Thousand Eyes", first appeared in his collection Among the Flowers (1878).
The songs given here are taken from Edmund H. Garrett's anthology Victorian Songs: Lyrics of the Affections and Nature (Boston: Little, Brown, 1895).

poets.name: Robert Dwyer Joyce
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Robert Dwyer Joyce (1830–1883), born in County Limerick, was a physician, journalist and poet. He emigrated to Boston in 1866, achieved distinction there, and returned to Dublin shortly before his death.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: John T. Campion
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John T. Campion contributed ballads to The Nation under the name "The Kilkenny Man". Sparling, writing in 1888, says he was born about 1830 and was then a medical practitioner in Dublin.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Stephen Nolan Elrington
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Stephen Nolan Elrington published Original Poems and Lyrics (Dublin, 1853; second edition 1856). A barrister, he was librarian of the King's Inns, Dublin, when Sparling wrote.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Ralph Varian
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Ralph Varian, who wrote as "Duncathail", published songs and poems and edited Street Ballads, Popular Poetry, and Household Songs of Ireland (Dublin, 1865).
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Francis Burdett Money-Coutts
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Francis Burdett Money-Coutts (1852–1923), fifth Baron Latymer, was a London solicitor, poet and librettist and heir to the Coutts banking fortune. He is remembered chiefly as a patron and collaborator of the composer Isaac Albéniz.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: John Henry Newman
poets.credit: Portrait: Herbert Rose Barraud — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Henry Newman (1801–1890) was an English theologian, historian and poet, who became a Roman Catholic and later a cardinal.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Caroline Clive
bio: Caroline Clive (1801–1873), who wrote under the pseudonym V., was an English writer, known chiefly as the author of IX Poems.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Isaac Williams
poets.credit: Portrait of Revd. Isaac Williams, unknown artist, c. 1864 (Welsh Portrait Collection, National Library of Wales) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Isaac Williams (1802–1865) was a Welsh-born clergyman and poet, a Fellow of Trinity College, Oxford, and a student and disciple of John Keble. A member of the Oxford Movement, he contributed verses to Lyra Apostolica and wrote Tract 80, “On Reserve in Communicating Religious Knowledge.”

His best-known verse is devotional. The Cathedral (1838) is a cycle of short poems in which the parts of a church — porch, cloisters, nave, transepts, choir, pillars and windows — stand for the Christian life and the Church of England. The Baptistery (1842), published anonymously “by the author of The Cathedral,” sets a long poem to each of twenty-three engraved “images” that follow the baptized soul’s way to eternal life.

poets.name: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poets.credit: Portrait of Elizabeth Barrett Browning · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Elizabeth Barrett Browning (1806–1861) was one of the most celebrated English poets of her day, an invalid for much of her youth who eloped to Italy with fellow poet Robert Browning in 1846.
Her Sonnets from the Portuguese, written to Robert during their courtship, remain her best-loved work, alongside socially engaged narrative poems on slavery, child labour, and women's lives.

poets.name: William Gilmore Simms
poets.credit: Portrait: Unidentified artist — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Gilmore Simms (1806–1870) was a Charleston, South Carolina, novelist, historian and poet, author of Guy Rivers and The Yemassee.
Griswold included 7 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Frederick W. Thomas
bio: Frederick W. Thomas (1806–1866) was a Providence-born lawyer, novelist and poet, author of the novel Clinton Bradshaw (1835).
Griswold included 1 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Ralph Hoyt
bio: Ralph Hoyt (1806–1878) was a New York Episcopal clergyman and poet, ordained in 1842.
Griswold included 5 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Emma Catharine Embury
bio: Emma Catharine Embury (1806–1863), née Manley, was a New York poet and writer of tales, whose verse appeared in Guido, a Tale; Sketches from History, and Other Poems (1828) and in the magazines of her day.
Edmund Clarence Stedman included her poem “Love Unsought” in An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Isaac McLellan, Jr.
bio: Isaac McLellan Jr. (1806–1899) was a poet of the sea and field sports, a native of Portland, Maine, and a graduate of Bowdoin College (1826).
Griswold included 4 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: George Allan
bio: George Allan (1806–1835) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 5 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Thomas Brydson
bio: Thomas Brydson (1806–1855) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Henry Inglis
bio: Henry Inglis (born 1806; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Michael Doheny
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Michael Doheny was born in County Tipperary and became a lawyer and a Young Ireland nationalist. After the failed rising of 1848 he escaped to America, where he wrote The Felon's Track (1849).
He died in New York in 1863.

poets.name: Rev. T. G. Torry Anderson
bio: Rev. T. G. Torry Anderson (died 1856) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William Anderson
bio: William Anderson (born 1805; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 4 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Joseph Grant
bio: Joseph Grant (1805–1835) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William M. Hetherington, D.D., LL.D.
bio: William M. Hetherington, D.D., LL.D. (born c. 1805; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Robert Hogg
bio: Robert Hogg (died 1834) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 6 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Dugald Moore
bio: Dugald Moore (1805–1841) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 7 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: George Outram
bio: George Outram (1805–1856) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: John Wright
bio: John Wright (born 1805) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 4 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Thomas Wade
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Wade (1805–1875) was a Victorian English poet.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Helen Selina Blackwood, Lady Dufferin
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Helen Selina Blackwood, Lady Dufferin, was a granddaughter of Richard Brinsley Sheridan and the mother of the diplomat Lord Dufferin. She wrote songs and verse and later became Countess of Gifford.
Her "Lament of the Irish Emigrant" is her best-known poem.

poets.name: Charles James Lever
bio: Charles James Lever (1806–1872) was an Irish novelist, born in Dublin, best known for the military and convivial romances Harry Lorrequer (1839) and Charles O'Malley (1841). His novels are studded with comic songs in Irish idiom.
The Widow Malone is the most famous of them.

poets.name: John Sterling
poets.credit: Portrait of John Sterling by J. Brown, 1830 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Sterling (1806–1844) was a Scottish-born writer and a friend of Thomas Carlyle, who later wrote his Life of John Sterling.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 4, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Sarah Flower Adams
bio: Sarah Flower Adams (1805–1848) was an English poet and hymn-writer, the author of “Nearer, My God, to Thee”.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Thomas Cooper
bio: Thomas Cooper, known as “the Chartist”, was born at Leicester in 1805. Self-educated under great disadvantages, he took an active part in political reform and lectured in England and Scotland.
He collected his poetical works in 1878 and died in 1892.

poets.name: William John Blew
bio: William John Blew, clergyman, was born about 1806, graduated at Wadham College, Oxford, in 1830 and was ordained in 1832.
He published several religious works and hymns. He died in 1894.

poets.name: Jonathan Lawrence
bio: Jonathan Lawrence (1807–1833) was a young New York poet who died early; friends collected his poems after his death.
Griswold included 4 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: J. O. Rockwell
bio: James Otis Rockwell (1807–1831) was a Connecticut-born journalist and poet, apprenticed as a printer in Utica, who died young.
Griswold included 7 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Micah P. Flint
bio: Micah P. Flint (c. 1807–1830) was a poet and lawyer, born in Lunenburg, Massachusetts, the son of the writer Timothy Flint, who grew up in the Mississippi valley and died young.
Griswold included 2 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: John H. Bryant
bio: John Howard Bryant (1807–1902) was a poet and farmer, born in Cummington, Massachusetts, and a younger brother of William Cullen Bryant, who settled in Illinois.
Griswold included 10 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Henry William Herbert
bio: Henry William Herbert (1807–1858) was born in London and settled in New York, where he wrote historical novels, translations and sporting books, the latter under the name “Frank Forester.”
Edmund Clarence Stedman included his poem “Come Back” in An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Theodore S. Fay
bio: Theodore S. Fay (1807–1898) was a New York novelist and poet, author of Norman Leslie (1835), who later served as a diplomat in Berlin.
Griswold included 2 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Thomas Ward
bio: Thomas Ward (1807–1873) was a physician and poet of Newark, New Jersey, who wrote under the name Flaccus.
Griswold included 3 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Ephraim Peabody
bio: Ephraim Peabody (1807–1856) was a Unitarian minister and writer, a graduate of Bowdoin College, later minister of King's Chapel in Boston.
Griswold included 4 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: John B. Magruder
poets.credit: Portrait of John B. Magruder (Wikimedia Commons) · Public domain
bio: John Bankhead Magruder (1807–1871) was a Confederate major general, born in Virginia and trained at West Point, who commanded on the Virginia Peninsula and later in Texas, where he recaptured Galveston in January 1863.
He is credited with the song "Imogen", reprinted here from W. L. Fagan's Southern War Songs (1890). He died in Houston.

poets.name: George Frederick Cameron
poets.credit: Portrait of George Frederick Cameron, from Canadian Poets (1916) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Frederick Cameron (1854–1885) was a Nova Scotian lawyer, journalist and poet who died young.

His collected Lyrics on Freedom, Love and Death appeared in 1887 after his death. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Barry Straton
bio: Barry Straton (1854–1901) was a Canadian poet of the Confederation generation.

Little biographical detail is recorded here beyond his appearance in Lighthall's anthology. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Annie Matheson
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Annie Matheson (1853–1924) was a British Victorian poet who wrote one of the first biographies of Florence Nightingale as well as several volumes of meditative and lyrical verse.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Thomas Herbert Warren
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir Thomas Herbert Warren (1853–1930) was a British academic and administrator, President of Magdalen College, Oxford, from 1885 to 1928 and Vice-Chancellor of the university from 1906 to 1910.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: George W. Patten
bio: George W. Patten (1808–1882) was an army officer and poet, born in Newport, Rhode Island, the son of the Rev. William Patten.
Griswold included 1 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: William D. Gallagher
bio: William D. Gallagher (1808–1894) was a poet and journalist, born in Philadelphia, who grew up in Cincinnati and edited Ohio and Kentucky papers.
Griswold included 11 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Ray Palmer
bio: Ray Palmer (1808–1887) was a Congregational minister of New York and Albany and a hymn-writer. His best-known hymn, “My faith looks up to Thee,” was written in 1830 and later set to music by Lowell Mason.
Edmund Clarence Stedman included it as “Faith” in An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Samuel Francis Smith
bio: Samuel Francis Smith (1808–1895) was a Baptist minister and hymn-writer of Massachusetts. He wrote “America” (“My country, ’t is of thee”) in 1831 as a student at Andover Theological Seminary.
Edmund Clarence Stedman included the poem, dated 1832, in An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Willis Gaylord Clark
poets.credit: Portrait: John Sartain — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Willis Gaylord Clark (1808–1841) was a poet and editor, born at Otisco, New York, who edited the Philadelphia Gazette and wrote for the Knickerbocker magazine, which was edited by his twin brother Lewis.
Griswold included 13 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Ellen Forrester
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Ellen Forrester (1831–1883) was born at Anyalla, County Monaghan, and died in Manchester. Her poems won favour for their simplicity and earnestness.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Louise Chandler Moulton
poets.credit: Photograph of Louise Chandler Moulton by James E. Purdy, 1904 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Louise Chandler Moulton (1835–1908) was an American poet and journalist, born at Pomfret, Connecticut, and long resident in Boston. She contributed to the Boston Herald, and spent many seasons in London, where she knew leading writers of the day.
Her verse, collected in several volumes, is lyrical and often melancholy.

poets.name: Dante Gabriel Rossetti
poets.credit: Portrait of Dante Gabriel Rossetti · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Dante Gabriel Rossetti (1828–1882) was an English poet and painter, a founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, who worked in sister arts of image and verse throughout his career.
His sonnet sequence The House of Life traces the arc of love and loss with dense, jewelled imagery, while The Blessed Damozel imagines a dead woman watching for her lover from heaven.

poets.name: Daniel Henry Deniehy
bio: Daniel Henry Deniehy (1828–1865) was an Australian-born lawyer, journalist, orator and poet, remembered for his 1853 speech mocking a colonial 'bunyip aristocracy'.
He wrote verse for Sydney newspapers and edited the weekly The Southern Cross (1859–60).

poets.name: Richard Rowe
bio: Richard Rowe (1828–1879) was an English-born journalist and writer who lived for some years in Australia and wrote for Sydney newspapers.
He published Peter 'Possum's Portfolio, a collection of his Australian sketches and verse.

poets.name: William McLennan
bio: William McLennan (1856–1904) was a Montreal lawyer and writer who published Songs of Old Canada (1886), translations of French-Canadian folk-songs.
Only his original poem is included here. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: James Nack
bio: James Nack (1809–1879) was a New York poet who lost his hearing in childhood after a fall, and whose poems were published as The Legend of the Rocks and Other Poems.
Griswold included 3 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: B. B. Thatcher
bio: Benjamin B. Thatcher (1809–1840) was a lawyer and writer, born in Warren, Maine, and a graduate of Bowdoin College (1826).
Griswold included 1 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Albert Pike
poets.credit: Portrait: Mathew Benjamin Brady / Levin Corbin Handy — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Albert Pike (1809–1891) was a Boston-born poet, lawyer and soldier who settled in Arkansas; he later became a Confederate general and a leading figure in Freemasonry.
Griswold included 11 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Park Benjamin
poets.credit: Portrait: Unknown authorUnknown author — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Park Benjamin (1809–1864) was a poet and editor born in British Guiana, active in the New York and Boston magazines of the 1830s and 1840s.
Griswold included 17 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Thomas Gordon Hake
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Gordon Hake by Dante Gabriel Rossetti, 1872 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Gordon Hake (1809–1895) was an English physician and poet. His verse appeared over more than fifty years, from The Piromides (1839) through Madeline, Parables and Tales and The New Day (1890), and was admired by Dante Gabriel Rossetti, who reviewed his work and drew his portrait.

He wrote long, solemn narrative poems in short stanzas, often about dream, sleep and the passage of the soul. The poems here are taken from the 1894 selection published by Elkin Mathews and John Lane, with a prefatory note by Alice Meynell.

poets.name: James Freeman Clarke
poets.credit: Portrait: No artist identified — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James Freeman Clarke (1810–1888) was a Unitarian minister and writer, born in Hanover, New Hampshire, a Harvard graduate and a friend of the Transcendentalists.
Griswold included 8 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Edmund Hamilton Sears
bio: Edmund Hamilton Sears (1810–1876) was a Unitarian minister in Massachusetts, who wrote the Christmas carol “It came upon the midnight clear” in 1849.
Edmund Clarence Stedman included it as “The Angels’ Song” in An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Robert T. Conrad
bio: Robert T. Conrad (1810–1858) was a Philadelphia judge, mayor, editor and poet, and the author of the play Aylmere.
Griswold included 4 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Robert Louis Stevenson
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Louis Stevenson · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Louis Stevenson (1850–1894) was a Scottish novelist and poet, best known for Treasure Island and Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, who also wrote widely loved verse.
A Child's Garden of Verses captures the imaginative world of childhood, while Songs of Travel, mostly written in his final years in Samoa, turns to restlessness, distance, and mortality.

poets.name: Philip Joseph Holdsworth
bio: Philip Joseph Holdsworth (1851–1902) was an Australian poet, born in Sydney, who spent time in the Queensland outback.
His books include Station Hunting on the Warrego.

poets.name: Theo Marzials
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Theo Marzials (1850–1920), born Théophile-Jules-Henri Marzials, was a British composer, singer and poet. Max Beerbohm described him in 1894 as a "poet and eccentric".
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: John Liddell Kelly
bio: John Liddell Kelly (1850–1925) was an Australian poet.
His verse was collected in Heather and Fern.

poets.name: Nasikh
poets.dates: dates not given in the source
bio: The book describes Nasikh as of Calcutta, belonging to the latter half of the nineteenth century, a Deputy Magistrate and Member of the Legislative Council of Bengal. This is the identification the book gives; it is not assumed here to be the earlier Lucknow poet of the same name, and no dates are given.

The 2 pieces given here are drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. They are free renderings, not literal translations, and the original Urdu poems are untitled; each is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Robert Richardson
bio: Robert Richardson (1850–1901) was an Australian clergyman and poet.
His verse was collected in Willow and Wattle.

poets.name: Michael Hogan
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Michael Hogan (1832–1899), the "Bard of Thomond", was a wheelwright from Thomondgate, Limerick, who published Lays and Legends of Thomond (1880). He left Ireland for New York in 1886.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: James Lister Cuthbertson
bio: James Lister Cuthbertson (1851–1910) was a Scottish-born poet and schoolmaster who emigrated to Victoria and taught at Geelong Grammar School.
He published Barwon Ballads (1893) and other verse, including the poem Australia Federata.

poets.name: Gleeson White
bio: Gleeson White (1851–1898) was an English art critic, editor and book designer. He edited The Studio, and for a time lived in the United States, where he conducted the Art Amateur.
He compiled Ballades and Rondeaus, Chants Royal, Sestinas, Villanelles, etc. (1887) and wrote a number of light and occasional poems.

poets.name: John Farrell
bio: John Farrell (1851–1904) was an Australian journalist and poet, born in Buenos Aires, who wrote for radical and labour newspapers.
His collected verse appeared as My Sundowner and Other Poems (1904).

poets.name: Eric Mackay
bio: Eric Mackay (1851–1898) was a poet, born in London, the son of the poet and journalist Charles Mackay. He was educated in Scotland and spent several years in Italy.
His Love Letters of a Violinist, and Other Poems appeared in 1886, followed by A Lover’s Litanies; he died in London.

poets.name: F. Wyville Home
bio: Francis Wyville Home was a Scottish poet, born in Edinburgh in 1851.
He published Songs of a Wayfarer (1878), Lay Canticles and Other Poems (1883) and The Wrath of the Fay (1887).

poets.name: Walter Herries Pollock
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Walter Herries Pollock (1850–1926) was an English writer, poet, lecturer and journalist, best known as editor of the Saturday Review from 1884 to 1894.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Arthur Patchett Martin
bio: Arthur Patchett Martin (1851–1902) was an English-born journalist and critic who worked in Australia and later settled in London.
He published The Withered Jester, and Other Verses.

poets.name: Robert H. Messinger
bio: Robert H. Messinger (1811–1874) was an American poet whose verses circulated chiefly in magazines and newspapers.
Griswold included 1 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Alfred B. Street
bio: Alfred B. Street (1811–1881) was a poet born at Poughkeepsie, New York, later State Librarian of New York.
Griswold included 7 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: John Osborne Sargent
bio: John Osborne Sargent (1811–1891) was an American lawyer and writer who also wrote verse.
The poem here is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1900).

poets.name: Harriet Beecher Stowe
bio: Harriet Beecher Stowe (1811–1896) was the Connecticut-born author of Uncle Tom’s Cabin (1852). She also published hymns and occasional verse.
Edmund Clarence Stedman included her poem “The Other World” in An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Elizabeth Lloyd Howell
bio: Elizabeth Lloyd Howell (1811–1896) was a Pennsylvania poet, a Quaker by upbringing and a friend of John Greenleaf Whittier.
Edmund Clarence Stedman included her poem “Milton’s Prayer of Patience” in An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Hardwicke Drummond Rawnsley
bio: Hardwicke Drummond Rawnsley (1851–1920) was an Anglican priest, poet, local politician and conservationist.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 8, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: John E. Logan ("Barry Dane")
bio: John E. Logan, who wrote under the pen-name Barry Dane, was born in Hamilton, Canada, in 1852. He later settled in Montreal, where he worked as an insurance adjuster, and spent some years in the Canadian North-West.
His poems appeared in Canadian newspapers and periodicals but, as Stedman noted in 1895, were never collected in a book. A Victorian Anthology prints several of them.

poets.name: Herbert Edwin Clarke
