bio: Herbert Edwin Clarke (1852–1912) was an English poet, born at Chatteris in the Isle of Ely and educated in Quaker schools. He worked as a commercial clerk and later as secretary to public companies.
He published Songs in Exile (1879), Storm-Drift (1882) and Tannhäuser and Other Poems (1896).

poets.name: Richard Dalton Williams
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Richard Dalton Williams (1822–1862), who wrote as "Shamrock", was a physician and journalist born in County Tipperary. He wrote for The Nation, was tried and acquitted in 1848, emigrated in 1851, and died in Louisiana.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: John Edward Pigot
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Edward Pigot (1822–1871), who wrote for The Nation as "Fermoy", was born at Kilworth, County Cork, the son of a Chief Baron of the Exchequer. He was called to the bar in 1845 and practised for some years in Bombay.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: John O'Hagan
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John O'Hagan (1822–1890), born at Newry, was a judge and accomplished linguist who translated the Song of Roland. The Nation poems signed "Sliabh Cuilinn" have been attributed to him, though Sparling notes he never acknowledged them.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: William H. Burleigh
bio: William H. Burleigh (1812–1871) was a Connecticut-born abolitionist and temperance poet and newspaper editor.
Griswold included 13 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Sarah Roberts Boyle
bio: Sarah Roberts Boyle was an American poet of the nineteenth century, remembered for the short lyric “The Voice of the Grass”.
The poem here is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1900).

poets.name: Louis L. Noble
bio: Louis L. Noble (1812–1882) was an Episcopal clergyman and writer, born in Otsego County, New York, and the biographer of the painter Thomas Cole.
Griswold included 2 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Thomas MacKellar
bio: Thomas MacKellar (1812–1899) was a New York-born printer and poet, later a partner in a Philadelphia type foundry.
Griswold included 3 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Matthew C. Field
bio: Matthew C. Field (1812–1844) was a London-born journalist and actor who wrote under the name Phazma for newspapers of the American South and West.
Griswold included 2 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: William Goldsmith Brown
bio: William Goldsmith Brown (1812–1906) was an American verse-writer, born at Whitingham, Vermont, who later settled in Wisconsin, where he died.
He is remembered for two popular poems of sentiment, "A Hundred Years to Come" and "Mother, Home, Heaven", both reprinted in The Home Book of Verse (1912).

poets.name: Dion Boucicault
poets.credit: Photograph of Dion Boucicault, photographer unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Dion Boucicault (c. 1820–1890) was a Dublin-born dramatist and actor, author of London Assurance (1841) and The Colleen Bawn, who spent much of his later life in the United States. His version of "The Wearing of the Green" is a rewriting of the older street ballad.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: William Cox Bennett
bio: William Cox Bennett (1820–1895) was an English poet and journalist, born at Greenwich. He is remembered chiefly for his domestic and patriotic songs, among them the nursery favourite "Baby May", collected in volumes such as Songs by a Song-Writer (1859).
The songs given here are taken from Edmund H. Garrett's anthology Victorian Songs: Lyrics of the Affections and Nature (Boston: Little, Brown, 1895).

poets.name: Ellen Sturgis Hooper
bio: Ellen Sturgis Hooper (1812–1848) was a Boston poet, a friend of Margaret Fuller and a member of the circle around the Transcendentalist journal The Dial. She married Robert William Hooper, a physician, and was the mother of Marian 'Clover' Hooper, later the wife of Henry Adams.
She published very little in her lifetime; her best-known lines, a six-line poem on beauty and duty, appeared unsigned and untitled in the first number of The Dial in July 1840.

poets.name: Jones Very
poets.credit: Portrait: Jonesvery.jpg: Unknown derivative work: Midnightdreary (talk) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Jones Very (1813–1880) was a Salem, Massachusetts, poet, tutor and preacher, a friend of the Transcendentalists, best known for his devotional sonnets.
Griswold included 18 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Charles T. Brooks
bio: Charles T. Brooks (1813–1883) was a Unitarian minister in Newport, Rhode Island, born in Salem, Massachusetts, and a translator from the German.
Griswold included 5 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Henry Theodore Tuckerman
poets.credit: Portrait: Mathew Benjamin Brady — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Theodore Tuckerman (1813–1871) was a Boston-born essayist, critic and poet, author of The Spirit of Poetry (1845).
Griswold included 14 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Epes Sargent
bio: Epes Sargent (1813–1880) was a poet, playwright and editor, born in Gloucester, Massachusetts, and the author of the play Velasco.
Griswold included 6 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Henry B. Hirst
bio: Henry B. Hirst (1813–1874) was a Philadelphia lawyer and poet, author of Endymion (1848).
Griswold included 5 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Charles Kingsley
poets.credit: Portrait of Charles Kingsley · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Kingsley (1819–1875) was an English clergyman, novelist, and poet, remembered as a children's author for The Water-Babies and as a muscular-Christian social reformer.
His poems range from the classical narrative Andromeda, written in unrhymed hexameters, to plain-spoken ballads and songs of the sea and English rural life.

poets.name: George Murray
bio: George Murray (1830–1910), born in Bermuda, was a Montreal schoolmaster and poet.
The poems here are those Lighthall selected for Songs of the Great Dominion (1889).

poets.name: Josiah Gilbert Holland
bio: Josiah Gilbert Holland (1819–1881) was an American writer and editor, born at Belchertown, Massachusetts. He trained as a physician, joined the Springfield Republican in 1849, and wrote popular prose under the name “Timothy Titcomb”; his verse includes Bitter-Sweet (1858) and Kathrina (1867). He helped found Scribner’s Monthly in 1870.
The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin, 1900).

poets.name: Amelia Coppuck Welby
bio: Amelia Coppuck Welby (1819–1852) was an American poet who wrote for the Louisville Journal and was popular in her day. Her verses were gathered in Poems by Amelia (1844).
The poem here is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1900).

poets.name: Harriet Winslow Sewall
bio: Harriet Winslow Sewall (1819–1889) was an American poet, and editor of the collected letters of Lydia Maria Child.
The poem here is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1900).

poets.name: Edward Kenealy
bio: Edward Vaughan Hyde Kenealy (1819–1880) was an Irish-born barrister, author and politician, best known as the defending counsel of the Tichborne Claimant, a case that led to his disbarment in 1874. He was elected Member of Parliament for Stoke-on-Trent in 1875.
He published several volumes of verse, among them Poems and Translations (1864), and wrote the eccentric prose work The Book of God (1867).

poets.name: W. H. C. Hosmer
bio: William H. C. Hosmer (1814–1877) was a lawyer and poet of Avon, New York, who wrote chiefly on Native American themes.
Griswold included 6 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Mikhail Lermontov
poets.credit: Portrait of Mikhail Lermontov by Pyotr Zabolotsky (1837) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mikhail Yuryevich Lermontov (1814–1841) was born in Moscow and raised largely by his grandmother on her estate at Tarkhany. He studied at Moscow University, then trained as a cavalry officer in St Petersburg and was commissioned in the Life-Guard Hussars. His poem on the death of Pushkin (1837) made him famous and led to his exile to the Caucasus, where he served again in 1840.

Lermontov wrote lyrics, narrative poems such as The Demon and Mtsyri, and the novel A Hero of Our Time. He was killed in a duel at Pyatigorsk in 1841, aged twenty-six. The Demon, begun in his teens and revised over many years, was finished in 1839 and first published abroad in 1856. The version here is by Francis Storr (1894), in rhymed couplets.

poets.name: Sarah Tittle Bolton
bio: Sarah Tittle Bolton (1814–1893) was an Indiana poet, best known for Paddle Your Own Canoe.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: Left on the Battle-Field.

poets.name: Francis Alexander Durivage
bio: Francis Alexander Durivage (1814–1881) was a Boston journalist and humorist who wrote verse and stories for newspapers and magazines.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: The Cavalry Charge.

poets.name: Alexander B. Meek
poets.credit: Portrait of Alexander Beaufort Meek (Wikimedia Commons) · Public domain
bio: Alexander Beaufort Meek (1814–1865) was an American lawyer, judge and poet, born in Columbia, South Carolina, who lived in Alabama and published Songs and Poems of the South (1857).
"Would'st Thou Have Me Love Thee?" is reprinted here from W. L. Fagan's Southern War Songs (1890). He died at Columbus, Mississippi.

poets.name: Samuel Ward
bio: Samuel Ward (1814–1884), known as “Uncle Sam” Ward, was an American banker, lobbyist and man of letters, brother of Julia Ward Howe. He published a volume of verse, Lyrical Recreations (1865).
The poem here is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1900).

poets.name: Frederick William Faber
poets.credit: Frederick William Faber, engraving by Joseph Brown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Frederick William Faber (1814–1863) was born at Calverley in Yorkshire and educated at Shrewsbury, Harrow and Balliol College, Oxford, later becoming a fellow of University College. He knew the Lake District well, and its lakes, rivers and fells fill his early verse; the Wordsworth circle at Ambleside and the Oxford Movement both shaped him. He published The Cherwell Water-Lily and other poems in 1840 and a larger collection of Poems in 1856.

Ordained in the Church of England, Faber was received into the Roman Catholic Church in 1845 and joined the Oratory of St Philip Neri, becoming head of its London house. His devotional prose and above all his hymns — among them ‘Faith of Our Fathers’ and ‘Hark! Hark! My Soul’ — made him one of the best-known Catholic writers of the Victorian age. The poems here come from the 1889 Baltimore printing of his Poems (a selection first published in 1856) and from a 1894 selection of his hymns.

poets.name: Jedediah V. Huntington
bio: Jedediah V. Huntington (1815–1862) was a physician turned Episcopal priest and novelist, the brother of the painter Daniel Huntington, and author of Alice, or the New Una.
Griswold included 3 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: William Jewett Pabodie
bio: William Jewett Pabodie (1815–1870) was a lawyer and poet of Providence, Rhode Island, and the author of Calidore (1839).
Griswold included 6 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Daniel Decatur Emmett
poets.credit: Portrait of Daniel Decatur Emmett (Wikimedia Commons) · Public domain
bio: Daniel Decatur Emmett (1815–1904) was an American entertainer and composer, born in Mount Vernon, Ohio, who helped found the Virginia Minstrels and wrote the minstrel songs "Old Dan Tucker" and "Dixie" (1859).
"I Wish I Was in Dixie's Land" was adopted as a marching song of the Confederacy; it is reprinted here from W. L. Fagan's Southern War Songs (1890).

poets.name: Edward Lear
poets.credit: Portrait of Edward Lear · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward Lear (1812–1888) was an English artist and writer who, alongside a career as a natural history and landscape painter, invented much of the English nonsense verse tradition.
His limericks, alphabets, and songs such as The Owl and the Pussy-cat and The Jumblies, collected across several Book of Nonsense volumes, delight in invented words and gentle absurdity.

poets.name: Francis Bennoch
bio: Francis Bennoch (born 1812; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 15 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Robert L. Malone
bio: Robert L. Malone (1812–1850) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: James Manson
bio: James Manson (born c. 1812; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 5 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William Miller
bio: William Miller (born c. 1812; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Allan Stewart
bio: Allan Stewart (1812–1837) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 4 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Charles Harpur
bio: Charles Harpur (1813–1868) was an Australian-born poet, born at Windsor, New South Wales, who spent much of his life in the bush as a farmer and later a gold-fields official.
He published Thoughts: A Series of Sonnets (1845) and The Bushrangers (1853), and wrote under the influence of Wordsworth and Shelley; his best work is in longer poems.

poets.name: Henry Parkes
bio: Sir Henry Parkes (1815–1896) was an English-born politician who emigrated to New South Wales in 1839, served several times as its Premier and is remembered as the 'Father of Federation'.
He was also a poet, publishing Stolen Moments (1842) and several further volumes of verse, among them Fragmentary Thoughts; he printed the early work of Henry Kendall in his paper The Empire.

poets.name: Norman Macleod
poets.credit: Portrait of Norman Macleod, artist unknown, before 1872 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Norman Macleod (1812–1872) was a Church of Scotland minister, born at Campbeltown, who served the Barony Church in Glasgow, edited the magazine Good Words, and was Moderator of the General Assembly in 1869. He was a Gaelic speaker and a much-loved figure in the Highlands.
Lyra Celtica prints his 'Farewell to Fiunary', named for the Morvern parish where he spent part of his youth.

poets.name: Philip Pendleton Cooke
bio: Philip Pendleton Cooke (1816–1850) was a Virginia lawyer and poet, born in Martinsburg, and author of Froissart Ballads (1847).
Griswold included 4 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Anna Peyre Dinnies
bio: Anna Peyre Dinnies (1816–1886) was an American poet. Her lyric “The Wife” was widely reprinted in the nineteenth century.
The poem here is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1900).

poets.name: Charles G. Eastman
bio: Charles G. Eastman (1816–1860) was a Vermont poet and newspaper editor, educated at the University of Vermont.
Griswold included 3 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Thomas Burbidge
bio: Thomas Burbidge (1816–1892) was an English poet, author of Poems, Longer and Shorter (1838) and Hours and Days (1851).
He was a friend of Arthur Hugh Clough, with whom he published Ambarvalia (1849).

poets.name: John G. Saxe
bio: John G. Saxe (1816–1887) was a Vermont poet and humorist, born in Highgate, Vermont.
Griswold included 4 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: William James Linton
poets.credit: Portrait of William James Linton · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William James Linton (1812–1897) was an English-born wood-engraver, landscape painter, political reformer and author who settled in the United States and also wrote poetry.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 4, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Thomas Caulfield Irwin
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Caulfield Irwin (1823–1892), born at Warrenpoint, County Down, was an essayist and poet who contributed to The Nation and the Dublin University Magazine and published several volumes of tales, translations and verse.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Cornelius Mathews
bio: Cornelius Mathews (1817–1889) was a New York novelist, playwright and poet, a leading voice of the Young America movement.
Griswold included 5 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: E. Spencer Miller
bio: E. Spencer Miller (born 1817) was a Philadelphia lawyer and poet, the son of the Princeton theologian Samuel Miller, born at Princeton, New Jersey, and a graduate of Nassau Hall.
Griswold included 6 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: James T. Fields
poets.credit: Portrait: Julia Margaret Cameron — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James T. Fields (1817–1881) was a Portsmouth, New Hampshire-born Boston publisher, a partner in Ticknor and Fields, editor of the Atlantic Monthly and a poet.
Griswold included 13 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Marion Paul Aird
bio: Marion Paul Aird (dates not given by Rogers) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: James Macdonald
bio: James Macdonald (1807–1848) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Charles Fenno Hoffman
poets.credit: Portrait of Charles Fenno Hoffman by Cephas Giovanni Thompson, 1843 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Fenno Hoffman (1806–1884) was an American poet, novelist and editor, born in New York City. He edited several magazines, including the Knickerbocker, and wrote travel sketches of the American frontier as well as songs and ballads.
He suffered a mental breakdown in 1849 and spent his last decades in a hospital for the insane. His song “Sparkling and Bright” was widely sung.

poets.name: Frederic S. Cozzens
bio: Frederic S. Cozzens (1818–1869) was a New York wine merchant and humorist, who wrote under the name Richard Haywarde.
Griswold included 1 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: George H. Colton
bio: George H. Colton (1818–1847) was a poet and founding editor of the American Review, born in Westford, New York, and the author of the poem Tecumseh (1842).
Griswold included 3 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Arthur Cleveland Coxe
bio: Arthur Cleveland Coxe (1818–1896) was an Episcopal clergyman, later bishop of Western New York, born in Mendham, New Jersey, and a poet.
Griswold included 5 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: William W. Lord
bio: William W. Lord (1818–1892) was a poet and clergyman from western New York, the son of a Presbyterian minister.
Griswold included 4 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: George W. Dewey
bio: George W. Dewey (born 1818) was a poet born in Baltimore who lived from boyhood in Philadelphia and contributed to its magazines.
Griswold included 6 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Charles Graham Halpine
poets.credit: Portrait: Unknown authorUnknown author — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Graham Halpine (1829–1868), born at Oldcastle, County Meath, was a journalist and poet who wrote anti-secession verse as "Miles O'Reilly" and rose to brigadier-general in the American Civil War. He died in New York.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Jean Ingelow
poets.credit: Portrait of Jean Ingelow · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Jean Ingelow (1820–1897) was an English poet and novelist, immensely popular in her lifetime, admired for narrative ballads and devotional lyrics of home, sea, and childhood.
Her poem The High Tide on the Coast of Lincolnshire (1571), a ballad of a great flood, remained a schoolroom favourite for generations.

poets.name: Gustave Nadaud
bio: Gustave Nadaud (1820–1893) was a French songwriter and chansonnier, born at Roubaix, who wrote and sang popular songs in the Paris cafés and salons of the Second Empire.
His song "Carcassonne" is known to English readers chiefly through the translation by the Virginian poet John R. Thompson.

poets.name: Menella Bute Smedley
bio: Menella Bute Smedley (1820–1877) was an English poet and novelist, a cousin of the novelist Frank Smedley, who published verse and prose fiction in the middle years of the century.
Elizabeth A. Sharp included two of her poems, “A Character” and “The Little Fair Soul”, in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Thomas Elliott
bio: Thomas Elliott (born 1820; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 8 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Allan Gibson
bio: Allan Gibson (1820–1849) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: James Dodds
bio: James Dodds (born 1815) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William Wetmore Story
bio: William Wetmore Story (1819–1895) was an American sculptor, poet and man of letters, born in Salem, Massachusetts. He lived for most of his life in Rome.
His Poems appeared in 1856 and in a larger edition in 1886; he also wrote Roba di Roma, a book on Roman life. He died at Vallombrosa, Italy.

poets.name: William Ross Wallace
bio: William Ross Wallace (1819–1881) was a poet born in Lexington, Kentucky, who lived in New York and is remembered for The Hand That Rocks the Cradle Is the Hand That Rules the World.
Griswold included 7 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Thomas Dunn English
poets.credit: Portrait: Uncertain — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Dunn English (1819–1902) was a Philadelphia-born physician, lawyer, politician and writer, the author of the song Ben Bolt.
Griswold included 1 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Augusta Webster
poets.credit: Portrait: unknown artist — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Augusta Webster (1837–1894), born Julia Augusta Davies, was an English poet, dramatist and essayist, and a supporter of women's suffrage who served on the London School Board. Her volumes include Dramatic Studies (1866), A Woman Sold and Other Poems (1867) and Portraits (1870).
She is admired for her dramatic monologues, among them “Circe”, which gives the enchantress her own voice; it and “English Stornelli” are in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: John Reade
bio: John Reade (1837–1919) was an Irish-born Canadian poet and journalist who settled in Montreal and long served as literary editor of the Montreal Gazette. He was a founding member of the Royal Society of Canada.
His best-known volume is The Prophecy of Merlin, and Other Poems (1870). One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: David Gray
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: David Gray (1838–1861) was a Scottish poet from Merkland, Kirkintilloch, who died in his home town aged twenty-three. His friend Robert Buchanan wrote his biography.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Michael O’Connor
bio: Michael O’Connor was a sergeant in the 140th regiment of New York volunteers; Eggleston notes that he died at the age of 25 at Potomac Station, Virginia, on 28 December 1862.
The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: Réveille.

poets.name: Charles Mair
poets.credit: Portrait of Charles Mair, University of Alberta Libraries · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Mair (1838–1927) was a Canadian poet and public figure, born in Lanark, Upper Canada, who lived for many years on the western frontier.

He published Dreamland, and Other Poems (1868) and the verse drama Tecumseh (1886); only his lyric and narrative poems are included here. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: E. Pauline Johnson
poets.credit: Portrait of E. Pauline Johnson (Tekahionwake) by Cochran, c. 1895 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: E. Pauline Johnson (Tekahionwake, 1861–1913) was a Mohawk-English Canadian poet and performer, born on the Six Nations reserve near Brantford, Ontario.

Her best-known collection is The White Wampum (1895); the poems here predate it. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Archibald Lampman
poets.credit: Portrait of Archibald Lampman by William James Topley, 1889 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Archibald Lampman (1861–1899), born at Morpeth, Ontario, was a Post Office clerk in Ottawa and the leading poet of the Confederation generation.
His first book, Among the Millet and Other Poems, appeared in 1888. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Frederick George Scott
poets.credit: Portrait of Canon Frederick George Scott, from his book The Great War as I Saw It · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Frederick George Scott (1861–1944) was a Canadian Anglican clergyman and poet, born in Montreal, who served as an army chaplain in the First World War.
His early volume The Soul's Quest (1888) supplies some of the poems here. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Henry Timrod
poets.credit: Portrait of Henry Timrod (Review of Reviews Co.) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Timrod (1828–1867) was an American poet, born at Charleston, South Carolina, and often called the poet laureate of the Confederacy. He worked as a tutor and journalist, and wrote several of the best-known poems of the Southern cause during the Civil War.
He died of tuberculosis at Columbia, South Carolina, in 1867, in poverty. “Katie” and “Carolina” are among his best-known poems.

poets.name: Charles J. Kickham
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Charles Joseph Kickham was born in County Tipperary and became a Fenian, a journalist, a poet and the author of the novel Knocknagow. An accident in youth left him with poor hearing and sight.
He died in 1882.

poets.name: Thomas Young
bio: Thomas Young (born 1815; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Henry R. Jackson
bio: Henry R. Jackson (1820–1898) was a Georgia lawyer, judge and soldier, a colonel in the Mexican War, later United States minister to Austria and a Confederate general.
Griswold included 2 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Henry Howard Brownell
bio: Henry Howard Brownell (1820–1872) was a Rhode Island-born poet of the Civil War. Admiral Farragut took him aboard his flagship at the Battle of Mobile Bay, which he described in The Bay Fight.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where they are printed under his or her name: The River Fight; The Bay Fight.

poets.name: Theodore O'Hara
bio: Theodore O'Hara (1820–1867) was a Kentucky soldier and journalist who served in the Mexican War and later as a Confederate officer. His elegy The Bivouac of the Dead honours Kentuckians who fell in the Mexican War.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: The Bivouac of the Dead.

poets.name: Margaret Junkin Preston
poets.credit: Portrait: AnonymousUnknown author — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Margaret Junkin Preston (1820–1897) was a Virginia poet and the sister-in-law of Stonewall Jackson, whose death she lamented in Under the Shade of the Trees.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: Under the Shade of the Trees.

poets.name: Christopher Pearse Cranch
poets.credit: Portrait of Christopher Pearse Cranch (1892) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Christopher Pearse Cranch (1813–1892) was an American poet, painter and Unitarian minister, born at Alexandria, Virginia. He belonged to the Transcendentalist circle, contributing to The Dial, and later lived for years in Europe as a landscape painter.
His volume Poems (1844) and his later books show a gentle idealism; he also translated Virgil’s Aeneid into blank verse.

poets.name: Ebenezer Jones
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Ebenezer Jones (1820–1860) was a London-born poet of Welsh parentage who was also involved in the Chartist and socialist movements. He published Studies of Sensation and Event (1843), a book of passionate and unconventional verse that was neglected in his lifetime.
Lyra Celtica prints two of his poems, 'When the World is Burning' and 'The Hand'.

poets.name: Alice Cary
bio: Alice Cary (1820–1871), elder sister of the poet Phoebe Cary, was an American poet and novelist, born near Cincinnati, Ohio.
The poem here is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1900).

poets.name: Anson Davies Fitz Randolph
bio: Anson Davies Fitz Randolph (1820–1896) was a New York publisher and writer of religious verse.
The poem here is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1900).

poets.name: George Frederick Root
poets.credit: Portrait of George Frederick Root · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Frederick Root (1820–1895) was an American songwriter and composer.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “The Battle-Cry of Freedom”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Anna Laetitia Waring
bio: Anna Laetitia Waring (1823–1910) was a Welsh poet and Anglican hymn-writer; the anthology prints her birth year as 1820.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Edward FitzGerald
poets.credit: Portrait of Edward FitzGerald · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward FitzGerald (1809–1883) was an English writer whose free translation and adaptation of the medieval Persian quatrains of Omar Khayyam, The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, became one of the most quoted poems in the English language.
Reworked by FitzGerald through several editions, its meditations on wine, transience, and fate gave English verse a strikingly fatalistic, epicurean voice unlike anything else in the period.

poets.name: Alfred Domett
bio: Alfred Domett (1811–1887) was an English poet and friend of Robert Browning, who emigrated to New Zealand in 1842 and served as its Premier in 1862–63.
His long poem Ranolf and Amohia: A South-Sea Day-Dream (1872) is set in New Zealand.

poets.name: Alexander Hume
bio: Alexander Hume (born 1811; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Alexander Maclagan
bio: Alexander Maclagan (born 1811) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 8 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

bio: Andrew Park (born 1811; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 9 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

bio: William Sinclair (born 1811; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 7 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Robert Lowe, Viscount Sherbrooke
bio: Robert Lowe, Viscount Sherbrooke (1811–1892), was a British statesman, born in Nottinghamshire and educated at Winchester and University College, Oxford. He practised at the New South Wales bar and sat in the colony's legislative council from 1843 to 1850, returning to England in 1851.

He was later Chancellor of the Exchequer under Gladstone and was created Viscount Sherbrooke in 1880. His satirical verse on colonial land administration, drawn from his Australian years, was reprinted in Stedman's Victorian Anthology (1895).

poets.name: Frances Sargent Osgood
bio: Frances Sargent Osgood (1811–1850), born Frances Sargent Locke in Boston, was an American poet and writer for children who published widely in the annuals and magazines of her day.
She married the painter Samuel Stillman Osgood, and is remembered for her literary friendship with Edgar Allan Poe. Stedman included several of her lyrics in An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Jane Francesca Wilde, Lady Wilde
poets.credit: Jane Wilde ("Speranza"), photograph by Bernard Mulrenin, 1864 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Jane Francesca Wilde, Lady Wilde (1821–1896), wrote for The Nation under the pen-name "Speranza" and was its leading woman poet. She was the mother of Oscar Wilde.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Rev. H. H. Dugmore
bio: Rev. H. H. Dugmore (Henry Hare Dugmore, 1810–1896, Wesleyan missionary in the Eastern Cape) is one of the named contributors to The Poetry of South Africa, collected and arranged by A. Wilmot (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle & Rivington; Cape Town: J. C. Juta & Co., 1887), an anthology of verse from the Cape Colony, Natal and the Transvaal.

This archive holds 18 poems printed under this name in that volume, in Wilmot’s spelling. His pieces carry datelines such as Stormberg (1874) and the English Channel (1859), and several are set at Cove Rock and Bathurst in the Eastern Cape. Dates are those of a standard reference.

poets.name: Sir Samuel Ferguson
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir Samuel Ferguson, from Lady Ferguson's Sir Samuel Ferguson in the Ireland of His Day (1896) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Samuel Ferguson was born in Belfast and trained as a barrister. He was Deputy Keeper of the Public Records of Ireland and was knighted in 1878.
His verse drew on Irish legend and history, notably in Lays of the Western Gael (1865) and the long poem Congal (1872).

This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.
