bio: Thomas Tod Stoddart (born 1810; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 4 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Arthur Henry Hallam
poets.credit: Drawing of the bust of Arthur Henry Hallam by Francis Chantrey, published 1898 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Arthur Henry Hallam (1811–1833) was an English poet and essayist, the close friend of Alfred Tennyson whose early death inspired In Memoriam.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 4, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Henry Ellison
bio: Henry Ellison (1811–1880; death year as printed in the anthology) was an English poet, represented here by pieces from his volumes of verse.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Roden Noel
poets.credit: Portrait of Roden Noel (Wikimedia Commons file 'Roden Noel by Richmond') · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Roden Berkeley Wriothesley Noel (1834–1894) was an English poet, a younger son of the first Earl of Gainsborough. His volumes include Beatrice and Other Poems (1868), The Red Flag and Other Poems (1872), A Little Child's Monument (1881) and Songs of the Heights and Deeps (1885).
Lyra Celtica gives him seven poems, among them 'The Swimmer', 'The Dance' and 'The Pity of It', and counts him among its Anglo-Celtic poets.

poets.name: Richard Coe
bio: Richard Coe (born 1821) was a Philadelphia poet of a Quaker family, a merchant by profession, whose Poems appeared in 1851.
Griswold included 2 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Eliza Scudder
bio: Eliza Scudder (1821–1896) was an American poet and hymn-writer of Massachusetts.
The poem here is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1900).

poets.name: John Crawford
bio: John Crawford (born 1816; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 6 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Anne Lynch Botta
poets.credit: Portrait of Anne Charlotte Lynch by Savinien Edme Dubourjal (watercolour, c. 1847) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Anne Charlotte Lynch Botta (1815–1891) was an American poet and teacher, born in Bennington, Vermont, and raised in Providence, Rhode Island.
From the 1840s she hosted a celebrated literary salon at her New York home, which drew the city’s writers and artists, and she published her Poems in 1848 and again in an enlarged edition in 1853.

poets.name: Edward N. Shannon
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Edward N. Shannon published the first volume of his works in London in 1842; Sparling could find no biography of him.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Michael Joseph Barry
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Michael Joseph Barry (1817–1889) was a Cork-born barrister and one of the Young Ireland writers of The Nation. He wrote many songs and ballads and edited a collection of Irish songs.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Denis Florence MacCarthy
poets.credit: Portrait of Denis Florence MacCarthy, artist anonymous · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Denis Florence MacCarthy (1817–1882), born in Dublin, was a barrister and poet who contributed to The Nation in its early days. He published volumes of original verse and translations, including a well-known version of Calderón's dramas.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Erastus W. Ellsworth
bio: Erastus W. Ellsworth (1822–1902) was a poet and inventor, born in East Windsor, Connecticut, and a graduate of Amherst College (1844).
Griswold included 1 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Thomas Buchanan Read
poets.credit: Portrait: Artist/photograrpher unidentified — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Buchanan Read (1822–1872) was a Pennsylvania-born poet and portrait painter, later the author of Sheridan's Ride.
Griswold included 9 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: James Lord Pierpont
poets.credit: Portrait of James Lord Pierpont (Wikimedia Commons) · Public domain
bio: James Lord Pierpont (1822–1893) was an American composer and songwriter, born in Boston, the son of the Unitarian minister and poet John Pierpont. He is best known for "One Horse Open Sleigh" (1857), later called "Jingle Bells".

He settled in the South before the Civil War and served the Confederacy; his Confederate lyrics include "We Conquer or Die" (1861). He died in Winter Haven, Florida. He is a different man from his father, the poet John Pierpont, who has his own file in the archive.

poets.name: Aubrey de Vere
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Aubrey de Vere was born at Curragh Chase, County Limerick, and published poetry, criticism and travel writing. He became a Roman Catholic in 1851.
His Irish poems include The Wedding of the Clans and The Bard Ethell. He is not to be confused with Edward de Vere, Earl of Oxford.

poets.name: Charles Heavysege
poets.credit: Portrait of Charles Heavysege, Canadian Illustrated News (17 April 1875) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Heavysege (1816–1876), born in England, settled in Montreal in 1853 and worked as a carpenter and later as a journalist. He is best known for the dramatic poem Saul (1857).

The pieces here are short lyrics and sonnets from his verse drama Jephthah's Daughter (1865); his plays are not included. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Sir Daniel Wilson
bio: Sir Daniel Wilson (1816–1892) was a Scottish-born archaeologist and educator who became president of the University of Toronto.
He also wrote occasional verse, represented here by a single piece. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: James Monroe Whitfield
bio: James Monroe Whitfield (1822–1871) was born in Exeter, New Hampshire, and made his living as a barber in Buffalo, New York. A free Black man who wrote in the intervals of his work, he became a prominent voice of the antislavery movement, and his verse appeared in Frederick Douglass's newspaper The North Star.

America and Other Poems (Buffalo, 1853), inscribed to Martin R. Delany, is his best-known collection of verse and opens with its famous indictment of the United States as a land of liberty that tolerates slavery. In the mid-1850s Whitfield turned from protest to emigrationism, the belief that Black Americans should seek a future outside the country. He moved to California in 1861 and died in San Francisco in 1871.

poets.name: William Batchelder Bradbury
bio: William Batchelder Bradbury (1816–1868) was a Maine-born American composer and publisher of hymn and Sunday-school music. Eggleston prints the song Marching Along under his name.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: Marching Along.

poets.name: Robert Lowell (Robert Traill Spence Lowell)
bio: Robert Traill Spence Lowell (1816–1891) was an American Episcopal clergyman, schoolmaster, novelist and poet, best known for The Relief of Lucknow. Eggleston prints his poem The Massachusetts Line under the name Robert Lowell.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: The Massachusetts Line.

poets.name: Severn Teackle Wallis
bio: Severn Teackle Wallis (1816–1894) was a Baltimore lawyer, scholar and writer, imprisoned in 1861 for his Southern sympathies; his The Guerillas appears in Eggleston’s anthology.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: The Guerillas.

poets.name: Catherine Ann Ware Warfield
bio: Catherine Ann Ware Warfield (1816–1877) was an American poet and novelist from Mississippi and Kentucky. Eggleston prints her as Catherine M. Warfield; her Manassas celebrates the first Confederate victory of the Civil War.
The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: Manassas.

poets.name: Archibald Stirling Irving
bio: Archibald Stirling Irving (1816–1851) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Eva Mary Kelly
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Eva Mary Kelly (1826–1910), the daughter of a Galway gentleman, wrote for The Nation as "Eva". She waited for her fiancé, Kevin Izod O'Doherty, through his sentence of transportation after 1848, and married him two days after his return.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Walter Mitchell
bio: Walter Mitchell (born 1826) was an American clergyman and poet, author of the sea-song “Tacking Ship off Shore”.
The poem here is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1900).

poets.name: Samuel Johnson
bio: Samuel Johnson (1822–1882) was an American Unitarian minister, born in Salem, Massachusetts. He preached for many years at Lynn, Massachusetts, and is remembered for his large study Oriental Religions and Their Relation to Universal Religion and for his hymns. He is not the eighteenth-century English lexicographer of the same name.
The two hymns given here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900).

poets.name: William Wye Smith
bio: William Wye Smith (1827–1917) was a Scottish-born Canadian journalist and poet who wrote in English and in Scots, and later published a translation of the New Testament into Scots.
His Poems appeared in 1888. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Lew Wallace
bio: Lew (Lewis) Wallace was an American soldier, lawyer, diplomat and novelist, born in Brookville, Indiana, in 1827, who rose to the rank of general in the Civil War and was United States minister to Turkey from 1881 to 1885.
He is best known for the novel Ben-Hur (1880); he also wrote The Fair God (1873) and The Prince of India (1893).

poets.name: Amir Minai
bio: Amir Minai of Rampur is described in the book as one of the best poets of the latest period and a great mystical poet whose qasidahs for Muhammad are sung by devotees. He was court poet of Rampur, travelled to Mecca and Medina, and after the death of his patron Nawab Kalbe Ali Khan came to Hyderabad, where he was a rival of Dagh and is buried by his side.

The 7 pieces given here are drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. They are free renderings, not literal translations, and the original Urdu poems are untitled; each is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Dagh Dehlvi
bio: The book describes Dagh as a court poet of Rampur who went to Hyderabad and became the Nizam’s teacher in poetry, living there in great honour as Poet Laureate with the title Fasih-ul-Mulk, "the eloquence of the nation". His poetry is described as natural and graceful in expression, and he is said to have been without a rival in the mushaira.

The 4 pieces given here are drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. They are free renderings, not literal translations, and the original Urdu poems are untitled; each is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Ethel Lynn Beers
bio: Ethel Lynn Beers (1827–1879), born Ethelinda Eliot, was an American poet whose The Picket Guard, first printed in 1861, became one of the best-known songs of the Civil War.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: The Picket Guard.

poets.name: Ellen Clementine Howarth
bio: Ellen Clementine Howarth (1827–1899) was an American poet whose lyric “’T Is but a Little Faded Flower” was widely reprinted.
The poem here is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1900).

poets.name: Zahir Dehlvi
bio: Zahir is described in the book as a well-known modern poet who lived at Rampur at the court of Nawab Kalbe Ali Khan, afterwards at the court of the Nawab of Tonk, and finally at Hyderabad, in the literary circle of the Nizam, by whom he was much appreciated and rewarded.

The 2 pieces given here are drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. They are free renderings, not literal translations, and the original Urdu poems are untitled; each is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Altaf Husain Hali
bio: Hali is described in the book as a modern poet, a pupil of Ghalib, greatly admired, chiefly by Muslims, for poems calling for a Muslim and Indian renascence; the British Government gave him the title Shams-ul-ulema. The book, which was prepared in 1918, speaks of him as recently dead.

The one piece given here is drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. It is a free rendering, not a literal translation, and the original Urdu poem is untitled; it is named here by its first line.

poets.name: John Francis O'Donnell
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Francis O'Donnell (1837–1874) was an Irish poet and journalist, born in Limerick, who contributed verse to the Irish nationalist press and later worked as a journalist in London, where he died in 1874.
Lyra Celtica prints his 'A Spinning Song', in which a girl at her wheel sings of her sweetheart going off to fight for Ireland.

poets.name: Hezekiah Butterworth
poets.credit: Portrait of Hezekiah Butterworth · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Hezekiah Butterworth (1837–1905) was an American author and poet.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “The Thanksgiving for America”, “The Legend of Waukulla”, “The Fountain of Youth”, “Verazzano” and “Ortiz” among others; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Francis Miles Finch
bio: Francis Miles Finch (1827–1907) was a New York judge and Cornell professor of law, whose poem The Blue and the Gray (1867) honoured the Northern and Southern dead alike.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where they are printed under his or her name: Nathan Hale; The Blue and the Gray.

poets.name: Caroline Atherton Mason
bio: Caroline Atherton Mason (1823–1890), born Caroline Atherton Briggs in Marblehead, Massachusetts, was an American poet.

She was popularly known as the author of "Do They Miss Me at Home?" and "The King's Quest", and published Utterance, a Collection of Home Poems (1852) and, posthumously, A Lost Ring and Other Poems (1891).

poets.name: Augustine J. H. Duganne
bio: Augustine J. H. Duganne (1823–1884) was a Boston-born poet and novelist, who later served as a colonel in the Union army.
Griswold included 1 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: J. M. Legaré
bio: J. M. Legaré (1823–1859) was a poet of Abbeville and Charleston, South Carolina, whose Orta-Undis and Other Poems appeared in 1848.
Griswold included 2 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: John R. Thompson
bio: John R. Thompson (1823–1873) was a Virginia poet and lawyer, born in Richmond, and editor of the Southern Literary Messenger.
Griswold included 2 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: John James Piatt
poets.credit: Photograph of John James Piatt, c. 1900 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John James Piatt (1835–1917) was an American poet born in Indiana and raised in Ohio. With William Dean Howells he published Poems of Two Friends (1860), and he worked as a journalist and government clerk in Washington before serving as United States consul at Cork, Ireland.
He was married to the poet Sarah Morgan Bryan Piatt, and several of their volumes of verse appeared under both names.

poets.name: Sarah Morgan Bryan Piatt
poets.credit: Portrait: Henry Howe — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sarah Morgan Bryan Piatt (1836–1919), also known as Sallie M. Bryan, was an American poet from Kentucky. She published hundreds of poems in newspapers, magazines and anthologies, and eighteen volumes of verse, two of them written jointly with her husband, the poet John James Piatt.

Her work was widely read and reviewed in the United States and Europe in her lifetime. Her poems, often dramatic monologues spoken by mothers and children, were collected in volumes such as A Woman's Poems (1871) and That New World (1876).

poets.name: Coventry Patmore
poets.credit: Portrait of Coventry Patmore · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Coventry Patmore (1823–1896) was an English poet best known for The Angel in the House, a long narrative sequence idealizing married domestic love that became one of the era's most influential, and later most contested, poems.
A convert to Catholicism, his later odes turn toward mystical and religious themes.

poets.name: George Henry Boker
poets.credit: Photograph of George Henry Boker, 1855–65, Brady-Handy Photograph Collection (Library of Congress) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Henry Boker (1823–1890) was an American poet and dramatist, born in Philadelphia. His blank-verse tragedy Francesca da Rimini (1855) is the best known of his plays, and he later served as United States minister to Turkey and to Russia.
During the Civil War he wrote patriotic Union verse, collected in Poems of the War (1864), including “The Black Regiment” and “Dirge for a Soldier”.

poets.name: George Douglas Campbell, Duke of Argyll
bio: George Douglas Campbell, 8th Duke of Argyll (1823–1900), was a Scottish statesman, Liberal cabinet minister, scientific writer and amateur poet.
His poem “Our Dead” was included in Palgrave’s The Golden Treasury, Second Series (1897).

poets.name: John Kells Ingram
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Kells Ingram was an Irish scholar, born in County Donegal, who became a fellow of Trinity College Dublin and later its librarian. He wrote on political economy as well as verse.
His ballad "The Memory of the Dead" was published in The Nation in 1843.

poets.name: James D. Burns
bio: James D. Burns (born 1823; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: John Bathurst Dickson
bio: John Bathurst Dickson (born 1823; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William Johnson Cory
poets.credit: Portrait of William Johnson Cory · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Johnson Cory (1823–1892), born William Johnson at Torrington in Devon, was an English poet and schoolmaster. Educated at Eton and King's College, Cambridge, he spent twenty-seven years as a master at Eton before retiring to Devon, and later took the name Cory.

His poems were gathered in Ionica, first published in 1858, enlarged in a privately printed second series of 1877 and reissued in 1891. The poems here follow the third edition of 1905, together with its appendix of pieces from the earlier volumes.

poets.name: Sara Jane Lippincott
bio: Sara Jane Lippincott (1823–1904) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Illumination for Victories in Mexico”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Sarah Hammond Palfrey
bio: Sarah Hammond Palfrey (1823–1914), who wrote under the pseudonym E. Foxton, was an American novelist and poet of Cambridge, Massachusetts.
The poem here is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1900).

poets.name: Edward Pollock
bio: Edward Pollock (1823–1858) was an American lawyer and poet, who lived in San Francisco. His best-known poem is “Olivia”.
The poem here is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1900).

poets.name: Robert Collyer
bio: Robert Collyer (1823–1912) was born in Keighley, Yorkshire, worked as a blacksmith, emigrated to America and became a Unitarian minister in Chicago and New York. He also wrote verse in Yorkshire dialect and English.
The poem here is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1900).

poets.name: William Philpot
bio: William Philpot (1823–1889) was an English poet of whose life little is recorded in the standard reference works.
His elegy "Maritæ Suæ", written for his wife, is printed in The Oxford Book of English Verse.

poets.name: Thomas Wentworth Higginson
bio: Thomas Wentworth Higginson (1823–1911), born in Cambridge, Massachusetts, was a Unitarian minister, abolitionist, essayist and soldier, who commanded the first regiment of formerly enslaved men raised for the Union army.

A frequent contributor to the Atlantic Monthly, he became the correspondent and later co-editor of Emily Dickinson's first posthumous volumes of poems. His own verse was collected in The Afternoon Landscape (1889) and later volumes.

poets.name: William Walsham How
bio: William Walsham How (1823–1897) was an English Anglican bishop and hymn-writer.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: William Caldwell Roscoe
bio: William Caldwell Roscoe (1823–1859) was an English journalist and poet.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 5, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Bartholomew Dowling
bio: Bartholomew Dowling (1823–1863) was an Irish poet, born in Limerick, where he worked as a clerk to the treasurer of the Corporation; he lived for a time in the United States. He is remembered for his lyric “Our Brigade at Fontenoy” and for “The Revel”, a drinking-song that was for a time wrongly attributed to Alfred Domett.
The poem here is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman (ed.), A Victorian Anthology, 1837–1895 (Boston and New York: Houghton Mifflin, 1895). Spelling is that of the anthology.

poets.name: William Brighty Rands
poets.credit: Portrait of William Brighty Rands · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Brighty Rands (1823–1882) was a British writer and one of the leading authors of nursery rhymes of the Victorian era.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 5, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Edward Polin
bio: Edward Polin (born 1816) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Imre Madách
poets.credit: Photograph of Imre Madách, c. 1860s · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Imre Madách (1823–1864) was a Hungarian dramatist and poet, born at Alsósztregova into an old landowning family of the county of Nógrád. He studied law, served as a county official, and after the failure of the 1848–49 revolution was imprisoned for sheltering a fugitive of the national cause. His marriage broke down in these years, and much of his writing was done in solitude on the family estate.

His reputation rests on The Tragedy of Man (Az ember tragédiája), finished in 1860 and published in 1861, a dramatic poem in fifteen scenes in which Adam, guided by Lucifer, sees the future of humankind in a series of dreams. It was little noticed at first, but came to be regarded as the Hungarian national classic of the stage. William N. Loew's English version appeared in New York in 1908.

poets.name: Sándor Petőfi
poets.credit: Miklós Barabás, 1848 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sándor Petőfi (1823–1849) is the national poet of Hungary. Born in Kiskőrös to a butcher's family, he lived a restless early life as a soldier, strolling actor and poor student before the success of his folk-flavoured verse made him famous in Pest in the mid-1840s. His plain speech, his songs of the Great Hungarian Plain and his comic and tender narrative poems, among them the folk epic János vitéz (1845), changed the tone of Hungarian poetry.

In March 1848 he became a leading voice of the revolution in Pest, and his 'Nemzeti dal' (National Song) was recited to the crowds on the first day of the uprising. He served as an officer in the war of independence that followed and was last seen at the battle of Segesvár (now Sighișoara) on 31 July 1849, aged twenty-six; he is presumed to have been killed there.

The English versions in this archive are by William N. Loew, a Hungarian-born American, from his 1912 volume published for the Hungarian Literary Society of New York: the long poems Simple Steve, Childe John and The Apostle, the sequence Cypress Leaves from the Grave of Dear Ethel, and a selection of lyrics.

poets.name: Elizabeth Stoddard
bio: Elizabeth Drew Barstow Stoddard (1823–1902) was an American novelist and poet, born at Mattapoisett, Massachusetts. In 1851 she married the poet Richard Henry Stoddard and thereafter lived in New York City.
She began to contribute poems to the periodicals a few years after her marriage; her verse was collected in Poems (1895). She is not to be confused with her husband, Richard Henry Stoddard.

poets.name: Charles G. Leland
poets.credit: Portrait: Photographer unidentified — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles G. Leland (1824–1903) was a Philadelphia-born humorist, folklorist and poet, later famous for his Hans Breitmann ballads.
Griswold included 4 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Phoebe Cary
bio: Phoebe Cary (1824–1871), sister of the poet Alice Cary, was an American poet and parodist.
The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: Ready.

poets.name: Annie Chambers Ketchum
bio: Annie Chambers Ketchum (1824–1904) was an American poet and teacher of the Southern states, associated with Memphis, Tennessee. Eggleston prints her version of The Bonnie Blue Flag among the Southern songs.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: The Bonnie Blue Flag.

poets.name: George H. Miles
bio: George Henry Miles (1824–1871) was an American poet and dramatist, a professor of English at Mount St. Mary's College in Emmitsburg, Maryland.

He wrote the words of "God Save the South" (1861), a Confederate "national hymn" set to music by C. W. A. Ellerbrock and published at New Orleans; the song is reprinted here from W. L. Fagan's Southern War Songs (1890).

poets.name: Henry David Thoreau
poets.credit: Daguerreotype of Henry David Thoreau by Benjamin D. Maxham, 1856 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry David Thoreau (1817–1862) was an American essayist, naturalist and poet, born and long resident in Concord, Massachusetts. He is best known for Walden (1854) and for the essay “Civil Disobedience”.
He wrote verse throughout his life, much of it printed in The Dial and in his prose works; it is plain, observant poetry of the seasons and the countryside around Concord.

poets.name: Philip James Bailey
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Philip James Bailey (1816–1902) was an English poet, best known as the author of the long philosophical poem Festus.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: William Allingham
poets.credit: Photograph of William Allingham · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Allingham (1824–1889) was an Irish poet born in Ballyshannon, County Donegal, where he spent his early working life as a customs officer. He published his first collection in 1850 and went on to Day and Night Songs (1854) and the long verse narrative Laurence Bloomfield in Ireland (1864), a portrait of the relations between landlords and tenants.

He later moved to England, edited Fraser's Magazine from 1874 to 1879, and married the illustrator Helen Paterson, who drew many of the pictures for his children's verse. He is remembered above all for the fairy poems, chiefly "The Fairies" ("Up the airy mountain"), and for the Donegal ballads and lyrics that W. B. Yeats chose for Sixteen Poems (1905) and the later Rhymes for the Young Folk.

poets.name: James Lionel Michael
bio: James Lionel Michael (1824–1868) was an English-born solicitor and poet who emigrated to Australia in the gold-rush years and practised in Sydney and later at Grafton on the Clarence River.
He gave early encouragement to the young Henry Kendall, who worked in his office; he wrote the poem John Cumberland and contributed verse to Sydney periodicals.

poets.name: J. H. Eccles
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: J. H. Eccles (1824–1883) was a Leeds dialect poet whose Yorkshire Songs, published in 1862, Moorman calls a notable contribution to the dialect movement of the industrial West Riding.
The two poems here are taken from Moorman's Yorkshire Dialect Poems (1916).

poets.name: Charlotte Brontë
poets.credit: Portrait: George Richmond — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio:
Charlotte Brontë (1816–1855) was an English novelist and poet, born at Thornton in Yorkshire and raised at Haworth parsonage, where her father was perpetual curate. With her sisters Emily and Anne she wrote from childhood, and in 1846 the three published a joint volume of verse under the pseudonyms Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell.

The 1846 Poems sold only a handful of copies, but it led all three sisters to prose fiction. Charlotte's Jane Eyre (1847) made her famous, followed by Shirley (1849) and Villette (1853). She died in 1855. Her nineteen poems in the 1846 volume are given here in the order printed.

poets.name: Alexander A. Ritchie
bio: Alexander A. Ritchie (1816–1850) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: James Henderson
bio: James Henderson (born 1824; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 4 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William Allen Butler
bio: William Allen Butler (1825–1902) was a New York lawyer and poet, born in Albany, the son of Attorney-General Benjamin F. Butler.
Griswold included 3 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Henry W. Parker
bio: Henry W. Parker (born 1825) was a poet and Presbyterian pastor in Brooklyn, born in Danby, New York, and a graduate of Amherst College (1843).
Griswold included 6 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Thomas Davis
poets.credit: Portrait: not identified — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Davis was born in Mallow, County Cork, and in 1842 helped to found the newspaper The Nation, the voice of the Young Ireland movement. He wrote the ballads collected in The Spirit of the Nation.
He died of scarlet fever in 1845, aged thirty.

poets.name: James Hedderwick
bio: James Hedderwick (born 1814; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 6 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Charles Mackay, LL.D.
bio: Charles Mackay, LL.D. (born 1814; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 17 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Robert Nicoll
bio: Robert Nicoll (born 1814) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 5 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Peter Still
bio: Peter Still (born 1814) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Hester Sigerson
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Hester Sigerson was an Irish poet, the wife of the physician and writer George Sigerson and the mother of the poet Dora Sigerson Shorter. She contributed verse to Irish periodicals.
Yeats printed her short "Mad Song" in A Book of Irish Verse (1900).

poets.name: Frances Brown
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Frances Brown (1816–1879), born at Stranorlar, County Donegal, lost her sight in infancy but educated herself and became a poet and novelist. Her first poem appeared in the Irish Penny Journal; she spent the later part of her life in England.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Charles Gavan Duffy
poets.credit: Charles Gavan Duffy, from his Autobiography (1880) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Charles Gavan Duffy (1816–1903), born in County Monaghan, founded The Nation in 1842 with Thomas Davis and John Blake Dillon and edited it. He emigrated to Australia in 1856, where he rose to high office, and later lived in southern Europe.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Thomas Westwood
bio: Thomas Westwood (1814–1888; death year as printed in the anthology) was an English poet and bibliographer of angling.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 4, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Shamshad
poets.dates: dates not given in the source
bio: Shamshad appears in the contents of Hindustani Lyrics but the book gives no biographical note and no dates for him; nothing further is claimed here.

The one piece given here is drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. It is a free rendering, not a literal translation, and the original Urdu poem is untitled; it is named here by its first line.

poets.name: James Maclardy
bio: James Maclardy (born 1824; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Timothy Daniel Sullivan
poets.credit: Photograph of T. D. Sullivan, photographer unknown, before 1914 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Timothy Daniel Sullivan (1827–1914), born at Bantry, County Cork, began contributing to The Nation as a young man and later became its proprietor and editor. His song "God Save Ireland" became one of the best known of the Irish nationalist songs.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Mortimer Collins
poets.credit: Mortimer Collins, portrait (1877; artist unknown) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mortimer Collins (1827–1876) was an English poet, novelist and journalist, born at Plymouth. He published light, graceful verse such as Summer Songs in Idleness (1860), alongside a long series of novels and newspaper work.
The songs given here are taken from Edmund H. Garrett's anthology Victorian Songs: Lyrics of the Affections and Nature (Boston: Little, Brown, 1895).

poets.name: Sydney Dobell
poets.credit: Portrait of Sydney Dobell · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sydney Thompson Dobell (1824–1874) was an English poet and critic, associated with the so-called "Spasmodic" school of the 1850s. He made his name with the dramatic poem The Roman (1850, as "Sydney Yendys") and followed it with Balder (1854) and, with Alexander Smith, Sonnets on the War (1855).
He was a frail man who spent his later years in the Cotswolds and on the Continent in search of health; his collected Poems appeared in 1875, after his death.

poets.name: Lucy Larcom
bio: Lucy Larcom (1824–1893) was an American journalist.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “Mistress Hale of Beverly”, “The Nineteenth of April” and “The Sinking of the Merrimack”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Adeline Dutton Train Whitney
bio: Adeline Dutton Train Whitney (1824–1903) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Peace”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: William Alexander
bio: William Alexander (1824–1911) was an Irish cleric of the Church of Ireland, later Archbishop of Armagh, and the husband of Cecil Frances Alexander.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Walter Chalmers Smith
bio: Walter Chalmers Smith (1824–1908) was a Scottish minister of the Free Church, hymn-writer and poet.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Francis Turner Palgrave
poets.credit: Portrait of Francis Turner Palgrave by Elliott & Fry · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Francis Turner Palgrave (1824–1897) was a British critic, anthologist and poet, best known as the compiler of The Golden Treasury (1861).

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vols. 5, 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Joseph Brownlee Brown
bio: Joseph Brownlee Brown (1824–1888) was born in Charleston, South Carolina, graduated from Dartmouth and died in Brooklyn, New York. He wrote for The Atlantic Monthly, and ill health kept him from fulfilling the promise of his youth.
His poem "Thalatta! Thalatta!" appears in Stedman's An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: George William Curtis
bio: George William Curtis (1824–1892) was an American essayist, orator and editor, born in Providence, Rhode Island. At eighteen he joined the Brook Farm community, and he later became a leading voice in social and political reform.
His early prose included "Nile Notes of a Howadji" (1851) and "The Potiphar Papers" (1853). His poem "Ebb and Flow" appears in Stedman's An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Adelaide Anne Procter
poets.credit: Portrait of Adelaide Anne Procter · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Adelaide Anne Procter (1825–1864) was an English poet and social activist, a devout Catholic and one of the best-selling poets of the Victorian era after Tennyson himself.
Her collection Legends and Lyrics gathers narrative ballads and devotional verse, often concerned with charity, suffering, and quiet endurance.

poets.name: Rolf Boldrewood (Thomas Alexander Browne)
bio: Thomas Alexander Browne (1826–1915), who wrote as 'Rolf Boldrewood', was an English-born pastoralist, police magistrate and gold commissioner in Australia.
He is best known for the bushranging novel Robbery Under Arms; he also wrote Old Melbourne Memories, and occasional verse.

poets.name: Richard Henry Stoddard
poets.credit: Photograph of Richard Henry Stoddard by Rockwood (before 1903) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Henry Stoddard (1825–1903) was an American poet and critic, born at Hingham, Massachusetts. He worked in an iron foundry as a young man, taught himself to write, and later became literary editor of the New York Mail and Express.
He was a central figure of the New York literary circle of his day, alongside Bayard Taylor and Edmund Clarence Stedman, and his polished lyrics were widely anthologised.

poets.name: Julia C. R. Dorr
poets.credit: Julia C. R. Dorr, frontispiece/portrait photograph · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Julia Caroline Ripley Dorr (1825–1913) was an American poet, novelist and travel writer, born in Charleston, South Carolina, and long associated with Vermont, whose centennial and landscape she celebrated in verse. She was best known for her poetry, which is gentle, devotional and carefully shaped, and which was widely printed in the American magazines of her day.

This selection follows her Complete Edition of Poems (Scribner, 1892), which gathers her earlier books in their own sections, and her later volume Afterglow (Scribner, 1900). Each book opens with a verse dedication to “S. M. D.”, her husband, and both dedications are kept here as poems.

poets.name: Charles Hamilton Aïdé
bio: Charles Hamilton Aïdé (1826–1906) was a novelist, song-writer, composer and poet, born in Paris and educated at the University of Bonn. His verse volumes include Eleonore, and Other Poems (1856), The Romance of the Scarlet Leaf, and Other Poems (1865) and Songs without Music (1882), and many of his songs were set to music.
The poem here is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman (ed.), A Victorian Anthology, 1837–1895 (Boston and New York: Houghton Mifflin, 1895). Spelling is that of the anthology.

poets.name: Bayard Taylor
poets.credit: Portrait of Bayard Taylor · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Bayard Taylor (1825–1878) was an American poet, travel writer and translator, born at Kennett Square, Pennsylvania. His accounts of journeys through Europe, Africa, and Asia made him a celebrated figure, and his verse translation of Goethe’s Faust (1870–71) was long standard.
He served as United States minister to Germany and died at Berlin in 1878. His lyrics, such as the “Bedouin Song”, were popular in his lifetime.

poets.name: Thomas D'Arcy McGee
poets.credit: Portrait: William Notman — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas D'Arcy McGee was born in Carlingford, County Louth, and was a Young Ireland writer and journalist. He emigrated, became a Canadian politician and one of the Fathers of Confederation.
He was assassinated in Ottawa in 1868.

poets.name: Andrew James Symington
bio: Andrew James Symington (born 1825; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Pamelia Vining Yule
bio: Pamelia Vining Yule (1825–1897) was a Canadian poet.
Her Poems of the Heart and Home appeared in 1881. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Francis James Child
bio: Francis James Child (1825–1896) was a Harvard professor and the editor of the great collection English and Scottish Popular Ballads. During the Civil War he wrote the satirical ballad Overtures from Richmond.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: Overtures from Richmond.

poets.name: Thomas Henry Huxley
bio: Thomas Henry Huxley (1825–1895) was an English biologist and teacher, best known as the defender of Darwin's theory of evolution and as a master of Victorian scientific prose.
He wrote very little verse. The poem here, written for the funeral of Tennyson in Westminster Abbey on 12 October 1892, is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman's A Victorian Anthology (1895).

poets.name: John Williamson Palmer
bio: John Williamson Palmer (1825–1906) was a Baltimore physician, author and journalist, who wrote the Confederate marching song Stonewall Jackson’s Way during the Civil War.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: Stonewall Jackson’s Way.

poets.name: L. Virginia French
bio: Louisa Virginia French (1825–1881) was an American poet and novelist who lived in McMinnville, Tennessee, and wrote under the name L. Virginia French.
Her Confederate-era verse includes "A Southern Gathering Song", written to the tune of "Hail Columbia" and reprinted here from W. L. Fagan's Southern War Songs (1890).

poets.name: Horatio Nelson Powers
bio: Horatio Nelson Powers (1826–1890) was an American Episcopal clergyman and poet. His devotional and nature verse was often reprinted in the anthologies of his day.
Our Sister and Chimney Swallows were included in Stevenson's Home Book of Verse (1912).

poets.name: Stephen Collins Foster
poets.credit: Portrait of Stephen Collins Foster, c. 1860 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Stephen Collins Foster (1826–1864) was an American songwriter, born at Lawrenceville, now part of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. He wrote both the words and music of songs such as “Oh! Susanna” (1848), “Old Folks at Home” (1851) and “My Old Kentucky Home” (1853).
He died in New York City in 1864. His song lyrics, printed here as poems, were among the most widely sung in the United States.

poets.name: A. E. Blackmar
bio: Armand Edward Blackmar (1826–1888) was an American music publisher and composer who worked in New Orleans, where he issued many songs of the Confederacy during the Civil War.
He is credited in W. L. Fagan's Southern War Songs (1890) with the words of "Allons Enfans", a Southern adaptation of the Marseillaise dated 1861, which is reprinted here.

poets.name: John William De Forest
bio: John William De Forest (1826–1906) was a Connecticut novelist and Union army officer, best known for his Civil War fiction and memoir.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: In Louisiana.

poets.name: Dinah Maria Craik
poets.credit: Portrait of Dinah Maria Craik by Hubert von Herkomer · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Dinah Maria Craik (1826–1887), born Dinah Maria Mulock in Stoke-on-Trent, was a novelist and poet, best known for the novel John Halifax, Gentleman (1856). In 1865 she married George Lillie Craik.
Her poems, which appeared in volumes from 1859, include the tender cradle-song “Philip, my King”; three of them are in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: George Donald, Jun.
bio: George Donald, Jun. (born 1826; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Robert Duthie
bio: Robert Duthie (born 1826) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Alexander Stephen Wilson
bio: Alexander Stephen Wilson (born 1826; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 3 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Emily Pfeiffer
poets.credit: Portrait of Emily Pfeiffer, 1890 (Charles Wells Moulton) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Emily Jane Pfeiffer (1827–1890), born Emily Davis, was an English-language poet who published Poems (1876), Songs and Sonnets (1880) and Under the Aspens (1882), and wrote on the position of women. She married Jurgen Edward Pfeiffer in 1853.
She left money in her will for the higher education of women. Five of her poems appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: James McIntyre
poets.credit: Frontispiece portrait from Poems of James McIntyre (Ingersoll: Chronicle office, 1889) · Public domain (Project Gutenberg)
bio: James McIntyre (1827–1906) was born in Scotland and emigrated to Upper Canada as a young man. He settled in Ingersoll, Ontario, where he kept a furniture shop and undertaking business. He is remembered as the "Cheese Poet" for his odes to the dairy industry of Oxford County.

His books Musings on the Banks of Canadian Thames (1884) and Poems of James McIntyre (1889) are filled with loyal verses on Canadian towns, rivers, hunting tales, patriotic occasions and the poets he admired. The lumbering rhymes and eccentric grammar, above all in the Ode on the Mammoth Cheese, have earned him a lasting reputation as one of the most charmingly awkward poets in English.

poets.name: Mary Bayard Clarke
poets.credit: Portrait of Mary Bayard Clarke (Wikimedia Commons) · Public domain
bio: Mary Bayard Clarke (1827–1886) was an American poet from North Carolina, born in Raleigh, who published under the pen name "Tenella". Her collection Wood-Notes; or, Carolina Carols appeared in 1854.
Her Civil War verse for the Confederacy, including two songs about Lee and Jackson, was reprinted in W. L. Fagan's Southern War Songs (1890) under the name "Tenella".

poets.name: William Haines Lytle
poets.credit: Portrait of William Haines Lytle · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Haines Lytle (1826–1863) was an American politician.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “The Siege of Chapultepec” and “The Volunteers”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Alexander Nicolson
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Alexander Nicolson (1827–1893) was a Scottish lawyer and man of letters, born on the Isle of Skye. A Gaelic scholar, he edited a collection of Gaelic proverbs and served as Sheriff of Kirkcudbright.
Lyra Celtica prints his poem 'Skye', in praise of his native island.

poets.name: Earl of Southesk
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: James Carnegie, ninth Earl of Southesk (1827–1905), was a Scottish peer, traveller and poet. He made his name with the verse tale Jonas Fisher (1875), followed by Greenwood's Farewell (1876), The Meda Maiden (1877) and The Burial of Isis (1884).
Lyra Celtica prints his lyric 'November's Cadence'.

poets.name: Rose Terry Cooke
poets.credit: Portrait of Rose Terry Cooke · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Rose Terry Cooke (1827–1892) was an American poet.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “The Death of Goody Nurse”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Richard Doddridge Blackmore
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Richard Doddridge Blackmore (1825–1900) was an English novelist, famous for Lorna Doone, who also wrote verse.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: John Townsend Trowbridge
poets.credit: Portrait of John Townsend Trowbridge · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Townsend Trowbridge (1827–1916) was an American author.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Columbus at the Convent”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: William Rodger Thomson
bio: William Rodger Thomson is one of the named contributors to The Poetry of South Africa, collected and arranged by A. Wilmot (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle & Rivington; Cape Town: J. C. Juta & Co., 1887), an anthology of verse from the Cape Colony, Natal and the Transvaal.

This archive holds 2 poems printed under this name in that volume, in Wilmot’s spelling. His poem on the Cape of Good Hope is dated Utrecht, 1856. Dates are not given by Wilmot and are not supplied here.

poets.name: E. B. Watermeyer
bio: E. B. Watermeyer is one of the named contributors to The Poetry of South Africa, collected and arranged by A. Wilmot (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle & Rivington; Cape Town: J. C. Juta & Co., 1887), an anthology of verse from the Cape Colony, Natal and the Transvaal.

This archive holds 2 poems printed under this name in that volume, in Wilmot’s spelling. His pieces are a translation of an ode by Horace and a poem on the morning after a storm at sea. Dates are not given by Wilmot and are not supplied here.

poets.name: G. Longmore
bio: G. Longmore is one of the named contributors to The Poetry of South Africa, collected and arranged by A. Wilmot (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle & Rivington; Cape Town: J. C. Juta & Co., 1887), an anthology of verse from the Cape Colony, Natal and the Transvaal.

This archive holds 3 poems printed under this name in that volume, in Wilmot’s spelling. His pieces are two sonnets of the Cape and a poem dated Cape Town, February 1862. Dates are not given by Wilmot and are not supplied here.

poets.name: John Stirling
bio: John Stirling is one of the named contributors to The Poetry of South Africa, collected and arranged by A. Wilmot (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle & Rivington; Cape Town: J. C. Juta & Co., 1887), an anthology of verse from the Cape Colony, Natal and the Transvaal.
This archive holds 1 poem printed under this name in that volume, in Wilmot’s spelling. His poem is a farewell to Madeira. Dates are not given by Wilmot and are not supplied here.

poets.name: William Selwyn
bio: William Selwyn is one of the named contributors to The Poetry of South Africa, collected and arranged by A. Wilmot (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle & Rivington; Cape Town: J. C. Juta & Co., 1887), an anthology of verse from the Cape Colony, Natal and the Transvaal.

This archive holds 11 poems printed under this name in that volume, in Wilmot’s spelling. His pieces are mostly dated from Port Elizabeth, between 1855 and 1886. Dates are not given by Wilmot and are not supplied here.

poets.name: A. Brodrick
bio: A. Brodrick is one of the named contributors to The Poetry of South Africa, collected and arranged by A. Wilmot (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle & Rivington; Cape Town: J. C. Juta & Co., 1887), an anthology of verse from the Cape Colony, Natal and the Transvaal.

This archive holds 9 poems printed under this name in that volume, in Wilmot’s spelling. His pieces are dated from Pretoria and the Transvaal (1874-82) and Kimberley (1875). Dates are not given by Wilmot and are not supplied here.

poets.name: C. F. Overton
bio: C. F. Overton is one of the named contributors to The Poetry of South Africa, collected and arranged by A. Wilmot (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle & Rivington; Cape Town: J. C. Juta & Co., 1887), an anthology of verse from the Cape Colony, Natal and the Transvaal.
This archive holds 1 poem printed under this name in that volume, in Wilmot’s spelling. His piece is a colonial ballad. Dates are not given by Wilmot and are not supplied here.

poets.name: A. W. Cole
bio: A. W. Cole is one of the named contributors to The Poetry of South Africa, collected and arranged by A. Wilmot (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle & Rivington; Cape Town: J. C. Juta & Co., 1887), an anthology of verse from the Cape Colony, Natal and the Transvaal.
This archive holds 3 poems printed under this name in that volume, in Wilmot’s spelling. His pieces are comic colonial ballads. Dates are not given by Wilmot and are not supplied here.

poets.name: H. Hartwell
bio: H. Hartwell is one of the named contributors to The Poetry of South Africa, collected and arranged by A. Wilmot (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle & Rivington; Cape Town: J. C. Juta & Co., 1887), an anthology of verse from the Cape Colony, Natal and the Transvaal.

This archive holds 2 poems printed under this name in that volume, in Wilmot’s spelling. His pieces are on the wreck of the Teuton and the hills of Africa. Dates are not given by Wilmot and are not supplied here.

poets.name: Stafford Cruikshanks
bio: Stafford Cruikshanks is one of the named contributors to The Poetry of South Africa, collected and arranged by A. Wilmot (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle & Rivington; Cape Town: J. C. Juta & Co., 1887), an anthology of verse from the Cape Colony, Natal and the Transvaal.

This archive holds 4 poems printed under this name in that volume, in Wilmot’s spelling. His pieces concern the Southern Cross, the 1820 Settlers’ Jubilee and the Cape statesman William Porter. Dates are not given by Wilmot and are not supplied here.

poets.name: G. Impey
bio: G. Impey is one of the named contributors to The Poetry of South Africa, collected and arranged by A. Wilmot (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle & Rivington; Cape Town: J. C. Juta & Co., 1887), an anthology of verse from the Cape Colony, Natal and the Transvaal.
This archive holds 1 poem printed under this name in that volume, in Wilmot’s spelling. His poem is dated Graham’s Town, 27 October 1851. Dates are not given by Wilmot and are not supplied here.

poets.name: Moodie
bio: Moodie is one of the named contributors to The Poetry of South Africa, collected and arranged by A. Wilmot (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle & Rivington; Cape Town: J. C. Juta & Co., 1887), an anthology of verse from the Cape Colony, Natal and the Transvaal.

This archive holds 3 poems printed under this name in that volume, in Wilmot’s spelling. Wilmot prints only the surname; the pieces are dated Tugela (1868) and Melsetter, Natal (January 1868). Dates are not given by Wilmot and are not supplied here.

poets.name: Rev. F. J. Ochse
bio: Rev. F. J. Ochse is one of the named contributors to The Poetry of South Africa, collected and arranged by A. Wilmot (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle & Rivington; Cape Town: J. C. Juta & Co., 1887), an anthology of verse from the Cape Colony, Natal and the Transvaal.
This archive holds 7 poems printed under this name in that volume, in Wilmot’s spelling. One piece is dated Beaconsfield. Dates are not given by Wilmot and are not supplied here.

poets.name: Garret Brown
bio: Garret Brown is one of the named contributors to The Poetry of South Africa, collected and arranged by A. Wilmot (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle & Rivington; Cape Town: J. C. Juta & Co., 1887), an anthology of verse from the Cape Colony, Natal and the Transvaal.
This archive holds 1 poem printed under this name in that volume, in Wilmot’s spelling. His poem is an elegy on General Gordon. Dates are not given by Wilmot and are not supplied here.

poets.name: H. W. Bidwell
bio: H. W. Bidwell is one of the named contributors to The Poetry of South Africa, collected and arranged by A. Wilmot (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle & Rivington; Cape Town: J. C. Juta & Co., 1887), an anthology of verse from the Cape Colony, Natal and the Transvaal.

This archive holds 12 poems printed under this name in that volume, in Wilmot’s spelling. His pieces are dated from Grahamstown and Uitenhage between 1862 and 1869. Dates are not given by Wilmot and are not supplied here.

poets.name: T. Fannin
poets.dates: d. before 1887; dates not given by Wilmot
bio: T. Fannin is named in the preface to The Poetry of South Africa, collected and arranged by A. Wilmot (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle & Rivington; Cape Town: J. C. Juta & Co., 1887), where Wilmot calls him “the late T. Fannin, who used in the olden days to sing his own rhymes in right good style”.
This archive holds the one poem, The Smouse, which Wilmot prints in his preface from lines received from Natal; no dates or biographical details are given there.

poets.name: Thomas Woolner
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Woolner by Dante Gabriel Rossetti · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Woolner (1825–1892) was an English sculptor and poet, one of the founding members of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 5, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Edward Henry Bickersteth
bio: Edward Henry Bickersteth (1825–1906) was an English Anglican bishop of Exeter, a poet and hymn-writer.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Henry Septimus Sutton
bio: Henry Septimus Sutton (1825–1901) was an English journalist and temperance activist, known as a religious poet.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: John Ellerton
bio: John Ellerton (1826–1893) was an English hymn-writer and hymnologist.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition.
