poets.name: Isa Blagden
poets.credit: Portrait of Isa Blagden (before 1873) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Isabella (Isa) Blagden (1817–1873) was an English writer who lived in Florence and was a close friend of Robert and Elizabeth Barrett Browning. She wrote novels, and her verse was collected in Poems (1873), published after her death.
Her short lyrics “Sorrow” and “Endurance” are included in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Wathen Mark Wilks Call
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Wathen Mark Wilks Call (1817–1890) was an English freethinker, poet and writer. He served as a deacon and priest in the Church of England from 1843 to 1856.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Alexander Buchanan
bio: Alexander Buchanan (1817–1852) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Robert Cathcart
bio: Robert Cathcart (born 1817; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: John De Jean Frazer
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John De Jean Frazer (c. 1809–1849), born near Birr and later a cabinet-maker in Dublin, was a song-writer. Sparling spells his name "Fraser" in his notes.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: John Keegan
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Keegan (c. 1809–1849), born in Queen's County, was a peasant poet educated at a hedge-school. He wrote of and for the country people among whom he lived and died.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: John Francis Waller
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Francis Waller (1809–1894), born in Limerick, was a barrister and poet whose songs and lyrics were widely admired.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Arthur Gerald Geoghegan
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Arthur Gerald Geoghegan (1810–1889), born in Dublin, wrote The Monks of Kilcrea, a series of verse stories with songs and interludes, which had reached a third edition by 1861.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Francis Davis
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Francis Davis (1810–1885), "The Belfast Man", was a weaver and poet born at Ballincollig, County Cork. He wrote his verses at the loom, contributed to The Nation, and published three volumes of verse.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Alexander Smith
bio: Alexander Smith (1829–1867) was a Scottish poet and essayist, born in Kilmarnock and trained as a designer of lace patterns in Glasgow. His long poem A Life-Drama (1853) made his name and linked him with the so-called Spasmodic school; in 1854 he became secretary to the University of Edinburgh, and his essays Dreamthorp appeared in 1863. He died in Edinburgh at thirty-seven.

The poems here are taken from the third edition of Poems (London: David Bogue, 1854). A Life-Drama is given as a work in thirteen scenes, with the scene settings and stage directions left out and the speakers’ names kept; the shorter poems and the untitled sonnets follow, each sonnet named by its first line.

poets.name: Rosanna Leprohon
poets.credit: Portrait of Rosanna Leprohon, from A Woman of the Century (1893) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Rosanna Eleanor Leprohon (1829–1879), born in Montreal, was a Canadian novelist and poet.
Her poems were collected in 1881. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: James Barron Hope
bio: James Barron Hope (1829–1887) was a Virginia poet, newspaper editor and Confederate officer, known for occasional verse and Southern patriotic poems.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: The Oath of Freedom.

poets.name: Guy Humphrey McMaster
bio: Guy Humphrey McMaster (1829–1887) was a New York lawyer and poet, remembered chiefly for the song Carmen Bellicosum, a stirring picture of the Revolution’s ragged continental soldiers.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: Carmen Bellicosum.

poets.name: Edna Dean Proctor
poets.credit: Portrait: Laura Carter Holloway — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edna Dean Proctor (1829–1923), born in Henniker, New Hampshire, was an American poet and traveller whose patriotic verse was widely printed during and after the Civil War.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: The Stripes and the Stars.

poets.name: Lamar Fontaine
poets.credit: Portrait of Lamar Fontaine from The Poets and Poetry of Texas (1885) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Lamar Fontaine (1829–1921) was an American Confederate soldier and writer from the South who claimed authorship of "All Quiet Along the Potomac To-Night".

That claim is disputed: the poem was first published in 1861 under the name of Ethel Lynn Beers. It is reprinted here under his name because W. L. Fagan's Southern War Songs (1890) attributes it to him, together with "Only a Soldier".

poets.name: Patrick Sarsfield Gilmore
poets.credit: Portrait of Patrick Sarsfield Gilmore · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Patrick Sarsfield Gilmore (1829–1892) was an Irish-American composer and bandmaster.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “When Johnny Comes Marching Home”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: David Taylor
bio: David Taylor (born 1817; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Silas Weir Mitchell
poets.credit: Portrait: Photo by Fr. GuteKunst.[1] ↑ Julie Bates Dock (1998) Charlotte Perkins Gilman's "The Yello — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Silas Weir Mitchell (1829–1914) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “Herndon”, “How the Cumberland Went Down”, “Kearsarge”, “Lincoln” and “The Song of the Flags”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Emily Brontë
poets.credit: Portrait of Emily Brontë · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Emily Brontë (1818–1848) is best known as the author of Wuthering Heights, but she also wrote intense, visionary lyric poetry, much of it set in the imagined world of Gondal she created with her sister Anne.

Published pseudonymously as "Ellis Bell" alongside her sisters' verse in 1846, her poems of longing, imprisonment, and the moors were far better received by contemporary critics than the sisters' novels first were.

poets.name: William Forster
bio: William Forster (1818–1882) was an Australian politician and writer who served as Premier of New South Wales in 1859–60.
He was also a poet and dramatist, the author of the verse drama Midas, from which Stevens takes his lyric.

poets.name: Eliza Cook
poets.credit: Portrait of Eliza Cook by William Etty, 1845 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Eliza Cook (1818–1889) was a London-born poet whose popular, plain-spoken verse made her one of the best-known women poets of the 1840s. Her first collection, Melaia and Other Poems, appeared in 1838, and “The Old Arm-Chair” became one of her best-loved songs.
From 1849 to 1854 she edited Eliza Cook's Journal, a weekly paper for working readers. Three of her lyrics appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: William Jamie
bio: William Jamie (born 1818; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Thomas C. Latto
bio: Thomas C. Latto (born 1818) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 4 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: William Stirling, M.P.
bio: William Stirling, M.P. (born 1818) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: M. E. Barber
bio: M. E. Barber (Mary Elizabeth Barber, 1818–1899) is one of the named contributors to The Poetry of South Africa, collected and arranged by A. Wilmot (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle & Rivington; Cape Town: J. C. Juta & Co., 1887), an anthology of verse from the Cape Colony, Natal and the Transvaal.
This archive holds 1 poem printed under this name in that volume, in Wilmot’s spelling. Her poem is dated Grahamstown, 9 March 1884. Dates are those of a standard reference.

poets.name: John Savage
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Savage (1828–1888), born in Dublin, was a Fenian, journalist and poet who was concerned in an attempted insurrection in Munster in 1849 and later lived in America, where he wrote on Irish revolutionary history and Celtic archaeology.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Joseph Brenan
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Joseph Brenan (1828–1857) was born in Cork and began as a contributor to the nationalist press. In 1848 he moved to Dublin and was imprisoned in Kilmainham; after his release he went to New York and in 1851 settled in New Orleans as a journalist, dying there in 1857.
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Ellen Mary Downing
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Ellen Mary Patrick Downing (1828–1869), of Cork, wrote for The Nation from the age of seventeen under the signature "Mary", and was known as "Mary of the Nation".
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: William Kenealy
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Kenealy (1828–1876) was an Irish poet; Sparling prints his "The Moon behind the Hill", subtitled "The Kilkenny Exile's Christmas Song".
The poems here are taken from H. Halliday Sparling's anthology Irish Minstrelsy (London: Walter Scott, 1888).

poets.name: Fitz-James O'Brien
poets.credit: Portrait of Fitz-James O'Brien · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Fitz-James O'Brien (1828–1862) was an American early science fiction and fantasy writer.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Kane”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Jeremiah Eames Rankin
poets.credit: Portrait of Jeremiah Eames Rankin · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Jeremiah Eames Rankin (1828–1904) was an American poet.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “The Word of God to Leyden Came” and “Fairest of Freedom's Daughters”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Arthur Joseph Munby
bio: Arthur Joseph Munby (1828–1910), born in York and educated at Cambridge, was a barrister and civil servant who wrote verse and kept a famous diary on the lives of working women.
His poems include Verses New and Old (1865), Dorothy: A Country Story in Elegiac Verse (1880) and Susan: A Poem of Degrees (1893). Stedman printed several of them in A Victorian Anthology (1895).

poets.name: Charles Doyne Sillery
bio: Charles Doyne Sillery (1807–1836) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. bio: John Mason Neale (1818–1866) was an English Anglican priest, scholar and hymn-writer.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Thomas Toke Lynch
poets.credit: Portrait: photographer William Elliott Debenham (1839–1924) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Toke Lynch (1818–1871) was an English nonconformist minister and hymn-writer.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Charles Hartley Langhorne
bio: Charles Hartley Langhorne was born at Berwick-on-Tweed in 1818 and educated at Glasgow University and at Oxford.
He was studying law when he died young, in 1845. His long, rolling lines in praise of the Greek pastoral poet Theocritus found a place in Stedman’s Victorian Anthology.

poets.name: Robert Brough
bio: Robert Barnabas Brough (1828–1860) was an English writer.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 5, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Theodore Winthrop
bio: Theodore Winthrop (1828–1861) was an American novelist and essayist, author of "Cecil Dreeme" and "John Brent". He was killed in the first weeks of the Civil War, at the battle of Big Bethel in June 1861.
His poem "But Once" appears in Stedman's An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Clarence Chatham Cook
bio: Clarence Chatham Cook (1828–1900) was an American art critic, born in Dorchester, Massachusetts. He edited The Studio of New York and published "The Central Park" (1868) and "The House Beautiful" (1877).
His poem on a death in spring appears in Stedman's An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Christopher Wordsworth
bio: Christopher Wordsworth (1807–1885) was an English Anglican bishop, a nephew of William Wordsworth, and a hymn-writer.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Richard Chenevix Trench
poets.credit: Portrait of Richard Chenevix Trench by John Richardson Jackson, 1863 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Chenevix Trench (1807–1886) was an Anglican churchman who became Archbishop of Dublin, and also a poet and philologist.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vols. 4, 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Frederick Tennyson
bio: Frederick Tennyson (1807–1898) was an English poet, the elder brother of Alfred, Lord Tennyson. His best-known volume is Days and Hours (1854), and he spent much of his life abroad.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 4, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: William Kirby
poets.credit: Portrait of William Kirby, c. 1865, from Le Chien d'or (1926 ed.) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Kirby (1817–1906) was an English-born Canadian writer who settled at Niagara-on-the-Lake. He is best known for the historical novel The Golden Dog (1877).
His verse includes the long poem The U. E.: A Tale of Upper Canada (1859). One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Alexander McLachlan
bio: Alexander McLachlan (1818–1896), born in Scotland, emigrated to Canada in 1840 and farmed in Ontario while writing popular verse in the manner of Burns.
He was often called the Burns of Canada. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Francis de Haes Janvier
bio: Francis de Haes Janvier (1817–1885) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “God Save Our President”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Henry Peterson
bio: Henry Peterson (1818–1891) was a Philadelphia poet, editor and novelist; his poem Lyon commemorates the Union general Nathaniel Lyon, killed in Missouri in 1861.
The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: Lyon.

poets.name: Mary Elizabeth Hewitt Stebbins
bio: Mary Elizabeth Hewitt Stebbins (1818–1894) was an American poet and writer (born Mary Elizabeth Hewitt).
Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900) prints two of her poems, "The Sunflower to the Sun" and "Harold the Valiant".

poets.name: Leconte de Lisle
poets.credit: Portrait of Leconte de Lisle by Jacques Blanquer, 1885 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Marie René Leconte de Lisle (1818–1894) was a French poet, born at Saint-Paul on the island of Réunion, who led the Parnassian school. His major collections are Poèmes antiques (1852), Poèmes barbares (1862) and Poèmes tragiques (1884), and he was elected to the Académie française in 1886.
The two poems here are English versions from W. J. Robertson's A Century of French Verse (1895), as reprinted in Lyra Celtica.

poets.name: Nathaniel Parker Willis
poets.credit: Photograph of Nathaniel Parker Willis, Mathew Brady studio · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Nathaniel Parker Willis (1806–1867) was an American poet, editor and journalist, born at Portland, Maine, and educated at Yale. He edited the New-York Mirror and later the Home Journal, and was among the best-paid magazine writers of his time.
His early scriptural and sentimental poems made him widely popular, and he was a prominent figure of the New York literary scene.

poets.name: Anne Brontë
poets.credit: Portrait of Anne Brontë by Charlotte Brontë (c. 1845) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Anne Brontë (1820–1849), the youngest of the three Brontë sisters, was born at Thornton, near Bradford, and died at Scarborough. She worked as a governess, first at Blake Hall, Mirfield, and from 1841 to 1845 at Thorp Green, near York, and published under the name Acton Bell. Her religious feeling, her grief for lost friends and her sense of duty run through her verse, and some of her early poems belong to the Gondal cycle she wrote with her sister Emily.

Twenty-one of her poems appeared in Poems by Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell (1846), given here in their 1846 text. The other thirty-three are taken from The Complete Poems of Anne Brontë, edited by Clement Shorter with a bibliographical introduction by C. W. Hatfield (Hodder and Stoughton, 1920), which first gathered all fifty-four. Where the volume gives a date of composition it is recorded in the poem's note; the editors' introductions, footnotes and variant readings are left out.

poets.name: John Esten Cooke
bio: John Esten Cooke (1830–1886) was a Virginia novelist and poet, born in Winchester, brother of Philip Pendleton Cooke.
Griswold included 4 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Christina Rossetti
poets.credit: Portrait of Christina Rossetti · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Christina Rossetti (1830–1894) was an English poet of devotional intensity and quiet formal mastery, sister of the painter-poet Dante Gabriel Rossetti.
Best known for ‘Goblin Market’ and the carol ‘In the Bleak Midwinter,’ she also wrote Sing-Song (1872), a book of nursery rhymes for children.

poets.name: Thomas Edward Brown
poets.credit: Portrait of T. E. Brown in his youth, from the Golden Treasury Series Selected Poems of T. E. Brown (Macmillan, 1908) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Edward Brown (1830–1897) was a Manx poet, scholar and schoolmaster. Born in Douglas, Isle of Man, the son of the vicar of Braddan, he was educated at King William’s College and at Christ Church, Oxford, and spent most of his working life teaching at Clifton College near Bristol.

His Fo’c’s’le Yarns (1881) and later volumes tell the stories of Manx fishermen, farmers and parsons in rhymed Anglo-Manx dialect, alongside English lyrics of nature, faith and memory. The Collected Poems (1900), prepared by his friends H. F. Brown, H. G. Dakyns and W. E. Henley, with an introduction by Henley, brought them together with some verse that had not been published in his lifetime.

poets.name: Isabella Craig
bio: Isabella Craig (dates not given by Rogers) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 4 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Henry Kingsley
poets.credit: Portrait of Henry Kingsley · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Kingsley (1830–1876) was an English novelist, the younger brother of Charles Kingsley. He spent about five years in Australia in the 1850s, which supplied the material for his first novel, The Recollections of Geoffry Hamlyn (1859); Ravenshoe (1862) was another popular success.
He wrote little verse; the ballad "The Blackbird's Song" is the one poem of his printed in this anthology.

poets.name: Ellen O'Leary
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Ellen O'Leary was an Irish poet, born in County Tipperary and the sister of the Fenian John O'Leary. Her collected verses, Lays of Country, Home and Friends, appeared in 1891, after her death.
She died in 1889.

poets.name: Isa Craig-Knox
bio: Isa Craig-Knox (1831–1903), born Isa Craig in Edinburgh, was a Scottish poet and journalist who worked with the women's movement of the 1850s and 1860s. In 1859 she won the prize for the ode written for the Burns centenary celebration at the Crystal Palace, and in 1866 she married John Knox.
Her “Ballad of the Brides of Quair” is the piece chosen for Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Robert Bulwer-Lytton, Earl of Lytton (Owen Meredith)
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Robert Bulwer-Lytton, first Earl of Lytton (1831–1891), was a British statesman and poet who wrote under the pseudonym Owen Meredith. He served as Viceroy of India from 1876 to 1880.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: C. S. Calverley
poets.credit: Portrait of Charles Stuart Calverley (published 1892) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Stuart Calverley (22 December 1831 – 17 February 1884) was an English poet and wit, a Cambridge man often called the literary father of the 'university school of humour'.
He is remembered for parody and light verse, collected in Verses and Translations (1862) and Fly Leaves (1872), and for his translations, including of Theocritus.

poets.name: Arthur Grey Butler
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Arthur Grey Butler (1831–1909) was a Victorian poet, represented here by two pieces from the anthology.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Mary Mapes Dodge
poets.credit: Portrait of Mary Mapes Dodge, unknown photographer, 1896 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mary Mapes Dodge (1831–1905) was an American author and editor, born in New York City. She made her name with the children's novel Hans Brinker; or, The Silver Skates (1865), a story of life in Holland, and wrote verse and prose for young readers throughout her career.

From 1873 until her death she edited St. Nicholas, the illustrated monthly for children, which she built into one of the leading American magazines of its kind. Rhymes and Jingles (1875) gathers the nursery verses, fables and songs she had written for it and for other periodicals.

poets.name: Will Wallace Harney
bio: Will Wallace Harney (1831–1912) was an American poet, teacher and journalist, born at Bardstown, Kentucky. He later lived in Florida.
Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900) reprints his "Adonais" and "The Stab".

poets.name: John Antrobus
bio: John Antrobus (born 1831) was an English-born painter, born in Walsall, Staffordshire. He lived in America from 1849 and made his home chiefly in Detroit.
His own painting "The Cowboy" suggested the poem of the same name printed in Stedman's An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Henry Sylvester Cornwell
bio: Henry Sylvester Cornwell (1831–1886) was an American poet. Two of his poems, the sonnet May and the lyric The Sunset City, were chosen for Stevenson's Home Book of Verse (1912).

poets.name: Franklin Benjamin Sanborn
bio: Franklin Benjamin Sanborn (1831–1917) was an American journalist, reformer and man of letters, born at Hampton Falls, New Hampshire. He settled at Concord, Massachusetts, where he knew Emerson, Thoreau and Alcott, and wrote lives of Thoreau and Emerson.
His occasional verse is represented in Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900) by "Samuel Hoar" and "Ariana".

poets.name: Edward Howland
bio: Edward Howland (1832–1890) was an American writer and social reformer, born in Charleston, South Carolina, and a graduate of Harvard.
After many years in business and literary work he became a socialist and took part in the Topolobampo colony in Sinaloa, Mexico, where he died.

poets.name: William Croswell Doane
bio: William Croswell Doane (1832–1913) was an Episcopal priest, later the first bishop of Albany, born in Boston, the son of Bishop George W. Doane.
Griswold included 3 of his poems in The Poets and Poetry of America (16th edition, Philadelphia: Parry & McMillan, 1855), the anthology from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Louisa May Alcott
bio: Louisa May Alcott (1832–1888) was an American novelist, born in Germantown, Pennsylvania, and raised in Concord, Massachusetts, among the circle of Emerson, Thoreau and her father, Amos Bronson Alcott. She is best known for Little Women (1868–69).
She also wrote poems throughout her life, among them elegies for her Concord neighbours.

poets.name: Mary Ashley Townsend
bio: Mary Ashley Townsend (1832–1901), who wrote as Xariffa, was a New Orleans poet.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: A Georgia Volunteer.

poets.name: Frédéric Mistral
poets.credit: Frédéric Mistral, photograph (c. 1880s) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Frédéric Mistral (1830–1914) was born at Maillane, near Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, the son of a prosperous farmer. After studying law at Aix he gave his life to the Provençal language: in 1854 he was one of seven poets who founded the Félibrige, a society for the revival of the language and literature of Provence, and he went on to compile its great dictionary, Lou Tresor dóu Felibrige.

His pastoral epic Mirèio (1859), in twelve cantos, tells of a farmer's daughter and a basket-weaver's son whose love is broken by her parents' pride. Lamartine hailed it, and the Académie française crowned it. Mistral wrote further long poems, including Calendau and Lou Pouèmo dóu Rose, and in 1904 he shared the Nobel Prize in Literature. The English version here is Harriet Waters Preston's translation (1872).

poets.name: Walt Whitman
poets.credit: Portrait of Walt Whitman (George Collins Cox, 1887) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Walt Whitman (1819–1892) was an American poet, essayist, and journalist from Long Island, New York, widely regarded as the father of free verse and one of the most influential poets in American literature.

His single, ever-expanding book ‘Leaves of Grass’, first published in 1855 and revised throughout his life into the 1892 ‘deathbed’ edition used here, celebrated democracy, the body, and the American landscape in a sweeping, unrhymed line.

poets.name: Herman Melville
poets.credit: Joseph Oriel Eaton, 1870 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Herman Melville (1819–1891) was an American novelist, short-story writer and poet, born in New York City. He is best known for the sea novel Moby-Dick (1851), which was little appreciated in his lifetime.

Battle-Pieces and Aspects of the War (1866) was his first book of verse, a sequence of poems on the American Civil War, from John Brown to the surrender at Appomattox and its aftermath. Melville turned chiefly to poetry in his later years and worked for many years as a customs inspector in New York.

poets.name: Emily Dickinson
poets.credit: Portrait of Emily Dickinson (daguerreotype, c. 1847) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Emily Dickinson (1830–1886) was an American poet who lived a famously reclusive life in Amherst, Massachusetts, writing nearly 1,800 poems of which barely a dozen were published in her lifetime.

Her tightly compressed, slant-rhymed verse on death, nature, faith, and the inner mind — much of it untitled and left in small hand-sewn booklets — was published posthumously and is now considered among the most original in American literature.

poets.name: Helen Hunt Jackson
poets.credit: Photograph of Helen Hunt Jackson by Charles F. Conly, c. 1884 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Helen Hunt Jackson (1830–1885) was an American writer, born at Amherst, Massachusetts, and a childhood friend of Emily Dickinson. She wrote poems, essays, and stories, signing some of them “H.H.”, and settled in Colorado Springs after her second marriage.
She is best known for A Century of Dishonor (1881), a protest against the treatment of Native Americans, and for the novel Ramona (1884).

poets.name: Paul Hamilton Hayne
poets.credit: Portrait: Unknown authorUnknown author — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Paul Hamilton Hayne (1830–1886) was a Charleston-born poet and critic, among the leading literary figures of the post-war South.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: The Battle of Charleston Harbor.

poets.name: Sebastian Evans
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sebastian Evans (1830–1909) was an English journalist, editor and poet of Welsh descent, the grandson of the astronomer the Rev. Lewis Evans and the brother of the archaeologist Sir John Evans.
Lyra Celtica prints his lyric 'Shadows'; this file also holds 'The Seven Fiddlers' from Popular British Ballads (1894).

poets.name: John Hunter-Duvar
bio: John Hunter-Duvar (1821–1899) was a Scottish-born poet and dramatist who settled on Prince Edward Island.

His verse dramas include The Enamorado (1879) and De Roberval (1888); only his lyric pieces are included here. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Frederick West Lander
bio: Frederick West Lander (1821–1862) was a Massachusetts-born civil engineer and explorer of western routes, and a Union general, who died in 1862 during the Civil War.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: Rhode Island to the South.

poets.name: George Martin
bio: George Martin (1822–1900) was a Canadian poet.

His poem Marguerite; or, The Isle of Demons (1887), a verse retelling of a sixteenth-century Quebec legend, supplies two of the pieces here. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Charles Sangster
poets.credit: Portrait of Charles Sangster, photographer unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Sangster (1822–1893) was born in Kingston, Upper Canada, and worked as a journalist and civil servant. He is often called the first important native-born Canadian poet.

His principal books are The St. Lawrence and the Saguenay, and Other Poems (1856) and Hesperus, and Other Poems and Lyrics (1860). One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Sir Noel Paton
poets.credit: Photograph of Sir Noel Paton by Thomas Annan, 1866 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Joseph Noel Paton (1821–1901) was a Scottish painter and poet, born in Dunfermline, who became Queen's Limner for Scotland and was knighted in 1867. He published two volumes of verse, Poems by a Painter (1861) and Spindrift (1867).
Lyra Celtica prints two of his poems, 'Midnight by the Sea' and 'In Shadowland'.

poets.name: William Harrison Safford
bio: William Harrison Safford (1821–1903) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “The Battle of Muskingum”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Maria White Lowell
bio: Maria White Lowell (1821–1853) was an American poet, born at Watertown, Massachusetts. In 1844 she married the poet James Russell Lowell, and she died at Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1853.
Her poems were printed privately after her death. Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900) reprints her "Song" and "The Morning-Glory".

poets.name: Edward Hayes Plumptre
bio: Edward Hayes Plumptre (1821–1891) was an English divine and scholar.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Francis Orray Ticknor
bio: Francis Orray Ticknor (1822–1874) was a Georgia physician and poet whose Little Giffen of Tennessee became one of the best-loved Southern war poems.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: Little Giffen of Tennessee.

poets.name: Edward Everett Hale
poets.credit: Portrait of Edward Everett Hale · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward Everett Hale (1822–1909) was an American historian and minister.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “Columbus”, “From Potomac to Merrimac”, “Adrian Block's Song”, “Anne Hutchinson's Exile” and “The Lamentable Ballad of the Bloody Brook” among others; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Harry McCarthy
bio: Harry McCarthy (also spelled Macarthy, 1834–1874) was an actor, comedian and songwriter who toured the Confederate States in "Personation Concerts" during the Civil War, billing himself as the Arkansas Comedian.
He wrote and sang "The Bonnie Blue Flag" (1861), one of the best-known songs of the Confederacy, together with other war songs reprinted here from W. L. Fagan's Southern War Songs (1890).

poets.name: Richard Realf
bio: Richard Realf (1834–1878) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “The Defence of Lawrence”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Frances Louisa Bushnell
bio: Frances Louisa Bushnell (1834–1899) was an American poet, born in Hartford, Connecticut, a daughter of the theologian Horace Bushnell.
She contributed verse to the Atlantic Monthly and other magazines.

poets.name: George Arnold
bio: George Arnold (1834–1865) was a New York journalist and humorist who first studied painting. His "McArone Papers" ran in Vanity Fair from 1860.
His verse was collected after his death in "Drift: A Sea-Shore Idyl, and Other Poems" and "Poems Grave and Gay" (1866), both edited by William Winter.

poets.name: Harriet McEwen Kimball
bio: Harriet McEwen Kimball (1834–1917) was an American poet and hymn writer, born in Portsmouth, New Hampshire. She was long devoted to charitable work, founding a cottage hospital in her native city.
Her books include Hymns (1867), Swallow-Flights of Song (1874) and a complete Poems (1889).

poets.name: Harriet Prescott Spofford
poets.credit: Photograph of Harriet Prescott Spofford by Brown Brothers, New York · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Harriet Prescott Spofford (1835–1921) was an American writer born at Calais, Maine, who lived for many years at Newburyport, Massachusetts. She became known in 1859 for her story “In a Cellar” in The Atlantic Monthly and wrote novels, stories, and poems.
Her verse is lyrical and compressed, and several short poems were taken up by anthologists of her time.

poets.name: Irving Browne
bio: Irving Browne (1835–1899) was an American lawyer, legal writer and book collector, born in Marshall, New York. He practised in Troy, edited the Albany Law Journal, and later lived in Buffalo.
Besides legal treatises and essays he wrote verse, including the volume The House of the Heart (1897) and ballads on books.

poets.name: William Augustus Croffut
bio: William Augustus Croffut (1835–1915) was an American journalist, editor and author, born in Redding, Connecticut. He worked on newspapers in several cities, including Washington, D.C., and wrote on a wide range of subjects.
His verse appeared in periodicals and was gathered in An American Anthology (1900) among the later poets of the century.

poets.name: Susan Coolidge
poets.credit: Portrait of Sarah Chauncey Woolsey (Susan Coolidge), unknown photographer, c. 1870 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Susan Coolidge was the pen name of Sarah Chauncey Woolsey (1835–1905), born in Cleveland, Ohio, the eldest of a family of five children. She is remembered chiefly as the author of the Katy Did books for children, beginning with What Katy Did (1872), but she also wrote verse throughout her life, mostly short religious and domestic lyrics, elegies and occasional pieces.

This selection gathers the three volumes of her verse: Verses (1880), A Few More Verses (copyright 1889) and Last Verses, published posthumously in 1906 with a memoir by her sister. Poems are given in that order, and each poem records the book it came from.

poets.name: Maurice Bell
bio: Maurice Bell is named as the author of the Confederate poem The Men in Eggleston’s anthology; his dates are not given there.
The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: The Men.

poets.name: Elizabeth Bogart
bio: Elizabeth Bogart, a New Yorker and the daughter of the Rev. D. S. Bogart, began writing about 1825 and contributed prose and verse to the Mirror under the pseudonym “Estelle.”
Her work was never collected into a volume; her best-known poem, “He Came Too Late,” was reprinted in Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Henry Lynden Flash
bio: Henry Lynden Flash (1835–1914) was a Southern poet and journalist who served in the Confederate army. Eggleston prints him as Harry L. Flash.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: Death of Stonewall Jackson.

poets.name: Theodore Tilton
poets.credit: Portrait of Theodore Tilton · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Theodore Tilton (1835–1907) was an American newspaper editor, poet, and abolitionist.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “The Great Bell Roland”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Maria La Conte
bio: Maria La Conte is named as the author of the Civil War poem Somebody’s Darling in Eggleston’s anthology; her dates are not given there.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: Somebody’s Darling.

poets.name: Frank Lee
bio: Frank Lee is named as the author of the Civil War poem He’ll See It When He Wakes in Eggleston’s anthology; his dates are not given there.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: “He’ll See It When He Wakes”.

poets.name: N. G. Shepherd
bio: N. G. Shepherd is named as the author of Roll-Call, a Civil War poem, in Eggleston’s anthology; his dates are not given there.
The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: Roll-Call.

poets.name: Edgar Allan Poe
poets.credit: Portrait of Edgar Allan Poe (daguerreotype, 1849) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edgar Allan Poe (1809–1849) was an American writer, editor, and literary critic best known for tales of mystery and the macabre, but he considered himself first a poet and a founder of the detective and horror genres.

His musical, tightly-wrought verse — including ‘The Raven’, ‘Annabel Lee’, and ‘The Bells’ — explores loss, beauty, and death, and made him one of the most widely imitated poets in the English language.

poets.name: Thomas Watson
bio: Thomas Watson (born c. 1807; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
poets.credit: Portrait of Henry Wadsworth Longfellow (Julia Margaret Cameron, 1868) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow (1807–1882) was an American poet and Harvard professor, and by far the most popular and widely read American poet of the 19th century, both at home and in Europe.

A leading figure among the ‘Fireside Poets’, he wrote narrative epics such as ‘The Song of Hiawatha’ and ‘Paul Revere’s Ride’ alongside shorter lyrics on nature, faith, and everyday life, in verse prized for its clarity and musicality.

poets.name: Charles Dawson Shanly
bio: Charles Dawson Shanly (1811–1875) was an Irish-born writer who spent part of his life in Canada and the United States.
He is remembered chiefly for the ballad The Walker of the Snow. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
poets.credit: Portrait of Ralph Waldo Emerson (Josiah Johnson Hawes, 1857) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803–1882) was an American essayist, lecturer, and poet from Concord, Massachusetts, and the leading voice of the Transcendentalist movement, which prized intuition, nature, and individual conscience over inherited tradition.

Best known for essays such as ‘Self-Reliance’ and ‘Nature’, he also wrote compact, philosophical verse — including ‘Concord Hymn’, ‘The Rhodora’, and ‘Brahma’ — that distilled his ideas into poetic form.

poets.name: George Henry Calvert
bio: George Henry Calvert (1803–1889) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Bunker Hill”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Thomas Miller
bio: Thomas Miller was born at Gainsborough in 1807 and worked as a basket-maker before publishing his first book of verse, Songs of the Sea Nymphs, in 1832.
A Day in the Woods (verse) followed in 1836. He wrote novels and books for children, contributed to the annuals and the London Journal, and died in London in 1874.

poets.name: William Cullen Bryant
poets.credit: Portrait of William Cullen Bryant — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Cullen Bryant (1794–1878) was an American poet and long-time editor of the New York Evening Post, whose meditative nature poetry helped establish a distinctly American Romantic voice.
Written when he was only seventeen, ‘Thanatopsis’ remains his best-known work, and poems such as ‘To a Waterfowl’ and ‘The Prairies’ celebrate the American landscape with a solemn, elevated calm.

poets.name: Alonzo Lewis
poets.credit: Portrait of Alonzo Lewis · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alonzo Lewis (1794–1861) was an American journalist.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Death Song”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: August Adolf Ludwig Follen
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: August Adolf Ludwig Follen was a German poet and political writer associated with the patriotic student movement. He later lived in Switzerland.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Wilhelm Müller
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Wilhelm Müller was born at Dessau, where he worked as a librarian and schoolmaster. His song cycles Die schöne Müllerin and Winterreise were set by Franz Schubert.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Joseph Rodman Drake
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of Joseph Rodman Drake, 19th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Joseph Rodman Drake (1795–1820) was an American poet born in New York City. Orphaned young, he studied medicine at Columbia College and married Sarah Eckford in 1816. He became a close friend of the poet Fitz-Greene Halleck, and the two wrote the satirical Croaker verses for the New York Evening Post in 1819.

His fairy poem The Culprit Fay, written in 1819, drew on the scenery of the Hudson Highlands. He died of consumption in 1820, aged twenty-five. His collected poems were published posthumously in 1835 by his daughter, and the 1836 edition is the source of this selection; Halleck's elegy for him, "Green be the turf above thee", is among the best remembered American elegies.

poets.name: John Richardson
bio: Major John Richardson (1796–1852), born at Queenston, Upper Canada, served in the War of 1812 and later wrote novels, notably Wacousta (1832).
His narrative poem Tecumseh; or, The Warrior of the West appeared in 1828. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: August Kuhn
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: August Kuhn was a German poet of the nineteenth century. His dates and biography are not established in this archive.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Conrad Wetzel
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Conrad Wetzel was a German poet of the nineteenth century. His dates and biography are not established in this archive.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Karl Egon Ebert
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Karl Egon Ebert was a German-Bohemian poet born at Prague, known for ballads and epic poems on Bohemian subjects.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Karl Immermann
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Karl Immermann was born at Magdeburg and worked for many years at Düsseldorf, where he directed a notable theatre. He wrote plays, poems and the novel Münchhausen.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Eben Fardd
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Eben Fardd (Ebenezer Thomas) was a Welsh schoolmaster and poet of Clynnog Fawr in Caernarfonshire, whose ode "Dinistr Jerusalem" ("The Destruction of Jerusalem") was among the most widely read Welsh poems of the nineteenth century.
Two extracts from it are given in English verse by Alfred Perceval Graves in A Celtic Psaltery (1917).

poets.name: Gwilym Hiraethog
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Gwilym Hiraethog (William Rees) was a Welsh Congregational minister, writer and publisher, born in Denbighshire, who published in Liverpool and was also a poet in the strict metres.
A passage from his poem "Emanuel", "Love Divine", is given in English verse by Alfred Perceval Graves in A Celtic Psaltery (1917).

poets.name: Karl Simrock
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Karl Simrock was born at Bonn, where he later became professor of German literature. He is known for his modern German versions of the Nibelungenlied and the Edda, and wrote poems of his own.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Susanna Moodie
bio: Susanna Moodie (née Strickland, 1803–1885) was an English-born writer, one of the Strickland sisters, who emigrated to Upper Canada in 1832 and described the settler's life in Roughing It in the Bush (1852). She also published verse, beginning with Enthusiasm, and Other Poems (1831).
The poems given here are taken from The Oxford Book of Canadian Verse, chosen by Wilfred Campbell (Toronto: Oxford University Press, 1913).

poets.name: Julius Mosen
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Julius Mosen was a German poet from the Vogtland. His ballad on the Tyrolean leader Andreas Hofer became the Tyrol's best-known song.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Joseph Howe
bio: Joseph Howe (1804–1873) was a Nova Scotian journalist, politician and champion of responsible government, who served as Premier of Nova Scotia and was long the best-known voice of the province. His poems were gathered after his death in Poems and Essays (1874).
The poems given here are taken from The Oxford Book of Canadian Verse, chosen by Wilfred Campbell (Toronto: Oxford University Press, 1913).

poets.name: Eduard Mörike
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Eduard Mörike was a Protestant pastor and, in his writing life, a poet and novelist of the Swabian school. His lyric poems are among the best loved in German, and many were set to music.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Louisa Macartney Crawford
bio: Louisa Macartney Crawford was a contributor to Chapman and Hall’s Metropolitan Magazine from about 1835, where she published a series of autobiographical sketches.

She wrote the words for several books of songs set by the composer F. Nicholls Crouch; “Kathleen Mavourneen” appeared in the first of the series, Echoes from the Lakes. The poem here is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s A Victorian Anthology, 1837–1895 (1895).

poets.name: James Russell Lowell
poets.credit: Portrait of James Russell Lowell (1855) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James Russell Lowell (1819–1891) was an American poet, critic, and diplomat from Cambridge, Massachusetts, who edited the Atlantic Monthly and later served as U.S. minister to Spain and Britain.

A member of the ‘Fireside Poets’, he wrote lyric and narrative verse — most famously ‘The Vision of Sir Launfal’ — alongside satirical and abolitionist poetry that engaged directly with the politics of his day.

poets.name: Julia Ward Howe
poets.credit: Photograph of Julia Ward Howe, 1895 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Julia Ward Howe (1819–1910) was an American poet, abolitionist and campaigner for women’s suffrage, born in New York City. She was married to the reformer Samuel Gridley Howe, with whom she edited the antislavery paper The Commonwealth.
Her “Battle Hymn of the Republic”, written in 1861 and printed in The Atlantic Monthly in February 1862, became the most famous song of the Union cause.

poets.name: Thomas William Parsons
bio: Thomas William Parsons (1819–1892) was an American poet and translator, born in Boston, who practised as a dentist. He spent decades translating Dante’s Inferno into English verse, a work that earned him a lasting if modest reputation.
His original poems, such as “On a Bust of Dante”, are classical in manner and were admired by his Boston contemporaries.

poets.name: Benjamin Franklin Taylor
bio: Benjamin Franklin Taylor (1819–1887) was a Chicago journalist, war correspondent and poet.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: The Cavalry Charge.

poets.name: George Eliot
poets.credit: Portrait of George Eliot by François d'Albert Durade (replica of a work of 1849) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans (1819–1880), the Warwickshire-born novelist of Adam Bede, The Mill on the Floss, Middlemarch and Daniel Deronda. She also translated Strauss and Feuerbach.

She wrote verse throughout her career, including the dramatic poem The Spanish Gypsy (1868) and the collection The Legend of Jubal and Other Poems (1874); her lines beginning “O, may I join the choir invisible” are among her most famous.

poets.name: William Cadenhead
bio: William Cadenhead (born 1819; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Ben Preston
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Ben Preston (1819–1902) was the Bradford poet who rose to local fame with "Natterin' Nan", first printed in a Bradford journal in 1856; a first edition of his poems followed in 1860. F. W. Moorman ranks him first among the poets of the artisan towns of Bradford, Leeds and Halifax.

His best pathos draws on the life of the handloom weaver in the "hungry forties", and Moorman holds "I Niver can call Her my Wife" to be his masterpiece. The three poems here come from Moorman's Yorkshire Dialect Poems (1916).

poets.name: John Campbell Shairp
poets.credit: Portrait of John Campbell Shairp by Robert Inerarity Herdman, 1886 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Campbell Shairp (1819–1885) was a Scottish scholar and poet, Principal of the United College at St Andrews and Professor of Poetry at Oxford. Lyra Celtica notes his Celtic descent through his mother.
His poems were gathered after his death in Glen Desseray and Other Poems, edited by F. T. Palgrave (1888). Lyra Celtica prints his ballad 'Cailleach Bein-y-Vreich'.

poets.name: John Ruskin
poets.credit: Portrait of John Ruskin by W. & D. Downey · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Ruskin (1819–1900) was an English writer, art critic and social thinker who also wrote verse, much of it in his youth.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 4, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: John Westland Marston
poets.credit: Portrait of John Westland Marston by J. & C. Watkins · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Westland Marston (1819–1890) was an English dramatist and critic who also wrote verse.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 4, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Ernest Charles Jones
poets.credit: Portrait of Ernest Charles Jones · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ernest Charles Jones (1819–1869) was an English poet, novelist and Chartist leader.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 4, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Thomas Hornblower Gill
bio: Thomas Hornblower Gill (1819–1906) was a British hymn-writer.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: William Henry Whitworth
bio: William Henry Whitworth was a Victorian sonneteer. According to Sharp’s Sonnets of the Century, he was head master of a large public school.
Only a few of his sonnets have been preserved in anthologies, and his dates are not recorded here.

poets.name: Charles Weldon
bio: Charles Weldon is little documented. Stedman’s Victorian Anthology notes that Linton and Stoddard’s English Verse describes him as an Englishman whose poems appeared over the signature “C. C.” in the New York Tribune between 1850 and 1856.
His dates are given here as the period of that activity.

poets.name: Edward Caswall
poets.credit: Photograph of Edward Caswall (19th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward Caswall (1814–1878) was a British clergyman and hymn writer who converted to Catholicism and became an Oratorian priest.
The poems printed here are those given in The Oxford Book of English Mystical Verse (1917), edited by D. H. S. Nicholson and A. H. E. Lee; the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Clarence A. Walworth
bio: Clarence Augustus Walworth (1820–1900) was an American attorney, writer, ordained Roman Catholic priest and missionary, well regarded as a writer on Catholic subjects.
The poems printed here are those given in The Oxford Book of English Mystical Verse (1917), edited by D. H. S. Nicholson and A. H. E. Lee; the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Albert Mathews
bio: Albert Mathews (born 1820), who wrote under the pen-name "Paul Siegvolk", was a New York lawyer and man of letters, a Yale graduate of 1842 and a cousin of the poet Cornelius Mathews.

He published "Walter Ashwood: A Love Story" (1860), "A Bundle of Papers" (1879) and "Ruminations, and Other Essays" (1893). His poem "To an Autumn Leaf" appears in Stedman's An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: John Greenleaf Whittier
poets.credit: Portrait of John Greenleaf Whittier — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Greenleaf Whittier (1807–1892) was an American Quaker poet and dedicated abolitionist from Massachusetts, who used verse throughout his life to campaign against slavery and to record New England legend and rural memory.
His long autobiographical poem ‘Snow-Bound’ (1866), recalling his family snowed in at their farmhouse, became one of the most beloved American poems of the 19th century.

poets.name: Caroline Norton
poets.credit: Portrait of Caroline Norton by George Hayter · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Caroline Norton (1808–1877) was a granddaughter of Richard Brinsley Sheridan, a poet and novelist of the 1830s and 1840s whose collections include The Sorrows of Rosalie (1829), The Undying One (1830) and The Dream and Other Poems (1840).

After a failed and bitter marriage she campaigned against the legal position of married women; her pamphlets helped bring about the Custody of Infants Act (1839) and the Matrimonial Causes Act (1857).

poets.name: James Ballantine
bio: James Ballantine (born 1808; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 12 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Horatius Bonar, D.D.
bio: Horatius Bonar, D.D. (dates not given by Rogers) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: John Finlay
bio: John Finlay (born 1808; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 2 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 5 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Evan M'Coll
bio: Evan M'Coll (born 1808; living 1855–57) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 1 song printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Augusta Theodosia Drane
poets.credit: Portrait of Augusta Theodosia Drane (before 1894, photographer unknown) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Augusta Theodosia Drane (1823–1894) was an English Catholic nun of the Dominican order, known as a poet and theologian as well as a writer of religious biography.

The two poems here are meditations that take their epigraphs from St John of the Cross. The poems printed here are those given in The Oxford Book of English Mystical Verse (1917), edited by D. H. S. Nicholson and A. H. E. Lee; the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: David Atwood Wasson
bio: David Atwood Wasson (1823–1887) was an American minister and Transcendentalist author, an essayist and poet, early influenced by Thomas Carlyle and usually regarded as a disciple of Ralph Waldo Emerson.
The poems printed here are those given in The Oxford Book of English Mystical Verse (1917), edited by D. H. S. Nicholson and A. H. E. Lee; the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Thomas Lake Harris
bio: Thomas Lake Harris (1823–1906) was an English-born American poet, Universalist and Swedenborgian preacher, and spiritualist. He founded the Brotherhood of the New Life, communities which settled at Brocton, New York, and later at Santa Rosa, California.
He published a number of long visionary poems in the 1850s and after. Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900) prints his "California" and "Fledglings".

poets.name: Oliver Wendell Holmes
poets.credit: Photograph of Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr., c. 1879 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. (1809–1894) was a Boston physician, Harvard professor of anatomy and physiology, essayist and poet, one of the Fireside Poets who made New England verse a household possession. His 1830 poem “Old Ironsides” is credited with helping to save the frigate Constitution from being broken up.

His genial comic and occasional verse — “The Deacon’s Masterpiece,” “The Last Leaf,” the dinner poems read for his Harvard classmates — sits beside the more serious “The Chambered Nautilus,” first printed in his Atlantic Monthly series “The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table” (1857–58). The poems here follow his collected Poetical Works as issued in 1893.

poets.name: Mary Cowden Clarke
poets.credit: Photograph of Mary Cowden Clarke by G. B. Sciutto & Co., c. 1870 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mary Victoria Cowden Clarke (1809–1898), born Novello, was the daughter of the music publisher Vincent Novello and in 1828 married Charles Cowden Clarke. She compiled The Complete Concordance to Shakespeare (1845), the first of its kind in English, and wrote The Girlhood of Shakespeare's Heroines.
Her poem “At Midnight of ‘All Souls’” was included by Elizabeth A. Sharp in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Frances Anne Kemble
poets.credit: Portrait of Fanny Kemble by Thomas Sully, 1834 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Frances Anne (Fanny) Kemble (1809–1893) came from the great theatrical family of Kemble and Siddons, and was herself a celebrated actress before her marriage to Pierce Butler of Georgia. Her Journal of a Residence on a Georgian Plantation records her experience of slavery.
She also wrote verse throughout her life, and published Poems in 1844; the nature sonnet “Winter” and two other sonnets appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: John Stuart Blackie
poets.credit: Portrait: Elliott & Fry — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Stuart Blackie (born 1809) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 4 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 6 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Alexander Hume
bio: Alexander Hume (1809–1851) is one of the Scottish song-writers whose lives Charles Rogers sketched in The Modern Scottish Minstrel (six volumes, Edinburgh: Adam & Charles Black, 1855–57).
This archive holds 8 songs printed under this poet's name in volume 4 of the anthology, in Rogers's spelling. Dates are those given in Rogers's memoir, which is the only source used here.

poets.name: Laughton Osborn
bio: Laughton Osborn (1809–1878) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “The Death of General Pike”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: August Schnezler
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: August Schnezler was a German poet and collector of legends from the Black Forest and Baden region.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Henry Nutcombe Oxenham
bio: Henry Nutcombe Oxenham (1829–1888) was an English ecclesiologist, theologian, author and translator. Originally ordained in the Church of England, he later became a Roman Catholic.
The poems printed here are those given in The Oxford Book of English Mystical Verse (1917), edited by D. H. S. Nicholson and A. H. E. Lee; the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Charles Dudley Warner
bio: Charles Dudley Warner (1829–1900) was an American essayist, editor and novelist, long resident in Hartford, Connecticut.
He wrote verse only occasionally; his sonnet "Bookra", on an Oriental theme, appears in Stedman's An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: James Aldrich
bio: James Aldrich (1810–1856) was an American poet, and has no connection with the better-known Thomas Bailey Aldrich. He is remembered almost entirely for one short poem, “A Death-bed”, widely reprinted in nineteenth-century anthologies.
Little is recorded about his life, and this archive makes no claim beyond his dates and the single poem Knowles printed.

poets.name: Margaret Fuller
bio: Margaret Fuller (1810–1850) was an American journalist, critic and women’s-rights advocate of the New England Transcendentalist circle, editor of The Dial and author of Woman in the Nineteenth Century (1845).
She wrote occasional verse; “Dryad Song” appeared in Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Frederick William Sawyer
bio: Frederick William Sawyer (1810–1875) is remembered for a single piece of light verse, “The Recognition”, a parody of Tennyson’s manner.
Burton E. Stevenson included it under his name in The Home Book of Verse (1912), subtitled “After Tennyson”.

poets.name: Lady John Scott
poets.credit: Portrait of Lady John Scott by David Octavius Hill, c. 1843 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alicia Ann Spottiswoode (1810–1900), who married Lord John Scott in 1836 and is known as Lady John Scott, was a Scottish songwriter and composer, born in Berwickshire. She is remembered for her version of 'Annie Laurie'.
Lyra Celtica prints her song 'Durisdeer'.

poets.name: James Sloan Gibbons
bio: James Sloan Gibbons (1810–1892) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Three Hundred Thousand More”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Elizabeth Clementine Kinney
bio: Elizabeth Clementine Kinney (1810–1889), born Elizabeth Clementine Dodge, was an American poet. By her first marriage, to David Stedman, she was the mother of the poet and critic Edmund Clarence Stedman.
Her second husband, William Burnet Kinney, was a newspaper editor and later American diplomatic representative at Turin, and she lived for some years in Italy.

poets.name: Sir Francis Hastings Doyle
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir Francis Hastings Doyle by Leslie Ward, 1877 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Francis Hastings Doyle (1810–1888) was a British poet and civil servant who served as Professor of Poetry at Oxford.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 4, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Henry Alford
poets.credit: Photograph published in the Encyclopædia Britannica, 1902 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Alford (1810–1871) was an English churchman, theologian, textual critic, scholar, poet and hymn-writer.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 10, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Ferdinand Freiligrath
poets.credit: Portrait: Johann Peter Hasenclever — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ferdinand Freiligrath was born at Detmold. He first made his name with vivid poems on exotic subjects, later became a political poet of 1848, and lived in exile in London for many years.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: James McCarroll
bio: James McCarroll (1814–1892) was an Irish-born journalist and writer who made his career in Canada, publishing verse, songs and humorous sketches in the newspapers of Ontario.
The poems given here are taken from The Oxford Book of Canadian Verse, chosen by Wilfred Campbell (Toronto: Oxford University Press, 1913).

poets.name: Elizabeth Cecilia Clephane
bio: Elizabeth Cecilia Clephane was born in Edinburgh in 1830 and died at Melrose in 1869.
Her poem “The Ninety and Nine”, first printed in the Family Treasury and afterwards in the Christian Age, was made famous by the evangelist Ira D. Sankey’s singing.

poets.name: William Ellery Channing
bio: William Ellery Channing (1817–1901), known as Ellery Channing, was an American Transcendentalist poet, born in Boston and nephew of the Unitarian minister of the same name. He contributed to The Dial and lived at Concord, Massachusetts.
A close friend and walking companion of Henry David Thoreau, he wrote the first full-length life of him, Thoreau: The Poet-Naturalist (1873). His own verse appeared in Poems (1843) and later volumes.

poets.name: Emily Chubbuck Judson
bio: Emily Chubbuck Judson (1817–1854) was an American author who wrote under the pen name "Fanny Forester". In 1846 she married the Baptist missionary Adoniram Judson, and she died at Hamilton, New York, in 1854.
Her verse, much of it written during her years in Burma and India, was printed in the magazines of her day. Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900) reprints her poems "My Bird" and "Watching".

poets.name: Emanuel Geibel
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Emanuel Geibel was born at Lübeck and became one of the most widely read German lyric poets of the mid-nineteenth century. He spent his later years in Munich.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Arthur Penrhyn Stanley
