bio: Arthur Penrhyn Stanley (1815–1881), born at Alderley, Cheshire, was educated at Rugby and Oxford, where he was tutor and later Professor of Ecclesiastical History. He was Canon of Canterbury and of Christ Church, and in 1863 was appointed Dean of Westminster.
He is best known as a church historian and for his Life of Dr. Arnold; his hymns appear in the hymnals. The poem here is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s A Victorian Anthology, 1837–1895 (1895).

poets.name: August Lamey
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: August Lamey was a poet and public man of Baden, a native of Strasbourg, who published verse in German.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Christopher Newman Hall
bio: Christopher Newman Hall (1816–1902), born at Maidstone, Kent, was a Congregational minister and a graduate of London University. He was pastor of Albion Chapel, Hull, and then of Surrey Chapel, London, and often visited America.
The poem here is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s A Victorian Anthology, 1837–1895 (1895).

poets.name: Georg Herwegh
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Georg Herwegh was born at Stuttgart. His Gedichte eines Lebendigen (1841) made him a leading political poet of the years before 1848; he lived in exile in Switzerland and France.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) translated this poet in his German Anthology (1845); the poems here are his English versions, as reprinted in Poems, ed. John Mitchel (New York, 1859).

poets.name: Edwin Waugh
bio: Edwin Waugh (1817–1890), born in Rochdale, was a printer and bookseller who turned to literature and became the best-loved Lancashire dialect poet of his day, known as the “Laureate of Lancashire”.

He also wrote Lancashire sketches and tales, and his collected works appeared in ten volumes in 1881–83. The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s A Victorian Anthology, 1837–1895 (1895).

poets.name: Tom Taylor
bio: Tom Taylor (1817–1880) was an English dramatist and critic, born at Sunderland and educated at Glasgow and Cambridge. He wrote The Ticket-of-Leave Man and many other plays, was art critic of the Times, and edited Punch from 1874 until his death.
His tribute to the murdered Abraham Lincoln appeared in Punch in 1865.

poets.name: Ford Madox Brown
bio: Ford Madox Brown (1821–1893), born at Calais, was a painter, a veteran leader of the Pre-Raphaelite circle, and a writer and lecturer on art. He spent eleven years on a series of frescoes for Manchester Town Hall.

He wrote sonnets to accompany his pictures, among them “The Last of England”, and a sonnet on the death of his son, the young writer Oliver Madox Brown. The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s A Victorian Anthology, 1837–1895 (1895).

poets.name: Charles Kent
bio: Charles Kent (William Charles Mark Kent, 1823–1902) was an English journalist and poet, born in London and educated at Prior Park and Oscott. He edited The Sun and the Weekly Register, and was called to the Bar in 1859.
His collected Poems appeared in 1870.

poets.name: Islwyn
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Islwyn (William Thomas) was a Welsh poet and Calvinistic Methodist minister of Monmouthshire, who took his bardic name from the hill above his home and is sometimes called the Welsh Wordsworth.
A passage from his blank-verse poem "The Storm" is given in English by Alfred Perceval Graves in A Celtic Psaltery (1917) as "Behind the Veil".

poets.name: Lucius Harwood Foote
bio: Lucius Harwood Foote (1826–1913) was an American diplomat and poet, long resident in California, who served as the first United States minister to Korea (1883–1885).
The poems printed here are those given in Stedman's An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1900); the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Samuel Laycock
bio: Samuel Laycock (1826–1893) was a Lancashire dialect poet who worked in a mill from his youth and began writing verse early. He later lived at Blackpool, where he died.

His books include Lancashire Rhymes (1864), Lancashire Songs (1866) and Lancashire Poems, Tales and Recitations (1875). The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s A Victorian Anthology, 1837–1895 (1895).

poets.name: Richard St John Tyrwhitt
bio: Richard St John Tyrwhitt (1827–1907) was an English clergyman and writer on art, educated at Oxford and vicar of St Mary Magdalen, Oxford, from 1858 to 1872.
His verse appeared in Free Field Lyrics, chiefly Descriptive (1888).

poets.name: John Veitch
bio: John Veitch (1829–1894) was a Scottish philosopher and critic, born at Peebles and educated at Edinburgh. He was professor of logic and rhetoric at St Andrews and later professor of logic at Glasgow.
His verse includes The Tweed and Other Poems (1875) and Merlin and Other Poems (1889).

poets.name: Mary Kyle Dallas
bio: Mary Kyle Dallas (died 1897) was an American writer, born in Philadelphia, who for many years contributed fiction and verse to family story papers; some of her novels were published in book form. She died in New York.
The poem printed here is taken from An American Anthology, 1787–1900, edited by Edmund Clarence Stedman (1900).

poets.name: Matthias Barr
bio: Matthias Barr (1831–1911) was born in Edinburgh, the son of a German-born watchmaker, and educated at the High School and Academy there. After a visit to Germany he settled in London, where he held a post and later kept a music-selling and publishing business.

His first volume of verse appeared in 1865, followed by several short collections of simple lyrics and verses for children. Two of his nursery poems, “Moon, so round and yellow” and “Only a baby small”, were widely reprinted.

poets.name: John Ceiriog Hughes (Ceiriog)
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: John Ceiriog Hughes, known as Ceiriog, was a Welsh poet born in the Ceiriog valley of Denbighshire, famed for the lyrics he wrote for old Welsh airs, and often called the Burns of Wales.
Four of his songs are given in English verse by Alfred Perceval Graves in A Celtic Psaltery (1917).

poets.name: Stopford A. Brooke
poets.credit: Photograph of Stopford Brooke by Frederick Hollyer, c. 1890 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Stopford Augustus Brooke (1832–1916) was an Irish-born clergyman, preacher and critic, born at Letterkenny in County Donegal and educated at Trinity College, Dublin. He became a well-known London preacher and a chaplain to Queen Victoria, and is remembered chiefly for his literary criticism, including his Primer of English Literature (1876).
He also wrote verse, publishing Riquet of the Tuft (1880) and a volume of Poems (1888). Lyra Celtica prints two pieces from the latter: 'The Earth and Man' and a song from his poem 'Six Days'.

poets.name: Joel Benton
bio: Joel Benton (1832–1911) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Grover Cleveland”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Nora Perry
poets.credit: Portrait of Nora Perry · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Nora Perry (1832–1896) was an American poet.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “Balboa” and “Running the Blockade”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Hiram Rich
bio: Hiram Rich (1832–1905) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Morgan Stanwood”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Theron Brown
bio: Theron Brown (born Willimantic, Connecticut, 1832) graduated from Yale in 1856 and entered the Baptist ministry in 1859. From 1870 he was editorially connected with The Youth’s Companion in Boston.
“His Majesty,” a tramp’s song, appeared in Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Henry Clay Work
poets.credit: Portrait of Henry Clay Work · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Clay Work (1832–1884) was an American songwriter and composer.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “Marching Through Georgia” and “The Year of Jubilee”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Elizabeth Akers Allen
poets.credit: Portrait: Artist unidentified — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Elizabeth Akers Allen (1832–1911), born Elizabeth Chase in Strong, Maine, was an American poet and journalist who wrote early under the pen name Florence Percy. She published Forest Buds from the Woods of Maine in 1856.
Her best-known poem, "Rock Me to Sleep", appeared in 1859 and was among the most widely reprinted American poems of its day.

poets.name: Theodore Watts-Dunton
poets.credit: Portrait of Theodore Watts-Dunton by Helen Bramwell Norris (1865-1927), 1902 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Theodore Watts-Dunton (1832–1914), printed in the anthology as Theodore Watts, was an English poetry critic and poet, the friend and housemate of Algernon Charles Swinburne.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 6, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: John James Ingalls
bio: John James Ingalls (1833–1900) was an American politician and writer, born in Middleton, Massachusetts. He moved to Kansas, where he served as United States Senator from 1873 to 1891.
His sonnet "Opportunity" brought him wide fame and was reprinted in countless anthologies.

poets.name: John Albee
bio: John Albee (1833–1915), born in Bellingham, Massachusetts, was an American poet and essayist who lived at New Castle, New Hampshire. He was acquainted with Emerson and the Concord circle.
He wrote verse, essays and Remembrances of Emerson (1901); Stedman's An American Anthology (1900) printed several of his poems.

poets.name: Emily Huntington Miller
bio: Emily Huntington Miller (1833–1913) was an American writer, editor and educator, born in Brooklyn, Connecticut, and graduated from Oberlin College in 1857. She edited the children’s magazine The Little Corporal and served as dean of women at Northwestern University.
She was active in the early Woman’s Christian Temperance Union and wrote many books of prose and verse, chiefly for young readers, together with hymns.

poets.name: Philip Gilbert Hamerton
bio: Philip Gilbert Hamerton (1834–1894), born at Laneside, Lancashire, was an artist and art critic who settled in France in 1861. He founded the art periodical The Portfolio in 1869 and edited it until his death.

He is best remembered for Etching and Etchers (1868) and The Intellectual Life (1873); his early verse appeared in The Isles of Loch Awe. The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s A Victorian Anthology, 1837–1895 (1895).

poets.name: Tracy Robinson
bio: Tracy Robinson (born 1833) was an American railway official and poet, born in Clarendon, New York, and educated at the University of Rochester. After service on railways in Tennessee and Louisiana he moved in 1861 to Colón, Panama, with the Panama Railroad.
His volume "Song of the Palm and Other Poems" appeared in 1889.

poets.name: Sabine Baring-Gould
bio: Sabine Baring-Gould (1834–1924) was an English clergyman, antiquary and novelist, and rector of Lew Trenchard in Devon from 1881. He is best remembered for the hymns “Onward, Christian Soldiers” and “Now the day is over”, and for collecting the folk songs of the West Country.

poets.name: Charles Pelham Mulvaney
bio: Charles Pelham Mulvaney (1835–1872) was a Canadian clergyman and writer whose verse appeared in Canadian periodicals and was later drawn on for anthologies of Canadian poetry.
The poems given here are taken from The Oxford Book of Canadian Verse, chosen by Wilfred Campbell (Toronto: Oxford University Press, 1913).

poets.name: Phillips Brooks
bio: Phillips Brooks (1835–1893) was an American Episcopal clergyman, rector of Trinity Church, Boston, and from 1891 Bishop of Massachusetts.
He wrote the Christmas carol "O Little Town of Bethlehem" in 1868 for the children of his Sunday school, after a visit to the Holy Land.

poets.name: William Hayes Ward
bio: William Hayes Ward (1835–1916) was an American Congregational minister, orientalist and editor. For many years he edited the New York weekly The Independent.
Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900) reprints his poems "To John Greenleaf Whittier" and "The New Castalia".

poets.name: Sir Alfred Comyn Lyall
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir Alfred Comyn Lyall by Elliott & Fry (before 1911) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Alfred Comyn Lyall (1835–1911) was a British civil servant in India, a literary historian and a poet. His Verses Written in India appeared in 1889.
The poems printed here are those given in The Oxford Book of English Mystical Verse (1917), edited by D. H. S. Nicholson and A. H. E. Lee; the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Augusta Cooper Bristol
bio: Augusta Cooper Bristol (born 1835) was an American educator and lecturer, born in Croydon, New Hampshire. She married Louis Bristol in 1866 and settled in Vineland, New Jersey, in 1872.
She wrote on social topics and published a volume of poems, "The Web of Life" (1895).

poets.name: Bret Harte
poets.credit: Napoleon Sarony, c. 1870s · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Francis Brett Harte (1836-1902) was an American short-story writer and poet, born in Albany, New York. He went to California in the 1850s, worked as a typesetter and journalist in San Francisco, and edited the Overland Monthly, in which his stories of the Gold Rush country, including The Luck of Roaring Camp (1868), first appeared.

His verse, notably the comic ballad known as Plain Language from Truthful James (1870), made him famous across the United States and Britain. From 1878 he lived abroad as a U.S. consul in Krefeld and Glasgow and then in London, where he died. East and West: Poems (1871), from which these poems are taken, gathers his Californian and Civil War verse with a second part of parodies and humorous pieces.

poets.name: Titus Munson Coan
bio: Titus Munson Coan (1836–1921) was an American physician and writer, born at Hilo in the Hawaiian Islands. He was educated in Honolulu, graduated at Williams College in 1859 and took his medical degree in New York City.
He practised and wrote in New York, contributing verse and essays to the magazines. Stedman included three of his poems in An American Anthology (1900), from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Mary Frances Butts
bio: Mary Frances Butts (1836–1902) was an American poet and writer of verse for children.
She is represented in Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900).

poets.name: Thomas Bailey Aldrich
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Bailey Aldrich (photograph, c. 1885–1907, photographer unknown) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Bailey Aldrich (1836–1907) was an American poet, novelist and editor, born in Portsmouth, New Hampshire. He edited The Atlantic Monthly from 1881 to 1890 and wrote the boyhood memoir The Story of a Bad Boy (1869).
In verse he was admired for small, polished lyrics and epigrams, which he refined steadily over his career.

poets.name: David Gray
bio: David Gray (1836–1888) was a Scottish-born American journalist and poet, born in Edinburgh. In 1856 he joined the staff of the Buffalo Courier in New York, of which he later became editor, resigning on account of ill health; he died at Binghamton.
His letters, prose writings and poems were collected and edited by J. N. Larned in 1888. He is not to be confused with the Scottish poet David Gray (1838–1861), author of The Luggie.

poets.name: John Hay
poets.credit: Portrait of John Hay (photograph, 1902, Library of Congress) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Hay (1838–1905) was an American diplomat and writer, born in Salem, Indiana, who served as private secretary to Abraham Lincoln and later as Secretary of State.
His dialect ballads, gathered in Pike County Ballads (1871) and including “Jim Bludso”, made him widely known as a poet.

poets.name: Abram Joseph Ryan (Father Ryan)
poets.credit: Photograph of Father Abram J. Ryan, c. 1875 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Abram Joseph Ryan (1838–1886) was an American Catholic priest and poet, born in Maryland or Virginia and raised in Missouri. Ordained in the 1860s, he served as a chaplain to Confederate troops during the Civil War, and afterwards ministered in parishes in the South, notably in Mobile, Alabama.

Known as the 'Poet-Priest of the South', he wrote devotional verse as well as elegies for the Confederate cause, among them 'The Conquered Banner' and 'The Sword of Robert Lee'. His collected Poems: Patriotic, Religious, Miscellaneous appeared in 1880 and was reprinted in the 1890s.

poets.name: Charlotte Fiske Bates
bio: Charlotte Fiske Bates (1838–1916), who also wrote as Madame Rogé after her marriage, was an American poet, critic and editor, a native of New England.
The poems printed here are those given in Stedman's An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1900); the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Basil W. Duke
poets.credit: Portrait of Basil W. Duke (Wikimedia Commons) · Public domain
bio: Basil Wilson Duke (1838–1916) was a Kentucky lawyer who served as a Confederate officer under his brother-in-law John Hunt Morgan and rose to the rank of brigadier general. He later wrote a History of Morgan's Cavalry (1867).
"Morgan's War-Song", set to a combination of the Marseillaise and "Old Granite State", is reprinted here from W. L. Fagan's Southern War Songs (1890).

poets.name: Samuel Hawkins Marshall Byers
bio: Samuel Hawkins Marshall Byers (1838–1933) was an Iowa-born Union soldier, later American consul and diplomat, who wrote the song Sherman’s March to the Sea.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: Sherman’s March to the Sea.

poets.name: William Reed Huntington
bio: William Reed Huntington (1838–1909) was an American Episcopal priest, for many years rector of Grace Church, New York, and a leading figure in the revision of the Book of Common Prayer.
Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900) prints two of his sonnets, "Tellus" and "Authority".

poets.name: Margaret Elizabeth Sangster
bio: Margaret Elizabeth Sangster (1838–1912) was an American author and editor, born at New Rochelle, New York. She wrote verse, stories and domestic advice, and edited Harper’s Bazar from 1889 to 1899.
Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900) prints her poems "Whittier" and "Awakening".

poets.name: Clara Doty Bates
bio: Clara Doty Bates (1838–1895) was born at Ann Arbor, Michigan, and in 1869 married Morgan Bates, a publisher.
She was chiefly known as a writer of verse and stories for children.

poets.name: Villiers de l'Isle-Adam
poets.credit: Portrait of Villiers de l'Isle-Adam, 1886 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Auguste de Villiers de l'Isle-Adam (1838–1889) was a French Symbolist writer, born at Saint-Brieuc in Brittany of Breton parentage. He is remembered for his tales, Contes cruels (1883), and his drama Axël (1890), and he published a first volume of poems when still very young.
The two poems here are in English verse renderings by W. J. Robertson from his A Century of French Verse (1895), as reprinted in Lyra Celtica.

poets.name: Carrie Bell Sinclair
bio: Carrie Bell Sinclair (1839–1883) was an American poet of the South who wrote lyrics for the Confederate cause during the Civil War.
Two of her songs, "The Homespun Dress" (to the air of "The Bonnie Blue Flag") and "The Soldier's Suit of Gray", are reprinted here from W. L. Fagan's Southern War Songs (1890).

poets.name: Laura Redden Searing
bio: Laura Catherine Redden Searing (1839–1923) was an American poet and journalist, born in Maryland. Deaf from childhood, she wrote for newspapers under the pen-name "Howard Glyndon".
She published Idyls of Battle, and Poems of the Rebellion (1864) and Sounds from Secret Chambers (1873), and later lived in California.

poets.name: Stephen Henry Thayer
bio: Stephen Henry Thayer (born 1839) was an American banker and poet, born at New Ipswich, New Hampshire. He attended Appleton Academy and, after moving to Tarrytown, New York, became a banker in New York City.

He published Songs of Sleepy Hollow (1886) and contributed verse and critical essays to the periodical press. Stedman included three of his poems in An American Anthology (1900), from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: William Tuckey Meredith
bio: William Tuckey Meredith (born 1839) was an American army officer, born in Philadelphia. He served under Admiral Farragut at the battle of Mobile Bay, became his secretary, and was afterwards a banker in New York City.
He published a novel, "Not of Her Father's Race" (1891); his ballad "Farragut" appears in Stedman's An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: William Winter
bio: William Winter (1836–1917) was an American poet and drama critic, born at Gloucester, Massachusetts. He wrote for the New York Tribune for more than forty years and became the leading theatre critic of his day, publishing many books on actors and the stage.
His own verse, gathered in several volumes, is quiet and elegiac; Knowles took “After All” from his collection Wanderers (1892).

poets.name: Mary Mathews Adams
bio: Mary Mathews Adams was an American poet, born in Brooklyn, New York, and educated at the Packer Institute. She married the publisher Alfred S. Barnes and, after his death, Charles Kendall Adams, president of the University of Wisconsin.
Her volume of poems, The Choir Invisible, appeared in 1897.

poets.name: Ellice Hopkins
bio: Ellice Hopkins (1836–1904) was an English writer and social-purity campaigner who worked for the protection of girls and for the moral reform of public life. She wrote prose and also devotional and reforming verse.
Two of her poems, “Life in Death” and “A Vision of Womanhood”, are included in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Daniel Bedinger Lucas
poets.credit: Portrait of Daniel Bedinger Lucas · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Daniel Bedinger Lucas (1836–1909) was an American judge.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “In the Land Where We Were Dreaming”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: William Henry Venable
bio: William Henry Venable (1836–1918) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “John Filson”, “Johnny Appleseed”, “The Founders of Ohio”, “El Emplazado” and “Battle Cry” among others; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: John Aylmer Dorgan
bio: John Aylmer Dorgan (1836–1867) was an American poet whose short career ended with his death in 1867.
Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900) prints two of his poems, "The Beautiful" and "The Dead Solomon".

poets.name: Mary Elizabeth Blake
bio: Mary Elizabeth Blake (1844–1923) was an Irish-born American poet. Born in Dungarvan, she was taken as a child to Quincy, Massachusetts, and lived in Boston after her marriage to Dr. John G. Blake.
She published several volumes of verse, beginning with Poems (1882), and wrote on Irish themes with warm affection.

poets.name: Robert Henry Newell
bio: Robert Henry Newell (1836–1901), who wrote as "Orpheus C. Kerr", was a New York journalist and humorist. He wrote for the New York Mercury and the World, edited Hearth and Home, and made his name with the satirical "Orpheus C. Kerr Papers" (1862–68).
His verse includes "The Palace Beautiful, and Other Poems" (1865) and "Studies in Stanzas" (1882).

poets.name: David Banks Sickels
bio: David Banks Sickels was an American diplomat who served as United States consul at Bangkok around 1879–80, and an occasional writer of verse.
His poem "Reincarnation" was printed in Edmund Clarence Stedman's An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Frances Laughton Mace
bio: Frances Laughton Mace (1836–1899) was an American poet, born at Orono, Maine.
Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900) prints her sonnet sequence "Alcyone" and her sonnet "The Succession".

poets.name: Sir Walter Besant
bio: Sir Walter Besant (1836–1901), born at Portsmouth, was a novelist and historian, educated at King’s College, London, and Christ’s College, Cambridge. He taught in Mauritius, and was for many years Secretary of the Palestine Exploration Fund.
His first book was Studies in Early French Poetry (1868). The song here comes from his novel Dorothy Forster and is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s A Victorian Anthology, 1837–1895 (1895).

poets.name: Anna Callender Brackett
bio: Anna Callender Brackett (born 1836) was an American educator, born in Boston. She taught at the State Normal School in Framingham and in Charleston, became principal of the Normal School in St. Louis, the first woman to hold such a post, and later conducted a school for girls in New York.
She wrote educational essays, stories and poems; her sonnet "In Hades" appears in Stedman's An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Charles Frederick Johnson
bio: Charles Frederick Johnson (1836–1904) was an American scholar and poet who taught English literature at Trinity College, Hartford, Connecticut.
Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900) prints his poems "The Modern Romans" and "Then and Now".

poets.name: Frank Sewall
bio: Frank Sewall (1837–1915) was an American Swedenborgian minister, author and educator, who served as president of Urbana University in Ohio.
He published several volumes of prose and verse, among them Swedenborg and Science and a book of poems.

poets.name: Mary Gardiner Brainard
bio: Mary Gardiner Brainard (1837–1905) was born in New London, Connecticut, the niece of the poet John Gardiner Calkins Brainard.
Her poem "Not Knowing" first appeared in The Congregationalist in 1869 and was later set to music as a hymn.

poets.name: Henry Ames Blood
bio: Henry Ames Blood (1836–1900) was an American poet whose verse appeared in the magazines of the 1890s.
Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900) prints his poems "Comrades" and "Shakespeare".

poets.name: John Burroughs
bio: John Burroughs (1837–1921) was an American naturalist and essayist, born in Roxbury, New York. He is remembered above all for his nature essays, which did much to popularise the study of birds and the countryside.
He also wrote a small body of verse, of which "Waiting" is by far the best known.

poets.name: Nicholas Flood Davin
bio: Nicholas Flood Davin (1840–1901) was an Irish-born lawyer, journalist and politician who settled in the North-West Territories, founded the Regina Leader and sat in the Canadian House of Commons. His long poem Eos: An Epic of the Dawn was published in 1889.
The poems given here are taken from The Oxford Book of Canadian Verse, chosen by Wilfred Campbell (Toronto: Oxford University Press, 1913).

poets.name: Agnes Maule Machar
bio: Agnes Maule Machar (1837–1927) of Kingston, Ontario, was a novelist, historian, essayist and poet who often wrote under the pen-name Fidelis, and a writer of strong religious and social interests.
The poems given here are taken from The Oxford Book of Canadian Verse, chosen by Wilfred Campbell (Toronto: Oxford University Press, 1913).

poets.name: Marguerite Elizabeth Easter
bio: Marguerite Elizabeth Easter (née Miller, 1839–1894) was born in Leesburg, Virginia, and married the Baltimore merchant James Washington Easter in 1859.
She is the author of Clytie, and Other Poems (1891).

poets.name: George Cotterell
bio: George Cotterell, born at Walsall in 1839, studied and practised law before entering literature as a profession. He became editor of the Yorkshire Daily Herald.

He published Poems: Old and New (1894), two privately printed volumes of verse (1870 and 1887), and a satire, The Banquet (1884). The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s A Victorian Anthology, 1837–1895 (1895).

poets.name: Chauncey Hickox
bio: Chauncey Hickox was an American journalist, born in Ravenna, Ohio, in 1837.
The poem printed here is taken from An American Anthology, 1787–1900, edited by Edmund Clarence Stedman (1900).

poets.name: Wendell Phillips Garrison
bio: Wendell Phillips Garrison (1840–1907) was an American editor and writer, born in Cambridgeport, Massachusetts, a graduate of Harvard and a son of the abolitionist William Lloyd Garrison.
He was literary editor of the New York Nation from its foundation in 1865 and lived for many years in Orange, New Jersey; he also wrote, with his brother Francis, a life of his father.

poets.name: John Lancaster Spalding
bio: John Lancaster Spalding (1840–1916) was an American Catholic bishop, the first Bishop of Peoria (1877–1908), an educator and a writer of essays and verse.
The poems printed here are those given in Stedman's An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1900); the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Robert Kelley Weeks
bio: Robert Kelley Weeks (1840–1876) was an American poet, born and died in New York City. A graduate of Yale and a member of the New York bar, he gave up law for literature.
He published Poems (1866) and Episodes and Lyric Pieces (1870). Stedman included three of his poems in An American Anthology (1900), from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Amelia Walstien Carpenter
bio: Amelia Walstien Carpenter (born 1840) was an American poet and story-writer, born at Stephentown, New York. At eighteen she married Cromwell Carpenter, with whom she lived in Kalamazoo and St. Louis, returning to her native town after his death.

Her poems and stories appeared in The Springfield Republican, The Christian Union, Lippincott's Magazine and other periodicals. Stedman included three of her poems in An American Anthology (1900), from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Ellen Mary Clerke
bio: Ellen Mary Clerke (1840–1906) was an Irish poet, linguist and journalist, born in County Cork and educated in Italy. She wrote in English and Italian.
The poems printed here are those given in The Oxford Book of English Mystical Verse (1917), edited by D. H. S. Nicholson and A. H. E. Lee; the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Henry Bernard Carpenter
bio: Henry Bernard Carpenter was an Irish Unitarian clergyman, orator, author and poet, educated at Oxford; his written works were principally in verse.

The dates given here, 1840–1887, are those printed in the 1917 anthology. The poems printed here are those given in The Oxford Book of English Mystical Verse (1917), edited by D. H. S. Nicholson and A. H. E. Lee; the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Joaquin Miller
poets.credit: Portrait of Joaquin Miller (photograph by Mathew Brady, c. 1870s) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Joaquin Miller (the pen name of Cincinnatus Heine Miller, 1841–1913) was an American poet of the Pacific coast who styled himself the “Poet of the Sierras”.
His Songs of the Sierras (1871) won him a reputation in England as well as in the United States, and he later lived in the hills above Oakland, California.

poets.name: James Herbert Morse
bio: James Herbert Morse (1841–1923) was an American poet, educator and editor.
The poems printed here are those given in Stedman's An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1900); the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Edward Rowland Sill
poets.credit: Portrait of Edward Rowland Sill (photograph, before 1887) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward Rowland Sill (1841–1887) was an American poet and teacher, born in Windsor, Connecticut, who taught English at the University of California.
His thoughtful short poems, among them “The Fool’s Prayer”, were widely admired and several were collected after his death.

poets.name: Minot Judson Savage
bio: Minot Judson Savage (1841–1918) was an American Unitarian clergyman and author, born in Norridgewock, Maine, and educated at Bowdoin College and Bangor Theological Seminary.
After mission work in California he was for many years pastor of the Church of the Unity in Boston, and wrote widely on religion and evolution.

poets.name: Sarah Knowles Bolton
bio: Sarah Knowles Bolton (1841–1916) was an American writer and reformer, born in Farmington, Connecticut. She was active in the temperance and woman suffrage movements and wrote for the periodical press.

She is best known for her collective biographies for young readers, including Lives of Poor Boys Who Became Famous (1885) and Lives of Girls Who Became Famous (1886); she also wrote verse, of which ‘The Inevitable’ was chosen for Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Thomas Stephens Collier
bio: Thomas Stephens Collier was an American poet of the later nineteenth century whose short verses appeared in periodicals and in Edmund Clarence Stedman's An American Anthology (1900).
He is represented there by a group of quatrains on large themes such as time, power and disappointment.

poets.name: Mathilde Blind
poets.credit: Portrait of Mathilde Blind by Lucy Madox Brown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mathilde Blind (1841–1896) was born Mathilde Cohen at Mannheim and came to England as a girl, taking the surname of her stepfather. She wrote poems, a biography of George Eliot and translations, and was a friend of the Rossettis and of Ford Madox Brown.
Her books include The Prophecy of Saint Oran (1881) and The Ascent of Man (1889). Five of her poems appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: James David Edgar
poets.credit: Portrait of James David Edgar by the Topley Studio, 1896 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James David Edgar (1841–1899), born in Quebec, was a lawyer and politician who became Speaker of the House of Commons of Canada, and wrote verse and songs.
The poems here are those Lighthall chose for his 1889 anthology, Songs of the Great Dominion.

poets.name: Sarah Williams
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sarah Williams (1841–1868) was an English poet and novelist, best known for "The Old Astronomer". She published under the pseudonyms Sadie and S.A.D.I.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Kate Putnam Osgood
bio: Kate Putnam Osgood (1841–1910) was an American poet whose Driving Home the Cows became a favourite of the Civil War.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: Driving Home the Cows.

poets.name: Robert Buchanan
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Buchanan by Herbert Rose Barraud, carbon print, c. 1893 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Williams Buchanan (1841–1901) was a Scottish poet, novelist and dramatist, born at Caverswall in Staffordshire and brought up in Glasgow. His books of verse include Undertones (1863), London Poems (1866) and The Book of Orm (1870), and in 1871 he published the attack on Rossetti and his circle called 'The Fleshly School of Poetry'.

Lyra Celtica calls him the foremost Scoto-Celtic poet of his time and takes four poems from him, including 'The Dream of the World without Death' from The Book of Orm. This file also holds his 'Ballad of Judas Iscariot' and 'Phil Blood's Leap' from Popular British Ballads (1894), songs from Victorian Songs (1895), and a broad selection of his shorter poems and ballads from The Complete Poetical Works (London: Chatto & Windus, 1901).

poets.name: Kate Brownlee Sherwood
bio: Kate Brownlee Sherwood (1841–1914) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “Molly Pitcher”, “Albert Sidney Johnston”, “Thomas at Chickamauga” and “Ulric Dahlgren”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: James Rhoades
bio: James Rhoades (1841–1923), born at Clonmel in County Tipperary and educated at Rugby, was an Anglo-Irish poet, translator and schoolmaster. He translated Virgil’s Georgics and Aeneid into English verse.
The poems printed here are those given in The Oxford Book of English Mystical Verse (1917), edited by D. H. S. Nicholson and A. H. E. Lee; the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Bertram Dobell
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Bertram Dobell (1842–1914) was an English bookseller and literary scholar. A largely self-taught man, he published or reissued works by writers including James Thomson and Thomas Traherne, and wrote poetry, criticism and biography himself.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Ina Coolbrith
bio: Ina Donna Coolbrith (1841–1928) was an American poet, born in Illinois and raised in California, where she became a central figure of the San Francisco literary circle around Bret Harte and Charles Warren Stoddard. She worked for many years as a librarian in Oakland and San Francisco.
Her books include A Perfect Day and Other Poems (1881) and Songs from the Golden Gate (1895). In 1915 she was named the first poet laureate of California.

poets.name: George Alfred Townsend
bio: George Alfred Townsend (1841–1914) was an American journalist who wrote under the pen name "Gath". He reported the Civil War for the New York Herald and later settled in Maryland.
Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900) prints his poems "Army Correspondent’s Last Ride" and "In Rama".

poets.name: William Gordon McCabe
bio: William Gordon McCabe (1841–1920) was an American soldier, schoolmaster and poet. He served as a Confederate artillery officer, notably at Petersburg, and afterwards founded schools in Petersburg and Richmond, Virginia.
Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900) prints his war poems "Christmas Night of ’62" and "Dreaming in the Trenches".

poets.name: Sidney Lanier
poets.credit: Portrait of Sidney Lanier — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sidney Lanier (1842–1881) was an American poet and musician from Georgia who served in the Confederate army, was imprisoned as a prisoner of war, and spent much of his short life battling the tuberculosis that eventually killed him.
A trained flautist, he brought a musician’s sense of rhythm and sound to poems such as ‘The Marshes of Glynn’ and ‘The Song of the Chattahoochee’, which celebrate the landscape of the American South.

poets.name: Ambrose Bierce
poets.credit: Portrait of Ambrose Bierce (photograph, c. 1866) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ambrose Bierce was born in 1842 in Meigs County, Ohio, and grew up in Indiana. He served as an officer in the Union Army through the Civil War, an experience that shaped his best-known short stories, and afterwards made his career in journalism, chiefly in San Francisco, where his newspaper column made him feared as a satirist. His prose includes the story collection In the Midst of Life (1892) and the dictionary of cynical definitions later published as The Devil's Dictionary.

His verse was mostly satire. Black Beetles in Amber (1892) gathers epigrams, mock-epitaphs and lampoons aimed at the politicians, editors, clergymen and businessmen of the Pacific Coast; Shapes of Clay (1903) collects later satires, fables and a few serious poems. In the autumn of 1913 he left for Mexico, then in revolution, and was last heard from in a letter of December 1913; his fate and the date of his death are unknown.

poets.name: Charles Goodrich Whiting
bio: Charles Goodrich Whiting (1842–1922) was an American critic of letters and art, born at St. Albans, Vermont. He grew up in Springfield, Massachusetts, and from 1866 was connected with the Springfield Republican, becoming its literary editor in 1874.

He wrote the poem for the unveiling of the soldiers' monument at Springfield in 1885 and published The Saunterer (1886), in prose and verse. Stedman included three of his poems in An American Anthology (1900), from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Charles Edward Carryl
bio: Charles Edward Carryl (1842–1920) was an American businessman and writer, born in New York City, and the father of the poet Guy Wetmore Carryl.
He is remembered for the children’s fantasy Davy and the Goblin (1885), whose nonsense verses include “The Plaint of the Camel”.

poets.name: May Riley Smith
bio: May Riley Smith (1842–1927) was an American poet whose verse appeared widely in magazines.
She is represented in Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900).

poets.name: Benjamin Dionysius Hill
bio: Benjamin Dionysius Hill was born in Buckinghamshire, England, in 1842, and educated at Oxford and Cambridge. He became a Passionist priest in the United States, taking the name Father Edmund of the Heart of Mary.
He published devotional verse, much of it addressed to the Virgin Mary and the saints.

poets.name: Annie Douglas Robinson
bio: Annie Douglas Robinson (née Green), who wrote as "Marian Douglas", was born in Plymouth, New Hampshire, in 1842 and lived in Bristol, New Hampshire.
She wrote verse and stories for children, including Picture Poems (1872) and Peter and Polly (1876).

poets.name: Charles Monroe Dickinson
bio: Charles Monroe Dickinson (1842–1924) was born in Lowville, New York. He was admitted to the bar in 1865 and later edited the Binghamton Republican.
His poem "The Children" gave its name to his volume The Children, and Other Verses (1889).

poets.name: Eliza Jane Nicholson ("Pearl Rivers")
poets.credit: Portrait of Pearl Rivers (Eliza Jane Nicholson) (Wikimedia Commons) · Public domain
bio: Eliza Jane Nicholson (1843–1896), who wrote as "Pearl Rivers", was an American poet and journalist born in Mississippi. After the death of her husband she became publisher of the New Orleans Picayune, one of the first women to run a major daily newspaper in the United States.
"True to the Gray" is reprinted here from W. L. Fagan's Southern War Songs (1890).

poets.name: Laurence Hutton
bio: Laurence Hutton (1843–1904) was an American man of letters and drama critic, born in New York City, who edited Harper's literary notes and wrote on authors, their haunts and their death masks.
Light verse such as "The Doves of Venice" appeared in anthologies of his day.

poets.name: Samuel Willoughby Duffield
bio: Samuel Augustus Willoughby Duffield (1843–1887) was an American clergyman and hymnologist, born in Brooklyn, New York, and a graduate of Yale. He was a Presbyterian minister and held a pastorate at Bloomfield, New Jersey, for most of his career.
He published a volume of poems, Warp and Woof (1870), and the hymnological study English Hymns: Their Authors and History (1886).

poets.name: Montgomery Schuyler
bio: Montgomery Schuyler was an American journalist and architectural critic, born in Ithaca, New York, in 1843 and educated at Hobart College.
He worked on the New York World from 1865 to 1883, wrote for Harper’s Weekly, and later joined the editorial staff of the New York Times.

poets.name: Edward Willard Watson
bio: Edward Willard Watson was an American physician, born in Newport, Rhode Island, in 1843, and educated at the University of Pennsylvania. He practised in Philadelphia.
He published two volumes of verse, To-day and Yesterday (1895) and Songs of Flying Hours (1897).

poets.name: Alfred Gurney
bio: Alfred Gurney (1843–1898) was an English cleric and writer, the second son of John Hampden Gurney and a brother of the psychical researcher Edmund Gurney.

The poem here carries a line from Tennyson as its epigraph. The poems printed here are those given in The Oxford Book of English Mystical Verse (1917), edited by D. H. S. Nicholson and A. H. E. Lee; the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Francis Fisher Browne
bio: Francis Fisher Browne (1843–1913) was an American editor and poet, born at South Halifax, Vermont. After serving as a volunteer in the Union army he went to Chicago, where in 1880 he founded the critical semi-monthly The Dial.
He wrote The Every-Day Life of Abraham Lincoln (1886) and the poems Volunteer Grain (1895). Stedman included three of his poems in An American Anthology (1900), from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Mollie E. Moore Davis
bio: Mollie Evelyn Moore Davis (1844–1909) was an American poet and novelist, born in Alabama and raised in Texas; after her marriage in 1874 she lived in New Orleans, where she became a leading Southern woman of letters.
Her Civil War poems, published under the name Mollie E. Moore, include "Lee at the Wilderness" and "Hood's Old Brigade", reprinted here from W. L. Fagan's Southern War Songs (1890).

poets.name: George Washington Cable
bio: George Washington Cable (1844–1925) was an American writer from New Orleans, best known for his Creole fiction such as Old Creole Days (1879) and The Grandissimes (1880).
He wrote occasional light verse, two examples of which are printed in Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900).

poets.name: Elizabeth Stuart Phelps Ward
poets.credit: Portrait of Elizabeth Stuart Phelps Ward · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Elizabeth Stuart Phelps Ward (1844–1911) was an American novelist.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “A Message” and “Conemaugh”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Mary Thacher Higginson
bio: Mary Thacher Higginson (1844–1941) was an American poet and the second wife of the writer and abolitionist Thomas Wentworth Higginson, whom she married in 1879. She published verse in magazines.
Her poems are short nature lyrics and sonnets, and four of them were chosen for Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: John Payne
poets.credit: Portrait of John Payne · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Payne (1842–1916) was an English poet and translator who had been associated with Dante Gabriel Rossetti.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 8, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Francis Howard Williams
bio: Francis Howard Williams (1844–1922) was an American poet and dramatist, born in Philadelphia, where he worked for a trust company and contributed to various journals.
He wrote the lyric drama The Princess Elizabeth (1880) and several comedies and pastorals. Stedman included three of his poems in An American Anthology (1900), from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Margaret Thomson Janvier
bio: Margaret Thomson Janvier (1844–1913), who wrote as "Margaret Vandegrift", was born in New Orleans and was the sister of the author Thomas Allibone Janvier.
She is best known for verse and stories for children, such as Under the Dog-Star (1881) and The Absent-Minded Fairy (1883).

poets.name: Mary Ainge De Vere
bio: Mary Ainge De Vere, who wrote under the pen-name “Madeline Bridges”, was an American poet born in Brooklyn, New York, in the 1840s. She lived in Brooklyn and contributed verse to the Galaxy, the Century, the Independent, Life and many other periodicals.
Her books include Love Songs, and Other Poems (1870) and Poems (1890). Edmund Clarence Stedman printed nine of her lyrics in An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Edward Carpenter
poets.credit: Portrait of Edward Carpenter by F. Holland Day · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward Carpenter (1844–1929) was an English socialist, poet, philosopher and anthologist, an early campaigner for gay rights and for prison reform. His free-verse sequence Towards Democracy appeared in 1883.

The pieces here are in the long, unrhymed lines of his free verse. The poems printed here are those given in The Oxford Book of English Mystical Verse (1917), edited by D. H. S. Nicholson and A. H. E. Lee; the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Eugene Fitch Ware
bio: Eugene Fitch Ware (1841–1911), who wrote as "Ironquill", was an American lawyer and politician, born in Hartford, Connecticut. He served as a cavalry officer in the Civil War and later lived in Kansas.
The poem printed here is taken from An American Anthology, 1787–1900, edited by Edmund Clarence Stedman (1900).

poets.name: Wallace Bruce
bio: Wallace Bruce (1844–1914) was an American lecturer and poet, born in Hillsdale, New York, and educated at Yale. He was United States consul at Edinburgh from 1889 to 1893 and published Old Homestead Poems (1887) and Wayside Poems (1895).
The poem printed here is taken from An American Anthology, 1787–1900, edited by Edmund Clarence Stedman (1900).

poets.name: Zitella Cocke
bio: Julia Zitella Cocke (1840–1929) was an American poet, born in Marion, Alabama, of a Virginian planter family. She wrote verse from childhood.
In the early 1890s she moved to Boston, where she worked as a translator at the Boston Public Library, and her poems appeared in the leading American magazines of her day.

poets.name: George Cooper
bio: George Cooper (1840–1927) was born in New York City and wrote song lyrics, among them “Sweet Genevieve” (1869).
He contributed songs and verse to children’s and other magazines.

poets.name: Will Carleton
poets.credit: Portrait of Will Carleton, steel engraving by Arthur Rice after a photograph by Sarony, 1890 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Will Carleton (William McKendree Carleton, 1845–1912) was an American poet from Michigan, whose verse most often drew on rural life. His ballads of farm and village speech, in the plain dialect of ordinary people, made him one of the most widely read popular poets of the United States in his day, and 'Over the Hill to the Poor-House' is the best known of them.

City Ballads (1885), one of the two books given here (with Farm Ballads, 1873), turns the same eye on the city. It is framed as the diaries of two country people newly arrived in New York, a young student, Arthur Selwyn, and an old farmer, Harrington, whose dated entries and inset ballads look at wealth, want, fire, water, vice, virtue, travel and home.

poets.name: John Henry Boner
bio: John Henry Boner (1845–1903) was an American poet born in Salem, North Carolina, of the Moravian community there. He worked as a printer and journalist and later held a post in the Library of Congress in Washington.
His collection Whispering Pines appeared in 1883 and a later volume of poems in 1903; he is remembered for his North Carolina verse and for “Poe’s Cottage at Fordham.”

poets.name: Gertrude Bloede
bio: Gertrude Bloede (1845–1905), who wrote also as Stuart Sterne, was an American poet, born in Dresden and brought to America in 1850. She lived in Brooklyn from 1861 and was a protégée of Bayard Taylor and his wife.

Her books include Poems (1874), Giorgio, and Other Poems (1881), Beyond the Shadow (1888) and Piero da Castiglione (1890). Stedman included three of her poems in An American Anthology (1900), from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: David Law Proudfit
bio: David Law Proudfit (1842–1897) was an American poet, born in Newburgh, New York. He enlisted in the Union army at the outbreak of the Civil War and rose to the rank of major, afterwards working in business in New York City.
He wrote for a time under the pseudonym "Peleg Arkwright", which he later gave up.

poets.name: Lydia Avery Coonley Ward
bio: Lydia Avery Coonley Ward (born 31 January 1845) was an American writer of devotional and reflective verse, who was living at Wyoming, New York, when The Home Book of Verse (1912) was compiled.
Her short poems "To-day" and "Heredity" were reprinted in that anthology.

poets.name: George Thomas Lanigan
bio: George Thomas Lanigan (1845–1886) was born in St. Charles, Quebec, and with Robert Graham founded the Montreal humorous paper Free Lance. He later worked on newspapers in New York and Chicago.
His comic "Threnody" on the death of the Ahkoond of Swat, first printed in 1873, was widely reprinted.

poets.name: John Campbell, 9th Duke of Argyll
bio: John Campbell, Marquess of Lorne and later 9th Duke of Argyll (1845–1914), was Governor General of Canada from 1878 to 1883 and a writer of verse and prose. His Canadian poems and his Canadian Pictures (1884) came out of his years in the country.
The poems given here are taken from The Oxford Book of Canadian Verse, chosen by Wilfred Campbell (Toronto: Oxford University Press, 1913).

poets.name: Julian Hawthorne
bio: Julian Hawthorne (1846–1934) was an American novelist and journalist, born in Boston, the son of Nathaniel Hawthorne.
The poem printed here is taken from An American Anthology, 1787–1900, edited by Edmund Clarence Stedman (1900).

poets.name: James Chapman Woods
bio: James Chapman Woods was a Victorian poet and writer, author of A Child of the People and Other Poems (1879), a guide to Swansea and the Mumbles, Gower and other places (1883), and In Foreign Byways (1887).
He also lectured on old and rare books. The poem here is taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s A Victorian Anthology, 1837–1895 (1895).

poets.name: Emma Huntington Nason
bio: Emma Huntington Nason (1845–1921) was an American poet, born in Hallowell, Maine, who lived in Augusta. Her books include White Sails (1888) and The Tower, with Legends and Lyrics (1895).
The poem printed here is taken from An American Anthology, 1787–1900, edited by Edmund Clarence Stedman (1900).

poets.name: Henrietta Robins Eliot
bio: Henrietta Robins Eliot (née Mack, born 1845) was born at Amherst, Massachusetts, and later lived in Portland, Oregon.
She wrote verse and short stories, and published Laura’s Holidays (1898).

poets.name: Frederick Keppel
bio: Frederick Keppel (1845–1912) was born at Tullow, Ireland, and settled in New York City as a dealer in prints and an art connoisseur.
He wrote on engravings and etchings, and occasional verse.

poets.name: Sir Frederick Pollock
bio: Sir Frederick Pollock, 3rd Baronet (1845–1937), was an English jurist, Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge, professor of jurisprudence at Oxford from 1883 and editor of the Law Quarterly Review.
His comic poem “The Six Carpenters’ Case”, a legal ballad, comes from Leading Cases Done into English (1876).

poets.name: Ella Dietz
poets.credit: Portrait of Ella Dietz Clymer (photographer unknown) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ella Dietz (1847–1920) was an American actress and author, known professionally by her maiden name; she was married first to a Mr Clymer and then to a Mr Glynes.
The poems printed here are those given in The Oxford Book of English Mystical Verse (1917), edited by D. H. S. Nicholson and A. H. E. Lee; the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Alice Wellington Rollins
bio: Alice Wellington Rollins (1847–1897) was an American poet.
Stedman included three of her poems in An American Anthology (1900), from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Henry Augustin Beers
bio: Henry Augustin Beers (1847–1926) was an American poet, critic and literary historian, for many years a professor of English at Yale.
The poems printed here are those given in Stedman's An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1900); the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Howard Weeden
bio: Howard Weeden (Maud Howard Weeden, 1847–1905) was an American poet and painter of Huntsville, Alabama. She is remembered for Songs of the Old South (1900), which paired dialect verse with her portraits of the Black men and women she knew in the South.
Edmund Clarence Stedman included two of her poems, “The Banjo of the Past” and “The Borrowed Child”, in An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Arthur Sherburne Hardy
bio: Arthur Sherburne Hardy (1847–1930) was an American mathematician, novelist and diplomat, born at Andover, Massachusetts. He graduated at West Point, taught civil engineering at Iowa College and from 1878 to 1893 was professor of mathematics at Dartmouth; he was later United States minister to Persia and then to Greece.
He published Francesca of Rimini, a poem (1878), and novels including But Yet a Woman (1883). Stedman included three of his poems in An American Anthology (1900), from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: William Young
bio: William Young (1847–1920) was an American poet and dramatist, the author of the stage version of Ben-Hur (1899).
He is represented in Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900).

poets.name: Lilian Whiting
bio: Lilian Whiting (1847–1942) was an American journalist and author, born in Niagara Falls, New York, who lived in Boston and wrote widely on spiritual and literary subjects.
The poem printed here is taken from An American Anthology, 1787–1900, edited by Edmund Clarence Stedman (1900).

poets.name: Grant Allen
bio: Grant Allen (1848–1899) was born near Kingston, Ontario, and made his career in England as a popular writer on natural science, a novelist and a journalist. He wrote verse only occasionally.
The poems given here are taken from The Oxford Book of Canadian Verse, chosen by Wilfred Campbell (Toronto: Oxford University Press, 1913).

poets.name: Alice Williams Brotherton
bio: Alice Williams Brotherton (1848–1930) was an American poet who lived in Cincinnati.
She is represented in Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900).

poets.name: Joel Chandler Harris
bio: Joel Chandler Harris (1848–1908) was an American journalist and folklorist from Georgia, creator of the Uncle Remus tales.
His plantation-dialect songs are represented in Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900).

poets.name: Edward King
bio: Edward King (1848–1896) was an American journalist and author, born in Middlefield, Massachusetts. From 1868 he was a correspondent in Paris.
His books include My Paris (1868), The Great South (1875) and the poems of A Venetian Lover (1887).

poets.name: Hjalmar Hjorth Boyesen
bio: Hjalmar Hjorth Boyesen (1848–1895) was a Norwegian-born American novelist and scholar, professor of German at Cornell and later of Germanic languages at Columbia.
He wrote tales of Norwegian life and verse, including the ballad "Thoralf and Synnöv".

poets.name: Digby Mackworth Dolben
bio: Digby Mackworth Dolben (1848–1867) was an English poet who died young by drowning. His poems were published after his death, edited by his cousin Robert Bridges.
The poems printed here are those given in The Oxford Book of English Mystical Verse (1917), edited by D. H. S. Nicholson and A. H. E. Lee; the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Edwin J. Ellis
bio: Edwin John Ellis (1848–1916) was a British poet and illustrator, remembered chiefly for the three-volume edition of the works of William Blake that he prepared with W. B. Yeats.
The poems printed here are those given in The Oxford Book of English Mystical Verse (1917), edited by D. H. S. Nicholson and A. H. E. Lee; the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Catherine C. Liddell
bio: Catherine C. Liddell, born Catherine C. Fraser-Tytler in 1848, married Edward Liddell. She published Songs in Minor Keys in 1881.
The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s A Victorian Anthology, 1837–1895 (1895).

poets.name: James Whitcomb Riley
poets.credit: Photograph of James Whitcomb Riley, 1913 (Library of Congress) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James Whitcomb Riley (1849–1916) was born in Greenfield, Indiana, and became the best-loved poet of the American Midwest, known as the “Hoosier Poet.” He worked as a sign painter and travelling performer before newspaper verse in Indiana dialect brought him a wide following, and he spent most of his later life in Indianapolis.

His most popular poems, such as “Little Orphant Annie” and “The Raggedy Man,” are written in rural Indiana speech and draw on childhood, farm life and storytelling. Riley toured widely as a reader of his own work, and Riley Child-Rhymes (1905), illustrated by Will Vawter, gathered many of his best-known verses for children.

poets.name: Francis Saltus Saltus
bio: Francis Saltus Saltus (1849–1889) was an American poet of New York, a younger brother of the novelist Edgar Saltus, whose verse draws on French and Oriental models.
The poems printed here are those given in Stedman's An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1900); the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: O. C. Auringer
bio: Obadiah Cyrus Auringer (born 1849) was an American clergyman and poet, born at Glens Falls, New York. He served in the United States Marine Corps from 1871 to 1875, farmed until 1889 and in 1890 was ordained a Presbyterian minister, becoming pastor of the Third Presbyterian Church of Troy, New York.
His volumes of poems include Scythe and Sword (1887) and The Heart of the Golden Rose (1891). Stedman included three of his poems in An American Anthology (1900), from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Elisabeth Cavazza Pullen
bio: Elisabeth Cavazza Pullen (1849–1926; née Jones, and published as Elisabeth Cavazza) was an American author and journalist who wrote verse, fiction and essays.
The poems printed here are those given in Stedman's An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1900); the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Eugene Field
poets.credit: Photograph of Eugene Field, c. 1890s (Library of Congress) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Eugene Field (1850–1895) was an American journalist and poet, born in St. Louis. He wrote a widely read newspaper column, first in Denver and then for the Chicago Daily News, and became known above all for his verses about children.

His best-loved poems, among them “Wynken, Blynken and Nod,” “Little Boy Blue” and “The Sugar-Plum Tree,” were gathered in With Trumpet and Drum (1892) and Love-Songs of Childhood (1894). The poems here follow the combined Poems of Childhood issued by Charles Scribner’s Sons in 1904.

poets.name: Emma Lazarus
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of Emma Lazarus (19th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Emma Lazarus (1849–1887) was an American poet and essayist, born in New York City to a prosperous Sephardic Jewish family. She published her first book of verse at seventeen, won the admiration and friendship of Ralph Waldo Emerson, and wrote narrative poems such as Admetus and Tannhauser before turning to lyric and sonnet forms.

From 1881, after the pogroms in Russia, she took up Jewish themes in poems such as The Banner of the Jew and The Crowing of the Red Cock, and worked on behalf of refugees. Her sonnet The New Colossus (1883), written for a fund-raising auction for the Statue of Liberty pedestal, is now inscribed there. She died in New York at the age of 38.

poets.name: Ella Wheeler Wilcox
poets.credit: Photograph of Ella Wheeler Wilcox (Library of Congress, LCCN 2014709802) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ella Wheeler Wilcox (1850–1919) was an American poet and journalist, born in Johnstown Center, Wisconsin. She began publishing verse as a girl and became one of the most widely read popular poets of her day, writing for newspapers and magazines as well as in book form.

Poems of Passion (1883), a collection of her love poems, drew a storm of public criticism for its frankness and, with it, a great many readers; Maurine and Other Poems appeared in 1888. Her best-known lines, such as “Laugh, and the world laughs with you” (from “Solitude”), became proverbial in English.

poets.name: Arthur Wentworth Hamilton Eaton
poets.credit: Portrait of Arthur Wentworth Hamilton Eaton, from Canadian Poets (1916) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Arthur Wentworth Hamilton Eaton (1849–1937), born in Kentville, Nova Scotia, was an Episcopal clergyman, historian and poet who spent much of his career in the United States.
He wrote on the history and legends of Acadia. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Laura E. Richards
poets.credit: Portrait of Laura E. Richards, photograph by Reynolds (before 1902) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Laura Elizabeth Howe Richards (1850–1943) was an American writer, the daughter of Julia Ward Howe, author of "The Battle Hymn of the Republic", and the physician and reformer Samuel Gridley Howe. She wrote many books for young readers, among them the verse collection In My Nursery (1890), which is dedicated to her mother.

With Maud Howe Elliott she won the 1917 Pulitzer Prize for Biography for a life of her mother. Her nonsense rhymes, with their coined words and rollicking rhythms, are among the best-loved comic verse for children in American writing; the best known, "Eletelephony", appeared in a later collection.

poets.name: E. W. Thomson
poets.credit: Portrait of Edward William Thomson, 1913 (Toronto Public Library) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward William Thomson (1849–1924) was a Canadian-born journalist and author who worked for many years in Boston.

He is best known for his short stories, such as Old Man Savarin and Other Stories (1895). One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Beverly Chew
bio: Beverly Chew (1850–1924) was an American book collector and bibliophile, born at Geneva, New York, and long resident in New York City.
His light verse "Old Books are Best", a rondeau in praise of old volumes, was widely reprinted in anthologies of the 1880s and after.

poets.name: Thomas Allibone Janvier
bio: Thomas Allibone Janvier (1849–1913) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Santiago”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Susan Marr Spalding
bio: Susan Marr Spalding was born at Bath, Maine, and educated at a young ladies’ seminary. After the death of her parents she went to live with relatives in New York, where she married, and a few years later she settled permanently in Philadelphia.
She published a volume of verse, The Wings of Icarus, and Other Poems (1892). Her birth and death dates are not given in the sources used here.

poets.name: Grace Denio Litchfield
bio: Grace Denio Litchfield (1849–1944) was an American novelist and poet, born in New York.
She is represented in Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900).

poets.name: George Augustus Baker
bio: George Augustus Baker (1849–1906) was born in New York City, graduated from the City College of New York and Columbia Law School, and practised as a lawyer.
His verse includes Point Lace and Diamonds (1875); he also wrote prose and a comedy.

poets.name: Edwin Markham
poets.credit: Portrait of Edwin Markham (portrait, 1919) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edwin Markham (1852–1940) was an American poet, born in Oregon City, Oregon, and raised in California, who later taught and lived in New York.
“The Man with the Hoe” (1899), written after seeing Millet’s painting, made him famous as a poet of social protest.

poets.name: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman
bio: Mary Eleanor Wilkins Freeman (1852–1930) was an American writer, born in Randolph, Massachusetts. She is known chiefly for her short stories and novels of New England village life, published first as Mary E. Wilkins and, after her marriage in 1902, under the name Freeman.
Her verse is slight beside her prose; the poem here appeared in Harper’s in 1890.

poets.name: C. E. S. Wood
poets.credit: Portrait of C. E. S. Wood (photograph, 1910) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: C. E. S. Wood (Charles Erskine Scott Wood, 1852–1944) was an American soldier, lawyer and writer, a West Point graduate who practised law in Portland, Oregon.
His long poem The Poet in the Desert (1915) is the best known of his verse.

poets.name: Maurice Francis Egan
bio: Maurice Francis Egan (1852–1924) was an American poet, critic and diplomat, born in Philadelphia. He taught English literature at Notre Dame and at the Catholic University of America and edited the New York Freeman’s Journal.
He served as United States Minister to Denmark from 1907 to 1918. His verse collections include Preludes (1880) and Songs and Sonnets (1892).

poets.name: Richard Edwin Day
bio: Richard Edwin Day (1852–1914) was an American poet and educator.
He is represented in Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900).

poets.name: Irwin Russell
bio: Irwin Russell (1853–1879) was an American poet from Port Gibson, Mississippi, who died at the age of twenty-six.
His “Christmas-Night in the Quarters” (1878) is often described as one of the earliest literary poems to use Black Southern dialect.

poets.name: Ben King
bio: Ben King (1857–1894) was an American humorist and reciter, born in Michigan, whose comic verse and parodies were widely recited at the end of the nineteenth century. His collected verse appeared as Ben King's Verse (1894).
If I Should Die To-night, a parody of a sentimental lyric, is his best-known piece.

poets.name: Katrina Trask
bio: Katrina Trask (née Nichols; 1853–1922), also known as Kate Nichols Trask, was an American author and philanthropist, and with her husband Spencer Trask the founder of the Yaddo estate at Saratoga Springs.
The four sonnets and short lyrics given here are those that Edmund Clarence Stedman printed under her name in An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900).

poets.name: Hall Caine
poets.credit: Photograph of Hall Caine (J. Willis Sayre Collection), 1922 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Thomas Henry Hall Caine (1853–1931) was a British novelist and playwright of Manx descent, born at Runcorn, Cheshire, whose best-known novels are The Deemster (1887) and The Manxman (1894). He edited Sonnets of Three Centuries (1882) and wrote little verse of his own.
Lyra Celtica prints his Manx ballad 'Graih my Chree' ('Love of my Heart').

poets.name: Robert Underwood Johnson
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Underwood Johnson · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Underwood Johnson (1853–1937) was an American writer, poet and diplomat.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “Dewey at Manila” and “To the Returning Brave”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Thomas Nelson Page
bio: Thomas Nelson Page (1853–1922) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “The Dragon of the Seas”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Katherine Miller
bio: Katherine (Wise) Miller (1853–1940) was an American poet, born at Spezia, Italy, the daughter of Commodore Henry A. Wise of the United States Navy and the wife of Commodore J. W. Miller of the naval reserve.
Her poem "Stevenson's Birthday" is based on an actual occurrence, and was included in Stedman's An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Richard Kendall Munkittrick
bio: Richard Kendall Munkittrick (1853–1911) was a humorist and poet who spent most of his life in the United States and worked on the staff of the New York weekly Judge, which he edited from about 1901 to 1906.
He wrote light verse for Judge and other magazines, including the verses that accompanied “Bugville Life”; his nature epigrams such as “A Bulb” were taken up by anthologists.

poets.name: William Cranston Lawton
bio: William Cranston Lawton (1853–1941) was an American classical scholar and poet.
He is represented in Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900).

poets.name: Julia Neely Finch
bio: Julia Neely Finch (1853–1926) was an American musician and composer of Birmingham, Alabama, born in Mobile.
Her poem "The Unborn", on motherhood, first appeared in an Atlanta periodical and was reprinted in Stedman's An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Katherine Eleanor Conway
bio: Katherine Eleanor Conway (1853–1927) was an American Catholic poet and journalist, long associated with the Boston Pilot.
She is represented in Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900).

poets.name: Edith M. Thomas
poets.credit: Portrait of Edith M. Thomas (photograph, 1890) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edith M. Thomas (1854–1925) was an American poet, born in Chatham, Ohio, who lived chiefly in New York City.
Her books of verse include A New Year’s Masque (1885) and The Inverted Torch (1890).

poets.name: Samuel Minturn Peck
bio: Samuel Minturn Peck (1854–1938) was an American poet born in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, who wrote graceful society verse and Southern lyrics. His books include Cap and Bells (1886) and Rings and Love-Knots (1892).
He was named poet laureate of Alabama in 1930.

poets.name: Danske Dandridge
bio: Danske Dandridge (1854–1914), born Danske Bedinger in Copenhagen, Denmark, was an American poet. In 1877 she married Stephen Dandridge, and she lived for many years at Shepherdstown, West Virginia.
Her books of verse were Joy, and Other Poems (1888) and Rose Brake (1890).

poets.name: Isabella Valancy Crawford
poets.credit: Portrait of Isabella Valancy Crawford, reproduced in E. S. Caswell, Canadian Singers and Their Songs (c. 1919) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Isabella Valancy Crawford (1850–1887) was born in Dublin and raised in Ontario, and supported herself and her family by writing poems and stories for periodicals.

Her only book in her lifetime was Old Spookses' Pass, Malcolm's Katie, and Other Poems (1884), which brought her little notice until after her death. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Arthur John Lockhart
bio: Arthur John Lockhart (1850–1926) was a Canadian clergyman and poet.
His poems here come partly from his Masque of Minstrels (1887). One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Francis Marion Crawford
poets.credit: Portrait of Francis Marion Crawford · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Francis Marion Crawford (1854–1909) was an American novelist.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “New National Hymn”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: George Houghton
bio: George Washington Wright Houghton (1850–1891) was an American poet, born at Cambridge, Massachusetts, and died at Yonkers, New York. He lived in New York, where he edited a trade paper.

His books of verse include Songs from over the Sea (1874), The Legend of St. Olaf's Kirk (1880) and Niagara and Other Poems (1882). Stedman included three of his poems in An American Anthology (1900), from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Charles Leonard Moore
bio: Charles Leonard Moore (1854–1923) was an American poet and lawyer, based in Philadelphia, author of The Book of Day-Dreams (1892).
He is represented in Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900).

poets.name: George Edward Woodberry
poets.credit: Portrait of George Edward Woodberry (photograph by Hollinger, by 1903) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Edward Woodberry (1855–1930) was an American poet, critic and scholar, born in Beverly, Massachusetts, and a professor of comparative literature at Columbia University.
His verse includes The North Shore Watch (1890) and Wild Eden (1899).

poets.name: H. C. Bunner
poets.credit: Portrait of H. C. Bunner (portrait, 1899) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: H. C. Bunner (Henry Cuyler Bunner, 1855–1896) was an American writer, born in Oswego, New York, who edited the humorous weekly Puck from 1877 until his death.
He was a master of light and occasional verse, collected in volumes such as Airs from Arcady and Elsewhere (1884).

poets.name: Wilbur Larremore
bio: Wilbur Larremore was an American lawyer and poet, born in New York City in 1855, editor of the New York Law Journal from 1890 and author of the verse volume Mother Carey’s Chickens (1888).
He is represented in Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900).

poets.name: Lucy White Jennison
bio: Lucy White Jennison (born 1850), who wrote under the pseudonym Owen Innsley, was an American poet, born at Newton, Massachusetts, and educated in Boston. She lived for many years in Italy.
She published Love Poems and Sonnets (1882). Stedman included three of her poems in An American Anthology (1900), from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Florence Earle Coates
poets.credit: Photograph of Florence Earle Coates (before 1912) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Florence Earle Coates (1850–1927) was an American poet, born in Philadelphia and educated at private schools there and in Europe. She was a prominent member of the Philadelphia literary world and was known for her devotional and patriotic poems.
Her volumes include Poems (1898), Mine and Thine (1904), Lyrics of Life (1909) and The Unconquered Air (1912); a two-volume collected Poems appeared in 1916.

poets.name: Louis James Block
bio: Louis James Block (1851–1928) was an American poet and critic who lived in Chicago. He published Dramatic Sketches and Poems (1891) and lectured on literature, and took part in the literary congresses held at the Chicago World’s Fair of 1893.
His verse ranges from sonnets on books and work to free-verse pieces such as “Tuberose,” and several of his poems appeared in Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Rose Hawthorne Lathrop
