bio: Rose Hawthorne Lathrop (1851–1926) was the youngest child of Nathaniel Hawthorne. She married the poet George Parsons Lathrop in 1871 and published verse (Along the Shore, 1888) and prose before turning to charity.
After her husband’s death she became a nurse to the poor dying of cancer, and as Mother Mary Alphonsa founded the Dominican Congregation of St. Rose of Lima (the Hawthorne Dominicans).

poets.name: Ellen Mackay Hutchinson Cortissoz
bio: Ellen Mackay Hutchinson Cortissoz (1851–1933) was an American poet, journalist and editor, born in Caledonia, New York. She joined the staff of the New York Tribune, where she looked after the literary department of its Sunday supplement.

With Edmund Clarence Stedman she edited A Library of American Literature (1888–90). She published Songs and Lyrics in 1881, and her ballads and lyrics with colonial and eighteenth-century settings were much admired. She married the art critic Royal Cortissoz.

poets.name: Arlo Bates
poets.credit: Portrait: published by L C Page and company Boston 1903 — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Arlo Bates (1850–1918) was an American novelist, poet and teacher, born at East Machias, Maine, and educated at Bowdoin College. He edited the Boston Sunday Courier from 1880 and later became professor of English literature at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
His verse includes Berries of the Brier (1886), Sonnets in Shadow (1887), A Poet and His Self (1891), Told in the Gate (1892) and The Torch-Bearers (1894).

poets.name: George Parsons Lathrop
poets.credit: Portrait: Unknown authorUnknown author — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Parsons Lathrop (1851–1898) was an American poet, novelist and editor, and the son-in-law of Nathaniel Hawthorne.

The poems here are taken from American War Ballads and Lyrics, edited by George Cary Eggleston (New York and London: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1889), where it is printed under his or her name: Keenan’s Charge.

poets.name: Robert Burns Wilson
poets.credit: Portrait: uncredited — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Burns Wilson (1850–1916) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “Battle Song” and “"Cut the Cables"”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Arthur Peterson
bio: Arthur Peterson (1851–1932) was an American poet, born in Philadelphia, the son of the editor and poet Henry Peterson. He published Sigurd (1910) and Andvari’s Ring (1916).
The poem printed here is taken from An American Anthology, 1787–1900, edited by Edmund Clarence Stedman (1900).

poets.name: David Starr Jordan
bio: David Starr Jordan (1851–1931) was an American ichthyologist, educator and writer, born in Gainesville, New York, and the first president of Stanford University.
The poem printed here is taken from An American Anthology, 1787–1900, edited by Edmund Clarence Stedman (1900).

poets.name: Lizette Woodworth Reese
poets.credit: Portrait of Lizette Woodworth Reese (portrait from A Woman of the Century (1893)) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Lizette Woodworth Reese (1856–1935) was an American poet, born near Baltimore, Maryland, who taught English in Baltimore schools for many years.
Her first book, A Branch of May (1887), began a long career of spare, finely made lyrics, among them the sonnet “Tears”.

poets.name: Mariana Griswold Van Rensselaer
bio: Mariana Griswold Van Rensselaer (1851–1934), also known as Mrs. Schuyler Van Rensselaer, was an American writer on art and architecture, born in New York. She is best remembered for her study Henry Hobson Richardson and His Works (1888) and for Art Out-of-Doors (1893).
She also wrote occasional verse; her lyric "Love's Prisoner" is printed in The Home Book of Verse (1912).

poets.name: Bertram Mitford
bio: Bertram Mitford (1855–1914) is one of the named contributors to The Poetry of South Africa, collected and arranged by A. Wilmot (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle & Rivington; Cape Town: J. C. Juta & Co., 1887), an anthology of verse from the Cape Colony, Natal and the Transvaal.

This archive holds 1 poem printed under this name in that volume, in Wilmot’s spelling. Wilmot prints his poem on the defence of Rorke’s Drift (22-23 January 1879). Dates are those of a standard reference.

poets.name: Benjamin Copeland
bio: Benjamin Copeland (1855–1940) was a Methodist Episcopal minister in western New York, and the author of pastoral and devotional verse. He wrote hymn-like pieces for the church year, nature lyrics, and occasional poems on public figures and events.

The poems here come from two of his books: Poems: Pastoral and Psalm (New York: Eaton & Mains, 1896) and Niagara, and Other Poems (Buffalo: Matthews-Northrup, 1904). Where a poem appears in both, the 1904 text is given.

poets.name: Oscar Fay Adams
bio: Oscar Fay Adams (1855–1919) was born in Worcester, Massachusetts. He lectured to classes on English literature and history and on Gothic architecture.

He is remembered for his Dictionary of American Authors (first published 1884, and much enlarged in later editions), and he also wrote Post-Laureate Idyls (1886) and a volume of stories, The Archbishop's Unguarded Moment (1899).

poets.name: Daniel Lewis Dawson
bio: Daniel Lewis Dawson (1855–1893) was born at Lewistown, Pennsylvania, attended La Salle College and completed his studies privately, and died at Philadelphia.
A posthumous collection, The Seeker in the Marshes, and Other Poems, appeared in 1893.

poets.name: William De Lancey Ellwanger
bio: William De Lancey Ellwanger (1855–1913) was born in Rochester, New York, studied at Yale and Albany Law School, and practised as a lawyer in Rochester.
He published verse, including A Summer Snowflake and Drift of Other Verse and Song (1902), and a book on oriental rugs.

poets.name: Armistead Churchill Gordon
bio: Armistead Churchill Gordon (1855–1931) was born in Albemarle County, Virginia, graduated from the University of Virginia and became a lawyer, later mayor of Staunton.
With Thomas Nelson Page he published Befo’ de War (1888), poems in negro dialect, and he wrote further verse including For Truth and Freedom (1898).

poets.name: Francis Barton Gummere
bio: Francis Barton Gummere (1855–1919) was born at Burlington, New Jersey, studied at Haverford College, Harvard and Freiburg, and from 1887 was professor of English at Haverford College.
He is best known as a scholar: The Anglo-Saxon Metaphor (1881), A Handbook of Poetics (1885) and Germanic Origins (1892).

poets.name: Annie Raymond Stillman
bio: Annie Raymond Stillman (1855–1922), who wrote as “Grace Raymond”, was born at Charleston, South Carolina, of Huguenot descent, and later lived in Birmingham, Alabama.
She wrote How They Kept the Faith (1889), a tale of the Huguenots of Languedoc, and occasional poems.

poets.name: May Probyn
bio: May Probyn (1856–1909) was an English poet whose verse appeared in the magazines and anthologies of the 1880s and 1890s.
Two of her poems, “Sudden Death” and a villanelle, are included in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: James Ernest Nesmith
bio: James Ernest Nesmith was an American artist and poet, born in Massachusetts in 1856, who lived in Lowell and died in 1898.
He published Monadnoc, and Other Sketches in Verse (1888) and Philoctetes, and Other Poems and Sonnets (1894).

poets.name: Fiona Macleod (William Sharp)
poets.credit: Photograph of William Sharp (Fiona Macleod) by Frederick Hollyer, 1894 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Sharp (1855–1905), born in Paisley, was a Scottish writer who published under his own name and, from 1893, under the woman's name 'Fiona Macleod', whose Celtic romances and lyrics (Pharais, 1894; The Mountain Lovers, 1895; The Sin-Eater, 1895) made her a leading voice of the Celtic Twilight. Who was behind the pen name was kept secret until his death in Sicily in 1905.
Sharp also wrote the Introduction to Lyra Celtica, which his wife, Elizabeth A. Sharp, edited. The seven poems here are those the anthology prints as Fiona Macleod's.

poets.name: Ernest Howard Crosby
bio: Ernest Howard Crosby (1856–1906) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “"Rebels"”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: James Berry Bensel
bio: James Berry Bensel was born in New York in 1856 and died there in 1886; much of his life was passed at Lynn, Massachusetts, where ill health hindered his literary work.
He wrote the novel King Kophetua’s Wife (1883) and the verse collection In the King’s Garden, and Other Poems (1885).

poets.name: William Hamilton Hayne
poets.credit: Portrait: Maurice Garland Fulton — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Hamilton Hayne (1856–1929) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “The Charge at Santiago”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Harrison Smith Morris
bio: Harrison Smith Morris (1856–1948) was an American poet, editor and arts administrator, born in Philadelphia. He was managing editor of Lippincott's Magazine and for many years managing director of the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts.
He knew Walt Whitman in the poet's last years and wrote of him. Stedman's An American Anthology (1900) printed his sonnet to Whitman and his poem "Destiny" (1899), among others.

poets.name: Frank Lebby Stanton
bio: Frank Lebby Stanton (1857–1927) was an American poet and newspaper columnist, born in Charleston, South Carolina, who worked for many years on the Atlanta Constitution, where his daily column of verse made him widely read in the South.

His books include Songs of the Soil (1892) and Up from Georgia (1902); he wrote in both literary English and Southern dialect, and “Mother” and “Just a Wearyin’ for You” were widely set to music. He was named poet laureate of Georgia in 1925.

poets.name: Horace Traubel
bio: Horace Traubel (1858–1919) was an American poet and editor, born in Camden, New Jersey, and a close friend and disciple of Walt Whitman.
He recorded Whitman’s last years in With Walt Whitman in Camden and edited the monthly The Conservator.

poets.name: William Morton Payne
bio: William Morton Payne (1858–1919) was an American educator, literary critic and writer, born at Newburyport, Massachusetts.

The four sonnets given here are those that Edmund Clarence Stedman printed under his name in An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900): two on the Wagner operas Tannhäuser and Lohengrin, one on the theatre, and one on the spring.

poets.name: Sam Walter Foss
bio: Sam Walter Foss was an American humorist and poet, born in Candia, New Hampshire, in 1858 and educated at Brown University.
He became librarian of the Somerville Public Library in 1898; his books include Back Country Poems (1892), Whiffs from Wild Meadows (1896) and Dreams in Homespun (1898).

poets.name: Constance Naden
bio: Constance Caroline Woodhill Naden (1858–1889) was born in Birmingham, studied science at Mason College, and wrote philosophical essays as well as verse. Her collections are Songs and Sonnets of Springtime (1881) and A Modern Apostle (1887).
Her poems often take evolution and the new science as subjects, sometimes with wit. She died at thirty. Two of her poems appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: E. Nesbit
poets.credit: Photograph of E. Nesbit · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edith Nesbit (1858–1924), who published verse as E. Nesbit, is best remembered today as the author of children's classics such as Five Children and It (1902) and The Railway Children (1906). She was a founder member of the Fabian Society.
Her early poems were collected in Lays and Legends (1886; second series 1892). Two of her poems appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Charles Francis Richardson
bio: Charles Francis Richardson (1851–1913) was an American critic and poet, born at Hallowell, Maine. He graduated at Dartmouth College, where he became professor of English literature in 1882, having served on the staff of the Independent from 1872 to 1878.

His books include a Primer of American Literature (1878), the verse collection The Cross (1879) and a two-volume History of American Literature (1887–89). Stedman included three of his poems in An American Anthology (1900), from which the poems here are taken.

poets.name: Nathan Haskell Dole
bio: Nathan Haskell Dole (1852–1935), born at Chelsea, Massachusetts, was a man of letters. He graduated from Harvard in 1874, taught at Derby Academy in Hingham, and worked as a critic for the Philadelphia Press and as editor of the New York Epoch.

He was an active translator, edited a twenty-volume edition of Tolstoy’s works and a multivariorum edition of the Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám (1896), and published a volume of verse, The Hawthorne Tree, and Other Poems (1895).

poets.name: Iwan Gilkin
poets.credit: Portrait photograph of Iwan Gilkin · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Iwan Gilkin (1858–1924) was a Belgian poet born in Brussels and associated with the Symbolist school in Belgium.
Jethro Bithell's 1911 anthology classes him as a Walloon with a Flemish mother and names him among the chief Parnassians, noting that his later Prométhée is nevertheless in free verse.

poets.name: John Eliot Bowen
bio: John Eliot Bowen (1858–1890) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “The Man Who Rode to Conemaugh”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Duffield Osborne
bio: Duffield Osborne was an American lawyer, novelist and poet, born in Brooklyn in 1858 and educated at Columbia College.
He wrote the historical romances The Spell of Ashtaroth (1888) and The Robe of Nessus (1890), and contributed verse to magazines.

poets.name: James Benjamin Kenyon
bio: James Benjamin Kenyon (1858–1924) was an American poet and clergyman of New York State.
The poems printed here are those given in Stedman's An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1900); the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Joseph B. Gilder
bio: Joseph B. Gilder (1858–1936) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “The Parting of the Ways”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Joseph Ernest Whitney
bio: Joseph Ernest Whitney was born in Cornwall, Connecticut, in 1858 and died in Colorado Springs in 1893. He graduated from Yale and was appointed instructor in English there in 1884, resigning in 1888 through ill health.
He was joint editor, with Henry S. Durand, of Elm Leaves, a collection of Yale verse.

poets.name: Robert Crewe-Milnes, Marquess of Crewe
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Robert Crewe-Milnes, first Marquess of Crewe (1858–1945), was a British Liberal politician, statesman and writer.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Sir James Rennell Rodd
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir James Rennell Rodd, later first Baron Rennell (1858–1941), was a British diplomat, poet and politician who served as Ambassador to Italy during the First World War.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: William Lindsey
bio: William Lindsey (1858–1922) was born in Fall River, Massachusetts, and was educated in the schools of that city. He entered business in 1877 and moved to Boston in 1888.
His verse was collected in Apples of Istakhar (1895); he also published fiction, At Start and Finish (1900). Edmund Clarence Stedman included two of his poems in An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: George Pellew
bio: George Pellew (1859–1892) was an American writer and poet. His verse was gathered after his early death in Poems of George Pellew (1892), edited by William Dean Howells.

poets.name: Clarence Urmy
bio: Clarence Urmy (1858–1923) was a California poet.
He is represented in Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900).

poets.name: Frank Dempster Sherman
poets.credit: Portrait of Frank Dempster Sherman (photograph by Bain News Service, 1900) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Frank Dempster Sherman (1860–1917) was an American poet and professor of graphics at Columbia University, born in Peekskill, New York.
His delicate, finely finished short lyrics were collected in volumes such as Madrigals and Catches (1887).

poets.name: Randall Parrish
poets.credit: Portrait of Randall Parrish · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Randall Parrish (1858–1923) was an American novelist.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Your Lad, and My Lad”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
poets.credit: Portrait of Charlotte Perkins Gilman (photograph by Charles Fletcher Lummis, c. 1900) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charlotte Perkins Gilman (1860–1935) was an American writer and lecturer on women’s rights and social reform, born in Hartford, Connecticut.
She is best known for Women and Economics (1898) and the story “The Yellow Wall-Paper”, and she also published satirical verse in In This Our World (1893).

poets.name: Edmond Holmes
bio: Edmond Gore Alexander Holmes (1850–1936) was an Anglo-Irish educationalist, writer and poet, an inspector of schools whose writings turned towards Eastern thought and mysticism.
The poems printed here are those given in The Oxford Book of English Mystical Verse (1917), edited by D. H. S. Nicholson and A. H. E. Lee; the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Frederika Richardson Macdonald
bio: Frederika Richardson Macdonald was a writer of the Victorian period, author of the novel Nathaniel Vaughan, Priest and Man (1874) and of Puck and Pearl, an account of the wanderings of two English children in India (1886).

poets.name: John Arthur Goodchild
bio: John Arthur Goodchild (born 1851) was an English physician and poet, educated at St George's Hospital, who practised in Ealing and later for many years at Bordighera in Italy.
His verse includes three series of Somnia Medici (the first in 1884) and Lyrics and Tales in Verse (1893).

poets.name: Percy Russell
bio: Percy Russell was an Australian journalist and poet who settled in London. He published King Alfred and Other Poems (1880) and My Strange Wife (1886).

poets.name: Harry Bache Smith
bio: Harry Bache Smith (1860–1936) was an American librettist and lyricist, born in Buffalo, New York.
He wrote the words for some three hundred comic operas and musical comedies, among them Robin Hood (1890), and also published occasional verse.

poets.name: Albert Giraud
poets.credit: Portrait: Unknown authorUnknown author — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Albert Giraud (born Marie Émile Albert Kayenbergh at Louvain, 23 June 1860; died Schaerbeek, 26 December 1929) was a Belgian Symbolist poet writing in French.
Jethro Bithell's 1911 anthology classes him as a Fleming and names him first among the chief Parnassians, those who cling to the traditional forms of French verse.

poets.name: George Meason Whicher
bio: George Meason Whicher was an American classical scholar and poet, born in Muscatine, Iowa, in 1860 and educated at Iowa College.
He was professor of classical languages at the Normal College of the City of New York, edited Greek and Latin school texts, and contributed essays and verse to periodicals.

poets.name: John Langdon Heaton
bio: John Langdon Heaton was an American journalist and writer, born in 1860 and a graduate of St. Lawrence University (1880).
His books include Stories of Napoleon (1895) and the verse collection The Quilting Bee, and Other Poems (1896).

poets.name: William Wilfred Campbell
poets.credit: Portrait of William Wilfred Campbell, from Canadian Poets (1916) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Wilfred Campbell (1860–1918), born at Newmarket, Ontario, was an Anglican clergyman who later became a civil servant and one of the Confederation poets.
His Lake Lyrics and Other Poems appeared in 1889. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Harriet Monroe
bio: Harriet Monroe (1860–1936), born in Chicago, was an American poet, critic and editor. She wrote the Columbian Ode, read at the dedication of the World’s Columbian Exposition on 21 October 1892, and in 1912 founded Poetry: A Magazine of Verse, which she edited until her death.

The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1900) and, for the Columbian Ode, from the edition published in Chicago in 1893.

poets.name: Harry Lyman Koopman
bio: Harry Lyman Koopman (1860–1937), born in Freeport, Maine, was an American librarian and poet. A graduate of Colby College, he became librarian of Brown University in 1893, and his verse appeared in Orestes, and Other Poems (1888), Woman’s Will, with Other Poems (1888) and Morrow-Songs (1898).
The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1900).

poets.name: John Elton Wayland
bio: John Elton Wayland, who wrote verse under the pen name “Idas”, was an American lawyer born in Waterbury, Connecticut, in 1860; he graduated from Yale in 1883 and from the Columbia Law School in 1895.
His poem An Epilogue at Wallack’s, written for the Yale Courant in 1882, honours the actor John Gilbert.

poets.name: Louise Imogen Guiney
poets.credit: Portrait of Louise Imogen Guiney (photograph, before 1894) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Louise Imogen Guiney (1861–1920) was an American poet and essayist, born in Boston, who spent her later years in England.
Her poems appeared in volumes such as Songs at the Start (1884) and A Roadside Harp (1893).

poets.name: Mary Augusta Mason
bio: Mary Augusta Mason, born in Windsor, New York, in 1861, was an American poet, author of With the Seasons.
She is represented in Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900).

poets.name: Sophie Jewett
bio: Sophie Jewett (1861–1909), born in Moravia, New York, was an American poet and teacher who also wrote under the name Ellen Burroughs. From 1889 she taught at Wellesley College, where she became associate professor of English literature, and her verse was collected in The Pilgrim, and Other Poems (1896).
The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1900).

poets.name: Virginia Woodward Cloud
bio: Virginia Woodward Cloud (1861–1938) was an American writer and poet.
The four lyrics given here are those that Edmund Clarence Stedman printed under her name in An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900).

poets.name: Hannah Parker Kimball
bio: Hannah Parker Kimball (born 1861) was an American poet, born in Boston.
Her volumes of verse include The Cup of Life (1892), Soul and Sense (1896) and Victory, and Other Poems (1897).

poets.name: Edmund Beale Sargant
bio: Edmund Beale Sargant (1861–1938) was an English educational administrator and poet.
His poem “The Cuckoo Wood” was printed in Georgian Poetry 1911–1912.

poets.name: Van Tassel Sutphen
bio: William Gilbert Van Tassel Sutphen (1861–1945) was an American editor, novelist, playwright and librettist, born in Philadelphia and a graduate of Princeton. He wrote under the name Van Tassel Sutphen.
His poem "Deep Waters" was included in Stedman's An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Bliss Carman
poets.credit: Portrait of Bliss Carman (photograph by Pirie MacDonald, 1903) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Bliss Carman (1861–1929) was a Canadian-born poet, born in Fredericton, New Brunswick, who spent much of his career in the United States.
With Richard Hovey he wrote the vagabond lyrics of Songs from Vagabondia (1894).

poets.name: Lucy Catlin Bull Robinson
bio: Lucy Catlin Bull Robinson (1861–1903) was an American poet, born in Hartford, Connecticut. As a child she published A Child's Poems, written in her tenth year.
She lived in New York from 1891, and in 1899 married the poet Tracy Robinson of Colón, Panama.

poets.name: Albert Bigelow Paine
bio: Albert Bigelow Paine (1861–1937) was born in New Bedford, Massachusetts, and was raised in Illinois. He worked in business in the West before his fiction and verse led him to settle in New York, where he joined the staff of St. Nicholas in 1899.
He published Rhymes by Two Friends (1893, with William Allen White), the fiction The Arkansaw Bear (1898) and The Bread Line (1900), and later became best known as the biographer of Mark Twain.

poets.name: Thomas Fleming Day
bio: Thomas Fleming Day, born in Weston-super-Mare, Somerset, in 1861, went to the United States as a child in 1868. He was the son of a professor of natural science at the Normal College, New York.
From 1895 he edited the yachting monthly The Rudder; his verse includes Songs of Sea and Sail, and “The Coasters” was printed in Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Charles Van Lerberghe
poets.credit: Photograph of Charles Van Lerberghe for Entrevisions, 1898 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Van Lerberghe (1861–1907) was a Belgian poet and playwright who wrote in French and is particularly identified with the Symbolist movement.
Jethro Bithell's 1911 anthology classes him as a Fleming, and notes that although he condemned free verse in a letter of 1905, his own work is a monument to its practicability.

poets.name: Jean Blewett
poets.credit: Portrait of Jean Blewett, from a book illustration, c. 1896 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Jean Blewett (born Jean McKishnie, 1862–1934) was a Canadian poet and journalist who wrote for the Toronto press and was widely read in Canada in her day.
Her verse, much of it in Scots and rural dialect, was gathered in Heart Songs (Toronto, 1897) and The Cornflower, and Other Poems (Toronto, 1906), both given here.

poets.name: Anna M. Pratt
bio: Anna Maria Pratt, born in Chelsea, Massachusetts, taught for some years in Cleveland, Ohio, and wrote verse for children, collected in Little Rhymes for Little People (1896).
She is represented in Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900).

poets.name: Grace Ellery Channing-Stetson
bio: Grace Ellery Channing (1862–1937), who as a married woman signed herself Grace Ellery Channing-Stetson, was an American writer and poet; her verse appeared often in The Land of Sunshine. She married the painter Charles Walter Stetson in 1894.
The four poems given here are those that Edmund Clarence Stedman printed under her name in An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900).

poets.name: Carolyn Wells
poets.credit: Portrait of Carolyn Wells (photograph, no later than 1904, from The Critic) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Carolyn Wells (1862–1942) was an American writer born in Rahway, New Jersey. She published a very large body of work, including detective novels, children’s books, anthologies and humorous verse, and was among the best-known American writers of nonsense and light verse in the early twentieth century.

The poems gathered here come from six books of her light verse: The Jingle Book (1899), illustrated by Oliver Herford; A Phenomenal Fauna (1901–02); Children of Our Town (1902); At the Sign of the Sphinx, Second Series (1906), a collection of verse riddles and charades; The Seven Ages of Childhood (1909); and The Re-echo Club (1913), a set of parodies of famous poets.

poets.name: Langdon Elwyn Mitchell
bio: Langdon Elwyn Mitchell (1862–1935), born in Philadelphia, was an American poet and playwright, the son of the physician and writer S. Weir Mitchell. His first book of verse, Sylvian, a Tragedy, and Poems (1885), appeared under the pen name John Philip Varley; his Poems followed in 1894, and he later wrote for the stage, notably The New York Idea (1906).

The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1900) and, for “To a Writer of the Day”, from his Poems (1894).

poets.name: John Kendrick Bangs
bio: John Kendrick Bangs (1862–1922) was an American humorist, editor and writer, born in Yonkers, New York.
He is best known for the comic fantasy A House-Boat on the Styx (1895), and also wrote light and occasional verse.

poets.name: Alice Learned Bunner
bio: Alice Learned Bunner, born in New London, Connecticut, in the 1860s, was the sister of Walter Learned and the wife of the journalist and poet H. C. Bunner, whom she married in 1880.
She contributed poems and sketches to periodicals; her sequence of two short poems, Vingtaine, was included in Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Ella Higginson
bio: Ella Higginson (1862–1940), born Ella Rhoads in Council Grove, Kansas, was an American poet and short-story writer who lived in Bellingham, Washington, and wrote of the Pacific Northwest. Her books of verse include When the Birds Go North Again (1898).
The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1900).

poets.name: Edith Wharton
bio: Edith Wharton (1862–1937) was an American novelist and writer, born Edith Jones in New York. She won the Pulitzer Prize for The Age of Innocence (1920).
She also wrote verse, collected in Artemis to Actaeon and Other Verse (1909) and Twelve Poems (1926); the sonnets "Experience" were printed in Stedman's An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Richard Burton
bio: Richard Burton (1861–1940) was an American poet, critic and teacher, born in Hartford, Connecticut, who taught English at the University of Minnesota.
His volumes of verse include Dumb in June (1895) and Lyrics of Brotherhood (1899).

poets.name: John S. McGroarty
bio: John Steven McGroarty (1862–1944) was an American journalist, poet and politician, born in Pennsylvania, who made his home in southern California. He wrote The Mission Play (1912) and served in the United States Congress in the 1930s.
His verse in the Home Book of Verse (1912) includes the soldiers' memorial lyric Blow, Bugles, Blow and the sailor's song The Port o' Heart's Desire.

poets.name: May Kendall
bio: May Kendall (1861–1943), born Emma Goldworth Kendall, was an English poet and novelist who wrote witty verse on science and modern life. Her books include That Very Mab (1885, with Andrew Lang) and Dreams to Sell (1887).
Her humorous poems on evolution, geology and the education of women made her popular in the 1880s. Two of them appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Mary C. Gillington
bio: Mary Clarissa Gillington (1861–1936) was an English poet, sister of the poet Alice E. Gillington.
Two of her poems, “A Dead March” and “The Home Coming”, appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Margaret L. Woods
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Margaret Louisa Woods (1855–1945), née Bradley, was an English writer known for her novels and for her lyrical and socially conscious poetry.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Henry van Dyke
poets.credit: Photograph of Henry van Dyke by Harris & Ewing (before 1918) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry van Dyke (1852–1933) was an American clergyman, professor and poet, born at Germantown, Pennsylvania. He was a Presbyterian minister in New York, a professor of English literature at Princeton, and United States minister to the Netherlands and Luxembourg from 1913 to 1916.
He wrote many volumes of verse and essays, and the story The Other Wise Man (1895). His nature lyrics on American birds were among his most anthologised poems.

poets.name: Brander Matthews
bio: Brander Matthews (1852–1929) was born in New Orleans and became professor of dramatic literature at Columbia University.
A critic, essayist and novelist, he also wrote light verse.

poets.name: Charles Henry Phelps
bio: Charles Henry Phelps was born at Stockton, California, in 1853, of the Phelps family of eastern Massachusetts. He was educated at the University of California and the Harvard Law School, and practised law in San Francisco.
He edited The Californian (afterwards the Overland Monthly) in 1880–82 and published Californian Verses (1882). He later became a leading member of the New York bar and an authority on copyright law.

poets.name: Craven Langstroth Betts
bio: Craven Langstroth Betts (1853–1941) was born at St. John, New Brunswick, of Loyalist descent, and educated in his native city. From 1879 he lived in New York, engaged in literary work.
His books include Songs from Béranger, translations (1888), The Perfume Holder: a Persian Love Poem (1892), Tales of a Garrison Town, written with A. W. Eaton (1892), and A Garland of Sonnets (1899).

poets.name: John Oxenham
bio: John Oxenham was the pen name of William Arthur Dunkerley (1852–1941), an English journalist, novelist and poet, born in Manchester. His devotional verse was widely read, notably in the collection Bees in Amber (1913).
The poems printed here are those given in The Oxford Book of English Mystical Verse (1917), edited by D. H. S. Nicholson and A. H. E. Lee; the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Ernest Francisco Fenollosa
bio: Ernest Francisco Fenollosa (1853–1908) was an American orientalist and art historian, born in Salem, Massachusetts, and a graduate of Harvard, who taught in Japan. He was the husband of the poet Mary McNeil Fenollosa.
The poem printed here is taken from An American Anthology, 1787–1900, edited by Edmund Clarence Stedman (1900).

poets.name: George Tracy Elliot
bio: George Tracy Elliot was born in Mason, New Hampshire, in 1853, and was educated at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. From 1884 he worked as a corrector at the Riverside Press, Cambridge, Massachusetts.
The poem printed here is taken from An American Anthology, 1787–1900, edited by Edmund Clarence Stedman (1900).

poets.name: Maybury Fleming
bio: Maybury Fleming, born at Boston, Massachusetts, in 1853, was a journalist. He was educated at the University of New York and joined the editorial staff of the New York Mail and Express.
He contributed verse to the magazines; Edmund Clarence Stedman included three of his poems in An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Homer Greene
bio: Homer Greene (1853–1940) was an American lawyer and author, born in Pennsylvania, who wrote novels for young readers and a popular poem, "What My Lover Said".
The poem printed here is taken from An American Anthology, 1787–1900, edited by Edmund Clarence Stedman (1900).

poets.name: William Henry Drummond
poets.credit: Portrait: unknown artist — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Henry Drummond (1854–1907) was born in Ireland and brought up in Canada, and practised medicine in Montreal. He became famous for his verse in the English of the French-Canadian country people, collected in The Habitant (1897), Johnnie Courteau (1901) and later volumes.
The poems given here are taken from The Oxford Book of Canadian Verse, chosen by Wilfred Campbell (Toronto: Oxford University Press, 1913).

poets.name: Charles Lotin Hildreth
bio: Charles Lotin Hildreth (1857–1896) was born in New York and worked as a journalist, writing for the New York World from 1883 and afterwards for Belford’s Magazine.
He published a novel, Judith (1876), a book of stories, The New Symphony (1878), and a volume of verse, The Masque of Death, and Other Poems (1889).

poets.name: Edward Sanford Martin
bio: Edward Sanford Martin (1856–1939) was born at Willowbrook, on Owasco Lake, New York, and graduated from Harvard. He edited the humorous weekly Life at its start in 1883.
His verse was collected in A Little Brother of the Rich (1888). He later wrote a department, This Busy World, for Harper’s Weekly.

poets.name: Harry Thurston Peck
bio: Harry Thurston Peck (1856–1914) was born at Stamford, Connecticut, graduated from Columbia, and became professor of Latin there. From 1895 he was American editor of The Bookman and was also literary editor of the New York Commercial Advertiser.
His books include The Semitic Theory of Creation (1886), Latin Pronunciation (1890), The Personal Equation (1897), What Is Good English? (1899) and a volume of verse, Greystone and Porphyry (1900).

poets.name: Andrew Bice Saxton
bio: Andrew Bice Saxton (born 1856) was born at Middlefield, New York, and graduated from Hartwick Seminary.
He worked as a farmer and teacher, and from 1890 as an editor on the Herald of Oneonta, New York.

poets.name: Ernest McGaffey
bio: Ernest McGaffey (1861–1941) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “Little Big Horn” and “Geronimo”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Max Elskamp
poets.credit: Portrait photograph of Max Elskamp · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Max Elskamp (born Antwerp, 5 May 1862; died Antwerp, 10 December 1931) was a Belgian Symbolist poet writing in French, and a member of the Académie royale de langue et de littérature françaises.

Jethro Bithell's 1911 anthology classes him as a Fleming with a French mother, notes that he illustrated his own books with quaint mediæval woodcuts, and observes that he is a free-verse poet only in his use of assonance.

poets.name: Grégoire Le Roy
bio: Grégoire Le Roy (born Ghent, 7 November 1862; died Ixelles, 5 December 1941) was a Belgian writer and engraver who wrote in French.
Jethro Bithell's 1911 anthology classes him as a Fleming, mentions that he was an amateur painter, and prints six of his poems.

poets.name: Maurice Maeterlinck
poets.credit: Portrait photograph of Maurice Maeterlinck · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Maurice Maeterlinck (1862–1949) was a Belgian playwright, poet and essayist who wrote in French, and was made a count in 1932.
Jethro Bithell's 1911 anthology classes him as a Fleming, remarking that he might equally have written in Flemish, and prints fifteen of his early poems together with a set of ten songs.

poets.name: Oliver Herford
poets.credit: Portrait of Oliver Herford (photograph, c. 1916) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Oliver Herford (1863–1935) was an English-born American humorist, illustrator and writer of light verse.
He wrote and drew many small books of whimsy, such as The Bashful Earthquake (1898).

poets.name: Winifred Howells
bio: Winifred Howells (1863–1889) was the eldest daughter of the novelist William Dean Howells, and wrote a small body of verse before her early death. She is a different person from her father, whose poems are filed separately here.
The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1900).

poets.name: Amélie Rives Troubetzkoy
bio: Amélie Rives (1863–1945), later Princess Troubetzkoy, was an American novelist and poet, born in Richmond, Virginia.
She published verse as well as fiction, and married the Russian painter Prince Pierre Troubetzkoy in 1896.

poets.name: Alice E. Gillington
bio: Alice E. Gillington (1863–1934) was an English poet and writer on Romani (Gypsy) life, sister of the poet Mary C. Gillington.
Two of her pieces, “A West-Country Love-Song” and “Nocturnes”, close Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Evaleen Stein
bio: Evaleen Stein (1863–1923) was an American poet and writer, also an illuminator of manuscripts, and the author of several books for young readers.
The four poems given here are those that Edmund Clarence Stedman printed under her name in An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900).

poets.name: Elaine Goodale Eastman
bio: Elaine Goodale Eastman (1863–1953) was an American poet and educator, born at Mount Washington, Massachusetts.
She published verse as a child with her sister Dora Read Goodale, later worked in Indian education, and married the Santee Sioux physician and writer Charles Alexander Eastman in 1891.

poets.name: Neil Munro
poets.credit: Portrait of Neil Munro by William Strang, 1903 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Neil Munro (1863–1930) was a Scottish novelist and journalist, born at Inveraray, remembered for his Highland romance John Splendid (1898) and for his comic Para Handy stories. He also wrote verse in Scots and English.
Lyra Celtica (1924) prints his poem 'Fingal's Weeping'.

poets.name: Arthur Quiller-Couch
poets.credit: Photograph of Arthur Quiller-Couch, from The Bookman, no later than 1898 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Arthur Quiller-Couch (1863–1944), who wrote as 'Q', was a Cornish novelist, critic and anthologist, born at Bodmin. He edited The Oxford Book of English Verse (1900) and became Professor of English Literature at Cambridge in 1912.
Lyra Celtica prints two of his poems, 'The Splendid Spur' and 'The White Moth', the latter described there as his most distinctively Celtic poem.

poets.name: Vance Thompson
bio: Vance Thompson (1863–1925) was an American journalist, critic and playwright of English parentage. He spent his boyhood in Pittsburgh, graduated at Princeton, studied at German universities and lived chiefly in New York.
He founded and edited the illustrated fortnightly M'lle New York, and published Songs and Symbols (1900) and French Portraits (1900).

poets.name: Richard Hovey
poets.credit: Portrait of Richard Hovey (photograph, before 1908) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Richard Hovey (1864–1900) was an American poet, born in Normal, Illinois, who lectured at Columbia University.
With Bliss Carman he wrote Songs from Vagabondia (1894), and he left unfinished a cycle of dramas on the Arthurian legend.

poets.name: Julie Mathilde Lippmann
bio: Julie Mathilde Lippmann (1864–1952) was an American writer, known as a novelist, critic and supporter of women's suffrage.
She also wrote verse, which appeared in periodicals and in anthologies of American poetry.

poets.name: Asif
bio: Asif is the pen-name of H.H. Mir Mahbub Ali Khan, Nizam of Hyderabad, who died in 1911; the book calls him a pupil of the poet Dagh and an esteemed poet and patron of poets. (The book names him, not the earlier Asaf-ud-Daula of Lucknow.)

The 4 pieces given here are drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. They are free renderings, not literal translations, and the original Urdu poems are untitled; each is named here by its first line.

poets.name: Elizabeth Gostwycke Roberts
bio: Elizabeth Gostwycke Roberts (1864–1922) was a Canadian poet, the sister of Charles G. D. Roberts.
The poem here is the one Lighthall chose for Songs of the Great Dominion (1889).

poets.name: Arthur Weir
bio: Arthur Weir (1864–1902) was a Montreal poet and journalist.
His volume Fleurs-de-Lys and Other Poems appeared in 1889. One of the poets chosen by W. D. Lighthall for Songs of the Great Dominion (London, 1889), an anthology of Canadian verse.

poets.name: Madison Cawein
poets.credit: Portrait of Madison Cawein (photograph, 1905) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Madison Cawein (1865–1914) was an American poet, born in Louisville, Kentucky, who wrote chiefly of the woods and fields of his native state.
He published many volumes of verse, beginning with Blooms of the Berry (1887).

poets.name: Mary McNeil Fenollosa
bio: Mary McNeil Fenollosa (1865–1954) was an American poet and novelist, born in Alabama. Under the pen name Sidney McCall she published novels such as Truth Dexter (1901); in 1895 she married the orientalist Ernest Fenollosa.
Much of her verse, including the collection Out of the Nest (1899), draws on Japanese scenes and subjects.

poets.name: André Fontainas
poets.credit: Portrait of André Fontainas by Félix Vallotton · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: André Fontainas (1865–1948) was a Belgian Symbolist poet and critic, born in Brussels, who spent much of his life in France.

Jethro Bithell's 1911 anthology classes him as a Fleming with some French admixture, and records that he translated Keats and Milton's Comus and Samson Agonistes and wrote a history of French painting.

poets.name: William Henry Gardner
bio: William Henry Gardner was an American song-writer, born in Boston in 1865, who devoted himself chiefly to writing verse for music.
His lyrics were set by both American and English composers, and he published Work and Play Songs (1899).

poets.name: Holman Day
poets.credit: Portrait of Holman Day (photograph, 1921), from Exhibitors Herald · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Holman Francis Day (1865–1935) was an American journalist, poet and novelist, born at Vassalboro, Maine, and long associated with Auburn, Maine. He wrote humorous and sympathetic dialect verse about Yankee farmers, fishermen, lumbermen and river-drivers, which earned him the title of the 'Kipling of Maine'.

Up in Maine: Stories of Yankee Life Told in Verse (1900) and Pine Tree Ballads (1902), both published in Boston by Small, Maynard & Company, made his name. He later turned to novels and plays, and several of his works were adapted for film.

poets.name: Bert Leston Taylor
poets.credit: Portrait of Bert Leston Taylor (photograph, 1921) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Bert Leston Taylor (1866–1921) was an American newspaper columnist and humorist, who conducted the column “A Line o’ Type or Two” in the Chicago Tribune.
His light verse and parodies appeared first in that column and were then gathered in book form.

poets.name: Anne Reeve Aldrich
poets.credit: Portrait: slowking4 — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Anne Reeve Aldrich (1866–1892) was an American poet and novelist. She died young, at the age of twenty-six.
Her works include The Rose and Flame and Other Poems and The Feet of Love.

poets.name: John Jerome Rooney
bio: John Jerome Rooney (1866–1934) was an American lawyer and poet, born in New York City. He is remembered for patriotic and occasional verse of the Spanish–American War period, above all "The Men behind the Guns" (1898).
Stedman's An American Anthology (1900) reprinted several of his poems, among them the Civil War reconciliation ballad "Joined the Blues".

poets.name: Dora Read Goodale
bio: Dora Read Goodale (1866–1953) was an American poet, born at Mount Washington, Massachusetts, and the younger sister of Elaine Goodale Eastman.
The sisters published Apple-Blossoms (1878) while still children; her later verse includes Mountain Dooryards (1946).

poets.name: Gelett Burgess
bio: Frank Gelett Burgess (1866–1951) was an American humorist, illustrator and critic, born in Boston. In San Francisco he founded the little magazine The Lark (1895–97), in which his quatrain The Purple Cow first appeared.
He went on to write the Goops books of comic manners for children and the Burgess Nonsense Book (1901), and is credited with coining the word blurb.

poets.name: Martha Gilbert Dickinson (Bianchi)
bio: Martha Gilbert Dickinson Bianchi (1866–1943), born in Amherst, Massachusetts, was the niece of the poet Emily Dickinson and grew up in the house next to hers. She wrote verse and fiction under the name Martha Gilbert Dickinson before her marriage to Alexander E. Bianchi.

Her best-known work as an editor was the posthumous publication of her aunt's poems and letters, but she also published her own poems, several of which Edmund Clarence Stedman reprinted in An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Edward Lucas White
bio: Edward Lucas White (1866–1934) was born in Bergen, New Jersey, and spent his career in Baltimore, Maryland, teaching Latin and Greek.
Besides his verse, which was gathered in later books, he became known for fiction, including the historical novel Helen (1925) and the weird tales of Lukundoo and Other Stories (1927).

poets.name: John Russell Hayes
bio: John Russell Hayes was an American poet, born in West Chester, Pennsylvania, in 1866. He studied at Swarthmore, Harvard and the University of Pennsylvania Law School and taught English at Swarthmore College.
His books of verse include The Old-Fashioned Garden, and Other Verses (1895), The Brandywine (1898), a West Chester Centennial Ode (1899) and Swarthmore Idylls (1899).

poets.name: Walter Malone
bio: Walter Malone (1866–1915) was born in De Soto County, Mississippi, and educated at the University of Mississippi. A lawyer, he later practised in Memphis, Tennessee.
His volumes include Songs of Dusk and Dawn (1894), Songs of December and June (1896) and The Coming of the King (1897).

poets.name: Albert Mockel
poets.credit: Portrait photograph of Albert Mockel · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Albert Mockel (born Ougrée, 27 December 1866; died Ixelles, 30 January 1945) was a Belgian Symbolist poet and writer, a Walloon militant, and a member of the Académie royale de langue et de littérature françaises.
Jethro Bithell's 1911 anthology classes him as a Walloon of distant German extraction and notes that he wrote a study of the sculptor Victor Rousseau.

poets.name: Oliver Madox Brown
poets.credit: Portrait of Oliver Madox Brown, by Ford Madox Brown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Oliver Madox Brown (1855–1874) was an English author and artist, the son of the painter Ford Madox Brown, who died aged nineteen.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 8, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Edward Cracroft Lefroy
bio: Edward Cracroft Lefroy (1855–1891) was a British poet.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 8, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Frances Bannerman
bio: Frances Bannerman (1855–1944), born in Halifax, Nova Scotia, was a painter and poet who later lived in Torquay, England. Ill health led her to give up painting for verse, and her collection Milestones appeared in 1899.
Her best-known poem, "An Upper Chamber", is printed in The Oxford Book of English Verse.

poets.name: Pakenham Beatty
bio: Pakenham Thomas Beatty (1855–1930) was an English poet. He published To my Lady (1878), Three Women of the People (1881) and Marcia, a Tragedy (1884).

poets.name: Lizzie M. Little
bio: Lizzie M. Little was a Victorian poet, author of Persephone, and Other Poems (1884).

poets.name: Dollie Radford
poets.credit: Portrait: Robert Bryden — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Dollie Radford (1858–1920), born Caroline Maitland, was an English poet and writer who published under her married name.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 8, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Ronald Ross
poets.credit: Photograph of Ronald Ross (U.S. National Library of Medicine) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Ronald Ross (1857–1932) was a British physician born in Almora, India. A surgeon in the Indian Medical Service, he showed that malaria is transmitted by mosquitoes, and received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1902. He later held a chair in tropical medicine at Liverpool and worked at the Ross Institute in London.

Alongside his scientific career he wrote poems, novels and plays. Edward Marsh included his lyric 'Hesperus', from Lyra Modulata, in the first Georgian Poetry volume (1911-1912), and it is the piece reproduced here.

poets.name: A. Mary F. Robinson
poets.credit: Portrait: Agnes Mary Frances Duclaux — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Agnes Mary Frances Robinson (1857–1944) was an English poet and scholar who later wrote under the names Madame Darmesteter and Madame Duclaux after her two marriages, to James Darmesteter (1888) and Emile Duclaux (1901). She lived much in France.
Her early volumes include A Handful of Honeysuckle (1878), The Crowned Hippolytus (1881) and An Italian Garden (1886). Four of her poems appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Marguerite Merington
bio: Marguerite Merington (1857–1951) was an American writer and playwright, author of the stage piece Captain Lettarblair and an editor of Custer correspondence.
Her lyric “Hey Nonny No” was printed among the additional selections of Stedman’s An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Marjory Kennedy-Fraser
poets.credit: Portrait of Marjory Kennedy-Fraser, c. 1900 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Marjory Kennedy-Fraser (1857–1930) was a Scottish singer and collector of folk song, born in Perth, who gathered and arranged the traditional songs of the Hebrides in her Songs of the Hebrides (1909–21).
Lyra Celtica (1924) prints three of her lyrics, 'Land of Heart's Desire', 'Ossian's Midsummer Day-Dream' and 'Kishmul's Galley'.

poets.name: Minna Irving
bio: Minna Irving (1857–1940) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Betsy's Battle Flag”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Tudor Jenks
poets.credit: Portrait of Tudor Jenks · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Tudor Jenks (1857–1922) was an American novelist.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “The Spirit of the Maine”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Richard Mansfield
bio: Richard Mansfield (1857–1907) was an English actor-manager.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “The Eagle's Song”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Alfred Hayes
bio: Alfred Hayes (1857–1936) was an English poet and translator, born at Wolverhampton.

The poems here are taken from Alfred H. Miles (ed.), The Poets and the Poetry of the Century (London: Hutchinson, 1891–1897), vol. 8, from the Internet Archive scans of that edition. Spelling is that of the anthology; Miles's biographical essay and extracts from longer poems are omitted, and only poems that could be read cleanly from the scan are included.

poets.name: Ada Foster Murray
bio: Ada Foster Murray was an American poet who lived in New York and was the wife of Henry Mills Alden, long the editor of Harper's Magazine. Her poems appeared in the magazines and in her single volume, Flower o' the Grass (Harper & Brothers, 1910).
Several of her poems were chosen for The Home Book of Verse (1912).

poets.name: Ethelwyn Wetherald
poets.credit: Portrait: http://www.poemhunter.com — CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ethelwyn Wetherald (1857–1940) was an Ontario poet and journalist whose nature lyrics were collected in The House of the Trees (1895) and later volumes.
The poems given here are taken from The Oxford Book of Canadian Verse, chosen by Wilfred Campbell (Toronto: Oxford University Press, 1913).

poets.name: Margaret Deland
poets.credit: Portrait of Margaret Deland, 1894 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Margaret Deland (1857–1945), born Margaretta Wade Campbell, was an American novelist, short-story writer and poet, best known for her fiction.
The poems printed here are those given in The Oxford Book of English Mystical Verse (1917), edited by D. H. S. Nicholson and A. H. E. Lee; the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: Annie Eliot Trumbull
bio: Annie Eliot Trumbull (1857–1949) was born at Hartford, Connecticut, where she spent her life.
She wrote novels and stories, among them White Birches (1893) and Mistress Content Cradock (1899), and occasional verse.

poets.name: Milicent Washburn Shinn
bio: Milicent Washburn Shinn (1858–1940) was born in Washington Township, Alameda County, California, and graduated from the University of California. In 1882 she took over the editorship of the new Overland Monthly, which she held until 1894.
She was a leading contributor to the magazines and later made a psychological study of children, for which her own university gave her the degree of Ph.D.

poets.name: Charles Henry Crandall
bio: Charles Henry Crandall (1858–1923) was born at Greenwich, New York, and worked as a journalist before settling at Springdale, Connecticut, where he gave his time to literature.
He published two volumes of verse by 1900, Wayside Music (1893) and The Chords of Life (1898); he also edited Representative Sonnets (1890).

poets.name: Henry Jerome Stockard
bio: Henry Jerome Stockard (1858–1914) was born in North Carolina and graduated from the University of North Carolina, where he was afterwards associate professor. He later taught at Fredericksburg College.
His verse appeared in Fugitive Lines (1897).

poets.name: James Buckham
bio: James Buckham (1858–1908) was born at Burlington, Vermont, the son of the president of the University of Vermont, and wrote also under the name Paul Pastnor.
His verse is collected in The Heart of Life (1897) and A Wayside Altar (1905).

poets.name: Arthur Edward Waite
poets.credit: Photograph of Arthur Edward Waite by J. Russell and Sons, 1911 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Arthur Edward Waite (1857–1942) was a British poet and scholarly mystic who wrote extensively on occultism and Western esotericism, and co-created the Rider–Waite tarot deck.
The poems printed here are those given in The Oxford Book of English Mystical Verse (1917), edited by D. H. S. Nicholson and A. H. E. Lee; the text is taken from that anthology.

poets.name: William Roscoe Thayer
bio: William Roscoe Thayer (1859–1923) was born at Boston, graduated from Harvard, and taught English there for several years. From 1892 he edited The Harvard Graduates’ Magazine, and he became a historian of modern Italy.
His verse includes The Confession of Hermes, and Other Poems (1884) and Poems, New and Old (1894); he published some of it under the name Paul Hermes.

poets.name: Katharine Lee Bates
bio: Katharine Lee Bates (1859–1929) was born at Falmouth, Massachusetts, graduated from Wellesley College, and became professor of English literature there. She also edited English classics.
Her verse includes The College Beautiful, and Other Poems (1887) and Sunshine, and Other Verses for Children (1890).

poets.name: Albert D. Watson
bio: Albert Durrant Watson (1859–1926) was a Toronto physician who wrote verse and took an interest in astronomy and psychical research.
The poems given here are taken from The Oxford Book of Canadian Verse, chosen by Wilfred Campbell (Toronto: Oxford University Press, 1913).

poets.name: John William Mackail
bio: John William Mackail (1859–1945) was a Scottish classical scholar and man of letters, translator of Virgil’s Aeneid into English prose, biographer of William Morris, and Oxford Professor of Poetry from 1906 to 1911.
With H. C. Beeching and J. B. B. Nichols he wrote the verse volumes Love in Idleness (1883) and Love’s Looking-Glass (1891).

poets.name: John Hall Ingham
bio: John Hall Ingham was born at Philadelphia in 1860 and practised as a lawyer.
His poems were printed in magazines and, as Stedman noted in 1900, had not been gathered into a volume.

poets.name: Cora C. Bass
bio: Cora C. Bass (1868–1928) was an American poet of Lowell, Massachusetts. Her verse appeared in periodicals such as The New York Observer, Zion's Herald, the Boston Transcript and the Portland Transcript before it was gathered into books.

She published Poems (Lowell: Lawler & Co., 1899), also issued under the name 'Harley Vane', and followed it with Songs for All Seasons, and Other Poems (Lowell: Lawler Printing Co., 1901). Her work is devotional, seasonal and patriotic, and includes pieces written for Memorial Day services at Huntington Hall.

poets.name: Philip Henry Savage
bio: Philip Henry Savage (1868–1899) was an American poet who died at the age of thirty-one.
The four poems given here are those that Edmund Clarence Stedman printed under his name in An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (1900).

poets.name: Herbert Bates
bio: Herbert Bates (1868–1929) was born in Hyde Park, Massachusetts, and graduated from Harvard in 1890. He was a teacher of English, serving at the University of Nebraska and, from 1897, at the Manual Training High School in Brooklyn.
He published Songs of Exile (1896) and edited several classics for school use.

poets.name: Edgar Lee Masters
poets.credit: Photograph of Edgar Lee Masters as a young man · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edgar Lee Masters (1868–1950) was an American lawyer and writer, born in Garnett, Kansas, and raised in Petersburg and Lewistown, Illinois. He practised law in Chicago for three decades, partly as law partner of Clarence Darrow, and wrote poetry, plays, novels and biography alongside his legal career.

Spoon River Anthology, first published in 1915 and expanded in 1916 with The Spooniad and the Epilogue, is a sequence of free-verse epitaphs spoken by the dead of an imagined Midwestern town, drawing on the Illinois towns of his youth. It was an immediate sensation and remains his most famous work; the later volumes never matched its success.

poets.name: William Vaughn Moody
poets.credit: Portrait of William Vaughn Moody (photograph by W. C. Ward, before 1906) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Vaughn Moody (1869–1910) was an American poet and dramatist, born in Spencer, Indiana, who taught at the University of Chicago.
His work includes the “Ode in Time of Hesitation”, the verse drama The Fire-Bringer (1904) and the play The Great Divide (1906).

poets.name: Margaret Gilman George Davidson
bio: Margaret Gilman George Davidson (1869–1897) was an American poet, born in Columbia, Missouri. In 1895 she married the journalist W. T. Davidson, and she died at Lewistown, Illinois, two years later.
Her poems were collected only after her death; "Moritura" appeared in Stedman's An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Algernon Tassin
bio: Algernon Tassin (1869–1931) was an American critic, teacher and writer. He took his degree at Harvard in 1892.
He taught English at Columbia University and wrote on the history of American periodicals, as in The Magazine in America (1916). His few poems were printed in college and magazine verse.

poets.name: Clarence Hawkes
bio: Clarence Hawkes (1869–1954) was an American author and lecturer, born at Goshen, Massachusetts, and known as the "Blind Poet of New England". He wrote short stories, nature sketches and verse.
His books include Pebbles and Shells (1895), Idyls of Old New England (1897) and The Hope of the World, and Other Poems (1900).

poets.name: George Sterling
poets.credit: Portrait of George Sterling (photograph by Johan Hagemeyer, 1926) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Sterling (1869–1926) was an American poet, born in Sag Harbor, New York, and a central figure of the bohemian literary circle of San Francisco and Carmel.
His books include The Testimony of the Suns (1903) and A Wine of Wizardry (1909).

poets.name: Philip Becker Goetz
bio: Philip Becker Goetz (1870–1950) was an American teacher and writer born in Buffalo, New York. He took his degree at Harvard in 1893.
He taught classics in the Buffalo schools and at the Nichols School, and helped found the College of Arts and Sciences of the University of Buffalo. He published verse, including Poems (1898).

poets.name: Alice Archer Sewall James
bio: Alice Archer Sewall James (1870–1955) was an American poet and painter, born in Glendale, Ohio.
Her verse appeared in Harper's and other magazines, and she published Ode to Girlhood, and Other Poems (1899).

poets.name: Stephen Crane
poets.credit: Photograph of Stephen Crane, c. 1899 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Stephen Crane (1871–1900) was an American novelist, short-story writer and poet, born in Newark, New Jersey. He is best remembered for the Civil War novel The Red Badge of Courage (1895) and for stories such as "The Open Boat", and worked as a journalist and war correspondent.

The Black Riders and Other Lines, his first book of verse, appeared in 1895. Its short, untitled, numbered pieces in unrhymed free verse, often parables addressing God, institutions and the self, were unusual for their time and are often compared with Emily Dickinson's. Crane died of tuberculosis in 1900, aged twenty-eight.

poets.name: Abbie Farwell Brown
bio: Abbie Farwell Brown (1871–1927) was an American writer born in Boston, Massachusetts. She wrote chiefly for children, publishing prose and verse for young readers.
Her books include The Book of Saints and Friendly Beasts (1900), In the Days of Giants (1902) and A Pocketful of Posies (1902), a volume of verses for children.

poets.name: Edwin Ford Piper
poets.credit: Portrait of Edwin Ford Piper (portrait, 1924) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edwin Ford Piper (1871–1939) was an American poet and professor of English at the University of Iowa, born in Nebraska.
He wrote poems of the Middle Western plains, such as those in Barbed Wire and Other Poems (1917).

poets.name: T. A. Daly
bio: T. A. Daly (Thomas Augustine Daly, 1871–1948) was an American newspaper columnist and poet, born in Philadelphia.
He was best known for comic verse in Italian-American dialect, collected in books such as Canzoni (1906) and Carmina (1909).

poets.name: Mary Berri Chapman Hansbrough
bio: Mary Berri Chapman Hansbrough (1872–1951) was an American poet and painter, born Mary Berri Chapman in Washington, D.C. In 1897 she married the senator Henry C. Hansbrough of North Dakota.
She wrote and illustrated Lyrics of Love and Nature (1895) and published Poems by MBCH in 1906.

poets.name: Herbert Bashford
bio: Herbert Bashford (1871–1920), born in Sioux City, Iowa, was an American librarian and poet who became state librarian of Washington. He wrote of the Pacific Northwest in Nature Stories of the Northwest and Songs from Puget Sea (1898).
The poems here are taken from Edmund Clarence Stedman’s An American Anthology, 1787–1900 (Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1900).

poets.name: Charles Augustus Keeler
bio: Charles Augustus Keeler (1871–1937) was an American naturalist, poet and writer, born in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and educated at the University of California. He lived in Berkeley, California.
His verse volumes include A Light through the Storm (1894), The Promise of the Ages (1896), The Siege of the Golden City (1896) and A Season's Sowing (1899).

poets.name: Cora Fabbri
bio: Cora Randall Fabbri (1871–1892) was an American poet, born in New York, who died in Italy at the age of twenty-one.
Her verses were published in the volume Lyrics (1892), just before her death.

poets.name: William M. MacKeracher
bio: William Mackay MacKeracher (1871–1913) was a Canadian poet. His verse was published in Montreal and Toronto between 1890 and 1909, and the library catalogue gives his dates as 1871–1913. The prefatory letter to Vacation Verse shows him writing as a student, composing during the intervals of study for a college examination.

His books are Verses of Feeling and Fancy (Montreal: W. Drysdale & Co., 1890), Vacation Verse (Montreal: “Witness” Printing House, 1891), Canada, My Land, and Other Compositions in Verse (Toronto: William Briggs, 1908) and Sonnets and Other Verse (Toronto: William Briggs, 1909). They range from patriotic Canadian pieces and sonnets on Milton, Burns, Wolfe and Montcalm to seasonal poems, Scottish and Irish dialect pieces, and light verse.

poets.name: James Weldon Johnson
poets.credit: Portrait of James Weldon Johnson, Library of Congress · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James Weldon Johnson (1871–1938) was born in Jacksonville, Florida, and became a poet, lyricist, novelist, diplomat and civil-rights leader. He graduated from Atlanta University, studied at Columbia, was admitted to the Florida bar, and served as U.S. consul in Venezuela and Nicaragua. With his brother J. Rosamond Johnson he wrote songs for the stage, including “Lift Every Voice and Sing.”

Fifty Years & Other Poems (1917), his first book of verse, marked the fiftieth anniversary of emancipation and gathered formal lyrics, sonnets and a closing group of dialect poems. He later became a leading secretary of the NAACP and a figure of the Harlem Renaissance, publishing God’s Trombones (1927) and editing The Book of American Negro Poetry.

poets.name: Hildegarde Hawthorne
bio: Hildegarde Hawthorne (1871–1952) was an American writer, the daughter of Julian Hawthorne and the granddaughter of Nathaniel Hawthorne. She wrote biographies, novels, and books for young readers, and also verse.
Edmund Clarence Stedman included two of her poems, “A Song” and “My Rose”, in An American Anthology (1900).

poets.name: Paul Laurence Dunbar
poets.credit: Photograph of Paul Laurence Dunbar, c. 1890 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Paul Laurence Dunbar (1872–1906) was an African American poet, novelist and short-story writer born in Dayton, Ohio, to parents who had been enslaved. He published his first poems while still in school and issued ‘Oak and Ivy’ (1893) at his own expense; ‘Majors and Minors’ (1895) and ‘Lyrics of Lowly Life’ (1896), the latter introduced by William Dean Howells, brought him national fame.

He wrote both in standard English and in the plantation dialect that audiences of his day expected, and was long best known for the latter, though he regretted that it overshadowed his other work. Poems such as ‘We Wear the Mask’, ‘Sympathy’ and ‘Ode to Ethiopia’ speak directly of race and hidden suffering. He died of tuberculosis at the age of thirty-three.

poets.name: Lola Ridge
poets.credit: Portrait: Unknown authorUnknown author — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Lola Ridge (1873–1941) was an Irish-born poet, raised in New Zealand and Australia, who settled in New York in 1907.
Her poems of immigrant life include those in The Ghetto and Other Poems (1918).

poets.name: Guy Wetmore Carryl
poets.credit: Portrait of Guy Wetmore Carryl (photograph, before 1902) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Guy Wetmore Carryl (1873–1904) was an American humorist and poet, born in New York City, the son of Charles Edward Carryl, who died young.
He is remembered for Fables for the Frivolous (1898), which retold Aesop and the fairy tales in comic verse.

poets.name: H. H. Knibbs
bio: H. H. Knibbs (Henry Herbert Knibbs, 1874–1945) was a Canadian-born American writer of verse and Western novels.
His poems of the desert and the trail include those in Riders of the Stars (1916).

poets.name: Olive Custance
bio: Olive Custance (1874–1944) was born at Weston Hall, Norfolk, the daughter of Colonel Custance. Her poems appeared in the leading English periodicals of the 1890s, and her first volume, Opals, was published in 1897.
In 1902 she married Lord Alfred Douglas.

poets.name: Douglas Hyde
poets.credit: Portrait: Alice Boughton — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Douglas Hyde was born in Castlerea, County Roscommon, and was a scholar of Irish. He founded the Gaelic League in 1893 and later served as the first President of Ireland (1938–45).
His English versions of Irish folk songs, such as those in Love Songs of Connacht (1893), were widely admired.

poets.name: Graham R. Tomson
poets.credit: Photograph of Rosamund Marriott Watson, c. 1880 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Graham R. Tomson was the name under which Rosamund Marriott Watson (1860–1911) published her poems in the late 1880s and early 1890s, after her marriage to the painter Arthur Graham Tomson; she later lived with the writer H. B. Marriott Watson. Her books include Tares (1884) and The Bird-Bride (1889).
She was admired for her ballades and other fixed forms. Three of her poems appear in Women Poets of the Victorian Era (1890).

poets.name: Elinor Sweetman
bio: Elinor Sweetman (c. 1860–1922) was an Irish poet, the sister of the novelists M. E. Francis and Agnes Castle. The family moved to Brussels in 1873.
Her pastoral dialogue "The Orchard by the Shore" is printed in The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse.

poets.name: Rosamund Marriott Watson
poets.credit: Portrait: Unknown authorUnknown author — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Rosamund Marriott Watson (1860–1911) was an English poet, nature writer and critic who wrote early in her career under the pseudonyms Graham R. Tomson and Rushworth Armytage.
The poems here are taken from Arthur Quiller-Couch's anthology The Oxford Book of Victorian Verse (Clarendon Press, 1912).

poets.name: Eleanor Elizabeth Montgomery
poets.era: Australian and New Zealand (19th and early 20th century)
bio: Eleanor Elizabeth Montgomery was a New Zealand poet of the 1880s and 1890s, who lived on a cattle farm in the Wanganui district and published several volumes of verse there under the name E. E. M. Montgomery.
Stedman's Victorian Anthology (1895) records that she wrote under the pseudonym "The Singing Shepherd".

poets.name: Elvet Lewis (Elfed)
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Howell Elvet Lewis, bardic name Elfed, was a Welsh Congregational minister, hymn-writer and poet, who served as Archdruid of Wales.
His poem "The High Tide" is given in English verse by Alfred Perceval Graves in A Celtic Psaltery (1917).

poets.name: Hamlin Garland
bio: Hamlin Garland (1860–1940) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Logan at Peach Tree Creek”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Clinton Scollard
poets.credit: Portrait of Clinton Scollard · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Clinton Scollard (1860–1932) was an American poet.

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poems here are “The First Thanksgiving”, “King Philip's Last Stand”, “The Eve of Bunker Hill”, “Montgomery at Quebec” and “The Boasting of Sir Peter Parker” among others; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Helena Coleman
bio: Helena Coleman (1860–1953) was a Toronto poet whose lyrics and sonnets appeared in Songs and Sonnets (1906) and later collections.
The poems given here are taken from The Oxford Book of Canadian Verse, chosen by Wilfred Campbell (Toronto: Oxford University Press, 1913).

poets.name: Albert E. S. Smythe
bio: Albert Ernest Stafford Smythe (1861–1947) was an Irish-born Toronto journalist and a leading Canadian Theosophist who also wrote verse.
The poems given here are taken from The Oxford Book of Canadian Verse, chosen by Wilfred Campbell (Toronto: Oxford University Press, 1913).

poets.name: Virna Sheard
bio: Virna Sheard (1862–1943) was a Canadian poet and novelist who lived in Toronto and published verse and fiction from the 1890s onward.
The poems given here are taken from The Oxford Book of Canadian Verse, chosen by Wilfred Campbell (Toronto: Oxford University Press, 1913).

poets.name: Arthur Colton
bio: Arthur Colton (1868–1943) was an American writer, born in Washington, D.C. He studied at Yale, took his doctorate there in 1893, taught English at Yale, and from 1906 was librarian of the University Club of New York.
He published essays and fiction, and one volume of poetry, Harps Hung Up in Babylon (1907).

poets.name: Violet Jacob
poets.credit: Portrait of Violet Jacob by Henry Harris Brown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Violet Jacob (born Violet Augusta Mary Frederica Kennedy-Erskine, 1863-1946) was a Scottish poet and novelist, born at the House of Dun in Angus. In 1894 she married Arthur Otway Jacob, a soldier, and spent a number of years abroad with him, including a period in India.

Her novel Flemington (1911) was followed by Songs of Angus (1915), with a preface by John Buchan, and More Songs of Angus and Others (1918). Her poems in the Scots of her native Angus are among the best-loved of the early twentieth century. She died in Kirriemuir in 1946.

poets.name: Freeman E. Miller
poets.credit: Frontispiece portrait of Freeman E. Miller from Oklahoma and Other Poems (Buffalo: Charles Wells Moulton, 1895) · Public domain (Project Gutenberg #14953)
bio: Freeman E. Miller (1864–1951) was an American poet and teacher. The title page of his first book, Oklahoma and Other Poems (Buffalo: Charles Wells Moulton, 1895), names him as Professor of English Language and Literature in the Agricultural and Mechanical College of Oklahoma Territory, and he dedicated the book to James Whitcomb Riley.

Oklahoma Sunshine (Stillwater: Advance Printing Company, 1905) gathers a year of the column of verse and prose he published in The Stillwater Advance from June 1904, much of it in homely farm and small-town dialect. This archive holds the verse of both books; the prose paragraphs of the second are left out.

poets.name: Robert Loveman
bio: Robert Loveman (1864–1923) is represented in this archive by verse from Burton E. Stevenson's anthology Poems of American History (1908; revised 1922).

Poems of American History gathers verse on events from the Norse voyages to the Spanish-American War, arranged by historical chapter. The poem here is “Hobson and His Men”; Stevenson's editorial headnotes are not reproduced.

poets.name: Phillips Stewart
