works.title: The Kasîdah of Hâjî Abdû El-Yezdî
works.author: Sir Richard Francis Burton
works.note: Presented as a translation from a Persian original by a certain Haji Abdu of Yezd, but the Persian poet is fictitious: the Kasidah is Burton's own English poem, privately printed in 1880. Nine parts in four-line stanzas (268 in all), each ending on the refrain of the camel-bell. Burton's prose apparatus (preface, notes, conclusion) is omitted.
works.blurb: A philosophical quatrain-sequence in which a desert traveller, Haji Abdu, reflects on faith, fate and the vanity of creeds. Burton's own composition, offered as a rendering from the Persian.

works.title: Keep Your Own Secret
works.author: Pedro Calderón de la Barca
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #63776 (Eight Dramas of Calderon, freely translated by Edward FitzGerald, Macmillan 1906, reprinting the Six Dramas of 1853 and the Two Dramas of 1865). FitzGerald's advertisement, footnotes and afterwords are omitted.
works.blurb: At the court of Parma the Prince, his secretary Don Cesar and the courtier Don Felix each hide a love from the rest, and every secret confided to the wrong ear tangles the plot further. The comedy ends with Nisida's hand placed in Felix's and a moral against trusting even a friend with a secret.

works.title: King Arthur
works.subtitle: Books I to XII
works.author: Edward Bulwer Lytton
works.note: Text of the Poetical Works (Routledge, Warne and Routledge, 1860). The Preface, the Note, the prose Arguments, the stanza numbers and the Notes to each book are omitted.
works.blurb: Bulwer Lytton’s twelve-book romantic epic in Spenserian stanzas, following Arthur and the wizard Merlin through the three labours of Fable-land.

works.title: King Horn
works.subtitle: Middle English text of Cambridge University Library MS Gg.4.27.2, ed. J. R. Lumby (1866), re-ed. G. H. McKnight (1901)
works.author: Anonymous
works.note: Middle English text of Cambridge University Library MS Gg.4.27.2, ed. J. R. Lumby (EETS 1866), re-ed. G. H. McKnight (1901); the Laud and Harley texts, notes and glossary are omitted.
works.blurb: The earliest surviving English verse romance: the exiled prince Horn, cast adrift as a boy after Saracens kill his father, wins the love of Rymenhild, proves himself in Ireland, and returns to reclaim his kingdom.

works.title: The Life and Death of King John
works.author: William Shakespeare
works.blurb: King John holds the English crown against the claim of his nephew Arthur, whom France backs, and the play follows the quarrel through the siege of Angiers, the bargained marriage of Louis and Blanche, and the grief of Arthur's mother Constance. Philip Faulconbridge, the Bastard, acknowledged as Richard Lionheart's son, becomes the play's sardonic commentator on politics and 'commodity'. Arthur dies leaping from the castle walls, the barons turn against John, and the king is poisoned at Swinstead Abbey, leaving England to young Henry.

works.title: The Tragedy of King Lear
works.author: William Shakespeare
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #100 (The Complete Works of William Shakespeare), revised 24 Aug 2025.
works.blurb: King Lear, old and weary of rule, divides his kingdom among his daughters according to their professions of love, banishing the plain-spoken Cordelia and Kent. Goneril and Regan soon strip him of his retinue and turn him out into the storm, where he goes mad upon the heath beside his Fool and the disguised Edgar. Meanwhile Gloucester, deceived by his bastard son Edmund, is blinded for helping the king. Cordelia returns with a French army, but Lear and she are defeated, and the play ends in the deaths of Cordelia, Lear and almost all the rest.

works.title: Kitty of the Sherragh Vane
works.subtitle: Fo'c's'le Yarns, Second Series: 2
works.author: Thomas Edward Brown
works.note: From The Collected Poems of T. E. Brown, with introduction by W. E. Henley (Macmillan, 1909 reprint of the 1900 first edition), Internet Archive scan; Fo'c's'le Yarns, Second Series (no. 2). The printer's footnote glosses are left out and Brown's Manx-English spellings are kept as printed.
works.blurb: A two-part dialect yarn set at the Sherragh Vane, a farm high up Sulby glen, with Kitty and Saul at its centre.

works.title: The Knight of Curtesy
works.author: Anonymous (Middle English)
works.note: Text from the undated black-letter quarto printed by William Copland (Bodleian Library, the only known copy), as Ritson gives it, as printed by Joseph Ritson (1802), revised by E. Goldsmid (1884–85); notes omitted.
works.blurb: A poem of 500 lines in four-line stanzas, an English version of the story of the Chastelain de Couci and the lady of Fayel: the knight of Curtesy and the lady of Faguell love in chastity, her jealous husband sends him to fight at Rhodes, and after the knight is killed the husband serves his heart to her at table.

works.title: Konrad Wallenrod
works.subtitle: An Historical Poem
works.author: Adam Mickiewicz
works.note: Project Gutenberg eBook #34050, transcribed from the 1882 London edition. The author's and translator's prefaces, Machiavelli epigraph, the prose notes and the note markers are omitted. The ballad of Alpujara and the Song of the Wajdelote stand in their places within the cantos.
works.blurb: Mickiewicz's narrative poem of 1828 in six cantos: a Lithuanian taken as a boy by the Teutonic Knights rises to be their Grand Master, and, hiding his vengeance behind a mask, leads the Order to ruin. Read in its day as a parable of Poland under Russian rule. Translated by Maude Ashurst Biggs.

works.title: The Kyng of Tars
works.author: Anonymous (Middle English)
works.note: Text from the Vernon manuscript in the Bodleian Library (a second, imperfect copy is in the Auchinleck manuscript, Advocates' Library, Edinburgh), as Ritson states; as printed by Joseph Ritson, Ancient Engleish Metrical Romanceës (1802), from the revised edition by E. Goldsmid (1884–85); notes omitted.
works.blurb: The Christian king of Tars refuses his daughter to the Sultan of Damascus, who attacks his kingdom; to save her father's people she marries the heathen lord, and bears him a shapeless lump of flesh. Christian baptism turns the lump into a living, fair child, the Sultan renounces his gods and is himself baptised, and the converted Sultan then conquers the lands of his enemies.

works.title: The Lady of the Lake
works.author: Sir Walter Scott
works.blurb: A romance of the Scottish Highlands, unfolding over six days on the shores of Loch Katrine, that made Sir Walter Scott the most popular poet in Europe.

works.title: Laili and Majnun
works.subtitle: A poem from the original Persian of Nizami, translated by James Atkinson
works.author: Nizami Ganjavi
works.note: Atkinson's rhymed English version in couplets (London: A. J. Valpy for the Oriental Translation Fund, 1836). Text from the Internet Archive OCR of two scans of the 1836 edition, checked line by line against each other and against the 1894 reprint (The Loves of Laili and Majnun). Atkinson's preface, the notes, the printed line numbers and running heads are omitted. His nineteen numbered divisions stand as the sections; the book's stanza spacing and indentation of short lines were not reliable in the OCR, so each division is set as continuous verse, flush left.
works.blurb: The Arab tale of Qays, who is driven mad by love and called Majnun, and of Laili, who is married to another and dies of longing, as Nizami told it in the twelfth century and Atkinson first rendered it into English verse.

works.title: Lalla Rookh
works.subtitle: An Oriental Romance
works.author: Thomas Moore
works.note: Project Gutenberg #8187 (Moore's poetical works) carries no edition year; Lalla Rookh was first published in 1817 and Moore died in 1852. Only the four verse tales are given here: Moore's prose frame (the journey of Lalla Rookh, Feramorz and the critic Fadladeen), the songs sung inside that frame, and his notes are omitted.
works.blurb: Thomas Moore's best-selling Oriental romance: four verse tales told to a princess on her journey from Delhi to Kashmir, by the young poet Feramorz.

works.title: Lamentations
works.subtitle: Authorized Version of Lamentations.
works.author: The Bible (Authorized King James Version)
works.blurb: Five laments for the fallen city of Jerusalem.

works.title: Lancelot, or the Knight of the Cart
works.subtitle: Lancelot, ou Le Chevalier de la charrette
works.author: Chrétien de Troyes
works.note: Prose translation of the Old French verse by W. W. Comfort, Everyman's Library (Dent, 1914); text from Project Gutenberg #831, checked against the 1914 Internet Archive record arthurianromance0000chre_x3s7.
works.blurb: Lancelot braves shame and peril to rescue Queen Guinevere from Meleagant; concluded by Godefroi de Leigni.

works.title: Lancelot of the Laik
works.subtitle: A Scottish Metrical Romance
works.author: Anonymous (Middle English)
works.note: Middle Scots text of Cambridge University Library MS Kk.1.5, ed. W. W. Skeat, EETS 6 (1865); preface, notes, sidenotes and glossary omitted. The long s is printed as s; the editor’s braces and tildes for the scribe’s abbreviations are kept as in the Project Gutenberg e-text, and square brackets mark the editor’s emendations. The poem breaks off unfinished in the manuscript.
works.blurb: A Middle Scots romance in decasyllabic couplets, after the French prose Lancelot. A lovesick poet is bidden by a vision to write of Lancelot, then tells of King Arthur at Carlisle, his dreams, the war with Galiot, and Lancelot’s love for Guinevere. The manuscript breaks off in mid-battle.

works.title: Lancelot
works.subtitle: A Poem
works.author: Edwin Arlington Robinson
works.note: Text of the Collected Poems (Macmillan, 1921; Lancelot first published by Thomas Seltzer, 1920), read from the Internet Archive scans and checked against the Seltzer edition. Paragraphs follow the printed page; short indented lines complete a verse line begun above.
works.blurb: Blank-verse Arthurian narrative in nine parts: Lancelot, Gawaine, Guinevere and the fall of Arthur's kingdom, as Lancelot rides out in search of the Light.

works.title: Laurence Bloomfield in Ireland
works.subtitle: A Modern Poem in Twelve Chapters
works.author: William Allingham
works.note: Text of the first edition (London and Cambridge: Macmillan, 1864), collated from two Internet Archive scans; the prose preface, contents and the author's footnotes are not reproduced, and the printed line numbers are omitted. The revised texts of 1869 and 1888 are not used.
works.blurb: Allingham's verse novel of Irish rural life: a young landlord returns to his Ulster-bordering estate and confronts agents, tenants, secret societies and evictions, in twelve chapters of heroic couplets.

works.blurb: The anonymous twelfth-century Castilian epic of Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, in three cantares: his banishment, the marriage of his daughters, and the affront of Corpes.

works.title: The Lay of the Last Minstrel
works.subtitle: A Poem
works.author: Sir Walter Scott
works.note: Text of the first edition (1805), from the proofread Wikisource transcription; Scott's preface and notes are omitted.
works.blurb: A verse romance of Border feud, magic and thwarted love in sixteenth-century Branksome Hall, framed as the song of the last of the old minstrels.

works.title: Le Bone Florence of Rome
works.author: Anonymous (Middle English)
works.note: Text from the paper manuscript in Bishop More's collections, Cambridge University Library (Num. 690), as Ritson gives it, as printed by Joseph Ritson (1802), revised by E. Goldsmid (1884–85); notes omitted.
works.blurb: A tail-rhyme romance of about 2,190 lines in twelve-line stanzas: Florence, daughter of the emperor Otes of Rome, is sought in marriage by the aged emperor Garcy, and after her father's death she marries the knight Emere. In his absence she is slandered, driven out and sold at sea, and at last becomes a nun at Beverfayre, where she heals her husband and her enemies.

works.title: The Legend of Good Women
works.author: Geoffrey Chaucer
works.note: Middle English text from W. W. Skeat, The Complete Works of Geoffrey Chaucer, vol. III (Clarendon Press, 1899; Gutenberg #45027). The Prologue survives in two versions, both given here (Text B, the later, and Text A, the earlier); Skeat's variant readings, introductions and notes are not reproduced. The collection is unfinished after the ninth legend; Skeat's Latin rubrics (Incipit/Explicit) are omitted.
works.blurb: Commanded by the God of Love to atone for Troilus and Criseyde, the poet dreams a Prologue among daisies and then tells nine legends of women who were faithful in love and betrayed by men.

works.title: The Legends of Saint Patrick
works.author: Aubrey de Vere
works.note: Text of the Cassell’s National Library edition (1892), which reprints the 1872 volume. The introduction, author’s preface, prose arguments and notes are omitted.
works.blurb: Fifteen narrative poems on the conversion of Ireland, from the infant baptism of Patrick to his dying Confession, drawn from the ancient Lives of the saint.

works.author: Sir Francis Kynaston
works.blurb: Kynaston's rhyme-royal romance of the Welsh prince Leoline and the Princess Sydanis, enchanted lovers parted by sorcery and reunited after many adventures, first printed in 1642 with the Cynthiades.

works.title: The Lesser Testament
works.subtitle: Le Lais, translated by John Payne
works.author: François Villon
works.note: Payne's English verse translation (1878) of Villon's Lesser Testament, in forty stanzas, as printed in the Mosher edition (Portland, Maine, 1909). Payne's introduction and notes are not included. Stanza numerals are Payne's.
works.blurb: Written at Christmas 1456, as Villon prepared to leave Paris, this is a comic will in which he bequeaths his imaginary property, and his scorn, to friends, enemies and officials of the city.

works.title: The Libation-Bearers
works.subtitle: The Oresteia
works.author: Aeschylus
works.note: Translated by E. D. A. Morshead (1881), from Project Gutenberg #8604, The House of Atreus. Text of the play only; the Harvard Classics introductory note is omitted.
works.blurb: Orestes, banished since boyhood, comes back to his father's tomb at Argos and meets his sister Electra there among the women bearing offerings for the dead. At Apollo's bidding he kills his mother Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus to avenge Agamemnon, and is driven out of his wits by the avenging Furies.

works.title: Liberty
works.subtitle: A Poem in Five Parts
works.author: James Thomson
works.note: Text of The Complete Poetical Works of James Thomson, ed. J. Logie Robertson (Oxford: Henry Frowde, 1908). The prose dedication, the prose summaries (the Contents of each part) and the editor's notes are omitted.
works.blurb: Thomson's blank-verse vision in five parts, in which the Goddess of Liberty traces her course from ancient Greece and Rome through the dark ages to her settled home in Britain.

sections.title: Part I: Ancient and Modern Italy Compared

works.title: The Life and Death of Jason
works.subtitle: A Poem
works.author: William Morris
works.note: Bell and Daldy, 1867 (first edition), read from an Internet Archive scan (lifedeathofjaso00morruoft) and collated with the Longmans 1902 tenth impression (lifedeathofjas00morr); where the first edition's OCR was damaged, the later scan was used to repair it. The text is the first edition's, so it differs in places from the revised later impressions. The seventeen books are kept as sections. The songs sung within the books (the Nereid's song 'I know a little garden close', the songs of Orpheus and of the Sirens) stay inside their books. The prose Argument at the head of the poem, the printer's errata, the 1902 prose summaries of the books and the publishers' lists are left out. The Nereid's song also appears, under the title 'A Garden by the Sea', among the poems on this poet's page.
works.blurb: Morris's first long narrative poem, in seventeen books of rhymed couplets: Jason's boyhood among the Centaurs, the voyage of the Argo, the winning of the Golden Fleece with Medea's help, and the tragedy of their later life at Iolchos and Corinth.

works.title: A Life-Drama
works.subtitle: In Thirteen Scenes

works.note: Text of Poems, third edition (London: David Bogue, 1854). Scene settings and stage directions are omitted; the speakers’ names are kept. The work is a dramatic poem, not a stage play.
works.blurb: The poem that made Smith’s name: the story of the young poet Walter, his ambition, loves and disillusion, told in blank verse and lyric in thirteen scenes.

works.title: The Light of Asia
works.author: Sir Edwin Arnold
works.blurb: Arnold's blank-verse life of the Buddha, narrated by a devout Buddhist, from the prince's birth through the Great Renunciation to his enlightenment and teaching.

works.author: Sir Edwin Arnold
works.blurb: Arnold's blank-verse life of Christ, told by Mary Magdalene to a visiting Indian sage in her house at Magdala, from the Nativity to the Resurrection.

works.blurb: A verse romance of the Scottish Wars of Independence, from Robert the Bruce's return to the Hebrides in 1307 to his victory at Bannockburn, woven round the story of Edith of Lorn.

works.blurb: The King of Navarre and his three lords swear off women, wealth and sleep for three years of study, only for the Princess of France and her ladies to arrive on an embassy and overturn the oath. Berowne, Longaville and Dumaine each write secret love-verses and are found out in turn, and the lords disguise themselves as Muscovites to woo the ladies, who mock them. A pageant of the Nine Worthies is interrupted by news of the French king's death, and the ladies set the lovers a year's penance, ending with the songs of Spring and Winter.

works.blurb: A verse novel in twelve cantos: the Comtesse de Nevers, once the lover of Lord Alfred Vargrave, calls him to Luchon on the eve of his marriage, and a story of renunciation and loyalty unfolds.

He rides out with the lady Elene and her dwarf to free the Lady of Synadowne, defeating Maugys, Lambard, Gyffroun and other champions on the way, and at last frees the lady from her enchantment by a kiss.

works.title: The Tragedy of Macbeth

works.blurb: Returning from battle, the Scottish general Macbeth is hailed by three witches as future king. Urged on by Lady Macbeth, he murders King Duncan in his sleep and seizes the throne, then kills Banquo and Macduff's family to secure it. Haunted by guilt, and by Banquo's ghost, he falls to the English army and Macduff at Dunsinane, as Birnam Wood seems to come against him. The play ends with Malcolm proclaimed king.

works.blurb: While Herakles is away in the Underworld on his last labour, the usurper Lykus threatens to kill his wife, sons and aged father; the hero returns in time to save them, only for Hera to send Madness upon him. Arthur Way renders Euripides' tragedy in English verse, with the choral odes in rhymed lyric measures.

The Sauptika Parva recounts the night massacre: Ashvatthama, resolving on revenge for the dying Duryodhana, kills the sleeping Pandava camp, and the Aishika weapon is loosed and turned aside.

The Stri Parva is the lament of the women: Dhritarashtra's grief and anger, Gandhari's curse, the widows moving over the field of Kurukshetra among the dead, and the funeral rites for the fallen.

The Santi Parva, the longest book of the epic, opens with Bhishma lying on his bed of arrows after the war, instructing the grieving Yudhishthira on the duties of kings, on conduct in times of distress, and on the paths to liberation.

The Aswamedhika Parva tells of the horse sacrifice by which Yudhishthira, once the war is over and the kingdom secure, claims the sovereignty of the earth. Before it Krishna relates the Anugita, a philosophical discourse to Arjuna, and Arjuna follows the sacrificial horse on its wanderings, fighting its opponents.

The Asramavasika Parva follows the old king Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Kunti as they leave the city for a hermitage in the forest, where the dead of the war are briefly seen again, and ends with the forest fire in which they die.

The Mausala Parva records the destruction of the Vrishni clan, who slaughter one another with iron clubs thirty-six years after the war, and the departure of Krishna and Balarama from the world.

In the Mahaprasthanika Parva the Pandavas renounce the kingdom and walk north toward the Himalaya, and one by one Draupadi and four of her husbands fall by the way.

The Svargarohanika Parva brings the epic to its close: Yudhishthira's trial at the gates of Heaven, his sight of Hell, the reunion of the heroes, and the closing words on the merit of hearing the Mahabharata.

works.blurb: Rustaveli's Georgian national epic of c. 1200: the knight Tariel, clad in a panther's skin, and Avt'handil, who sets out to find him, search for the lost Nestan-Daredjan, in a tale of love, loyalty and chivalry.

works.blurb: Byron's Faustian drama of a Count in the high Alps, tormented by guilt over the death of Astarte, who summons the spirits of the universe, refuses to bow to Arimanes, and defies the demons who come for his soul.

The prologue, The Lawyer’s First Tale (printed in five parts, numbered I to V), The Clergyman’s First Tale, The Mate’s Story and The Clergyman’s Second Tale already stand among Clough’s poems, together with the linking passages that close each of them. The italics of the printed text are not reproduced.
works.blurb: Tales told by passengers on an Atlantic steamer, on the subject of love and marriage: here the traveller’s own tale and the lawyer’s second.

works.title: Marino Faliero, Doge of Venice
works.subtitle: An Historical Tragedy
works.author: George Gordon, Lord Byron
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #20158, The Works of Lord Byron: Poetry, vol. 4, ed. E. H. Coleridge (1901). The editor's introduction, the appendix, footnotes, variant readings and line numbers are omitted; stage directions are given in brackets.
works.blurb: Byron's tragedy in five acts, first published in 1821, on the fourteenth-century Doge of Venice. Marino Faliero, an old man whose appeal for justice against the patrician Michel Steno's insult is dismissed by the Forty as a trifling punishment, is drawn by the plebeian leader Israel Bertuccio into a conspiracy to overthrow the aristocratic Council. The plot is betrayed, the conspirators are condemned by the Council of Ten, and the Doge is sentenced to death and beheaded on the Giants' Staircase.

works.title: Marmion
works.subtitle: A Tale of Flodden Field
works.author: Sir Walter Scott
works.blurb: A verse romance of treachery and doomed love set against the Scottish army's march to its catastrophic defeat at Flodden in 1513.

works.title: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
works.author: William Blake
works.note: Text of the Luce edition (Boston, 1906), via Project Gutenberg #45315; Blake's plate designs are not reproduced.
works.blurb: Blake's satirical prophetic book, engraved in the early 1790s, overturns the moral order of Heaven and Hell: Energy is Eternal Delight, and the Devil's party speaks for Genius and Imagination. Blending verse, aphorism, parable and prose, it sets the Proverbs of Hell beside five Memorable Fancies and closes with A Song of Liberty, a visionary salute to the revolutions of his age.

works.title: The Masnavi (abridged), Books I–VI
works.subtitle: The Spiritual Couplets, abridged and translated by E. H. Whinfield
works.author: Jalal al-Din Rumi
works.note: Abridged translation by E. H. Whinfield (Kegan Paul, Trübner's Oriental Series, 2nd ed., London, 1898; first edition 1887), the text of sacred-texts.com. All six books of the Masnavi are present in this abridgement, but Whinfield renders only selected passages in verse and summarises the rest in prose. Only his verse is given here: his prose summaries, marginal headings and footnotes are omitted, as are the few stories he gives in prose alone. Obvious keying slips in the online text have been corrected. Whinfield is also the translator of the archive's Khayyam quatrains. The archive's other Masnavi is Redhouse's version of Book I (1881). Marginal headings and prose arguments have been removed; a few may remain.
works.blurb: Rumi's great Persian Sufi teaching poem in six books, here in E. H. Whinfield's abridged English version, opening with the lament of the reed-flute torn from its reed-bed and moving through tales of the prince and the handmaid, the lion and the beasts, the harper and 'Omar, and the elephant in the dark room.

works.subtitle: A Monodrama
works.author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
works.note: From Maud, and Other Poems, a new edition (London: Edward Moxon, 1859), Project Gutenberg ebook 56913. The poem alone, in the two parts and numbered divisions of the 1859 edition; the printed stanza numbers are left out. First published 1855.
works.blurb: A young man, embittered by his father's ruin and death, finds love and hope in Maud, then loses her in a duel, and passes through madness toward a stern new purpose.

works.subtitle: till the death of Iulius Caesar
works.author: Thomas May
works.note: From A Continuation of Lucans Historicall Poem (London, 1630), transcribed by the Text Creation Partnership (EEBO-TCP A07324). May's own Latin and English poem completing Lucan's narrative to the death of Caesar. Printers' VV/vv given as W/w and long s as s; marginal glosses, prose annotations, dedication and commendatory matter omitted. Letters the transcribers could not read are shown as •, except where one letter alone completes the word; the printer's unrecognised punctuation marks are kept as ▪.
works.blurb: Thomas May's own seven-book English epic in heroic couplets, written to carry Lucan's unfinished story of the civil war on from Caesar at Alexandria to his assassination.

works.title: The Mayor of Zalamea
works.author: Pedro Calderón de la Barca
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #63776 (Eight Dramas of Calderon, freely translated by Edward FitzGerald, Macmillan 1906, reprinting the Six Dramas of 1853 and the Two Dramas of 1865). FitzGerald's advertisement, footnotes and afterwords are omitted.
works.blurb: Soldiers of Philip II are quartered at Zalamea, and the Captain dishonours the daughter of Pedro Crespo, a prosperous farmer. Crespo, newly made Mayor, arrests the Captain and has him judged and executed, and the King upholds his justice. The one play in the volume FitzGerald says was already well known.

works.title: Measure for Measure
works.author: William Shakespeare
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #100 (The Complete Works of William Shakespeare), revised 24 Aug 2025.
works.blurb: Duke Vincentio of Vienna pretends to leave the city and, disguised as a friar, hands his strict deputy Angelo the enforcement of laws long neglected. Angelo condemns Claudio to death for fathering a child out of wedlock, then offers to spare him if Claudio’s sister Isabella, a novice nun, will yield herself to him. Isabella refuses, and the Duke, watching in disguise, contrives a bed-trick that substitutes Angelo’s abandoned betrothed Mariana, and finally unmasks himself in a public reckoning of justice and mercy.

works.title: Medea
works.author: Euripides
works.note: Text from Internet Archive scans of The Tragedies of Euripides in English Verse, vol. I (1894), checked against a second scan and the 1912 Loeb Classical Library revision for OCR errors only. Way's prose argument, footnotes, running heads and line numbers are omitted.
works.blurb: Abandoned in Corinth by Jason, who has taken the king's daughter as his new bride, the sorceress Medea plans a vengeance that will cost her what she loves most. Arthur Way renders Euripides' tragedy in rhymed English verse, with the choral odes in lyric measures.

works.title: The Merchant of Venice
works.author: William Shakespeare
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #1515 (The Merchant of Venice), cross-checked against #100 (The Complete Works of William Shakespeare).
works.blurb: To fund his friend Bassanio's courtship of the heiress Portia, the merchant Antonio borrows three thousand ducats from the moneylender Shylock, pledging a pound of his own flesh against default. When Antonio's ships are lost, Shylock demands his bond in open court, and Portia, disguised as a young lawyer, turns the letter of the law against him. Beside the trial run the riddle of the three caskets, the elopement of Shylock's daughter Jessica, and the comedy of the rings.

works.blurb: Blank-verse Arthurian narrative in seven parts: the ruin of Camelot and the old enchanter Merlin, held by Vivian in the forest of Broceliande.

works.blurb: The first book of Rumi's great Persian Sufi teaching poem, opening with the lament of the reed-flute torn from its reed-bed, and moving through tales of the prince and the handmaid, the parrot and the oilman, and the lion and the beasts, each tale unfolding a lesson of love and the soul's return to God.

works.title: Much Ado About Nothing
works.author: William Shakespeare
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #100 (The Complete Works of William Shakespeare), revised 24 Aug 2025.
works.blurb: In Messina, Claudio, fresh from the wars, woos Hero with the help of his prince, Don Pedro, while Hero's cousin Beatrice and the soldier Benedick trade barbed wit and swear they will never love. Friends contrive to make each believe the other is secretly in love, even as Don John, the prince's embittered bastard brother, plots to shame Hero on her wedding day. The slander is exposed by the bumbling constable Dogberry and his watch, Hero is restored, and the sparring pair are brought to marriage.

The speakers' names appear only where the edition prints them.
works.blurb: Samuel Daniel's long verse dialogue in defence of poetry and learning. Philocosmus, the lover of the world, scorns the poet's idle art; Musophilus, the lover of the Muses, answers him at length on fame, the worth of the English language, the dangers of ignorance and the place of learning in a commonwealth. It is dedicated, in a sonnet, to Fulke Greville.

works.blurb: The story of King Nala of Nishadha and Damayanti, princess of Vidarbha: the swan messenger, the choice among the gods, the possession of Nala by the demon Kali, the dice, the desertion in the forest and the long wanderings, until husband and wife are reunited and his kingdom restored.

works.subtitle: Verse sections only

works.note: From The Collected Poems of Roden Noel, with a notice by John Addington Symonds (Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner, 1902), Internet Archive scan (text rebuilt from the scan's word coordinates). A Modern Faust is a vision-poem in six books that mixes verse with prose. Only the verse sections are given here: the Prologue, Books I and II, Book III Cantos I and II, Book V Cantos II and III, and Book VI. The prose Preface, Summary, Book IV and the prose-led Cantos (Book III Canto III, Book V Canto I) are left out, as are the author's notes.
works.blurb: Noel's long visionary poem of a modern Faust, a pilgrim who goes from faith through doubt and disorder to a vision of order.

The song 'Lost', sung within Book IV, is left out here and appears as a separate poem; the author's notes are omitted.

First published in 1874. The prose Preface and the author's notes are left out; the song 'Mosi-oa-Tunya' is kept inside Canto IV, where it stands in the book.
works.blurb: A blank-verse narrative in seven cantos of David Livingstone's last years in Africa, his death, and the carrying of his body home, with the lyric 'Mosi-oa-Tunya' set within it.

works.subtitle: From Songs of the Heights and Deeps
works.author: Roden Noel
works.note: From The Collected Poems of Roden Noel, with a notice by John Addington Symonds (Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner, 1902), Internet Archive scan (text rebuilt from the scan's word coordinates). Melcha stands in Songs of the Heights and Deeps (1885). It has three parts; the small numerals II and III did not survive the scan's OCR, so those divisions follow the spacing of the printed pages (checked against the page image for II). The author's notes are omitted.
works.blurb: A narrative poem in three parts about the pensive maiden Melcha, wooed by the fairy knight O'Donoghue and carried under the waters of an Irish lake as his bride.

The dedication, the notes and the other apparatus are not reproduced. In Canto VI Sotheby abridges the tale told by Sherasmin (his own note says he has omitted nearly the whole of it), and the stanzas run on without it. Text from the University of Toronto scans of the 1805 edition (Internet Archive, oberonpoem01wieluoft and oberonpoem02wieluoft), checked against a second scan of the same edition.
works.blurb: Wieland's romance of the knight Huon of Bordeaux, sent by Charlemagne to Babylon and helped by the fairy king Oberon, who has sworn to reconcile with his queen Titania only when a faithful pair keep their vows through every trial; Sotheby's English verse version of the German epic.

Theseus gives him shelter and defends him against Creon and the pleas of his son Polynices, and Oedipus passes mysteriously from the sight of men, a blessing to Athens.

works.title: Oedipus the King
works.author: Sophocles

Oedipus vows to find him, and the search leads step by step to the truth about his own birth and to the fulfilment of the oracle: Jocasta hangs herself, and Oedipus blinds himself.

works.author: William Shakespeare
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #100 (The Complete Works of William Shakespeare), revised 24 Aug 2025.
works.blurb: Othello, the Moor who commands Venice's forces, secretly marries Desdemona, the daughter of the senator Brabantio, and is sent to defend Cyprus against the Turks. His ensign Iago, passed over for promotion, poisons his mind with the lie that Desdemona is unfaithful to him with the lieutenant Cassio. Driven to jealous rage by a lost handkerchief and Iago's insinuations, Othello smothers Desdemona in her bed, and learns the truth too late to do anything but take his own life.

works.blurb: Weston's 1894 verse rendering, the first complete English Parzival, in long rhyming couplets.

works.title: The Passage of the Red Sea
works.author: Reginald Heber
works.note: From The Poetical Works of Reginald Heber, D.D. (London and New York: Frederick Warne, The Lansdowne Poets, n.d.; 1874 per Internet Archive metadata). The author's prose notes are omitted.
works.blurb: A poem on the Israelites' crossing of the Red Sea and the overthrow of Pharaoh's host.

sections.title: The Passage of the Red Sea

works.title: The Pastime of Pleasure
works.subtitle: An Allegorical Poem
works.author: Stephen Hawes
works.note: First printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1509; this is the text of the 1845 Percy Society edition (ed. Thomas Wright), Project Gutenberg #58037, with the introduction and notes omitted. Original spelling kept.
works.blurb: Hawes's allegorical romance in rhyme royal: the young Graunde Amoure learns the seven liberal arts in the Tower of Doctrine, wins the hand of La Bell Pucell by slaying giants and monsters, and is brought through age and death to the judgement of Fame, Time and Eternity.

works.title: Patience
works.author: Gawain Poet
works.note: Middle English text of BL Cotton Nero A.x, ed. Richard Morris, Early English Alliterative Poems, EETS 1 (2nd ed. 1869); sidenotes, notes and glossary omitted.
works.blurb: A retelling of the Book of Jonah in about 530 alliterative lines, preceded by a prologue on the Beatitudes of poverty and patience. The reluctant prophet flees by sea, is swallowed by the whale and is finally rebuked for his anger at God's mercy.

works.title: Pearl
works.author: Gawain Poet
works.note: Anonymous Middle English original (Cotton Nero A.x). This is Sophie Jewett's 1908 verse translation, made in the metre and stanza-form of the original and long in the public domain.
works.blurb: A grieving father falls asleep on the grave of his infant daughter and dreams her transfigured into a maiden of Heaven, radiant among the elect — an elegy of loss answered by consolation, in interlocking rhymed stanzas.

works.title: Pearl (Middle English text)
works.subtitle: The Pearl
works.author: Gawain Poet
works.note: Middle English text of BL Cotton Nero A.x, ed. Richard Morris, Early English Alliterative Poems, EETS 1 (2nd ed. 1869); sidenotes, notes and glossary omitted.
works.blurb: The original Middle English text of the dream-vision elegy, in 101 twelve-line stanzas of interlocking rhyme and alliteration. A bereaved father falls asleep by the grave of his lost pearl and sees her, transfigured, across a stream in the heavenly city.

works.title: Peer Gynt
works.subtitle: A Dramatic Poem
works.author: Henrik Ibsen
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #66239 (The Collected Works of Henrik Ibsen, vol. IV, Heinemann, 1907), translated by William and Charles Archer. Introduction, translators' footnotes and appendix omitted.
works.blurb: Peer Gynt, a boastful young peasant, steals a bride, flees into the mountains and the hall of the Troll King, and goes out into the world: a rich trader in Morocco, a prophet among the Bedouin, an emperor in a Cairo madhouse. Returning old and empty-handed, he meets the Button-Moulder, who has come to melt him down, and the faithful Solveig, who has waited.

works.title: The Psalms of David (Psalms 44–150)
works.subtitle: Metrical paraphrase from the Sidney Psalter, in the 1823 printed text
works.author: Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke
works.note: Text from the first printed edition (1823), spelling kept as printed; Psalm 119 is printed in 22 parts, one for each Hebrew letter. Psalms 1–43 are by Sir Philip Sidney.
works.blurb: The Countess of Pembroke's verse paraphrase of Psalms 44–150, each psalm in a different stanza form, completing the psalter begun by her brother Sir Philip Sidney.

works.title: The Persians
works.author: Aeschylus
works.note: Translated by E. D. A. Morshead (1908), from Project Gutenberg #8714, Four Plays of Aeschylus. Text of the play only; the introduction and argument are omitted.
works.blurb: At the Persian court of Susa, the elders and the queen mother Atossa wait anxiously for news of Xerxes and his vast army, gone to conquer Greece. A messenger arrives with the tale of Salamis and the ruin of the fleet, and the ghost of Darius is raised from the tomb to name the king's pride as the cause. Xerxes returns in rags to a chorus of lament.

works.title: Peru
works.subtitle: A Poem in Six Cantos
works.author: Helen Maria Williams
works.note: The revised text printed in volume II of Williams's Poems (1786), London: T. Cadell, as transcribed by Project Gutenberg (ebook 11054) and compared with the Internet Archive scan of the same volume. It is the author's revision of the 1784 first edition (Peru, a Poem in Six Cantos, 1784). The dedication, advertisement, cantos' arguments and her footnotes are omitted, as are the line numbers.
works.blurb: A poem in six cantos on the Spanish conquest of Peru, the fall of the Inca Ataliba and the sufferings of his queen Alzira, ending in an appeal against cruelty and the lust for gold.

works.title: The Phenomena and Diosemeia
works.author: Aratus of Soli
works.blurb: A heroic-couplet version of Aratus’s star-poem and its weather signs by John Lamb, Dean of Bristol, published in 1848.

works.title: Phaenomena
works.author: Aratus
works.note: Prose translation, Loeb Classical Library (1921), from theoi.com. Mair’s own divisions are kept; line numbers follow the Greek and are given in the section titles.
works.blurb: Aratus’s hexameter account of the constellations, the celestial circles, the risings of the zodiac and the weather signs, a poem of the stars that was widely read and translated in antiquity.

sections.title: A. Constellations north of the ecliptic (Lines 19–318)
B. Constellations south of the ecliptic (Lines 319–453)
D. Circles of the celestial sphere (Lines 462–558)

works.title: Pharonnida
works.subtitle: A Heroick Poem
works.author: William Chamberlayne
works.note: William Chamberlayne’s heroic poem, from the 1659 first edition (EEBO-TCP A31613). Original spelling; long s and VV normalised. Letters the transcribers could not read are shown as •, except where one letter alone makes a word of the period, where it is supplied; unreadable words are shown as […].
works.blurb: A heroic romance in rhymed couplets, in five books of five cantos each, of love and adventure among Christians and Turks; text from the 1659 edition (EEBO-TCP), in original spelling.

works.title: Pharsalia
works.subtitle: De Bello Civili (The Civil War)
works.author: Lucan
works.note: Verse translation; the poem was left unfinished at Lucan’s death.
works.blurb: Lucan’s unfinished epic of the Roman civil war between Julius Caesar and Pompey, notable for banishing the gods from its narrative entirely.

works.title: The Civil War (Pharsalia)
works.subtitle: Books I-X, Loeb translation by J. D. Duff
works.author: Lucan
works.note: Prose translation, Loeb Classical Library 1928; text from the unrevised 1962 reprint.
works.blurb: J. D. Duff's plain prose translation of Lucan's unfinished epic of the Roman civil war between Caesar and Pompey, ten books ending where Lucan's text breaks off.

works.title: Pharsalia
works.subtitle: Lucan's Pharsalia, containing the civil wars between Caesar and Pompey
works.author: Lucan
works.note: From Lucans Pharsalia (London, 1614), transcribed by the Text Creation Partnership (EEBO-TCP A06411). 1614 spelling kept; long s normalised; commendatory verses and marginal glosses omitted.
works.blurb: Sir Arthur Gorges's 1614 rhymed translation of Lucan's epic of the Roman civil war, in octosyllabic couplets, with a verse argument before each book.

works.title: Pharsalia (May)
works.subtitle: Lucans Pharsalia: or The Civill Warres of Rome, betweene Pompey the Great, and Iulius Caesar
works.author: Lucan
works.note: From Lucans Pharsalia (London, 1631; third edition of May's complete translation, first published 1627), transcribed by the Text Creation Partnership (EEBO-TCP A06415). Printers' VV/vv given as W/w and long s as s; marginal glosses, prose annotations, dedication and commendatory matter omitted. Letters the transcribers could not read are shown as •, except where one letter alone completes the word; the printer's unrecognised punctuation marks are kept as ▪.
works.blurb: Thomas May's rhymed heroic-couplet translation of Lucan's epic of the Roman civil war, the first complete English version in pentameter couplets, with May's own verse argument before each book.

works.title: Pharsalia (Rowe)
works.subtitle: Lucan's Pharsalia, translated into English verse by Nicholas Rowe
works.author: Lucan
works.note: Nicholas Rowe's verse translation, first published 1718 (Tonson); text from the 1812 reprint, checked against the 1718 and 1722 editions (Internet Archive).
works.blurb: Nicholas Rowe's version of Lucan's epic of the Roman civil war between Caesar and Pompey, in heroic couplets, published after the translator's death in 1718.

works.title: Philoctetes
works.author: Sophocles
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #14484 (Sophocles: The Seven Plays in English Verse), Lewis Campbell's translation, first published 1883, World's Classics revision of 1906. Campbell's introductions, footnotes and notes are omitted.
works.blurb: Odysseus brings the young Neoptolemus to Lemnos to trick the exiled Philoctetes out of the bow of Heracles, without which Troy cannot fall. Neoptolemus, moved by pity and shame, gives the bow back, and only the appearance of the deified Heracles persuades the wounded archer to sail for Troy and healing.

works.title: The Phoenician Maidens
works.author: Euripides
works.note: Text from the Internet Archive scan of The Tragedies of Euripides in English Verse, vol. III (1898). Way's prose argument, footnotes, running heads and marginal line numbers are omitted; OCR errors were corrected by hand.
works.blurb: Thebes is besieged by Polyneikes and his Argive host, and the house of Oedipus stands on the edge of its last catastrophe: Jocasta, Kreon, the blind seer Teiresias and a chorus of Phoenician maidens watch as the brothers move toward single combat. Arthur Way renders Euripides' tragedy in rhymed English verse.

works.title: The Phoenix
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.translator: trans. Cosette Faust Newton & Stith Thompson (1918)
works.blurb: A richly decorative description of the mythical phoenix and its cyclical death and rebirth in a paradisal eastern land, allegorized in the poem's second half as a figure of Christian resurrection.

works.title: The Phoenix (Old English)
works.subtitle: Old English text
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.note: The Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records, ed. Krapp and Dobbie, vol. III (1936). Old English text as in ASPR; hand-keyed e-text via sacred-texts.com.
works.blurb: The Old English verse of a richly decorative description of the mythical phoenix and its cyclical death and rebirth in a paradisal eastern land, allegorized in the poem's second half as a figure of Christian resurrection.

works.title: The Piccolomini
works.author: Friedrich Schiller
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #6786. Coleridge did not translate the prelude, Wallenstein's Camp. His preface and footnotes are omitted.
works.blurb: At Pilsen, in the Thirty Years' War, the imperial generals gather round their commander Wallenstein while a plot against him is already being laid by Octavio Piccolomini, whose son Max loves Wallenstein's daughter Thekla. Octavio holds a secret commission to take the generalship, and father and son are drawn toward a collision of loyalties.

works.title: Piers Plowman
works.subtitle: The Vision of Piers Ploughman
works.author: William Langland
works.note: Original Middle English text, B-text, edited by Thomas Wright (1842 edition, Library of Old Authors; text as reprinted on Project Gutenberg).
works.blurb: Falling asleep on the Malvern Hills, the dreamer Will sees a field full of folk and sets out through a sequence of visions to find Do-well, Do-bet, and Do-best — a vast alliterative satire of church, court, and commons.

works.title: The Pilgrims of the Sun
works.author: James Hogg
works.note: Text of the Blackie edition (Glasgow, 1838), vol. 2. The Notes to the poem are omitted.
works.blurb: A visionary poem in four books, in Spenserian stanzas, in which a Scottish girl, Mary Lee, is borne in spirit through the planets and the sun, with a dedication to Lord Byron.

works.title: Pippa Passes
works.subtitle: A Drama
works.author: Robert Browning
works.note: Text of the Cambridge Edition (Houghton Mifflin, 1895), from Project Gutenberg. Browning's 1841 advertisement and the editor's headnote are omitted. Speakers are given in capitals; Browning's prose passages (the students' talk in Noon, the Bishop's scene in Night) are kept as prose. The drama has no epilogue.
works.blurb: Browning's drama of New Year's Day at Asolo follows Pippa, a silk-mill girl on her one holiday, whose songs, passing unheard by, break in on four scenes of love, guilt, plot and temptation and change the lives of those who hear them.

works.title: The Pleasures of Memory
works.subtitle: In Two Parts
works.author: Samuel Rogers
works.note: Text of Rogers's Poems (London: T. Cadell and W. Davies, 1814), from Project Gutenberg eBook #13586. The prose analyses, prefaces, arguments, epigraphs and notes are omitted.
works.blurb: Samuel Rogers's best-known poem, in heroic couplets, on the association of ideas and the consolations of memory, from a revisited village to the afterlife.

works.title: The Poetic Edda
works.subtitle: Lays of the Gods and Lays of the Heroes, translated from the Icelandic with the stanza numbering of the standard editions
works.author: Anonymous (Old Norse)
works.blurb: The great Old Norse collection of mythological and heroic lays preserved in the Codex Regius, in Bellows's 1923 verse translation, with the Eddas' own prose links kept in place.

works.title: The Elder Edda
works.subtitle: The Poetic Edda of Sæmund
works.author: Anonymous (Old Norse)
works.blurb: The Old Norse mythological and heroic lays of the Codex Regius in Benjamin Thorpe's 1866 prose translation, with the manuscripts' own prose links kept in place.

sections.title: Fragments of the Lay of Sigurd and Brynhild

works.title: The Poet's Pilgrimage to Waterloo
works.subtitle: Proem and two parts (1816)
works.author: Robert Southey
works.note: Text of the collected Poetical Works (1845 printing), read from two Internet Archive scans (completepoetica00soutgoog and poeticalworksro24soutgoog) collated line by line; the argument, Southey's prose notes and the footnote quotations are omitted. The stanzas are numbered in the print; the numbers are dropped here. Damaged lines and stanzas (the scans are torn or smudged in several places) were restored from three Internet Archive scans of the 1816 first edition (poetspilgrimage01soutgoog, poetspilgrimaget00sout, poetspilgrimage00soutgoog), whose spelling differs slightly in a few words.
works.blurb: Southey's account in six-line stanzas of his journey in 1815 through Flanders and Brussels to the field of Waterloo, followed by a dream-vision on the Mountain of the Muse in which he is shown the hopes of mankind after the victory.

Part I, Canto IV: The Scene of War
Part II, Canto I: The Tower
Part II, Canto II: The Evil Prophet
Part II, Canto III: The Sacred Mountain
Part II, Canto IV: The Hopes of Man

works.title: Politian: Scenes from an Unpublished Drama
works.author: Edgar Allan Poe
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #79019 (The Poetical Works of Edgar Allan Poe); the five scenes first printed in the Southern Literary Messenger, 1835-36.
works.blurb: Poe's only drama, left unfinished, survives in five blank-verse scenes set in Rome. Politian, Earl of Leicester, loves Lalage, a ward whose betrothal to the Count Castiglione stands in the way; haunted by melancholy and fatal premonition, he is drawn toward a challenge that the scenes break off before resolving.

works.title: Poltava
works.subtitle: A poem in three cantos
works.author: Alexander Pushkin
works.blurb: Pushkin's narrative poem of Mazeppa, Kotzubei and his daughter Marie, set against the Ukrainian hetman's betrayal of Peter the Great and the battle of Poltava (1709), in Charles Edward Turner's 1899 English version.

works.title: Poly-Olbion
works.subtitle: A Chorographicall Description of Great Britain, in thirty Songs
works.author: Michael Drayton
works.note: Drayton’s Poly-Olbion, Part I (1612, EEBO-TCP A20847) and Part II (1622, EEBO-TCP A20849): thirty songs; Selden’s prose Illustrations and the marginal notes are left out. Original spelling; long s and VV normalised. Letters the transcribers could not read are shown as •, except where one letter alone makes a word of the period, where it is supplied; unreadable words are shown as […].
works.blurb: Drayton's topographical poem in alexandrines on the rivers, hills, forests and history of England and Wales, in thirty Songs (Songs 1-18 printed 1612, Songs 19-30 in 1622), each opening with its verse Argument; Selden's prose Illustrations are omitted.

works.title: Garrick's Looking-Glass; or, the Art of Rising on the Stage
works.subtitle: A Poem in Three Cantos
works.author: Samuel Jackson Pratt
works.blurb: A satirical poem in three cantos on the theatrical world of David Garrick, published in 1776 (TCP K040357).

works.title: Humanity, or the Rights of Nature
works.subtitle: A Poem in Two Books
works.author: Samuel Jackson Pratt
works.blurb: Pratt’s verse attack on the slave trade and on cruelty to the weak, in heroic couplets, published in 1788 (TCP K038048).

works.title: Sympathy; or, a Sketch of the Social Passion
works.subtitle: A Poem
works.author: Samuel Jackson Pratt
works.blurb: A two-book poem in praise of fellow-feeling as the bond of society, published in 1781 (TCP K094645).

works.title: Prince Arthur
works.subtitle: An Heroick Poem in Ten Books
works.author: Sir Richard Blackmore
works.note: Text from the 1695 first edition (EEBO-TCP A28298), with original spelling; the preface, errata and publisher's advertisement are omitted.
works.blurb: Blackmore's first epic, in ten books of rhymed couplets, follows the British prince Arthur against the Saxons, with Lucifer and the powers of Hell working to thwart him.

works.title: Prince Hohenstiel-Schwangau, Saviour of Society
works.author: Robert Browning
works.blurb: A dramatic monologue in blank verse in which a disgraced ruler, a thinly veiled Napoleon III, defends his career to a woman in London.

works.title: The Prince's Quest
works.author: William Watson
works.note: Text from The Poems of William Watson (Macmillan, New York and London, 1893); the poem first appeared in The Prince's Quest and Other Poems (1880).
works.blurb: A romance in ten parts of a prince who sets out in search of the meaning of life and love, written in rhymed couplets.

works.title: Prometheus Bound
works.author: Aeschylus
works.note: Translated by E. D. A. Morshead (1908), from Project Gutenberg #8714, Four Plays of Aeschylus. Text of the play only; the volume's introduction and the prefatory Argument are omitted.
works.blurb: For giving fire to mortals against the will of Zeus, the Titan Prometheus is nailed to a crag in the Scythian wastes by Strength and Force, while a reluctant Hephaestus does the work. Visited by the sea-nymphs, by Oceanus and by the wandering, cow-horned Io, he foretells the fall of Zeus, until Hermes comes to demand the secret and the rocks collapse upon him.

works.title: Prometheus Unbound
works.subtitle: A Lyrical Drama in Four Acts
works.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg no. 4800 (Hutchinson, Oxford edition, 1914), which follows the edition of 1820 as corrected from the 1839 text and the Bodleian fair copy. Shelley's prose Preface, the Dramatis Personae, the Greek epigraph, the editor's line numbers and textual notes, and Mrs Shelley's note are left out. The scene directions are given in square brackets at the head of each section.
works.blurb: Shelley's lyrical drama in four acts, in which the Titan chained to the Caucasus is freed when Jupiter is overthrown and love takes the place of tyranny.

works.title: Psalm of the West
works.author: Sidney Lanier
works.note: From The Poems of Sidney Lanier (Scribner, 1884); dated June 1876 in the volume's contents. Parts of it also appear among the poet's poems as excerpts from Poems of American History (1908).
works.blurb: Lanier's long poem on the making of America, running from Columbus's night voyage and the Norse landing in Vinland through the Mayflower and Lexington.

works.title: Psyche
works.subtitle: or, The Legend of Love
works.author: Mary Tighe
works.note: Text of the 1816 Longman edition (Psyche, with Other Poems), read against two scans. The author's prose Preface and her prose Arguments to the cantos, and the Notes at the end of the volume, are left out. The five proem stanzas open Canto I.
works.blurb: Mary Tighe's retelling of the myth of Cupid and Psyche, from Apuleius, in six cantos of Spenserian stanzas.

sections.title: Dedicatory Sonnet, Addressed to My Mother

works.title: Punica
works.subtitle: The Second Punick War between Hannibal and the Romanes
works.author: Silius Italicus
works.note: Heroic couplets. From The Second Punick War (London, 1661), transcribed by the Text Creation Partnership (EEBO-TCP A60230). 1661 spelling kept; dedications, the Life of Silius and marginal notes omitted; lost passages marked. Each book opens with Ross's verse Argument. Where the transcribers could not read letters or printer's marks, the loss is shown as […]. A page is missing in the source copy twice each in Book XI and Book XII (marked in the text). Ross's own continuation after the poem (the triumph of Scipio to the death of Hannibal) is not included.
works.blurb: Silius Italicus's Latin epic of the war between Rome and Hannibal, the longest surviving Latin epic, in seventeen books of heroic couplets by Thomas Ross.

works.title: The Purgatorio (Okey)
works.subtitle: Prose translation by Thomas Okey (Temple Classics)
works.author: Dante Alighieri
works.note: Thomas Okey's prose Purgatorio for the Temple Classics (Dent, 1901); Italian text, arguments and notes left out.
works.blurb: Dante's climb of the mountain of Purgatory in Thomas Okey's plain, literal prose for the Temple Classics, printed in 1901 as the facing English of the Italian text.

works.title: The Purple Island
works.subtitle: or, The Isle of Man
works.author: Phineas Fletcher
works.note: Text from EEBO-TCP A00977 (the 1633 Cambridge edition), keyed from the ProQuest page images; Fletcher's marginal notes and the stanza numbers are left out. The dedication to Edward Benlowes, the address 'To the Readers' and the commendatory verses are omitted; the Piscatorie Eclogs and miscellanies that follow are given among the poems. The 1633 spelling is kept (no long s or VV occurs in the transcription). Printer's abbreviation strokes are expanded (commands, Io); five end-of-line marks that the transcribers could not identify are given as full stops (Cantos VII, VIII, IX, XI and XII). The transcription's two illegible places fall within Fletcher's marginal notes, which are omitted, so no word of the verse is lost to a gap.
works.blurb: The body of man allegorised as an island, its anatomy described in Spenserian-derived stanzas, and the war of the virtues and vices for it in the last cantos.

works.title: Queen Hynde
works.author: James Hogg
works.note: Text of the Blackie edition (Glasgow, 1838-40), vol. 3. The Notes to the poem are omitted.
works.blurb: Hogg's long romance in six parts, in tetrameter couplets, of a legendary Queen of Scotland in the age of St Columba, and the Norse suitors who beset her.

works.title: The Queen's Wake
works.subtitle: A Legendary Poem
works.author: James Hogg
works.note: Text of the Blackie edition (Glasgow, 1838), vol. 1. The Notes to the poem are omitted.
works.blurb: Hogg's legendary poem of a minstrel contest at Holyrood, where the bards of Scotland sing before Mary, Queen of Scots, in the first weeks after her return from France. Twelve of the seventeen songs are given, among them Kilmeny and The Witch of Fife, together with the framing narrative divided into the Introduction, the three Nights, and the interludes between the songs.

sections.title: Interlude before The Witch of Fife
Interlude after The Witch of Fife
Interlude before The Fate of Macgregor

works.title: The Quest of the Sangraal
works.author: Robert Stephen Hawker
works.note: First published 1864. Text from The Poetical Works of Robert Stephen Hawker, ed. J. G. Godwin (London: Kegan Paul, 1899). Five lines of black-letter inscription (a runic line and heraldic mottoes) were illegible in the scan and are omitted.
works.blurb: Hawker's blank-verse narrative of King Arthur's knights setting out from Tintagel on the quest for the Holy Grail (the Sangraal), with Merlin's prophecy and the lots cast for the four quarters of the world.

works.title: The Raghuvamsa (The Story of Raghu's Line)
works.subtitle: Raghuvamsa
works.author: Kalidasa
works.note: A complete blank-verse translation of the 19 cantos (J. M. Dent, London, 1902; title page: The Raghuvança: The Story of Raghu's Line). Kalidasa's Cloud-Messenger and Birth of the War-God are already in the archive. Johnstone's spelling of names is kept; the Introduction, notes and plate captions are omitted.
works.blurb: Kalidasa's epic of the solar dynasty of Raghu, from King Dilipa's vow at the hermitage of Vasishtha through Rama's life and banishment of Sita to the decline of the line under the last king, Agnivarna.

sections.title: Canto I: How King Dilipa went to Vaçishtha's Hermitage

works.author: Valmiki
works.note: Dutt's condensed verse rendering in long rhymed couplets, in twelve books. Source: sacred-texts.com (via the Wayback Machine). Dutt's prose introduction, his prose summaries at the head of each book, the conclusion and epilogue (both prose) and the footnotes are left out. The Books are headed with Dutt's English titles and the Sanskrit names he gives them.
works.blurb: Romesh Chunder Dutt's condensed English rendering of the Sanskrit epic of Rama, in twelve books of rhymed couplets, from the bridal of Sita to the sacrifice of the horse and the recognition of Lava and Kusa. Published by J. M. Dent and Co., London, 1899.

works.author: Claudian
works.note: Verse translation by Leonard Digges (1588–1635), London: G. P. for Edward Blount, 1617, from the EEBO-TCP transcription (A18949). Original 1617 spelling kept, with long s normalised and printers' VV set as W. Each book is preceded by the printed verse Argument, given here in the section note. Digges's prose commentary is omitted. Two illegible places in the Argument of Book I are marked […]. One printer's punctuation mark in Book II is rendered as a hyphen (swift-drawne) and one at a line end in Book III is dropped.
works.blurb: The first English verse translation of Claudian's unfinished epic of Pluto's abduction of Proserpine, by Leonard Digges, the editor of Shakespeare's Poems (1640).

works.title: The Rape of the Bucket
works.subtitle: La Secchia Rapita, an heroi-comical poem in twelve cantos
works.author: Alessandro Tassoni
works.note: Text of James Atkinson's English verse translation (London: J. M. Richardson, 1825), in the original ottava rima, transcribed from Internet Archive scans of both volumes. The speeches keep their printed quotation marks. Atkinson's preface, life of Tassoni, cantos' arguments, stanza numbers and all notes are omitted.
works.blurb: Tassoni's mock-heroic epic of the war between Modena and Bologna over a stolen wooden bucket, the first of its kind in Italian, in James Atkinson's English ottava rima.

works.title: The Rape of the Lock
works.subtitle: An Heroi-Comical Poem, in Five Cantos
works.author: Alexander Pope
works.blurb: A mock-epic on a society scandal — a lock of hair snipped in jest — blown up with the full machinery of Homeric epic, sylphs and all.

works.title: Red Cotton Night-Cap Country; or, Turf and Towers
works.author: Robert Browning
works.blurb: A narrative in four parts, in blank verse, of a rich young Parisian's religious mania and fatal leap, based on a recent Normandy law case.

works.title: The Regement of Princes
works.subtitle: De Regimine Principum
works.author: Thomas Hoccleve
works.note: Original Middle English text from Thomas Wright's edition, De Regimine Principum: A Poem by Thomas Occleve (London: printed for the Roxburghe Club by J. B. Nichols and Sons, 1860), read from two independent scans of that edition on the Internet Archive and cross-checked against each other. Wright's preface, notes and Latin marginal glosses, the running heads and the page and signature marks are left out; the edition's own quotation marks, damaged in the scans, are omitted, and only plain scanning slips are corrected. The edition prints no chapter divisions: the Prologue (the poet's sleepless night and his dialogue with the Old Man, 288 stanzas) is set apart from the Regement proper that he then writes for Prince Henry. The three closing stanzas, the envoy to the book itself, are in eight lines.
works.blurb: Sleepless at Chester's Inn, the clerk Hoccleve meets an old beggar who talks him into writing a book of counsel for Prince Henry: a verse mirror for princes on justice, mercy, patience, prudence, largesse and peace, in rhyme royal.

works.title: Rhesus
works.author: Euripides
works.note: Text from the Internet Archive scan of The Tragedies of Euripides in English Verse, vol. III (1898), checked against the 1912 Loeb Classical Library English text for names and OCR errors only. Way's prose argument, footnotes, running heads and marginal line numbers are omitted.
works.blurb: On the night after Hector's victory, the Trojan sentinels rouse their chief, a spy is sent into the Greek camp, and the Thracian king Rhesus arrives with his famous snow-white horses, only to be murdered in his sleep by Odysseus and Diomedes. Arthur Way renders the play, whose authorship has long been disputed, in rhymed English verse, with the choral odes in lyric measures.

works.title: The Tragedy of King Richard the Second
works.author: William Shakespeare
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #100 (The Complete Works of William Shakespeare), revised 24 Aug 2025.
works.blurb: Richard II banishes Bolingbroke and Mowbray, seizes the estate of the dying John of Gaunt, and sails for Ireland, only to find on his return that the exiled Bolingbroke has come home with an army. Deposed in Westminster Hall and imprisoned, Richard loses his crown to the man who becomes Henry IV. He is murdered at Pomfret Castle by Sir Pierce of Exton, and Henry is left to mourn the deed he wished for.

works.title: The Tragedy of King Richard the Third
works.author: William Shakespeare
works.blurb: Richard, Duke of Gloucester, plots his way to the crown through the deaths of his brother Clarence, the wooing of Lady Anne, the murder of the princes in the Tower and the use and discarding of Buckingham. On the eve of Bosworth the ghosts of his victims curse him in his sleep and bless his rival, and Richmond's victory begins the Tudor line as Henry VII.

works.title: Roderick, the Last of the Goths
works.subtitle: A Tragic Poem
works.author: Robert Southey
works.note: Text of "A New Edition" (London: Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, 1844); the prefaces and Southey's notes are omitted. First published 1814.
works.blurb: A blank-verse epic in twenty-five sections on the last Visigothic king of Spain, who after his defeat by the Moors lives on as a penitent and fights again beside Pelayo.

sections.title: IV. The Monastery of St. Felix
XXI. The Fountain in the Forest

works.title: Rokeby
works.subtitle: A Poem in Six Cantos
works.author: Sir Walter Scott
works.note: Text of the 1923 Houghton Mifflin volume, checked line by line against Black's Poetical Works (1861) and Ballantyne's first edition (1813). Scott's advertisement, introduction and notes are omitted; the songs stay in their places in the cantos.
works.blurb: A verse romance of the English Civil War, set around Barnard Castle and the River Greta just after Marston Moor, whose outlaw songs — 'Brignall Banks' and 'Allen-a-Dale' among them — became favourites.

works.title: The Romaunt of the Rose
works.author: Geoffrey Chaucer
works.type: Allegorical dream vision (translation from Guillaume de Lorris and Jean de Meun)
works.note: Original Middle English text from W. W. Skeat, The Complete Works of Geoffrey Chaucer, vol. I, 2nd ed. (Clarendon Press, 1899), via Project Gutenberg #43089. This is the Middle English rendering of the French Roman de la Rose. Skeat accepts only Fragment A as Chaucer's own work and prints Fragments B and C as the work of other hands. The French text that Skeat prints beside Fragment A, his marginal headings, line numbers and bracket marks have been removed; the words he supplied in brackets are kept.
works.blurb: A dreamer enters the walled Garden of Love and sets his heart on a rosebud, helped and hindered by allegorical figures such as Fair Welcome, Danger and Reason, in the English version of the great French allegory.

works.title: The Tragedy of Romeo and Juliet
works.author: William Shakespeare
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #100 (The Complete Works of William Shakespeare), revised 24 Aug 2025.
works.blurb: In Verona, the children of two feuding houses, Romeo Montague and Juliet Capulet, fall in love at a masked ball and marry in secret with the help of Friar Lawrence. When Tybalt kills Mercutio and Romeo kills Tybalt, Romeo is banished, and Juliet, pressed to marry Paris, takes a sleeping potion that makes her seem dead. The message to Romeo goes astray, and both lovers die in the tomb, ending their parents' quarrel too late.

works.title: Rose Mary
works.author: Dante Gabriel Rossetti
works.blurb: A ballad in three parts of the magic Beryl-stone, of the maiden Rose Mary who must read it, and of the spirits that dwell in it, with a Beryl-song between the parts.

works.title: The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam
works.subtitle: Fifth Edition
works.author: Edward FitzGerald
works.translator: trans. Edward FitzGerald (1889), from Omar Khayyam
works.note: From Project Gutenberg etext 246. FitzGerald's preface, the Third Edition material and the notes are left out.
works.blurb: FitzGerald's free English version of the quatrains attributed to Omar Khayyam, the fifth edition of 1889.

works.title: The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam
works.subtitle: First Edition
works.author: Edward FitzGerald
works.translator: trans. Edward FitzGerald (1859), from Omar Khayyam
works.note: From Project Gutenberg etext 246. FitzGerald's preface, the Third Edition material and the notes are left out.
works.blurb: FitzGerald's free English version of the quatrains attributed to Omar Khayyam, the first edition of 1859.

works.title: Rubáiyát of Doc Sifers
works.author: James Whitcomb Riley
works.note: Text of the first edition (The Century Co., 1897; Project Gutenberg #32944). The poem is in 105 numbered stanzas, here grouped by tens; the dedicatory verses to Dr. Franklin W. Hays come first. Illustrations omitted.
works.blurb: A Hoosier country doctor, Doc Sifers, is sketched in numbered quatrain-stanzas in Indiana dialect, from his rounds on horseback and his fire-fighting to his plain-spoken kindness.

works.title: Salaman and Absal
works.subtitle: An Allegory
works.author: Jami
works.note: FitzGerald's free verse rendering of Jami's Persian allegory, first published anonymously in 1856; text of the FitzGerald Centenary Edition (1909) from Project Gutenberg. The editor's notes, the Life of FitzGerald, Emerson's essay on Persian poetry and FitzGerald's own preface and notes are not reproduced here. The edition prints the poem in thirty numbered sections; the section titles Prologue, The Story and Epilogue are the edition's own, and underscored emphasis has been dropped.
works.blurb: Jami's allegory of a king of Greece whose son Salaman, nursed and then seduced by the beautiful Absal, flees with her, is saved from a funeral pyre, and is finally freed from earthly love by the heavenly Venus, with the closing section explaining the story as the soul's journey.

works.title: Samson Agonistes
works.subtitle: A Dramatic Poem
works.author: John Milton
works.blurb: A tragedy on the Greek model — the blinded, captive Samson among the Philistines, moving toward his final act.

works.title: Sardanapalus
works.subtitle: A Tragedy
works.author: George Gordon, Lord Byron
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #23475, The Works of Lord Byron: Poetry, vol. 5, ed. E. H. Coleridge (1901). The editor's introduction, Byron's dedication and preface, footnotes, variant readings and line numbers are omitted; stage directions are given in brackets.
works.blurb: Byron's tragedy in five acts, first published in 1821, on the last king of Assyria. Sardanapalus, a pleasure-loving monarch who prefers peace and his Ionian slave Myrrha to war and empire, is roused too late when the Mede Arbaces and the priest Beleses rebel; after fighting bravely he builds a funeral pyre in his palace and dies upon it with Myrrha.

works.title: Ane Pleasant Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis
works.subtitle: In Commendatioun of Vertew and Vituperatioun of Vyce
works.author: Sir David Lyndsay
works.note: Text of David Laing's edition (The Poetical Works of Sir David Lyndsay, Edinburgh: William Paterson, 1871), vol. II, collated against a second scan of the same volume. Speaker names and stage directions are kept as printed; the cast list, line numbers, running heads, notes and glossary are omitted, and the appendix interlude (The Auld Man and his Wife) is not included. The scans' blank lines follow the page layout rather than the stanzas, so speeches are given without stanza breaks.
works.blurb: A long Scots morality play in rhyme, first staged in 1552, in which the young King Humanitas, led astray by Wantonnes and Sensualitie, is brought to reform by Divyne Correctioun and Dame Veritie, while Johne the Common-weill and the poor man Pauper accuse the clergy, lords and merchants of the Thrie Estaitis.

works.title: The School of the Heart
works.author: Henry Alford
works.blurb: A long blank-verse poem in six lessons: a young man's meditation on love, nature, the Church and death, which the author later called a collection of detached passages of youthful feeling.

works.title: The Second Shepherds' Play
works.subtitle: Wakefield (Towneley) Cycle
works.author: Anonymous (Middle English)
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #19481 (Everyman and Other Old Plays, Everyman's Library, ed. Ernest Rhys, 1909), in the editor's modernised spelling; the Wakefield Master's play of the Towneley cycle.
works.blurb: Three Yorkshire shepherds, grumbling on a cold moor, are joined by the sheep-stealer Mak, who steals a lamb and hides it in a cradle at home, passing it off as his newborn son. When the shepherds find it, they toss Mak in a blanket; then an angel sings of Christ's birth, and they go to adore the true child in Bethlehem. The play is famous for its comic parody of the Nativity.

works.subtitle: Selections, trans. Florence Lederer (Wisdom of the East, 1920)

works.blurb: A Persian Sufi poem of 1311 in reply to fifteen questions about the mystic path, in Florence Lederer's selective English verse.

works.title: The Secrets of the Self (Asrar-i Khudi)
works.subtitle: A philosophical poem, translated from the Persian
works.author: Muhammad Iqbal
works.note: This is the masnavi that made Iqbal's name, and Nicholson's is the first English version. Nicholson read the Persian soon after its Lahore publication in 1915 and wrote to Iqbal for leave to translate it; Iqbal agreed warmly, and Nicholson's Introduction draws on notes on his philosophy communicated by Iqbal himself. Text from the Macmillan edition of 1920 (Project Gutenberg); Nicholson's prose Introduction, notes and footnote markers are omitted. The original, first published at Lahore in 1915, is in Persian.
works.blurb: Iqbal's Persian masnavi of 1915, the poem that made his name, in Nicholson's English verse: a Prologue and eighteen chapters on the strengthening of the Self through love and desire, with tales of a tiger and sheep, a diamond and a coal, and a Brahmin and a Sheikh.
