works.title: The Seven Against Thebes
works.author: Aeschylus
works.note: Translated by E. D. A. Morshead (1908), from Project Gutenberg #8714, Four Plays of Aeschylus. Text of the play only; the introduction and the translator's argument are omitted.
works.blurb: Oedipus's sons Eteocles and Polynices, doomed by their father's curse, face each other across the walls of Thebes. As a scout reports the seven champions of the Argive host, one to each gate, Eteocles assigns a defender to six of them, and then, learning that his own brother stands at the seventh, resolves to meet him in person. The brothers kill each other, and the play closes on the dirge for them and the defiance of Antigone.

works.title: The Shahnama of Firdausi
works.subtitle: Done into English by Arthur George Warner and Edmond Warner
works.author: Firdausi
works.translator: trans. Arthur George Warner and Edmond Warner (1905–1925)
works.note: The Warner brothers' complete English translation of the Shahnama, in blank verse, published by Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner in nine volumes between 1905 and 1925 (the Introduction and notes of vol. I are by Arthur Warner, and Edmond Warner completed the work after his brother's death in 1903). All nine volumes are given here: the Prelude and the reigns from Gaiumart to Sikandar (Alexander the Great), then the Ashkanians and the Sasanian dynasty from Ardshir Papakan to the fall of the dynasty and the Arab conquest. Volumes III and IV (1908, 1909) continue from there through the whole reign of Kai Khusrau, in the Warners' seven Parts, and the reign of Luhrasp; their text is taken from the Toronto scans shahnama03firduoft and shahnama04firduoft, checked against the scans in.ernet.dli.2015.102318 and in.ernet.dli.2015.52963 (vol. III) and in.gov.ignca.35448 (vol. IV). Volume V (1910) gives the reign of Gushtasp in the Warners' four Parts (the coming of Zarduhsht and the war with Arjasp, the Seven Stages of Asfandiyar, Asfandiyar's fight with Rustam, and the death of Rustam), then Bahman and Humai; volume VI (1912) gives Darab, Dara and Sikandar, then the Ashkanians and the Sasanian reigns from Ardshir Papakan to Yazdagird son of Shapur (the section for Yazdagird carries Bahram Gur's boyhood and his winning of the crown from between the lions, which the Warners print under his father's reign). Volume VII (1915) gives Bahram Gur, Yazdagird son of Bahram, Hurmuz, Piruz, Balash, Kubad, and the first four of the six Parts of Nushirwan (his administration, wars and the revolt of Nushzad; Buzurjmihr and the seven banquets; Mahbud and other matters; the game of chess and the book of Kalila and Dimna). Volume VIII (1923) gives the last two Parts of Nushirwan (the fall and restoration of Buzurjmihr, and the Shah's last years), Hurmuzd son of Nushirwan and Khusrau Parwiz. Volume IX (1925) completes the poem: the short reigns of Kubad (called Shirwi), Ardshir son of Shirwi, Guraz (Farayin), Purandukht, Azarmdukht and Farrukhzad, then Yazdagird, the last of the Sasanians, in the Warners' fifteen Parts, which are given here as one section for the reign (Parts 1–14: the Arab invasion, the death of Rustam at Kadisiya, the flight to Khurasan and the murder of Yazdagird in the mill) and a final section, 'The Completion of the Shahnama' (Part 15), Firdausi's own closing verses. Their text is taken from the Toronto scans shahnama05firduoft, shahnama06firduoft, shahnama07firduoft and shahnama08firduoft, checked against the scans in.gov.ignca.35449 (vol. V), in.gov.ignca.35450 (vol. VI), in.ernet.dli.2015.530039 and in.gov.ignca.35451 (vol. VII) and in.gov.ignca.35452 and in.ernet.dli.2015.169865 (vol. VIII), and, for vol. IX, from the Toronto scan shahnama09firduoft (title page: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner, London, 1925), checked line by line against the scan in.gov.ignca.35453 (the Archaeological Survey of India copy). In these volumes the Warners spell the hero's name Asfandiyar, and that spelling is kept. The Warners' prose arguments, introductory notes, footnotes, sub-headings and verse numbers have been left out, and each reign is one section; Kai Kaus, Kai Khusrau, Gushtasp and Nushirwan are each divided into the Warners' Parts, and the epilogue of vol. IX stands apart from the reign of Yazdagird. Text from OCR of two independent scans of each volume (three for vols. VII and VIII); some eighty lines in vols. III–VIII, on pages where the second scans are unreadable, rest on the Toronto scan alone, and in vol. IX one line (in Guraz) rests on the Archaeological Survey scan alone because the Toronto scan is illegible there. Names appear in plain ASCII spelling without the Warners' diacritics.
works.blurb: The Warners' complete blank-verse English translation of Firdausi's Persian national epic; all nine volumes, from the creation of kingship under Gaiumart to the war with Mazandaran, Suhrab, Siyawush and the coming of Kai Khusrau, then Kai Khusrau's long wars with Turan (Piran, Kamus, the Khan of Chin, Bizhan and Manizha, the Twelve Rukhs, the fall of Afrasiyab) and the reign of Luhrasp, then the reign of Gushtasp (the coming of Zarduhsht, the wars with Arjasp, Asfandiyar's Seven Stages, the fight of Rustam and Asfandiyar, the death of Rustam), Bahman, Humai and Darab, and the last two reigns of the Kaianian line, Dara and Sikandar, the legend of Alexander; then the Sasanian dynasty, from the Ashkanians and the rise of Ardshir Papakan through the reigns of his successors, Bahram Gur's hunts and adventures, Nushirwan's justice with the tales of Buzurjmihr and Mahbud and the invention of chess, and Hurmuzd, to the long reign of Khusrau Parwiz (the revolt of Bahram Chubina, Khusrau's flight to Rum, Shirin, and his fall), then the brief reigns of his successors (the lament of Barbad, the death of Shirin, the women Shahs Purandukht and Azarmdukht), and last the reign of Yazdagird: the Arab conquest, the death of Rustam at Kadisiya, the flight to Khurasan and the murder of Yazdagird by the miller, ending with Firdausi's own closing words.

works.subtitle: Shakuntala and the Ring of Recognition
works.author: Kalidasa
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #16659 (Translations of Shakuntala and Other Works, Everyman's Library, 1912). Prologue and seven acts only; Ryder's introduction, cast list and notes omitted.
works.blurb: King Dushyanta, hunting in the forest, comes to the hermitage of the sage Kanva and falls in love with his foster-daughter Shakuntala; they marry by mutual consent, and he leaves her a signet ring. Cursed by the irascible Durvasas, the king forgets her, and rejects her when she comes to court, until a fisherman finds the lost ring and his memory returns. Years later, in the heavenly hermitage of Kashyapa, he is reunited with Shakuntala and their son Bharata.

works.title: The Shepheard’s Calender

works.blurb: Spenser’s first major work: twelve eclogues, one for each month, mixing pastoral love-complaint, satire of the clergy, and elegy in a deliberately archaic English.

works.title: The Shepherd's Week
works.subtitle: In Six Pastorals
works.author: John Gay
works.note: Text of The Poetical Works of John Gay, ed. John Underhill (Muses' Library, Lawrence and Bullen, 1893), vol. I, following Gay's quarto of 1720; the editor's notes and Gay's own are omitted.
works.blurb: Gay's six burlesque pastorals, one for each day of the week, in which English rustics quarrel, court, mourn and get drunk in mock-Spenserian dialect, a parody of Ambrose Philips's pastoral manner

works.title: The Shield of Hercules
works.author: Hesiod
works.note: Verse translation by Charles Abraham Elton, from The Remains of Hesiod the Ascraean (second edition, London, 1815). Elton’s own notes are omitted.
works.blurb: Elton’s blank-verse version of the poem traditionally, though doubtfully, attributed to Hesiod, on Heracles’ duel with Cycnus and the description of his shield.

works.author: Hesiod
works.note: Prose translation, Loeb Classical Library. Line numbers follow the Greek.
works.blurb: An epic fragment on Heracles’ duel with the brigand Cycnus, built around a long description of the hero’s richly decorated shield and traditionally, though doubtfully, attributed to Hesiod.

works.author: Hesiod
works.note: Prose translation, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1908.
works.blurb: A prose version of the poem on Herakles’ combat with Kyknos, son of Ares, built around a long description of the hero’s decorated shield; ancient tradition ascribed it to Hesiod, though its authorship is doubtful.

works.blurb: A narrative poem in heroic couplets of a merchant ship's voyage from Alexandria and its loss on the coast of Greece, drawn from the author's own experience at sea.

Terry (New York: Hunt & Eaton; Cincinnati: Cranston & Stowe, 1890), text from the Internet Archive scan; his introduction, argument and notes are omitted, as are his line numbers. Terry numbers the last four books IX–XII and gives the manuscript numbers XI–XIV in parentheses; those titles are kept. His asterisks and rows of dots mark gaps in the Greek. works.blurb: Twelve books of Greek hexameter prophecy put into the mouth of the pagan Sibyl by Jewish and Christian writers between the second century BC and the fifth century AD, from the creation and the flood to the fall of Rome and the last judgment.

works.author: Sir Philip Sidney
works.note: From the first printing, The Psalmes of David (Chiswick Press for R. Triphook, 1823), transcribed from John Davies of Hereford's copy of the manuscript; Psalms 1–43 are by Sidney, the rest by his sister. Spelling is kept as printed.
works.blurb: Sir Philip Sidney's verse paraphrase of the first forty-three Psalms, each in a different metre and stanza form, begun in the early 1580s and completed by his sister Mary, Countess of Pembroke.

works.title: The Siege of Valencia
works.subtitle: A Dramatic Poem
works.author: Felicia Hemans
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #66785 (The Poems of Felicia Hemans). The author’s own footnotes and the editor’s annotations are omitted.
works.blurb: Valencia, held by the Christian governor Alvar Gonzalez, a descendant of the Cid, lies under siege by the Moors. Abdullah, the Moorish chief, has taken two of Gonzalez’s sons prisoner and offers their lives in exchange for the city. Gonzalez refuses, and the play follows his wife Elmina, his daughter Ximena and the priest Hernandez through the city’s last days, to the deaths of the sons and of Gonzalez himself, as Castilian help arrives.

works.title: The Story of Sigurd the Volsung and the Fall of the Niblungs
works.subtitle: In four books: Sigmund, Regin, Brynhild, Gudrun
works.author: William Morris
works.note: Project Gutenberg #18328, from the eighth impression (Longmans, Green, 1904); first published 1876. Each of Morris's chapters is a section, titled with its book and its chapter heading as printed above the chapter. The title page, contents, the prose argument at the head of each book and the transcriber's notes are left out. Morris's long lines, which the book wraps, are rejoined as single lines.
works.blurb: Morris's epic retelling of the Volsunga Saga in long anapaestic lines: the Volsung kings, Sigurd's slaying of Fafnir, his waking of Brynhild, the Niblungs' treachery, and the vengeance of Gudrun, in four books.

works.title: Sir Amadace
works.subtitle: A verse rendering
works.author: Anonymous (Middle English)
works.note: The Middle English original is anonymous; Jessie L. Weston's bibliography records two manuscripts (Auchinleck and Irland), both defective at the commencement, and her rendering likewise begins partway through the story, with the steward's counsel to the indebted knight. This is Jessie L. Weston's 1914 verse rendering, in twelve-line tail-rhyme stanzas, from The Chief Middle English Poets (Boston: Houghton Mifflin). Her line numbers, notes and bibliography are omitted; the sections are about 430-line ranges.
works.blurb: Sir Amadace, ruined by his own open-handedness, sets out with what money is left and finds a dead man refused burial because of his debts. He spends everything to lay the corpse in the ground, and the favour is repaid when a mysterious White Knight helps him win a princess and a kingdom, on one terrible condition.

works.title: Sir Eglamour of Artois
works.author: Anonymous (Middle English)
works.note: Middle English text of the Thornton MS (Lincoln Cathedral 91), ed. J. O. Halliwell, Camden Society 1844; notes and variants omitted. Stanza numbers and line numbers are not reproduced.
works.blurb: A tail-rhyme romance of Sir Eglamour, who wins the love of Christabel, daughter of the Earl of Artois, by slaying a giant and a monstrous boar, and by killing a dragon at Rome. After long separation, their child, carried off by a griffin, grows up to be a knight and, unknowing, is wed to his own mother, until a token reveals the truth and the family is reunited.

works.title: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
works.subtitle: A Middle-English Arthurian Romance
works.author: Gawain Poet
works.note: Anonymous Middle English original (Cotton Nero A.x). This is Jessie L. Weston's 1898 prose translation (David Nutt, London), long in the public domain — chosen over any 20th-century verse translation (Tolkien, Borroff, Armitage), which remain under copyright.
works.blurb: A green-skinned knight rides into Arthur's Christmas feast with an impossible challenge; Sir Gawain's answer sends him on a year-long quest that tests his courage, his courtesy, and his honesty alike.

works.title: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
works.subtitle: A verse rendering
works.author: Gawain Poet
works.note: Anonymous Middle English original (Cotton Nero A.x). This is Jessie L. Weston's 1912 verse rendering, made in the original metres and published in Romance, Vision and Satire (Boston: Houghton Mifflin), distinct from her 1898 prose version also on the site. The four Books are given in full; the bob-and-wheel lines closing each stanza are indented.
works.blurb: A green-skinned knight rides into Arthur's Christmas feast with an impossible challenge; Sir Gawain's answer sends him on a year-long quest that tests his courage, his courtesy, and his honesty alike. Here the poem is rendered in rhymed, bobbed-and-wheeled stanzas.

works.title: Sir Gawayne and the Grene Knyȝt (Middle English text)
works.subtitle: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
works.author: Gawain Poet
works.note: Middle English text of BL Cotton Nero A.x, ed. Richard Morris, EETS 4 (2nd ed. 1869); prefaces, sidenotes, notes and glossary omitted.
works.blurb: The original alliterative Middle English of the great Arthurian romance: a green-skinned knight rides into Camelot at Christmas, and Gawain's answer to his beheading game leads him through a year of trial to the castle of Bertilak, the temptations of the lady, and the green girdle.

works.title: Sir Isumbras
works.author: Anonymous (Middle English)
works.note: Middle English text of the Thornton MS (Lincoln Cathedral 91), ed. J. O. Halliwell, Camden Society 1844; notes and variants omitted. Halliwell's square brackets, which mark letters and lines he supplied, are kept, and his stanza numbers are followed; stanza divisions in the edition are sometimes irregular. The manuscript's thorn-like and yogh-like letters appear as printed (yogh as ȝ).
works.blurb: A tail-rhyme romance of a proud and prosperous knight who is warned by a bird to choose penance in this life. He loses wealth, wife and three sons, serves as a smith and a palmer, and at last regains all by God's mercy and wins a Christian kingdom from the Saracens.

works.title: Launfal
works.subtitle: Sir Launfal
works.author: Thomas Chestre
works.note: Middle English text of BL Cotton Caligula A.ii as printed by Joseph Ritson, Ancient Engleish Metrical Romanceës (1802), from the revised edition by E. Goldsmid (1884–85); notes omitted.
works.blurb: A tail-rhyme Breton lay of about 1,040 lines, adapted from Marie de France's Lanval and the anonymous Graelent: a knight of Arthur's court, impoverished and slighted by Guinevere, is loved by the fairy Tryamour.

works.title: Sir Orpheo
works.subtitle: Sir Orfeo
works.author: Anonymous (Middle English)
works.note: Text from the Harleian manuscript 3810 (British Museum), as Ritson gives it, as printed by Joseph Ritson (1802), revised by E. Goldsmid (1884–85); notes omitted.
works.blurb: A Middle English Breton lay of about 510 lines, the Orpheus story moved into fairyland: King Orpheo's queen Heurodis is carried off by the king of Faerie, and Orpheo gives up his crown to live as a harper in the wilderness, follows the fairy riders into their country, and wins her back with his playing.

works.title: Sir Perceval of Galles
works.author: Anonymous (Middle English)
works.note: Middle English text of the Thornton MS (Lincoln Cathedral 91), ed. J. O. Halliwell, Camden Society 1844; notes and variants omitted. One printed line (l. 1540) is wanting in the edition and is not supplied.
works.blurb: A tail-rhyme romance of the boy Perceval, reared in the wilds by his widowed mother, who rides to Arthur's court, avenges his father's death on the Red Knight and wins a lady's release from a Saracen sultan.

works.title: Sir Tristrem
works.subtitle: A verse rendering
works.author: Anonymous (Middle English)
works.note: The Middle English original is anonymous; the narrator names Thomas of Erceldoune as his authority, and Jessie L. Weston's bibliography records its sole manuscript as the Auchinleck MS (Advocates' Library, Edinburgh). This is Jessie L. Weston's 1914 verse rendering, in eleven-line stanzas, from The Chief Middle English Poets (Boston: Houghton Mifflin). Weston's line numbers, her bracketed "(End of MS.)" marker, headnote, notes and bibliography are omitted. The printed text marks no fyttes, so the sections are about 400-line ranges.
works.blurb: Tristrem, son of Roland Riis and of Blancheflower, King Mark's sister, is brought up by the loyal Rohant and educated in the courtly arts before he comes to his uncle Mark in Cornwall. He kills the Irish champion Moraunt, is healed by Ysonde, wins her as Mark's bride, and shares with her a love that survives suspicion, banishment and exile.

works.title: Sister Songs
works.subtitle: An Offering to Two Sisters
works.author: Francis Thompson
works.note: Text from the Burns & Oates edition of 1908 (Project Gutenberg). The prose Preface is omitted.
works.blurb: Published in 1895, Sister Songs is Thompson’s offering to Monica and Madeline (Sylvia) Meynell, daughters of his patrons Wilfrid and Alice Meynell. It moves from a Proem addressed to Spring through two long parts to a closing Inscription.

works.title: Solomon and Saturn
works.subtitle: The poetic dialogues
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.translator: trans. J. M. Kemble, The Dialogue of Salomon and Saturnus (Ælfric Society, 1848)
works.note: Kemble's line-for-line verse translation, printed facing the Old English in his edition. Only the two verse dialogues are given here, not the prose Pater Noster dialogue the manuscript inserts between them. Asterisks and dots mark gaps and damage in the manuscript.
works.blurb: Old English verse dialogues in which the wise King Solomon answers the riddling questions of the Chaldean prince Saturn.

works.title: Solomon and Saturn (Old English)
works.subtitle: The poetic dialogues: Old English text
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.note: The Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records, ed. E. V. K. Dobbie, vol. VI (1942). Old English text as in ASPR; hand-keyed e-text via sacred-texts.com.
works.blurb: Old English verse dialogues in which the wise King Solomon answers the riddling questions of the Chaldean prince Saturn.

works.title: Solomon on the Vanity of the World
works.subtitle: A Poem in Three Books
works.author: Matthew Prior
works.blurb: Prior's longest poem: Solomon looks for happiness in knowledge, pleasure and power, and finds that all is vanity. Each book opens with the poet's prose argument.

works.title: The Song of Hiawatha
works.author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
works.blurb: A trochaic epic drawing on Ojibwe legend, following the life of the hero Hiawatha — his childhood, wooing, feats, and eventual departure — in a rhythm modeled on the Finnish Kalevala.

sections.title: The Son of the Evening Star

works.title: The Song of the Merchant Kalashnikov
works.subtitle: A Song of the Tzar Ivan Vasilyevich, of the Young Oprichnik and of the Bold Merchant Kalashnikov
works.author: Mikhail Lermontov
works.note: Voynich's unrhymed version, from Six Lyrics from the Ruthenian of Taras Shevchenko, also The Song of the Merchant Kalashnikov (London: Elkin Mathews, 1911). Lermontov wrote the Russian poem in 1837 in the manner of the folk bylina; its publication was punished by his exile to the Caucasus. The prologue and the three parts are printed as in the book; the translator's footnotes are omitted, and the stress marks on proper names (Ivan, Kalashnikov, Alyona and the rest) are not reproduced. Internet Archive item sixlyricsfromrut00shevrich, checked against the page images.
works.blurb: In the Moscow of Ivan the Terrible, the merchant Kalashnikov fights and kills the Tsar's favourite oprichnik to avenge the insult to his wife, and pays for it on the block.

works.title: The Song of Los
works.author: William Blake
works.note: Text from The Poetical Works of William Blake, ed. John Sampson (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1913).
works.blurb: Los sings the long history of the laws and religions that bound Africa and Asia, until Orc's fires break out in Europe and America.

works.title: The Song of Roland
works.subtitle: La Chanson de Roland
works.author: Anonymous (Old French)
works.note: Anonymous Old French epic of c. 1100. This is C. K. Scott Moncrieff's English verse translation, transcribed by Project Gutenberg (#391); the Gutenberg text carries no date, and 1919 is taken from the Internet Archive catalogue record of the Chapman & Hall edition (songofroland00scot). The 291 laisse numerals and the manuscript's AOI marks are kept. The Gutenberg text misnumbers a few laisse headings; they have been restored to their running order.
works.blurb: Betrayed by his stepfather Ganelon, Charlemagne's nephew Roland holds the pass at Roncevaux against the Saracens, refuses to sound his horn until too late, and dies a martyr; the Emperor then avenges him.

works.title: The Song of Roland
works.subtitle: La Chanson de Roland
works.author: Anonymous (Old French)
works.note: Anonymous Old French epic of c. 1100. This is John O'Hagan's English verse translation, first published by Kegan Paul in 1880, as reprinted in The Harvard Classics, vol. 49, Epic and Saga (ed. C. W. Eliot, 1910), Project Gutenberg #14019. The editor's introduction and the footnotes are omitted. The stanzas that O'Hagan adds from other manuscripts are kept as he printed them. The Gutenberg text prints laisse CLXXXIX as a second CLXXIX; it is restored to its running order. Part II, being much the longest, is divided here at the laisse of the horn.
works.blurb: John O'Hagan's version renders the epic of Roland's last stand at Roncevaux in rhymed octosyllabic couplets, divided into three Parts and numbered laisses, with scene headings of his own.

sections.title: Part I: The Treason of Ganelon
Part II: The Prelude of the Great Battle (Laisses LXXXIII–CXLVII)
Part II: The Great Battle Continued (Laisses CXLVIII–CXCVII)

works.title: The Song of Songs
works.subtitle: Authorized Version of the Song of Solomon.
works.author: The Bible (Authorized King James Version)
works.blurb: An anthology of Hebrew love lyrics, traditionally ascribed to Solomon.

works.title: Sordello
works.author: Robert Browning
works.note: Text of the Riverside Edition (Houghton Mifflin, Boston, 1887), collated with the Ticknor and Fields edition of 1864 and a second copy of the Riverside volume; this is Browning's revised text (first published 1840, revised 1863). The wording and punctuation are a collation of these scans and so draw on both the 1887 and the 1864 printings, not on one alone. Verse paragraphs follow the paragraph indentation of the 1887 Riverside page layout; the 1864 Ticknor layout was used only where the Riverside scan could not be read, and it paragraphs somewhat differently in places. Spaces that the scans' typography put before 's, 'll, 're, 've and 'd have been closed (there 's is printed there's); the printed 't is and 't was are kept. The dedication to J. Milsand and the running page headlines are omitted.
works.blurb: Browning's long narrative poem in six books follows the thirteenth-century Mantuan troubadour Sordello through the Guelf and Ghibelline wars of northern Italy, and is chiefly a study of the growth and failure of a poet's soul.

works.title: The Romaunce of the Sowdone of Babylone and of Ferumbras His Sone Who Conquerede Rome
works.subtitle: The Sowdone of Babylone
works.author: Anonymous (Middle English)
works.note: Middle English text of the unique Phillipps MS (now Princeton, Garrett 140), ed. Emil Hausknecht, EETS ES 38 (1881); introduction, notes, sidenotes and glossary omitted. The editor’s braces round expanded abbreviations, his footnote numbers and his typographical flourishes on final letters are printed as plain letters; thorn, yogh and the other marks of the transcription are kept as the Gutenberg text gives them. Stanza breaks are not marked in the Gutenberg text and have been restored from the rhymes (mainly abab quatrains). The text breaks off in a damaged leaf near the end, where gaps are marked with dots.
works.blurb: A Middle English romance in rhymed quatrains. The Saracen Soudan Laban of Babylon sacks Rome; his son Ferumbras is defeated and converted, and his daughter Floripas helps the imprisoned peers of Charlemagne win their freedom before Charles himself defeats Laban in Spain. Preserved in a single manuscript.

works.title: The Spanish Gypsy
works.author: George Eliot
works.note: Text from the Internet Archive copy of the 1893 printing of the 1868 poem (spanishgypsypoem00elio_0), checked against the 1883 Cabinet edition (legendofjubaloth02elio). Books I to V complete. Speakers' names stand above their speeches as in a play; narrative verse is left unattributed, with the printed square brackets around the narrator's interludes, and stage directions are kept in parentheses.
works.blurb: A dramatic poem of fifteenth-century Spain, in five books. Fedalma, a Gypsy foundling brought up in the household of the Duke Silva, is about to marry him when her father Zarca, chief of the Zincali, claims her for the cause of his people. She renounces her love, and after her father's death sails with the exiled Gypsies for Africa. It mixes narrative blank verse, dramatic dialogue with named speakers, and songs.

works.title: The Spanish Student
works.subtitle: A Play in Three Acts
works.author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #1365 (The Complete Poetical Works of Henry Wadsworth Longfellow); the editor's headnote and notes omitted; speakers' names are printed in capitals as abbreviated in the source, and unclosed square-bracket stage directions have been closed.
works.blurb: A verse play set in Spain. The student Victorian loves Preciosa, a gypsy dancer of Madrid, whom the profligate Count of Lara also pursues. Her gypsy guardian, jealousies and a slandering plot divide the lovers, and the story passes from Madrid to the Guadarrama mountains, with serenades and gypsy songs set within the dialogue, before her true parentage is revealed.

works.title: The Spanish Tragedy
works.subtitle: Containing the lamentable end of Don Horatio and Bel-imperia, with the pitiful death of old Hieronimo
works.author: Thomas Kyd
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #35330, the quarto 'newly corrected and amended of such gross faults as passed in the first impression' (Edward Allde for Edward White). Editorial bracketed insertions and stage directions have been removed; the Chorus of the Ghost of Andrea and Revenge is kept between the acts.
works.blurb: The ghost of the Spanish courtier Don Andrea, slain in battle, is led back from the underworld by Revenge to watch his killer Balthazar punished. Instead he sees Andrea's friend Horatio murdered in his father's arbour and Hieronimo, the Knight-Marshall of Spain, driven half mad by grief as he seeks justice from a corrupt court. Hieronimo at last stages a play before the court in which the real deaths are carried out.

works.title: The Spirit of Discovery by Sea
works.subtitle: A Descriptive and Historical Poem
works.author: William Lisle Bowles
works.blurb: A blank-verse poem in five books on the history of maritime discovery, from the Ark to the voyages of the eighteenth century.

works.title: The Historie of Squyer Meldrum
works.author: Sir David Lyndsay
works.note: Text of David Laing's edition (Edinburgh: William Paterson, 1871), vol. I pp. 161-224, collated from several scans. Lyndsay's last major narrative poem, written about 1550, with the Testament of the hero as its second part.
works.blurb: Lyndsay's verse romance of William Meldrum of Cleish and Binns, a Fife laird: a gallant, fighting, loving squire who defends a lady from robbers, wins a tournament in Ireland and a wife at home, and dies in his bed, leaving a Testament that is part mock-heroic, part valediction.

sections.title: The Historie of Squyer William Meldrum, of Cleische and Bynnis
The Testament of the Nobill and Vailyeand Squyer William Meldrum of the Bynnis

works.title: The Squyr of Lowe Degre
works.author: Anonymous (Middle English)
works.note: Text from the undated black-letter quarto printed by William Copland (British Museum, Garrick collection), as Ritson gives it, as printed by Joseph Ritson (1802), revised by E. Goldsmid (1884–85); notes omitted.
works.blurb: A romance of about 1,130 lines in rhymed couplets: a squire of low degree loves the king of Hungary's daughter. She bids him win fame in arms abroad, the king's steward betrays him, and after seven years of mourning over a body she wrongly takes to be his, the princess finds him alive and they are married.

works.title: Le Morte Arthur
works.subtitle: The stanzaic Morte Arthur
works.author: Anonymous (Middle English)
works.note: Middle English text of BL Harley MS 2252, ed. S. B. Hemingway (1912); notes and glossary omitted. Sections are titled by line count of this text (the edition's own marginal numbering, which runs to 3970 and allows for lines lost with a missing leaf, is not reproduced). Stanza breaks are inferred from rhyme and sense; a few stanzas are short in the manuscript, among them the six lines at 1177-1182 before the missing leaf (the editor's bracketed notes on the gap and on a missing line are omitted).
works.blurb: An English verse romance of about 1400 in eight-line stanzas, telling the last days of King Arthur: the love of Lancelot and Guinevere, the Maid of Ascolot, the war between Arthur and Lancelot, Mordred's treason, the passing of Arthur and the deaths of Lancelot and Guinevere. It was a main source of Malory's last books.

works.title: The Story of Rimini
works.author: Leigh Hunt
works.note: From the London: C. and J. Ollier 1819 edition (first published 1816), Internet Archive scans storyofriminipoe00hunt (University of California) and storyriminiapoe00huntgoog (New York Public Library / Google), read against one another where the OCR is doubtful. The prose preface and dedication to Lord Byron, the contents and the notes at the end are left out, as is the author's footnote. The canto subtitles are kept as printed.
works.blurb: Hunt's retelling of the story of Paolo and Francesca, from Dante's Inferno, in four cantos of heroic couplets: the bride fetched to Rimini, her journey, the fatal passion and its end.

works.title: Such Stuff as Dreams Are Made Of
works.subtitle: A drama taken from Calderón's La Vida es Sueño
works.author: Pedro Calderón de la Barca
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #63776 (Eight Dramas of Calderon, freely translated by Edward FitzGerald, Macmillan 1906, reprinting the Six Dramas of 1853 and the Two Dramas of 1865). FitzGerald's advertisement, footnotes and afterwords are omitted.
works.blurb: Basilio, King of Poland, confines his son Segismund from birth because of a prophecy, then drugs him and lets him wake in the palace for a day to test it. FitzGerald's free version of La vida es sueño, whose title he turns into a joke on the stolen phrase.

works.title: The Suppliant Maidens
works.author: Aeschylus
works.note: Translated by E. D. A. Morshead (1908), from Project Gutenberg #8714, Four Plays of Aeschylus. Text of the play only; the introduction, dedication, argument and footnotes are omitted.
works.blurb: The fifty daughters of Danaus flee Egypt to escape forced marriage to their cousins, the sons of Aegyptus, and beg sanctuary at Argos. King Pelasgus must choose between sheltering them and war; the Argive assembly votes to protect them, and the Egyptian herald's threats are turned back as the maidens give thanks.

works.title: The Suppliants
works.author: Euripides
works.note: Text from Internet Archive scans of The Tragedies of Euripides in English Verse, vol. I (1894), checked against a second scan and the 1912 Loeb Classical Library revision for OCR errors only. Way's prose argument, footnotes, running heads and line numbers are omitted.
works.blurb: After the failed assault of the Seven against Thebes, the mothers of the fallen Argive chiefs come to Eleusis and beg Theseus to win back the unburied bodies of their sons. Arthur Way renders Euripides' tragedy in rhymed English verse, with the choral odes in lyric measures.

works.title: Sylvia; or, The May Queen
works.subtitle: A Lyrical Drama
works.author: George Darley
works.note: Text from The Complete Poetical Works of George Darley, edited by Ramsay Colles (London: Routledge, 1908), Internet Archive scan (OCR), collated with the first edition (London: Published for John Taylor, 1827), a second Internet Archive scan. Where the 1908 scan is garbled or incomplete (some speeches in Acts IV and V, and the last line of the closing chorus) the 1827 text is used. The preface, editor's notes, line numbers, running heads and footnotes are left out. The songs (such as Sylvia's Song and Romanzo to Sylvia) stay in place within the scenes; the prose speeches remain prose.
works.blurb: A lyrical drama set in the Apennines. The traveller Romanzo falls in love with Sylvia, May Queen of a glen shared between the fairy queen Morgana and Ararach, king of the fiends. The fiends plot to seize Sylvia and to torment Romanzo with a phantom show, while the comic servant Andrea, transformed by the fiends, blunders between the two parties, until the fairy host drives off the fiends and the lovers are reunited. Blank verse, songs and comic prose.

works.title: Syphilis
works.subtitle: A Poetical History of the French Disease
works.author: Girolamo Fracastoro
works.note: The original is Latin verse, published in 1530; this is Nahum Tate's English translation of 1686 (EEBO-TCP A40375). The 1686 spelling and capitals are kept; the transcription marks no book divisions, so none are shown.
works.blurb: Fracastoro's Latin didactic poem on the origin, nature and cure of the new disease that gave syphilis its name, in Nahum Tate's English couplets.

works.title: The Táin
works.subtitle: Táin Bó Cúailnge, the Cattle-Raid of Cooley, in English verse
works.author: Anonymous (Old Irish)
works.note: Internet Archive scan of the second edition (Talbot Press, Dublin, 1924; first published by Maunsel, Dublin, 1907), archive.org/details/tinOOhutt. Hutton's verse rendering from 'The Finding of the Táin' to 'The Writing of the Táin', one section per Book. Her preface, introduction, pronunciation keys, appendices, notes and index of names, and the plate captions, are omitted. Her phonetic spellings and stress marks (Shen'-cawn, Cucullin, Maev) are kept exactly. Only the 1924 scan was available, so no chapter was compared with 1907; the text follows 1924. Her double quotation marks, damaged in the scan, have been restored, and running heads, page numbers and line-end hyphenation removed.
works.blurb: The central epic of the Ulster cycle in Mary Hutton's English blank verse: Queen Maev of Connaught and King Ailill gather the Four Fifths of Ireland to seize the Brown Bull of Cooley, and the boy-hero Cúchulainn (her Cucullin) holds the Ulster border alone until Ulster rises. It opens with the tale of how the poets recovered the lost Táin from the ghost of Fergus.

works.title: The Taking of Ilios
works.subtitle: Prose translation by A. W. Mair
works.author: Tryphiodorus
works.note: Prose translation, Loeb Classical Library (1928), from theoi.com.
works.blurb: A short late-antique epic on the last night of the Trojan War, from the building of the wooden horse to the sacrifice of Polyxena.

works.title: A Tale of Eternity
works.subtitle: The Haunted Hurst
works.author: Gerald Massey
works.note: Text of the first edition, A Tale of Eternity, and Other Poems (London: Strahan and Co., 1870). The poem was later reprinted, revised, as "The Haunted Hurst, a Tale of Eternity" in My Lyrical Life, First Series (1889). Sections are the poem's own parts: a short prologue and Parts I-VII.
works.blurb: Gerald Massey's long narrative poem of haunting and the afterlife, in seven parts, first published in 1870.

works.title: The Tale of Gamelyn
works.author: Anonymous (Middle English)
works.note: Text from W. W. Skeat, The Tale of Gamelyn (Oxford, 1884); the editor's apparatus, notes and line numbers are omitted.
works.blurb: A younger son, Gamelyn, is cheated of his inheritance and kept in servitude by his elder brother. He wrestles his way to fame, escapes his bonds, and becomes king of the outlaws in the greenwood. When his brother has him arraigned, Gamelyn returns, takes the judge's seat and hangs the corrupt justice, the sheriff and the jury. The story is the source of Shakespeare's As You Like It.

works.title: A Tale of Paraguay
works.subtitle: Dedication, Proem and four cantos (1825)
works.author: Robert Southey
works.note: Text of the collected Poetical Works (1845 printing), read from two Internet Archive scans (completepoetica00soutgoog and poeticalworksro24soutgoog) collated line by line; the preface, Southey's prose notes and the Latin extracts are omitted. Where one scan was torn or illegible the other was followed, and doubtful readings were checked against two separate Internet Archive scans of the 1825 and 1827 editions (ataleparaguay00soutgoog, taleofparaguay00sout), so a few words carry the spelling of those texts.
works.blurb: Southey's Spenserian tale of the Guarani Indian pair Quiara and Monnema, left alone by a plague of smallpox, and of their son Yeruti and daughter Mooma, whom the Jesuit missionary Dobrizhoffer receives into the mission of St Joachin; written in 1824-25 and dedicated to his daughter Edith May.

works.title: Tamburlaine the Great: Part 1
works.author: Christopher Marlowe
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg (ebook 1094), the edition of the Rev. Alexander Dyce (1850; 1858), taken from the 8vo of 1592 and collated with the 4tos of 1605-6. The date given is that of first performance (c. 1587-88); the play was first printed in 1590. The editor's footnotes, address to the readers and list of persons are left out; words the editor supplied in square brackets are printed without them, and stage directions stay bracketed.
works.blurb: Marlowe's first great play, in blank verse, follows the Scythian shepherd Tamburlaine from his seizure of the Persian crown to his triumph over Bajazeth, the Soldan of Egypt and the city of Damascus.

works.title: Tamburlaine the Great: Part 2
works.author: Christopher Marlowe
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg (ebook 1589), the edition of the Rev. Alexander Dyce (1850; 1858), taken from the 8vo of 1592 and collated with the 4tos of 1605-6. The date given is that of first performance (c. 1587-88); the play was first printed in 1590. The editor's footnotes, address to the readers and list of persons are left out; words the editor supplied in square brackets are printed without them, and stage directions stay bracketed.
works.blurb: The sequel in blank verse follows Tamburlaine through the death of Zenocrate, the killing of his faint-hearted son Calyphas and the burning of Babylon, to his own death.

works.title: Tartuffe; or, The Hypocrite
works.author: Molière
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #2027 (Curtis Hidden Page's English verse translation, 1908). The translator's introductory note, Molière's prefaces and placets, and the footnotes are omitted.
works.blurb: Orgon, a prosperous Parisian householder, has taken the pious Tartuffe into his home and fallen wholly under his spell, promising him his daughter's hand and his fortune. Orgon's family, led by the sharp-tongued maid Dorine and his wife Elmire, try to open his eyes to the impostor, who is in fact scheming to seize the house and seduce Elmire. Molière's comedy of religious hypocrisy was banned for five years after its first performance in 1664.

works.title: Temora: An Ancient Epic Poem
works.subtitle: In Eight Books
works.author: James Macpherson
works.note: Published by Macpherson as translations from the Gaelic of Ossian (Fingal 1762, Temora 1763); now regarded as largely his own composition from Gaelic ballad matter. Text of the 1824 Griffin edition (vol. II), collated against the 1807 printing; the arguments, footnotes and dissertations are omitted.
works.blurb: Ossian's epic of Cairbar's murder of King Cormac and Fingal's expedition to Ireland to restore the throne, ending in the battle with Cathmor, in measured prose.

works.title: The Tempest
works.author: William Shakespeare
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #100 (The Complete Works of William Shakespeare), revised 24 Aug 2025.
works.blurb: Prospero, the usurped Duke of Milan, has lived twelve years on an enchanted island with his daughter Miranda, served by the spirit Ariel and the savage Caliban. When his enemies sail past, he raises a storm and wrecks their ship, and through illusion, music and a courtship between Miranda and Ferdinand he brings them to repentance. In the end he forgives his brother, frees Ariel, and abjures his magic.

works.title: The Temple of Nature
works.subtitle: or, The Origin of Society
works.author: Erasmus Darwin
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg (ebook 26861). The preface, contents, the author's philosophical footnotes, the Additional Notes and the printed line numbers are omitted.
works.blurb: Darwin's last poem, published after his death, traces in four cantos the progress of life from its first stirrings in the ocean to the rise of mind, society and morality. Written in heroic couplets, it versifies his evolutionary speculations in the mysteries of an ancient temple.

sections.title: Canto III. Progress of the Mind
Canto IV. Of Good and Evil

works.title: The Testament of Beauty
works.subtitle: A Poem in Four Books
works.author: Robert Bridges
works.note: Text of the first edition (Clarendon Press, Oxford, 1929), from the proofread Wikisource transcription. Bridges's reformed spellings are kept as printed. The marginal line numbers, running heads, dedication, contents and index are omitted.
works.blurb: Published on Bridges's eighty-fifth birthday, in his last year as Poet Laureate, this long meditative poem in loose Alexandrines sets out his philosophy of beauty as the meeting-point of instinct and spirit in the mind of man. It is in four books: Introduction, Selfhood, Breed and Ethick.

works.title: Thalaba the Destroyer
works.author: Robert Southey
works.note: Text of the first edition (London: Longman and Rees, 1801), as reproduced in the Woodstock Books facsimile; Southey's prose notes are omitted.
works.blurb: An Arabian romance in twelve books, in irregular unrhymed verse: the orphan Thalaba is chosen to destroy the sorcerers of the Domdaniel caverns that murdered his family.

works.title: The Apostle
works.subtitle: Az apostol
works.author: Sándor Petőfi
works.note: Internet Archive scan of Alexander Petöfi: The Apostle, Childe John, Simple Steve, Cypress Leaves, Selected Lyrics (Hungarian Literary Society, New York, 1912). English version by William N. Loew. The printed numeral of Part X is absent at its break in the scan and was restored from the sequence; the translator's preface, glossary and index are omitted.
works.blurb: Petőfi's long poem of democratic faith: the foundling Szilveszter, raised in cruelty, grows up to become a wandering preacher of liberty and brotherhood, here in twenty parts in English verse by William N. Loew.

works.title: The Bride's Prelude
works.author: Dante Gabriel Rossetti
works.blurb: An unfinished narrative poem begun in 1848: on the morning of Aloyse's wedding she tells her sister Amelotte the story of her lost love.

works.title: The Bridge
works.subtitle: A Poem
works.author: Hart Crane
works.note: Crane’s sequence in eight parts, with the Proem, as printed by Horace Liveright (New York, 1930). The epigraphs and the italic marginal glosses are kept where they stand; the glosses are set as indented lines.
works.blurb: Hart Crane’s long poem of America, taking the Brooklyn Bridge as its emblem: from Columbus’s landfall in Ave Maria through the Pocahontas section, Cutty Sark, the Whitmanic Cape Hatteras, the Three Songs, Quaker Hill and The Tunnel, to the closing hymn of Atlantis.

sections.title: II. Powhatan’s Daughter: 1. The Harbor Dawn
V. Three Songs: 2. National Winter Garden

works.title: The Cenci
works.subtitle: A Tragedy in Five Acts
works.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
works.note: Text from the Hutchinson edition (Oxford, 1914), Project Gutenberg #4800. The dedication, Shelley's preface and the editorial notes are not included. Stage directions are given in brackets.
works.blurb: Shelley's blank-verse tragedy of the Roman nobleman Francesco Cenci, whose cruelty to his family drives his daughter Beatrice to plot his murder; she is tried and executed for the deed. Based on a sixteenth-century Roman crime, it was written in 1819.

works.title: The Doctor
works.subtitle: Fo'c's'le Yarns, Second Series: 1
works.author: Thomas Edward Brown
works.note: From The Collected Poems of T. E. Brown, with introduction by W. E. Henley (Macmillan, 1909 reprint of the 1900 first edition), Internet Archive scan; Fo'c's'le Yarns, Second Series (no. 1). The printer's footnote glosses are left out and Brown's Manx-English spellings are kept as printed.
works.blurb: The longest of the Fo'c's'le Yarns: a seaman's tale in rhymed Manx dialect of the Doctor and the people around him, told to a forecastle audience that suspects him of spinning stories.

works.title: The Excursion
works.author: William Wordsworth
works.note: Text of William Knight's edition (The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. V, Macmillan, 1896; Project Gutenberg #56361). Knight's introduction, the 1814 prose Preface, the prose Arguments, footnotes, variant readings, notes and appendix are omitted. First published 1814.
works.blurb: Wordsworth's nine-book blank-verse poem follows the poet, the Wanderer, the Solitary and the Pastor through a Lake District excursion in which grief and despondency are met with reflections on nature, faith, human suffering and the moral life.

sections.title: Book Sixth: The Church-yard among the Mountains
Book Seventh: The Church-yard among the Mountains (continued)
Book Ninth: Discourse of the Wanderer, and an Evening Visit to the Lake

works.title: The Golden Violet
works.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon (L.E.L.)
works.note: From The Poetical Works of Letitia Elizabeth Landon, in four volumes, 'A New Edition' (London: Longman, Orme, Brown, Green and Longmans), vol. III, University of Toronto scan on the Internet Archive (OCR, volume III title page dated 1839); words doubtful in the OCR read against the 1839 one-volume Poetical Works of Miss Landon (Brussels: Meline, Cans and Co.; Internet Archive). Prefaces, dedications, engraving credits, running heads and the author's notes are left out. Volume III, The Golden Violet. Printed 1827.
works.blurb: A frame poem of a two-day minstrel contest in Provence for the prize of the Golden Violet, in which each minstrel sings his or her own tale.

works.title: The Improvisatrice

I, University of Toronto scan on the Internet Archive (OCR, volume I title page dated 1839); words doubtful in the OCR read against the 1839 one-volume Poetical Works of Miss Landon (Brussels: Meline, Cans and Co.; Internet Archive). Prefaces, dedications, engraving credits, running heads and the author's notes are left out. Volume I, The Improvisatrice and Other Poems. Printed 1824.
works.blurb: An Italian poet-improvisatrice tells her own story of art, song and an unhappy love for Lorenzo, with the songs and tales she sings along the way as their own sections.

sections.title: Song (Farewell! we shall not meet again)

works.title: The Indiaman
works.subtitle: Fo'c's'le Yarns, Third Series: 3
works.author: Thomas Edward Brown
works.note: From The Collected Poems of T. E. Brown, with introduction by W. E. Henley (Macmillan, 1909 reprint of the 1900 first edition), Internet Archive scan; Fo'c's'le Yarns, Third Series (no. 3). The printer's footnote glosses are left out and Brown's Manx-English spellings are kept as printed.
works.blurb: A seaman's dialect yarn of Fanny Graeme, who caught her frock boarding at the Prince's dock, and of Peter Young, whom she married.

works.title: The Inn Album
works.author: Robert Browning
works.blurb: A blank-verse tale in eight parts of a young man, an older cardsharp and the woman between them, set in the parlour of a country inn.

works.title: The Jacquerie
works.subtitle: A Fragment
works.author: Sidney Lanier
works.note: From the group of Unrevised Early Poems in The Poems of Sidney Lanier (Scribner, 1884); the fifth chapter is dated Macon, Georgia, 1868. The text breaks off unfinished, and two lines are marked in the source as partly lost.
works.blurb: Lanier's unfinished early narrative poem about the French peasant revolt known as the Jacquerie, left in five chapters.

works.title: The King's Tragedy
works.subtitle: James I. of Scots, 20th February 1437
works.author: Dante Gabriel Rossetti
works.blurb: A ballad in which Catherine Douglas, called Kate Barlass, tells the murder of King James I of Scotland in 1437.

works.title: The Lost Pleiad
works.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon (L.E.L.)
works.note: From The Poetical Works of Letitia Elizabeth Landon, in four volumes, 'A New Edition' (London: Longman, Orme, Brown, Green and Longmans), vol. IV, University of Toronto scan on the Internet Archive (OCR, volume IV title page dated 1839); words doubtful in the OCR read against the 1839 one-volume Poetical Works of Miss Landon (Brussels: Meline, Cans and Co.; Internet Archive). Prefaces, dedications, engraving credits, running heads and the author's notes are left out. Volume IV. Printed 1829. The verse prelude before the poem is kept as its opening.
works.blurb: A story from the stars: the legend of the Pleiad that left her sisters, and what it costs a heavenly love to touch the earth.

works.title: The Manx Witch
works.subtitle: A Story of the Laxdale Mines
works.author: Thomas Edward Brown
works.note: From The Collected Poems of T. E. Brown, with introduction by W. E. Henley (Macmillan, 1909 reprint of the 1900 first edition), Internet Archive scan; Fo'c's'le Yarns, Third Series (no. 1). The printer's footnote glosses are left out and Brown's Manx-English spellings are kept as printed.
works.blurb: A dialect-verse story of the Laxdale mines, in which a witch's spells trouble Nessy Brew and the miners who court her.

works.title: The Passing Bell
works.author: John S. B. Monsell
works.note: The title poem of The Passing Bell and Other Poems (London: Bell and Daldy, 1868), in five parts of four-line stanzas, each part opening with the same refrain.
works.blurb: A meditation in five parts on the old custom of tolling the church bell for a dying soul, each part turning its warning on a different temptation: the man of business, the domestic man, the young and giddy, the sinful, and the pastor.

works.title: The Prelude
works.subtitle: or Growth of a Poet's Mind
works.author: William Wordsworth
works.note: Text of William Knight's edition (The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 3, Project Gutenberg #12383), giving the 1850 Prelude; Knight's introduction, footnotes, variant readings and appendices are omitted, though the bracketed footnote letters inside verse lines are left as printed. Composed 1799–1805, published posthumously in 1850.
works.blurb: Wordsworth's blank-verse autobiography traces the growth of his imagination from boyhood in the Lake District through Cambridge, London and revolutionary France to the recovery of his poetic vocation.

works.blurb: Tennyson's blank-verse medley of a prince who woos Princess Ida, founder of a women's university, framed by a summer fete at Vivian-place and broken by its famous songs, among them 'Tears, idle tears' and 'The splendour falls'.

works.title: The Ring and the Book
works.author: Robert Browning
works.note: Text of the Cambridge Edition (1895, Houghton Mifflin) from Project Gutenberg #50954; Scudder's headnote is omitted. The poem first appeared in four volumes in 1868-1869.
works.blurb: Browning's twelve-book epic retells a seventeenth-century Roman murder trial through the conflicting voices of the town, the lawyers, the killer, his victim and the Pope.

works.blurb: Hogg's burlesque fragment of an epic, in two books, supposedly by a Selkirk cobbler.

works.author: Thomas Edward Brown
works.note: From The Collected Poems of T. E. Brown, with introduction by W. E. Henley (Macmillan, 1909 reprint of the 1900 first edition), Internet Archive scan; Fo'c's'le Yarns, Second Series (no. 3). The printer's footnote glosses are left out and Brown's Manx-English spellings are kept as printed.
works.blurb: A shorter dialect yarn on the three schools of the parish and their masters, told by the speaker of the earlier Christmas Rose.

works.title: The Seasons
works.author: James Thomson
works.note: Text of the 1791 edition, from the proofread Wikisource transcription.
works.blurb: Thomson's blank-verse poem on the four seasons of the year, with a closing hymn, a landmark of eighteenth-century nature poetry.

works.title: The Task
works.subtitle: A Poem, in Six Books
works.author: William Cowper
works.blurb: Begun as a joke on the subject of a sofa, The Task grew into Cowper’s masterpiece — a long, ruminative blank-verse walk through rural retirement, nature, solitude, and faith.

sections.title: Book V: The Winter Morning Walk
Book VI: The Winter Walk at Noon

works.title: The Temple of Glass
works.author: John Lydgate
works.note: Original Middle English text, from the 1905 Cambridge University Press facsimile of William Caxton's c. 1477 printing.
works.blurb: A Chaucerian dream vision in which the poet, carried in sleep to a temple of glass, overhears a lady and her knightly lover lament and console each other in unrequited love — modelled closely on Chaucer's House of Fame and Parliament of Fowls.

works.title: The Troubadour
works.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon (L.E.L.)
works.note: From The Poetical Works of Letitia Elizabeth Landon, in four volumes, 'A New Edition' (London: Longman, Orme, Brown, Green and Longmans), vol. II, University of Toronto scan on the Internet Archive (OCR, volume II title page dated 1839 (the OCR reads 1830)); words doubtful in the OCR read against the 1839 one-volume Poetical Works of Miss Landon (Brussels: Meline, Cans and Co.; Internet Archive). Prefaces, dedications, engraving credits, running heads and the author's notes are left out. Volume II, The Troubadour and Poetical Sketches of Modern Pictures. Printed 1825.
works.blurb: A verse romance in four cantos of the troubadour Raymond, set in Provence, with songs and tales worked into the story.

works.title: The Venetian Bracelet
works.author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon (L.E.L.)
works.note: From The Poetical Works of Letitia Elizabeth Landon, in four volumes, 'A New Edition' (London: Longman, Orme, Brown, Green and Longmans), vol. IV, University of Toronto scan on the Internet Archive (OCR, volume IV title page dated 1839); words doubtful in the OCR read against the 1839 one-volume Poetical Works of Miss Landon (Brussels: Meline, Cans and Co.; Internet Archive). Prefaces, dedications, engraving credits, running heads and the author's notes are left out. Volume IV, The Venetian Bracelet, The Lost Pleiad, A History of the Lyre and Other Poems. Printed 1829.
works.blurb: A tale of Venice in fourteen numbered parts, centred on a serpent bracelet and the doomed love of Amenaide.

works.title: The Wanderer
works.subtitle: A Vision, in Five Cantos
works.author: Richard Savage
works.blurb: A visionary meditation in heroic couplets, in which a wanderer in retirement weighs the still life against the active and finds that misfortune can refine the mind.

works.title: Thebaid
works.author: Statius
works.note: Prose translation, Loeb Classical Library (1928), from theoi.com.
works.blurb: Statius’s epic of the war of the Seven against Thebes, in twelve books, from the quarrel of Oedipus’s sons to the burial of the dead.

works.title: The First Book of Statius's Thebais
works.author: Statius
works.note: Verse translation in heroic couplets, made in 1703 and first published in 1712; Book I only.
works.blurb: Pope's youthful heroic-couplet version of the first book of Statius's epic of the war of the Seven against Thebes, from the curse of Oedipus to the hymn to Apollo at the court of Adrastus.

works.title: The Theogony
works.author: Hesiod
works.note: Verse translation by Charles Abraham Elton, from The Remains of Hesiod the Ascraean (second edition, London, 1815). Elton’s own notes are omitted.
works.blurb: Elton’s blank-verse version of Hesiod’s account of the birth of the gods, from Chaos and Earth through the Titans to the victory of Zeus.

works.title: Theogony
works.author: Hesiod
works.note: Prose translation, Loeb Classical Library. Line numbers follow the Greek.
works.blurb: Hesiod’s account of the birth of the gods, from Chaos and Earth through the Titans to the victory of Zeus, opened by his own story of being called to poetry by the Muses on Mount Helicon.

works.title: Theogony
works.author: Hesiod
works.note: Prose translation, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1908.
works.blurb: A prose version of Hesiod’s account of the origin of the gods, opening with the Muses of Helikon and tracing the line from Chaos and Earth through the Titans to the rule of Zeus and the unions of gods with mortals.

works.title: The City of Dreadful Night
works.author: James Thomson (B.V.)
works.note: From The City of Dreadful Night and Other Poems (Reeves and Turner, 1880), Internet Archive scan (text rebuilt from the scan's word coordinates). The opening section keeps the epigraphs from Dante and Leopardi and the Proem. Two leaves (pages 20 and 21) are missing from the Internet Archive copy of the 1880 book, so the end of section VI (six tercets) and the whole of section VII are supplied from a later reprint, the Dobell selection of 1899 (Internet Archive 'cityofdreadfulni00thom_0'). Three corrections in the City (Ogni, not, blessing) come from the 1880 volume's own list of errata; the other four errata fall in the Heine versions. Stanza breaks follow the printed page.
works.blurb: James Thomson's poem of a nocturnal city of despair, in twenty-one numbered sections, with an epigraph from Dante, one from Leopardi and a Proem.

works.title: Three Judgments at a Blow
works.author: Pedro Calderón de la Barca
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #63776 (Eight Dramas of Calderon, freely translated by Edward FitzGerald, Macmillan 1906, reprinting the Six Dramas of 1853 and the Two Dramas of 1865). FitzGerald's advertisement, footnotes and afterwords are omitted.
works.blurb: In the Aragon of Pedro IV, a quarrel between two noble houses and a blow struck in the dark bring three sentences down together on the House of Urrea and the King's Minister. The title is Calderón's own riddle, answered in the closing lines: three judgments summed up in a single blow.

works.title: Tiriel
works.author: William Blake
works.note: Text from Poems by William Blake, selected by Alice Meynell (Blackie, Red Letter Library, 1911).
works.blurb: The blind and aged king Tiriel curses his sons, wanders to the vales of Har, and dies at last before the feet of his gentle, childlike parents.

works.title: Tommy Big-Eyes
works.subtitle: Fo'c's'le Yarns, First Series: IV
works.author: Thomas Edward Brown

IV). The printer's footnote glosses are left out and Brown's Manx-English spellings are kept as printed.
works.blurb: A dialect yarn about Tommy Gellin, a shy man with a head of his own, and how he won his darling little wife.

works.title: Torrent of Portyngale
works.author: Anonymous (Middle English)
works.note: Middle English text of Chetham's Library MS 8009, ed. E. Adam, EETS ES 51 (1887); introduction, notes, sidenotes and glossary omitted. The editor's expansions of scribal abbreviations are printed without their braces; the editor's bracketed line numbers, folio marks and apparatus are left out.
works.blurb: A Middle English verse romance in tail-rhyme stanzas. Torrent, the son of a Portuguese earl, loves the king's daughter Desonell, is sent to fight giants and a dragon, and after many adventures is crowned emperor of Rome. Preserved in a single fifteenth-century manuscript.

works.title: The Trachinian Maidens
works.author: Sophocles
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #14484 (Sophocles: The Seven Plays in English Verse), Lewis Campbell’s translation, first published 1883, World’s Classics revision of 1906. Campbell’s introductions, footnotes and notes are omitted.
works.blurb: Deianira, fearing she is losing Heracles to the captive princess Iole, sends him a robe smeared with what she believes is the centaur Nessus' love-charm. It is a poison, and Heracles is carried home in agony to die on a pyre on Mount Oeta, while Deianira takes her own life.

works.title: The Tragedy of Man
works.subtitle: A dramatic poem in fifteen scenes
works.author: Imre Madách
works.note: Text from the Internet Archive scan of The Tragedy of Man, dramatic poem, translated by William N. Loew (New York: Arcadia Press, 1908). Translator's preface and running heads omitted; speakers' names and stage directions retained.
works.blurb: Adam and Eve, newly cast out of Eden, are shown by Lucifer in a series of dreams the future course of humankind, from Egypt, Athens and Rome to the medieval church, Renaissance Prague, revolutionary Paris, a mechanised London and a frozen end of the world. In each dream Adam takes up a new ideal and sees it fail. Waking from the last, he is ready to end his life, until Eve tells him she is to bear a child and God bids him to strive and to trust.

works.title: Troilus and Cressida
works.author: William Shakespeare
works.note: Text from Project Gutenberg #1528 (Troilus and Cressida), updated 19 Sep 2025.
works.blurb: Seven years into the siege of Troy, the young prince Troilus, sick with love, enlists Cressida's uncle Pandarus to bring him to her bed, and the two swear eternal faith. Almost at once Cressida is traded to the Greek camp in exchange for the captured Antenor, where she yields to Diomedes while Troilus looks on. Around this affair the Greek leaders quarrel, Akhilleus sulks in his tent with Patroclus, Ajax is puffed up as a champion, and Thersites rails at the whole war. Hector is killed by Akhilleus' Myrmidons, and the play closes on Troy's coming fall and Pandarus' bitter epilogue.

works.blurb: In rime royal, Chaucer tells how the Trojan prince Troilus wins the love of Criseyde through her uncle Pandarus, and then loses her to the Greek camp, in the original Middle English.

Meanwhile Olivia's kinsmen and servants gull her pompous steward Malvolio with a forged love letter, while Viola's twin brother Sebastian, believed drowned, turns up to untangle the confusions of identity and desire. Feste the fool sings the songs that frame the play's wistful mirth.

works.blurb: Leontes, King of Sicilia, is seized by a sudden jealousy and accuses his pregnant queen, Hermione, of adultery with his oldest friend, Polixenes of Bohemia. He casts out the newborn Perdita, defies the oracle of Apollo, and loses both his son and, as he believes, his wife. Sixteen years pass, announced by the figure of Time, and Perdita, raised by shepherds in Bohemia, falls in love with Prince Florizel amid a sheep-shearing feast enlivened by the rogue Autolycus and his songs. The lovers flee to Sicilia, where the truth comes out and a statue of Hermione, in Paulina’s house, comes to life.

poems.title: A Hymn To The Setting Sun
poems.excerpt:
“Homage to thee, O Rā, when thou risest [as] Tem-Heru-khuti (Tem-Harmachis). Thou art adored [by me when] thy beauties are before mine eyes, and [when thy] radiance [falleth] upon [my] body. Thou goest forth to thy setting in the Sektet boat with [fair] winds, and thy heart is glad; the heart of the Mātet boat rejoiceth. Thou stridest over the heavens in peace, and all thy foes are cast down; the never-resting stars sing hymns of praise unto thee, and the stars which rest, and the stars which never fail glorify thee as thou sinkest to rest in the horizon of Manu, O thou who art beautiful at morn and at eve, O thou lord who livest and art established, O my lord!

“Homage to thee, O thou who art Rā when thou risest, and Tem when thou settest [in] beauty. Thou risest and shinest on the back of thy mother [Nut], O thou who art crowned king of the gods! Nut doeth homage unto thee, and everlasting and never-changing order embraceth thee at morn and at eve. Thou stridest over the heaven, being glad of heart, and the Lake of Testes is content [thereat]. The Sebau Fiend hath fallen to the ground; his arms and his hands have been hacked off, and the knife hath severed the joints of his body. Rā hath a fair wind; the Sektet boat goeth forth and sailing along it cometh into port. The gods of the south and of the north, of the west and of the east, praise thee, O thou divine substance, from whom all forms of life come into being. Thou sendest forth the word, and the earth is flooded with silence, O thou only One, who didst dwell in heaven before ever the earth and the mountains came into existence. O Runner, O Lord, O only One, thou maker of things which are, thou hast fashioned the tongue of the company of the gods, thou hast produced whatsoever cometh forth from the waters, and thou springest up from them over the flooded land of the Lake of Horus. Let me snuff the air which cometh forth from thy nostrils, and the north wind which cometh forth from thy mother [Nut]. Oh, make thou to be glorious my shining form (khu), O Osiris, make thou to be divine my soul (ba)! Thou art worshipped [in] peace (or [in] setting), O lord of the gods, thou art exalted by reason of thy wondrous works. Shine thou with thy rays of light upon my body day by day, [upon me], Osiris the scribe, the teller of the divine offerings of all the gods, the overseer of the granary of the lords of Abtu (Abydos), the royal scribe in truth who loveth thee; Ani, victorious in peace.”

poems.title: Hymn And Litany To Osiris
poems.excerpt: “Praise be unto thee, O Osiris, lord of eternity, Unnefer, Heru-khuti (Harmachis), whose forms are manifold, and whose attributes are majestic, Ptah-Seker-Tem in Annu (Heliopolis), the lord of the hidden place, and the creator of Het-ka-Ptah (Memphis) and of the gods [therein], the guide of the underworld, whom [the gods] glorify when thou settest in Nut. Isis embraceth thee in peace, and she driveth away the fiends from the mouth of thy paths. Thou turnest thy face upon Amentet, and thou makest the earth to shine as with refined copper. Those who have lain down (i.e., the dead) rise up to see thee, they breathe the air and they look upon thy face when the Disk riseth on its horizon; their hearts are at peace inasmuch as they behold thee, O thou who art Eternity and Everlastingness!”

poems.title: Litany

“Homage to thee, O An in Antes, (?) Heru-khuti (Harmachis), with long strides thou stridest over heaven, O Heru-khuti. Oh, grant thou unto me a path whereon I may pass in peace, for I am just and true; I have not spoken lies wittingly, nor have I done aught with deceit.” …

poems.title: Hymn To Rā
poems.excerpt:
“Hail, thou Disk, thou lord of rays, who risest on the horizon day by day! Shine thou with thy beams of light upon the face of Osiris Ani, who is victorious; for he singeth hymns of praise unto thee at dawn, and he maketh thee to set at eventide with words of adoration. May the soul of Osiris Ani, the triumphant one, come forth with thee into heaven, may he go forth in the Mātet boat. May he come into port in the Sektet boat, and may he cleave his path among the never-resting stars in the heavens.”

Osiris Ani, being in peace and in triumph, adoreth his lord, the lord of eternity, saying: “Homage to thee, O Heru-khuti (Harmachis), who art the god Khepera, the self-created; when thou risest on the horizon and sheddest thy beams of light upon the lands of the North and of the South, thou art beautiful, yea beautiful, and all the gods rejoice when they behold thee, the King of heaven. The goddess Nebt-Unnut is stablished upon thy head; and her uræi of the South and of the North are upon thy brow; she taketh up her place before thee. The god Thoth is stablished in the bows of thy boat to destroy utterly all thy foes. Those who are in the Tuat (underworld) come forth to meet thee, and they bow in homage as they come toward thee, to behold [thy] beautiful Image. And I have come before thee that I may be with thee to behold thy Disk every day. May I not be shut up in [the tomb], may I not be turned back, may the limbs of my body be made new again when I view thy beauties, even as [are those of] all thy favored ones, because I am one of those who worshipped thee [whilst I lived] upon earth. May I come in unto the land of eternity, may I come even unto the everlasting land, for behold, O my lord, this hast thou ordained for me.” …

poems.title: Hymn To The Setting Sun (2)
poems.excerpt:
The lady Mut-hetep, victorious, singeth hymns of praise to thee [saying]: “O Rā-Tem, in thy splendid progress thou risest, and thou settest as a living being in the glories of the western horizon; thou settest in thy territory which is in Manu. Thy uræus is behind thee, thy uræus is behind thee. Homage to thee, O thou who art in peace, homage to thee, O thou who art in peace. Thou art joined unto the Eye of Tem, and it chooseth its powers of protection [to place] behind thy members. Thou goest forth through heaven, thou travellest over the earth, and thou journeyest onward. O Luminary, the northern and southern halves of heaven come to thee and they bow low in adoration, and they pay homage unto thee, day by day. The gods of Amentet rejoice in thy beauties and the unseen places sing hymns of praise unto thee. Those who dwell in the Sektet boat go round about thee, and the Souls of the East pay homage to thee, and when they meet thy Majesty they cry: ‘Come, come in peace!’ There is a shout of welcome to thee, O lord of heaven and governor of Amentet! Thou art acknowledged by Isis who seeth her son in thee, the lord of fear, the mighty one of terror. Thou settest as a living being in the hidden place. Thy father [Ta-]tunen raiseth thee up and he placeth both his hands behind thee; thou becomest endowed with divine attributes in [thy] members of earth; thou wakest in peace and thou settest in Manu. Grant thou that I may become a being honored before Osiris, and that I may come to thee, O Rā-Tem! I have adored thee, therefore do thou for me that which I wish. Grant thou that I may be victorious in the presence of the company of the gods. Thou are beautiful, O Rā, in thy western horizon of Amentet, thou lord of Maāt, thou mighty one of fear, thou whose attributes are majestic, O thou who art greatly beloved by those who dwell in the Tuat (underworld); thou shinest with thy beams upon the beings that are therein perpetually, and thou sendest forth thy light upon the path of Re-stau. Thou openest up the path of the double Lion-god, thou settest the gods upon [their] thrones, and the Khus in their abiding places. The heart of Naarerf is glad [when] Rā setteth, the heart of Naarerf is glad when Rā setteth.”

“Hail, O ye gods of the land of Amentet who make offerings and oblations unto Rā-Tem, ascribe ye glory [unto him when] ye meet him. Grasp ye your weapons and overthrow ye the fiend Seba on behalf of Rā, and repulse the fiend Nebt on behalf of Osiris. The gods of the land of Amentet rejoice and lay hold upon the cords of the Sektet boat, and they come in peace; the gods of the hidden place who dwell in Amentet triumph.” …
