poems.excerpt: LAUREL-groves, plane-groves, and aery pine-groves, and a bath not made for one, you keep to yourself, and your colonnade stands high on a hundred columns, and trodden under your foot gleams the alabaster; and the flying hoof makes ring your dusty drive, and CD every side babbles the water of a stream crossing your ground; your halls lie open without end. But nowhere is there a place for dining or for sleep How well you are — not housed!

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 51 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Do you wonder, Aulus, that our friend Fabullinus is so often taken in? A good man is always a greenhorn.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 52 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: He who was wont to bind his temples with the Muses' crown, whose eloquence was no less famed among dismayed defendants, here, here he lies, Sempronia, who was once thy own Rufus, whose very ashes glow with love for thee. Sweetly mid Elysian fields is thy story told, and dazed is even Tyndarus' daughter i at thy ravishment; thy fame is the happier, for, quitting thy ravisher, thou didst return; she, even when sought again, would not join her spouse. Menelaus - listens to a Trojan love-tale and smiles: the story of your rape makes Phrygian Paris guiltless. When the joyous abodes of pious souls shall some day receive thee, no shade more famed will dwell in the house of Styx; Proserpina looks not strangely on the ravished, but loves them: that love thou hast shown shall win thy Queen's good-will.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 53 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Though you have moneys and wealth such as only a citizen here and there owns, you bestow nothing, Paternus, and brood over your treasui-e like the great dragon that poets sing of as guardian once of the Scythian grove. But the reason, as you report, and yourself repeat, is a son of dreadful rapaciousness. Are you looking, then, for simpletons and ignoramuses to delude and rob of sense? To this vice you have always been father.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 54 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Of hair red, swarthy of face, short of foot, of eye blear, you show yourself to be a portent, Zoilus, if you are virtuous.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 55 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: He who bids you, girls, give your favours for nothing, is a most foolish and impudent fellow. Do not give them for nothing, kiss for nothing. This Aegle refuses, this in her greed she sells. But let her sell it: how precious is a good kiss! This she sells, I say, and for no small plunder too; she asks for either a pound of Cosmian unguent, or four times two gold coins of the new mintage, that her kisses may not be silent ones or grudgingly given, that she may not with shut lips deny their approach. Yet this one thing she does graciously; Aegle, who refuses to give a kiss, a single kiss, for nothing, does not refuse to for nothing.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 56 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You are ill in a single year ten times, or oftener, Petilian domain whose ground floor looks down on the hill tops, and where you have country in the town, and a Roman for your vine-dresser — not on Falernian hills is there a greater crop — and within your boundary a broad drive for your curricle, and unfathomed depths of ' slumber, and a stillness broken by no tongues, and no daylight unless you let it in. As for me, the laughter of the passing throng wakes me, and Rome is at my bed's head. Whenever, worn out with worry, I wish to sleep, I go to my villa.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 58 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Your wife calls you an admirer of servant maids, and she herself is an admirer of litter-bearers. You are a pair, Alauda.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 59 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Rome gives you as many kisse.s, when after fifteen years you have just returned, as Lesbia never gave Catullus. Upon you all the neighbourhood presses, upon you the bristly farmer with a kiss like a he-goat's; on this side the weaver crowds you, on that the fuller, on this the cobbler who has just been kissing his hide, on this the owner of a perilous chin; on this side the one-eyed and on that the blear-eyed, and many a rascal with foulest lips. By now you find it was not worth while to return.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 60 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Thou day, nursling of Mars, whereon I first saw the rosy light and the mighty visage of the star-encircled god, if it shall shame thee to be worshipped in the country and at green altars, who wert worshij ped by me in the Latian city, grant thy pardon in that I refuse to be a slave on my kalends, but wish to live on the day I was born. To grow pale on one's birthday lest Sabellus lack warm water; and, that Alauda may drink his wine strained, anxiously to pass the turbid Caecuban through the bag; and to go to and fro among one's tables; to receive these and those guests, and all through the dinner to be getting up, treading on marble colder than ice — what reason is there why one should suffer and endure these things of one's own accord, which, if your lord and master bade you, you would refuse?

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 61 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You are afi-aid, Ligurra, I should write verses on you, and some short and lively poem, and you long to be thought a man that justifies such fear. But vain is your fear, and your longing is vain. Against bulls Libyan lions rage, they are not hostile to butterflies. Look out, I advise you, if you are anxious to be read of, for some dark cellar's sottish poet, one who with coarse charcoal or crumbling chalk scrawls poems which people read in the jakes. Your brow is not one to be marked by my brand.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 62 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Great king of the ancient heaven and of a bygone world, under whose reign was lazy rest and no toil, nor over-tyrannous thunderbolt, nor men that deserved the bolt, when, earth was not cleft to its nether deeps but kept her riches for herself, gladly and graciously come thou to Priscus' festival of joy: it befits thee to attend thy own rites. Thou in the sixth winter. Father most good, bringest him back to his fatherland from peaceful Numa's Latin city.'' Seest thou how, as in a Roman market, hangs cheer, to honour thee, how full is festive luxury? how unsparing the hand? and the tokens on the loaded board? what rich gifts, Saturnus, are measured out to thee? And, to give value and greater praise to such worth, 'tis a father and a frugal man who so celebrates thy rites. And do thou, hallowed Sire (so mayst thou be ever loved thus in thy own December), bid days like these return upon him oft.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 63 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: CoRDUBA, more prolific than oil-bearing Venafrum,' nor less perfect than the jars of Istria, thou that dost outvie the sheep of white Galaesus, not by the aid of any cheating shell-fish or blood, but by flocks coloured in native hues,® tell your poet, I beg you, to have some shame, and not to recite my poems scot-free. I could bear it if a good bard did this, one I could visit with pain in his turn. A bachelor debauches without reprisal, a blind man cannot lose that whereof he robs you. Nothing is worse than a naked robber, nothing more safe than a bad poet.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 64 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: A slave surpassing with his face and locks the rosy-cheeked attendants Cinna has made his cook. Cinna, you are a lickerish fellow!

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 65 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: When lovely Phyllis had all the evening yielded herself bounteously to me in every way, and I was considering next morning what present to give her, whether a pound of unguent of Cosmus' or Niceros' make, or full weight of Baetic wool, or ten yellow boys of Caesar's mintage, Phyllis, embracing my neck, and wheedling me with a kiss as lingering as that of wedded doves, began to ask me for a — jar of wine!

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 66 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: A town house was bought by you for twice fifty tliousand sesterces, and you long to sell it even for a scantier sum. But you seek to seduce a purchaser with crafty art, Amoenus; and a cottage lies disguised pretentiously in riches. Couches gleam bright, inlaid with peerless tortoiseshell, and there are pieces, choice and weighty, of Moorish citrus-wood; an elaborate sideboard is loaded with silver and gold plate; young slaves are standing there whom I would wish my masters! Then you loudly prate of two hundred thousand sesterces, and say the place is not worth less. Furnished as it is, Amoenus, you are selling your town house cheap.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 67 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You, Ides of May, brought forth Mercurius; on August's Ides return Diana's feasts; Maro has hallowed the Ides of October. Oft may you keep these Ides and those, you, who celebrate great Maro's Ides!

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 68 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Morning client, the cause of my leaving Rome, you would court, were you wise, the halls of greatness. No pleader am I, nor fitted for bitter lawsuits, but an indolent man and one growing old, and the comrade of the Muses. Ease and sleep attract me, and great Rome denied me these; I return if I am sleepless even here.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 69 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Just like your pictures and cups, Paulus, all the friends you possess are "genuine antiques."

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 70 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: When of late a bow-legged home-born slave carried his towels for Aper, and a one-eyed old crone sat guard o\'er his scanty toga and a ruptured anointer offered him his drop of oil, he was a stern and harsh censor of drinkers; he used to shout that the cups ought to be smashed, and the Falernian poured away that the knight, just bathed, was drinking. But after tliree hundred thousand sesterces came to him from an old uncle, he doesn't know how to go home from the warm baths sober. Oh, how great is the influence of fretwork chalices and five long-haired slaves! Til en, when he was poor, Aper was not thirsty!

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 71 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: There is nothing you do not deny me, Ljgdus, when I ask; but once there was nothing, Lygdus, you denied.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 72 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Having purchased the acres of a small farm lying hid near the tombs, and an ill-built cottage with a shored-up roof, you desert the city law-suits, that were your landed estate, Pannychus, and the small but certain reward of your threadbare gown. Wheat, millet, and barley and beans you used to sell when you were an attorney: you buy them now you are a farmer.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 73 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You say I am your heir, Catullus. I won't believe it unless I read my name, Catulhis.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 74 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: While a fleet from Nile is bnn<Ting you crystal glass, accept some cups from the Flaminian Circus. Are these the more "dreadnought" or are they who send such presents? But in cheap vessels is a double advantage: these embossed cups attract no thief, Flaccus, and they are not cracked by water too hot. What of this, too, that the attendant is not nervous while a guest drinks, and shaky hands do not fear a slip? This, also, is something: you will drink a health in these vessels, Flaccus, if you have to break the cup afterwards.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 75 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: PoLYTiMUS hurries off to girls, Hypnus unwillingly confesses that he is a boy, Secundus has buttocks yard-fed, Dindymus is effeminate but wishes not to seem so, Amphion might have been born a girl. The caprice of these boys, and their haughtiness, and their querulous disdain, I prefer, Avitus, to five times two hundred thousand sesterces of dower.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 76 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: A flagon of wine is sold for twenty pence, a peck of corn for four. The husbandman is drunk and overfed, but has nothing.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 77 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: While with many prayers he addressed Jupiter, standing all the time, with eyes upturned, on the tips of his toes, Aethon in the Cajiitol broke wind. Men laughed, but the Father of the Gods himself was offended, and amerced his client in domiciliary dinners for three nights. After this outrage wretched Aethon, when he is minded to enter tlie Capitol, makes beforehand for Paterclius' latrines, and lets off his piece ten and twenty times. But, however much he has taken precautions by this crepitation, 'tis with constricted buttocks he addresses Jove!

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 78 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: I wrote nothing against you, Bithynicus. Do you refuse to believe me, and require me to swear? I prefer to pay the debt.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 79 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: I have given you much you asked; I have given you more than you asked; yet you do not cease continually to ask me. He who refuses nothing, Atticilla, is capable of anything.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 80 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: To avoid praising the worthy, Callistratus praises everybody. Who can be good in his eyes to whom no man is bad?

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 81 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: In the days of winter and at the feast of Saturn, Umber used to send me a cape: he was poor. Now he sends me capers: for he has become rich.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 82 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: To escape Menogenes in the warm baths and about the baths is impossible, try what artifice you will. He will grab the warm hand-ball with right and left, that he may be able often to score to your account the balls he catches.' He picks up and will restore to you the flaccid bladder-ball from the dust, even if he has already bathed, is already in his dinner slippers. If you take your towels, he will speak of them as whiter than snow, although they are dirtier than an infant's bib. While you are arranging with a comb your scanty hairs, he will say these are Achilles' locks that you have ordered. He will with his own hands bring you the dregs from the bottom of the smoky wine-jar, and he wipes the moisture on your brow. Everything he will praise, will admire everything, until, having endured to the end a thousand boredoms, you say "Come and dine."

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 83 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Fabianus, who derided hernia, whom of late all lewd fellows dreaded, when he inveighed against swelling ruptures in tones even two Catulluses could not match, suddenly beheld himself — wretched fellow! — in Nero's warm baths, and began to hold his tongue.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 84 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: I was loth, Polytimus, to mar those locks of thine, but glad am I to have granted that much to thy prayers. Such wert thou, O Pelops lately shorn, and thus, when thy hair was laid aside, didst thou shine, so that thy spouse saw all the ivory of thy shoulder.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 85 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You say that the breath of unnatural rascals smells. If this be, as you say, true, Fabullus, what do you imagine is the smell of some others?

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 87 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: CoTTA, after complaining that he had twice lost his house-shoes while he brought with him a careless attendant, the only slave that serves for and makes up his staff, thought out — sagacious and acute man I — how to avoid such a loss too often. He now goes out to dine without outdoor shoes!

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 88 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: ToNGiLiANus has a nose: I know, I don't deny it. But now Tongilianus has nothing but a nose.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 89 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You swathe your head in wool, Charinus; but it is not with your ears that it goes sadly, but with your hair.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 90 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: For his old friend, ill of a severe and burning semi-tertian fever, Maro — and aloud — made a vow that, if the sick man were not sent down to the Stygian shades, there should die a victim welcome to mighty Jove. The doctors begin to guarantee a certain recovery. Maro now makes vows not to pay his vow.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 91 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Although, Magulla, you have a couch, and have a concubine in common with your husband, tell me why you have not a cupbearer also. You sigh: the reason is, you fear the wine-cup.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 92 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You are often wont to ask me what sort of person I should be, Priscus, if I became rich and were suddenly powerful. Do you think any man can declare his character in future .'' Tell me, if you became a lion, what sort of lion will you be?

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 93 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Labulla has discovered how to kiss her lover in the presence of her husband. She gives repeated kisses to her dwarf fool; this creature, slobbered with many kisses, the lover at once pounces upon, fills him up with his own kisses, and hands him back to the smiling lady. How much bigger as a fool is the husband!

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 94 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: I was writing an epic; you began to write one: left off, that my poems should not stand in rivalry with yours. My Thalia shifted to tragic buskins: you also fitted on yourself the long train of tragedy. I struck the strings of a lyre practised by the Calabrian Muses: you, ambitious man, snatch from me the new quill. I venture satire: you strain to be a Lucilius. I sport with light elegies: you, too, sport with the same thing. What lesser art can there he? I begin to model epigrams: in this quarter, too, my fame is already sought after by you. Pick out something you do not want — for what modesty is there in wanting everything? — and if there is anything you don't want, Tucca, leave it to me.

poems.title: Book XII, Epigram 98 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Baetis, with thy hair wreathed with the olive crown, that dippest thy golden fleeces in sparkling waters, whom Bromius, whom Pallas loves, to whom the king of waters, Albula, opens a path that wafts the ships over the seas, with glad omens may Instantius first tread thy shores, and this year pass for the peoples as the last. He is not blind to the burthen of succeeding Macer: he that gauges his load can bear it.

poems.title: Book XIII, 1 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: That tunny-fry may not lack a gown, and olives a capote/ nor the foul black beetle fear pinching hunger, destroy, ye Muses — the loss is mine — papyrus from the Nile: see tipsy winter calls for new pleasantries, No die of mine contends with dauntless weapon, nor does sice together with ace shake my ivory box: this paper is my nuts, this paper is my dice-box; hazard that brings me no loss nor yet any gain.

poems.title: Book XIII, 2 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Although you have always a critic's nose, are in a word a nose so great that Atlas on request would not have consented to shoulder it, and though you can deride even Latinus himself, you cannot say more against my trifling effusions than I have said myself. What pleasure is there in tooth gnawing tooth? you require flesh if you want to be fat. Lest you should waste your time, keep your venom for those that fancy themselves; I know these efforts of mine are nothing worth. And yet not altogether nothing if you come to me with a just ear, and not with a morning aspect.

poems.title: Book XIII, 3 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The whole collection of Mottoes in this slender little volume will cost you to buy four sesterces. Is four too much. it can cost you two, and bookseller Tryphon would make his profit. These distichs you can send to your guests instead of a gift, if a coin shall be as rare with you as with me. In addition you will get the names of the things on the headings: pass it by if anything is not to your stomach.

poems.title: Book XIII, 4: Incense (Ker)
poems.excerpt: That it may be late ere Germanicus rule the palace of Heaven, and that he may long rule earth, give pious incense to Jove.

poems.title: Book XIII, 5: Pepper (Ker)
poems.excerpt: When a beccafico, with its bright waxen flesh and plump sides, falls to you by lot, if you have taste, add pepper.

poems.title: Book XIII, 6 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: I can send you barley-water, a rich man will be able to send you mead. If the rich man be unwilling to send it, you will buy.

poems.title: Book XIII, 7 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If pale beans bubble for you in a red earthenware pot you can often decline the dinners of sumptuous hosts.

poems.title: Book XIII, 8 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Flavour common jars with pulse from Clusium, that, after dinner, you may drink from them, when empty, new wine.

poems.title: Book XIII, 9 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Receive lentils of Nile, a present from Pelusium; tliey are cheaper than spelt, dearer than beans.

poems.title: Book XIII, 10 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: One cannot enumerate the properties or the uses of flour, seeing that it is so often handy for the baker and the cook.

poems.title: Book XIII, 11 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Receive something for your muleteer to withhold from your mules that will not blab. I have given this to the inn-keeper, not to you, as a gift.

poems.title: Book XIII, 12: Com (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Take three hundred pecks from the harvest of the Libyan farmer, that your suburban land may not gi"ow sterile.

poems.title: Book XIII, 13 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: That insipid beet the noon-meal of artizans, may acquire flavour, oh, how often will the cook ask for wine and pepper!

poems.title: Book XIII, 14 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Tell me, why is it that lettuce, which used to end our grandsires' dinners, ushers in our banquets?

poems.title: Book XIII, 15 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If you till fields near to me at Nomentum, I remind you, rustic, to bring wood to my villa.

poems.title: Book XIII, 16 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: These rapes, delighting in winter's cold, which I give you, in heaven Romulus is wont to eat.'

poems.title: Book XIII, 17 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: In order that pale sprouts may not move your disgust, let the cabbage become green in water and soda.

poems.title: Book XIII, 18 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: As often as you have eaten the strong-smelling shoots of Tarentine leeks, give kisses with shut mouth.

poems.title: Book XIII, 19: Headed Leeks (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Woody Aricia sends the finest leeks: observe on the white stem the green blades.

poems.title: Book XIII, 20 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: These the land of Amiternum nurtures in its fertile gardens; the round rapes of Nursia you will be able to eat at less cost.

poems.title: Book XIII, 21 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The succulent stalk that has grown in watery Ravenna will not be more palatable than wild asparagus.

poems.title: Book XIII, 22 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: I am a grape unfit for the wine-cup and worthless to LyaeuSj but, if you do not drink me, I shall be nectar to you.

poems.title: Book XIII, 23: Chian Figs (Ker)
poems.excerpt: A Chian fig is like the old wine Setia has sent you; it carries in itself new wine, and in itself salt too.

poems.title: Book XIII, 25 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: We are Cybele's apples "; depart far hence, traveller, lest our downfall descend on your wretched head.

poems.title: Book XIII, 26 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: We are service berries that astrict too relaxed bowels; you will better give these apples to your boy than to yourself.

poems.title: Book XIII, 27 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: A gilt date is offered on the kalends of January; but yet this is wont to be the gift of a poor man.

poems.title: Book XIII, 28: A Jar of small Syrian Figs (Ker)
poems.excerpt: These Syrian figs, which, stored in a round conical jar, have reached you, would, if largei-, be figs.

poems.title: Book XIII, 29 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Take plums wrinkled by shrivelling old age abroad: they are used to lighten the load of an obstinate stomach.

poems.title: Book XIII, 30 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Cheese, stamped with the crest of Etruscan Luna, will afford your slaves a thousand lunches.

poems.title: Book XIII, 31 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If you wish without meat to take a frugal breakfast, this lump comes to you from a Vestinian flock.

poems.title: Book XIII, 32 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: It is not every heat, or every smoke that a cheese imbibes; but that which has imbibed V elabran has flavour.

poems.title: Book XIII, 33 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Trebula gave us birth; a double excellence recommends us; we are tamed by a moderate fire or by water.

poems.title: Book XIII, 34 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Since your wife is an old woman, and your members are nerveless, you can do nothing but satisfy your hunger with bulbs.

poems.title: Book XIII, 35 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Daughter of a Picenian sow, here I come, a Lucanian sausage; with me you may put a toothsome garnish round white pottage.

poems.title: Book XIII, 36: A Small Box of Olives (Ker)
poems.excerpt: These olives which have reached you, withdrawn from the oil presses of Picenum, begin and also end our repasts.

poems.title: Book XIII, 37 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: These were either from the branches of Corcyra's garden, or they were apples, the Massylian dragon's charge.

poems.title: Book XIII, 38 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Beestings, whereof the shepherd has robbed the kids while not yet able to stand, I give you fi-om the first milk of the dams.

poems.title: Book XIII, 39: Kid (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Let the wanton beast, and one of no service to the green vine, pay the penalty; though young, it has already injured the god.

poems.title: Book XIII, 40: Eggs (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If a white liquid surround the saffron-coloured yolks, let the sauce of Spanish mackerel season the eggs.

poems.title: Book XIII, 41 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Let a rich man set before me the nursling, fed on milk alone, of a lazy mother, and let him eat of an Aetolian boar.

poems.title: Book XIII, 42 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: I do not give you tuber-apples and pomegranates from Libyan boughs, but from my Nomentan trees.

poems.title: Book XIII, 43: The Same (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Culled from suburban boughs are sent you pomegranates and home-grown tuber-apples. What do you want with Libyans?

poems.title: Book XIII, 44: Sows Paps (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You would think it not yet a dish of udder, so full-flowing is the dug, and so does the pap swell with living milk.

poems.title: Book XIII, 45: Fonds (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If I possessed guinea-fowls and pheasants you should receive them; but now receive the birds of the farmyard.

poems.title: Book XIII, 46 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Of little worth should we peaches have been on the branches of our mother tree; now on adoptive boughs we peaches are prized.

poems.title: Book XIII, 47 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The bread of Picenum jrrows big with its white nectar as a light sponge swells when it has taken in water.

poems.title: Book XIII, 48: Mushrooms (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Silver and gold, and a mantle, and a toga it is easy to send; to send mushrooms is difficult.

poems.title: Book XIII, 49 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Seeing that figs nourish me, seeing that I am fed on sweet grapes, why did not the grape rather give me my name .''

poems.title: Book XIII, 50 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: We truffles that burst through the nurturing soil with our soft heads are of earth's apples second to mushrooms.

poems.title: Book XIII, 51 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: A circlet woven of roses or rich spikenard perhaps pleases you, but one made of fieldfares pleases me.

poems.title: Book XIII, 52 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: LI I. — Ducks Let a duck certainly be served up whole; but it is tasty only in the breast and neck: the rest return to the cook.

poems.title: Book XIII, 53: Turtle-doves (Ker)
poems.excerpt: When I shall have a fat turtle-dove, good-bye, lettuce; and keep the snails for yourself. I don't want to spoil my appetite.

poems.title: Book XIII, 54 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Let me have Cerretanian gammon served to me, or it may be sent from the Menapians; let gourmets devour ham.

poems.title: Book XIII, 55: Ham (Ker)
poems.excerpt: It is freshly cured: make haste, and do not put off your dear friends; for let me have nothing to do with an old ham.

poems.title: Book XIII, 56 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You perhaps the womb of a virgin pig may allure more: the maternal womb of a pregnant sow allures me.

poems.title: Book XIII, 57: Egyptian Beans (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You will scoff at this vegetable from Nile and its tenacious threads when with teeth and hands you draw out its stubborn fibres.

poems.title: Book XIII, 58 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: See how the liver is swollen bigger than a big goose! In wonder you will say: "Where, I ask, did this grow?"

poems.title: Book XIII, 59 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: All my winter is passed in sleep, and I am fatter at that season during which nothing but sleep nourishes me.

poems.title: Book XIII, 60 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: A rabbit delights in dwelling in burrowed holes: he taught foes the art of secret paths.

poems.title: Book XIII, 61 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Of all flavours of fowls the most tasty is said to be that of Ionian heathcocks.

poems.title: Book XIII, 62 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The hen is easily fattened on sweetened meal; it fattens, too, on the dark. Ingenious is gluttony!

poems.title: Book XIII, 63 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: That the cock might not grow thin by over indulgence, he has been gelded. Now he will be to me a Gaul.

poems.title: Book XIII, 64: The Same (Ker)
poems.excerpt: In vain the hen submits to her sterile husband. This bird it beseemed to have been the bird of Mother Cybele. LX V. — Partridges This bird is very rarely served on Italian tables: one often sees it playing in the fishpond.

poems.title: Book XIII, 65: Doves (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Do not violate with profane tooth tender doves, if the rites of the goddess of Cnidos have been entrusted to you.

poems.title: Book XIII, 67 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Ringdoves check and blunt the manly powers: let not him eat this bird who wishes to be lickerish.

poems.title: Book XIII, 68 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The green bird is beguiled by canes and nets at the season when the young grape is swelling with juice yet immature.

poems.title: Book XIII, 69 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Umbria has never supplied us with Pannonian cattae; these are the gifts Pudens prefers to send to his lord.

poems.title: Book XIII, 70 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Dost thou admire it, oft as it spreads its spangled wings, and hast the heart, unfeeling man, to deliver this bird to a cruel coo'li?

poems.title: Book XIII, 71 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: My ruddy wing gives me a name, but my tongue is a delicacy to gluttons. What if my tongue were to speak?

poems.title: Book XIII, 72 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: I was transported first by Argo's keel; ere that Phasis was all I knew.

poems.title: Book XIII, 73 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Although Hannibal ate his fill of Roman geese, yet the barbarian never ate the birds of his own land.

poems.title: Book XIII, 74 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: This bird saved the Thunderer's Tarpeian fane. Do you wonder.'' a god had not yet built it.

poems.title: Book XIII, 75 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You will disorder the lines, and the letter will not fly complete if you make away with a single bird of Palamedes.

poems.title: Book XIII, 76 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Whether I am woodcock or partridge, what does it matter if the flavour be the same > A partridge is dearer. 'Tis thus it has better flavour.

poems.title: Book XIII, 77: Swans (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The swan gives forth its sweet measured song with failing tongue itself the minstrel of its own death.

poems.title: Book XIII, 78 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Has so small a bird the name of a great giant? [t has, too, the name of Porphyrion of the Green.

poems.title: Book XIII, 79 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The mullet breathes in the sea-water brought A'ith him, but, already torpid, he begins to languish. 3ive him the fresh sea; he will be strong.

poems.title: Book XIII, 80 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The big lamprey that swims in the Sicilian deep;ea has not the strength to plunge when its skin is jcorched by the sun.

poems.title: Book XIII, 81 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: However wide is the dish that bears the turbot, y et the turbot is wider than the dish.

poems.title: Book XIII, 82: Oysters (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Drunken with the water of Baiae's Lucrine,! have I, a shell-fish, just arrived. Now, luxurious that I am, I thirst for the noble pickle.

poems.title: Book XIII, 83 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Cerulean Liris, which Marica's wood guards, is fond of us: from hence we prawns come in greatest numbers.

poems.title: Book XIII, 84 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Of this sea-bream, which has come lean from the sea-waves, the entrails are good eating; as to the rest it has poor flavour.

poems.title: Book XIII, 87 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Cloaks dyed in our blood/ ingrate, you put on; and this is not enough: we are your food.

poems.title: Book XIII, 88 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: In Venetian territory, however choice may be the entertainment, the beginning of the dinner is wont to be a gudgeon.

poems.title: Book XIII, 89 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Soft and white the bass breasts the mouths of Euganean Timavus, fed on fresh water and the salt of the sea.

poems.title: Book XIII, 90 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Not every gilthead deserves praise and a big price, but the one that feeds only on Lucrine shell-fish.

poems.title: Book XIII, 91 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Send sturgeon to Palatine tables; let rare offering adorn ambrosial feasts.

poems.title: Book XIII, 92: Hares (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Amongst birds the fieldfare, if my judgment can aught decide, amongst quadrupeds the primest delicacy is a hare.

poems.title: Book XIII, 93: Boar (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The terror in the land of Diomedes, the bristly beast that fell beneath an Aetolian spear/ was such as this.

poems.title: Book XIII, 94: Doe (Ker)
poems.excerpt: For his tusk is the boar dreaded, his horns defend the stag; we, unwarlike does, what are we but a prey?

poems.title: Book XIII, 95 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Not the meanest quarry among the beasts of morning shows, the savage oryx costs me the death of how many dogs!

poems.title: Book XIII, 96: The Stag (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Was this the stag tamed by your halter, Cyparissus, or rather was it your stag, Silvia .''

poems.title: Book XIII, 97 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: While he is a young wild ass, and is fed by his mother alone, the lalisio has, as a nursling, this name, but one short-lived.

poems.title: Book XIII, 98 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You will see a roe "poised on the summit of a rock; one can only hope she will fall; she is showing contempt of the dogs.

poems.title: Book XIII, 99 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You shall give a gazelle as a pet to your little son. The crowd loves to procure its dismissal by fluttering their togas.

poems.title: Book XIII, 100: The Wild Ass (Ker)
poems.excerpt: A beautiful wild ass comes; the hunt of the Indian tusk must be sent away; now shake your togas no longer.

poems.title: Book XIII, 101 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: This oil the berry of Campanian Venafrum has distilled for you; your unguent, as often as you use it, smells too of that oil.

poems.title: Book XIII, 102 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Receive this proud sauce, made of the first blood of a mackerel breathing still, an expensive gift.

poems.title: Book XIII, 103: A Jar of Tunny-fish Sauce (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Daughter of the tunny of Antipolis I confess I aui. Were I of the mackerel, I should not have been sent to you.'

poems.title: Book XIII, 104 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: This the bee, spoiler of Thesean Hymettus, has sent you, noble nectar from the woods of Pallas.

poems.title: Book XIII, 105 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: When you make a present of Sicilian combs from amid Hybla's hills ' you may say they are Attic combs.

poems.title: Book XIII, 106 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The vintage of Gnossos in Minoan Crete brought forth for you this, which is wont to be the poor man's mead.

poems.title: Book XIII, 107 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: That this pitch -flavoured wine came from vine-bearing Vienna do not doubt; Romulus himself sent it to me.

poems.title: Book XIII, 108 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You, Attic honey, thicken the nectarous Falernian. It is meet that such a drink be mixed by a Ganymede.

poems.title: Book XIII, 109: Alban Wine (Ker)
poems.excerpt: This wine the mild grape, proud of itself on the Julian mount, sends you from Caesar's cellars.

poems.title: Book XIII, 110 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Drink you Surrentine .'' Take not beakers ot painted murrine, nor of gold: these wines will supply you with their native cups.

poems.title: Book XIII, 111: Falernian Wine (Ker)
poems.excerpt: From presses of Sinuessa has the Massic come. Stored in what consul's year do you ask .'' there was no consul then.

poems.title: Book XIII, 112 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Setia high-poised, that looks on the Pomptine levels, has sent from a tiny city casks of aged wine.

poems.title: Book XIII, 113 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: This Fundanian the rich autumn of Opimius' year produced. The consul squeezed out the must, and himself drank the wine.

poems.title: Book XIII, 114 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: I am not, I confess, of the first brand of Lyaeus; yet among wines my vintage shall be the seventh.

poems.title: Book XIII, 115 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: I Generous Caecuban is ripened at Amyclae by Fundi, and the vine grows green, born in the middle of the marsh.

poems.title: Book XIII, 116 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Paei.ignian wine-growers send you turbid Marsic,vine. Do not driuk it yourself, but let your freednan do so.

poems.title: Book XIII, 122: Vinegar (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Let not a jar of Egyptian vinegar be mean in your syes. When it was wine it was more mean.

poems.title: Book XIII, 123 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: When your dole shall strike off the list a hundred citizens, you can serve them the smoky wines of Massilia.

poems.title: Book XIII, 124 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Let Nepos serve Caeretan, you will imagine it Setine. He does not serve it to a crowd: with three guests he drinks it.

poems.title: Book XIII, 125 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Let Aulon, renowned for wool and blest in vines, give precious fleeces to you, wines "to me.

poems.title: Book XIII, 126: Unguent (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Unguent or wine never bequeath to your heir; let him have your cash: the whole of these give to your own self.

poems.title: Book XIII, 127: A Crown of Roses (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Forced coronals winter gives thee, Caesar: erewhile the rose was Spring's: now has it become thine.

poems.title: Book XIV, 1 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: While the knight and My Lord the Senator rejoice in dinner-dress, while wearing freedom's cap beseems our Jove, and the home-bred slave, as he shakes the dice-box, does not fear to look the Aedile in the face, when he sees the cold tanks so near, receive these lots, gifts of rich and poor alternate; let everyone give his own guest his proper prize. "They are worthless and gira-cracks, or anything still meanei", if possible." Who does not know it? Or who denies what is so plain? But what else am I to do, Saturn, on the unsober days your son himself gave you in exchange for Heaven? Do you wish me to write of Thebes, or Troy, or guilty Mycenae? "Play with nuts," you say. I don't want to lose my nuts.

poems.title: Book XIV, 2 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You can finish this little book at whatever point you like; every subject is summed up in two verses. If you ask why headings are added, I will explain: it is that, if you prefer, you may read the headings only.

poems.title: Book XIV, 3: Tablets of Citrus-wood (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Had not our wood been cut into thin plates, we should have been the noble burden of a Libyan tusk.

poems.title: Book XIV, 4: Five-leaved Tablets (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The glad court of our master is warm with the slaughter of steers, when by the five-leaved waxen tablet is conferred on him high honour.

poems.title: Book XIV, 5: Ivory Tablets (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Lest dark-coloured waxen tablets dim your failing eyesight, let black letters dye for you snow-white ivory.

poems.title: Book XIV, 6: Three-leaved Tablets (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You will then deem my three-leaved tablets no mean gift, when your mistress shall write to you that she will come.

poems.title: Book XIV, 7: Parchment Tablets (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Imagine these tablets are waxen, although they are calltd parchment. You will rub out as often as you wisli to write afresh."

poems.title: Book XIV, 8 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Although she may not as yet have read them, a girl knows what Vitellian tablets wish for.

poems.title: Book XIV, 9: The Same (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Because you see we are very small, you believe we are being sent to a mistress. You are mistaken: a tablet of that sort also duns for money.

poems.title: Book XIV, 10 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: There is no reason you should think the offering puny when a poet gives you blank sheets.

poems.title: Book XIV, 11: Letter-paper (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Whether sent to a slight acquaintance or to a dear comrade, this paper is accustomed to address everyone as its "Dear friend."

poems.title: Book XIV, 12 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: To fill these money-boxes with anything but yellow money is unfitting: let cheap wood carry silver.

poems.title: Book XIV, 13 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If anything still remain at the bottom of me, a little money-box, it shall be a gift. Is there nothing.'' The little box itself shall be the gift.

poems.title: Book XIV, 14: Ivory Knuckle-bones (Ker)
poems.excerpt: When no one of the bones you throw stands with the same face as another you will say I have given you a great present.

poems.title: Book XIV, 15 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Let us dice be not equal in number to the knuckle-bones," if only our stakes be often greater than with the knuckle-bones.

poems.title: Book XIV, 16 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If the cheating hand, that knows how to arrange and throw the bones, has thrown them through me, he will achieve nothing beyond prayers.

poems.title: Book XIV, 17 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: On this side of rne dice ai-e counted by double sixes: on this other the piece of hostile colour is taken by twin foemen.

poems.title: Book XIV, 18 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Nuts appear a small stake, and one not ruinous; yet often has that stake made prize of boys' buttocks.

poems.title: Book XIV, 19 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Having won the case in the raffle, remember to equip it with pens: we have given you all else, do you provide the slighter things.

poems.title: Book XIV, 20: Draught Pieces (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If you play the war-game of robbers in ambush, these glass pieces will be your soldiers and their enemies.

poems.title: Book XIV, 21: A Style-case (Ker)
poems.excerpt: This style-case, fitted with its proper iron styles, shall be for you: if you give it to your boy, it will be no slight gift.

poems.title: Book XIV, 22 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Mastick is better; but if pointed wood be not forthcoming, a quill can relieve your teeth.

poems.title: Book XIV, 23 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If your ear is troubled with a persistent itching, I give you an instrument appropriate to such vagaries.

poems.title: Book XIV, 24 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: That your moistened hair may not soil your bright silks, let a pin fix and hold up your knotted locks.

poems.title: Book XIV, 25: Combs (Ker)
poems.excerpt: What will be the use, when it will find here no hair, of this many-toothed piece of box which is given you?

poems.title: Book XIV, 26 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The spume of the Chatti turns to flame Teutonic locks: you can be smarter with the hair of a captive slave.

poems.title: Book XIV, 27 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If white-haired you are set on dyeing your aged locks, accept — why be hairless? — these balls from Mattiacum.

poems.title: Book XIV, 28 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Accept a sunshade to subdue the overpowering heat; even though there be a wind, your own awning will cover you.

poems.title: Book XIV, 29 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: I will be a spectator with you in Ponipey's theatre for blasts of wind are apt to deny the people an awning.

poems.title: Book XIV, 30: Hunting-spears (Ker)
poems.excerpt: They will counter boars, and will wait for the lion's rush; they will pierce bears if the hand be but firm enough.

poems.title: Book XIV, 31 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If you lament that your hunting spear with its long blade has been struck down, this short weapon will closely engage a huge boar.

poems.title: Book XIV, 32 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: A soldier's decoration is this, and it will be a sign of a prized honour, a weapon worthy to gird a tribune's side.

poems.title: Book XIV, 33 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: This dagger, which a narrow circle marks with its rounded groove, Salo dipt while it was hissing in his chilling waters.

poems.title: Book XIV, 34: Sickle (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Me our Captain's assured peace has bent to serve quiet uses: the husbandman's am I now, the soldier's was I aforetime.

poems.title: Book XIV, 35: A Small Axe (Ker)
poems.excerpt: When a melancholy auction for payment of debts was held, this was bought for four hundred thousand sesterces.

poems.title: Book XIV, 36 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: These instruments are suitable for the cutting of your hair; this one is serviceable to long nails, that to your cheeks.

poems.title: Book XIV, 37 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Unless you provide me '' with choice books I will let in moths and savage bookworms.

poems.title: Book XIV, 38 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The land of Memphis supplies reeds handy for writing: let your roof be thatched with the reeds from other marshes.

poems.title: Book XIV, 39 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: I am a lamp, privy to the pleasures of your couch: you may do what you will, I shall be silent.

poems.title: Book XIV, 40 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The lot has given you the lamp's handmaid, which is awake and dispels complete darkness.

poems.title: Book XIV, 41 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Although I illume whole entertainments with my flames, and carry so many wicks, I am called a single lamp.

poems.title: Book XIV, 42 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: This taper will afford you light by night, for your lamp has been stolen from your slave.

poems.title: Book XIV, 43 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Candles gave me my name of old; the oil-lamp had no knowledge of our thrifty sires.

poems.title: Book XIV, 44 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You see I am wood; unless you guard the light, a great lamp will be made of your candelabrum.

poems.title: Book XIV, 45 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: This ball which swells with tip;htly-crammed feathers is less flaccid than the bladder-ball and less compact than a hand-ball.

poems.title: Book XIV, 46 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If you know how to bandy me with your nimble left-handers, I am yours. Don't you know how .'' You clown, give back the ball.

poems.title: Book XIV, 47 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Go far off, you young men; unstrenuous age befits me: with the bladder-ball it becomes boys to play, with the bladder-ball old men.

poems.title: Book XIV, 48 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: These the dissolute youth, who with empty labour makes big his neck, swiftly catches at on the dusty ground of Antaeus.

poems.title: Book XIV, 49 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Why is strength of arm wasted on the silly dumb-bell.'' Trenching a vineyard better employs men.

poems.title: Book XIV, 50: A Small Cap (Ker)
poems.excerpt: That the wrestler's dirty oil may not soil your sleek locks, you may cover your moist hair with this skin cap.

poems.title: Book XIV, 51 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Pergamus sent these; scrape yourself with the curved blade: the laundryman will not so often wear out your towels.

poems.title: Book XIV, 52 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: A steer bore me lately on his forehead: you fancied me a real rhinoceros horn.

poems.title: Book XIV, 53 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: This shalTbe for you, that horn, lately seen in our Master's Italian arena, to which a bull was as a straw-dummy.

poems.title: Book XIV, 54 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If any little home-born slave shall hang on your neck in tears, let him shake this noisy rattle with his infant hand.

poems.title: Book XIV, 55: Whip (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You will make no way with this whip though you may continually use the lash, if your courser be of the Purple faction.

poems.title: Book XIV, 56 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: What have you to do with me.'' Let a young maid use me: I am not wont to polish purchased teeth.

poems.title: Book XIV, 57 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: ThiSj which neither Virgil nor Homer mentions in his poems/ is compounded of unguent and ben-nut.

poems.title: Book XIV, 58 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Are you a countryman? You do not know what I am styled by a Greek name: I am called the froth of nitre. Are you a Greek? Aphronitrum.'

poems.title: Book XIV, 59 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Balsams attract me; these are the unguents of men ': ye matrons, exhale the choice perfumes of Cosmus.

poems.title: Book XIV, 60: Bean-meal (Ker)
poems.excerpt: 'Twill be a welcome gift, and one not without use to a wrinkled belly, if in broad daylight you go to Stephanus' bath.

poems.title: Book XIV, 61: A Horn Lantern (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Guide of your way am I carried, a lantern golden with fenced flame, and safe in my bosom is a small light.

poems.title: Book XIV, 62: A Lantern made of Bladder (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If I be not of horn, am I the dimmer? or does he that meets mc think me a bladder?

poems.title: Book XIV, 63: Pipe of Reed (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Why do you laugh at me, compact of wax and reed? The first pipe that was made was such as I.

poems.title: Book XIV, 64 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The drunken flautist bursts our ears with her bibulous cheeks; often she uses two pipes at once, often only one.

poems.title: Book XIV, 65 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If it happens your slave is not at hand, and you want to put on your house-shoes, your foot will itself be its own slave.

poems.title: Book XIV, 66: A Bosom-hand (Ker)
poems.excerpt: "With a bull's hide" you might well have braced up your bosom; for this skin stomacher of yours is too small for your breasts.

poems.title: Book XIV, 67 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: This which forbids foul flies to taste your meal was the proud tail of a peerless bird.

poems.title: Book XIV, 68 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Don't strike with your fist the teeth of your offending servant; let him eat the biscuit illustrious Rhodes has sent you.

poems.title: Book XIV, 69 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If you want to satisfy your hunger you can eat my Priapus; you may gnaw his very appendage, yet you will be undefiled.

poems.title: Book XIV, 70: Pig (Ker)
poems.excerpt: This pig will make you a "Good Saturnalia ": he was fed on acorns among the foaming boars.

poems.title: Book XIV, 71 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If your dress has been soiled with yellow dust let this light ox-tail emend this with a gentle flap.

poems.title: Book XIV, 72: A Sausage (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The sausage that has reached you at the mid-season of winter had reached me before Saturn's seven days."

poems.title: Book XIV, 73 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: I, A PARROT, will learn of you the names of others: this I learned of my own accord to say, "Caesar, hail!"

poems.title: Book XIV, 75 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Philomela laments the crime of incestuous Tereus: she who was a silent maiden is acclaimed as a bird of song.

poems.title: Book XIV, 76: Magpie (Ker)
poems.excerpt: A chattering pie, I with intelligible voice salute you, my master; did you not see me you -will say I am no bird.

poems.title: Book XIV, 77 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If you shall have such a bird as Lesbia, beloved of Catullus, mourned, here it can dwell.

poems.title: Book XIV, 78 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You see a medicine chest, the ivory equipment of a doctor's art: you will have a gift which Paccius would wish his own.

poems.title: Book XIV, 79 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Play, ye jovial slaves, but play only; I will keep these sealed up for five days.

poems.title: Book XIV, 80 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Hated much by boys and welcome to school-masters, we are the wood made famous by Prometheus' gift.

poems.title: Book XIV, 81: Wallet (Ker)
poems.excerpt: That he may not carry the mendicant scraps of a half-clad bearded philosopher, nor sleep with a sour cynic, is the prayer of the wallet.

poems.title: Book XIV, 82 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The palm-tree testifies that brooms were once in demand, but the crumb-collector has now given a rest to brooms.

poems.title: Book XIV, 83 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: This hand will protect your shoulder-blades when "an irritating flea is biting you, or any insect fouler than a flea.

poems.title: Book XIV, 84 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: To prevent your toga or cloak making your books frayed, this fir-wood will give long life to your paper.

poems.title: Book XIV, 85 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The bird, most lovely with its painted plumage, gives its name to a couch; it is now the bird of Juno, but once it was Argus.

poems.title: Book XIV, 86 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Take, hunter, the housing of a nimble steed, for from a bare-backed horse piles are wont to spring.

poems.title: Book XIV, 87 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Rf.ceive a horse-shoe couch inlaid with crescent lines of tortoise-shell. It takes eight: let everyone come who shall be my friend.

poems.title: Book XIV, 88 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If you think shell of a female land-tortoise is part of me, you are deceived: I am the male catch of the sea.

poems.title: Book XIV, 89 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Receive this wood of a fruitful tree, the offering of Atlas: he who shall give you golden gifts will give you less.

poems.title: Book XIV, 90 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: I am indeed not veined, nor the daughter of a Moorish forest, but even my wood knows sumptuous feasts.

poems.title: Book XIV, 91 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Tusks that upbear the huge bodies of bulls ® — do you ask whether they can uphold tables of Libyan wood?

poems.title: Book XIV, 92: Five-foot Rule (Ker)
poems.excerpt: An oaken rule, marked off into lengths and ending in a sharp point, is often apt to detect a contractor's fraud.

poems.title: Book XIV, 93: Antique Cups (Ker)
poems.excerpt: That is no recent work, nor pride of Roman chisel; Mentor made these cups and first drank from them.

poems.title: Book XIV, 94 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: We are plebeian chased cups of dreadnought glass, and our ware is not cracked by boiling water.

poems.title: Book XIV, 95: Chased Gold Bowl (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Though I am noble and ruddy with Gallician ore, I gloiy more in my workmanship, for of Mys was the labour you see.

poems.title: Book XIV, 96 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Receive a cup, a cheap memento of cobbler Vatinius, but that nose was longer.

poems.title: Book XIV, 97: Gold-inlaid Dishes (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Do not insult large gold-inlaid dishes with a small mullet: at the least it ought to weigh two pounds.

poems.title: Book XIV, 98 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: We advise you not overmuch to despise Arretian vases: Tuscan earthenware was luxury to Porsena.

poems.title: Book XIV, 99: Basket (Ker)
poems.excerpt: I have come, a barbarian basket, from the woad-stained Britons; but Rome now prefers to call me her own.

poems.title: Book XIV, 100 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If the country of the elegant Catullus is not unknown to you, you have drunk Rhaetian wine from my crock.

poems.title: Book XIV, 101 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Although mushrooms have given me so noble a name, yet I am a slave — alas! I am ashamed to own it — to early greens.

poems.title: Book XIV, 102 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Receive chalices not sprung of common clay, out the smooth embossed work of a Surrentine potter's-wheel.

poems.title: Book XIV, 103 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: With the snow I contain, I warn you, subdue your cups of Setine: in a poorer wine you may dip linen bags.

poems.title: Book XIV, 104 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: My linen also knows how to liquefy snow: no colder spirts the water from your strainer.

poems.title: Book XIV, 105: Small Jugs for -Table-service (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Cold water will not be wanting; there will not be wanting hot, if you ask for it; but do not you be dainty with a craving thirst.

poems.title: Book XIV, 106 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Here is given you a red jug with a spreading handle: Stoic Fronto used to go to this for cold water.

poems.title: Book XIV, 107 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The Satyrs love us, Bacchus loves us; us, too, the drunken tigress which has been taught to lick the wine-dabbled feet of her master.

poems.title: Book XIV, 108 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Take cups made of Saguntine clay, which without anxiety your servant may handle and guard.

poems.title: Book XIV, 109 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: See how the gold gleams, gemmed with the fire of Scythian emeralds! How many fingers has that chalice stripped!

poems.title: Book XIV, 110 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: In this jewelled flask that bears the name of Cosmus you may drink, luxurious man, if your thirst is for perfumed wine.

poems.title: Book XIV, 111: Crystal Cups (Ker)
poems.excerpt: So long as you fear to break them, you will break crystal cups: hands too careless and too anxious alike offend.

poems.title: Book XIV, 112 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The storm-cloud that comes from Jove will pour you water in plenty to blend your cups: this one will give you wine.

poems.title: Book XIV, 113 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If you drink your wine warm, murrine suits the burning Falernian, and better flavour comes therefrom to the wine.

poems.title: Book XIV, 114 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: This platter, her own townsman, ruddy with the soil of. Cumae, the chaste Sibyl has sent you.

poems.title: Book XIV, 115: Glass Chalices (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You observe the ingenuity of Egypt. Ah, how often has the artist, in wisliing to make additions, ruined his work!

poems.title: Book XIV, 116 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You drink Spoletine, or wine stored in Marsian cellars: what is the use to you of the noble coolness of boiled water?

poems.title: Book XIV, 117: The Same (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The drinking, not of snow, but of water fresh from the snow, the ingenuity of thirst has devised.

poems.title: Book XIV, 118 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Boy, forbear to mix Massilia's smoke with iced water, that the water may not cost you more than the wine.

poems.title: Book XIV, 119 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: While I am called for by a snapping of the fingers,® and the home-born slave lingers, oh, how often has a pillow been made my rival!

poems.title: Book XIV, 120 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: However much both knights and senators may call me ligula, I am called by ignorant grammarians lingula.

poems.title: Book XIV, 121: A Snail-pick (Ker)
poems.excerpt: I am convenient for eating snails, and no less useful for eating eggs. Do you know why I am rather called a snail-pick?

poems.title: Book XIV, 122: Rings (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Formerly many a friend gave us as presents, but now here and there a friend. Happy is he whose, comrade is a knight he himself has made '&

poems.title: Book XIV, 123 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Often a heavy ring slips from fingers moist with unguent; but your gem will be made safe in my faithful charge.

poems.title: Book XIV, 124: Toga (Ker)
poems.excerpt: He makes the Romans "lords of the world and the race that wears the toga," who granted his mighty sire immortality.

poems.title: Book XIV, 125: The Same (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If it comes easily to you to lose your morning sleep, by wearing out your toga a dole will often come to you.

poems.title: Book XIV, 126 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: 'Tis a poor man's offering but not a poor man's wear. This wrapper I send you in place of a cloak.

poems.title: Book XIV, 127 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: This cloak of Canusian wool, very like in colour to turbid mead, shall be your present. Rejoice: it will not quickly become old.

poems.title: Book XIV, 128 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Gaul clothes you in a Santonian cowled cloak. Formerly it was the frock of long-tailed monkeys.

poems.title: Book XIV, 129 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Rome is clad more in brown, Gaul in red, and this colour pleases boys and soldiers.

poems.title: Book XIV, 130 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Although you may set out on your journey when the sky is continuously serene, let a leather surtout nowhere be wanting against sudden showers.

poems.title: Book XIV, 131: Scarlet Mantle (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If you favour the Blue or the Green, why will you assume scarlet? See that by this lot you do not become a deserter,

poems.title: Book XIV, 132: Cap (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If I could, I should have wished to have sent a mantle complete: now I send you a present only for your head.

poems.title: Book XIV, 133 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: My wool is not deceptive, nor am I transformed in the vat. Let Tyrian mantles please you by such means: my own sheep dyed me.

poems.title: Book XIV, 134 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Stomacher, compress the swelling breasts of my mistress that there may be something for my hand to seize and cover.

poems.title: Book XIV, 136 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: In the winter season smooth coverings do not much avail: my wool makes warm your outer garment.

poems.title: Book XIV, 137: White Mantles (Ker)
poems.excerpt: We recommend ourselves by our use in the amphitheatre, when a white mantle shall cover a chilly toga.

poems.title: Book XIV, 138 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Let woollen cloths cover your nobler citrus wood: on my round tables a circular mark may stand.

poems.title: Book XIV, 139 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: CXXXIX,— Libumian Hood You have not known, O foolish fellow, how to match your mantle with me: you put it on white; take it off now green.

poems.title: Book XIV, 140 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Wool did not supply these, but the beard of the noisome husband: your foot will be able to take refuge in a Cinyphian nest.

poems.title: Book XIV, 141 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: While the toga gladly rests for five days, you may assume this garb as of right.

poems.title: Book XIV, 142 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Iv, meaning to recite, I shall perhaps have sent you a note of invitation, let this comforter emancipate your ears.

poems.title: Book XIV, 143 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Paduan garments of triple thread use up many fleeceSj and only a saw can sever the thick tunics.

poems.title: Book XIV, 144: A Sponge (Ker)
poems.excerpt: This sponge is given you by lot: it is useful for wiping tables when it lightly swells after the water has been squeezed out.

poems.title: Book XIV, 145 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Such is my whiteness, the beauty of my wool is such, that you would choose to wear me even in the midst of harvest.

poems.title: Book XIV, 146: Pillow (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Anoint your head with Cosmus' unguent, your pillow will smell of it: when your hair has lost the fragrance the feathers retain it.

poems.title: Book XIV, 147 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Your coverlet of wool is bright with purple bro-cade. What is the use of it if an aged wife freeze you .''

poems.title: Book XIV, 148 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: That the sacking on your bare bed might not show, we sisters, knit together, have come to you.

poems.title: Book XIV, 149 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: I shrink from big-breasted women: hand me over to some young girl, that my linen may enjoy a bosom of snow.

poems.title: Book XIV, 150 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: This present the land of Memphis makes you: now has the needle of Babylon been surpassed by the sley of the Nile.

poems.title: Book XIV, 151: A Female Girdle (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Long enough am I now; but if your shape should swell under its grateful burden, then shall I become to you a narrow girdle.

poems.title: Book XIV, 152 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Blankets the country of elegant Catullus will send you: we are from the region of Helicaon.

poems.title: Book XIV, 153 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Let a rich man give a tunic: I can gird you in front. Were I rich, I would give both gifts.

poems.title: Book XIV, 154 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Drunken as I am with the blood of Sidon's shell-fish, I do not see why I am called sober wool.''

poems.title: Book XIV, 155: White Wool (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Apulia is renowned for the finest wool/ Parma for second quality; its sheep, third in rank, commend Altinum.

poems.title: Book XIV, 156: Tyrian Wools (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Us the shepherd gave to his Lacedaemonian mistress i of less worth was the purple of her mother Leda.

poems.title: Book XIV, 157 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: This land is wont to supply not only wool that mourns with its black fleece: it supplies also its native chalices.

poems.title: Book XIV, 158: The Same (Ker)
poems.excerpt: My wool is indeed sad in hue, but 'tis fit for closeclipt attendants, such as — but not from the first rank of slaves — the table summons.

poems.title: Book XIV, 159 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Is the bed-girth "too near the feather pillow you crush down. Accept fleeces shorn for Leuconian cloaks.

poems.title: Book XIV, 160 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Marsh-reed chopped up is called Circensian stuffing. This litter the poor man buys in lieu of Leuconian.

poems.title: Book XIV, 161: Feathers (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Tired you may rest on feathers of Amyclae which the swan's inner down has given you.

poems.title: Book XIV, 162 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: I.ET your rustling mattress swell with thefts from your mule: pale Care comes not to hard couches.

poems.title: Book XIV, 163 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Give up the ball: the bell of the warm baths is sounding. Do you go on playing .'' You want to go home after a bath in the Virgin water only.

poems.title: Book XIV, 164 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: While the burnished weight of the Spartan quoit is flying, keep far off, ye boys: let that quoit be guilty only once.

poems.title: Book XIV, 165 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: It restored Eurydice to her bard; but he himself lost her, trusting not himself, nor loving with patience.

poems.title: Book XIV, 166: The Same (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Often has that been driven from Pompey's theatre, which drew after it woods and stayed wild beasts. CLXVIL— Quill for Playing the Lyre That an angry blister may not arise on your chafed thumb, let an ivory quill embellish your responsive lyre.

poems.title: Book XIV, 168: Hoop (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The wheel must be fitted with a tyre: you give me a useful present; this to boys will be a hoop, but to me a tyre.

poems.title: Book XIV, 169: The Same (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Why do noisy rings wander round the wide orbit? That the crowd that meets them may give way to tinkling hoops.

poems.title: Book XIV, 170: Golden Statue of Victory (Ker)
poems.excerpt: She is given without a drawn lot to him to whom Rhine has given a true victor's name. Ten times pour Falernian, boy.

poems.title: Book XIV, 171 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The renown of so small a statue is not unknown. Of this boy was Brutus the lover.

poems.title: Book XIV, 178: J Hercules in Clay (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Fragile am I, but do not you, I charge you, despise my small statue: it shames not Alcides to bear my name.

poems.title: Book XIV, 179: A Minerva in Silver (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Tell me, gallant maid, whereas thou hast thy helm and thy spear why hast thou not thine aegis? "Caesar has it."

poems.title: Book XIV, 180 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Better, most excellent Father of the Gods, couldst thou have been changed into a bull when lo was to thee a heifer.'

poems.title: Book XIV, 181: Marble Leander (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Daring Leander cried amid the swelling waters: "Drown me, ye waves, when I am turning home."

poems.title: Book XIV, 182 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: 'TvvAS a drunken Prometheus, I fancy, made for the earth this monster; he himself, too, played viith Saturnalian clay. CLXXXIIL— //07ner' "Battle of Frogs and Mice"

poems.title: Book XIV, 183 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Read through the story of the frogs sung in Homer's lay, and learn to smooth your brow by means of my trifles.

poems.title: Book XIV, 184 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The Iliad and the tale of Ulysses, foe to Priam's realm, both lie stored in many-folded skins.

poems.title: Book XIV, 185: Virgil's Gnat (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Receive, studious reader, the Gnat of eloquent Maro; you need not then lay aside your nuts to read "Arms and the Man."

poems.title: Book XIV, 186 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: How short a parchment has comprised the mighty Maro! The features of the man himself the first leaf beai-s.

poems.title: Book XIV, 187 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: With this first he lightly touched youth's wanton love, and Glycera was not the mistress of his boyhood: 'twas Thais.

poems.title: Book XIV, 188: Cicero in Parchment (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If this parchment shall be your travelling companion, imagine you are taking a long journey with Cicero.

poems.title: Book XIV, 189 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Cynthia, the theme of eloquent Propertius' youthful song, won from him fame; no less she herself bestowed.

poems.title: Book XIV, 190 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Narrowed into scanty skins is bulky Livy, the whole of whom my library does not contain.

poems.title: Book XIV, 191 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Here will be Crispus, first of Roman historians, as the judgment of learned men declares.

poems.title: Book XIV, 192 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: This bulk, that has been formed of many a leaf, contains the fifteen books of Naso's poems.

poems.title: Book XIV, 193 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Wanton Nemesis fired her lover Tibullus, whom it pleased to be "of no account in his own house."

poems.title: Book XIV, 194 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Some are there that say I am no poet: but the bookseller that sells me thinks I am.

poems.title: Book XIV, 195: Catullus (Ker)
poems.excerpt: As much great Verona owes to her Catullus as small Mantua owes to her Virgil.

poems.title: Book XIV, 196 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: These sheetSj that speak to you of fountains and of the names of rivers themselves will better swim in the waters they tell of.

poems.title: Book XIV, 197: Dwarf Mules (Ker)
poems.excerpt: From these mules no fall is to be apprehended: you are used to sit almost higher on the ground.

poems.title: Book XIV, 198 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If you wish to hear the tricks of a small lapdog, for the telling a whole page of mine is too short.

poems.title: Book XIV, 199 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: This little horse, that picks up its hurrying hoof in measured time, has come from tribes rich in gold, an Asturian steed.

poems.title: Book XIV, 200 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Not for himself, but for his master, hunts the keen greyhound, who will bring you a hare unwounded by his tooth.

poems.title: Book XIV, 202 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: A monkey cunning to avoid darts hurled at me, I should be a "long-tailed ape" had I a tail.

poems.title: Book XIV, 204 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: The brazen cymbals that mourn for the boy of Celaenae, the darling of the Great Mother, her priest is often wont to sell when hungry.

poems.title: Book XIV, 205: Young Slave (Ker)
poems.excerpt: May I have a boy with a cheek smooth with youth, not with pumice, for whose sake no maid would please me.

poems.title: Book XIV, 206: Cestus (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Round thy neck twine, boy, love's very essence, a cestus warm from the bosom of Venus.

poems.title: Book XIV, 207: The Same (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Take thou the cestus imbued with Cytherea's nectar: this girdle fired the lover Jove.

poems.title: Book XIV, 208 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Albeit the words speedy the hand is swifter than they: not yet has the tongue, the hand has finished its work.

poems.title: Book XIV, 209: Sea-shell (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Let the rind of the Mareotic rush be made smooth by the sea-shell: the reed-pen will run on an unimpeded path.

poems.title: Book XIV, 210: A Natural (Ker)
poems.excerpt: His dulness is not assumed, or pretended by crafty art. He that has wits no more than is enough has his wits.

poems.title: Book XIV, 211: Rams Head (Ker)
poems.excerpt: You have cut the soft throat of the lord of the flock, a ram of Phryxus; did he deserve this who gave you, cruel man, your tunic

poems.title: Book XIV, 212 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: If you regard the man's head alone you would believe him Hector; if you saw him standing you would deem him Astyanax.

poems.title: Book XIV, 213: Small Shield (Ker)
poems.excerpt: This, which is wont oft to be overcome, rarely to win, will be to you a small buckler, but a dwarf's great shield.

poems.title: Book XIV, 214 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: In all tins troupe will be no one "Tlie Hated"; [but any one of them can be "The Double Deceiver."

poems.title: Book XIV, 215 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Tell me candidly, O clasp, what do you guarantee to comedians and harp-players } "The greater value of their favours."

poems.title: Book XIV, 216 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: He preyed once upon birds; the servant of the fowler now, he strikes them down, and is sad the birds are not taken for his own behoof.

poems.title: Book XIV, 217 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: CCXVIL— /f Caterer Say with how many and at what cost you want to dine, and do not add another word: your dinner is ready for you.

poems.title: Book XIV, 218 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Not only by canes, but by a bird's note also is the bird deceived while the cunning reed is being lengthened by the noiseless hand.

poems.title: Book XIV, 219 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Seeing that you, a poor lawyer, write poems thai do not bring you in a penny, take from me pluck like your own.

poems.title: Book XIV, 220: Cook (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Insufficient is his art alone for a cook: I would not have his palate that of a slave; a cook ought to possess the taste of his master.

poems.title: Book XIV, 221 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Let your grated gridiron be unctuous with the rounded cutlet; on the long pointed spit let a foaming boar smoke.

poems.title: Book XIV, 222 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: A thousand toothsome shapes of handiwork that hand will construct for you; for him alone labours the frugal bee.

poems.title: Book XIV, 223 (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Get up: already the baker is sellino-to boys their breakfast, and the crested fowls of dawn are crowing on all sides.

poems.title: Book XIV, 224: Epigram of Uncertain Position (Ker)
poems.excerpt: Flavian family, of how much glory has thy third heir robbed thee! Well nigh had it stood us in stead not to have possessed the twain!

poems.title: Book XI, 418
poems.excerpt: If you put your nose pointing to the sun and open your mouth wide, you will show all passers-by the time of day.

poems.title: Book VI, 332
poems.excerpt: To Casian Zeus did Trajan, the descendant of Aeneas, dedicate these ornaments, the king of men to the king of gods: two curiously fashioned cups and the horn of a urus? mounted in shining gold, selected from his first booty when, tirelessly fighting, he had overthrown with his spear the insolent Getae. But, Lord of the black clouds, entrust to him, too, the glorious accomplishment of this Persian war, that thy heart’s joy may be doubled as thou lookest on the spoils of both foes, the Getae and the Arsacidae.

poems.title: Book VII, 674
poems.excerpt: This is the tomb of Archilochus, whom the Muse, out of kindness to Homer, guided to furious iambics.

poems.title: Book IX, 387
poems.excerpt: Hector of the race of Ares, if thou hearest where’er thou art under ground, hail! and stay a little thy sighs for thy country. Ilion is inhabited, and is a famous city containing men inferior to thee, but still lovers of war, while the Myrmidons have perished. Stand by his side and tell Achilles that all Thessaly is subject to the sons of Aeneas.

poems.title: Book XIV, 63: On the Sphinx
poems.excerpt: A CREEPING, flying, walking maiden; a lioness lifting up feet not her own as she ran; she was a woman winged in front, in the middle a roaring lioness, and behind a curling snake. She ran away neither making a trail nor as a woman, nor either bird or beast in her whole body; for she seemed to be a maiden without feet, and the roaring beast had no head. She had an irregularly mixed nature, made up of imperfect and perfect parts.

poems.title: Book XVI, 323: On the Invention of Glass
poems.excerpt: The workman having quarried it, brought the glass and put in the fire the mass hard as iron, and the glass, set afire by the all-devouring flames, ran out melted like wax. And to men it was a marvel to see a trail flowing from the fire, and the workman trembling lest it should fall and break; and on the points of the double forceps he put the lump.

poems.title: Book XI, 19
poems.excerpt: Drink and love now, Damocrates, for we shall not drink for ever or be for ever with the lads. Let us bind our heads with garlands and scent ourselves before others bear flowers and scent to our tombs. Now may my bones inside me drink all the more wine, and when they are dead let Deucalion’s flood cover them.

poems.title: Book XI, 21
poems.excerpt: Agathon’s lizard was rosy-fingered the other day ; now it is already even rosy-armed.

poems.title: Book XI, 117
poems.excerpt: The physician Capito anointed Chryses’ eyes then when he could see a high tower from a mile off and aman from a furlong and a quail from ten yards and a louse even from a foot. Now from a furlong he cannot see the town and from two hundred feet cannot see that the lighthouse is alight ; he scarcely sees a horse from half a foot off and as for the quail he once saw, he can’t even see a large ostrich. If he manages to give him another dose, he won’t ever after be able to see even an elephant standing close to him.

poems.title: Book XII, 1
poems.excerpt: “Let us begin from Zeus,’ as Aratus said, and you, O Muses, I trouble not to-day. For if I love boys and associate with boys, what is that to the Muses of Helicon?

poems.title: Book XII, 2
poems.excerpt: Look not in my pages for Priam by the altar, nor for the woes of Medea and Niobe, nor for Itys in his chamber and the nightingales amid the leaves; for earlier poets wrote of all these things in profusion. But look for sweet Love mingled with the jolly Graces, and for Bacchus. No grave face suits them.

poems.title: Book XII, 4
poems.excerpt: I delight in the prime of a boy of twelve, but one of thirteen is much more desirable. He who is fourteen is a still sweeter flower of the Loves, and one who is just beginning his fifteenth year is yet more delightful. The sixteenth year is that of the gods, and as for the seventeenth it is not for me, but for Zeus, to seek it. But if one has a desire for those still older, he no longer plays, but now seeks “ And answering him back.”

poems.title: Book XII, 5
poems.excerpt: I like them pale, and I also love those with a skin the colour of honey, and the fair too; and on the other hand I am taken by the black-haired. Nor do I dismiss brown eyes; but above all I love sparkling black eyes.

poems.title: Book XII, 8
poems.excerpt: Just now, as I was passing the place where they make garlands, I saw a boy interweaving flowers with a bunch of berries. Nor did I pass by unwounded, but standing by him I said quietly, “For how much will you sell me your garland?” He grew redder than his roses, and turning down his head said, “Go right away in case my father sees you.” I bought some wreaths as a pretence, and when I reached home crowned the gods, beseeching them to grant me him.

poems.title: Book XII, 9
poems.excerpt: Now thou art fair, Diodorus, and ripe for lovers, but even if thou dost marry, we shall not abandon thee.

poems.title: Book XII, 10
poems.excerpt: Even though the invading down and the delicate auburn curls of thy temples have leapt upon thee, that does not make me shun my beloved, but his beauty is mine, even if there be a beard and hairs.

poems.title: Book XII, 11
poems.excerpt: Yesterday I had Philostratus for the night, but was incapable, though he (how shall I say it?) was quite complaisant. No longer, my friends, count me your friend, but throw me off a tower as I have become too much of an Astyanax.

poems.title: Book XII, 13
poems.excerpt: I once found some beardless doctors, not prone to love, grinding a natural antidote for it. They, on being surprised, besought me to keep it quiet, and I said, “I am mum, but you must cure me.”

poems.title: Book XII, 15
poems.excerpt: If a plank pinched Graphicus in the bath, what will become of me, a man? Even wood feels.
