Tarry, ye twain, and listen : I will tell you, since ye ask : [I am] a man who wages war against his cousin, while [the King is] a man bereaved, repentant sore !

And I swear that had it not been for those who stood in the way, this keen sword, bright in its steel, had mingled the blood of both together. …

poems.title: Ode LXXXIX: Far away has Salma gone, and
poems.excerpt:
Far away has Salma gone, and taken up her abode among enemies, towards whom thou urgest on the unbroken young she-camels ;

And my people inhabit the mountain-side of Qanawan, while she dwells in the meadows of Bishah and ar-Rubab. …

poems.title: Ode XCI: Who will carry a message to
poems.excerpt:
Who will carry a message to Sa'd son of Nu'man, and Sa'd son of Dhubyan who binds his turban so pompously—

The two branches of the Children of Dhubyan, since their judgement is perverted, and they have been given a drench of bitterness against us ? …

poems.title: Ode XCII: May a forgiving Lord and an
poems.excerpt:
May a forgiving Lord and an Intercessor who is listened to pour blessings upon Yahya and his followers !

A folk were they to whom God decreed that the call [to die] should go forth : and setting aside God's command is a thing that may not be. …

poems.title: Ode XCIII: Many the host of horse, far-spreading
poems.excerpt:
Many the host of horse, far-spreading like birds in flight, have I stayed on its way down to battle, what time the faint-heart shouts his name and lineage, but turns aside himself from the fight —

Mounted thereon warriors clad in iron — some of them the hunted of the spear-points, others the hunters thereof : …

poems.title: Ode XCIV: Goodly, in sooth, were the young
poems.excerpt:
Goodly, in sooth, were the young warriors of the morning raid whom ye met, what time the women with heads bare were [pale with fright] like the white root of the papyrus —

One of them casting off her veil, and her sister running with her girdle slipped down to the place of the izar : …

poems.title: Ode XCV: By thy life ! I am
poems.excerpt:
By thy life ! I am a man who defends stoutly his folk, no fighter unskilled in the day of trouble ;

I give generously to strangers who come from afar to seek my bounty, and I withhold it not from those who are my kin or bound to me by covenant ; …

poems.title: Ode CXXIV: Dost thou recognize the abodes of
poems.excerpt:
Dost thou recognize the abodes of the household of Maiy, by the side of ash-Shaqiq, now empty and desolate ?

The gazelles and the oryx therein seem as though they had clad themselves in thin white muslin of Rai. …

poems.title: Ode XCVI: Ramah and its hill no longer
poems.excerpt:
Ramah and its hill no longer bear traces of Sulaima, and her journeyings and their divergencies have carried her far away from thee ;

There has changed her that which has changed men before her : she is gone, and the longings of my heart seek her out. …

poems.title: Ode XCVII: Ah, gone on her way is
poems.excerpt:
Ah, gone on her way is Idam ; and every tie to a fair one must one day wear out and snap !

Thou hast been her lover in earnest and in jest, until now that thou hast grown old, and men say — ' Verily thou art distraught ! ' …

poems.title: Ode XCVIII: Ah, our partners have departed and
poems.excerpt:
Ah, our partners have departed and cannot be reached, and thy heart is in the keeping of the ladies as they journey away !

The drivers make their way with them towards the waters of Nakhl, and they turn aside from the twin peaks of Aban. …

poems.title: Ode XCIX: To whom belong the dwellings thou
poems.excerpt:
To whom belong the dwellings thou hast lighted on at al-An'um, the traces of which stand forth like the markings of a spotted snake ?

The East wind has played with them, and they have become unrecognizable, but for a remnant of their trench with its sides broken in. …

poems.title: Ode C: Say to al-Muthallam and Malik son
poems.excerpt:
Say to al-Muthallam and Malik son of Hind — ' If thou desirest to assail our strength, come on !

' Thou shalt find among us what our enemies have to face, and thou shalt be given a morning draught from a cup the dregs of which are bitter as colocynth. …

poems.title: Ode CI: If now I complain not to
poems.excerpt:
If now I complain not to any of my pain, and if I cannot direct my steps unless I have one to guide me,

Yet time was when I have brought at dawn upon the pasturing camels of a tribe a host of raiders, far-spreading, one following another, besetting them suddenly from lowland and upland alike ; …

poems.title: Ode CII: Ye Sons of Manulah ! in
poems.excerpt:
Ye Sons of Manulah ! in sooth I obeyed your chiefs, hoping that there might be a way to avoid war with friends ;

And the Sons of Umayyah — all of them would be leaders and captains, and the Sons of Kiyah the same, when a matter is debated in council. …

poems.title: Ode CIII: Does not their knowledge of Zabban
poems.excerpt:
Does not their knowledge of Zabban suffice to restrain the Sons of al-Laqitah, that they attack him with lampoons, while he sleeps [and gives no heed to them] ?

They go about with the Weak-eyed one, while there is poured forth upon them a tongue keen like the edge of an Indian sword. …

poems.title: Ode CIV: Umamah came to me by night
poems.excerpt:
Umamah came to me by night, and far was the distance she had to travel in the darkness, when all my comrades were sleeping by their camel-saddles.

' How didst thou find thy way hither ? and never wast thou strong afoot ' : and of the people some were awake and some plunged in slumber. …

poems.title: Ode CV: My heart settled firmly upon quitting
poems.excerpt:
My heart settled firmly upon quitting Salma, and cut short its desires, after that she and I had both grown grey ;

And grey too are now my contemporaries, and they turn away from me, as thou strippest off garments and wearest them no more. …

poems.title: Ode CVI: Of a truth the Chiefs of
poems.excerpt:
Of a truth the Chiefs of Hawazin know well that I am the knight who defends the cause of the House of Ja'far ;

And al-Maznuq too knows well that I urged him again and again against the enemy's host, as one puts back into the bag again and again the blank arrow, denounced by the gamers. …

poems.title: Ode CVII: Now let Asma ask — for
poems.excerpt:
Now let Asma ask — for she is kind and cares for our fortunes — let her ask her counsellors whether I was driven away or not.

They said to her — 'Yea, we drove away and scattered his horsemen'. The yellow-toothed dogs ! it was not I that was wont to be driven away ! …

poems.title: Ode CVIII: When we drew near to the
poems.excerpt:
When we drew near to the leather tents and their folk, there was ordained to us a wolf, crafty and dangerous when night comes on :

Bakr were ordained to us, and under their banner were troops of horse which the strong, glorying in his strength, would look upon well pleased ; …

poems.title: Ode CX: She spent the night reviling me
poems.excerpt:
She spent the night reviling me and pressing me to sell Thadiq, and her rebellion against me was violent.

[I said :] ' Verily thy talking in secret about Thadiq is all one to me as if it were shouted abroad ! ' …

poems.title: Ode CXI: I have revealed my love for
poems.excerpt:
I have revealed my love for Juml — what a revelation ! and her case with me has come to light after being long kept hidden ;

And tale-bearers have been busy between us, and carried their stories abroad, until I had to avoid her, though I meant not to break the bond. ($) Shall there carry me to her a fleet camel, good as a stallion, strong, bulky under the saddle, tractable, easy in hand ? …

poems.title: Ode CXII: Saduf has departed, and her lover's
poems.excerpt:
Saduf has departed, and her lover's heart has been reft away : far off is Saduf, and alienated from thee.

She has left in thy keeping a crippling disease — her phantom to visit thee nightly in thy sleep and possess thy dreams. …

poems.title: Ode CXIV: Her journey has carried Laila ever
poems.excerpt:
Her journey has carried Laila ever further and further away, in place of our former sweet converse : yet somewhat of gain it is that I have memory to feed on.

Yet shall we have pleasance with Laila : her travel has not taken her utterly away : the hard stony plan of Kamatan is the place that holds her now. …

poems.title: Ode CXV: The Sid do not regard Zaid
poems.excerpt:
The Sid do not regard Zaid in their hearts as the Sons of Kuz and Marhub regard him.

If ye ask for that which is due, we will give his due to the asker, while the mail-coat is in its bag and the sword in its sheath : …

poems.title: Ode CXVI: O Jubail, verily thy father's day
poems.excerpt:
O Jubail, verily thy father's day is drawing in : so when thou art called to great deeds, make haste !

I leave with thee the testament of a man who counsels thee with sincerity, skilled in the deceitfulness of Fortune and not heedless thereof. …

poems.title: Ode CXVII: I have become sober, and lightness
poems.excerpt:
I have become sober, and lightness has left me — by the life of thy father! — a long, long leaving:

No more am I ready in the strife of reviling, nor greedy to feed on the flesh of my friends. …

poems.title: Ode CXVIII: We brought up our horse from
poems.excerpt:
We brought up our horse from the two sides of Arik to AjaR, to the ribs of ar-Rikham,

A vast host that [by shaking the earth] drove the field-rats from their holes, mighty in its array, a sure defence against enemies. …

poems.title: Ode CXIX: A heart quick to thrill when
poems.excerpt:
A heart quick to thrill when touched by Beauty has drawn thee far, although Youth has sped long since, and grey hairs invade thy brow.

It fills all my thought with Laila, distant though now her home, and matters of weight stand twixt us, obstacles manifold. …

poems.title: Ode CXX: Is that which thou knowest [i
poems.excerpt:
Is that which thou knowest [i. e., her inclination to thee], and that which she gave to thee in trust [i. e., her love], still kept as a hidden treasure [with her], or is the bond of affection which bound her to thee severed, now that to-day she is far from thee ?

Or is an old man who weeps, without coming to the end of his tears, after loved ones on a day of parting, requited for his pains ? …

poems.title: Ode CXXI: The tent-traces in al-Jaunani refuse to
poems.excerpt:
The tent-traces in al-Jaunani refuse to show signs of change, although they have added a whole year to the year that had sped before ;

And they have gotten in exchange for Laila, in the place where once she dwelt, wild kine of the wide Deserts, that feed in ad-Dakhul and Haumal : …

poems.title: Ode CXXVI: Is thy heart distrest at the
poems.excerpt:
Is thy heart distrest at the spite of Fate and the stroke of Doom ? Nay, Fortune pays no heed to him who bemoans his lot.

' What ails thy body ', Umaimah asked, ' and thy haggard face, lined deep with pain? thou hast wealth enough to be free from toil. …

poems.title: Flowers and Moonlight on the Spring River
poems.excerpt:
The evening river is level and motionless--
The spring colours just open to their full.
Suddenly a wave carries the moon away …
poems.collection: A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918)

poems.title: A Political Prisoner Listening to a Cicada
poems.excerpt:
While the year sinks westward, I hear a cicada
Bid me to be resolute here in my cell,
Yet it needed the song of those black wings …
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)

poems.title: Tell Me Now
poems.excerpt:
“Tell me now, what should a man want
But to sit alone, sipping his cup of wine?”
I should like to have visitors come and discuss philosophy …
poems.collection: A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918)

poems.title: On Going to a Tavern
poems.excerpt:
These days, continually fuddled with drink,
I fail to satisfy the appetites of the soul.
But seeing men all behaving like drunkards, …
poems.collection: A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918)

poems.title: In Absence
Ichabod
A King of Tang
poems.excerpt:
There looms a lordly pleasure-tower o’er yon dim shore,
Raised by some King of Tang.
Jade pendants at his girdle clashed, and golden bells …

poems.title: Farewell to Vice-Prefect Tu Setting Out for His Official Post in Shu
poems.excerpt:
By this wall that surrounds the three Ch'in districts,
Through a mist that makes five rivers one,
We bid each other a sad farewell, …
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)

poems.title: On a Walk in the Early Spring
poems.excerpt:
Only to wanderers can come
Ever new the shock of beauty,
Of white cloud and red cloud dawning from the sea, …
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)

poems.title: A Sunday in the Week of the Great Fast
poems.excerpt:
By fruit, the ancient Foe's device
Drave Adam forth from Paradise:
Christ, by the cross of shame and pain, …

poems.title: Stichera for Great Thursday
poems.excerpt:
O the mystery, passing wonder,
When, reclining at the board,
"Eat," Thou saidst to Thy Disciples, …
poems.collection: Hymns of the Eastern Church (1862; 5th ed. 1884)

poems.title: Troparia for Palm Sunday
poems.excerpt:
Jesus, hastening for the world to suffer,
Enters in, Jerusalem, to thee:
With His Twelve He goeth forth to offer …
poems.collection: Hymns of the Eastern Church (1862; 5th ed. 1884)

poems.title: The Great Canon, Called Also the King of Canons
poems.excerpt:
Whence shall my tears begin?
What first-fruits shall I bear
Of earnest sorrow for my sin? …
poems.collection: Hymns of the Eastern Church (1862; 5th ed. 1884)

poems.title: Stichera for the Second Week of the Great Fast
poems.excerpt:
Christian! dost thou see them
On the holy ground,
How the troops of Midian …
poems.collection: Hymns of the Eastern Church (1862; 5th ed. 1884)

poems.title: The Hymn for conquering Martyrs raise
poems.excerpt:
The Hymn for conquering Martyrs raise:
The Victor Innocents we praise:
Whom in their woe earth cast away, …

poems.title: Bede's Death Song: Northumbrian Version (Old English)
poems.excerpt:
Fore thaem neidfaerae    naenig uuiurthit
thoncsnotturra,    than him tharf sie
to ymbhycggannae    aer his hiniongae …

poems.title: Bede's Death Song: The Hague Version (Old English)
poems.excerpt:
Fore ðaem nedfere    nenig wiorðeð
ðonosnottorra    ðon him ðearf riae
to ymbhycgenne    aer his hinionge …

poems.title: Bede's Death Song: West Saxon Version (Old English)
poems.excerpt:
For þam nedfere    næni wyrþeþ
þances snotera,    þonne him þearf sy
to gehicgenne    ær his heonengange …

poems.title: Business Men
poems.excerpt:
Business men boast of their skill and cunning
But in philosophy they are like little children.
Bragging to each other of successful depredations …
poems.collection: A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918)

poems.title: The Last Revel
Regrets
Against Idols
On a Gate-Tower at Yu-chou
poems.excerpt:
Where, before me, are the ages that have gone?

poems.title: Metrical Preface to the Pastoral Care
poems.excerpt: This message Augustine over the salt sea brought from the south to the islanders, as the Lord's champion had formerly decreed it, the pope of Rome. The wise Gregorius was versed in many true doctrines through the wisdom of his mind, his hoard of cunning thoughts. For he gained over most of mankind to the Guardian of heaven, best of Romans, wisest of men, most gloriously famous. Afterwards king Alfred translated every word of me into English, and sent me to his scribes south and north; ordered more such to be brought to him after the example, that he might send them to his bishops, for some of them needed it, who knew but little Latin.
poems.collection: King Alfred's West-Saxon Version of Gregory's Pastoral Care, ed. and trans. Henry Sweet (EETS o.s. 45, 1871)
poems.translator: trans. Henry Sweet, King Alfred's West-Saxon Version of Gregory's Pastoral Care (Early English Text Society, 1871)

poems.title: Metrical Epilogue to the Pastoral Care
poems.excerpt: These are now the waters, which the God of Hosts promised as a solace to us earthdwellers. He said that he wished in the world ever-living waters to flow from the hearts of those who believed in him well under the sky. There is little doubt that the source of the waters is in the kingdom of heaven; that is, the Holy Ghost. Whence saints and the elect drew it, after those who obeyed God had directed it through holy books on this earth through the minds of men variously. Some dam it in within their minds, the stream of wisdom, hold it with their lips, so that it flows not out to no purpose. But the well remains in the man's breast, by the grace of the Lord, deep and still. Some let it flow away over the tract of land in rills. That is not a wise thing, if so pure water is dispersed in murmuring, shallow streams over the fields, till it becomes a marsh. But draw water now to drink, since the Lord has granted that Gregory should direct to your doors the Lord's stream. Let him now fill his vessel, who has brought hither a watertight pitcher. Let him come back soon. If any man here has brought to this spring a leaky pitcher, let him repair it carefully, lest he spill the clearest of waters, or lose the drink of life.
poems.collection: King Alfred's West-Saxon Version of Gregory's Pastoral Care, ed. and trans. Henry Sweet (EETS o.s. 50, 1871)

poems.title: On Waking from Sleep
Prologue
poems.excerpt:
Those to whom God has given the gift of comely speech, should not hide their light beneath a bushel, but should willingly show it abroad. If a great truth is proclaimed in the ears of men, it brings forth fruit a hundred-fold; but when the sweetness of the telling is praised of many, flowers mingle with the fruit upon the branch.

According to the witness of Priscian, it was the custom of ancient writers to express obscurely some portions of their books, so that those who came after might study with greater diligence to find the thought within their words. The philosophers knew this well, and were the more unwearied in labour, the more subtle in distinctions, so that the truth might make them free. They were persuaded that he who would keep himself unspotted from the world should search for knowledge, that he might understand. To set evil from me, and to put away my grief, I purposed to commence a book. I considered within myself what fair story in the Latin or Romance I could turn into the common tongue. But I found that all the stories had been written, and scarcely it seemed the worth my doing, what so many had already done. Then I called to mind those Lays I had so often heard. I doubted nothing--for well I know--that our fathers fashioned them, that men should bear in remembrance the deeds of those who have gone before. Many a one, on many a day, the minstrel has chanted to my ear. I would not that they should perish, forgotten, by the roadside. In my turn, therefore, I have made of them a song, rhymed as well as I am able, and often has their shaping kept me sleepless in my bed. …

poems.title: The Lay of Gugemar
poems.excerpt:
Hearken, oh gentles, to the words of Marie. When the minstrel tells his tale, let the folk about the fire heed him willingly. For his part the singer must be wary not to spoil good music with unseemly words. Listen, oh lordlings, to the words of Marie, for she pains herself grievously not to forget this thing. The craft is hard--then approve the more sweetly him who carols the tune. But this is the way of the world, that when a man or woman sings more tunably than his fellows, those about the fire fall upon him, pell-mell, for reason of their envy. They rehearse diligently the faults of his song, and steal away his praise with evil words. I will brand these folk as they deserve. They, and such as they, are like mad dogs--cowardly and felon--who traitorously bring to death men better than themselves. Now let the japer, and the smiler with his knife, do me what harm they may. Verily they are in their right to speak ill of me.

Hearken, oh gentles, to the tale I set before you, for thereof the Bretons already have made a Lay. I will not do it harm by many words, and here is the commencement of the matter. According to text and scripture, now I relate a certain adventure, which bechanced in the realm of Brittany, in days long gone before. …

poems.title: The Lay of the Dolorous Knight
poems.excerpt:
Hearken now to the Lay that once I heard a minstrel chanting to his harp. In surety of its truth I will name the city where this story passed. The Lay of the Dolorous Knight, my harper called his song, but of those who hearkened, some named it rather, The Lay of the Four Sorrows.

In Nantes, of Brittany, there dwelt a dame who was dearly held of all, for reason of the much good that was found in her. This lady was passing fair of body, apt in book as any clerk, and meetly schooled in every grace that it becometh dame to have. So gracious of person was this damsel, that throughout the realm there was no knight could refrain from setting his heart upon her, though he saw her but one only time. Although the demoiselle might not return the love of so many, certainly she had no wish to slay them all. Better by far that a man pray and require in love all the dames of his country, than run mad in woods for the bright eyes of one. Therefore this dame gave courtesy and good will to each alike. Even when she might not hear a lover's words, so sweetly she denied his wish that the more he held her dear and was the more her servant for that fond denial. So because of her great riches of body and of heart, this lady of whom I tell, was prayed and required in love by the lords of her country, both by night and by day. …

poems.title: The Lay of Eliduc
poems.excerpt:
Now will I rehearse before you a very ancient Breton Lay. As the tale was told to me, so, in turn, will I tell it over again, to the best of my art and knowledge. Hearken now to my story, its why and its reason.

In Brittany there lived a knight, so courteous and so brave, that in all the realm there was no worthier lord than he. This knight was named Eliduc. He had wedded in his youth a noble lady of proud race and name. They had long dwelt together in peace and content, for their hearts were fixed on one another in faith and loyalty. Now it chanced that Eliduc sought his fortune in a far land, where there was a great war. There he loved a Princess, the daughter of the King and Queen of those parts. Guillardun was the maiden's name, and in all the realm was none more fair. The wife of Eliduc had to name, Guildeluec, in her own country. By reason of these two ladies their story is known as the Lay of Guildeluec and Guillardun, but at first it was rightly called the Lay of Eliduc. The name is a little matter; but if you hearken to me you shall learn the story of these three lovers, in its pity and its truth. …

poems.title: The Lay of the Nightingale
poems.excerpt:
Now will I tell you a story, whereof the Breton harper already has made a Lay. Laustic, I deem, men name it in that country, which, being interpreted, means rossignol in French, and nightingale in good plain English.

In the realm of Brittany stands a certain rich and mighty city, called Saint Malo. There were citizens of this township two knights, so well spoken and reputed of all, that the city drew therefrom great profit and fame. The houses of these lords were very near the one to the other. One of the two knights had to wife a passing fair lady, right gracious of manner and sweet of tongue. Wondrous pleasure found this dame to array herself richly, after the wont and fashion of her time. The other knight was yet a bachelor. He was well accounted of amongst his fellows as a hardy knight and as an honourable man. He gave hospitality gladly. Largely he gained, largely he spent, and willingly bestowed gifts of all that he had. …

poems.title: The Lay of Sir Launfal
poems.excerpt:
I will tell you the story of another Lay. It relates the adventures of a rich and mighty baron, and the Breton calls it, the Lay of Sir Launfal.

King Arthur--that fearless knight and courteous lord--removed to Wales, and lodged at Caerleon-on-Usk, since the Picts and Scots did much mischief in the land. For it was the wont of the wild people of the north to enter in the realm of Logres, and burn and damage at their will. At the time of Pentecost, the King cried a great feast. Thereat he gave many rich gifts to his counts and barons, and to the Knights of the Round Table. Never were such worship and bounty shown before at any feast, for Arthur bestowed honours and lands on all his servants--save only on one. This lord, who was forgotten and misliked of the King, was named Launfal. He was beloved by many of the Court, because of his beauty and prowess, for he was a worthy knight, open of heart and heavy of hand. These lords, to whom their comrade was dear, felt little joy to see so stout a knight misprized. Sir Launfal was son to a King of high descent, though his heritage was in a distant land. He was of the King's household, but since Arthur gave him naught, and he was of too proud a mind to pray for his due, he had spent all that he had. Right heavy was Sir Launfal, when he considered these things, for he knew himself taken in the toils. Gentles, marvel not overmuch hereat. Ever must the pilgrim go heavily in a strange land, where there is none to counsel and direct him in the path. …

poems.title: The Lay of the Two Lovers
poems.excerpt:
Once upon a time there lived in Normandy two lovers, who were passing fond, and were brought by Love to Death. The story of their love was bruited so abroad, that the Bretons made a song in their own tongue, and named this song the Lay of the Two Lovers.

In Neustria--that men call Normandy--there is verily a high and marvellously great mountain, where lie the relics of the Two Children. Near this high place the King of those parts caused to be built a certain fair and cunning city, and since he was lord of the Pistrians, it was known as Pistres. The town yet endures, with its towers and houses, to bear witness to the truth; moreover the country thereabouts is known to us all as the Valley of Pistres. …

poems.title: The Lay of the Were-Wolf
poems.excerpt:
Amongst the tales I tell you once again, I would not forget the Lay of the Were-Wolf. Such beasts as he are known in every land. Bisclavaret he is named in Brittany; whilst the Norman calls him Garwal.

It is a certain thing, and within the knowledge of all, that many a christened man has suffered this change, and ran wild in woods, as a Were-Wolf. The Were-Wolf is a fearsome beast. He lurks within the thick forest, mad and horrible to see. All the evil that he may, he does. He goeth to and fro, about the solitary place, seeking man, in order to devour him. Hearken, now, to the adventure of the Were-Wolf, that I have to tell. …

poems.title: The Lay of the Ash Tree
poems.excerpt:
Now will I tell you the Lay of the Ash Tree, according to the story that I know.

In ancient days there dwelt two knights in Brittany, who were neighbours and close friends. These two lords were brave and worthy gentlemen, rich in goods and lands, and near both in heart and home. Moreover each was wedded to a dame. One of these ladies was with child, and when her time was come, she was delivered of two boys. Her husband was right happy and content. For the joy that was his, he sent messages to his neighbour, telling that his wife had brought forth two sons, and praying that one of them might be christened with his name. The rich man was at meat when the messenger came before him. The servitor kneeled before the dais, and told his message in his ear. The lord thanked God for the happiness that had befallen his friend, and bestowed a fair horse on the bringer of good tidings. His wife, sitting at board with her husband, heard the story of the messenger, and smiled at his news. Proud she was, and sly, with an envious heart, and a rancorous tongue. She made no effort to bridle her lips, but spoke lightly before the servants of the house, and said, …

poems.title: The Lay of the Honeysuckle
poems.excerpt:
With a glad heart and right good mind will I tell the Lay that men call Honeysuckle; and that the truth may be known of all it shall be told as many a minstrel has sung it to my ear, and as the scribe hath written it for our delight. It is of Tristan and Isoude, the Queen. It is of a love which passed all other love, of love from whence came wondrous sorrow, and whereof they died together in the self-same day.

King Mark was sorely wrath with Tristan, his sister's son, and bade him avoid his realm, by reason of the love he bore the Queen. So Tristan repaired to his own land, and dwelt for a full year in South Wales, where he was born. Then since he might not come where he would be, Tristan took no heed to his ways, but let his life run waste to Death. Marvel not overmuch thereat, for he who loves beyond measure must ever be sick in heart and hope, when he may not win according to his wish. So sick in heart and mind was Tristan that he left his kingdom, and returned straight to the realm of his banishment, because that in Cornwall dwelt the Queen. There he hid privily in the deep forest, withdrawn from the eyes of men; only when the evening was come, and all things sought their rest, he prayed the peasant and other mean folk of that country, of their charity to grant him shelter for the night. From the serf he gathered tidings of the King. These gave again to him what they, in turn, had taken from some outlawed knight. Thus Tristan learned that when Pentecost was come King Mark purposed to hold high Court at Tintagel, and keep the feast with pomp and revelry; moreover that thither would ride Isoude, the Queen. …

poems.title: The Lay of Equitan
poems.excerpt:

That these marvellous things should not be forgotten they fashioned them into Lays. Amongst these Lays I have heard tell of one which is not made to die as though it had never been.

Equitan, lord of Nantes, was a loyal and courteous gentleman, of great worth, beloved by all in his own country. He was set on pleasure, and was Love's lover, as became a gentle knight. Like many others who dote on woman, he observed neither sense nor measure in love. But it is in the very nature of Love that proportion cannot enter into the matter. …

poems.title: The Lay of Milon
poems.excerpt:
He who would tell divers tales must know how to vary the tune. To win the favour of any, he must speak to the understanding of all. I purpose in this place to show you the story of Milon, and--since few words are best--I will set out the adventure as briefly as I may.

Milon was born in South Wales. So great was his prowess that from the day he was dubbed knight there was no champion who could stand before him in the lists. He was a passing fair knight, open and brave, courteous to his friends, and stern to his foes. Men praised his name in whatever realm they talked of gallant deeds--Ireland, Norway, and Wales, yea, from Jutland even to Albania. Since he was praised by the frank, he was therefore envied of the mean. Nevertheless, by reason of his skill with the spear, he was counted a very worshipful knight, and was honourably entreated by many a prince in divers lands. …

poems.title: The Lay of Yonec
poems.excerpt:
Since I have commenced I would not leave any of these Lays untold. The stories that I know I would tell you forthwith. My hope is now to rehearse to you the story of Yonec, the son of Eudemarec, his mother's first born child.

In days of yore there lived in Britain a rich man, old and full of years, who was lord of the town and realm of Chepstow. This town is builded on the banks of the Douglas, and is renowned by reason of many ancient sorrows which have there befallen. When he was well stricken in years this lord took to himself a wife, that he might have children to come after him in his goodly heritage. The damsel, who was bestowed on this wealthy lord, came of an honourable house, and was kind and courteous, and passing fair. She was beloved by all because of her beauty, and none was more sweetly spoken of from Chepstow to Lincoln, yea, or from there to Ireland. Great was their sin who married the maiden to this aged man. Since she was young and gay, he shut her fast within his tower, that he might the easier keep her to himself. He set in charge of the damsel his elder sister, a widow, to hold her more surely in ward. These two ladies dwelt alone in the tower, together with their women, in a chamber by themselves. There the damsel might have speech of none, except at the bidding of the ancient dame. More than seven years passed in this fashion. The lady had no children for her solace, and she never went forth from the castle to greet her kinsfolk and her friends. Her husband's jealousy was such that when she sought her bed, no chamberlain or usher was permitted in her chamber to light the candles. The lady became passing heavy. She spent her days in sighs and tears. Her loveliness began to fail, for she gave no thought to her person. Indeed at times she hated the very shadow of that beauty which had spoiled all her life. …

Through love of them I called out behind their riding-camels, 'O ye who are rich in beauty, here am I, a beggar! …

The watercourses were flooded and the breeze wafted perfume, and a ringdove flapped her wings and a twig put forth leaves. …

poems.excerpt:
She said, 'I wonder at a lover who in conceit of his merits walks proudly among flowers in a garden.'
I replied, 'Do not wonder at what thou seest, for thou hast beheld thyself in the mirror of a man.'

poems.excerpt:

Have pity! Do not reveal, by wailing and weeping, my hidden desires and my secret sorrows!
I respond to her, at eve and morn, with the plaintive cry of a longing man and the moan of an impassioned lover. …

poems.title: At Dhú Salam and the monastery in the abode of al-Ḥimá
poems.excerpt:

Therefore I watch spheres and serve in a church and guard a many-coloured meadow in the spring.
And at one time I am called the herdsman of the gazelles in the desert, and at another time I am called a Christian monk and an astrologer. …

poems.title: A ringdove wailed and a sad lover complained
poems.excerpt:
A ringdove wailed and a sad lover complained, and he was grieved by her trilling note and complaint.
Tears flowed from their eyes in distress for her complaint, and ’twas as tho’ they (the tears) were fountains.
I responded to her in the bereavement caused by the loss of her only child: one who loses an only child is bereaved indeed. …

poems.title: He saw the lightning in the east and he longed for the east
poems.excerpt:
He saw the lightning in the east and he longed for the east, but if it had flashed in the west he would have longed for the west.
My desire is for the lightning and its gleam, not for the places and the earth.
The east wind related to me from them a tradition handed down successively from distracted thoughts, from my passion, from anguish, from my tribulation, …

poems.title: They left me at al-Uthayl and an-Naqá shedding tears and…
poems.excerpt:
They left me at al-Uthayl and an-Naqá shedding tears and complaining of the fire (that consumed me).
My father be the ransom of him for whose sake I melted with anguish! My father be the ransom of him for whose sake I died of fear!
The blush of shame on his cheek is the whiteness of dawn conversing with the redness of eve. …

poems.excerpt:
They (the women) mounted the howdahs on the swift camels and placed in them the (damsels like) marble statues and full moons,
And promised my heart that they should return; but do the fair promise anything except deceit?
And she saluted with her henna-tipped fingers for the leave-taking, and let fall tears that excited the flames (of desire). …

poems.title: O driver of the reddish-white camels
poems.excerpt:

Stop the camels and tighten their reins! I beseech thee by God, by my passion, by my anguish, O driver!

poems.title: Halt at the abodes and weep over the ruins and ask the…
poems.excerpt:
Halt at the abodes and weep over the ruins and ask the decayed habitations a question.
'Where are the loved ones? Where are their camels gone?' (They answer), 'Behold them traversing the vapour in the desert.
Thou seest them in the mirage like gardens: the vapour makes large in the eyes the figure (of one who walks in it).' …

poems.title: O mouldering remains
poems.excerpt:
O mouldering remains (of the encampment) at al-Uthayl, where I played with friendly maidens!
Yesterday it was cheerful and smiling, but to-day it has become desolate and frowning.
They went far away and I was unaware of them, and they knew not that my mind was watching over them, …

poems.title: My lovesickness is from her of the lovesick eyelids
poems.excerpt:
My lovesickness is from her of the lovesick eyelids: console me by the mention of her, console me
The grey doves fluttered in the meadows and wailed: the grief of these doves is from that which grieved me.
May my father be the ransom of a tender playful girl, one of the maidens guarded in howdahs, advancing swayingly among the married women! …

poems.title: O garden of the valley
poems.excerpt:
O garden of the valley, answer the lady of the preserve and her who hath shining front-teeth, O garden of the valley
And let a little of thy shades o’ershadow her for a short time until she be settled in the meeting-place.
And her tents be pitched in thy midst. Then thou wilt have as much as thou wishest of dew to feed the tender shoots, …

poems.title: Turn the camels aside towards the stony tract of Thahmad
poems.excerpt:
Turn the camels aside towards the stony tract of Thahmad, where are the tender branches and the humid meadow,
Where the lightnings show to thee their flashes, where the clouds pass at eve and morn,
And lift thy voice at dawn to invoke the bright-faced damsels and the fair lissome virgins, …

poems.title: At dawn they alighted in Wádí ’l-‘Aqíq after having…
poems.excerpt:
At dawn they alighted in Wádí ’l-‘Aqíq after having traversed many a deep ravine,
And at daybreak they descried a cairn shining on the top of a mountain peak.
When the vulture desires to reach it he is unable, and the eggs of the anúq are below it. …

poems.title: Halt by the ruined abodes at La‘la‘ and mourn for our loved…
poems.excerpt:
Halt by the ruined abodes at La‘la‘ and mourn for our loved ones in that wilderness.
Halt by thy dwelling-places and call to them, wondering at their loneliness, with exquisite lamentation.
'Beside thy bán tree I have seen many a one like myself plucking the fruit of comely forms and the roses of a verdant meadow. …

poems.title: O grief for my heart
poems.excerpt:
O grief for my heart, O grief! O joy for my mind, O joy!
In my heart the fire of passion is burning, in my mind the full moon of darkness hath set.
O musk! O full moon! O bough of the sand-hills! How green is the bough, how bright the moon, how sweet the musk! …

poems.title: In the valley-curve between the two stony tracts is the…
poems.excerpt:
In the valley-curve between the two stony tracts is the trysting-place. Make our camels kneel, for here is the journey's end.
Do not seek (any other spot) and do not call after this, 'O Báriq! O Ḥájir! O Thahmad!'
And play as friendly full-breasted damsels played, and pasture as shy gazelles pastured …

poems.title: O ancient temple
poems.excerpt:
O ancient temple, there hath risen for you a light that gleams in our hearts.
I complain to thee of the deserts which I crossed, where I let my tears flow unchecked,
Taking no joy in rest at dawn or dusk, continuing from morn to morn and passing from eve to eve. …

poems.title: Between an-Naqá and La‘la‘ are the gazelles of Dhát al-Ajra‘
poems.excerpt:
Between an-Naqá and La‘la‘ are the gazelles of Dhát al-Ajra‘,
Grazing there in a dense covert of tangled shrubs, and pasturing.
New moons never rose on the horizon of that hill …

poems.title: May my father be the ransom of the boughs swaying to and…
In the tamarisk groves of an-Naqá is a flock of qaṭá birds…
poems.excerpt:
In the tamarisk groves of an-Naqá is a flock of qaṭá birds over whom Beauty has pitched a tent,
And in the midst of the deserts of Iḍam are camels which graze beside them and gazelles.
O my two friends, stop and beg speech of the relics of an abode which has become ruined after them, …

poems.title: A lightning-cloud gleamed at Dhát al-Aḍá
poems.excerpt:
A lightning-cloud gleamed at Dhát al-Aḍá, with light flashing over the plain thereof,
And the thunder of its secret converse cracked, and its rain-cloud let fall copious showers.
They called to one another: 'Make the camels kneel!' but they did not listen, and I in my passion cried out: 'O driver, …

poems.title: Our talk between al-Ḥaditha and al-Karkh recalls to me the…
poems.excerpt:
Our talk between al-Ḥaditha and al-Karkh recalls to me the period of youth and its prime.
I said to myself: 'After fifty years, when through long meditation I have become as weak as a young bird,
It recalls to me the neighbourhood of Sal‘ and Ḥájir, and brings to my mind the period of youth and its prime, …

poems.title: I respond with diverse notes of grief to every cooing dove…
poems.excerpt:
I respond with diverse notes of grief to every cooing dove perched upon a bough in a grove.
She weeps for her mate without tears, but from my eyelids the tears of sorrow are streaming.
I say to her, when my eyelids have shed their abundant tears in token of my inward state, …

poems.title: At the hill among the mountains of Zarúd are haughty lions
poems.excerpt:
At the hill among the mountains of Zarúd are haughty lions, by the looks of lissome women
Overthrown, though they were bred in the carnage of war. What match are the lions for the black eyes?
The women's looks murdered them. How sweet are those looks from the daughters of kings!

poems.title: Three full moons
poems.excerpt:
Three full moons, unadorned by any ornament, went forth to at-Tan‘ím with veiled faces.
They unveiled shining faces like suns and cried with a loud voice 'Labbayka', visiting the holy shrines.
And they approached, walking slowly as the qaṭá birds walk, in gowns of striped Yemen cloth.

poems.title: O earth of the Highland
poems.excerpt:
O earth of the Highland, mayst thou be a blessed highland! May the rain-clouds water thee abundantly with shower on shower!
And may he who has greeted thee for fifty years greet thee once and twice and then once again!
I crossed every desert and wilderness to meet her, riding on the big-humped she-camel and the old dromedary, …

poems.title: O my two comrades
poems.excerpt:
O my two comrades, approach the guarded pasture and seek Najd and yonder sign that marks the way,
And come down to a well at the tents of the curving sand and beg shade of its ḍál and salam trees.
And whenever ye come to the valley of Mind—for then ye have come to that in which is my heart's being— …

poems.title: The dearest place on God's earth to me after Ṭayba and…
poems.excerpt:
The dearest place on God's earth to me after Ṭayba and Mecca and the Farther Temple is the city of Baghdán.
How should I not love the (City of) Peace, since I have there an Imám who is the guide of my religion and my reason and my faith?
’Tis the home of a daughter of Persia, one whose gestures are subtle and whose eyelids are languid. …

poems.title: My soul be the ransom of fair-complexioned and coy virgins…
poems.excerpt:
My soul be the ransom of fair-complexioned and coy virgins who played with me as I was kissing the Pillar and the Stone!
When thou art lost in pursuit of them, thou wilt find no guide but in their scent, the sweetest of traces.
No moonless night darkened o’er me but I remembered them and journeyed in moonlight. …

poems.title: Between Adhri‘át and Buṣrá a maid of fourteen rose to my…
poems.excerpt:
Between Adhri‘át and Buṣrá a maid of fourteen rose to my sight like a full moon.

Every full moon, when it reaches perfection, suffers a waning that it may make a complete month, …

poems.title: God save a bird on a bán tree
poems.excerpt:
God save a bird on a bán tree, a bird that has revealed to me the true story
How the loved ones bound the saddles on their camels and then gat them away at dawn.
I journeyed—and in my heart for their sake was a blazing fire because of their departure— …

poems.title: O men of intelligence and understanding
poems.excerpt:
O men of intelligence and understanding, I am distraught between the sun and the gazelles.
He who forgets Suhá is not forgetful, but he who forgets the sun is forgetful.
Let him offer himself to his herd, for gifts open the mouth to utter praise. …

poems.title: Let me never forget my abode at Wána and my saying to…
poems.excerpt:
Let me never forget my abode at Wána and my saying to camel-riders as they departed and arrived,
'Stay beside us a while that we may be comforted thereby, for I swear by those whom I love that I am consoled (by thinking of you).'
If they set out they will journey with the most auspicious omen, and if they halt they will alight at the most bountiful halting-place. …

poems.title: The full moon appeared in the night of hair
poems.excerpt:
The full moon appeared in the night of hair, and the black narcissus bedewed the rose.
A tender girl is she: the fair women were confounded by her, and her radiance outshone the moon.
If she enters into the mind, that imagination wounds her: how, then, can she be perceived by the eye? …

poems.title: The loved ones of my heart
poems.excerpt:
The loved ones of my heart—where are they? Say, by God, where are they?
As thou sawest their apparition, wilt thou show to me their reality?
How long, how long was I seeking them! and how often did I beg to be united with them, …

poems.title: There is a war of love between the entrails and the large…
poems.excerpt:
There is a war of love between the entrails and the large eyes, and because of that war the heart is in woe.
Dark-lipped and Swart is she, her mouth honeyed: the evidence of the bees is the white honey which they produce.
Full-ankled, a darkness o’er a moon; in her cheek a red blush; she is a bough growing on hills. …

poems.title: O dove on the bán tree at Dhát al-Ghaḍá
poems.excerpt:
O dove on the bán tree at Dhát al-Ghaḍá, I am oppressed by the burden thou hast laid upon me.
Who can support the anguish of love? Who can drain the bitter draught of destiny?
I say in my grief and burning passion, 'O would that he who caused my sickness had tended me when I am sick!' …

poems.title: O camel-driver
poems.excerpt:
O camel-driver, turn aside at Sal‘ and halt by the bán tree of al-Mudarraj,
And call to them, imploring their pity and grace, 'O my princes, have ye any consolation?'
At Ráma, between an-Naqá and Ḥájir, is a girl enclosed in a howdah. …

poems.title: Who will show me her of the dyed fingers
poems.excerpt:
Who will show me her of the dyed fingers? Who will show me her of the honeyed tongue?
She is one of the girls with swelling breasts who guard their honour, tender, virgin, and beautiful,
Full moons over branches: they fear no waning. …

poems.title: Oh, the traitress
poems.excerpt:
Oh, the traitress! She has left bitten by her viper-like locks one who would fain approach her,
And she bends her soft eye and melts him and leaves him sick on his bed.
She shot the arrows of her glances from the bow of an eyebrow, and on whatever side I came I was killed.

poems.title: At Dhát al-Aḍá and al-Ma’zimán and Báriq and Dhú Salam and…
poems.excerpt:
At Dhát al-Aḍá and al-Ma’zimán and Báriq and Dhú Salam and al-Abraqán to the traveller by night
Appear flashes of swords from the lightnings of smiling mouths like musk-glands, the odour whereof none is permitted to smell.
If war is waged against them, they draw the swords of their glances; and if peace is made with them, they break the bonds of constraint. …

poems.title: I am content with Raḍwá as a meadow and a lodging-place
poems.excerpt:
I am content with Raḍwá as a meadow and a lodging-place, for it has a pasture in which is cool water.
May be, those whom I love will hear of its fertility, so that they will take it as an abode and lodging-place.
For lo, my heart is attached to them and listens silently whenever the camel-driver urges them on with his chant. …

poems.title: Whenever we meet to take farewell thou wouldst deem us
poems.excerpt:
Whenever we meet to take farewell thou wouldst deem us, as we clasp and embrace, to be a doubled letter.
Although our bodies are dual, the eye sees only a single one.
This is because of my leanness and his light, and were it not for my moaning, I should have been invisible to the eye.

poems.title: They said, 'The suns are in the heavenly sphere
poems.excerpt:
They said, 'The suns are in the heavenly sphere.' Where should the sun dwell but in heaven?
When a throne is set up, there must be a king to sit erect upon it.
When the heart is purged of its ignorance, then must. the angel descend. …

poems.title: I am absent, and desire makes my soul die
poems.excerpt:
I am absent, and desire makes my soul die; and I meet him and am not cured, so ’tis desire whether I am absent or present.
And meeting with him creates in me what I never imagined; and the remedy is a second disease of passion,
Because I behold a form whose beauty, as often as we meet, grows in splendour and majesty. …

poems.title: (My goal is) the corniced palace of Baghdád
poems.excerpt:
(My goal is) the corniced palace of Baghdád, not the corniced palace of Sindád,
The city set like a crown above the gardens, as though she were a bride who has been unveiled in the most fragrant chamber.
The wind plays with the branches and they are bent, and ’tis as though the twain had plighted troth with one another. …

poems.title: O breeze of the wind
poems.excerpt:
O breeze of the wind, bear to the gazelles of Najd this message: 'I am faithful to the covenant which ye know.'
And say to the young girl of the tribe, 'Our trysting-place is at the guarded pasture beside the hills of Najd on the Sabbath morn,
On the red hill towards the cairns and on the right hand of the rivulets and the solitary landmark.' …

poems.title: Oh, is there any way to the damsels bright and fair
poems.excerpt:
Oh, is there any way to the damsels bright and fair? And is there anyone who will show me their traces?
And can I halt at night beside the tents of the curving sand? And can I rest at noon in the shade of the arák trees?
The tongue of inward feeling spoke, informing me that she says, 'Wish for that which is attainable.' …

poems.title: Ṭayba hath a gazelle from whose witching eye
poems.excerpt:
Ṭayba hath a gazelle from whose witching eye (glances like) the edge of a keen blade are drawn,
And at ‘Arafát I perceived what she desired and I was not patient,
And on the night of Jam‘ we had union with her, such as is mentioned in the proverb. …

poems.title: Approach the dwelling of dear ones who have taken covenants
poems.excerpt:
Approach the dwelling of dear ones who have taken covenants—may clouds of incessant rain pour upon it!—
And breathe the scent of the wind over against their land, in desire that the (sweet) airs may tell thee where they are.
I know that they encamped at the bán tree of Iḍam, where the ‘arár plants grow and the shíḥ and the katam.

poems.title: O bán tree of the valley
poems.excerpt:
O bán tree of the valley, on the bank of the river of Baghdád!
A mournful dove that cooed on a swaying bough filled me with grief for thee.
His plaintive song reminds me of the plaintive song of the lady of the chamber. …

poems.title: Love Song of Alcharisi
poems.excerpt:
I.
The long-closed door, oh open it again, send me back once more my fawn that had fled.
On the day of our reunion, thou shalt rest by my side, there wilt thou shed over me the streams of thy delicious perfume. …

Whosoever there doth dwell

poems.excerpt:
All roots of wood and wold

poems.excerpt:
Ill-luck is mine, and that hath often made me grieve:
Thus, ere I drunk a drop, a lake I had to leave,
From which a cool stream took its course …

poems.title: The Lot of All
poems.excerpt:
This blade of straw we praise, for produce it hath borne.
The season hath been fair and plentiful of corn,
And glad thereat the world hath been. …

poems.title: Clothed in Honour
poems.excerpt:
Though a chaste woman may not wear a costly dress,
Full sure am I, she's clad in her own worthiness,
So that in brave attire she goes, …

A lady surely ought to let
Me look on her in loving wise.
At her I wish (and none could yet …

poems.excerpt:
Leaves are thrusting, flowers are springing,
And the breath of May to birds their music hath restored.
I can sometimes fall a-singing …

poems.title: Splendide mendax
poems.excerpt:
Ever I feel that the world is my own,
Yes, and that over it all I can fly.
Lightly I spring where my thoughts may have gone; …

poems.title: Crusader's Song
poems.excerpt:
Life's true worth at last beginneth,
Now my sinful eyes behold
The holy land, the earth that winneth …

poems.title: Lord of All
poems.excerpt:
Whoso, Lord God, shall feel no fear
To speak Thy ten commandments clear
And break them — no true love does that betoken! …

poems.title: Viaticum
poems.excerpt:
With blessing may I rise this day,
Lord God, to wend upon my way,
And wheresoe'er I ride, do Thou defend me! …

poems.excerpt:
King Constantine, he gave of yore
Spear, Cross, and Crown, no less, no more,
Unto the See of Rome: I tell you truly. …

poems.excerpt:
Most blessed God, how seldom dost Thou hear me praying?
Since 'tis from Thee I have my singing and my saying,
How dare I wanton thus beneath the sceptre of Thy swaying? …

No Stronger than a Flower
poems.excerpt:

Every joy that e'er to me was sent …

All that hitherto you've heard …

poems.excerpt:
Ah me, where are my years all gone, without a sign?

poems.excerpt:
Whoso were minded to grow old in pain

poems.excerpt:
85. Having great pity, our Eternal Father lighteneth the dark night of ignorance, manifesting Himself in that Land of Joy as the Buddha of Infinite Light which enlighteneth all the worlds with its immeasurable glory.

86. That Lord most compassionate, the Buddha of immeasurable Light, He who had attained unto the Supreme Wisdom even before the myriads of Kalpas were, pitying them that know not, made himself manifest in the Palace of Kapila as the Lord Sakya-muni. …

94. He that hath unending pity, the Buddha of Infinite Life, hath given unto us in the Sutra of Golden Light a teaching concerning long life, that the way of long life and the welfare of the people might be made known unto them.

95. Dengyo-Daishi, he who taught the Tendai-shu in the mount of Hiye, hath compassionately instructed us that we should recite Namuamida-butsu, that Holiest Name, as a sure shield against the seven sorts of calamities. …

118. For the Lord Buddha declared in prophecy that in India, in the Southern Parts, should arise a great Teacher, trampling upon the false teachings of affirmation and denial. …

poems.excerpt:

128. Only to Him who is above all things is known the glory of the Land of Peace. Wide as the sky and boundless is it spread forth. …

poems.excerpt:

138. Having thus cast from him the writings that he had so many years diligently studied, he preached unto all men the doctrine of the Divine Promise, and, so teaching, he led men that are fast bound in the fetters of illusion, in at the Gate of the Great Peace. …

There is nothing but water at the holy bathing places; and I know that they are useless, for I have bathed in them.
The images are all lifeless, they cannot speak; I know, for I have cried aloud to them.
The Purana and the Koran are mere words; lifting up the curtain, I have seen. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XLIII: I laugh when I hear that the fish in the water is thirsty:
poems.excerpt:
I laugh when I hear that the fish in the water is thirsty:
You do not see that the Real is in your home, and you wander from forest to forest listlessly!
Here is the truth!  Go where you will, to Benares or to Mathura; if you do not find your soul, the world is unreal to you.
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XLIV: The Hidden Banner is planted in the temple of the sky
poems.excerpt:
The Hidden Banner is planted in the temple of the sky; there the blue canopy decked with the moon and set with bright jewels is spread.
There the light of the sun and the moon is shining: still your mind to silence before that splendour.
Kabîr says: "He who has drunk of this nectar, wanders like one who is mad."
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XLV: Who are you, and whence do you come?
poems.excerpt:
Who are you, and whence do you come?
Where dwells that Supreme Spirit, and how does He have His sport with all created things?
The fire is in the wood; but who awakens it suddenly?  Then it turns to ashes, and where goes the force of the fire? …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XLVI: O sadhu!  purify your body in the simple way.
poems.excerpt:
O sadhu!  purify your body in the simple way.
As the seed is within the banyan tree, and within the seed are the flowers, the fruits, and the shade:
So the germ is within the body, and within that germ is the body again. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XLVII: There is a strange tree
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XLVIII: I have stilled my restless mind, and my heart is radiant
poems.excerpt:
I have stilled my restless mind, and my heart is radiant: for in Thatness I have seen beyond That-ness.  In company I have seen the Comrade Himself.
Living in bondage, I have set myself free: I have broken away from the clutch of all narrowness.
Kabîr says: "I have attained the unattainable, and my heart is coloured with the colour of love."
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XLIX: That which you see is not: and for that which is, you have no words.
poems.excerpt:
That which you see is not: and for that which is, you have no words.
Unless you see, you believe not: what is told you you cannot accept.
He who is discerning knows by the word; and the ignorant stands gaping. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song L: The flute of the Infinite is played without ceasing
poems.excerpt:
The flute of the Infinite is played without ceasing, and its sound is love:
When love renounces all limits, it reaches truth.
How widely the fragrance spreads!  It has no end, nothing stands in its way. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LI: Dear friend, I am eager to meet my Beloved!  My youth has flowered
poems.excerpt:
Dear friend, I am eager to meet my Beloved!  My youth has flowered, and the pain of separation from Him troubles my breast.
I am wandering yet in the alleys of knowledge without purpose, but I have received His news in these alleys of knowledge.
I have a letter from my Beloved: in this letter is an unutterable message, and now my fear of death is done away. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LII: When I am parted from my Beloved, my heart is full of misery
poems.excerpt:
When I am parted from my Beloved, my heart is full of misery: I have no comfort in the day, I have no sleep in the night.  To whom shall I tell my sorrow?
The night is dark; the hours slip by.  Because my Lord is absent, I start up and tremble with fear.
Kabîr says: "Listen, my friend!  there is no other satisfaction, save in the encounter with the Beloved."
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LIII: What is that flute whose music thrills me with joy?
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LIV: Have you not heard the tune which the Unstruck Music is playing
poems.excerpt:
Have you not heard the tune which the Unstruck Music is playing? In the midst of the chamber the harp of joy is gently and sweetly played; and where is the need of going without to hear it?
If you have not drunk of the nectar of that One Love, what boots it though you should purge yourself of all stains?
The Kazi is searching the words of the Koran, and instructing others: but if his heart be not steeped in that love, what does it avail, though he be a teacher of men? …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LV: Subtle is the path of love!
poems.excerpt:
Subtle is the path of love!
Therein there is no asking and no not-asking,
There one loses one's self at His feet, …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LVI: He is the real Sadhu
poems.excerpt:
He is the real Sadhu, who can reveal the form of the Formless to the vision of these eyes:
Who teaches the simple way of attaining Him, that is other than rites or ceremonies:
Who does not make you close the doors, and hold the breath, and renounce the world: …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LVII: Receive that Word from which the Universe springeth!
poems.excerpt:
Receive that Word from which the Universe springeth!
That word is the Guru; I have heard it, and become the disciple.
How many are there who know the meaning of that word? …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LVIII: Empty the Cup!  O be drunken!
poems.excerpt:
Empty the Cup!  O be drunken!
Drink the divine nectar of His Name!
Kabîr says: "Listen to me, dear Sadhu! …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LIX: O man, if thou dost not know thine own Lord
poems.excerpt:
O man, if thou dost not know thine own Lord, whereof art thou so proud?
Put thy cleverness away: mere words shall never unite thee to Him.
Do not deceive thyself with the witness of the Scriptures: …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LX: The savour of wandering in the ocean of deathless life has rid me of…
poems.excerpt:
The savour of wandering in the ocean of deathless life has rid me of all my asking:
As the tree is in the seed, so all diseases are in this asking.
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXI: When at last you are come to the ocean of happiness
poems.excerpt:
When at last you are come to the ocean of happiness, do not go back thirsty.
Wake, foolish man!  for Death stalks you.  Here is pure water before you; drink it at every breath.
Do not follow the mirage on foot, but thirst for the nectar; …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXII: Who has ever taught the widowed wife to burn herself on the pyre of…
poems.excerpt:
Who has ever taught the widowed wife to burn herself on the pyre of her dead husband?
And who has ever taught love to find bliss in renunciation?
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXIII: Why so impatient, my heart?
poems.excerpt:
Why so impatient, my heart?
He who watches over birds, beasts, and insects,
He who cared for you whilst you were yet in your mother's womb, …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXIV: Now hard it is to meet my Lord!
poems.excerpt:
Now hard it is to meet my Lord!
The rain-bird wails in thirst for the rain: almost she dies of her longing, yet she would have none other water than the rain.
Drawn by the love of music, the deer moves forward: she dies as she listens to the music, yet she shrinks not in fear. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXV: O brother! when I was forgetful, my true Guru showed me the Way.
poems.excerpt:
O brother! when I was forgetful, my true Guru showed me the Way.
Then I left off all rites and ceremonies, I bathed no more in the holy water:
Then I learned that it was I alone who was mad, and the whole world beside me was sane; and I had disturbed these wise people. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXVI: The Yogi dyes his garments
poems.excerpt:
The Yogi dyes his garments, instead of dyeing his mind in the colours of love:
He sits within the temple of the Lord, leaving Brahma to worship a stone.
He pierces holes in his ears, he has a great beard and matted locks, he looks like a goat: …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXVII: I do not know what manner of God is mine.
poems.excerpt:
I do not know what manner of God is mine.
The Mullah cries aloud to Him: and why?  Is your Lord deaf?  The subtle anklets that ring on the feet of an insect when it moves are heard of Him.
Tell your beads, paint your forehead with the mark of your God, and wear matted locks long and showy: but a deadly weapon is in your heart, and how shall you have God?
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXVIII: I hear the melody of His flute, and I cannot contain myself:
poems.excerpt:
I hear the melody of His flute, and I cannot contain myself:
The flower blooms, though it is not spring; and already the bee has received its invitation.
The sky roars and the lightning flashes, the waves arise in my heart, …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXIX: If God be within the mosque, then to whom does this world belong?
poems.excerpt:
If God be within the mosque, then to whom does this world belong?
If Ram be within the image which you find upon your pilgrimage, then who is there to know what happens without?
Hari is in the East: Allah is in the West.  Look within your heart, for there you will find both Karim and Ram; …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXX: He who is meek and contented., he who has an equal vision
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXI: Go thou to the company of the good
poems.excerpt:
Go thou to the company of the good, where the Beloved One has His dwelling place:
Take all thy thoughts and love and instruction from thence.
Let that assembly be burnt to ashes where His Name is not spoken! …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXII: The jewel is lost in the mud, and all are seeking for it;
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXIII: The palanquin came to take me away to my husband's home
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXIV: O my heart! you have not known all the secrets of this city of love
poems.excerpt:
O my heart! you have not known all the secrets of this city of love: in ignorance you came, and in ignorance you return.
O my friend, what have you done with this life?  You have taken on your head the burden heavy with stones, and who is to lighten it for you?
Your Friend stands on the other shore, but you never think in your mind how you may meet with Him: …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXV: The Vedas say that the Unconditioned stands beyond the world of…
poems.excerpt:
The Vedas say that the Unconditioned stands beyond the world of Conditions.
O woman, what does it avail thee to dispute whether He is beyond all or in all?
See thou everything as thine own dwelling place: the mist of pleasure and pain can never spread there. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXVI: Open your eyes of love
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXVII: O my heart!  let us go to that country where dwells the Beloved
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXVIII: Kabîr says: "O Sadhu! hear my deathless words
poems.excerpt:
Kabîr says: "O Sadhu! hear my deathless words.  If you want your own good, examine and consider them well.
You have estranged yourself from the Creator, of whom you have sprung: you have lost your reason, you have bought death.
All doctrines and all teachings are sprung from Him, from Him they grow: know this for certain, and have no fear. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXIX: I am neither pious nor ungodly, I live neither by law nor by sense,
poems.excerpt:
I am neither pious nor ungodly, I live neither by law nor by sense,
I am neither a speaker nor hearer, I am neither a servant nor master, I am neither bond nor free,
I am neither detached nor attached. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXX: The true Name is like none other name!
poems.excerpt:
The true Name is like none other name!
The distinction of the Conditioned from the Unconditioned is but a word:
The Unconditioned is the seed, the Conditioned is the flower and the fruit. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXXI: In the beginning was He alone, sufficient unto Himself: the formless
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXXII: Kabîr ponders and says: "He who has neither caste nor country
poems.excerpt:
Kabîr ponders and says: "He who has neither caste nor country, who is formless and without quality, fills all space."
The Creator brought into being the Game of Joy: and from the word Om the Creation sprang.
The earth is His joy; His joy is the sky; …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXXIII: The harp gives forth murmurous music
poems.excerpt:
The harp gives forth murmurous music; and the dance goes on without hands and feet.
It is played without fingers, it is heard without ears: for He is the ear, and He is the listener.
The gate is locked, but within there is fragrance: and there the meeting is seen of none. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXXIV: The Beggar goes a-begging, but
poems.excerpt:
The Beggar goes a-begging, but
I could not even catch sight of Him:
And what shall I beg of the Beggar He gives without my asking. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXXV: My heart cries aloud for the house of my lover
poems.excerpt:
My heart cries aloud for the house of my lover; the open road and the shelter of a roof are all one to her who has lost the city of her husband.
My heart finds no joy in anything: my mind and my body are distraught.
His palace has a million gates, but there is a vast ocean between it and me: …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXXVI: Serve your God, who has come into this temple of life!
poems.excerpt:
Serve your God, who has come into this temple of life!
Do not act the part of a madman, for the night is thickening fast.
He has awaited me for countless ages, for love of me He has lost His heart: …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXXVII: Clouds thicken in the sky!  O
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXXVIII: This day is dear to me above all other days
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song LXXXIX: Is there any wise man who will listen to that solemn music which…
poems.excerpt:
Is there any wise man who will listen to that solemn music which arises in the sky?
For He, the Source of all music, makes all vessels full fraught, and rests in fullness Himself.
He who is in the body is ever athirst, for he pursues that which is in part: …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XC: To whom shall I go to learn about my Beloved?
poems.excerpt:
To whom shall I go to learn about my Beloved?
Kabîr says: "As you never may find the forest if you ignore the tree, so He may never be found in abstractions."
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XCI: I have learned the Sanskrit language, so let all men call me wise:
poems.excerpt:
I have learned the Sanskrit language, so let all men call me wise:
But where is the use of this, when I am floating adrift, and parched with thirst, and burning with the heat of desire?
To no purpose do you bear on your head this load of pride and vanity. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XCII: The woman who is parted from her lover spins at the spinning wheel.
poems.excerpt:
The woman who is parted from her lover spins at the spinning wheel.
The city of the body arises in its beauty; and within it the palace of the mind has been built.
The wheel of love revolves in the sky, and the seat is made of the jewels of knowledge: …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XCIII: Beneath the great umbrella of my King millions of suns and moons and…
poems.excerpt:
Beneath the great umbrella of my King millions of suns and moons and stars are shining!
He is the Mind within my mind: He is the Eye within mine eye.
Ah, could my mind and eyes be one!  Could my love but reach to my Lover!  Could but the fiery heat of my heart be cooled! …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XCIV: O sadhu! my land is a sorrowless land.
poems.excerpt:
O sadhu! my land is a sorrowless land.
I cry aloud to all, to the king and the beggar, the emperor and the fakir--
Whosoever seeks for shelter in the Highest, let all come and settle in my land! …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XCV: Came with my Lord to my Lord's home
poems.excerpt:
Came with my Lord to my Lord's home: but I lived not with Him and I tasted Him not, and my youth passed away like a dream.
On my wedding night my women-friends sang in chorus, and I was anointed with the unguents of pleasure and pain:
But when the ceremony was over, I left my Lord and came away, and my kinsman tried to console me upon the road. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XCVI: O friend, dear heart of mine, think well!  if you love indeed
poems.excerpt:
O friend, dear heart of mine, think well!  if you love indeed, then why do you sleep?
If you have found Him, then give yourself utterly, and take Him to you.
Why do you loose Him again and again? …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XCVII: The Lord is in me, the Lord is in you, as life is in every seed
poems.excerpt:
The Lord is in me, the Lord is in you, as life is in every seed. O servant!  put false pride away, and seek for Him within you.
A million suns are ablaze with light,
The sea of blue spreads in the sky, …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XCVIII: The month of March draws near: ah, who will unite me to my Lover?
poems.excerpt:
The month of March draws near: ah, who will unite me to my Lover?
How shall I find words for the beauty of my Beloved?  For He is merged in all beauty.
His colour is in all the pictures of the world, and it bewitches the body and the mind. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song XCIX: Oh Narad!  I know that my Lover cannot be far:
poems.excerpt:
Oh Narad!  I know that my Lover cannot be far:
When my Lover wakes, I wake; when He sleeps, I sleep.
He is destroyed at the root who gives pain to my Beloved. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: Song C: Hang up the swing of love to-day
poems.excerpt:
Hang up the swing of love to-day!  Hang the body and the mind between the arms of the Beloved, in the ecstasy of love's joy:
Bring the tearful streams of the rainy clouds to your eyes, and cover your heart with the shadow of darkness:
Bring your face nearer to His ear, and speak of the deepest longings of your heart. …
poems.translator: trans. Rabindranath Tagore, with Evelyn Underhill (1915)

poems.title: He Who Longs for Ruby Lip's Kiss May
poems.excerpt:
He who longs for ruby lip's kiss may not calm of soul remain:
He his head must yield who hopes the dusky locks' sweet scent to gain.
 …

How that a Dog, because that he wes pure,

The profound wit of God Omnipotent

poems.title: The Fox, the Wolf, and the Husbandman

In elderis dayis, as Esope can declair,
Thair wes ane husband, quhilk had ane pleuch to steir.
